### *To my Most Gracious Lord and Prince.*

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'N' featuring ornate foliate scrollwork and a human figure, possibly a putto, entwined within the architecture of the letter.</image-desc>Neither undeservedly, nor for any trivial reason, did the Ancients consecrate two very vigorous and lively animals—in a <term>hieroglyphic sense<note>Here meaning "symbolic" or "emblematic," as was common in Renaissance scholarship.</note></term>—to Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of healing and medicine.</note> (whom they believed to be the son of Apollo): the Rooster and the Serpent <note>original Latin: *Draconem*</note>. ...reminded him. For a Physician, as **Macrobius** writes, foreknows either the benefits or the ailments that will arise in the body: thus, as **Hippocrates** says, it behooves the Physician to speak concerning the sick man of *the present, the past, and the things that are yet to come* <note>original Greek: τὰ τε παρεόντα, καὶ τὰ προγεγονότα, καὶ μέλλοντα ἔσεσθαι</note>, that is, those things which are, those which were, and those which will soon follow: which corresponds to **Divinations**—or as we might interpret it, skillful conjecture. Therefore, he who excels in these two gifts (allowing others to rest for now) shall be heard of through the herald **Homer** as being *worth many other men* <note>original Greek: πολλῶν ἀντάξιος ἄλλων</note>; and by the promise of **Sirach**, *he shall receive glory from the king* <note>original Greek: παρὰ βασιλέως λήψεται δόξαν</note>, or as others read, *a gift* <note>original Greek: δόμα</note>. Truly, histories testify that the more civilized Nations held the guardians of **Health** in distinguished honor. Thus, as **Suetonius** records, **Gaius Julius Caesar** granted **Citizenship** to all who practiced Medicine in Rome; and **Augustus**, having been delivered from a life-threatening crisis by the skill and aid of **Antonius Musa**, besides a more generous reward, granted the right to wear gold rings <note>The "jus annulorum aureorum" was a mark of high social status, effectively elevating the recipient to the equestrian rank.</note> both to him and to his present fellow-practitioners <note>original Greek: ὁμοφύλοις (*homophylois*)</note>, as well as to all future ones, according to the account of **Caelius Rhodiginus**. With no less favor, **Valentinian I** granted **Immunity to Physicians**, through which they and their families might be relieved from all trouble and from all public burdens. Indeed, the dignity of the **Medical Art** reveals itself to such an extent that it makes a **true** <note>original Greek: γνήσιον (*gnēsion*)</note> and noble possessor of it most acceptable even to enemies. For what else did **Artaxerxes, King of the Persians**, intend when he wrote to **Histanes**, Governor of the Hellespont, that he should entice **Hippocrates of Cos, the Physician**, by whatever rewards possible, inviting him to join his household? "Take care," he said, "to give him as much gold as he desires, and likewise other things which he needs, and [send him] to me..."

...dismiss them: for he shall be equal in honor to the highest men in Persia. <note>The author likely refers to a historical anecdote where a physician's status was compared to Persian nobility.</note> But let the faction of Physicians be far from here—those of whom that **Old Man of Cos** <note>original: *Senex ille Cous* — a common epithet for Hippocrates (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE), the "Father of Medicine."</note> declared many to be so in name only. Men fashioned after their character are found even today, who resemble those two mentioned by **Aetius** <note>Aetius of Amida, a 6th-century Byzantine Greek medical writer.</note>, who relied solely on medicinal formulas while being utterly ignorant of the **Method of Healing** <note>original: *Methodo Medendi* — referring to the systematic approach to medical practice popularized by Galen.</note>. Of those two, one—having lost his notebooks either by accident or the malice of another—wasted away in grief, while the other ceased to profess the art of Healing altogether. 

<margin>
Tetrabiblos 4,
Series 2,
chapter 25.
</margin>

Just as one must labor with continuous vigils in cultivating the knowledge of things, which belongs to **Reason**; so too must that very thing be carried out through prudent conjecture, born and increased through **Experience**, which that hard "weapon of necessity" demands in respect to every afflicted body. Hence, like any other arts, **Medicine** is supported by both **Reason** and **Experience**. Indeed, it is not without cause that the ancients are observed to have wished to define the tireless labor of knowledge by the **Rooster** (the symbol of vigilance), and the circumspect **application** <note>original Greek: παρεγχείρησιν — *parepicheiresin*, meaning manual intervention or the practical application of skill.</note> and handling of things known by the **Serpent**. 

This excellence of the perfected Art has not only ensured that Great Men of old, and even Kings themselves, devoted their efforts to it; but even today it remains dear to the hearts of Princes. This is beautifully evident through their Authority and Example, and it is greatly cultivated by their munificent support. Among these patrons of truly **Salubrious Letters**, as well as of learned men, I grant no small place to **Your Highness** <note>original: *Celsitudo Tua*</note>, **Most Illustrious Prince**, **Most Merciful Lord**, who from your earliest age have wished not only to devote yourself to the most choice studies, but also to strive with all your desires toward this: that nothing in Your Highness might be found want-

...would be held, which could be deemed worthy of Princely height. Regarding the Emperor **Albert II** <note>Albert II of Habsburg (1397–1439), King of Hungary, Croatia, and Bohemia, and King of the Romans.</note>, **Dubravius** <note>Jan Dubravius (c. 1486–1553), a Czech bishop and historian known for his "History of Bohemia."</note> relates that at **Buda** <note>The western part of modern-day Budapest, then a royal seat.</note>, from an immoderate eating of melons, he contracted a looseness of the bowels; and, having disregarded the advice of his Physicians, he undertook a journey toward **Vienna**. Thus, by unworthily neglecting his medicines, he was snatched away by a premature death not far from **Strigonium** <note>Esztergom, Hungary.</note>. Truly, with a far different mind, whenever something is commanded by necessity, Your Highness demonstrates that the medical prescriptions of the **disciples of Asclepius** <note>original: *Æsculapiorum*; referring to physicians as followers of the Greek god of healing.</note> are commended to you—rightly determining that **Medicine**, having been created by God (according to the aforementioned **Wise Man** <note>Referring to the author of the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:1: "Honor the physician... for the Lord created him."</note>), is by no means to be neglected by a man of consummate judgment. 

Moreover, many years ago I experienced this very thing in person, when I was called all the way from **Hesse** to **Montbéliard** <note>original: *Montisbelgardum*; a county then ruled by the House of Württemberg, now in France.</note> on account of the fragile health <note>original: *vitream valetudinem* — literally "glassy health," meaning delicate or easily broken.</note> of Your Highness’s former most Illustrious consort—alas! most missed, and of most pious memory. Furthermore, even in this most unfavorable time, the matter speaks for itself: for Your Highness, with God thus directing human affairs, has been brought closer to us. This occurred after your most Illustrious and exalted Prince and Lord, **Johann Friedrich, Duke of Württemberg**, etc.—your most closely joined eldest brother, who is **now among the saints** <note>original: *τῷ νῦν ἐν ἁγίοις* (tō nyn en hagiois). Duke Johann Friedrich died in 1628.</note>—was taken away by an all-too-sudden death (oh, the misfortune of the age!). You now most gravity sustain the guardianship of those most ample fraternal territories and the administration you have undertaken. At the beginning of this reign, just as you are piously solicitous for the welfare of the entire Fatherland, so you are especially concerned for the abundant advancement of the studies of the **Academy** <note>Referring to the University of Tübingen, the primary university of the Duchy of Württemberg.</note> itself and of the Schools.

# DEDICATION.

*where he lived, so that he would not seem to be the only one idle from duty among so many workers, he began to roll [his tub] back and forth: and when he was asked in a familiar way by a friend why he was doing this, he hinted that in the midst of the burning occupation of the entire State* <note>original: *Reipublicæ*; literally "Republic," but used here to refer to the Commonwealth or the Duke's domain.</note> *he too should by no means remain quiet. Since, therefore, it was also my duty to congratulate Your Highness* <note>original: *C. T.* abbreviation for *Celsitudo Tua*; a formal title for a Prince or Duke.</note> *on your Administration of such great weight, undertaken under lucky auspices: I found nothing left for me to do but to shake my "Vessel"* <note>original: *Vas*; referring to Diogenes’ famous tub. The author is saying his book is his "tub" that he rolls to show he is working for the public good.</note> *along with Diogenes: that is, while others are applauding, to dedicate in one way or another these night-studies of mine,* <note>original: *lucubrationes*; scholarly works produced by the light of a lamp, implying diligent labor after hours.</note> *otherwise intended for the public Good, to Your Highness, and to consecrate them to your most Illustrious name with the declaration of a most solemn Vow. For this is what the heroic Virtue of Your Most Illustrious Highness deserved long ago; and what my meager resources* <note>original: *copiolæ*; literally "little forces," a humble way of describing his own intellect or wealth.</note> *confessed long ago they owed to the same, on account of the singular Grace and Most Clement Beneficence shown to me for many years. Therefore, when even by the measure of a small jar* <note>original: *sextarioli*; a Roman measure of capacity, used here to contrast his "small" gift with the Duke's "great" status.</note> *my humble poverty can be compared with the Princely Magnificence of Your Highness; I shall rejoice that I have attained the goal of my desire, and while I reflect upon this, I see that I must at the same time make an end to my preamble: seizing upon this one closing thought, by which I devoutly worship GOD, [praying] that He may command Your Most Illustrious Highness, along with your family and the lands taken into your Protection, to HAPPILY survive; and that we all may reach that part of the final age in which we may hear sung, both publicly and privately, what we observe on ancient coins:* THE RESTORATION OF HAPPY TIMES <note>original: *FELICIUM TEMPORUM REPARATIO*; a famous inscription found on Roman coins, particularly those of the 4th century, signaling a return to prosperity.</note>. *May it be so; make it so, O GOD,*
->*may it be so!*<-

# PREFACE TO THE BENEVO-
## LENT READER.

That saying of *Solon* is well known: "I grow old always learning many things" <note>original Greek: *γηράσκω δ' αἰεὶ πολλὰ διδασκόμενος*; original Latin: *senesco semper multa addiscens*. Solon was one of the Seven Sages of Greece.</note>. This is what *Plato* repeats in his *Dialogue on Philosophy* and applies to the study of Wisdom: what else, he asks, is *Philosophy* than doing what *Solon* said? For he said that "for the one who learns constantly, old age arrives with many things." We say the same thing, by right and merit, concerning true Physicians, whose Art *Hippocrates* solemnly pronounced to be long <note>A reference to the famous aphorism *Ars longa, vita brevis* (Art is long, life is short), suggesting that the medical craft is too vast to master in one lifetime.</note>, so that they never fail to have something they can learn, even up to extreme old age. For although we do not deny that other disciplines possess their own difficulties—since our mind, for the purpose of knowing things, is (according to <term>the Philosopher</term><note>Referring to Aristotle.</note>) like a <term>blank slate</term><note>original: *tabula rasa*; the philosophical idea that the mind is born without innate ideas.</note> upon which nothing is actually written, yet all things can be inscribed upon it, though not without labor and continuous practice—this is nonetheless most especially verified in the Medical Art. Granted indeed, Medicine is not called a <term>Science</term> in the strict sense, but an <term>Art</term> <note>In the 17th century, a "science" referred to theoretical, certain knowledge, while an "art" referred to a practical skill or application involving judgment.</note>, because it has a Subject of Operation rather than a purely scientific one; yet it is not called the Most Noble of all Arts without reason. Hence its knowledge extends most widely and requires the most perfect investigation of many things. Whether you consider the *Subject of Operation*—namely Man, whose present health must be defended and whose absent health must be restored—or the *means through which* this must be accomplished, a wide-open field of contemplation presents itself everywhere. The *Subject of Operation* is that matter in which health is to be defended or restored, specifically Man himself; if one lacks the most perfect knowledge of him, surely he must frequently deceive others and be deceived himself. The *means through which* health is preserved and defended designates all those things which, by whatever reasoning, are designed to defend and preserve our body in its state according to nature, as well as to alter, correct, and reduce it back to suitable health when it is in a state contrary to nature.

And indeed, by Hercules, how great those things are! For one must track down the most hidden powers of herbs, examine the qualities of plants, investigate the nature of four-footed animals, birds, and fish, and unlock the faculties of metals and minerals—

<vocab>Solon, Plato, Philosophy, Physician, Hippocrates, Medicine, Science, Art, Man, Herb, Metal, Mineral</vocab>

<summary>In this preface, Horstius argues that medicine is an inexhaustible field of study requiring lifelong learning. He defines medicine as a noble "Art" focused on the complex study of Man and the vast natural world of remedies.</summary>

<keywords>medical philosophy, lifelong learning, Solon, Hippocrates, tabula rasa, medical ethics, anatomy, pharmacology, 17th-century medicine</keywords>

LENT READER.

...to distinguish useful things from harmful ones, to apply the various operations of the surrounding air at the right time and in the right manner, and finally—to say much in a few words—to guard against harmful things and choose what is healthy in all matters: is this not a work of extreme difficulty and labor, and often full of dangerous risk? For what, I ask, is left in the entire Universe that does not fall under the Physician's consideration, since nothing is contained in the world for which the Medical art does not require knowledge? 

Perhaps you doubt the importance of the heavenly bodies? Stop being suspicious: for these are not entirely neglected by the Physician. Since it contributes to the healing of diseases to know the risings and settings, and the various positions and changes of the stars—whose force and power over these lower things is clearer than the midday light—who, unless blinder than a mole, does not see that a Physician cannot be ignorant of these things? *Hippocrates* emphasizes this very thing in his book *On Airs, Waters, and Places* <note>original: *Hipp. lib. de aëre, aq. & loc.*</note>, where he says: 

> One must especially observe the great changes of the seasons, so that we neither willingly administer medicines in those times, nor perform cauterizations <note>original: *uramus* (we burn/cauterize)</note> around the belly, until ten or more days have passed: both Solstices are most dangerous, especially the summer one; the Equinox is also dangerous, especially the Autumnal. One must also consider the rising of the Stars, especially the Dog Star <note>Sirius</note>, then the setting of Arcturus and the Pleiades: for diseases are mostly judged <note>original: *judicantur*; referring to the "crisis" or turning point of an illness</note> at these times, etc.

From all this, it appears clearer than midday light that the field of the medical art is widely open, and a man’s lifespan is hardly—indeed, not even hardly—sufficient for an exact knowledge of it.

Therefore, it is no wonder that a true Physician, who takes to heart that verse of Holy Scripture—"Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord deceitfully" <note>original: *maledictus qui facit opus Domini fraudulenter*; see Jeremiah 48:10</note>—says rightly with *Solon*: "I grow old always learning many things" <note>original Greek: γηράσκω δ' αἰεὶ πολλὰ διδασκόμενος; original Latin: *senesco semper multa addiscens*</note>. For this reason, our *Hippocrates*, in his *Epistle to Democritus*, confesses that even as an old man he has not yet reached the end of Medicine. Since this is the case, we must labor with all our strength so that "no day passes without a line being drawn" <note>original: *nulla dies abeat, quin linea ducta supersit*; a reference to the proverb *Nulla dies sine linea*, suggesting constant practice or writing.</note>, so that by diligence and constant observation we may somehow compensate for the shortness of life. 

This is what has moved me as well; although by God's grace I have already passed my fiftieth year, I nevertheless desire to learn daily, as much as my professional duties allow, which I attempt to continue through the diligent annotation of <term>Singular Cases</term> <note>original: *Casuum singularium*; individual medical case studies or clinical observations.</note>.

Since I have been informed that this method of my annotations was not unwelcome to students of Medicine when I published the first four books of *Singular Observations* a few years ago, I did not want to miss the opportunity—at the frequent request of friends—to also commit the following four books to the press. I do not indeed deny,

<meta>catchword: teor,</meta>

<meta>This page continues the preface. The text picks up mid-sentence from the previous page's discussion on the challenges of the medical profession, concluding the thought that the author admits some may find his work incomplete, but he hopes it serves the public good.</meta>

->PREFACE TO<-

...I confess <note>original: *teor*, likely the end of *confiteor*</note>, that many things might be found wanting by many people here and there; yet I have no doubt that good men, weighing my intention, will be fully satisfied.

Together with my own, I have also brought forward remarkable observations shared by certain friends from various places—as was also done in the added Letters and Consultations of the second book—for no other reason than to satisfy the expectations of the **friends of medicine** <note>original Greek: *Φιλιατρων* (Philiatron)</note> in this way, as well as to honor the Authors.

Indeed, I would have added more bundles of epistolary debates, if the final conclusion had not been added to the eleventh section during my absence, contrary to my intention.

But what is delayed is not taken away: perhaps an opportunity will be given, if it pleases God, for the remainder to see the light of day along with other things that time and age provide.

Meanwhile, let the Reader take in good part what we publish here for the benefit of our neighbor regarding the promised observations. Here, the first part treats the **Diseases of Women** <note>original: *Morbis Mulierum*</note>, mainly noting only those cases that contain something remarkable in themselves, though not neglecting those which occur more frequently and are explained for the benefit of beginners along with others.

To this book we have added a unique appendix, namely an **examination** <note>original Greek: *ἐξέτασιν* (exetasin)</note> **regarding the diseases of children** <note>original: *morbis puerorum*</note>, which was once subjected by us to public examination in the Academy according to the Hippocratic doctrine. This section is adorned with easily obtainable medicines and resolved pleasant questions, along with the doctrine of smallpox and measles translated into Latin by the most famous Mr. Daniel Stolz from our German treatise. The second book is titled **On Contagious and Malignant Diseases** <note>original: *Morbis contagiosis & malignis*</note>, in which various cures for the venereal pox <note>original: *lue venerea*; a historical term for syphilis</note> and other diseases of this kind—which often deceive both patients and doctors through their malignancy and contagion—are discussed. In these, many medicines prepared **chemically** <term>original: *Spagyricè*; spagyric medicine refers to early modern alchemy focused on separating and recombining the "pure" parts of minerals and plants for healing</term> from minerals are proposed. These include Sweetened Mercury <note>original: *Mercurius dulcificatus*, also known as calomel</note>, Compound Mineral Laxative, Simple Mineral Laxative, Salt of Antimony, the Golden Panacea, the Saffron of Metals <note>original: *Crocus Metallorum*, a prepared form of antimony</note> of our own preparation, Mercury of Life <note>original: *Mercurius vitæ*</note>, and similar purgatives; as well as Diaphoretic <note>sweat-inducing</note> Gold, Golden Diaphoretic Sulfur, Cinnabar of Antimony, Mineral Bezoar <note>an alchemical preparation intended to act as an antidote</note>, etc., among the diaphoretics and others. **Chemical physicians** <term>Chymiatri: early modern doctors who used laboratory chemistry to create mineral-based medicines</term> will very easily gather from the recorded operation of the said medicines that they were prepared from chosen and purified minerals in such a way that they may be administered without any harm—as the outcome testifies. It will be their task to investigate the cause from the effect and to infer, by their own effort <note>original Latin idiom: *proprio Marte*, meaning by one's own strength or skill</note>, a similar purification of minerals and the separation of healthy qualities from harmful ones. Nevertheless, for the sake of beginners, we will add a few general points about the said medicines—not because we wish to withhold anything from our neighbor, but rather because it is impossible for the **practical procedure** <note>original Greek: *ἐγχείρησις* (encheiresis)</note> to be exactly described unless we put our own hands to the coals with **personal observation** <note>original Greek: *αὐτοψίᾳ* (autopsia)</note>.

Let it suffice that we make **Sweetened Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurium dulcificatum*, often referring to calomel</note> from **Quicksilver** <note>original: *Argento vivo*</note> (which native **Cinnabar** provides with the help of **Vulcan** <note>an alchemical name for fire</note>), most carefully purified and reduced with the same into a **sublimated state** <note>original: *Meteoron*, referring to the vaporized and re-solidified state of the mineral</note>. This preparation is repeated five or even seven times until it shows us the marks of perfection in the proper manner, where at last the medicine becomes entirely harmless, to be given even to children and women in childbirth without any harm.

Let it suffice that the **Simple Mineral Laxative** is made from the hyacinth-colored **glass of Antimony** through repeated digestions of **spirit of vitriol** <term>spirit of vitriol: a concentrated form of sulfuric acid</term> and various corrections with **spirit of wine** <term>spirit of wine: ethanol or high-proof alcohol</term>. By this diligence—which many have so often desired—the vomiting power is entirely taken away, and the Antimony itself is accustomed to draw out the offending matter only through the lower parts <note>i.e., through the bowels</note>, unless something is fluctuating around the opening of the stomach.

Let it suffice that the **Compound Mineral Laxative** is made from Antimony and Mercury, which we possess through almost the same progress of labor as the **Emetic Powder** and the **Mineral Bezoartic** <note>a chemical compound used as an antidote or counter-poison</note>. Let it suffice that the **Crocus of Metals** <note>a medicinal preparation of antimony with a saffron-like color</note> owes its origin to the **Regulus** <note>the metallic form of a mineral</note> rather than to raw Antimony; and likewise, that the **Golden Panacea** has Sweetened Mercury and that same Crocus as integral parts, mixed in just proportion. Let it suffice that the **Mercury of Life** <note>also called *Antimony oxychloride*</note> can be successfully corrected by the correction of spirit of vitriol and repeated digestion of spirit of wine, so that it may afterward be safely applied both internally and externally. Let it suffice to have named only **vomiting vitriol** (or **Gilla** <note>likely *Gilla Theophrasti*, a sulfate of iron or zinc</note>), **Golden diaphoretic Sulfur**, and others, since the preparations of such things are very well known to those even moderately practiced.

To this second book we have added our treatise on **Scurvy** <note>original: *Scorbuto*</note>, written in Latin twenty years ago, for the reason that a singular contagious malignancy is discovered here as well. For although the same booklet, translated by us into the vernacular tongue, has already been printed and published several times, I do not doubt that this Latin edition will be pleasing to the **friends of medicine** <note>original Greek: *Philiatris*</note> as the original version which explains the matter itself more fully.

# TO GREGOR HORST, DOCTOR
## AND CHIEF PHYSICIAN,
### My greatly respected patron and
#### promoter,
#### Much health and humble service.

When I recently saw your Excellency's medical observations on the *Diseases of Women* in print, and had read through the appendix to the second observation concerning the obstruction of the menses producing various preternatural <note>original: *p. n.*, an abbreviation for *praeter naturam*, meaning "beyond nature" or abnormal</note> excretions, there occurred to me the memorable history of a certain woman living in our hospital <term>Xenodochium: an institution for the care of the poor, pilgrims, or the sick</term>, which I wished to write out in full for your Excellency, and to submit to your judgment—if your duties permit and it is not a burden.

There is, I say, in our hospital, a certain unmarried woman named **Barbara Maurer**, forty-six years old, of a stature small yet moderately tall, who, about twenty years ago, suffered from a certain swelling of the entire abdomen. This was not indeed dropsical <term>Dropsy: an old medical term for edema or swelling caused by the accumulation of fluids</term>, nor did it sensibly harm her bodily functions, but it caused her distress whenever her body was bent toward the ground. After an enema was administered but not returned, she was seized by an enormous and astounding flow of purple blood from her right ear. This flow recurred at intervals every single day and lasted for an entire year, despite many remedies being applied in vain by the most excellent doctors. When that year had passed, with the patient emaciated and rendered almost bloodless, the flow finally ceased of its own accord. In the course of time, as her strength and blood were somewhat recovered, she suffered a relapse. Although her menses (which she first experienced in her twelfth year) always flowed for her properly and in an orderly fashion, that flow from the ear was nevertheless not prevented. Instead, in the course of time, it grew so strong that the ear was not sufficient; the blood, surging upward <term>Anarrhopos: a Greek medical term describing the movement of humors or fluids toward the upper parts of the body</term> and overflowing, began—about two years ago—to break forth in heaps, primarily through vomiting, sometimes also through the nose, though never through the eyes.

This vomiting and the flow from the ear did not thereafter observe a fixed and orderly schedule, but occurred sometimes in the third, sometimes the fourth, and occasionally the fifth or following week, in a quantity quite large and worthy of mention, and it re-

...and she maintained this pattern and period for many years. During the times when the blood did not break out, a swelling appeared either in the right hypochondrium <term>hypochondrium: the upper region of the abdomen, just below the ribs, traditionally associated with the liver and spleen</term> or across the entire abdomen. When this swelling vanished, the flow of blood returned through the upper parts of the body. To drive away this condition, although various remedies were carefully attempted by various doctors—namely, diverting and revulsive measures <note>Treatments intended to draw "bad humors" away from an affected area to another part of the body</note>, treatments to induce the menses, altering, purging, and strengthening agents—she received no benefit from any of them. Instead, she was only relieved and revived by bloodletting <note>original: "sanguinis missione"</note>, with as many as three veins sometimes being opened at once, and additionally by certain hepatic rolls <note>Small medicinal lozenges intended to treat the liver</note>.

She could not bear the use of baths which were to be continued for three weeks according to the doctor's prescription; instead, immediately after the first entry, she was accustomed to feel so poorly that she was forced to be confined to her bed for a long time afterward. A year ago, when I first began to visit the Hospital <term>Xenodochium: a charitable institution or infirmary for the sick and poor</term>, I very often saw her there vomiting purple blood and ejecting it copiously through the right ear, lying in bed like someone half-dead. 

Moved by the rarity of the illness, I wished to explore and record her history more diligently and attentively. I noted that before the vomiting and that bloody flow, she would suffer a certain heavy and tensive pain in the right hypochondrium accompanied by a certain hardness. Or, if the affliction settled in the lower parts, she would perceive a swelling of the right foot with significant heat and a stinging pain, which could not be resolved, digested, or softened by any poultices or ointments, but was accustomed to go away on its own. 

Alternatively, if the blood crept upward, she felt a painful hardness of the breast reaching all the way to the throat, or a bruising and swelling of the right arm—resembling an ecchymosis <term>ecchymomatis: a discoloration of the skin resulting from bleeding underneath, typically caused by bruising</term>—from the copious influx of blood. And if by chance that swelling of the foot vanished, the heaviness of the right hypochondrium would return; if this ceased, the breast or arm would swell; if this abated, a redness and heat of the face would follow, and from this came that vomiting and the bloody flow from the ear. 

This was preceded by nausea, fainting, fear of suffocation, a whistling and ringing in the ears, stinging sensations, and a heaviness of hearing—though the operations of her mind and her internal senses remained unharmed. This would last sometimes for one, two, or three days, after which, as if a crisis <note>In Galenic medicine, the "crisis" was the turning point of a disease where the body either overcame the illness or succumbed</note> had occurred, the sick woman would return to herself, feel somewhat better, and take food and drink. She was never urged by severe thirst either before or after the vomiting. 

Meanwhile, the affliction granted a truce for sometimes fourteen days, sometimes eight, and occasionally barely three days. At the present time, it is perhaps more exacerbated because her menstrual cleansings <note>original: "menstruas purgationes"</note> have now been blocked for two years. And since I have long and deeply pondered the origin, causes, and cure of this chronic condition in my mind, various thoughts have come to me for consideration; however, I have decided to leave all these to Your Excellency's judgment and to abide by your decision.

I. Whether this affliction arose from natural causes, or perhaps was intentionally provoked by the wickedness and malice of the sick woman herself—especially since the bystanders claimed that this woman was able, and even now is able, to provoke this movement of blood at her own whim and will, so that she might be kept longer in the Hospital <term>Xenodochium: a charitable institution for the sick and poor</term>, drawing the bystanders into pity on account of the severity of her illness? However, this did not seem consistent with the truth to me, as the natural causes and signs accompanying the illness were sufficient evidence: for that periodic movement of blood, moving now from the leg into the right upper abdomen <term>hypochondrium: the area of the abdomen just below the ribs</term>, now from there into the arm <note>original: "brahium"</note>, now from there into the head, as well as that bloody excretion which relieved her constitution, and similar examples occurring everywhere in medical practice, proved otherwise.

II. Whether the cause of this flow was menstrual blood regurgitating to the upper parts; or truly the blood-making power of an over-heated liver <note>original: "jecoris"</note>, generating an abundance of blood? For although it might seem that a reflux <note>original: "palindromen," a Greek term for a recurrence or backward movement</note> of menstrual blood produced this vomiting alone—especially at this time when, for two years, the veins of the womb having been obstructed or perhaps entirely closed up, she had no longer flowed monthly in the required manner—nevertheless, since many years before, when her monthly cycles were always flowing legitimately, it had nonetheless broken out through the upper parts, it was more credible that this reflux happened due to a powerful blood-production of the liver. By this, a more copious amount of blood was created, overabounding in the whole body, which could not be governed by the body's faculties nor sufficiently evacuated through the veins of the womb. Thus, by a certain necessity, seeking an exit for itself but finding it nowhere except in the upper parts, it was cast out through the mouth, ear, and nostrils. This was also attested by the fact that all the affected parts were on the right side, which alone used to be occupied by this evil, while the parts of the left side always remained untouched. For daily experience taught that when this periodic flow was about to come, the region of the liver first swelled, then the blood turned toward the right leg, and when an exit was denied here, it rushed to the upper parts and broke out from there through the mouth and the right ear.

III. Whether this vomiting of blood went out through the stomach, or truly through other paths? For although everything which is copiously cast back by vomiting is said to come from the stomach—the blood in our suffering subject doubtless being diverted there through the mesenteric <note>original: "mesaraicas"</note> veins and the branches of the portal vein, which end in the lowest part of the stomach and its second lining, and are opened by an opening <term>anastomosis: a connection or opening between two vessels</term>—nevertheless, since it is established among authors that a great eruption of blood does not happen from the veins of the stomach on account of their thinness, and furthermore, that blood transmitted abundantly from the liver to the duodenum would, on account of its natural weight, descend to the lower intestines—

**IV.** Should this bloody vomiting be hindered, repressed, or at least diminished by remedies? For although other discharges of blood—occurring together through the womb, hemorrhoids, nose, mouth, ears, etc.—would be ordered by practitioners to be restrained by proper protections unless they were "critical" <term>critical: a "crisis" in early medicine was a turning point where nature expelled harmful fluids to heal the body</term>: since Hippocrates, in *Aphorisms* 4, 25, pronounced that blood coming from the upper parts, wherever it might exit, is a bad sign. If it were hindered, it would bring about significant harm. Therefore, I determined that those other types should be stopped, but this one should be allowed to finish and by no means hindered. This is in accordance with observations 55 and 56 of the 3rd book of Schenck <note>Johannes Schenck von Grafenberg, a famous 16th-century medical observer</note>, in which mention is made first of a certain Abbess who, having passed her 58th year, was freed from illness by a spontaneous, copious vomiting of blood whenever she was seized by coughing and pain around the upper abdomen without a fever. Secondly, mention is made of a certain noblewoman of a sanguine and fleshy temperament who, for 20 years—both during marriage and as a widow—labored several times a year with a very copious vomiting of blood without any distress, even though her monthly cycles proceeded lawfully. Yet, if the vomiting was hindered, either by itself or by medicines, she felt unwell and perceived a great weariness of the whole body.

**IV.** Should this vomiting of blood be hindered, repressed, or at least diminished? For although other discharges of blood—through the womb, hemorrhoids, nose, mouth, ears, and so on—when occurring in abundance, are ordered by practitioners to be restrained with proper remedies (unless they are **critical** <term>an event signaling the turning point of a disease, often involving a sudden discharge that provides relief</term>): and although **Hippocrates** <note>original: "Hipp. 4. aph. 25."</note> pronounced in his 25th Aphorism of the 4th book that blood coming from the upper parts, wherever it exits, is a bad sign: nevertheless, those other eruptions often prostrate a person's strength and rob the body of its life-treasure, making them **symptomatic** <term>a sign of the disease itself rather than a cure</term>. Therefore, I rightly decided that while those other types should be stopped, this one should be allowed to finish and by no means hindered. This follows observations 55 and 56 of the 3rd book of **Schenckius** <note>Johann Georg Schenck von Grafenberg (1560–1620), a physician famous for his massive collection of medical rarities</note>, which mention first a certain Abbess over 58 years old who, every year, was seized by pain around the **upper abdomen** <term>hypochondria: the regions of the upper abdomen below the ribs</term> without fever; by coughing and a spontaneous, copious vomiting of blood, she was freed from her illness. Secondly, he mentions a noblewoman, full-blooded and fleshy, who for 20 years (both while married and as a widow) suffered several times a year from a very copious vomiting of blood without any distress, even though her **monthly periods** <term>menses</term> proceeded normally. If the vomiting was hindered, either on its own or by medicines, she felt unwell and experienced a great weariness throughout her whole body.

**V.** Could this flow from the ear and the unnatural vomiting be diverted or mitigated by **bloodletting** <term>venæsectionibus</term>, ligatures, cupping glasses, **medical drains** <term>fonticulis: small, intentional sores kept open to drain "bad humors"</term>, **remedies to provoke menstruation** <term>menagogis: emmenagogues</term>, baths, and similar aids? Regarding bloodletting: since this had brought her notable relief some years before when the upper and lower veins were pierced with a lancet, and since **Schenckius** noted in observation 57 of book 3 that a certain young woman suffering severely from vomiting felt well after blood was drawn from the lower vein near the ankle (at which point her menstrual cleansing followed), this aligns with the **Aphorism** <note>original: "Aph. 34. s. 5. Mulieri sanguinem evomenti, menstruis erumpentibus, solutio."</note>: *To a woman vomiting blood, if the menses break out, it is the solution.* Therefore, it could not unjustly be decided that bloodletting should not be neglected but repeated, as the blood here was at fault not in its quality, but in its excessive quantity. However, since an opening of the veins of the right side (both in the arm and near the ankle) had been attempted on alternate days six months ago, as well as on the left side, and only the vein of the left ankle flowed—with not even a droplet then flowing from the veins of the right side—from this I conjectured...

# TO THE KIND READER.

**I.** Whether this condition arose from natural causes, or perhaps from the wickedness and malice of the sick woman herself, provoked by her own will and whim? This was considered especially since those standing by affirmed that this woman had been able—and was still able—to call forth this movement of blood as she pleased, so that she might be kept longer in the **hospital** <term>Xenodochio: an infirmary or guest-house for the poor and sick</term>, the bystanders having been moved to pity by the severity of the illness. However, this did not seem believable to me, as the natural causes and signs accompanying the illness were sufficient to explain it. For that periodic movement of blood—shifting now from the leg into the right **upper abdomen** <term>hypochondrium: the region of the abdomen under the ribs, where the liver is located</term>, now from there into the arm, now from there into the head—as well as that discharge of blood which relieved her physical state, and similar examples occurring everywhere in the writings of **medical practitioners** <note>original: "Practicos"</note>, proved otherwise.

**II.** Whether the cause of this flow was menstrual blood regurgitating to the upper parts; or indeed the blood-making power of an overheated liver generating an abundance of blood? For although it might seem that a **reflux** <note>original: "palindromen"</note> of menstrual blood produced this vomiting—especially at this time when, for two years, the veins of the womb had been obstructed or perhaps entirely closed up, and she had no longer flowed monthly in the proper way—nevertheless, since many years ago, even when her periods were always flowing lawfully, it had nonetheless erupted through the upper parts. Therefore, it was more credible that this reflux occurred due to a powerful **blood-production** <note>original: "sanguificatione"</note> in the liver. By this process, a more copious amount of blood was generated, overabounding in the whole body, which could not be governed by the body's faculty nor sufficiently evacuated through the veins of the womb. Hence, by a certain necessity, the blood sought an exit for itself; finding it nowhere but in the upper parts, it was cast out through the mouth, ear, and nostrils. This was also attested by the fact that all the affected parts were on the right side, which alone used to be occupied by this evil, while the parts of the left side always remained untouched. For daily experience taught that when this periodic flow was about to come, the region of the liver first swelled, then the blood leaned toward the right leg, and when an exit was denied there, it rushed to the upper parts and broke forth from the mouth and right ear.

**III.** Whether this vomiting of blood exited through the stomach, or indeed through other paths? For although everything cast out in abundance by vomiting is said to come from the stomach—blood doubtless being derived there in our suffering subject through the **mesenteric veins** <term>venas mesaraicas: vessels that carry blood from the intestines</term> and the branches of the **portal vein** <term>venae portae: the large vein carrying blood to the liver</term> which end in the bottom of the stomach and its second coating, and are opened by **anastomosis** <term>a connection or opening between two vessels</term>—nevertheless, it is held among authors that a great eruption of blood does not happen from the veins of the stomach because of their thinness. Furthermore, blood transmitted in abundance from the liver to the **duodenum** <term>the first part of the small intestine</term> would, because of its natural weight, descend toward the lower intestines

For although other discharges of blood—from the uterus, hemorrhoids, nostrils, mouth, ears, etc.—occurring in abundance are ordered by **medical practitioners** <note>original: "Practicis"</note> to be restrained by the proper remedies unless they are **critical** <term>critical: a "crisis" in early medicine was a turning point where the body naturally expelled harmful "humors" to heal itself</term>; and although **Hippocrates** <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460 – c. 370 BC)</note> in the 4th book of his *Aphorisms*, aphorism 25, pronounced that blood coming from the upper parts, wherever it exits, is a bad sign: nevertheless, while those other eruptions might utterly exhaust the strength and rob the body of its "treasure" <note>a common metaphor for blood as the vital spirit of the body</note>—and thus be symptomatic of disease—this vomiting and flow in our patient occurred with a relief of nature. It was like a critical movement; if it were hindered, it would bring about significant harm. Therefore, I decided that those other types of bleeding should be stopped, but this one should be allowed and by no means hindered. 

I based this on observations 55 and 56 of the 3rd book of **Schenckius** <note>Johann Georg Schenck von Grafenberg (1560–1620), a physician famous for collecting rare medical cases</note>, which mention, first, a certain Abbess over 58 years of age. Every year, she was seized by pain around the **upper abdomen** <term>hypochondria: the area under the ribs</term> without a fever, and by coughing; she was freed from her illness by a spontaneous and copious vomiting of blood. I conjectured that even **bloodletting** <term>venæsectiones: the surgical practice of opening a vein to withdraw blood, a standard treatment at the time</term> would no longer benefit her, since the blood was now accustomed to exiting via vomiting and the flow from the ear. For this reason, I also believed that ligatures, **cupping glasses** <term>cucurbitulas: glass vessels used to create a vacuum on the skin to draw out "bad humors"</term>, friction, **setons** <term>fonticulos: small, intentionally created wounds kept open to allow "corrupt" fluids to drain</term>, **emmenagogues** <term>menagoga: medicines used to stimulate menstrual flow</term>, and similar aids would bring her no benefit. Consequently, I strongly advised against the use of baths, which she had greatly desired, and I warned her not to impede the course of nature. I urged her to focus primarily on a proper diet as much as possible, while entirely omitting other stronger medications.

**VI.** Would this flow and ebb of blood cease of its own accord as she aged? Or would it be followed by frequent vomiting, wasting, **cachexia** <term>cachexia: a state of ill health involving weight loss and muscle wasting</term>, or eventually **dropsy** <term>hydrops: swelling caused by excess fluid, which historical doctors often linked to liver failure</term>? Regarding the first possibility, there might be a glimmer of hope that as she grows older and her **menstrual purgings** <note>original: "menstruis purgationibus"</note> naturally cease—due to the lack of blood that younger people have in abundance—this ailment would be either entirely removed or at least diminished. However, because nature—her cycles having been interrupted for two years—had sought a path toward the upper parts of the body more and more through these vomitings, and because **Schenckius** <note>Johannes Schenck von Grafenberg (1530–1598), a German physician known for his massive encyclopedia of rare medical cases</note> recorded an observation from **Cardanus** <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath and physician</note> concerning a woman who experienced frequent vomiting of blood and yet lived past her 96th year, it seemed more consistent with reason that this reflux would last until the end of her life. Alternatively, once nature was stripped of its "treasure" <note>a common metaphor for blood as the vital spirit</note>, the liver "cooled," and the blood-making process was impaired, her strength would be exhausted, and a poor bodily state or dropsy would undoubtedly follow in the course of time.

And these are the matters concerning this remarkable case which I chose to write to Your Excellency (who is perhaps hindered by other more serious affairs) on July 12th of the current year. But behold, on August 12th, while I was visiting her again, I was informed by her that her periods had flowed most copiously for fourteen days. By the benefit of this, that flow from the ear and the vomiting had ceased until this very day—namely October 8th—although a swelling of the right foot persisted at that time. When the menses had spontaneously disappeared again after fourteen days and had not yet returned, a hardness of the right **hypochondrium** <term>hypochondrium: the upper area of the abdomen; "hardness" here usually indicated an enlarged liver or spleen</term> returned alongside that swelling of the foot. Because of this, she was forced to remain in bed. Three days ago, when she leaned down from the bed toward the floor, she suffered a **nosebleed** <note>original: "hæmorrhagiam narium"</note> of nearly half a measure; since that occurred, she has felt well until now and takes her food with an appetite. I am entirely uncertain as to what final outcome this history will have, and I leave it to Your Excellency to consider. If you judge these matters worthy of further examination <note>original: "sub examinis incudem" — literally, "under the anvil of examination"</note>, it would be a most welcome favor to my studies.

Your diligent record of that case was most welcome to me, most illustrious Doctor; the rarity of the matter moves me to consider it a little further. I confess that, as you gather from those printed observations, I too have observed remarkable **metastases** <term>metastases: from the Greek μεταστάσεις (metastaseis), referring to the displacement or shifting of a disease or bodily fluid from one part of the body to another</term> regarding the movement of the menstrual material; however, I have seen none quite like those that could be fully compared with this long-term eruption of blood described here.

You add that after a **clyster** <term>clyster: an enema or liquid injection into the rectum used for medicinal or purgative purposes</term> was administered and not returned, a flow of purple blood followed from the right ear. In that case, blood collected copiously in the hypochondria, and due to the injection of the **enema** <note>original: "Enematis"</note>, as the internal spaces were constricted, the blood rushed toward the upper parts of the body and found an exit near the right ear; and this [continued] through the years—

This was perhaps because the material was collected anew in the distended spaces of the vessels of the lower belly, which then vanished again once the volume of blood was moved toward the accustomed areas of excretion. 

It is not at all surprising that various prescribed medications achieved little here, with the sole exception of bloodletting from a vein. By this method—repeatedly opening three veins at once—she found relief, because the blood, offending by its quantity and sharpness, required reduction and swift alteration. For this reason, she could by no means endure the use of baths, as her blood would immediately begin to boil and strike the vital organs with its sharpness.

The *second question* is also skillfully determined, where an abundance of blood produced by the strong action of the internal organs’ blood-making is placed as the principal cause of this hemorrhage. The obstruction of the menses serves greatly in the collection of this blood, as does the weakness of the remaining body parts, which draw too little from the blood supply for their daily nutritional needs. Consequently, the constitution of the rest of the body—in proportion to the copious blood—shows none of the **well-fleshed condition** <note>original: εὐσαρκίαν (eusarkia); a term for a healthy, well-muscled physique</note> that would otherwise correspond to such a superabundance of blood.

Thirdly, what is proposed concerning the causes of *Vomiting of blood* is judged worthy of further discussion, especially since the occasion for it can be manifold. I shall say nothing here of those vomitings of blood which happen to women because of the "regurgitation" <note>Early modern physicians believed that if menstruation was blocked, the blood could be diverted or "regurgitated" to other organs, such as the stomach or lungs.</note> of their menses. However, those points proposed in Book 4 of the *Observations*, Part 2, Observation 2, on the occasion of a notable history of vomiting blood, are worthy of note. It is pleasing to share similar cases here along with their outcomes. 

The first is that of a **man of the senatorial order**, who several years ago was frequently afflicted by vomiting blood and simultaneously by black stools. At last, as his strength was dissipated along with his blood, he perished. Even outside of these paroxysms, he was often tortured by very heavy twisting pains and bloating in the lower belly and especially the back—perhaps because a sharp **black bile** <note>original: atrabilaris materia; one of the four humors in ancient medicine, thought to cause melancholy and physical irritation when "sharp" or "burnt."</note> material became fixed around the sensitive membranes of the **mesentery** <note>The fold of membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall.</note>, provoking them with its sharpness for so long until it was separated with the help of the "expulsive faculty" <note>The body's natural power to push out waste or harmful substances.</note>. 

The *second* case is that of a certain **tanner**, who in the previous year suffered a relapse of such a symptomatic evacuation through vomiting blood and black stools. Having been restored from this after a fashion, a few months later he became **dropsical** <note>original: hydropicus; suffering from edema or "dropsy," an accumulation of fluid in the body.</note>. Finally, as his expulsive faculty grew faint and the offending material accumulated in great quantity, he died, his strength having been suffocated.

The *third* is a **certain patrician**, nearly forty years of age, who after a long-lasting, heavy pain on his left side, finally fell into a **semitertian fever** <note>original: febrim quasi semitertianam; a specific type of recurring fever, historically associated with malaria, where the patient experiences both a daily fever and a more severe one every other day.</note> due to rotting matter in the **hypochondria** <note>The upper abdominal region under the ribs.</note>. This was immediately followed by a copious vomiting of blood and lethal black stools, so that toward the end of April 1625, he exchanged life for death. 

The *fourth* is a **certain nobleman**, of senatorial rank, about 56 years old, with a lean constitution of body and a facial color just like all the others whom we have known to be seized by this affliction...

<meta>This page continues the medical discussion regarding "vomiting of blood." The previous page concluded a case study of a learned man who died from internal bleeding; this page explains the anatomical findings of the autopsy and moves into a comparison with non-fatal vomiting of blood in women, while addressing theoretical doubts about treatment methods like bloodletting.</meta>

# PREFACE TO [THE READER]

...[the blood] having been stirred up, through the **gastric coronary vein**, communicated to the stomach from the splenic branch. The intestines, especially the large ones along with the **Ileum** <note>The final and longest segment of the small intestine</note>, were seen to be smeared with a blackish fluid like ink; when this was wiped away, the **mesenteric veins** <note>original: venæ meseraicæ; the veins that drain blood from the digestive tract</note> poured out a fluid of that sort mixed with blood. From these observations, and from what has been said elsewhere, it is easily gathered that these bloody vomitings accompanied by black stools are far different from those produced in women by a healthy abundance of blood when the menstrual flow is obstructed.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In this regard, I recall a certain woman, the wife of a Cooper <note>A barrel-maker</note> living here near the Gate of the Holy Mother, who suffered for many years from menstrual obstruction. Up until her later years, she frequently endured bloody vomiting without significant harm, until on June 17, 1625, she sought medical advice. By addressing the obstructions with medicated wine, and also by strengthening the stomach with moderate **astringents** <note>Medicines that cause the contraction of body tissues to stop blood flow</note>, we successfully restored her menses, and the vomiting of blood never returned. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I am also persuaded that such a vomiting of blood in the example you proposed of that woman occurs through not only the gastric and coronary veins connected to the stomach, but also through any others whatsoever, because boiling and effervescing blood very easily finds a way out—just as is sometimes seen in other copious hemorrhages. 

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The fourth doubt is correctly resolved by presupposing the stated principle: namely, that blood is generated in great abundance because of the health of the liver, yet it is not at all consumed because of the sluggish **attractive faculty** <note>The power of an organ to draw in the nourishment it needs from the blood</note> of other parts of the body. This is also apparent in those who have had a limb—such as a foot or a hand—amputated. In these patients, a greater abundance of blood later requires evacuation at certain times; if this is neglected, it usually causes recurring hemorrhages.

<margin>*Fifth, it was asked whether **bloodletting** and other means of **revulsion** <note>original: revulsio; a medical practice of drawing blood or humors away from a diseased area to a healthy part of the body</note> still have a place, especially since such treatments are usually applied in vain when one is of a declining age?*</margin> 

Since, however, "custom is second nature" <note>original: consuetudo sit altera natura</note> according to the common proverb, I very readily concede that these accustomed modes of excretion can only be reversed with difficulty after such a long span of time. This is also apparent in other long-standing diseases of **fluxions** <note>The flow of excess humors to a specific part of the body</note>. It happens especially to those with confirmed **Gout** <note>original: Podagricis</note>, who provoke a **paroxysm** <note>A sudden attack or intensification of symptoms</note> when bloodlettings and purgatives are used. This occurs because the stirred-up **humors** <note>The bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow and black bile—that were thought to determine health</note> tend to seek their accustomed paths toward the weaker parts of the body, rather than following the intended paths of **derivation** and **revulsion** <note>Two methods of bloodletting: derivation draws blood from a vein near the affected part; revulsion draws it from a distant part.</note>. Finally, in the sixth case, the outcome is investigated, where I do not doubt that this excretion will eventually introduce a poor bodily condition, [becoming...]

<meta>catchword: becoming,</meta>

<header>TO THE KIND READER.</header>

*...it happens, as we observe in others as well, in whom a more vigorous force of nature is accustomed to stir up abundant hemorrhages from an early age during bouts of weakness. Over time, these people incur damage to their nutritive capacity; and if they do not perish suddenly from a loss of strength due to a more violent symptomatic effusion of blood, they are nevertheless gradually consumed by **Cachexia** <term>A state of severe physical wasting and malnutrition associated with chronic illness</term>.*
*As for what is added at the end—that the menstrual flow, which had ceased for two years, returned in the preceding weeks with signs of matter being transferred here and there, as well as an ensuing nosebleed—this very fact confirms what was said before: namely, that **blood production** <note>original: "sanguificationem"</note> is still quite abundant. For this reason, nature tries to seek some relief for itself through these customary evacuations. I think the outcome to be expected is either sudden death due to a collapse of strength—the "retentive faculty" <note>The biological power to hold onto necessary fluids and nutrients; the OCR "lætâ" is likely a typo for "læsâ" meaning injured or damaged</note> failing suddenly while nature expels not only the superfluous blood but also the very support necessary for life—or a lethal **Cachexia** will ensue, which the gradual dissipation of the **spirits** <note>In 17th-century medicine, "spirits" were subtle fluids believed to animate the body and mind</note> will produce. All these things an **autopsy** <note>original: "corporis post mortem apertio"; literally, "the opening of the body after death"</note> would most strongly confirm. These are the things I wished to reply regarding the present case. Take them in good part, and continue to hold me in your affection. Quickly, from Ulm, October 18, 1628.*

### I.

There is a place on earth, near to the squalid underworld,
The pale house of diseases and of **Tisiphone**. <note>In Greek mythology, Tisiphone was one of the Furies, often depicted as a bringer of disease and madness</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the specific medical consultation of the previous page to a series of commendatory poems—common in early modern medical texts—praising the physician Gregor Horst for his wisdom and his published medical observations. The poem personifies disease as the Fury Tisiphone and portrays Horst's book as the ultimate shield for humanity.</meta>

Tisiphone, the mother of diverse plagues
And of a hundred sorrows, had thrust forth her viperous head from the depths.
And, not yet satisfied—not yet filled with the sight of funeral biers—
She said, "I am fashioning an immense, unspeakable work."
"With me as leader, with me as the foul overseer of losses, the **Fevers** <term>Febres; referring to various types of recurring or intermittent fevers</term>
Have learned their alternating cycles;
With me as their mother, the heavy strokes of **Apoplexy** <term>Apoplectica sidera; literally "apoplectic stars," referring to sudden strokes or paralysis once thought to be caused by celestial influence</term>
Hurl down their power; from me, the bitter **Dropsy** <term>Hydrops; an accumulation of fluid in the body (edema)</term> swells.
From me, the hands took up their sluggish chains: the **Gout of the hand** <term>Cheragra</term>;
From me, with the **Gout of the foot** <term>Podagra</term>, come the sluggish chains of the feet.
In short, imagine whatever evil you wish, whatever you might seek,
You will find that the evil had me as its mother.
But it is not yet enough: within my heart I turn over new
Chariots of death, by which the journey of fate may be hastened."
She spoke; and turning her eyes toward her **Colchian teachers** <note>original: "Colchas magistras"; a reference to Medea, the famous witch-priestess of Colchis, symbolizing the dark arts of poisoning</note>,
She stirred herself to the wicked **Thessalian work** <note>Thessaly was renowned in antiquity as the home of powerful witches and sorcerers</note>.
New Fevers are sought for the lands, a new **Hectic fever** <term>Hectica; a wasting fever often associated with consumption or tuberculosis</term>
Is sought for the world; a single pestilence is not enough to please her.
**Ulcers** known neither to **Phoebus** <note>Apollo, the god of healing</note>, nor to **Galen** <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire, whose works were still foundational in the 17th century</note>,
Are ordered to crawl through the vital pathways of the body.
A troop of diseases never seen before, never believed possible,
Was advancing—a certain ruin for the head of mankind.
And now nothing was lacking; now, O World, you were to be slaughtered at so many altars,
You were destined to become a sepulchral pit;
When suddenly, she checked her step and fled backward—
The mother Tisiphone, with her dire threats.
For she saw (for your labor is everywhere, with **lamp and oil** <note>A classical metaphor for late-night study and scholarly dedication</note>)
She saw the **Machaonian writings** <note>original: "scripta Machaonia"; Machaon was the son of Asclepius, the god of medicine, and a legendary physician in the Trojan War</note>:
A book full of your counsels and medical **Providence** <note>original: "Pronoâ"</note>
Tisiphone saw—and she fell silent.
Evidently, she perceived that here, both new diseases and old
Could perish at the hands of a physician.
Hence she checked her step, surrendered the palm of victory,
And carried herself away from there in desperate flight.

### II.

Neither the **Great** <note>original: "MAGNUS"; a reference to Alexander the Great</note> of the Greeks, nor the **Greatest** <note>original: "MAXIMUS"; likely referring to the Roman general Fabius Maximus</note> of the Latin race themselves,
Nor King nor Father, saw an equal to this man.
Hannibal yielded to the one; almost the whole world to the other;
Thus was glory won by the sword and by **cautious delay** <note>original: "cauta mora"; a reference to the strategy of Fabius "The Delayer" (Cunctator) against Hannibal</note>.
The club of Hercules, which knew not how to be broken, 
Was able to tame those fire-breathing monsters and dragons.
By his word, his pen, his right hand, and by a favorable star, 
How great a slaughter of diseases does **Horst** alone perform?
How many heads of the venomous **Hydra** does he not cut off?
How many ghastly monsters of the sick does he not subdue?
Hence, like a Prince, he rightly shines among the medical ranks,
And holds a name of merited honor.
To this man, therefore, may you be "Famous" and "Fortunate"; to that one, "Great";
But to me, you who are greater than the **GREAT**, be the **GREATEST**.

*With dutiful affection and applause, in the name of an old friendship, inscribed by:*
->**Johannes Plachetius**, Doctor, Ordinary Physician to the Most Illustrious Court of Württemberg.<-

### III.

# A Double Epigram.

## To the Author.

This GARDEN <note>original: "HORTUS"; a pun on the author's name, Horstius</note> is yours, HORST, which full breasts have watered,
And which this double PANACEA <term>A mythological universal remedy or "all-healing" herb</term> fosters:
HERMES <note>representing Hermetic or chemical medicine</note> and HIPPOCRATES <note>representing classical Greek medicine</note> are the Mothers; you have sucked
Both breasts for a long time: you have become the honor of a double Art.
O happy SON OF THE ART: O splendid cultivator of the GARDEN:
Hail to the sweet garden-beds which you arrange!
We have seen how you cut away the weeds <note>original: "zizania"; literally "tares," often used biblically to refer to harmful things growing among the good</note> with each scythe;
This extraordinary GARDEN demonstrates your double work.
I predict: from here anyone will pluck herbs and balsams,
Both the men of the Spagyric <term>Alchemical medicine, focusing on the separation and recombination of natural elements</term> and the Dogmatic <term>Traditional medicine based on the ancient Greek teachings of Galen</term> sects!
For what they observe HERE, he performs THIS; so that we may rightly
Leave these primary observations to his own age!

## To the Reader.

You should read practical writings: imitate practical things;
May your Practice be good, if the present HORST adds his aid.
The present "Gregorian Practice" is good beyond many others:
Imitate this: in a short time I shall call you a Chymiattrist <term>A physician who combines chemical remedies with traditional medicine</term>!
Add to it the Practice of Wittenberg <note>original: "Leucoream"; the Latinized Greek name for the University of Wittenberg</note> and the great Galen,
Whom Altdorf <note>The University of Altdorf</note> holds and whom Wittenberg fosters.
If you join these three, rising as both a Chemist by art,
And a Sage, and a Physician; then you shall sing these good words:
HORST, HOFMANN, and SENNERT <note>Caspar Hofmann and Daniel Sennert were, along with Horst, the most famous German medical authorities of the early 17th century</note>, the Lights of the World,
These three are the Physicians: Greatest Trio, FAREWELL!

->Made out of gratitude, respect, and kinship by<-

->*of Darmstadt.*<-

### IV.

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal band consisting of repetitive floral and geometric woodcut ornaments runs across the top of the page above the poem number.</image-desc>

Among the honored Physicians whom the German world
Boasts of, and whom she adores among her ancient ancestors:
Forgive me, happy souls! Now **Horst** is worthy of honor,
renowned for his genius and powerful in his art.
To be sure, **Hartmann** <note>Johannes Hartmann (1568–1631), the first professor of "Chymiatria" (chemical medicine) in Germany</note> reigns in the Hessian lands,
celebrated for your discoveries, divine **Chemistry** <term>Chymia: the early modern term for the art of extracting and purifying medicinal substances through fire and distillation</term>.
The famous **Sennert** <note>Daniel Sennert (1572–1637), a titan of 17th-century medicine who sought to reconcile Aristotle and Galen with new chemical theories</note> is heard by the Saxon Elbe,
the greatest in eloquence, the greatest in reliability.
And others in other lands, who are praised together,
Physicians are held in high price and in their own honor.
But to me, our man sees neither diseases nor medicines
more slowly, nor does he see Causes and Aid worse
than they; with what an easy method, with what learned daring
Horst explains the immense riches of the wealthy art.
Though these same things may be common in learned books—
whether in yours, **Forestus** <note>Pieter van Foreest (1521–1597), known as the "Dutch Hippocrates"</note>, or yours, **Platerus** <note>Felix Platter (1536–1614), a Swiss physician famous for his clinical observations and anatomical studies</note>—
Yet he does no less for medical uses;
(if I may speak with your leave) he has no less authority regarding causes.
Just as the **Citrus** tree rises in fragrant gardens,
and illuminates all the soil with its fruits:
So, among the divinely inspired initiates of Apollo <note>Apollo was the Greek god of healing and the father of Asclepius</note>,
the Virtue and dexterity of his good genius shines forth.
Just as the honey of Mount **Hymettus** <note>A mountain range in Greece famous in antiquity for its high-quality honey</note> drips in Athenian lands,
everywhere with pure, dew-covered honeycombs:
So Horst shines in eloquence, and so he flourishes in his art,
and pours out words that rival the pressed honeycombs.
Therefore **SWABIA** will owe you deserved praises,
the City of **ULM**, and the whole World alike, will give thanks,
Because you now build up and amplify with your writings
not only the people of Augsburg <note>original: "Vindelicos"</note> and the City, but the whole world.
What shall I say? Your fame will travel to the **Don** <note>original: "Tanaim," the river marking the boundary between Europe and Asia</note> and the powerful **Scythians**:
it will enter the rapid waters of the **Danube**.
Fame which the **Oder** <note>original: "Viadrus"</note> already, and the **Lahn**, the **Main**, and the **Elbe**
celebrate with their neighboring shallows, not without praise.
Now even the mindful **Swans** <note>a common poetic metaphor for poets or learned men</note> that these rivers nourish
loosen their tuneful mouths in your praise.

### V.

This was in our prayers, this we all asked with our voices:
that **Horst** would expand the riches of Medicine.
He has done so, and has added new publications to his printed books,
monuments that future generations will marvel at.
Whatever others may do, I offer the highest thanks from my heart

You ensure that the people of **Paeon** <note>original: "gens Pæonis." Paeon was the physician of the gods in Greek mythology; the phrase refers to the medical community or the "tribe of doctors."</note> become more learned throughout the whole world,

Beyond your other writings, O Leader of Wisdom! O Star of Health! <note>original: "Sydus Hygeiæ." Hygeia was the Greek goddess of health and cleanliness.</note>

> These things also spread the fame of the House of Horst through the ages,

> Truly, though you may not be able to grasp the whole at once, the honor of the 
> Frontispiece marks out gifts worthy of the highest man.
> It teaches what the mind of a Physician is, what his hope is; in what 
> matters he may burn with zeal, and what Light of prayer may rule his judgments.
> And whatever of these things you see standing there, he desires to strike 
> not so much the eyes as the mind with a short motto.
> Behold! someone from the race of Ancient Sages cries out:
> "I OBSERVE": and he urges on the work of everlasting study. <note>The word "OBSERVO" (I Observe) was a central theme in Horst's work, emphasizing empirical bedside observation over mere theory.</note>
> For whoever ponders the wandering World with his senses or his heart, 
> is tossed about in innumerable ways:
> Until he distinguishes the fragile from the eternal, the moving from the dull:
> And, having set aside the dross, reaches out for the serenity of God.

## ANALYSIS.

<margin>Origin of the illness.</margin>
I determined that a complicated condition was present here, which had its origin from an excessive collection of blood gathered along with <term>excrementitious humors</term> <note>In 17th-century medicine, these were "waste" fluids produced when the body failed to properly digest or "cook" food into healthy blood.</note>, primarily in the veins of the <term>mesentery</term> <note>The membrane attaching the intestines to the abdominal wall.</note>, the liver, the spleen, and the stomach.

<margin>Preceding cause.</margin>
The cause for this collection was the weaker <term>concoction</term> <note>The "cooking" or metabolic process of digestion.</note> of the stomach and the imperfect digestion of the liver, which the *white and thick urine* demonstrated more than enough. Because of this, impurities were not cleared from the blood mass, and for that reason the *menstrual flow was also found to be only imperfectly* performed, <margin>Derivation of the symptoms.</margin> since the aforementioned veins of the uterus were also obstructed by the causes already stated. Thus, it was no surprise that the most Illustrious Patient was very frequently subject to *dysentery and bloody fluxes of the bowels*. The *thick and white urine* is easily traced to its cause here, insofar as the weaker digestion of the liver does not separate from the blood mass that which is bilious and <term>tartareous</term> <note>Sediment-like matter, named after the crust in wine barrels, thought to cause obstructions in the body.</note> (which gives the serum its color), but—

<column-break/>

—leaves sharp and salty impurities in the blood. These impurities, once collected and somewhat coagulated around the minor veins of the internal organs, produce a strange <term>concurrence</term> <note>original Greek: "syndromen," from which we derive the modern word "syndrome."</note> of various symptoms. Hence the pain around the <term>xiphoid cartilage</term> <note>The lower tip of the breastbone.</note> of the chest, which occurs because the upper opening of the stomach—endowed with very sensitive feeling—is unnaturally affected, either because some matter is collected there or because it is irritated by salty and sharp vapors. The sides of the <term>hypochondria</term> <note>The upper abdominal region below the ribs.</note> are bloated, both due to the large amount of matter hidden there and the "boiling" of the hidden obstructions; this is also why the illness has its periods of remission. There is difficulty in breathing, not because the breathing organs themselves are the primary cause of the trouble, but insofar as the diaphragm is pressed upward and its free movement is hindered. The *incipient fainting spells and heart palpitations* occur because harmful vapors—rising from the effervescing obstruction around the splenic veins—are communicated upward to the heart by means of the many arteries connected to the spleen. Therefore, through a "sympathy" between the organs, such incidents are felt occasionally rather than constantly. These are accompanied by *headaches*, as these same fumes penetrate further to the brain, where they produce sharp, vehement pains by affecting the membranes—mostly around the front of the head, where—

...abundant vessels permeate the outer membrane; this usually happens not at just any time, but especially when the time of the monthly period is imminent, when nature stirs the blood mass and attempts to secrete <margin>Indications.</margin> impurities.
