### BOOK I. PART II.

Because the smaller, delicate veins of the lower abdomen are so narrow, this abundance of blood cannot yet be directed toward the womb. Thus, even though the girl’s age seems to have surpassed puberty, a lack of menstruation still persists.

<margin>Explanation of the symptoms.</margin>
For this reason, around the **New Moon** <note>original: "Novilunium"; early modern medicine often linked bodily fluids and blood flow to the lunar cycle</note>, when the blood is naturally stirred to motion and seeks an exit as if it were boiling, she is afflicted by pains around the navel and the region of the spleen. At that time, a commotion is stirred up from waste material, causing gases to rise around the colon, which produce rumblings and belchings from the stomach. **Anxiety** is present because of a tightness in the chest; this is caused by the diaphragm being compressed by the bloating of the abdomen. From this, **difficult breathing** follows, and consequently, as the watery fluids <note>original: "serosis humoribus"</note> also bubble up around the heart, a **palpitation** of the heart occurs. This is accompanied by **bloating of the belly**, which is very often merely a kind of tension, as the abdominal muscles themselves suffer from what is improperly called a convulsion. Therefore, such **tension** is usually joined with **exquisite, but only momentary pains**, which would not happen if the pain always arose from a physical substance. She passes urine that is "crude" <note>undigested or unprocessed</note> and straw-colored, because the retention of unprocessed blood necessarily means the watery serum is also colored by "Tartar" <note>original: "Tartari"; a term for metabolic sediment or byproduct</note> that has been minimally processed by the body’s filtration.

<margin>Prognosis.</margin>
Having considered these things, I predicted the illness would be long-lasting, both because the girl has had weak internal organs since she was small, and because the menstrual flow is pressing but cannot yet find its way to action. Although it is not to be doubted that once her periods arrive, the aforementioned symptoms will be removed of their own accord, the matter should not be totally neglected in the meantime due to the difficulty of the menstruation. Rather, it is necessary to proceed according to the following goals for the sake of preventing <term>cachexia</term><note>A general state of wasting, weakness, and poor health.</note>.

<margin>Indications and Goals.</margin>
1. The collection of phlegmatic and sticky matter around the stomach and neighboring parts must be gradually prepared and gently cleared out.

2. The digestive organs, which are weak due to being "chilled," must be warmed and strengthened.

3. Each month, as the moon wanes, those things should not be neglected which can serve to open the veins and prepare the body and blood for the menstrual discharge.

<margin>Regarding Point 1.</margin>
Regarding Step 1: After the Full Moon <note>original: "Plenilunium"</note>, let her use 2 ounces <note>symbol: ℥</note> of **Manna** <note>a sweet, mild laxative derived from the sap of the flowering ash tree</note> dissolved in a broth of prunes, adding 1 scruple <note>symbol: ℈</note> of Cream of Tartar as a stimulant. Or, to more effectively drive out the more stubborn phlegm, let her take 1 dram <note>symbol: ʒ</note> of the finest white **Mechoacan** <note>original: "Mechoacannæ"; a root from the Americas used as a purgative</note>, recently powdered, with the addition of half a scruple of **Vitriolated Tartar** <note>original: "Tartari Vitriolati"; potassium sulfate, used as a diuretic and laxative</note>. Or let a Laxative Wine be made, which [contains]:

Take: **Rhubarb**, 1 dram.

Fol. <note>catchword for "Folia" (Leaves)</note>

### Obstruction of the menses producing various preternatural excretions.

<margin>Observation on</margin> Not only do the aforementioned accidents frequently arise from the obstruction of menses, but it also happens not rarely that the abundance of excess blood seeks other preternatural <note>original: "p. n." or *praeter naturam*; meaning "beyond the natural order" or abnormal</note> paths when the usual ones are obstructed. We observed this in a most noble young lady in the year 1608 near Giessen <note>a university town in Germany</note>, who,

<margin>the excretion of menses through the bowels.</margin> being deprived of the usual menstrual flow, discharged blood through the bowels for several days every month. This was because the finer veins of the womb were obstructed. We attempted to help her in the same way as the previous case, regarding which see *Therapeutic Problems*, Decade 9, Question 1. To this also belongs the story proposed in Book 1 of *Medical Epistles*, Section 19, concerning a woman whose natural parts had grown shut <note>original: "consolidatis"</note> and who was purged through the bowels every month.

<margin>Menses rejected through vomiting.</margin> Thus, a few years ago, I treated a maidservant, about 20 years of age, who had suffered for several years from menstrual obstruction due to the "coldness of the womb" <note>in humoral medicine, a lack of vital heat in the uterus was thought to prevent the thinning and flow of blood</note>; every month, a *vomiting of blood* occurred for two or three days. Other modes of excretion may be 
<margin>Incomplete transformation of menses. Observation.</margin> observed among practitioners—though they are imperfect—such as the case we knew in the year 1614, where a certain young woman was seized by joint pains almost every month because of menstrual obstruction.

<margin>Observation 3. Cachexia from a lack of menstruation.</margin>
It happens not rarely that an incipient Cachexia <note>a state of general ill health and physical wasting, often involving anemia in this historical context</note> arises around the time of puberty due to a lack of the menses. An example of this occurred to us here in Ulm this past year, 1622, which I am pleased to add to the others. A girl, about 15 years old and from a respected family, was being gradually consumed by atrophy; she was frequently afflicted by a crushing sensation in the chest, stomach pain, and similar symptoms, while her urine remained crude and thick <note>original: "spicea," likely referring to a sediment-heavy or cloudy appearance indicating poor digestion of humors</note>. I concluded that a Cachexia from suppressed menstruation was present here, for which reason I evacuated the "crudities" <note>undigested or harmful bodily fluids</note> collected around the primary passages using a Laxative Wine.

# OBSERVATION III.

### The Virgin’s Disease or <term>Leucophlegmatia</term><note>Literally "white phlegm," a condition characterized by a pale, bloated appearance caused by an excess of cold, moist humors</note> with difficulty of the menses.

A NOBLE VIRGIN, of mature age, has complained for several years of difficulty with her monthly periods and a "white flow" <note>Leucorrhea, a common gynecological symptom</note>. Her entire body, and especially her face and lips, is pale. She is frequently affected by palpitations of the heart and difficulty breathing. A spontaneous exhaustion of the limbs comes upon her, and not rarely a convulsive-like tremor; headache; and swelling and bloating around the <term>hypochondria</term><note>The upper abdominal region just below the ribs</note>, particularly when her periods are imminent. For this reason, she called me for a consultation at the beginning of winter in the year 1622.

# RESOLUTION.

<margin>Classification of the affliction.</margin>
It is manifest that <term>Leucophlegmatia</term> is present here (<gloss>white phlegm</gloss> <note>original Greek: λευκὸν Φλέγμα</note>, as described by Hippocrates in his book *On Affections*). This is surely a cold

<column-break/>

and moist imbalance, involving phlegm and watery humors, both in the organs of blood-making and in the overall habit of the body. This has taken root over many years, so that the disease now appears quite established. Consequently, regarding the digestive organs, it threatens a type of dropsy called <term>Anasarca</term><note>General swelling of the whole body due to fluid in the tissues</note>; regarding the vital organs, it threatens <term>tabes</term><note>A wasting or consumption of the body</note> due to raw "distillations" <note>harmful fluids flowing from one part of the body to another</note> toward the chest; and regarding the state of the brain, it threatens convulsions and epilepsy. The difficulty of the menses is present because of the phlegmatic blood obstructing and cooling the veins; these end in a white flow because impure and raw blood is abundant throughout the whole. From this, paleness occupies the entire body, insofar as this kind of phlegm is converted into the substance of the skin—especially the face and lips. This is noticed sooner in these parts because, due to the thinness of their substance, they are otherwise flooded with a natural redness. She is frequently affected by palpitations of the heart because of the abundance of phlegmatic fluid gathering and boiling around the <term>capsule of the heart</term><note>The pericardium, or the sac surrounding the heart</note>, and by difficulty in breathing due to the compression of the diaphragm caused by the bloating of the upper abdomen. In these moments, her breath seems to fail, especially if she has to climb stairs, because of the necessity of exhaling to expel thicker vapors when the weakened faculty <note>the body's natural strength</note> must compensate for its deficiency through more frequent effort.

## OBSERVATION IV.

## Leucophlegmatia with total obstruction of the menses,

**A** respectable girl, the daughter of a merchant from Ulm, 18 years of age, fell into a state of menstrual obstruction lasting six months; there followed paleness of the face, wasting <term>atrophy: a thinning or weakening of the body</term> of the entire body, a feeling of pressure in the stomach, difficulty breathing, exhaustion of the whole body, etc.

### RESOLUTION

<margin>
Determination of the disease.
Indications.
</margin>
**W**HEN I was called into consultation at the beginning of September in the year 1623, I immediately stated that **Leucophlegmatia** <note>A condition involving pale, "doughy" swelling caused by an excess of cold, moist humors (phlegm)</note> was occurring alongside a total obstruction of the menstrual flow. Therefore, I said we must work with all our might so that the **phlegmatic cachexia** <note>A general state of poor health and "bad habit" of the body caused by an imbalance of phlegm</note> might be corrected, the blocked smaller veins of the lower belly might be opened, and the cooled organs of digestion might be warmed and strengthened.

For this reason, we immediately ordered a **Laxative Wine** to be used for several days.
**Take:** Roots of **Elecampane**.

<column-break/>

**Sweet Flag**, 3 drams each.

### OBSERVATION IV.

### Pale-phlegm swelling with a total obstruction of the menses.

A respectable young woman, the daughter of a merchant from Ulm, 18 years of age, fell into an obstruction of her menses <note>amenorrhea</note> for six months; there followed a paleness of the face, a wasting of the entire body <note>atrophy</note>, a feeling of pressure in the stomach, difficulty breathing, general exhaustion, etc.

### RESOLUTION

<margin>
Determination of the disease.
Indications.
</margin>
When I was called to consult at the beginning of September in the year 1623, I immediately stated that a pale-phlegm swelling <term>Leucophlegmatia; a condition where the body appears pale and bloated, thought to be caused by an excess of cold, moist phlegm</term> was occurring alongside a total obstruction of the menses. Therefore, I said we must work with all our strength to correct the phlegmatic poor health <note>original: "Cachexia"</note>, open the obstructed smaller veins of the lower belly, and warm and strengthen the digestive organs that had become chilled.

For this reason, we immediately ordered a Laxative Wine to be used for several days.

**Take:** Roots of **Elecampane**.

## OBSERVATION V.

->*Difficulty of menstruation with*<-
->*very severe*<-
->*symptoms.*<-

The noble young lady, Maria Sabina, daughter of the Illustrious Count Ernest of Solms, seventeen years of age and of a thin physical constitution, complains of very severe pains in her head and stomach, especially when her monthly periods are imminent. These are frequently accompanied by vomiting or sometimes even diarrhea. Her menstrual flow is painful and difficult, accompanied by torment in the lower abdomen, heart palpitations, and subsequent fainting. Her urine is passed in a raw and thick state, depositing a white, bran-like sediment.

### THE RESOLUTION.

<margin>Determination of the disease.</margin>
Called to her aid in the year 1614 near the beginning of November, when the aforementioned symptoms were afflicting the patient more severely due to the harshness of the oncoming winter, I soon concluded that her difficult menstrual flow was primarily due to a <term>phlegmatic cachexia</term> <note>A state of ill health or "bad habit" of the body caused by an excess of cold, moist humors (phlegm).</note>. Hence her physical constitution was thin—not by her natural temperament, but because her nutritional processes were hindered. The pain in her head and stomach afflicted her most when her periods were approaching because, at that time, the viscid humors were stirred up, and the imperfectly purified blood would surge back toward the upper parts of the body, transmitting putrid vapors to the sensitive organs.

<column-break/>

Frequent vomiting and bowel movements occurred because nature, as the contents of the stomach "boiled" or became agitated, stimulated the expulsive power of the stomach and intestines. The menstrual flow was painful and difficult insofar as the "raw" (undigested) and viscid blood is separated only with great effort; this is due to the distension of the vessels and passages, as well as the bitterness of the blood itself, which increases because of its retention and the beginning of decay. From this arose pains in the lower belly similar to those of childbirth, and—as the heart was affected by "consensus" <note>An early medical term for "sympathy," where one organ reacts to the distress of another via the nervous or vascular system.</note>—palpitations and fainting followed. The raw, thick urine, which deposited a white, bran-like sediment, did not come from a "melting" or "scorching" of the bodily juices, but from a weakness of the <term>concoction</term> <note>The "cooking" or metabolic process by which the body refines food into blood and energy.</note>; it deposits such a sediment due to the weight of the matter, which usually signifies a long-lasting illness, according to the 31st Aphorism in the 3rd Section of Hippocrates <note>original: "Aphor. 31. sect. 3. Hipp."</note>.

<meta>The text on the following page likely begins with the word "Hic" (Here/This).</meta>

<margin>Treatment Goals.</margin>
For this case, we have established the following plan: 1. first of all, the primary passages <note>the digestive tract</note> must be cleared; 2. the material of the <term>cachexia</term> <note>a state of ill health</note> around the organs of the "second digestion" <note>the liver and spleen, where the ancients believed food was turned into blood</note> must be processed and separated; 3. the thick and sticky blood must be thinned and cut through; 4. the monthly periods must be encouraged; and 5. the internal organs must be strengthened.

<margin>Regarding goal 1.</margin>
As for the first goal, we initially administered a mild laxative, which was:
> Take: Half an ounce of <term>Tamarind Electuary</term> <note>a medicinal paste made from tamarind fruit</note> with senna leaves.
> One and a half drachms of <term>Caryocostinum</term> <note>a classic purgative made with cloves and costus</note>. Mix.

<margin>Regarding goal 2.</margin>
As for the second goal, let the "digestion" <note>the ripening of humors</note> be performed by a decoction of <term>opening roots</term> <note>usually a combination of fennel, parsley, asparagus, butcher's broom, and smallage</note> with appropriate herbs and seeds. To this, add syrups of <term>Maidenhair fern</term>, the "Five Roots," Marshmallow, and similar items. For each dose, mix in half a scruple of Cream of Tartar. This digestive treatment should be continued for four days, followed by a more complete purging, which was accomplished with half a drachm of <term>Mechoacan</term> <note>a root from Mexico used as a strong laxative</note>.

<margin>Regarding goal 3.</margin>
As for the third goal, let a syrup of <term>Steel Filings</term> <note>original: "Limaturâ Chalybis"; iron was a standard treatment for "greensickness" or anemia</note> be made in this manner:
> Take: Half a pound of steel filings dissolved in sulfur and prepared.
> One pound each of Lemon Balm water, Fennel water, and <term>Scordium</term> <note>Water Germander</note> water.
> Let them infuse for eight days in a [suitable] place, then boil down to a third. Let them be strained, and
> Add:
> One handful each of Lemon Balm, Betony, and Maidenhair fern.
> One drachm of Fennel seed.
> One and a half drachms of Sassafras.
> Let them stand overnight; in the morning, boil them in turn,

<column-break/>

and let them be strained. Add a sufficient quantity of sugar to make a syrup. Two ounces or three drachms of this should be diluted with a decoction of Fennel root, <term>Eryngo</term> <note>Sea Holly</note>, raisins, and red chickpeas, and taken twice daily for eight days.

<margin>Regarding goal 4.</margin>
As for the fourth goal, after the previous steps are completed and near the time her period is due, she should use a morning bath made from the herbs Lemon Balm, <term>Mugwort</term> <note>Artemisia, a plant traditionally used for uterine health</note>, Chamomile, Asarabacca root, Juniper berries, and similar plants, on an empty stomach for several days. Before the bath, she should first take half a drachm of the following mixture:
> Take: Six drachms of <term>Dwarf Elder juice</term> <note>original: "Rob Ebuli"</note>.
> One drachm of <term>Theriac of Andromachus</term> <note>a complex, ancient "universal" medicine</note>.
> Half a scruple of <term>Castoreum</term> <note>a yellowish secretion from beaver scent glands, used for hysteria</note>.
> Sufficient Juniper berry syrup to mix. For 2 doses.

After the morning bath is finished, let her take one scruple of "hysteric pills" in the evening before dinner, which consist of:
> Take: Two drachms of <term>Succotrine Aloe</term>.
> One scruple of the best Myrrh.
> Half a scruple each of extracts of Aromatic Calamus and <term>Blessed Thistle</term>.
> Two grains of Saffron.
> Five grains each of Gentian root, Long Birthwort, and <term>Dittany</term>.
> With Elderberry juice, make into pills.

Finally, regarding goal 5: We ordered a suitable diet and prescribed a "stomachic wine" made from an infusion of Elecampane root, Aromatic Calamus, Blessed Thistle, Lemon Balm, Lesser Centaury, Scordium, etc. Frequently, on an empty stomach, we administered several drops of the <term>Elixir of Property of Paracelsus</term> <note>a famous tonic made of aloe, myrrh, and saffron</note> before sleep.

## OBSERVATION VI.

### Menstrual blockage with the bowels suppressed for 11 days.

A peasant girl in the village of Wustrow, in the Old March of Brandenburg, in the year 1607—while I was practicing medicine in Salzwedel <note>original: "Soltquellæ"</note>—suffering from a long-term and total blockage of her periods, fell into abdominal pain with a blockage of the bowels. There followed a crushing sensation in the chest, heart palpitations, headache, swelling of the face, and the retention of stool for 11 days.

## THE RESOLUTION.

This patient begged for medical help on the 12th day. Although various symptoms were present, nevertheless, since they all seemed to have their origin in the long-term bowel obstruction, I immediately ordered a

<column-break/>

clyster <note>an enema</note>, but in vain; the patient would have sooner exchanged life for death than allow its use. Therefore, in place of that, the following potion—though unpleasant—was prescribed:

Take:
One handful of Mallow.
Two <term>drachms</term> <note>about 3.9 grams</note> of Marshmallow root.
One and a half drachms of Fenugreek seed.
Make a decoction in a sufficient quantity of water to 4 ounces.
Add one and a half drachms of <term>Galen's Simple Hiera</term> <note>original: "Spec. Hieræ simp. Gal."; Hiera Picra was a famous "holy bitter" purgative made of aloes and spices</note>.
Mix and let a draught be made.

Also: Three suppositories were employed to stimulate the bowel, so that the medicine she had taken might work more quickly.

By this method, that vehement bowel obstruction was opened quite copiously, and the girl herself gradually recovered from those most severe symptoms.

## OBSERVATION VII.

### The recognition and cure of menstrual blockage.

A young woman of 20 years, suffering from a chronic affliction, frequently complains of headache around the crown and the front part of the head, of a general weariness of the whole body, of a weakness of the stomach, of tightness in the chest, and other symptoms...

<header>ON DISEASES OF WOMEN.</header>
<sig>C 3</sig>

...is finished: almost every month there occurs an exacerbation of the mentioned symptoms, accompanied by pains in the lower abdomen and loins. The natural skin color is changed to a pale hue, and for the most part, the urine passed is quite crude <note>In Galenic medicine, "crude" (original: *cruda*) urine indicated that the body's "internal heat" had not properly "cooked" or processed the humors.</note>.

## THE ANALYSIS.

The present patient was affected by a menstrual obstruction contrary to nature due to thick and phlegmatic <note>original: *pituitosum*; referring to the humor of phlegm</note> blood obstructing the narrower veins of the uterus. This was the cause of the frequent flare-up of symptoms around the time of the menstrual flow, when the "peccant matter" <note>the harmful or diseased substance in the body</note> is otherwise stirred up and attempts to find an exit for itself. A headache was present due to the "sympathy" <note>an old medical concept where one organ's distress affects another via shared membranes or nerves</note> between the uterus and the brain regarding their membranes, especially around the crown and the frontal part, where the <term>dura mater</term> <note>original: *crassa meninx*; the tough outermost membrane surrounding the brain</note> is significantly folded. 

There was a weariness of the whole body because of the retained waste-like humors; a weakness of the stomach due to the humors surging back and hindering digestion; and pain in the lower abdomen and loins as the matter sought an exit and affected the sensitive parts. The natural color changed to pale because the blood of the entire body had been rendered more phlegmatic. Finally, the urine was mostly passed in a crude state because the "workshop of the blood" <note>original: *sanguinis officinam*; a reference to the liver, where Galenic medicine believed blood was produced</note> was infected by the retained phlegmatic waste.

<margin>Indications.</margin>
Regarding the treatment, the bowels had to be light-

<column-break/>

-ened <note>original: *alvus levanda*; meaning to relieve constipation or soften the stool</note>, the peccant matter had to be prepared, and the menses were to be moved through appropriate remedies, while not neglecting those things which assist the weaker parts.

For this reason, a <term>lenitive</term> <note>a mild laxative</note> was first ordered, followed by "digestion" <note>the process of thinning or preparing humors for evacuation</note> through the frequent use of a decoction of <term>aperient</term> <note>opening</note> roots and "cutting" <note>substances that break up thick fluids</note> and warming herbs, along with other appropriate items. Finally, with a suitable purging, the "second region" <note>the liver and vascular system</note> was also assisted. 

<margin>Concerning Thermal Baths.</margin> 
Once these things were completed, the use of the Wiesbaden thermal baths (to which she was nearby at that time) was granted. By these, she perfectly recovered her health, as these baths are rightly credited with the powers of warming, resolving <note>dissolving or dispersing morbid matter</note>, and cleansing.

## OBSERVATION VIII.

### Excessive Menstruation.

An honorable woman, who had been sterile for 40 years—the wife of Master Ludovicus Wagner, Pastor of Holzhausen in Hesse—complained to me on October 20, 1619, regarding excessive menstruation <note>original: *superfluo menstruo*</note>. Vertigo threatened as soon as her head became cold; crushing pains haunted the region of the heart; and she was subject to obstructions of the bowels...

# THE ANALYSIS

**A**mong the various causes that are accustomed to excite excessive menstruation in women, two things especially came to be considered in this case: namely, a sharper blood <note>original: *sanguis acrior*; blood that is too "hot" or acidic</note>, greatly diluted by a copious and crude watery fluid <note>original: *sero*; serum or whey-like humor</note>, and a uterine substance that is too loose, making it quite unfit for retention. For this reason, the patient was sterile, as the female parts were overflowing with continuous moisture and were therefore unfit for conception. Dizziness <note>original: *vertigo*</note> looms as soon as the head is cooled, caused by a weakened heat, and by the "sympathy" of the uterus occurring alongside the weakness of the head. Compressive pains haunt the region of the heart, because the "internal heat" in the <term>hypochondria</term> <note>the upper abdomen, just below the ribs</note> is daily dissolved by frequent hemorrhages; consequently, superfluous crude humors collect there, producing gas and belching. She is prone to obstructions of the bowels, as the watery and serous fluids are diverted elsewhere; thus, the drier waste matter of the "first digestion" is forced to linger longer in the folds and windings of the intestines. She passes sandy and crude urine, both because of an impaired "second digestion" <note>the stage of digestion where food is turned into blood</note> which processes the blood imperfectly, and because the kidneys, being also weaker, more readily receive the impure, tartareous <note>original: *tartareum*; referring to stony or gritty deposits</note> serum.

<column-break/>

<margin>The Indication</margin>
Here we thought this should be addressed: 1. that by first using universal remedies, we might prevent the production of sharp and serous blood; and 2. that we might strengthen the weakened uterus.

Regarding the first point, we established a universal evacuation using a laxative <term>hydromel</term> <note>a medicinal drink made of honey and water</note>, as follows:

Take: 
Roots of Elecampane and Orris, 1 ½ ounces of each.
Peony, 2 ounces.
Senna leaves, 1 ounce.
Mechoacan root and Larch Agaric, 1 ½ ounces of each.
Elderberry tips collected in Spring, 6 drams.
Herbs: Lemon Balm, Lesser Centaury, and Blessed Thistle, half a handful of each.
Elderflowers, 2 pinches.
Safflower seeds, 2 drams.
Red chickpeas, 1 ½ drams.
Fennel, ½ dram.
Sassafras, 1 scruple.
Galangal, 1 scruple.
Small raisins, 6 ounces.

Make an infusion in 3 pounds of hydromel. Let them boil once and let them sit in infusion in a warm place for 24 hours. Take half a pound of this on an empty stomach for several days. After this, we judged that the abundance of sharp watery fluids should be dispersed through suitable sweating; for this reason, we prescribed the following <term>electuary</term> <note>a medicinal paste made with honey or syrup</note>.

Take: 
Elderberry Rob <note>a thickened fruit juice</note>, 1 ½ ounces.
Confection of Rosemary and Lemon Balm, ½ ounce of each.
Syrup of Juniper berries, as much as suffices.
Mix to make an electuary, of which 1 ½ drams should be taken on an empty stomach with ½ ounce of Water.

## OBSERVATION IX

### Recognition and Cure of the 
### Suffocation of the
### Womb.

An honorable woman, the wife of *Johann Hartmann at the Wood-Mill near Giessen*, a woman of a bad humoral disposition <term>cacochymic: a state where the bodily fluids, or humors, are unhealthy or unbalanced</term> and failing in her dietary habits, suddenly collapsed in the spring of the year *1610*. She complained of pains in the abdomen, and her breathing was so obstructed that she appeared to be suffocating; her external limbs were somewhat convulsed, her voice failed, and she lay as if stunned, without sensation or movement. As the seizure <note>original: *paroxysmo*</note> waned, she felt griping pains in the abdomen, stomach pain, nausea, and a futile attempt to vomit. On the second day, after she had endured several such seizures, she begged for medical assistance.

---

### ANALYSIS.

<margin>
Determination of the disease.
</margin>
Having been called to this patient and inquiring into the nature of the illness, I was informed both by her husband and

<column-break/>

by those standing by that the patient had been affected by epileptic attacks several times. However, having considered the listed signs, I concluded that she was suffering more from *suffocation of the Womb* <note>original: *suffocatione Matricis*; also historically called hysteria</note>, especially since, when I questioned her, she reported that during the attacks, although she was almost completely suffocated, she observed everything that the bystanders attempted—something that cannot happen in epilepsy <note>where the patient typically loses consciousness and memory of the event</note>. I was confirmed in my assertion by the nature of the suffering subject: she had been quite fertile in her first marriage but was now sterile, which led to a suspicion of corrupt, retained seminal matter <note>referring to the early medical theory that retained reproductive fluids could putrefy and cause disease</note>. Furthermore, it was springtime, a season in which such corrupt matters "seethe" or boil up, and the other listed symptoms were present which typically happen to those suffering from strangulation of the womb. *For she suddenly collapsed*, the origin of her nerves being affected by poisonous exhalations <note>original: *venenatas exhalationes*</note> that affect her by their specific property, as *Leonardo Giachini* <note>original: *Iachinus*</note> notes in his commentary on the 9th book of *Al-Razi* <note>original: *Rhasis*</note>. She feels abdominal pains at the start of the seizure because of the disordered movement of the womb, by which nature tries to expel the harm of the stirred-up corrupt matter. *With her breathing cut off, she seems to be suffocated*, not because the womb itself is carried upward and blocks the air passages <note>a reference to the ancient "wandering womb" theory, which the author is here refining</note>, but because foul vapors rising to the brain block the free access of the animal spirits <note>the subtle substances then believed to transmit sensation and motion through the nerves</note> to the organs of respiration, as witnessed by *Mercato* in book 2, chapter 3 of *On the Diseases of Women*. From this also...

### OBSERVATION X.

### Various symptoms in a pregnant woman.

A most noble lady, wife of the most noble Lord Victor von Bülow in Gartow <note>original: *Victor à Bülaw in Garthaw*</note>, about 30 years of age and the mother of several children, possessed a choleric constitution <note>in the theory of the four humors, a "choleric" person was thought to be hot and dry, prone to anger and digestive heat</note>. When she had been pregnant for about three months, in the summer of the year 1607, she began to suffer first from stubborn obstructions of the bowels, soon followed by nausea of the stomach, vomiting, palpitations of the heart, kidney pains, <term>suffocation of the womb</term> <note>a condition where the uterus was believed to move or exert pressure upward, causing respiratory distress and anxiety</note>, thirst, and painful vapors rising

<column-break/>

to the head, discharges <note>original: *defluxiones*; catarrh or fluids moving through the body</note> to the chest, a cough and spitting of phlegm, along with a total exhaustion of her strength.

# ON THE DISEASES OF WOMEN.

When such obstructions occur, the waste-like bile and other harmful humors—which nature normally separates daily through the movements of the bowels—are transferred elsewhere. It is no wonder, then, that kidney pains <note>original: *nephritici dolores*</note> arise, as the aforementioned harmful matter is distributed to the urinary pathways. This was evidenced by the *turbid, thick, and dark urine*. Likewise, the <term>suffocation of the womb</term> <note>original: *suffocatio matricis*; a historical term for a condition where the uterus was thought to press against other organs, causing respiratory distress or anxiety</note> occurred because the blood boiled around the veins of the uterus for the same reason—especially since a large amount of blood had already collected there due to the conception and the subsequent pause in monthly cycles. There was also a great *thirst*, caused by the boiling of the bile and an increased hot imbalance <note>original: *intemperie calidâ*</note> of the digestive organs. For this reason, painful vapors also affected the head; once these exhalations condensed and were released there, they flowed down to the chest. This could not help but provoke *coughing* and *coughing up phlegm*, along with a total loss of strength, as the free movement of the spirits and the blood seemed almost to be stifled.

<margin>The Plan</margin>
Having considered these things, I decided that we must look to these goals: *1. That the hot and dry imbalance be altered as much as possible across the whole body; 2. That the daily obstruction of the bowels be corrected; 3. That the weakened digestive organs be strengthened; 4. Finally, that the more serious symptoms not be neglected, especially for the sake of the fetus.* Therefore, having arranged a suitable regimen of the <term>six non-natural things</term> <note>the "six non-naturals" were the core of Galenic lifestyle medicine: air, food/drink, sleep/waking, motion/rest, excretion/retention, and passions of the mind</note>, we ensured that the surrounding air

<column-break/>

was not excessively hot (or was at least corrected), that the *food* was easy to digest and possessed the power to moisten rather than dry the body, and that the *drink* was laxative and easy on the digestion—neither increasing raw humors nor producing inflammation of the internal organs. We also advised that violent *movements of the mind and body*, which stir up the bile and worsen the blood, should be avoided, and so on.

<margin>Regarding point 1.</margin>
*According to the first goal*, I prescribed a decoction of Chicory Root with Raisins in meat broth, and a decoction of chicken that had first been stuffed with Rose Conserve. I also ordered the use of the following Electuary <note>a medicinal paste</note>:
> ℞. *Rose Conserve.*
> *Lemon Balm. ½ oz. of each.*
> *Pickled Lettuce Stalks. 1 oz.*
> *Pickled Citron Peel. 2 drachms.*
> *Pickled Orange Flowers. 6 drachms.*
> *Powder of Diarrhodon Abbatis <note>a cooling rose-based spice blend</note>. 1 drachm.*
> *Citron Juice, as much as is sufficient to make an Electuary.*

In addition to these, she frequently drank the following decoction for the sake of quenching her thirst:
> ℞. *Hulled Barley. 1 ½ oz.*
> *Mallow Seed.*
> *Marshmallow Seed. 2 drachms of each.*
> *Red Chickpeas. 2 drachms.*
> *The four major cold seeds <note>seeds of cucumber, melon, pumpkin, and gourd, used to cool the body</note>. 2 drachms of each.*
> *Fat Figs. Number 9.*
> *Scraped Licorice Root. 6 drachms.*
> Let a decoction be made in a sufficient quantity of water, down to 3 pounds.
> Near the end of the boiling, add:
> *Fresh Sorrel herb.*
> *Beet. 2 handfuls of each.*

# OBSERVATION XI.

## Concerning the lack of milk in a woman who has recently given birth.

# THE CASE

## Proposed through letters by the Reverend and most Renowned MAN N. N.

<margin>Serious uterine hemorrhage after a difficult birth.</margin>
Greetings. Most Renowned and Excellent Man, honored godfather and kinsman: since for more than two months after a laborious birth of twins, my wife has suffered from a lack of milk, I did not want to neglect to propose this case to you with its circumstances, and to implore your healing help. On the 20th of September of the current year, my aforementioned wife gave birth to twin daughters by the blessing of God; during this difficult birth, such a huge amount of blood was lost that her natural heat <note>the vital warmth believed in early medicine to drive all bodily functions</note> was so entirely dissipated that she was like one dying, so that even for her

<column-break/>

external parts and her whole body, heated linens were scarcely sufficient to warm her. This remarkable hemorrhage was followed by weakness of the whole body, headache, feverish heat, loss of appetite, and a sense of taste that was almost abolished. As these most serious accidents subsided by the grace of God, her appetite for food and drink returned over four weeks, yet the lack of milk still persists. For although she not only puts the little daughters to the breast to help the generation of milk, but even arranges for suction by a female assistant <note>likely a woman hired to help draw the milk manually or by nursing</note>, nothing follows, while the breasts remain flaccid. Since this is the case, we greatly ask that you, most Renowned Godfather, do not fail us with your counsel; in turn, we promise our most ready services to you at all times, and commend you and all your family to God, the best and greatest. November 16, 1623.

---

## Of MR. GREGOR HORST to the preceding case.

Greetings. For the service of Christian charity performed, Reverend and most Renowned Man, patron...

# ON THE DISEASES OF WOMEN.

<margin>The cause of the lack of milk in this case.</margin>
My most honored godfather and kinsman, there is no need for you to give thanks: may God the best and greatest grant that your twin daughters grow by divine blessing and be raised in piety and virtue, so that one day you may see them joined in marriage, and even see twin sons born to them in a long succession. Regarding the condition of your most beloved wife, I gather from the description of the circumstances that this lack of milk had its origin in an immoderate evacuation <note>excessive loss of bodily fluids, in this case, blood</note>. This occurred because a huge quantity of blood was lost during the birth—undoubtedly, as you write, due to the rupture of the more significant veins of the uterus. It was so severely drained that, through the dissipation of the spirits and the heat <note>the 'vital spirits' and 'natural heat' were believed to be the essential energies that powered the body's functions</note>, the entire body appeared utterly bloodless and half-dead. This was followed by other symptoms which usually follow injuries to the heat and spirits. Although later the headache, preternatural heat <note>fever</note>, loss of appetite, and general exhaustion subsided, and her strength was somewhat restored as her appetite for food returned, you nevertheless write that a lack of milk remains, and that frequent attempts at suckling have been instituted in vain, with the breasts themselves remaining flaccid. You wish to know from me whether your most beloved wife, and consequently the twins who are in need of a supply of milk, can be helped by some means to procure the generation of milk? To this I briefly re-

<column-break/>

<margin>Response to the proposed question.</margin>
-spond that nothing at all can be hoped for here unless the total depletion, caused by the preceding hemorrhage, is first abundantly restored through a suitable dietary regimen. This is because nature does not grant any blood for the generation of milk except for that which is superabundant <note>early medicine taught that milk was refined from 'extra' blood not needed for the mother's own survival</note>, since the nourishment of all the body's parts is prior to the generation of milk in terms of preserving the individual. Therefore, first, let the foods be of good juice <note>term: <term>good juice</term> (Latin: *boni succi*), referring to foods that produce healthy, nutritious blood</note> and well-nourishing: 

<margin>Dietary regimen for a lack of milk.</margin>
white bread, fresh soft-boiled eggs, beer broths with egg yolks, gruels made with fresh milk and wheat flour prepared with sugar and egg yolks, and the meat of wethers <note>castrated rams</note>, lambs, hens, and capons; panadas <note>bread soups</note> with a decoction of hulled barley, rice cooked with milk, almond-milk preparations, etc. For drink, let there be well-clarified beer which has lost the bitterness of the hops through proper fermentation; also a light wine seasoned with raisins. Let there also be frequent use of the roots of the domestic parsnip, boiled until soft with mutton broth (on this matter, see *Galen, Book 5 on Simple Medicines*, or among the more recent authors, *Varandæus, Treatise on the Diseases of Women, Chapter 10*). Assuming that the restoration of the whole body can be conveniently achieved in this way, it is necessary that we look further ahead to whether a superabundant supply of blood might, in turn, return to the breasts in its own time—namely, in the 3rd month after birth.

He prescribes a restorative diet of eggs, broths, and specific meats to replenish her strength before milk production can be expected.</summary>

be sent back to the breasts, especially since you write that the breasts are tried in vain by suckling, and that their substance is entirely flaccid. But truly, since a supply of milk-producing matter is not enough on its own, but the <term>milk-making power</term> <note>original Greek: galaktopoiētike</note>—which follows the appropriate and natural condition of the breasts—is necessarily required, I do not see what can be hoped for regarding the restoration of milk. The only exception might be if, perhaps through daily rubbing with rough cloths and through fomentation <note>applying warm, moist substances to the body</note> with new sponges soaked in warm water, the veins of the breasts might be dilated in turn and rendered more capable of attracting blood. This is how the shepherds of Mount Oeta, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>, used to provoke milk even from virgin goats; see on this our treatment of milk production in Book 1 *On Human Nature*. However, I strongly doubt whether the conjugal embrace <note>sexual intercourse</note> can promote surplus blood to the breasts (which are currently less capable for the reasons mentioned) rather than to the womb. For this reason, once the monthly cycles reappear, the generation of milk will be hoped for in vain, as nature cannot be forced. As for <term>milk-promoting medicines</term> <note>original Greek: gala thrōskonta</note>, they are of two different kinds: namely, they either convert colder juices into blood—and consequently into milk—by moderate heat, or they increase the milk by a suitable moisture through a similarity of substance. For a

<column-break/>

further determination of these, see our *Pharmaceutical Exercises*, decade 4, thesis 8. These are the things, honored Godfather, which I wished to answer; take them in good part, and continue to love your Horst as you do. Written in haste at Ulm, December 3, 1623.

### OBSERVATION XII.

Just as it is common knowledge to everyone that, according to the author Hippocrates, an "Iliad of evils" <note>a classical expression meaning a vast series of troubles</note> can emerge from the suppression of menstrual blood, so no less evils arise from its excessive evacuation. A certain honest matron, a widow in her sixties, experienced this very thing in her own case; for two years and more, she was troubled by a quite distressing hemorrhage <note>excessive bleeding</note> of the womb, along with a great

below the navel, the size of a human head, a tumor with a heavy feeling of weight. This matron, since she would take no medicine by mouth, called no physician for that reason out of shame, but by using her own familiar remedies to stop this bleeding <note>original: "hæmorrhagiam"</note>, she incurred the greatest danger to her life. Finally, when she realized from her own well-tested strength that this condition would not cease of its own accord or without a doctor's hands, but was instead taking deeper roots, at the persuasion of certain friends, she called me to her for counsel and committed the care of her body to my faith. Having made a prognosis with her based on the patient's reports, I immediately told her that this bleeding threatened her with imminent death; and if life were dear to her, and she wished to avoid the danger of <term>dropsy</term> <note>a historical term for swelling caused by excess fluid, now called edema</note>, into which such cases usually end over time, she must be helped by timely medicines. Nor did my prediction fail me: for after a short time, her feet and belly swelled to a massive size. Therefore, so as not to leave her entirely to my predictions, I prescribed both external treatment to soften and disperse the hardness of the tumor—since I believed it to consist of mixed <term>gases</term> <note>original: "flatibus"; in early medicine, "wind" trapped in the body was believed to cause various swellings and pains</note>—and internal treatment to stop the blood. After she used these for four days, she obtained the greatest benefit from their use:

<column-break/>

for the tumor vanished somewhat, and the bleeding was suppressed for a time. But after no long interval of days—which truly is not without cause for wonder—a piece of flesh, resembling the appearance of a large ox's spleen in both color and length, with many small veins and membranes like tendons interspersed here and there, was expelled through the womb. <margin>A putrid fleshy piece expelled from the womb.</margin> When I cut through this piece of flesh with a knife, such a heavy stench exhaled as if from the <term>Lake of Avernus</term> <note>a volcanic crater lake in Italy believed by the Romans to be the entrance to the Underworld; used here to describe a hellish or sulfurous smell</note>, which struck both my nostrils and those of the bystanders, so that they were forced to flee far from me against their will. Although the aforementioned tumor had subsided somewhat, nevertheless, a few days later it began to grow anew, and as it rolled from side to side it caused her the greatest agonies, which lasted until the final day of her life, when she died of dropsy.

# BOOK I. PART II.

<columns>2</columns>

A woman aged about forty-five years, who was suffering from the most cruel pains of the <term>rectum</term> <note>original: "intestini recti"</note>, such that she could neither sit comfortably nor even sleep on her back, called me to her for counsel. Having first made a prognosis with her regarding the pain, I immediately ordered an <term>enema</term> <note>original: "clysterem"</note> of milk and a decoction of flaxseed to be administered, both to soothe the pain and to temper the <term>humors</term> <note>in early medicine, bodily fluids believed to cause illness if they became too "sharp" or "acrid"</note>, should any particularly sharp ones be clinging to the intestines. After this was administered, a short time later, she expelled—with the greatest agony—fish scales and spines, henbane seeds <note>original: "semen hyoscyami", a plant often used as a sedative but highly toxic</note>, small pieces of wood, and stone shavings; also, what is truly worthy of wonder, a piece of sheepskin, still covered with wool, exceeding half the size of a hand. I saw all these things with my own eyes, and handled them with my hands after they were cleaned of the feces. Although this woman expelled these preternatural objects, her pains nonetheless did not vanish; rather, treating this wretched woman miserably day and night, and gradually consuming her strength, they brought about a swift death.

# OBSERVATION XV.

->Lethal bleeding of the gums<-
->in a pregnant woman, with<-
->subsequent red spots and<-
->bloody sweat.<-

A respectable young woman, the wife of a pastor in the neighborhood, seven months pregnant, fell ill in the month of May in the year 1624. She suffered a sudden hemorrhage from the gums, with blood flowing out in great bursts, day and night, for three continuous weeks. It flowed in such quantity that it could have filled several large vessels; thus, the most immediate danger hung not only over the mother but also over the fetus. At last, from head to heel, blood-colored spots <note>likely petechiae or purpura, which are small purple or red spots caused by bleeding under the skin</note> appeared. When she attempted to dispel these with a sweating-bath, a bloody sweat <note>a rare condition known as hematidrosis, where blood seeps through the skin</note> broke out, especially around the upper part of the body in those places where the blood-spots had previously shown themselves. This sweat later appeared with such force...

# BOOK I. PART II.

<columns>2</columns>

...a collapse of all her faculties followed, so that a few days later she exchanged her life for death.

### ANALYSIS.

<margin>A similar observation</margin>
When this singular case was described in a letter from the husband of the aforementioned woman on June 17, 1624, I immediately recalled a certain fatal hemorrhage of a respectable matron, the wife of a Professor at Giessen <note>a prominent university town in Germany</note>. In the year 1622, at the beginning of March, she was suffering from a continuous fever. Although she was freed from this through the application of suitable remedies, around the time her monthly period was due at the start of April, she fell into a most severe hemorrhage from the nostrils. This was followed by a continuous secretion of blood through the gums, which continued in such great quantity for four days that finally—after a bloody flux of the bowels also occurred—her strength was exhausted, and on April 8th she paid her debt to nature <note>a common euphemism for dying</note>. 

In this case, there was a lean constitution of the body, naturally disposed to the collection of "sharp" blood <note>early medicine classified humors as 'sharp' or 'acrid' if they caused irritation or eroded tissues</note>. This condition had been greatly increased by the "scorching" <note>original: "adustione"; the theoretical overheating of bodily humors</note> of the preceding fever. Consequently, due to the weakness left behind by the previous illness, the sharp blood—diluted with much serum—turned upward instead of following the usual path of menstrual evacuation through the uterus (perhaps because the paths there were blocked by the remains of the offending matter). It then flowed out symptomatically through the nose and gums. 

<column-break/>

Although Dodonaeus <note>Rembert Dodoens (1517–1585), a famous Flemish physician and botanist</note> writes in his *Observations*, chapter 15, of a certain eighteen-year-old girl whose periods were not occurring, he notes that the nature of the body attempted to expel the superfluous blood through the corners of the eyes as continuous bloody tears, and in others through the gums. In those cases, the outcome was healthy, just as we noted various other modes of expulsion at the end of Observation 3. 

However, a distinction must be made: in those instances, such an event occurs while the strength of "nature" <note>the body's internal healing force</note> is still present. This was lacking in our current patient, whose natural powers had been shattered by the preceding disease. The case of that pregnant woman seemed truly similar to us; in her, the absence of periods was quite correct because she was carrying a child in her womb, yet a symptomatic hemorrhage of such magnitude came upon her through the gums. 

This happened because of an unnatural constitution of sharp, serous, and watery blood. On account of this, not only was a weakness of all powers introduced (since adequate nutrition and restoration were denied to the body), but furthermore, the "mouths" of the veins <note>original: "osculis," referring to the theoretical openings of blood vessels</note> were forced open by the sharp, watery moisture. Thus, an unnatural excretion occurred in the gums, as they are softer parts and otherwise disposed to bleeding. 

<margin>Copious flow from the gums without harm.</margin>
An example of this is recorded by Marcellus Donatus in Book 4 of *Wonderful Histories*, chapter 9, citing Matthaeus de Grado. He describes a certain nun who—not from an abundance of humors, nor from any violent cause—began to bleed from everywhere: through her spit, through her nose...

# ON THE DISEASES OF WOMEN
E 3
<meta>catchword: acrimony</meta>

<columns>
...due to the severity of the [acrimony] of the fluids, someone observed a discharge of blood through the urine amounting to 18 pounds, even though the woman was by nature slender, thin, and phlegmatic <note>one of the four humors, associated with a cool and moist temperament</note>. He says, however, that she was saved from death by a narcotic. Indeed, Marcellus <note>Marcellus Donatus, a 16th-century physician</note> himself testifies that for a certain blacksmith with a diseased spleen, more than eight pounds of blood were evacuated through a small vein in the gums within the space of a single natural day; this occurs in those where blood diluted with sharp serum is abundant. 

Therefore, given the aforementioned danger, we would have advised in vain those remedies which might soothe the "swelling" <note>original: *ὀργασμὸν* (orgasmòn); a state of medical excitement or rushing of the humors</note> of the effervescing blood, temper its sharpness, and strengthen the patient's nature—especially since a very rare symptom, namely a bloody sweat, appeared along with a total failure of strength. 

As for the cause of the observed bloody sweat, Rondeletius <note>Guillaume Rondelet, a prominent French physician</note>, in his book *On the Diagnosis of Diseases*, chapter 11, refers the cause in a certain student to the thinness of the veins, the laxity of their openings, and the thinness of the blood. 

<margin>
The cause of 
bloody sweat.
</margin>

Aristotle, however, in *On the Parts of Animals*, Book 3, Chapter 5, and *History of Animals*, Book 3, Chapter 19, says that a "bloody sweat" <note>original: *ἐξίδρωμα αἱματῶδες* (exidrōma haimatōdes)</note> happens to some because of a corrupted state of the body—specifically when the body is loose and leaky, and also because the blood, due to a lack of internal heat, becomes watery and (as the latter passage says) "becomes like serum" <note>original: *γίνεται ἰχωροειδὴς* (ginetai ichōroeidēs)</note>, almost like whey. So here too, we conclude that this dangerous occurrence was produced first by the thinness and wateriness of the blood (caused by a weakness of bodily heat), as well as by the laxity of the skin and its pores, and finally

<column-break/>

by a weakness of the "retentive faculty" <note>the biological power believed to keep fluids within their proper vessels</note>. Consequently, because suitable remedies were neglected from the start—and because measures were even applied that increased the intensity of the disease (among which was a sweat-inducing bath)—a fatal outcome followed.

## CASE STUDY XVII.

### Joint pains and convulsions in a woman after childbirth.

A respectable woman, the wife of a schoolmaster in the village of Lützellinden near Giessen, in August of the year 1617, when she was in her fourth week after childbirth, was afflicted with *joint pains and also convulsive movements of the external parts*. Since an incomplete purging after birth <note>original: "puerperij purgatio"; refers to the lochia, the normal discharge after delivery</note> had preceded this, I judged that we must labor toward first removing the *bad humors* <term>cacochymia; an unhealthy state of the body’s fluids</term>. For this reason, because of her weakened strength, I decided she should be purged gradually, immediately ordering a *laxative wine*. Half of this, before the infusion is made, should be diluted with a decoction of chicory roots. After using this for eight days, a *sweat* should be provoked by a drink of speedwell water, to which is added 1 dram of Theriac <term>a complex herbal "universal" antidote and restorative</term> and half a dram of spirit of Dwarf Elder <note>original: "spiritus Ebuli"</note>. This is to be repeated for three days. Once the sweat is achieved, the *extremities* should be rubbed with wine from a decoction of sage and lemon balm, or "swallow water" <note>original: "aq. hirund."; a traditional distillation involving young swallows, used for nerve disorders</note> distilled with Castoreum <note>a secretion from beaver glands used for nervous ailments</note>, as well as those external

<column-break/>

means which are otherwise frequently used in "false paralysis" <note>original: "paralysi spuria"</note> following the pains of colic.

### OBSERVATION XIX.

## Pains of the back, loins, and upper abdomen after childbirth.

A young wife, about 25 years of age and of a sanguine constitution <term>a temperament traditionally associated with an abundance of blood, resulting in a ruddy complexion and energetic personality</term>, after her first labor,

<column-break/>

on January 2, 1617, complained of continuous pain in her back and loins. Although she was said to have been moderately purged during childbed <note>original: "in puerperio purgata"; referring to the lochia, the normal discharge of blood and tissue after birth</note>, it was nonetheless gathered from the continuation of the symptom that a quantity of impure blood remained. This manifested in those parts where the major vessels pass, so that in this way, pain arose around the back and loins. This occurred because, for the generation of milk, the more "praiseworthy" or healthy part of the blood was drawn to the breasts, while the remainder moved downward and introduced a state of bad humors <term>cacochymia; an unhealthy state of the body’s fluids</term> into the lower belly.

Therefore, in respect to this preceding cause, I prescribed a laxative bundle <note>original: "nodulum laxativum"; a small bag of herbs steeped in liquid</note> so that the superfluous collected matter might be led out little by little while she was nursing the infant. At the same time, cupping glasses with scarification <term>the practice of drawing blood to the surface using heated glass cups and making small incisions</term> were applied to the back and loins. These were applied to the aching part after a fomentation <note>a warm, moist medicinal compress</note> made from a decoction of sage in wine. Simultaneously, I ordered that a sweat be induced several times during the morning hours in bed, after she had first taken a small drink made of elderberry syrup <note>original: "Rob. sambucino"</note> with a little Mithridatum <term>a famous complex herbal "universal antidote" used here as a restorative</term> dissolved in speedwell water. Shortly after these treatments, she felt better.

However, a more severe and stubborn pain was felt in the left side around the region of the spleen in the wife of a coachman from Butzbach. Shortly after her labor, on February 3 of the same year, she was gravely afflicted due to matter left behind in the upper abdomen <term>hypochondria; the regions of the upper abdomen under the ribs</term> from an incomplete purging. In her case, the urine was being passed "raw" <note>original: "urina cruda"; urine that appears thin or lacks the typical signs of "digestion" or processing by the body's heat</note>, for which reason the matter first had to be concocted <note>matured or processed by the body's internal heat</note>...

## OBSERVATION XX.
### Cachexia after the carriage
### of a dead 
### fetus.

A woman of thirty years, from a respected family of the Imperial City of Dinkelsbühl, came here at the beginning of the year 1625 to seek medical advice. After carrying a fetus that had died in the womb, she fell in subsequent years into a weakness of the stomach accompanied by an unnatural thirst. This was followed by a swelling of the feet along with a chilling of the extremities and a convulsive tension in them. Sometimes a colicky pain, and soon after bloating, took hold of her, along with an onset of diar-

<column-break/>

rhea; furthermore, an ulceration of the breasts occurred.

## THE ANALYSIS.

It is certain that a fetus that has died in the womb, if it is neglected or unnoticed for too long, creates incurable damage to the mother. The present case provides us with an example of this, where a cachexia <note>a state of severe physical wasting and malnutrition</note> of the whole body was present. This was first manifested by a notable weakness of the stomach, along with an unnatural thirst, which was produced by "false fluids" <note>original: "serum falsum"; refers to degraded bodily humors</note> throughout the body due to the impaired digestion <note>original: "concoctionem"; the process of the liver refining nutrients</note> of the liver. The swelling of the feet occurred as the watery blood, which was less suitable for nutrition, descended toward the lower parts. This was accompanied by a chilling of the extremities because of the weakness of the "natural heat" <note>the vital warmth thought to be generated in the heart</note> in places further removed from the heart. A convulsive tension followed because the muscular parts, intended for free movement, were—contrary to nature—soaked with "raw vapors" instead of the purer "animal spirits" <note>the refined essence believed to travel through nerves to enable sensation and motion</note>. Sometimes colicky pain occurred, as the sharpness of the superfluous fluids irritated the sensitive parts; soon after, bloating followed, as the membranous parts of the intestines and the abdomen were unnaturally stretched. This was accompanied by an onset of diarrhea, in which nature finally overcame the offending matter and sent it away through the customary paths of urinary excretion. Of the breasts...

### OBSERVATION XXI.

### The afterbirth retained after delivery.

An honorable woman, the wife of a primary citizen, having a choleric constitution of body <note>meaning she was thought to have an excess of "yellow bile," leading to a warm and dry temperament</note> and prone to the "burning" of the humors and other hysterical incidents, gave birth in the year *1624, near the end of January*, to a small boy in the eighth month of gestation. The infant was entirely weak and died on the same day shortly after receiving holy baptism. The mother was in great danger due to a violent hemorrhage, with the afterbirth <note>original: "secundinis"; the placenta and membranes</note> remaining inside into the third day.

### THE RESOLUTION.

A fermentation <note>original Greek: ἐργασμὸς (ergasmos); a term used here to describe a violent "working up" or agitation of the blood and heat</note> of heat and blood produced this premature birth; this was indicated, among other things, by the violent hemorrhage, which introduced an extreme weakness in the laboring woman. From this it happened that the afterbirth was left behind, partly because it seemed still firmly attached to the womb, having been expelled before its natural time...

I believe this happened not so much because of the retained afterbirth, but by reason of the injury to the major arteries and veins, which discharged themselves internally into the cavity of the womb or the space between the organs of the lower belly, and in this way brought about the collapse of the vital faculty <note>the body's ability to maintain life</note>.

Around the middle of her pregnancy, she is seized by pains in the head, and especially in the eyes, with very troublesome flows to the throat and a lack of sleep, while at the same time a painful compression of the stomach afflicts her, which also very often [causes] distress**

->THE RESOLUTION<-

When this case was proposed to us by letter, we immediately gathered through skillful conjecture that there was a serious internal cause for this miscarriage, specifically because at that time of gestation, pregnant women do not normally miscarry easily. In fact, in this very month, they usually bear the necessary purgings <note>original: *purgationes*; likely referring to the body's natural cleaning or the discharge of fluids</note> without difficulty, according to the decree of Hippocrates.
<margin>*See Decade 9, Medical Problems, Question 7.*</margin>
Therefore, it is no wonder—*since such miscarriages are more serious to Hippocrates than full-term births*—that after the mother's nature was weakened by the preceding miscarriage, and a new conception occurred shortly thereafter, various symptoms arose. This was especially true around the middle of the pregnancy, when blood retained for too long introduced *cacochymia* <term>an imbalance of the bodily humors, literally "bad juices"</term>. This led to headache and eye pain, caused by the sharp vapors of blood seething in the larger vessels; it also caused flows <note>drainage or catarrh</note> to the throat, produced by the weakness of the head. Furthermore, there was a lack of sleep because the body was denied proper restorative material due to "rawness" <term>original: *cruditas*; a state where humors are undigested or poorly processed</term>, whereas the pleasant vapor of good digestion usually facilitates sleep. At the same time, she suffered from a painful compression of the stomach due to the remains of depraved digestion trapped in the folds of the stomach itself. It is also common in pregnant women for

<column-break/>

copious corrupt matter to seek the stomach, trigger nausea, and ruin the appetite. This more often brings about a tightening of the chest and difficulty in speaking, as the "spiritual organs" <note>the heart and lungs, which manage the *spiritus* or vital breath</note> are affected at once. When the vapors of this retained matter invade the "citadel of the heart," it is not uncommon in such cases for fainting and heart palpitations to occur.

<margin>*The Indications*</margin>
Here, *1. the "peccant matter" <term>the harmful or "sinning" excess humors causing the disease</term> indicated it needed to be removed; 2. the fetus in the womb required strengthening; 3. and various symptoms required correction.*

<margin>*Regarding the 1st.*</margin>
Regarding the first point, let a beginning be made with a mild clyster <term>an enema</term>, by which the lower parts of the abdomen may be washed out, so that a fuller evacuation can later be performed with less violence. Note, however, that clysters here must be injected in a smaller quantity than usual, lest some harm be brought upon the fetus by the intestines being too greatly distended. Once the bowels are opened and softened by the clyster, let the evacuation be carried out through a **Laxative Claret** <note>a medicated wine</note>, which is made as follows:

℟. <note>Recipe</note> *Senna leaves, 1 drachm.*
*Selected Rhubarb, 2 drachms.*

*Wormwood, of each, 1 pinch.*

*Anise, 1.5 scruples.*

*White wine, 6 pounds.*

## OBSERVATION XXIV.

->Severe uterine suffocation with loss of speech.<-

A young woman of 22 years, prone to <term>hysterical</term> <note>At the time, "hysteria" (from the Greek word for womb) was a catch-all term for various physical and emotional symptoms believed to be caused by the uterus moving or "suffocating" other organs.</note> conditions, suffered a severe <term>uterine suffocation</term> <note>A condition where the patient felt as though they were choking or could not breathe, attributed to the womb "rising" in the body.</note> toward the end of *February* in the previous year, **1627**, just as her menstrual period was approaching. This was followed by a loss of speech for three days.

## RESOLUTION.

Having been called at once, I prescribed those things which might correct the fit that was still distressing her, which I have described above. Once this was eased, the patient began to recover herself, though the impediment to her voice remained. Since the cause of the evil arose from a difficulty

<column-break/>

with her menstruation, I judged that efforts must immediately be directed toward correcting the origin of the symptoms. Therefore, after the primary passages were evacuated by means of an <term>enema</term>, I prescribed <term>hysterical pills</term> of the usual description so that the impending menstrual flow might be opened. As this broke through, I judged that the symptom of impaired speech must not be neglected. To this end, she not only frequently took *Antihysteric water with Cephalic Theriac* <note>Theriac was a complex, prestigious "cure-all" containing many ingredients; a "Cephalic" version was specifically tailored for head or brain disorders.</note>, but furthermore, she frequently chewed a medicinal paste in the quantity of 2 ounces. This was prepared as follows: *Take: Conserve of Rosemary 1 ounce. Old Mithridatium 1 ounce.* <note>Mithridatium was a famous semi-legendary tonic and antidote named after King Mithridates VI.</note> *Confection of Anacardium ½ ounce. Syrup of peony flowers, as much as suffices. Mix to make a preserve.* Once these were used and the menses were flowing correctly, her strength gradually returned. We then advised that whenever her period was about to begin, she should use a laxative wine to draw out phlegmatic and watery humors and assist nature by using the "hysterical pills" adapted for excretion.

<margin>*A similar, more severe observation.*</margin>
We noted a similar and far more severe and frequently recurring *Loss of Speech*, along with very heavy convulsions, in a certain high-born noblewoman in previous years. She had been sterile for several years and, at the onset of her menses, was seized first by a most severe uterine suffocation, then by mild <term>epilepsy</term>, and finally by terrifying partial convulsions of the arms, feet, *spine*, and the entire body.

<margin>
*Foul-smelling things are harmful to some hysterical patients.*
</margin>

## ANALYSIS

<margin>Definition of the maidenly disease.</margin>
**W**E stated that a most noble young lady was suffering from the <term>maiden’s disease</term> <note>Historically known as chlorosis or "green sickness," a form of anemia often attributed to the onset of puberty in young women.</note> on December 2, 1625. Its origin consists in the collection of a raw and <term>phlegmatic</term> <note>Relating to the humor of phlegm, which was considered cold, moist, and sluggish.</note> matter which accumulates around the stomach and its folds, and afterwards obstructs the vessels—otherwise quite narrow—of the <term>mesentery</term> <note>The membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall and contains blood vessels.</note> and other organs of the lower belly. From this, not only is the first <term>concoction</term> <note>The "cooking" or breaking down of food in the stomach.</note> of food corrupted, so that raw humors are increased daily through congestion, but even the distribution of <term>chyle</term> <note>The milky fluid produced from digested food before it is turned into blood.</note> is greatly hindered, and the <term>sanguification</term> <note>The biological process of blood-making.</note> itself is made worse. Consequently, not only the nutrition of the whole body but also its growth proceeds less than it should for her age. *No natural menstrual flow appears around the time of puberty*, insofar as the organs of digestion are everywhere overflowing with raw superfluities. Because of this, nature—being frequently burdened—*also rejects undigested food through vomiting*. When this food is retained, *compressive pain and gas* arise, because the <term>native heat</term> <note>The innate internal warmth believed to drive all metabolic processes.</note> is weakened and overwhelmed by the abundance of raw matter, and is insufficient to transform what has been consumed.

<column-break/>

*Spontaneous exhaustion is also frequently present*, due to the raw and phlegmatic blood received into the muscle tissue, which hinders the free and constant flow and return of the <term>animal spirits</term> <note>In early medicine, these were subtle fluids that traveled through the nerves to facilitate movement and sensation.</note>. In these cases, a *slight chill and momentary heat* are also observed, resulting from the struggle of the remaining native heat against the offending matter, when the movement of the flowing heat is affected by the abundance of raw juices. Just as the change of age usually serves to help correct this condition, so too this illness must not be entirely neglected, lest something worse follow in the meantime.

<margin>Indications.</margin>
*Therefore, the following must be addressed: 1. that the tenacious and viscous matter collected in the stomach and its folds, as well as in the mesenteric veins and neighboring parts, be digested, softened, and cleansed; 2. that the digested matter be evacuated in stages; 3. that the primary and secondary organs of concoction, being weak and chilled, be strengthened and warmed; 4. Finally, besides the use of medicines, a diet accommodated to the preceding goals should not be neglected.*

*Regarding the first goal*, let there be frequent use of *Mindererus’s opening syrup* <note>A medicinal preparation attributed to the physician Raymond Mindererus (1570–1621).</note>, *of which 1 ounce should be taken morning and evening, two hours before food on a fasting and empty stomach, either alone or mixed with the waters of lemon balm, <term>blessed thistle</term> <note>Cnicus benedictus, a plant widely used in the period as a tonic and digestive aid.</note>, or fumitory. Likewise, a digestive powder will be of great benefit here, which...*

->TO GREGORIUS HORSTIUS, Doctor.<-

Greetings. You know, most distinguished sir, for what purpose the most noble Matron so greatly desired the use of the wild hot springs <note>original: "thermarum ferinarum." These were natural mineral springs, often used in this period to treat infertility or "cold" disorders of the womb.</note>. But please accept, in a few words, the reason why she was forced to break off their continuation. Since she suspected she was pregnant due to the lack of menstrual flow and other signs, and her belly was immediately raised into an immense mass—not without subsequent distress and weakness—she immediately abstained from further use of the springs on the advice of the physicians present. You can therefore easily gather the cause of the symptoms! Without a doubt, because of a conception that had occurred previously, the powers of the springs in correct-

<column-break/>

-ing, drying, and strengthening the womb were not able to sufficiently exert themselves. Consequently, the thick and cold impurities were not enough consumed and dissipated, but were instead resolved into "winds" <note>original: "flatus." In early modern medicine, "wind" or gas was believed to be a byproduct of poorly digested or "cold" humors in the body.</note>, which produced such inconveniences as she still suffers from today. Otherwise, a "windy mole" <term>mola flatuosa</term> <note>A "mole" (mola) referred to a fleshy, non-viable mass in the uterus; a "windy" mole was a false pregnancy where the belly swelled with gas rather than a fetus.</note> is also sometimes known to be born, and a false pregnancy is produced, where the accidents and signs following a true impregnation concur at the same time. This happens when—on account of the crudeness and imperfection of both "seeds" <note>At this time, it was often believed both male and female contributed a "seed" to conception.</note>, or because of a cold <term>intemperies</term> <note>A humoral imbalance where one quality (like coldness) dominates an organ.</note> of the womb which destroys the woman's spirit, or due to a lack of proper blood if a crude humor flows in its place—the formative power <note>original: "facultas formatrix." The biological force believed to be responsible for shaping the embryo.</note> is imperfect or hindered. It does not perfectly work the material of generation, but turns it into winds or waters, whence the belly then swells and the other indications of pregnancy follow. I have, however, not rarely seen such swelling of the belly and a windy mole (if I may call it so) joined with a true conception, which brings the greatest difficulties and usually precedes a miscarriage. Lest that happen here, since I have almost no doubt regarding a true pregnancy, I have prescribed those things which help to consume and discuss <note>To "discuss" a humor meant to break it up and disperse it.</note> the winds and moisture, and at the same time strengthen the womb and retain the fetus within it by a moderate <term>astriction</term> <note>The use of tightening or "binding" medicines to prevent the womb from releasing the fetus prematurely.</note>. These include a *Strengthening conserve with oil of anise, Embryo Balsam with anise water, etc.* and externally a "shield" or *Plaster of Ladanum* <note>original: "Emplastrum ex Ladano." Ladanum (or Labdanum) is a sticky resin from the Rockrose plant, used in plasters to warm and "fix" the womb.</note>.
