# OBSERVATION XXX.

## A severe asthmatic condition in a hysterical woman.

->*The Distinguished and Excellent*<-

->*Master Johann Christoph Eisenmenger,*<-
->*Doctor of Medicine and*<-
->*Ordinary Physician of the*<-
->*Republic of Heilbronn,*<-

->TO GREGOR HORSTIUS, Doctor.<-

Most Distinguished and Excellent Doctor, etc. There lives among us a certain noblewoman who has been afflicted by a certain chronic condition,

<column-break/>

for the sake of overcoming which she has used various medications prescribed by me for many years, though without the desired success of lasting health. At length, I was led—nearly a year ago in the month of August—to record the entire history of this illness at greater length, to be submitted to the more expert judgments of other physicians. However, because she did not feel worse through the following winter but began to improve, she stopped sending that record elsewhere. But when, in recent days, the ailment flared up again with nighttime tightness in the chest and its usual symptoms, with a somewhat increasing and pressing effort and labor of coughing, she and her husband requested that I present the case, detailed in all its circumstances, to Your Excellence. They ask that you would not find it burdensome to open your mind and counsel to me in writing regarding what and of what sort this condition is, or what is to be hoped for or done. Especially, they ask whether the Hot Springs of Zell or rather the Baths of Baden <note>The "Baden" mentioned here likely refers to the famous mineral springs of Baden-Baden or Baden in Switzerland, often used for "cold" ailments.</note> might be of benefit and health to her this summer—due to the actual coldness of the brain which she feels—since at other times, upon entering the baths, she is always accustomed to feel worse because of the symptoms attacking more severely. This kind of service she and her husband will honorably repay, not without the highest expression of gratitude and the due fee for your labors, with me acting as their representative.

BOOK I. PART II.

### Case presented, translated from German.

<columns>
A certain woman, about thirty-eight years of age, possessed a praiseworthy temperament—as is evident from her bodily functions, the graceful shape of her limbs, and the lively color of her face—and while in the flower of her youth, she was of a sanguine <note>original: "sanguineo"; in the medical theory of the time, a 'sanguine' temperament was associated with an abundance of blood, resulting in a healthy, energetic, and optimistic disposition</note> nature. Twelve years ago, she married a certain widower; a year and a half later, she gave birth to a small son, whom she lost to an untimely death after only ten weeks. Shortly thereafter, consumed by grief, she fell into an epidemic fever <note>original: "febrem Epidemialem"</note> which was then spreading lethally through the neighboring regions and which she greatly dreaded. For six weeks she was tossed and tormented by this fever, at great risk to her life, until at last, by the breathing of divine grace, she was freed from it. It happened, however,
<margin>the occasion of the illness.</margin>
that because her physician at the time feared a serious relapse, he forbade her from drinking wine—which she was then demanding quite eagerly, contrary to her usual habit—until her health was fully restored. Instead, he allowed her to drink nothing but barley water, prepared without any other additions, for the sake of quenching her thirst. Consequently, she contracted a notable weakness of the stomach and indigestion <note>original: "dyspepsiam"</note>,

<column-break/>

and experienced a sensible change in her entire temperament. From this, in the course of time, fluxions <term>fluxion: the movement of excess bodily fluids or "humors" from one area to another</term> gathered in her whole body and head in such a way that, during the night, they would rush in a heap into the stomach after her first sleep, frequently provoking bouts of vomiting. Sometimes these fluids settled in the chest,
<margin>Nighttime asthma.</margin>
producing distress and difficulty in breathing; however, all these symptoms would cease immediately after the vomiting and sleep. Although the medicinal hot springs were proposed to her as a remedy shortly after the first onset of this evil, she neglected them for several years. Finally, however, as the condition became more urgent, she used the nearby springs at Leonstein under her own roof for two successive summers, and in the following third year, she went to the springs at Zell. Yet the use of all these waters brought her either nothing or certainly very little toward a lasting recovery of her health. Two years ago, the previous attacks began to worsen during the night after she first lay down; she was suddenly seized by such distress in the chest and difficulty in breathing that she could not remain in bed. Indeed, drawing her breath with her neck held straight, she narrowly escaped the danger of suffocation with great effort, a rattling sound <note>original: "stertore"</note>, and a dry cough—though her mind remained unimpaired. During this attack, she was troubled by a pain with actual coldness beneath the skull around the crown of the head, and a pressure of the hands

This condition has worsened; even now that her menstrual purgings are completed, the paroxysms <note>original: "paroxysmis"; periodic attacks or fits of a disease</note> often invade repeatedly at night, usually when she first lies down, as was said above. When these attacks subside, she has no other complaint except for a weariness of the limbs, and in these most recent years, a compression of the chest, so that the patient is almost forced to squeeze out her breath with the greatest labor and not without a whistling sound. And if the fuel and occasion <note>In Galenic medicine, the "fomes" or "fuel" refers to the underlying material cause of a disease</note> of these occurrences is investigated, she says she perceives no discomfort in the lower belly; for that reason, she cannot affirm with certainty (since the affliction attacks her while she is sleeping) whether something ascends from the lower parts or whether it instead falls from above into the parts below. The invasion itself, mostly around evening time, is usually preceded by frequent sneezing, which sometimes provides the starting point for the attack, though the sneezing no longer appears once the fit is over. In the middle of the struggle, a thin serum <note>A watery discharge or fluid</note> sometimes drips down, which is of a nature to cause a cough. Outside of the attacks, however, she is moderately well and enjoys ordinary food and drink, except for the weakness of the stomach that occurs and, as is clear from the signs, an excessive heat of the liver.

<margin>The origin and cause of the illness.</margin>
To drive away this serious affliction, various physicians were employed with various medicines; these did not all aim at a single goal, but were mostly directed at fluxes <note>original: "fluxiones"; the movement of "bad humors" or fluids through the body</note> and the lungs. The household physician, however, is of the opinion that the origin of these attacks is drawn primarily from the <term>womb</term> <note>original: "matrice"</note> itself and the surrounding small veins. From these, malignant vapors ascending to the head first excite sneezing; afterwards, having been thickened by the coldness of the brain, they produce thin and subtle fluids. These fluids, partly dripping into the esophagus, provoke vomiting, and partly falling down to the lungs, bring on <term>asthma</term> <note>At this time, "asthma" was a general term for any intense difficulty in breathing</note> and difficulty in breathing. This occurs because the <term>diaphragm</term> <note>The muscle separating the chest from the abdomen</note> is otherwise constricted and compressed by the fumes from below; this difficult breathing persists until the poisonous vapors are dissipated by suitable and appropriate medicines, and a freer ability to breathe returns.

Once these occurrences are dispersed, the patient—who is otherwise naturally quite drowsy—falls into a most peaceful sleep and enjoys it without hindrance. Within a few days, she gathers her strength again so that she can once more manage her household affairs, except perhaps if she is in the countryside on the ground...

But because, despite all the diligence applied, this disease could not be pulled out by its roots using remedies sought from every possible source, and because the husband and wife both fear that over time her life may be thrown into the greatest danger by this evil, it seemed advisable to them to propose the entire history of this condition—described in all its parts and circumstances—to more **Excellent and Skilled Doctors** for their deliberation. They most dutifully ask these physicians to freely and kindly share their thoughts on the disease's true origin, and what should be changed or corrected in the method and course of treatment. They ask whether some excellent, specific protection might be found for this condition, and whether the use of **thermal baths**—and if so, of what kind—would be most profitable for her, so that, being freed from this most heavy disease by divine help, she may again take possession of her former health.

Given at **Heilbronn** on the 22nd day of August, in the year 1622.

This condition is frequently made worse by both **congestion** <note>A buildup of fluids or "humors" in the body</note> and a sudden **afflux** <note>A rapid flow of humors to a specific organ</note> of matter. Regarding the **antecedent cause** <note>the underlying internal predisposition to the illness</note>, I would prescribe half a dram of "hysterical pills" to be taken every day on an empty stomach for eight days before the expected time of menstruation. After the menstrual flow has finished, while the "passageways" are still open, I would use several uterine **pessaries** <note>Medicated plugs inserted into the vagina</note> to purge the corrupt matter contained there. # There follow eight observations of rare female ailments, kindly communicated by the same most distinguished man, Lord Doctor Johann Christoph Eisenmenger.

## I.
## A swelling of the belly in a woman caused by many blisters filled with water attached to the Mesentery.

Among the ailments of women, there not infrequently occur swellings of the belly which, <column-break/> in the first months, mimic pregnancy; these are usually attributed either to a **mole** <term>mola: a 'false conception' or non-viable mass of tissue in the uterus</term>, or to "winds" [gas], or to a collection of bloody or watery fluids contained within the uterus. However, the following case history makes it clear that the matter distending the belly is sometimes contained even outside the uterus, enclosed in peculiar membranes.

<margin>Observation 31.</margin>
The young wife of a certain prominent citizen of ours, in the second year after her marriage, began to be tormented by various pains in the lower belly and the upper abdomen, which sometimes disappeared entirely and sometimes raged to the point of fainting. Her face was suffused with paleness and her belly rose in a swelling—though an uneven one—which indeed had been somewhat turgid since her early youth; nevertheless, her menses flowed at the proper time. She first sought the advice of various **empirics** <note>Self-taught or unlicensed practitioners</note>, one of whom ascribed the whole matter to **sorcery** <term>veneficium: the use of poisons or witchcraft</term>. When, however, the pains grew urgent and she received no help from their foolishness, she called my late father <note>original: 'p. m.' (piae memoriae); meaning of pious memory</note> and me into consultation. Besides general remedies, we then applied a certain **carminative** <note>A medicine used to relieve gas and bloating</note> oil; following its use, on February 9th, 1622, she felt such intense pains around the womb (like those of a woman in labor) that the midwife <term>obstetrix: a woman who assists in childbirth</term> was summoned, expecting either a 'mole' or something similar to come forth from the uterus.

<margin>A discharge of water rejected through the uterus.</margin>
But except for certain watery flows, nothing appeared, and the pains gradually subsided entirely. Since, however, after a few days had passed, both the swelling of the belly and...

The pains increased again, and the most distinguished Lord Doctor Johann Ulian, a colleague of mine who is to be highly respected, was called in. He approached the matter again with purgatives, and then sought to soothe the pains with a **poultice** <term>cataplasma: a soft, moist mass of herbs applied to the body</term> and **sitz-baths** <note>original: 'insessionibus'; a medicinal bath taken in a sitting position</note>; this was not without success. For not only was the swelling significantly diminished as a result, but the pains also seemed so relieved that she began to perform her domestic duties in the house once more. 

However, it was by an unhappy omen. For on the 7th of March, on a colder day, while she was standing by a butcher slaughtering a pig, she suddenly collapsed with an **epileptic fit** <term>Epileptica: used here to describe a sudden seizure or loss of consciousness</term>, and on that very day, she exchanged life for death. So that the cause of this condition and her sudden death might be investigated, with the permission of her parents and husband, the body was opened the next day. In it, the stomach, liver, spleen, and intestines were found to be in their natural state; the womb was also found whole, healthy, and in its natural place. 

But in place of the **mesenteric glands** <term>mesenterij: the membranes that attach the intestines to the abdominal wall</term>, more than twenty blisters of various sizes appeared, swollen with the clearest water, entwined and hidden by the small veins of the mesentery and attached to it here and there. One of these was the largest of all (the size of an infant's head); it soon showed itself during the dissection and covered the entire womb, so that the surgeon at first glance pronounced it to be **dropsy of the womb** <term>Hydropem matricis: a collection of fluid in the uterus</term>. However, when the matter was inspected more deeply, the uterus, as I said, lay healthy underneath. Next to this largest one, six slightly smaller ones were equal to a fist in size;

<column-break/>

the rest were like chicken or pigeon eggs. All of these were connected to one another, remarkably resembling a cluster of chicken eggs, some brought to maturity and some still growing in various sizes, <note>original German: 'wie ein Eyerstock'</note> **like an ovary**.

<margin>A similar observation</margin> There was also the wife of an innkeeper among us who for several years carried a similar mass in her belly, but because her **monthly cycles** [periods] were also retained, it was larger than the other woman’s. She used the **Baths of Zell** <note>Thermis Zellensibus: likely referring to mineral springs in Zell, Germany</note> and other medicines in vain. In the year 1625, in the month of March, after she had perceived a certain sound like a bursting bladder in the bottom of her belly (as she told me), she fell into the greatest pains of the abdomen, such that she cried out loudly at even a slight movement. Lying there for two days, she refused to take any medicine. 

Finally overcome by the pains, she took **opiate laudanum** <note>Laudanum opiatum: a tincture of opium used as a powerful painkiller</note> provided by me, by which the pains were so quieted that the next day she rose from her bed. Afterward, she frequently used that remedy to calm such unexpected, prostrating pains. Ultimately, however, she also died miserably when convulsions came upon her.

From these cases, it appears that we labored in vain with purgatives, and others would too in such instances; for the **offending matter** <note>original: 'materia peccans'; the pathological substance believed to cause the disease</note>, being enclosed within its own membranes or vesicles that have no passage out, easily evaded the power of medicines. Indeed, because of the long delay, perhaps conceiving a malignancy, it sent **poisonous vapors** to the brain, from which the convulsions and death could follow.

->2.<-

### Menstrual flow in pregnant
### women is harmless.

<margin>Observation 32.</margin>
Although most women tend to judge that they are pregnant based on the retention of their menses, and from that point calculate the time of birth, I have known many who, after conception, are still purged <note>original: 'expurgantur'; referring to the menstrual flow as a cleansing process</note> in the ordinary way once or even twice. Indeed, three years ago, one of my female relatives, in the second month after conception, felt the usual flow (as she thought), which afterwards persisted continuously for more than three months. Whenever it was restrained by medicines, it excited pains in the **hypochondria** <term>hypochondriorum: the upper abdominal regions located just below the ribs</term> and **fainting spells** <term>lypothymias: a historical term for sudden loss of consciousness or severe weakness</term>. Therefore, after administering a purgative made of rhubarb, and likewise after **letting blood** <note>original: 'venâ item Epaticâ ſectâ'; the 'hepatic vein' in the arm was traditionally bled to treat liver or blood-related issues</note> from the hepatic vein, and establishing a diet to blunt the sharpness of the blood, we committed the whole matter to nature. Nature, gradually recovering itself, eventually brought the fetus to maturity; however, it was quite weak and was delivered at the end of the eighth month, and so it died in the fifth or sixth month [of its life]. From this, it is clear that the **Hippocratic rule** <note>Hippocrates, the 'Father of Medicine,' famously warned that bleeding a pregnant woman would cause a miscarriage</note>—that a woman miscarries if a vein is cut—can admit many exceptions. Indeed, I know another woman, who was abundant in blood, who had a vein cut three times while carrying a child in her womb, and at the proper

<column-break/>

time gave birth to a healthy child; whereas otherwise, on account of a cough and the sheer quantity of blood, there had been a greater fear of miscarriage. Nevertheless, I have noted that at other times, bloodletting administered to pregnant women without sound judgment has turned out poorly.

### 5.

## A dead fetus, identified by its own signs and skillfully expelled.

<margin>Observation XXXV.</margin>

She underwent care established by Dr. Johannes Pistorius of Nidd, involving frequent purges and other medications. However, as everything was rushing for the worse—with a ghastly paleness of the face following, a heavily foul-smelling breath, constant burning of the stomach, frequent fainting spells, pains in the head and eyes, and even **epileptic convulsions** <note>likely referring to eclampsia or severe seizures</note> (though of a milder sort), along with an increase in the mass of the belly, etc.—my Master Father was also called. Although the aforementioned Pistorius maintained that the patient, besides the cachexia, was merely carrying a shapeless and empty **mole** <term>mola: a "false pregnancy" or a non-viable mass of tissue in the uterus</term> formed from the sterile seed of both parents; nevertheless, when my Master Father examined the details more deeply—especially that in the first months the patient had suffered from **pica** <term>pica: a craving for unusual or non-food items</term>, vomiting, an aversion to food, itching of the breasts, pain in the teeth and eyes, etc., and after the fourth month had ended, she had felt a certain unmistakable movement—he reached the opinion that a formed fetus was being carried, but that it was now dead. This he proved further, primarily from the coldness of the belly (both apparent to the touch and from the symptoms listed above). # ON THE DISEASES OF WOMEN.

...of the territory of Württemberg, bringing with him his daughter, a maiden of about 22 years of age. In the presence of her father, she reported that in the preceding month of July, while she was suffering from her menstrual flow, she fell from a ladder. Because of this, the flow immediately stopped, followed by an extreme shortness of breath; however, after three days, this ceased when a vein in her arm was opened. Yet her menses have remained stopped for half a year until now, and she has recently suffered from a cough, difficulty breathing, stomach pains after consuming food, and similar symptoms. For these reasons, she sought my advice. A sample of her urine was provided, which differed from that of a healthy person, as its color was fading from gold and was not a little thin, suggesting a wasting condition.

Therefore, having weighed the matter, and placing trust in the account of the father as much as the daughter, I prescribed a **Medicated Wine** made from aperients <note>medicines used to "open" obstructions in the body's channels</note>. I ordered her to continue this for the eight days preceding the new moon, and afterward to open the right **saphenous vein** <note>a large vein in the leg/ankle, traditionally bled to stimulate menstrual flow</note>. When these measures did not help, I advised her to repeat the same wine after a month had passed and to also cut the left saphenous vein. She followed these instructions, but because her menses did not yet flow after the first bloodletting, she became impatient of the delay; eight days later, she saw to it that the vein at the ankle of her other foot was also punctured. Once this was done, on the following day, she expelled from her womb not only a great quantity of clotted blood and other humors, but also a <term>mola: a "mole" or fleshy mass of tissue that grows in the uterus, once thought to be a "false conception"</term>. This mass lacked life, but in every respect it resembled

<column-break/>

a house mouse (except that the body was smooth and lacked hair, though it exceeded a common mouse in size). After this, following a period of rest and a proper diet, she was freed from all her distress.

The matter, however, was not free from suspicion <note>the expulsion of such a mass often led to accusations of illicit pregnancy or witchcraft</note>. She herself was brought before the Magistrate, cast into prison, and severely examined—not without threats. She testified to nothing else than that she was conscious of no sexual encounter, and she gave the greatest thanks to God and the Doctor that she had been freed from this monster. Indeed, when I was questioned by the judge, I responded that it could certainly happen that from retained menstrual blood and "female seed," perhaps with the addition of some power of the **imagination**, Nature (which always strives to impress a form) might generate such a mouse-shaped mole.

Indeed, examples are recorded by physicians of **moles** being brought forth not only in the form of an **Eagle**, **Hawk**, **Toad**, **Frog**, **Mole** <note>the burrowing animal</note>, **Elephant**, **Lion**, **Pig**, **Cat**, **Hare**, **Lizard**, or **Serpent**, or other animals, but *Mercurialis* and *Paré* <note>Girolamo Mercuriali (1530–1606) and Ambroise Paré (c. 1510–1590), two of the most famous medical authorities of the Renaissance</note> make special mention of a mouse, and even a living one. Although such moles are most often brought to light in married women and those having intercourse with men (usually alongside true offspring), it is not impossible for something similar to happen even to virgins. On this subject, see *Levinus Lemnius*, book 4 of *The Secret Miracles of Nature*, chapter 19.

### 8.
->Various Uterine Suffocations.<- <note>original: "Uterinæ Suffocationes" — a term for what was later called hysteria, though here describing physical symptoms of choking or fainting believed to originate in the uterus.</note>

<margin>
Observation 38.
</margin>
Although women are subject to many different conditions, I believe none is more worthy of wonder than uterine suffocations. For who would not marvel that a woman can lie down for several hours without movement or sense, and even without breathing [to say nothing of other symptoms]? Especially since no man can live even for a quarter of an hour without breathing.

<column-break/>

I have, in my practice thus far, observed a great variety and range in this condition. I saw a certain noble young girl who was fully conscious—hearing, seeing, and even moving her limbs—lie for two hours without breathing or voice; she returned to herself only after the scent of amber <note>original: "fuccini" — fossilized resin used in medicinal fumigation</note> was applied several times to her nostrils. Another woman, regarding whose case I sought the advice of Your Excellency some years ago, had such difficult breathing with snorting <note>original: "ftertore"</note> and such great distress that she was forced to sit in a sloping position, gasping for air with an open mouth and clutching at any obstacle with great force; by the grace of God, she was freed from that condition by using the thermal baths at Baden <note>original: "thermarum Baden fium" — likely Baden-Baden or a similar spa town known for medicinal waters</note>.

Again, two years ago, I undertook the care of a noble and virtuous virgin who was frequently afflicted by this same condition, arising from an obstruction of the mesenteric veins <note>term: mesenteric veins — the veins that drain blood from the intestines</note>, the spleen, and the uterus. The onset of her attack was as follows: first, pains in the hypochondria <note>term: hypochondria — the upper regions of the abdomen, below the ribs</note>, especially on the left side, heralded the illness. She endured these until she was forced to take to her bed. At the very moment she lay down, she immediately began to lose her mind and say many ridiculous things; this delirium lasted sometimes for one or two hours. Then convulsions followed, though they were light, primarily in the right arm (which sometimes even preceded the paroxysm). Her breathing became more and more difficult until at last it failed completely, and she lay there senseless...

There is a noble religious woman <note>Likely a nun or a particularly devout woman.</note> still living who, many years ago—specifically in the year 1596 <insert>November 30, 1596</insert> and following—frequently experienced such a paroxysm attacking her unexpectedly. Then, carried to bed, she lay without breathing for half an hour, more or less; then she returned to herself and recognized those standing around, though always complaining of extreme exhaustion and sometimes even an inability to move, though this lasted only briefly.

Certain eminent doctors called this condition a "convulsion of the diaphragm." Although most suspected a "uterine connection" <note>The medical theory that the uterus caused symptoms in distant parts of the body via "sympathy."</note>, nevertheless, because she claimed to be wonderfully refreshed during the attack itself by highly fragrant scents—musk, ambergris, rose water, and the like—and her periods flowed at the appointed time, they were forced to leave the matter in doubt. Eventually, as she grew older, and through I know not what remedies (for she had various ones from various people), the evil was entirely removed. Now in her sixties, though frequently subject to ailments of the spleen, joints, and <term>catarrhs</term> <note>An excessive buildup of mucus or fluid drainage.</note>, she feels nothing of the sort anymore.

->1.<-

### Menstrual flow harmless to certain pregnant women.

<margin>Observation XXXIX</margin>
Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine" (c. 460 – 370 BCE).</note> asserts in *Book 5, Aphorism 60* that it is impossible for a fetus to be healthy if the mother’s menstrual periods continue their course during pregnancy. I have observed the contrary more than once, especially in a woman of a plethoric <note>original: "plethorici" — meaning an overabundance of blood or bodily fluids.</note> constitution, the wife of Master N. Linsius, a Patrician of Augsburg living in Lauingen in the year 1590. This woman, as often as she carried a child in her womb, experienced her monthly periods copiously throughout the entire time of her pregnancy (as she herself reported to me more than once), while in the meantime she gave birth to perfectly healthy, stout, and very lively children.

---

->2.<-

### A severe uterine suffocation occurring only once.

<margin>Observation XL.</margin>
The wife of the most distinguished Master Dr. Sebastian Halbmayer—intimate counselor to the most Reverend Lord, Lord Johann Otto, Bishop of Augsburg—while traveling from Würzburg to Dillingen with her family in the year 1592, fell ill with uterine pains and a "suffocation" <note>original: "suffocatio uteri" — a condition where the womb was believed to rise up and compress the internal organs, causing fainting or respiratory distress.</note> so severe that she was without sensation or motion and was taken for dead. Called from Lauingen, I applied frictions <note>therapeutic rubbing of the limbs</note> and ligatures to her feet, anointed her navel with civet <note>term: "Zibeto" — a pungent musk obtained from civet cats, used in medicine to "attract" the womb back down to its proper place.</note>, and blew a powder made of castoreum <note>term: "Castoreo" — a yellowish secretion from beaver sacs, prized for its strong odor and medicinal effects.</note> and pepper into her nostrils. Once this irritation was made, she began to sneeze after half an hour and to recover herself. She remained well thereafter and suffered nothing further from her womb.

Simon von Welden, bore for a long time a belly swollen like a drum <term>tympanites</term> <note>A condition where the abdomen is distended by gas or air, sounding like a drum when tapped.</note>, while her monthly periods meanwhile occurred regularly. After her husband died, she moved to Dillingen with her whole household. There, in 1594, while living in widowhood, she experienced delayed periods, occurring only every 8 weeks, but with great force, especially on the 4th of July; so much so, that at one time she filled buckets and basins of considerable size with clotted blood. From this followed fainting spells <term>lipothymiae</term>, pains in the nape and back of the head, piercing pains in the loins and abdomen, swelling and paleness of the face, and many other horrific symptoms, which subsequent vomiting usually made milder. Having ordered a diet, she used a decoction of mastic wood and a reddish wine for her drink. Meanwhile, ligatures and rubbings were applied; and according to her strength, blood was let from the right arm. This potion was given:

*1 scruple and a half.*

From the use of this, a swift bowel movement removed all danger of the violent flow by the kindness of God, and she lived very well thereafter. But, so that she might enjoy a health more fortified against attacks of this kind, she went to the <term>baths of Grumbach</term> <note>A historical German spa known for its mineral springs.</note>, which are very helpful for flows of this kind, and she used them with great benefit to her health. But after one whole year had passed, when she had decided to return to these waters again, behold, beyond all hope and expectation, that flow attacked the wretched woman more cruelly than ever, and exhausted her strength with the loss of her life.

### 8.

### Menstrual flow and bloodletting in the 8th month of pregnancy without harm.

<margin>Observation XLVI.</margin> The wife of the noble and most famous man, Master Albrecht Fabri—Doctor of Both Laws and the most excellent Chancellor to the Most Reverend Lord Johannes Otto, Bishop of Augsburg—was a woman of quite corpulent and <term>plethoric</term> <note>original: "plethorica" — in humor-based medicine, this meant having an overabundance of blood, which was thought to cause heat and pressure.</note> constitution. In the year 1592, while she was in her eighth month of pregnancy, she did not notice that a flow of blood had begun during her sleep. In the morning, following her usual habit, she underwent a copious <term>bloodletting</term> <note>original: "venæ-sectio." At the time, doctors believed bleeding a pregnant woman could be dangerous, but here it was done accidentally or out of habit.</note>. Because the fetus was kicking violently—as was reported to me in writing—she fell into such mental distress and fear, believing the child was in immediate danger, that she would accept almost no consolation. However, after remedies were ordered to strengthen both the fetus and the mother, she happily completed the remaining time of her pregnancy and gave birth to a living and healthy child. This same most honored matron, in the year 1597, complained of an excessive flow of blood while the fetus was in its seventh month and quite weak. The following restorative <term>Tragea</term> <note>A medicinal powder mixed with sugar, intended to be eaten or sprinkled on food.</note> was prescribed:

With this and an astringent <term>fomentation</term> <note>A warm, medicinal soak or poultice.</note>, along with the "Countess's Ointment" being applied, she reached the proper term for birth. This woman, whenever no excessive flows occurred while she was pregnant, would always give birth with great difficulty and danger to the child unless she had let blood two or three times—even in the final month. I pass over the bouts of asthma and very sharp, burning fevers which she mostly endured in the middle of her pregnancies; these, however, were several times successfully driven away through bloodletting and <term>purging</term> <note>The use of laxatives to clear the bowels and balance the humors.</note>, even without strictly observing the timing of conception, by the help of God and diligent care.

->9.<-

### Repeated purging and bloodletting in a pregnant woman, without harm.

<margin>Observation XLVII.</margin> The most honored matron Maria Zechin, of Lauingen—the wife of the most esteemed Master Georg Zech, my honored fellow-godfather—similarly had to be purged two or three times while she was pregnant. Just as many times, she had to be relieved by bloodletting, often for a third time, and occasionally even in the final month. When these treatments were omitted, neither she nor the fetus fared well during or after the birth. These histories teach us that it is not <term>universally</term> <note>original: "καθόλου" (*katholou*) — a Greek term meaning generally or universally true.</note> true that one must abstain from bloodletting and purging in the first and last months when the fetus is still tender or quite large.

### Convulsive attacks from the sympathy of the womb.

<margin>Observation XLVIII.</margin> In the year 1626, Maria—the daughter of Master Jeremias Majer, the consul of Lauingen, living in Maryhann—complained that six months earlier, after a sudden and unexpected fright, she immediately felt griping pains in her belly. She described a "vapor" rising from the left <term>hypochondrium</term> <note>The upper region of the abdomen, below the ribs; in this period, it was often thought to be the source of "vapors" affecting the mind or nerves.</note> with pain, followed by her falling down with her arms and mouth stretched in a convulsive motion. Once she was revived, she did not know what had happened to her. Since that time, she has experienced this disaster once; she fears that this evil, by taking root, may recur more often in the future, as her arms still always ache, she feels a weariness in all her limbs, and nausea persists along with a total loss of her menstrual flow. After ordering a proper diet, I advised the following:

Take:

*Ammoniacum* — 15 grains.
*Opoponax* <note>A medicinal gum resin.</note> — 15 grains of each.
*Galbanum* — 5 grains.

# OBSERVATION XLIX.

## A remarkable long-lasting sneezing in a girl.

A girl about 11 years of age, of a rather delicate constitution, fell into a nosebleed at the beginning of the current year 1628. As this subsided, sneezing followed for several days, afflicting her at certain intervals with great effort.

## THE RESOLUTION

<margin>What sneezing is and how many kinds there are.</margin>
Although sneezing is not rarely called a work of nature, it is nevertheless not undeservedly reduced to the category of symptoms "contrary to nature" as well. It seems to be nothing other than a depraved <note>In this context, "depraved" means abnormal or malfunctioning.</note> motion of the brain, breaking out with a most vehement blowing-out through the nostrils. This arises from the expulsive faculty, irritated by some biting or stinging cause around the nostrils and the anterior parts of the brain, with the muscles of the chest and head cooperating—just as described by Galen in book 2 of *On the Causes of Symptoms*.

<meta>catchword: causes.</meta>

### ON THE DISEASES OF WOMEN.

<margin>
The usual benefits of sneezing.
</margin>
...as collected from cause, chapter 4. Since sneezing commonly brings its own benefits with it, while purging the head and brain, and appearing once the disease has been concocted, <note>In Galenic medicine, "concoction" refers to the body "cooking" or ripening raw humors into a form that can be safely expelled.</note> it indicates the strength of nature. Therefore, we are not particularly anxious about correcting what happens commonly.
<margin>
Dangerous sneezing.
</margin>
Yet it can happen, though rarely, that this symptom is dangerous—not only in all diseases of the lungs, as **Hippocrates** holds in his *Prognostics*, but also by its own nature, due to the gravity of the cause. For this reason, **Cardanus** in *Book 4, Aphorism 45*, reports that a young man afflicted by many empty sneezes died the following day of the Comitial disease <note>original: "Comitiali morbo"; a historical name for epilepsy, so called because a seizure during a Roman assembly (comitia) was considered a bad omen that required the meeting to be cancelled.</note>. Likewise, he records a sixty-year-old man who, after many signs of a badly affected brain and having lain in bed with a long illness, perhaps sneezed twenty-five times in the morning with a light and empty effect, and died on the third day following. Indeed, it is possible that something contrary to nature, retained around the anterior parts of the head, may cause a most troublesome sneezing as long as the troublesome cause is held there. A memorable case of this is in **Alexander Benedictus**, *Book 4 on the Cure of Diseases, Chapter 4*, concerning a certain Greek man. Having been wounded near the temples by an arrow, twenty-five years later, after sneezing beyond measure with a great itch and among the greatest efforts, he cast out from his nostrils a fragment of the arrow, the length of a middle finger, with an iron tip. **Forestus** in his *Book of Observations, 127*,

<column-break/>

testifies that troublesome, continuous sneezings arose from an acrid catarrh <note>A "catarrh" was historically understood as a "down-flowing" of excess mucus from the brain.</note> which could be soothed in no way until he, being asked, shared this advice: that lukewarm milk should be drawn up through the nostrils quite often. Once this was done three or four times, like a miracle, all sneezing was dispelled; the milk tempered the saltiness of the catarrh which was stimulating the expulsive faculty, and thus its acrimony was corrected. So too, **Amatus Lusitanus**, in his *4th Century of Cures, Observation 3*, observed *habitual and stubborn* sneezing in a twenty-year-old youth, who was bilious <note>Having a temperament dominated by yellow bile, associated with heat and irritability.</note> by nature and had quite thick blood. His hot vapors, carried to the head, produced the sneezings by which the head was infested, narrowed, and disturbed, according to **Hippocrates** in *Aphorism 51, Book 7*, where the generation of sneezing is proposed. He restored him and freed him from this trouble by bloodletting, with cooling and evacuating medicines, together with a plaster applied to the head made of pumpkin marrow, barley flour, a little purslane, several egg yolks, oil of roses, vinegar, etc.; and also by drawing oil of roses, pumpkin, and water-lily through the nostrils. **Forestus**, in the place cited, proposes *various remedies for more vehement sneezing*, and before him **Paulus Aegineta**, *Book 3, Chapter 24*, and also others of the ancients whom **Amatus** joins together in the commentary on his observation. As for *our own observation*, although at first the stubborn symptom seemed...

...appeared, so that sometimes she would be seized by a fit of sneezing a hundred times, almost continuously with great effort and a shaking of the whole body. Local remedies were of little or no help, such as milk by itself, or even combined with the mucilage of quince seeds and psyllium <note>Both quince seeds and psyllium were used to create soothing, viscous liquids to coat and calm irritated membranes.</note>, as well as oil of sweet almonds and similar substances drawn into the nostrils. Strengthening and drying juices were applied to the crown of the head, and footbaths were ordered using herbs that "digest" and "draw out" humors, etc. At last, however, the condition was rendered milder once the stomach was first cleared with common pills, and afterward the lower belly was greatly unburdened of a copious amount of waste <term>saburra: a medical term for a collection of undigested matter or "foul humors" in the digestive tract</term> by a sharper clyster <note>original: "clystere acriore"; an enema containing more potent or irritating ingredients intended to stimulate a bowel movement.</note>.

<column-break/>

Since, however, this ailment had been preceded by frequent nosebleeds, and these had arisen not from a surplus of blood, but rather from a corruption or sharpness <note>original: "acrimonia"; in Galenic medicine, this refers to a quality of the humors where they become "acrid" or "stinging," causing irritation to the tissues.</note> of the blood, it must certainly be concluded that some of this sharper blood remained in the frontal membranous parts of the brain. At certain times, due to vapors rising from the <term>cacochymia: a state of "bad juice" or unhealthy humors in the body</term> of the lower belly, this blood irritated the expulsive faculty <note>The body's natural power to drive out harmful or superfluous substances; in this case, the brain was trying to "expel" the sharp humors through sneezing.</note>. This continued until the underlying cause was corrected and the fullness of the head was gradually consumed by the power of the <term>native heat: the innate vital warmth that early physicians believed drove all metabolic processes and the "cooking" of humors</term>, etc.

## TO BOOK I, PART TWO OF THE MEDICINAL OBSERVATIONS
# APPENDIX,
### ON THE DISEASES OF CHILDREN.

ALTHOUGH THE EGYPTIANS lacked specialized physicians for children, and the diseases of children—along with their specific remedies—were not diligently treated by the ancients, and because children themselves are almost impossible to manage <note>original: "intractabiles"; referring to the difficulty in getting young children to cooperate with examinations or swallow bitter medicines.</note> and their very tender bodies do not easily tolerate the use of just any medicine, we do not believe that childhood diseases should be neglected for these reasons. Instead, we approach their cure by applying singular medical wisdom, always looking to the condition of the suffering subject, by which reasoning we are forced to vary the medicines as well. Hence, following the guidance of Hippocrates, we once established a public exercise in the Academy regarding *The Diseases of Children*, which it will by no means displease the lovers of medicine <note>original: "philiatros"; from the Greek for "friends of medicine," usually referring to medical students or practitioners.</note> to see repeated here with other works.

## GREGOR HORSTIUS, DOCTOR
### ACADEMIC EXERCISE, IN THE YEAR 1619,
### SUBJECTED TO PUBLIC EXAMINATION.
## ON THE DISEASES OF CHILDREN,
### According to Hippocrates.

->*Aphorism 24, Book 3.*<-

greatest changes according to

when he starts: *according to age
such things happen*, proceeding to child-

APPENDIX TO BOOK I, PART II.

[The author continues discussing] the diseases of children, which he first reviews with respect to those who are called small and newborn, in comparison to those who reach the time of teething.
<margin>Diseases of newborns.</margin>

---

### Question I.
## Do diseases happen according to age?

The negative view seems probable: 1. Because the change of age is natural; but things that are according to nature do not produce diseases. 2. Because age is a sign of change; but that which has the nature of a sign does not immediately also obtain the nature of a cause. 3. Because age is a determination of time, which does not act by itself. 4. Because the temperament of a specific age does not differ from the native temperament. *See Mercatus, On Temperaments, question 54.* 5. Because an antecedent disease-causing factor changes the properties of the age. But since the constitution of the body varies by reason of age, and for that reason—depending on how the body is rendered such or such—it is therefore more disposed to these or those diseases; thus it is clear that the assertion of Hippocrates is consistent with the truth. *Regarding the aforementioned objections, we respond:* To the 1st: Age does not produce diseases by itself, but through other concurrent causes, which

<column-break/>

more quickly produce an unnatural disposition in this or that age. To the 2nd: Both a cause and a sign can coincide. To the 3rd: It acts insofar as it includes motion. To the 4th: With respect to the foundation and the root [of the temperament]. To the 5th: This is conceded when the violence of an external cause concurs.

<margin>1. Ulcers of the mouth, called aphthae</margin> He establishes that ulcers of the mouth often happen to these [infants] first; they are called *aphthai* <note>original: ἄφθαι</note> by the Greeks, arising superficially because of the softness of the throat and the bitterness of the milk. These prevent the closing of the mouth and the sucking of milk. For this evil, near the beginning, *fresh butter, as well as starch diluted in rose water, iron-infused milk <term>chalybeate milk: milk in which hot iron has been quenched, believed to have astringent or strengthening properties</term>, powder of dried roses with rose syrup, and a mouthwash made from a decoction of fresh bugloss root* are suitable. This is done while not neglecting those things which serve to correct the milk, either by changing the nurse, or by altering her milk through cold and moist remedies and foods. Care should be taken that she does not use salty, sharp, or watery foods; and furthermore, she should be purged with cassia, tamarinds, and syrup of violets.

---

This is affirmed, insofar as the Thrush <term>Aphthae: oral yeast infections or small ulcers</term> is considered in its beginning stage. But it is doubted, 1. because...

2. ### Question 3.

### Whether Honey of Roses is suitable in mouth inflammations.

It is affirmed, because the medicines with which it is mixed acquire a power of 

<column-break/>

cleansing from the honey, and a power of cooling from the roses. *On the other hand*, it is doubted: 1. because of the heating and fiery quality of honey; 2. because it is readily turned into bile; 3. because honey of roses is more suitable for phlegmatic conditions. *But I respond* to the 1st: the heating quality of honey is tempered by the roses, so that it acquires the power of cleansing along with cooling; hence it is also not easily converted into bile, as if it were alone; 3. indeed, an influx of phlegm is joined here.

3. Once these steps are taken, let the ulcerated parts be cleansed with a decoction of barley prepared with steel <note>water in which hot steel was quenched, believed to add medicinal properties</note> mixed with honey of roses; afterward, they should be led to scarring <note>forming a cicatrix</note> by the following decoction, which contains: *plantain water, shepherd's purse water, and white wine, two ounces each; burnt alum, one drachm; strained honey of roses, one ounce. Mix.*

<margin>Elongation of the uvula</margin>
In this case, it must not be neglected if an elongation of the *Columella* <note>the uvula, the fleshy hanging part at the back of the throat; literally "little column"</note> is joined with inflammation. In the cleansing decoctions, astringents should be increased; and for the sake of suspending <note>lifting the sagging tissue</note> it, an *Acacia plaster* with *vinegar and burnt oak galls* should be applied to the coronal suture <note>the seam at the top of the skull</note>, with a sufficient amount of *rose ointment* added.

<margin>2. Vomiting</margin>
Furthermore, among the diseases of children are numbered *vomitings* <note>original Greek: εμετοὶ (*emetoì*)</note>, which occur because of the stomach or the milk, insofar as the stomach itself—unaccustomed to food due to the novelty of its operation—is not sufficient for the transformation of the milk, or insofar as the milk itself becomes watery in the stomach...

## Question 4.

->Why do children frequently have<-
->vomitings and hiccups?<-

Mercurialis responds in his book *On the Diseases of Children* that it is because they possess a stomach that is exceptionally relaxed and moist; indeed, they do not spit anything out, nor do they discharge through the nose as readily as adults do, which causes more phlegm to accumulate in the stomach. But given such a cause, the reasons we propose seem insufficient, being external rather

<column-break/>

than internal. But note that the condition can be considered both as it currently exists <note>Latin: *in facto*</note> and as it is still developing <note>Latin: *in fieri*</note>: with respect to the latter, the stated cause holds, without excluding the instances that confirm the disease once it has already formed.

<margin>3. Coughs.</margin>
In the third place are listed coughs <note>Greek: *βῆχες* (bēches)</note> and little coughs, which frequently happen to children due to the breathing in of air—especially cold air—by which the parts of the chest are irritated; this is particularly true when, for the same reason, the resolved moisture of the head drips down <note>Referring to the "catarrh" theory where fluids were thought to drip from the brain to the lungs</note> and burdens the chest. Hence, an external anointing of the chest with oil of sweet almonds is appropriate. Internally, if the flowing matter is joined by a more viscous substance, the juice of a succulent radish with powdered white sugar candy—made layer upon layer and extracted overnight—should be frequently administered in the quantity of half a spoonful. Indeed, oil of sweet almonds mixed slightly with *penidium* sugar <note>A traditional twisted barley sugar used for throat irritation</note> and taken by licking is also suitable. A hollowed-out apple filled with sugar candy and a little added saffron, then roasted and applied like a pap or pulp, is highly praised. There are some who provide musk-scented *alipta* <note>A medicinal paste or confection</note> with milk, especially where vomiting is also present.

# ON THE DISEASES OF CHILDREN.

### Question 5.

->Whether the humidity of the head<-
->is released by cold<-
->air.<-

**W**e affirm this very point, in so far as a warm and moist constitution of the head, when external cold approaches, promptly sends down released fluxions <note>original: *fluxiones*; the flow of excess bodily fluids or humors, often resulting in a runny nose or catarrh</note> to the emunctories <note>original: *emunctoria*; the organs or channels that carry off waste, such as the nostrils or sweat glands</note>, provided the dew-like moisture is resolved into liquid by the cold. But there are objections: 1. that coldness causes condensation; 2. that distillations <note>the "dripping" of humors from the head</note> in fevers often arise because of a release caused by heat; 3. that the release of humidity presupposes a thinning of the fluids, which is not performed by cold. *In truth, we respond:* 1. nothing prevents cold from condensing, specifically by collecting the dew-like moisture more densely; 2. indeed, there is also another way they are generated, where in fevers the heat dissolves phlegmatic <note>original: *pituitoſos*; relating to phlegm or mucus</note> humors, while at the same time a weakness of digestion occurs; 3. the thinning of thicker humidity is presupposed, but not that of the dew-like variety.

-><image-desc>A decorative printers' ornament consisting of stylized floral or leaf patterns</image-desc><-

<column-break/>

### Question 6.

->Whether anointing the chest<-
->is appropriate for a<-
->cough?<-

**T**he negative view seems probable: 1. because every anointing blocks the pores of the skin; 2. nor does the strength of a liniment <note>a medicated liquid or lotion</note> on the chest penetrate to the lowest parts; 3. not to mention the warm friction of the anointing itself, by which more flow is drawn toward the affected area. *But instead, we maintain the affirmative view,* insofar as liniments of this kind possess the power of softening, digesting, and dissipating. *Hence, to the 1st objection we respond:* that anointing which is cold in action blocks the pores of the skin, but certainly not that which is warm in both action and potential. To the 2nd: it is sufficient that it aids nature, so that it may more quickly move the "sinning matter" <note>harmful or diseased humors</note> toward the exterior, even through occult transpiration <note>original: *transpirationem*; invisible perspiration through the skin, thought to release internal toxins</note>. To the 3rd: it is granted that a certain attraction occurs, but it is from the interior to the exterior, and toward a healthy part.

---

<margin>4. Sleeplessness.</margin>
In the fourth place are <term>ἀγρυπνίαι</term> <note>Greek: *agrypniai*; sleeplessness or insomnia</note>, or vigils. These should be neglected even less because an abundance of sleep is naturally appropriate for children. If, therefore, they occur because of the sharp vapors of spoiled milk rising to the head, let the milk be corrected by a suitable dietary regimen prescribed for the nurse, for whom broths... <note>original catchword: *cula*, completing the word *juscula* or "broths"</note>

# APPENDIX TO BOOK I. PART II.

...[remedies], after <term>cacochymia</term> <note>original: *cacochymiam*; an imbalance of bodily humors</note> and <term>plethora</term> <note>original: *plethoram*; an overabundance of blood or humors</note> have been corrected, should be prescribed from *lettuce, purslane, and the seeds of white poppy*. Indeed, even for children themselves, to prevent rising vapors, a little *poppy syrup* mixed with *violet syrup* may be granted, and *violet oil* with a little saffron, or *dill oil mixed with lettuce juice*, should be prescribed for application to the nostrils and temples. But if a lack of sleep occurs due to internal pains or other causes, one must look to those causes which introduce wakefulness <note>original: *pervigiliam*; a state of abnormal sleeplessness or insomnia</note> as a secondary symptom: thus, a scruple <note>a small unit of pharmaceutical weight</note> of *anise powder* mixed with a spoonful of porridge and administered corrects the griping of the stomach that prevents sleep.

---

## Question 7.
### Whether saffron is appropriate for sleeplessness?

The *negative view seems probable:*
1. because saffron possesses a power of heating and drying;
2. indeed, it excites the senses; 3. and it introduces mobility to the <term>spirits</term> <note>original: *spirituum*; the vital vapors believed to carry life and sensation through the body</note>, by which it is said to refresh the heart. *But note,* that it should not be prescribed alone in this case, but mixed with a cooling syrup, to which it adds a power of penetration. *Therefore, although it possesses the power of heating and drying when used alone,*

<column-break/>

yet when mixed with other substances, it induces sleep more quickly by exciting pleasant vapors; hence, by itself it excites the senses; 3. and when mixed with warm cordials—but not with cold ones—it refreshes the heart by introducing mobility to the spirits.

---

<margin>5. Night Terrors.</margin>
Fifthly, **Night Terrors** <note>original Greek: *Φόβοι* (Phoboi)</note> are numbered; specifically those which occur when corrupt humors weigh down the stomach in great quantity and "bite" at its opening, sending foul vapors upward. Due to the disturbance of the spirits, the <term>phantasia</term> <note>the faculty of imagination</note> creates terrifying images. So that those things which are more difficult to digest may be more easily processed, and that which is corrupt and separated may be driven down to the bowels, something of *syrup of citron peel* should frequently be administered where a hotter temperament is present, or *syrup of wormwood*. Nor should one neglect *simple rose syrup*, by which the stomach is strengthened and nature is assisted in expelling waste, especially if sleep is avoided too soon after eating in older children.

---

## Question 8.
### Whether Wormwood is appropriate for the night terrors of children?

We affirm this very thing, for the reason that the juice of Wormwood <note>original: *Absynthij*</note> tempered with sugar...

...appropriate for the preceding cause, namely the corruption of food in the stomach. Nor does it stand in the way that Wormwood <note>original: *Absynthium*</note> is said to weigh down the head; that by heating it may increase exhalations; and that it may introduce sleep before the proper time, which is most harmful here. For 1. the addition of sugar corrects the first harm while it is being prepared into a syrup; 2. when used in the right manner and time, the second harm is also not to be feared; 3. nor is untimely sleep to be dreaded here in the least, since the remedy corrects the very cause of the sleepiness.

---

<margin>6. Inflammations of the navel.</margin>
Sixthly, *inflammations of the navel* <note>original: *ὀμφαλῆ Φλεγμοναὶ*</note> occasionally arise in the first days due to the treatment of the umbilical cord, the said part being painful and drawing blood, especially at that time when midwives act without sufficient care. In this case, the nurse should, above all else, choose a cooling and moistening diet. For the child, *rose oil mixed with earthworm oil* <note>original: *ol. lumbricorum*; oil infused with earthworms, traditionally used to soothe nerves and reduce swelling</note> should be applied externally over the navel until the inflammation subsides. Then, *chamomile oil* and finally even *dill oil* <note>original: *Anethinum*</note> may be added for the sake of dispersing the fluids. Powdered *Mastic* <note>original: *Mastix*; a resin from the mastic tree</note>, mixed with egg white and applied to the navel in the form of a plaster, is also sometimes effectively prescribed for the further drying out of the matter.

---

### Question 9.

### Whether earthworm oil is suitable in inflammation of the navel?

Someone might doubt this because it is otherwise usually prescribed for "cold" afflictions of the nerves, and they might fear that it would increase the inflammation by its own heat. But *note* that earthworm oil, when mixed with rose oil, tempers the inflammation and is suitable for the nervous substance of the navel. Thus, nothing stands in the way, even if it might heat and increase inflammation if used on its own.

---

<margin>7. Moisture of the ears.</margin>
Lastly, *moisture of the ears* <note>original: *ὠτῶν ὑγρότητες*</note> are listed—moistness and discharges from the ears—due to the great humidity and impurity of the brain, which nature cannot sufficiently evacuate through the mouth and nostrils in small children. Such discharges should be left to nature for a while, because they serve to evacuate the brain, unless pain occurs alongside inflammation. In that case, *white of egg kneaded with breast milk* and instilled into the ear is recommended; goose fat with fresh butter and woman's milk also helps...

### Question 10.

->Why does Hippocrates mention<-
->moisture of the ears, but not<-
->of the nostrils and palate?<-

Is it because excretions of the nostrils and palate are natural, whereas those of the ears are morbid <note>diseased or abnormal</note>, as Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> implies? Or indeed, as Mercurialis <note>Girolamo Mercuriali (1530–1606), an Italian physician and author of the first systematic treatise on pediatric diseases</note> adds, is it because they occur through the ears by force—that is, by morbid matter stimulating nature—and not spontaneously, as occurs through the nostrils and palate?

<image-desc>Ornate decorative centerpiece featuring floral and scrollwork motifs surrounding a central oval.</image-desc>

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Horizontal floral divider composed of small repeating flower icons.</image-desc>

### Question 11.

->Whether egg white is suitable<-
->in the inflammation<-
->of the ears.<-

This may be doubted, because: 1. it has a repellent power <note>the ability to drive humors away from a site</note>; 2. it may also hinder the expulsive faculty; 3. add to this that the matter producing the inflammation seems rather to require warm, moist, and resolving <note>treatments that dissipate or "resolve" inflammatory fluids</note> agents. But since the intense pain of the ears necessarily requires some soothing treatment, we approve of egg white <note>original: *albumen ovi*</note> beaten with breast milk <note>original: *lacte mulieris*</note>. We grant to this a modest repellent power, having regard for the greater influx of fluids which otherwise tends to occur by reason of persistent pain. Indeed, we determine that the expulsive faculty should not be hindered when there is little matter; but where there is a great influx, one must consider not only the humors that have already flowed in, but also those about to flow. By this reasoning, the third objection is also very easily resolved: where matter is already impacted in the laboring part, it indicates that it must be resolved and thinned; however, this is not the case for that matter which is still in the process of flowing.

# ON THE DISEASES OF CHILDREN.

[Signature mark M 3]

...[Hippocrates] says that during the eruption of all the teeth, there occur irritations, fevers, convulsions, and diarrheas, especially when they bring up the canine teeth <note>the "eye teeth" or fangs</note>, and particularly in the fattest of children and those who have hard bellies. <note>original Greek: γησιν ὅλων ὀδαξισμοὶ, πυρετοὶ, σπασμοὶ, διάῤῥοιαι, καὶ μάλισα ὅταν ἀνάγωσι τοὺς κυνόδοντας, καὶ τοῖσι παχυτάτοισι τῶν παιδίων, καὶ τοῖσι τὰς κοιλίας σκληρὰς ἔχουσιν.</note>

<margin>Diseases of children at the time of teething.</margin>
Having determined the diseases of newborns, Hippocrates proceeds to the time of teething, which usually begins around the seventh month, although sometimes teeth break through earlier for some and later for others.

<margin>1. Itching of the gums.</margin>
Here first are placed "irritations of all the teeth" <note>original Greek: ὅλων ὀδαξισμοὶ (holon odaxismoi)</note>, which are the troublesome itching of the gums. These occur when the teeth, by their progress, twitch at the gums; for this reason, those things which facilitate an easier breakthrough and temper the pain are of great service. These include fresh butter mixed with honey and a portion of **hare’s brain** <note>a traditional folk remedy believed to soften the gums and ease the passage of teeth</note>, smeared upon the gums. Externally, also, frequently anointing the jaws and neck with oil of sweet almonds will assist nature not a little.

---

### On Aphorism 25.
### Question I.
### Whether hare’s brain is suitable during teething.

It is affirmed by Experience: and it may be that by its coldness it tempers the heat of the gums, or that by its astringency <note>the power to shrink or tighten body tissues</note> it strengthens those parts, or that it performs such a thing by some specific property. But it can be doubted, because here a warm thinning power is required rather than a cold astringent one,

<column-break/>

especially since the eruption of teeth ought to be aided by the former. To which we respond, that moderately cold and mildly astringent things strengthen nature, so that the heat, having obtained a balance in this way, can more conveniently complete its operation.

---

<margin>2. Fevers.</margin>
To these are added "fevers" <note>original Greek: πυρετοὶ (pyretoi)</note>, which occur very easily when, at the time of teething—because of the stimulating and twitching itch, the continued pain, and through sleeplessness—inflammations arise on account of the abundance of heat and moisture which children possess. Here, before all things, the teething and the itching must be considered as the nourishing causes: then the fever itself indicates the regimen, such as eating wholesome <note>original: *euchymis*, referring to foods that produce good humors or bodily fluids</note>, moistening, and cooling foods. Nor should those things be neglected which can be given to children, such as Julep of roses or violets, common barley-water <note>original: *ptisana vulgaris*</note>, etc., with prepared **burnt hartshorn** <note>the carbonized horn of a stag, used in historical medicine to absorb acid and reduce fever</note>. Also, for the sake of tempering heat and decay, syrups of lemon acidity, of sour pomegranates, or of Verjuice <note>original: *de Agresta*, a highly acidic juice made from unripe grapes</note> may be taken by licking to repress and halt the febrile exhalations.

<margin>Whether children are hot and moist? See Mercado <note>Luis Mercado (1525–1611), a prominent Spanish physician</note> on temperaments, question 57.</margin>

### Question 2.

## Can every kind of fever occur in children?

Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine," c. 460–370 BCE</note> seems to deny this toward the end of his book *On the Nature of Man*, where he Refuses to attribute **Quartan fever** <note>a fever that recurs every four days, often associated with malaria</note> to children. However, Mercurialis <note>Girolamo Mercuriale (1530–1606), an Italian physician famous for writing the first systematic treatise on pediatric diseases</note> notes in Book 2 of *On the Diseases of Children*, chapter 1, that because of their natural temperament, a **Synochus** <note>a continuous, non-intermitting fever</note> is most common to children, although other varieties of fever can also arise by accident or specific circumstances.

---

### Question 3.

## Should blood be let from children suffering from fever?

Rhasis <note>Rhazes (865–925 CE), a Persian polymath and influential physician</note> affirms in his work *On the Pestilence*, chapter 4, that **cupping glasses** <note>a method of bloodletting using heated glass jars to create suction</note> can be applied after the fifth month of age, a point which Prosper Alpinus <note>An Italian physician and botanist (1553–1617) known for his study of Egyptian medicine</note> elaborates upon in Book 2 of *Egyptian Medicine*, chapter 5. On the contrary, Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the "Prince of Physicians," whose Canon of Medicine was a standard textbook</note> (Book 4, Treatise 1, Chapter 21) denies this, arguing it should not be done before the first year. Mercurialis, in the passage cited above, approves the assertion of the "Prince" <note>referring to Avicenna</note> and says that he himself only applied cupping glasses to children after their first year, and then only if: 1. They are of a sanguine and robust constitution; 2. The cups are applied only to the legs, because the blood drawn from there does not so greatly weaken the 

<column-break/>

vital strength; 3. and no more than one or two drachms <note>a small unit of weight, roughly 3.5 to 7 grams</note> are evacuated.

---

<margin>3. Convulsions.</margin>
Furthermore, frequent **convulsions** occur at this time, especially alongside the aforementioned fevers, insofar as the crude humors <note>unprocessed bodily fluids</note> are liquefied and rushed toward the nervous parts, which are weak at this age. When the nerves are thus overwhelmed, a contortion arises at their source. For this reason, **Epilepsy** is common in children, particularly when, in addition to the cause mentioned, there is a quick and ready collection of "crudities" <note>undigested matter</note> and the corruption of milk in the stomach is observed. Here, excessive fullness should be avoided, and a stomach oppressed by too much food should occasionally be provoked to vomit using a finger or a feather dipped in oil. Externally, near the region of the **ensiform cartilage** <note>the pointed lower part of the breastbone</note>, a small bag should be hung on the chest containing fresh **male peony root**, if it can be obtained, and it should be hung together with the crushed seeds of the same plant. Internally, one should administer syrup of betony, of stoechas <note>French lavender</note>, of citron peel, etc., with a few drops of **spirit of vitriol prepared from Mars** <note>an acidic preparation of iron sulfate, used as a tonic</note>, mixed to a pleasant acidity. Also useful are spirit of black cherries with water distilled from linden flowers, etc. A small amount of these should be given even during the seizure itself, without neglecting other things that liberate one from a paroxysm, such as **rue** ground with vinegar and applied to the nostrils, **balsam of amber** rubbed onto the nostrils and the crown of the head, and the rubbing of the extremities with oil of sweet almonds.

### Question 4.
#### Do children suffer from convulsions caused by repletion? <note>original: "ex repletione"; in early medicine, this refers to an overabundance of bodily fluids or "humors" that overwhelms the system</note>

A *probable negative* seems likely: 1. because the nerves are very soft and can give way to the flowing matter; 2. for this reason, **paralysis** <note>a loss of sensation or movement</note> should occur from the stated cause rather than a convulsion; 3. furthermore, it seems the weakness of the nerves would hinder the creation of a convulsion. *We assert the affirmative*, regarding light and momentary convulsions which cannot be traced to dryness or malignancy. *Hence we respond to the first point:* although the nerves are very soft, they cannot give way indefinitely; *to the second:* we acknowledge the similarity, yet in children we call this state **convulsive** rather than **paralytic**; *to the third:* just as the nerves are still weak, the convulsion is likewise lighter and less painful.

<margin>4. Diarrhea.</margin>

Finally, **diarrhea** is addressed in this age group, which occurs due to an abundance of crude moisture, caused by sleeplessness, restlessness, feverish heat, pain in the gums, and other causes where digestion is impaired. Because of this, when nature is exhausted, the humors <note>the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were thought to determine health</note> rush through whatever gate is open; hence this is frequent during the time of **teething**. Such outflows of the bowels should not be stopped easily, because children of this sort are less subject to convulsions than others whose bowels are harder and who have a thicker constitution. For this reason, *Hippocrates* <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine," c. 460–370 BCE</note> established that they are subject to the aforementioned diseases, especially when they are cutting their **canine teeth** <note>original: "caninos dentes," also known as the eye teeth or cuspids; their eruption was historically considered particularly dangerous for infants</note>, which bring about more vehement pains due to their sharpness. But if a loss of strength is feared due to continuous bowel movements, it is necessary that we assist nature by providing **milk boiled down to a third and treated with iron** <note>original: "chalybeato"; milk in which hot steel or iron has been dipped, thought to infuse the liquid with strengthening properties</note>, **myrtle syrup**, **syrup of dried roses**, **syrup of quinces**, **syrup of the tips of oak leaves**, etc. Externally, the belly should be anointed with **quince oil**, and a **plaster made of bread crust** should be applied at the same time.

<margin>Diseases of children.</margin>
### Aphorism 26.

> As they grow older, they suffer from inflammation of the tonsils, inward protrusions of the vertebra at the nape of the neck, asthma, stones <note>bladder or kidney stones</note>, roundworms, pinworms, warts, satyriasis <note>here referring to abnormal genital inflammation or priapism in children</note>, strangury <note>painful, drop-by-drop urination</note>, scrofula <note>tuberculous swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck</note>, and other growths, but especially the aforementioned. <note>original: Πρεσβυτέροισι δὲ γινομένοισι παρίσθμια... The author is quoting the Greek text of Hippocrates' Aphorisms, Book 3, Aph. 26.</note>

<margin>1. Tonsillitis</margin>
Furthermore, as age advances slightly, other diseases are recorded from the time of teething until puberty. These all share a general cause, insofar as there is an overabundance of moisture <note>original: "humiditas"; referring to the "moist" humor common in children</note> throughout the body. This moisture, which was previously dormant, as it were, now begins to swell as it is slightly warmed; it is moved by the stirred-up heat, which attempts more powerfully to expel the superfluous matter, while at the same time the passages and vessels undergo a greater dilation. Here, first, is generated **tonsillitis** <note>original: "παρίσθμια" (paristhmia)</note>, which are tumors of the glands around the throat (some call them "tonsils" or "almonds" <note>original: "tonsillæ & amygdalæ"</note>). Because of the spongy nature of these parts, these tumors are quickly produced there by fluids <note>original: "fluxiones"</note> flowing from the brain. For this reason, inflammation of the throat, narrowing, and consequently difficult swallowing and breathing arise. First, the bowels should be provoked to excretion by an enema, or at the very least, by a sharp...

<column-break/>

...suppository. Then, soon in the early stages—if the disease presents with little matter—a very thin diet should be prescribed along with a gargle such as this: ℞ <note>Recipe</note> Take half a drachm of Bistort root, one handful each of Plantain herb and Self-heal <note>original: "prunella"</note>, half a handful of Oak leaves, and half a handful each of Pomegranate flowers <note>original: "balaust."</note> and Red roses. Boil these in a sufficient quantity of water until reduced by a third. Strain half a pound [of the liquid] and add six drachms each of Walnut Rob <note>a thickened fruit juice</note> and Syrup of Mulberries <note>original: "Diamoron"</note>. Mix. Externally, let an ointment be made with a mixture of sweet almond oil and rose oil. But if the ailment involves much matter, so that suppuration <note>the formation of pus</note> is to be expected, then in addition to general remedies, nature must be assisted by gargles made from a decoction of dried figs <note>original: "caricar."</note>, marshmallow seeds, etc. Externally, do not omit poultices <note>original: "cataplasmata"</note> made from barley flour and fenugreek, prepared with a decoction of dried figs, marshmallow, and honey.

### Regarding Aphorism 26.
### Question I.

->Why does Hippocrates place tonsillitis only after the time of teething?<-
**Response:** Galen says it is because they are so severe that they immediately kill <note>original: "jugulent," literally "cut the throat"</note> in the first stage of life. Mercurialis <note>Girolamo Mercuriale (1530–1606), a famous physician who wrote the first systematic treatise on pediatric diseases</note> adds that in infants, there is not such a copious attraction of matter to those parts; or if it does occur, the matter is not retained, since the generation of this condition requires that the matter flows with a certain force and is also held there.

### Question 2.

->Should enemas be used<-
->for children during inflammation<-
->of the tonsils?<-

This is denied by some because, first, the action of an enema <note>original: "clysteris"</note> cannot reach the affected site; second, the use of an enema seems dangerous due to the thinness of children's intestines; and third, a small, localized amount of inflammation does not justify a treatment aimed at preserving the whole body. However, since effort must be made to prevent further buildup of fluids <note>original: "affluxus"; the flow of humors toward the throat</note> and to create a "revulsion" <note>a medical technique of drawing excess humors away from an inflamed area to a distant part of the body</note> toward the lower parts, we instead defend the affirmative position. Responding to the objections: to the first, it does not hinder the treatment, because a greater buildup is nonetheless prevented; to the second, no danger is to be feared from gentle enemas; and to the third, indeed, a great deal of trouble can arise from a small amount of matter, especially when accompanied by blockages of the bowels.

<column-break/>

vertebra at the back of the head occurs. This happens when the bones are distorted because the ligaments have been loosened by the flow of fluids. Consequently, the swallowing of food and the drawing in of air are hindered, eventually resulting in a *type of Quinsy* <note>original: "Anginæ species"; a historical term for severe throat inflammation that threatens suffocation</note> in which a certain hollow appears in the neck. This is quite dangerous, which is why care must be taken at the beginning to prevent *such a condition from arising*.
