### Question 3.

->Can inflammation<-
->be the cause of<-
->dislocation?<-

This is denied because: 1. Dislocation and inflammation differ in kind, as the latter is an imbalance of qualities <note>original: "intemperies"; a humoral imbalance</note> while the former is a structural malformation; 2. Inflammation indicates nothing regarding the nature of a dislocation; and 3. The treatment for inflammation does nothing to cure a dislocation. *But we approve the affirmative view*, insofar as a flow of fluids to the tendons and ligaments occurs accidentally due to the nearby inflamed parts, which a dislocation very easily follows. *Therefore, we respond to the first point* that inflammation can be an accidental cause of dislocation; hence, *to the second*, it serves as a "necessary cause" <note>original: "causa sine qua non"</note> as long as it is present; and thus, *to the third*, although it does not by itself...

Furthermore, as age advances slightly, other diseases are noted from the time of teething until puberty. These all have a general cause, insofar as there is an overabundance of moisture <note>original: humiditas</note> in the whole body. This moisture, which was previously dormant as it were, now becomes somewhat heated and begins to swell <note>original: turgere</note> as it is stirred by the aroused heat of the growing body. This heat attempts more powerfully to expel these "superfluous" fluids, while at the same time the passages and vessels undergo a greater dilation. Produced here are:

-> Regarding Aphorism 26. <-

### Question I.

**W**hy are *paristhmia* <note>tonsillitis</note> placed only after the time of teething by Hippocrates? Response: Galen says it is because they are so severe that they would immediately kill an infant in its earliest age. Mercurialis <note>Girolamo Mercuriali, a famous 16th-century physician</note> adds that in infants, there is not such a copious attraction of fluids to those parts; or if there is, the matter is not retained, whereas the generation of this condition requires that the matter flow with a certain force and also be held there.

# ON THE DISEASES OF CHILDREN.

### Question 2.

### Whether Enemas are suitable for children during inflammation of the tonsils.

It is argued in the negative, first, because the action of an enema <note>original: clyster</note> cannot reach the affected site (the throat); second, because the use of an enema seems dangerous due to the thinness of the intestines in children; and third, because the small, localized matter of the inflammation does not warrant a treatment for the whole body. *However, since efforts must be made to prevent further flow of fluids to the throat and to create a diversion <note>original: revulsio; the practice of drawing fluids away from a diseased part to another part of the body</note> toward the lower parts, we support the affirmative position by responding to these objections. Specifically, to the first: nothing stands in the way, because a greater flow to the throat is nonetheless prevented; to the second: no danger is to be feared from mild enemas; and to the third: indeed, from a small amount of matter, much can arise, especially when constipation <note>original: alvi obstructionibus</note> occurs at the same time.*

<margin>
1. Displacement of the cervical vertebrae inward.
</margin>

Furthermore, when the muscles near the inflamed glands around the root of the tongue contract, <term>inward displacements of the vertebra at the nape of the neck</term> <note>original Greek: σπονδύλῳ τῷ κατὰ τὸ ἰνίον εἴσω ὤσιες</note>,

<column-break/>

dislocations of the vertebra located in the back of the head occur toward the interior. This happens when the ligaments are loosened by the discharge of fluids and the bones become distorted; as a result, the swallowing of food and the drawing of breath are hindered. Eventually, a type of <term>Quinsy</term> <note>original: Angina; a severe throat inflammation that threatens suffocation</note> develops, in which a certain hollow appears in the neck. This is quite dangerous, which is why care must be taken at the beginning so that such a thing does not arise.

### Question 3.

### Whether inflammation can be the cause of a dislocation?

It is argued in the negative because: 1. dislocation and inflammation differ in kind, since the latter is an imbalance of humors and the former is a structural deformity; 2. inflammation provides no indication of how to treat a dislocation; and 3. the treatment of inflammation does nothing to cure a dislocation. *But we approve of the affirmative view, insofar as an accidental flow of fluids to the tendons and ligaments occurs because of the neighboring inflamed parts, which a dislocation very easily follows. Therefore, in response to the first point: inflammation can be an indirect cause of dislocation. From this, regarding the second: it serves as an indicator as a "necessary cause" as long as it is present. And thus, regarding the third: by itself, it does not indeed*

<margin>3. Asthma</margin>
In the third place, **asthmas** <note>original Greek: άσθματα</note> are addressed. Children at this age become short of breath and asthmatic due to the flow of crude humors <note>unrefined or undigested fluids in the body's four-humor system</note> trickling from the brain to the lungs. In this situation, one must ensure that the **peccant matter** <note>original: materia peccans; the harmful substance or "morbid matter" causing the disease</note> does not increase further through intemperance. Therefore, if catarrh is present, drying and diverting agents should be prescribed; for the collected matter, preparing and evacuating remedies are used. In such cases, a fumigating powder made from **mastic**, **tacamahac**, and **frankincense** <note>original: olibano</note> is appropriate, used as incense in the bedroom and near the beds morning and evening. The matter should be prepared and thinned with syrup of **cat’s foot** <note>original: hispidula; also known as mountain everlasting</note>, **jujube**, or **hyssop**, unless some feverish heat is present, in which case something like syrup of violets, wild poppy, or purslane may be mixed in. If these remedies are insufficient, one must progress to **oxymel of tobacco** <note>original: oxymel de Peto vel Nicotiana; a medicinal syrup of vinegar, honey, and tobacco</note>, which has a remarkable power for thinning fluids and clearing them through vomiting; for this reason, it must be used cautiously and primarily in older children. Externally, a liniment of roasted onions and crushed chicken fat rubbed onto the chest is recommended.

<column-break/>

---

### Question 4.

## Whether Syrup of Cat’s Foot is suitable for asthma in children?

It seems to be opposed, because: 1. The herb **cat’s foot** <note>original: hispidula; also called pes cati</note> has an astringent <note>binding or contracting</note> quality, yet here it seems necessary to open and thin the fluids. 2. It serves to heal **solutions of unity** <note>original: consolidationem Unitatis; a medical term for healing wounds or ulcers where the tissue's natural continuity is broken</note> in lung ulcerations, which is hardly a concern in children here. Finally, 3. it cannot prepare or thin viscous <note>thick and sticky</note> matter. *But in fact, experience confirms that this syrup is highly effective for chest conditions, regarding which one may consult Ronodeus in his Pharmaceutical Dispensatory.* Note these points regarding the objections: to the 1st, that astringent power is tempered by other ingredients so that it better supports the strengthening of the lungs; hence, to the 2nd, we respond that the "unity" of the lungs is better preserved; and to the 3rd, through the strengthening of the internal organs, the viscous matter is prepared by the process of digestion.

<margin>4. Dispositions toward stones.</margin>
In the fourth place are **lithiases** <note>original Greek: λιθιάσιες; the formation of stones in the body</note>, or the disposition toward stones, specifically regarding the bladder, where a stone is easily generated at this age: 1. because of the accumulation of **crude humors** <note>undigested or unrefined fluids</note> due to the greediness of children; 2. the strength of the **expulsive faculty** <note>the body’s natural ability to push out waste</note>; 3. the narrowness of the bladder’s passage; and 4. aided at the same time by a more robust **innate heat** <note>the vital warmth believed to drive biological processes</note>. Here, the opportunity for the stone's generation should be cut off, such as ill-timed movements after eating, constant undigested matter, thick drinks, sticky foods, etc. Once the signs of a future stone are noted (which frequent **strangury** <note>painful, interrupted urination</note>, urinating drop by drop, and sand <note>original: fabulum; likely a typo for "sabulum," meaning gravel or sediment</note> flowing with the urine indicate), baths made from a decoction of **marshmallow root**, **mallow herb**, **melilot**, and **chamomile** should be frequently applied on a fasting and empty stomach. First, one or two spoonfuls of **oil of sweet almonds** should be administered with a draught of **elecampane wine**, or if feverish heat is feared, with a chicken broth boiled with **parsley root**. This is done so that by relaxing the passages, that which has collected may be expelled, and new matter may not easily collect again. Externally, **oil of scorpions** <note>a traditional medicinal oil infused with scorpions, believed to break up stones</note> should be frequently used as an ointment around the root of the member and the pubic area.

### Question 5.

->Whether crude humors are<-
->the cause of stones in<-
->children?<-

It can be doubted, because: 1. all [children] are equally greedy, yet not all suffer from the stone; add to this 2. that undigested matter and a more robust innate heat are rarely present together; and furthermore 3. **Galen** <note>the influential 2nd-century Roman physician</note> himself, in his commentary on the *Epidemics* (Book 6, Commentary 3, Text 15), attributes this instead to the property of coagulation. *But the thicker urine of children, with its sandy sediment, confirms the affirmative view; however, it must be noted* regarding the first point, that one cause is not sufficient, but the others are also necessary. Indeed, 2. undigested matter and a more robust innate heat can exist together when the **concocting heat** <note>digestive fire</note> and the food do not meet in the right proportion. Finally, 3. we concede Galen’s point, but without excluding the other causes; on this matter, see those things proposed in our *Problems*, as well as in Book 1 of our *Medicinal Letters*, Sections 8 and 9.

### Question 6.

->Whether the strength of<-
->the expulsive faculty<-
->can also be a cause?<-

This is denied for the following reasons: 1. the strength of the **expulsive faculty** <note>original: facultatis expultricis; the body's natural power to drive out waste</note> preserves against the formation of a stone; 2. a weakened expulsive faculty is the cause of this malady in the elderly; 3. it does not seem to be present in children, insofar as nature is concerned with retaining as much as possible for the growth of the body. *However, we affirm the opposite*, insofar as the serum <note>the watery part of the humors</note> is separated from the "workshops of digestion" <note>the stomach and liver</note> along with **crude tartar** <note>original: crudo tartaro; gritty, undigested sediment or waste</note> too quickly and before the time of complete perfection. *Hence, we respond to the first point:* the strength of the expulsive faculty preserves with respect to the kidneys and bladder, but not with respect to the whole body, by expelling matter before its time. Thus, the second instance also proceeds concerning the urinary passages and the bladder. Regarding the third point, it should be noted that where there is the most nourishment, there is also the most waste left behind.

<margin>5. Worms.</margin>
In the fifth place are **worms** <note>original Greek: ἑλμινθες</note>; their production in 

<column-break/>

this stage of childhood is more frequent than in the preceding wetter age or the subsequent drier age. They are created from putrid **phlegmatic matter** <note>original: materia pituitosa; a thick, cold humor</note>, to which they are believed to owe their origin, life, and nourishment. They are categorized here into two varieties: **roundworms** <note>original Greek: στρογγύλαι</note> and those called **ascarids** <note>original Greek: ἀσκαρίδες; pinworms</note>, which are smaller worms that appear in the lower part of the large intestines, following the gluttony of children. Therefore, once the causes serving the generation of worms have been cut off and an optimal diet established, one must look toward killing the generated worms, or at least rendering them senseless, and afterwards expelling them from the body itself. Therefore, the use of **Oxymel** <note>a medicinal syrup made of honey and vinegar</note> is appropriate, prepared from honey, very sharp vinegar, and a decoction of **wormwood** <note>original: absynthij</note>; likewise, **wormseed** <note>original: semen Chinæ; a plant used to expel parasites</note> lightly prepared with sugar, and similar remedies. After using these, a suitable quantity of <gloss>a specific preparation of turbith with Rhubarb</gloss> <note>original: spec. diaturbith cum Rhab.; "turbith" is a root used as a purgative</note> is correctly prescribed for expulsion in wormwood wine, or pills may be given to older children made from one part **aloes**, and half a part each of **myrrh**, **water germander**, and **white dittany** <note>original: Myrrhæ, Scordij & Dictamni albi</note>, prepared with wormwood syrup. Externally, anointing the navel with crushed **cumin** mixed with **ox gall** <note>the bile of a bull, traditionally used for its bitter properties</note> and reduced into the form of a liniment with wormwood oil is also recommended. ### Question 7.

->Whether worms derive their life from phlegmatic matter?<-

This itself seems less probable, because: 1. matter cannot possess the nature of an "efficient cause" <note>the active agent that brings something into being</note>; 2. the heat of putrefaction <note>the warmth generated by rotting</note> generates nothing; 3. the inanimate cannot be the cause of the animate. However, *we assert the contrary*, insofar as worms born from this same matter increase and are sustained by it. *To these doubts we respond*: to the 1st, although matter does not by itself act as an efficient cause, it nevertheless contributes to the preservation of life when the heat of putrefaction is present. To the 2nd, it does not stand in the way that the heat of putrefaction—if we consider only the starting point—generates nothing; yet it does produce something new by preparing the matter for its final form. To the 3rd, indeed it can, insofar as it is activated by **innate heat** <note>original: nativo calore; the vital heat believed to exist in all living bodies</note>, since in this case not only "univocal" generation <note>life from like life</note> 

<column-break/>

but also **equivocal generation** <note>original: æquivocæ generationes; the archaic belief that life, like worms or insects, could spontaneously arise from non-living matter like rot or phlegm</note> has a place.

<margin>6. Hanging warts</margin>
Furthermore, we find *hanging warts* <note>original Greek: ἀκροχορδόνες (akrochordones)</note>, which arise from a thicker matter that a stronger heat has separated and pushed through the tiny filaments of the veins to the surface of the body. 
<margin>7. Facial swellings.</margin>

(This is the interpretation of *Galen in book 8 of On the Doctrines, chapter 6, and his book on the Language of Hippocrates*, whom *Cardanus* and others follow. *Mercurialis* argues that "priapism" <note>a persistent, painful erection</note> should be understood here. *Brassavola and Fuchsius* understand it as Elephantiasis; but they are in error, as that is not a disease of children.) These begin due to down-flowing phlegm.

Eighthly, **stranguries** <note>original: στραγγουρίαι; a condition where urine is passed drop by drop with pain</note>, arising from acrid matter.

### Question 8.

->Whether scrofulous swellings in children arise from phlegm?<-
<note>original: "strumæ," referring to scrofula, a swelling of the lymph nodes, typically in the neck.</note>

Hippocrates, in his *Book on Glands*, seems to affirm this when he determines that scrofula is formed from a copious, sticky, and slow-moving flow. Celsus, in *Book 5, Chapter 28*, posits that the matter hardened under the skin is composed of blood and pus. From this, Plutarch, in the second volume of his *Table Talk*, suggests that scrofula is produced from bloody humor and heat. Note from Girolamo Mercuriali’s *On the Diseases of Children*, Book 1, Chapter 5: since the glands are nourished by <term>phlegmatic blood</term> <note>blood mixed with phlegm, one of the four bodily humors</note>, it is evident that scrofula is formed primarily from phlegm, and secondarily from blood with which pus is sometimes mixed, etc.

---

In conclusion, it should be noted that we may also conveniently refer here to **skin eruptions** <note>original: ἐξανθήματα (exanthemata)</note> accompanied by fever—namely, **smallpox** <note>original: variolas</note> and **measles** <note>original: morbillos</note>. These afflict childhood most of all, as they are unnatural "flowering out" of the human body caused by the defects of impure blood drawn in during the final months in the womb.

<column-break/>

As nature purges itself from deep within, these eruptions emerge accompanied by fever. They are formed either from a thicker humor—becoming raised and filled with pus, called **smallpox**—or from a thinner humor, appearing as broad spots called **measles**. In both cases, care must be taken to halt the boiling and heat of the humors, to assist a sluggish nature in the process of expulsion, and to defend the external parts as much as possible from dangerous accidents. We achieve the first of these through a gentle evacuation of the primary passages <note>the digestive tract</note>, by bloodletting in older or full-blooded children, and by using "alteratives" that resist inflammation and rot. The second goal—settling the heat of the blood—is accomplished through the use of tempered **protective antidotes** <note>original: ἀλεξιφηρτικῶν (alexipharmics); substances believed to ward off poison or contagion</note>, such as **Bezoar stone** <note>a stone-like mass found in the stomachs of animals, prized as a universal antidote</note>, prepared burnt **hartshorn** <note>deer antler</note>, **Sealed Earth** <note>medicinal clay stamped with an official seal</note>, seeds of **Columbine**, and so on. The third goal consists of defending the eyes, nostrils, and throat; we do this by using treatments that prevent the generation of **pustules** <note>original: ἐκθυμάτων (ekthymata)</note> in those parts at the start by repelling them, or by soothing those already formed and bringing them to maturity without damage to the underlying parts. Regarding all these matters, we once established a specific **formal inquiry** <note>original: σύζητησιν (syzetesis)</note> which we explained more fully in a German Treatise, the translation of which into the Latin language we are pleased to provide below.

## On the Diagnostic Signs
## of this Disease.

Now it is necessary that we descend to the diagnostic signs of this disease; where above all it is important to notice the symptoms and marks from which we may gather that this disease is to be expected.

<margin>Diagnostic signs from impaired functions.</margin>
Those symptoms are taken first from **impaired functions** <note>original: "actionibus læsis"; a traditional medical category referring to bodily processes that are no longer working normally.</note>: namely when **headache appears along with heaviness of the eyes and neck**, because of the rising vapors of the <term>boiling blood</term> <note>original: "ebullientis sanguinis"; early modern doctors believed fevers were caused by blood "boiling" or fermenting like new wine.</note> in the larger veins.

When the **back hurts** from the same cause.

When the **nostrils itch**, because of sharp vapors rising upward, from which sharp <term>catarrhs</term> <note>original: "catarrhi"; an excessive buildup or discharge of fluid, often from the nose or throat.</note> take their origin from the head.

When the **whole body is rendered heavy and sluggish, and pain is stirred up as if in the skin**, specifically when that sharp and hot blood is expelled toward the outer parts of the body.

When **infants are terrified in sleep, or adults** 

<column-break/>

speak as if in a slight delirium; because the thicker and hotter vapors rising upward occupy the head itself.

When **spasm and signs of epilepsy appear**, because of the commotion of the corrupted and impure blood.

When **breathing is shortened**, because of the hot vapors which hinder the chest from being able to draw in free air.

When a **dry cough appears**, which happens while sharp catarrhs occupy the <term>windpipe</term> <note>original: "asperam arteriam"</note> or the lungs within.

When the **feet tremble** as the sick person turns themselves, because of the abundant matter which occupies and weakens the nerves.

When **sneezing is frequent**, because of the sharp vapors which attack the <term>meninges</term> <note>original: "meninges"; the membranes that envelop the brain.</note> or the coverings of the brain.

When **frequent stretching and yawning is present**, because of the vaporous blood which hides between the skin and the flesh.

When **palpitation of the heart appears**, because of the hot vapors of the blood, by which the <term>Vital Power</term> <note>original: "facultas Vitalis"; the biological force believed to be responsible for the heartbeat and pulse.</note> is, as it were, oppressed.

<margin>Diagnostic signs in altered excretions.</margin>
SECONDLY, the **symptoms which appear in altered excretions** <note>original: "excretis mutatis"; changes in the body's fluids or waste products.</note> are considered: such as eyes tearing without cause, either because they suffer from sharp vapors, or because of the watery moisture which is collected by the boiling of the blood.

## On the treatment of this disease.

<margin>Indications for a cure.</margin>
Since this illness begins with a great "boiling" of the blood, from which all kinds of more serious symptoms are to be feared, we must first pay close attention to how we can assist with our aid.

So that (2) **Nature** <note>In this context, "Nature" refers to the body’s innate healing power and its effort to expel the disease.</note> may achieve its purpose more quickly, it must be helped with purgative means. Then (3) it must be seen immediately how the various parts of the body heavily damaged by the smallpox are to be defended and preserved.

Regarding the first point, in adults and <term>sanguine</term> <note>People with a "sanguine" temperament were thought to have an abundance of blood, making them more prone to "boiling" or inflammatory diseases.</note> individuals, this is easily achieved through <term>bloodletting</term> <note>original: "Venæ sectionem"; the practice of opening a vein to restore the balance of humors.</note>. This could also be done in younger children of 7 or 8 years, if it were as accepted in our custom as it was among the ancient physicians. We frequently see that in these children, **Nature** helps itself through a nosebleed <note>original: "narium hæmorrhagiam"</note>, which is why such children recover much more easily than others.

After bloodletting, a gentle purgation is helpful to prevent hardness of the bowels, even in infants; this can be successfully accomplished through the use of <term>Manna</term> <note>A sweet, gummy sap from the flowering ash tree, used as a mild laxative.</note>, or syrup of roses or violets, or the raisin wine mentioned above.

Malignant symptoms must also be resisted.
</margin>
If, however, an internal poisonous corruption of the blood is mixed in with the smallpox—which usually happens when this disease rages most severely beyond its usual custom, even in the winter time, and very quickly prostrates the strength of the heart—this condition is easily recognized by a changed pulse, frequent <term>fainting</term> <note>original: "lipothymia"</note>, excessive anxiety, and the **Hippocratic face** <note>A classic medical term for a face with sunken eyes, hollow temples, and pinched nose, indicating the patient is near death.</note>, with the eyes sinking deeply, and similar symptoms. One could also boil some water germander and the aforementioned viper's grass root together with sweating potions, to be used as a daily drink.

<margin>
Diet should not be neglected along with the aforesaid.
</margin>
While these and similar means are used in the first few days to encourage sweating, nature will also be assisted by a certain prescription of **Diet**. Here it must first be diligently observed that patients guard themselves against the outside air, especially if it is cold, since Nature would be hindered in that way from expelling the smallpox and measles <note>The "expulsion" refers to the belief that the rash must be pushed out from the internal organs to the skin to save the patient.</note>.

<margin>
The surrounding air.
</margin>
For this reason, the heated rooms <note>original: "hypocausta"</note> must always be kept warm, yet not so much that the patient's strength is weakened by excessive heat; this can be easily recognized by a resulting tightness of the chest and the onset of fainting.

<margin>
Food.
</margin>
As for food, moderation is first and foremost best. Those foods should be used which are easy to digest, not "hot" in nature, but rather helpful in the process of expulsion. These include hulled barley, or a wine-broth mixed with half-part rose water and a little mace and saffron. <margin>Decoction of lentils.</margin>
Since the common people err somewhat in preparing the decoction of lentils mentioned here, we have decided to add a few words here regarding its preparation and use. It must be noted, therefore, that the skins of lentils have an **astringent** <note>original: "stipticam," meaning they tend to shrink or constrict body tissues.</note> property; for this reason, care must be taken that they are discarded if they are to help in the expulsion of the rash.

<margin>Is red wine appropriate?</margin>
Wine in this disease—especially
from the beginning—is harmful, since
feverish heat is always present: and although
the common people think that ***Red wine*** is 
appropriate here, experience demonstrates 
otherwise. For if it is 
strong, it promotes inflammation; 
but if it is weak and sour, it hinders 
the "expulsion" <note>The process of the rash moving from the internal organs to the skin.</note>.

It should be noted here, however, that in those 
places where wine is in use, in the second 
week—namely when the measles 
and smallpox have been properly led 
out to the exterior, and the feverish symptoms 
have ceased—a ***thin Rhenish*** or 
***Neckar wine***, diluted with a decoction 
of barley, can be used for the 
strengthening of the stomach.

<column-break/>

<margin>Sleep.</margin>
Regarding sleep, in the first days 
it is not necessary to violently 
provoke it; since Nature always 
performs the duty of expulsion better 
when the sick are enjoying moderate 
sleep.

For this reason, if at the beginning too much 
sleep appears, it is necessary to lead the 
sick away from it, by offering rose 
vinegar to the nostrils to be smelled. But 
if sleep remains deep-seated, it is a sign 
of greater internal inflammation, 
and of the rising of hot vapors, which 
we can meet through the above-mentioned means 
intended for the "boiling of the blood."

<margin>Loosening of the bowels.</margin>
A daily movement of the stool is 
also necessary, but through 
mild and temperate means, just as 
was said above.

<margin>Affections of the mind.</margin>
<gloss>Softening of the bowels</gloss>
As for disturbances of the mind—
fear, consternation, sadness, 
and the like—these are excessively 
harmful, because through them the blood 
recurs from the exterior to the interior, 
and in this way generates greater 
anxiety.

<margin>Regarding the third [point]</margin>
After all these things have been 
diligently provided for, right from the 
beginning of this disease, this third 
point must also be well observed: 
namely, how we may protect 
the various members which 
could easily be harmed by the smallpox.

<margin>Protection of the eyes.</margin>
Here, first, the eyes must be well 
guarded; since for very many 
people, sight is lost through this 
disease.

...if the throat <note>The Latin text begins mid-sentence; context suggests the throat or gullet.</note> is seized by pustules, the following barley decoction will be beneficial if it is drunk frequently by the spoonful: Take: 1 pound of barley decoction, 4 ounces each of rose syrup and endive syrup, and 1 ounce of myrtle berry syrup. <margin>Protection of the lips.</margin>
To protect the lips, where the smallpox causes great pain due to their sensitivity and delicate substance, it is useful to soak *quince seeds* in *rose water* overnight, and then thoroughly rub the lips with that mucilaginous water.

In this way, if care is established, parents and others serving the sick have fulfilled their duty. In the end, nature helps itself and does not require many means or remedies.

<column-break/>

<margin>Judgment on topical remedies.</margin>
Although many labor anxiously over how they might open and dry out those pustules through external means, experience itself nevertheless demonstrates that there is less danger if nature's ordinary course is left alone; for we could easily go astray in such external care.

However, it must be carefully noted that patients should not cause themselves harm by scratching and opening the pustules before the proper time. Indeed, not only could unsightly marks <note>original: "naevi"</note> arise from this, but even long-lasting and malignant ulcers. By doing this, the natural heat is hindered in its operation and cannot complete the necessary suppuration <note>The process of forming or discharging pus, which the author views as a necessary stage of the disease's "cooking" or "maturation."</note>.

<margin>Legitimate use of external remedies.</margin>
But if the maturation of the pustules is delayed too long, and they appear white and full of purulent matter, they should be lightly anointed with *sweet almond oil*. In this way, the pain will be lessened, the pus will mature, and the opened pustules will heal more easily.

Opening [the pustules] with silver or gold or other small needles can also be permitted, provided that the pustules already appear mature and well-suppurated.

# CONCLUSION.

<margin>On the serious accidents <note>In a medical context, "accidents" refers to complications or symptoms.</note> of smallpox and measles.</margin>
By way of a concluding flourish, it is necessary to add something here regarding the grave and dangerous symptoms that sometimes occur both alongside the smallpox itself and afterward. Indeed, these symptoms appear more frequently today as this disease spreads among the people, bringing a **contagious malignancy** with it.

<column-break/>

<margin>Epilepsy.</margin>
Experience demonstrates that sometimes *Epilepsy* <note>Seizures or "the falling sickness."</note> coincides with the disease, if nature has not been strong enough, nor able to promptly expel those evil and corrupt **humidities** <note>The "humors" or bodily fluids believed to cause disease.</note> to the skin. For this reason, with the help of the rising vaporous blood, they are carried straight to the head, and there they attack the beginning of the nerves—namely, the brain itself.

When this happens, it is necessary to add to the previously mentioned remedies required by this disease those which are suitable for the head and which resist the Epileptic disease. Therefore, **male peony root** <note>original: "Radix pæoniæ masculæ." Specific genders of plants were often distinguished in old herbalism.</note>, if it can be had fresh, crushed together with its seed and tied in a small pouch, can be most usefully hung around the necks of infants as an **amulet**.

Internally, one spoonful of syrup of citron peel may be administered occasionally with the best **Spirit of Vitriol from Mars** <note>original: "Spir. Vitrioli ex Marte." An acidic preparation of iron sulfate, used here as a tonic.</note>, tempered to a pleasant acidity; likewise, water of **black cherries** distilled two or three times with linden flowers.

<margin>2. Convulsive disease.</margin>
Furthermore, there is sometimes found a convulsive disease, called *Kriebelkranckheit* by the Germans <note>Literally "itching-sickness." This likely refers to ergotism, a poisoning from fungus on grain that caused painful muscle spasms and gangrene.</note>, similar to that which raged most fiercely in neighboring regions twenty years ago. I had patients of this kind both here in the City and round about in the district of **Grünberg** <note>Likely Zielona Góra in modern-day Poland.</note> nearly ten years ago, and by the help of God and my counsel, I successfully helped them all.

### THE RESOLUTION.

<margin>Malignant gonorrhea.</margin>

Since the sufferer voluntarily confessed that, from impure intercourse, he had first suffered for some time from gonorrhea—not a simple flow of seminal matter, but one joined with corrosive sharpness and malignancy—communicated by contagion from an infected harlot when the genital organs became heated during the act of Venus <note>A common euphemism for sexual intercourse.</note> and their pores were opened, with the prostate glands becoming inflamed internally, from which part the semen afterwards flows with pus; it was

<column-break/>

<margin>Prognosis.</margin>
We pronounced that this pox <note>original: "Luem" — referring here to the "Great Pox" or syphilis.</note> would be quite stubborn and rebellious, because from the mentioned symptoms it was gathered that the seeds of the malignant disease had crept in more deeply and taken firm root. This was further aided by the patient's phlegmatic disposition of body. Just as such a constitution is more difficult to infect—since a warm constitution, combined with a ready boiling of the blood, looseness of the passages, and softness of the parts, is much more suited to receive the contagion—so, once it has received the poisonous stain, it makes the cure more difficult. This is because the disease becomes more fixed in such thick and viscous humors <note>In traditional medicine, "phlegmatic" humors were thought to be cold and sticky, making them harder to clear from the body.</note>, and the body’s natural power to expel waste is more hindered.

<column-break/>

After making this prognosis in the form of advice (since the patient lived many miles away from our practice), we attempted to help him in the following manner. 
<margin>Indications.</margin>
Before all things, truly, according to the "Preservatory Indication," it is right first to demolish the fuel of the evil. Once that is done, the second goal looks to the disease itself and its immediate containing cause; finally, in the third place, a particular correction of the symptoms and concurrent defects is also required.

<margin>Regarding the 1st.</margin>
*Regarding the first*, the fuel of the sickness is withdrawn by convenient preparation, digestion, and evacuation <note>The medical process of softening "bad humors" and then purging them from the body.</note>. This includes no neglect of the dietary regimen and other factors pertaining to the "six non-natural things" <term>Six non-natural things: In early medicine, these were external factors like air, diet, sleep, and exercise that affected health but were not part of the body's internal nature.</term>. Therefore, after first performing the following mild evacuation, the median vein of the right arm should be cut, so that nature might be freed for a little while from the burden of excessive blood;

> Take: Agaric <note>A medicinal fungus used as a purgative.</note>, 2 drams.
> Ginger, 1/2 dram; Anise seed, 1 scruple.
> Infuse overnight in a sufficient quantity of Mint and Blessed Thistle <note>original: "Card. bened." (Carduus benedictus)</note> water. In the morning, let it boil slightly and strain 5 and 1/2 ounces. Add:
> Syrup of Safflower, 1 ounce.
> Extract of Diacarthamum <note>A strong laxative made from safflower seeds.</note>, 2 and 1/2 scruples.
> Cinnamon water, 1 dram.
> Mix and make a draught.

With the excessive blood thus diminished, the preparation, digestion, and evacuation should be performed in the following manner:

> Take: Roots of Valerian and Fennel, 1/2 dram each.
> Herbs of Blessed Thistle and Water Germander <note>original: "Scordy." (Scordium), a plant traditionally used for its antiseptic and drying properties.</note>.

For meat, the following are suitable: veal, kid, mutton, chicken, wild venison, and mountain birds. Eggs should be fresh and soft-boiled. Seasoning should be modest and sparing, made with roots of parsley and fennel, onions, garlic, mus-

tard, wild radish, ginger, mace, cinnamon, pepper, saffron, etc.; these are naturally suited to cut through and digest phlegmatic and viscous humors and prepare them for evacuation.
For drink, let there first be Neckar or Rhenish wine of middling strength. Later, movement of the body should be performed by walking about in a room, since by this means the limbs grow warmer and the expulsive force [of the body] is more quickly excited. Customary excretions <note>Natural bodily functions such as bowel movements and urination.</note> should be promoted as much as possible.
Sleep should be at night only, so that by day the Natural faculties may more effectively fulfill their duty in the expulsion and separation of heterogeneous <note>Foreign or waste matter in the body.</note> substances. The passions of the mind should be moderate; for by their exacerbation, which throws everything into total disorder, nothing worse can happen to those suffering from illness.

### SECOND BOOK OF PART II.

<margin>
The method of proceeding by wood decoction.
</margin>
While simultaneously observing the method of procedure, I answer that for the common method of healing—which is completed by the administration of a sweat-inducing decoction—nothing at all can be desired [to be added]. This is because the bodies are first duly prepared not only by prior digestions, purgings, and bloodletting, but also by cleansing baths. Furthermore, the wood decoction itself <note>Likely Guaiacum or "Holy Wood," a standard 16th-17th century treatment for syphilis.</note>, combined with a suitable diet, is diligently continued until the patients seem perfectly restored, while not neglecting external means required by the specific symptoms of each sufferer. However, since many are not perfectly healed despite all diligence and even repeated treatments, and others suffer a relapse shortly after being "cured," it is not without reason that we ask:

<margin>
Why is the Wood Treatment not always sufficient?
</margin>
Whether, besides the *Wood Treatment* <note>original: "Ligni Curam"</note> (which excels in the early stages of the Pox), it is hardly sufficient for a rooted or long-standing disease? This seems especially true among the Germans, whose bodies are well-fleshed <note>original Greek: "ευσαρκα" (eusarka)</note>, more compact, and solid—and thus more prone to retaining and rooting the Venereal malignancy than the Italians and similar peoples. In the latter, due to a less dense muscular constitution, such malignancy is more quickly driven out by the force of sweat. Therefore, should not Mercurial and Metallic Remedies also be employed, whether by a suitable *Ointment* <note>original: "Inunctio"</note>,

<column-break/>

or by fumigation, or by the administration of *Turpeth Mineral* <term>Turpeth Mineral: A yellow basic mercury sulfate used as a powerful emetic and purgative to "drive out" humors.</term>, or similar duly prepared remedies? This is also observed in the neighboring Imperial Republics, where the restoration of those suffering in the hospitals is more exquisite, shorter, and more certain. There, after the universal remedies—namely digestion, purging, and bloodletting—have been performed, Mercurials are administered, such as *Fumigation* <note>original: "Suffitus"</note> or *Ointment*, depending on whether the pox has occupied external or internal parts. For "French nodes" <note>original: "tophis Gallicis," referring to bony swellings or gummata caused by syphilis.</note> and joint pains, *Mercurial Caustic Water* is used simultaneously; indeed, *Turpeth Mineral* is more often given internally, especially

The method of proceeding in Ointments, Fumigation, etc.

This consists of a spoonful or two of Theriac Water <note>original: "Aqua Theriacali," a complex herbal distillate used against poisons.</note> mixed with a certain antidote. Afterward, the *Fumigation* or *Ointment* is undertaken in a Spartan bath <note>original: "Laconico," a dry sweating room.</note>; then the wood decoction is given, and sweat is provoked in bed, with another draught of the decoction given at midday for the sake of sweating. Such *Fumigation* and *Ointment*, and even the administration of *Turpeth Mineral*, is repeated three, four, or even more times, until the treatment's effect—principally *salivation* <term>Salivation: A process where the patient was induced to drool excessively (sometimes pints a day), which doctors believed carried the "venereal poison" out of the body.</term>—follows. This continues until the malignancy of the disease is exhausted by it, while in the meantime the wood decoction is taken every morning and evening for...

# OBSERVATION III.

->**The Venereal Pox contracted from a shared bed.**<-

**A** girl about 18 years of age, serving in the household of a Noble master who was suffering from the <term>Venereal Pox</term> <note>original: "lue Venerea"; Syphilis.</note>, and sharing a common bed with his concubine, was finally infected everywhere with <term>French pustules</term> <note>original: "pustulis Gallicis"; the characteristic skin sores of syphilis.</note> and <term>condylomas</term> <note>Wart-like growths or skin lesions, often appearing in the genital area.</note> in her private parts, after suffering various symptoms of nocturnal pains, tightness of the chest, and the like.

# RESOLUTION.

<margin>
French pustules.
Nocturnal pains of the limbs and chest.
</margin>
**I**t was concluded that this girl was first infected by the shared bed because the entire household was suspect on account of this pox. This infection was first cutaneous, manifesting as French pustules—reddish-yellow, round, covered with a dry crust, creeping around the body, and in some places ulcerating the skin more deeply. These were preceded by nocturnal pains in the limbs and chest, indicating that the malignancy was still deeper within...

### OBSERVATION V.

## Confirmed Syphilis in a robust body.

Catharina Heblerin, a farm servant from near Geyßlingen, twenty-two years of age and endowed with a rather robust constitution, was infected through sexual contact with <term>French pustules</term> <note>original: "pustulis Gallicis"; a common historical name for the sores associated with syphilis.</note> over her entire body, as well as <term>fissures</term> <note>original: "Rhagadibus"; painful cracks or slits in the skin or mucous membranes.</note> and ulcerated sores on her private parts, to such a degree that she could no longer conceal the affliction.

### THE RESOLUTION.

She was therefore admitted on the first of October in the year 1623. First, she took a digestive powder <note>A "digestive" in this context was a medicine intended to "cook" or prepare the diseased humors for evacuation.</note> consisting of 15 grains of <term>Starch of Cuckoo-pint</term> <note>original: "Faeculae Aronis".</note>, 1 scruple of <term>vitriolated Tartar</term> <note>original: "Tartari vitriolati"; potassium sulfate, used as a laxative.</note>, and 8 grains of red Coral. Mixed.
This was taken with a broth of distilled Chicory root. On the following day, she took pills composed as follows:
Take: 1 scruple of Golden Pills <note>original: "Pil. Aurear."; a standard strong purgative pill.</note>.
1.5 scruples of <term>Universal Extract</term> <note>original: "Extr. cathol. Th."; likely the "Extractum Catholicum," a multi-purpose laxative resin.</note>.

<column-break/>

15 grains of <term>sweetened mercury</term> <note>original: "Merc. dulcific."; calomel, a common mercurial treatment for syphilis.</note>.
3 drops of Oil of Anise.
With Fumitory water, make into standard pills.

After these had opened the bowels only three times, we proceeded to stronger measures. On October 3rd, the <term>Golden Panacea</term> <note>original: "Panacea aurea"; a potent chemical medicine made from a "balanced mixture" of Crocus of Metals (antimony) and sweetened mercury.</note> was administered at a dose of 12 grains with a <term>laxative raisin</term> <note>original: "Zibeba laxativa"; a large dried grape or raisin stuffed with purgative medicine.</note>. As this worked only once, her nature required an even more powerful medicine; for this reason, on the fourth day of October, 18 grains of the same Panacea were given with three raisins, which resulted in one instance of vomiting and three bowel movements. On the fifth day, 1 scruple of the Panacea provoked two bouts of vomiting and three stools. On the sixth of October, she rested from internal medicine while <term>Caustic Water</term> <note>original: "Aqua Caustica"; a corrosive chemical solution used to burn away diseased tissue.</note> was applied to the external pustules and ulcers after a bath. On the seventh, she continued with the evacuation, taking 1 scruple of Golden Panacea, 6 grains of prepared <term>Scammony</term> <note>original: "Diagryd. praep."; a harsh purgative resin.</note>, 8 grains of Cuckoo-pint starch, and 2 scruples of Rose preserve, administered as a <term>bolus</term> <note>A soft, rounded mass of medicine, often mixed with honey or sugar to make it easier to swallow.</note> with sugar. On the eighth, after a preliminary cleansing bath, the Surgeon moistened the ulcerated parts with the Caustic Water. On the ninth and tenth of October, the previously mentioned purgative was repeated, which performed its work five or six times daily through the bowels alone. On the eleventh, resting again from purging, we applied the Caustic Water. On the twelfth, the purging dose was increased in this manner...

<margin>French pustules on the forehead.</margin>
**W**hen the current patient had suffered from severe <term>tympanites</term> <note>a condition where the abdomen is stretched by gas, like a drum</note> about two years ago, and was finally recovering with difficulty, he was seized by <term>cachexia</term> <note>a general state of ill health and wasting</note>. This was preceded and accompanied by spontaneous exhaustion and pains in the joints, especially in the evening and at night, which gave rise to a suspicion of the <term>Venereal plague</term> <note>syphilis</note>. This was particularly suspected since he had previously suffered from <term>gonorrhea</term>, which undoubtedly arose from the malignancy of that same plague. Thus, the hidden disease afflicted the sufferer for some time, until it manifested itself through pustules around the forehead—reddish, raised, and covered with a dry crust—<margin>Aphthæ.</margin> through <term>aphthæ</term> <note>mouth sores</note> (or foul little ulcers of the mouth, turning lead-blue at the edges), <margin>Serpigo.</margin> through <term>serpigo</term> <note>a creeping skin eruption</note> around the arms and chest, and through a dry, hard, and callous condition in other parts arising from viscous, metallic, and "burnt" humors. <margin>Hard tophi.</margin> It also showed itself through hard <term>tophi</term> <note>original: "tophi duri"; stony deposits often found in the joints or under the skin in chronic syphilis</note>, etc., which are frequently seen in confirmed cases of this plague when the malignancy is complicated by phlegmatic and metallic humors, as was said above. <margin>Indications.</margin> Therefore, as the patient's overall strength was otherwise still very stable, the indications were directed toward this: that after a suitable preparation of the body, the malignancy—which had been absorbed into the habit of the body, the entire mass of the blood, and even the organs of blood-making—should be expelled outward both through <term>cathartics</term> <note>purgatives</note> and through <term>diaphoretics</term> <note>medicines that induce sweating</note>, while not neglecting in-

<margin>Derivation of symptoms.</margin>
By sharing the same lodging, bed, and laundry, and through the daily interaction of her lifestyle, even while eating with those already infected, she herself contracted the malignancy of the <term>pox</term> <note>original: "luis"; referring to the "French Pox" or syphilis</note>. Indeed, since this malignancy was joined with a <term>Melancholic Cacochymia</term> <note>an imbalance of the "four humors" characterized by an excess of corrupted black bile</note>, abounding in tartareous and "burnt" humors, it was not surprising that the evil remained hidden for some time. In such a bodily constitution, the disease is accustomed to fix its roots firmly before it erupts onto the surface of the body. Hence, the *left side of the head*—due to its relationship with the *spleen*—*ached at night*, which is a characteristic of putrefying matter corrupted by the "French" malignancy. She suffered from *insomnia*, as the withdrawal of heat and spirits from the sensory organs (which normally happens during sleep) was hindered by the hostile sensation of pain. The *color of her face was livid* due to the failure of digestion, as the nutritive faculty languished. This was accompanied by *heaviness of the stomach and spleen*, specifically a bloating of the <term>hypochondria</term> <note>the upper regions of the abdomen</note> caused by the concurrent obstruction of the <term>mesaraic</term> <note>mesenteric</note> and splenic veins. This was further indicated by *belching* that frequently rose up from an empty stomach, along with *raw, lead-colored urine*. Finally, *hard tumors* appeared *around the head and forehead*, not unlike those swellings the Greeks call *scirrhos* <note>hard, painless lumps</note>, and *livid pustules like warts* invaded the entire body, arising from the "burnt" and viscous humors combined with the infection of the pox.

## OBSERVATION VIII.

### The French Pox contracted after Scarification in a public bath.

When I came here four years ago in the year 1622, having been called to the office of <term>Chief Physician</term> <note>original: "Archiatrus"; the senior medical officer of a city or court</note>, among others who met with me for medical advice was a certain citizen, a weaver by trade named Johannes König. He complained of fixed and most vehement nocturnal pains in his joints. I prescribed various medicines for these in vain, until finally in the following year a <term>tophus</term> <note>a hard, bony swelling or knot typical of advanced syphilis</note> manifested itself around his left shin, preceded and accompanied by the greatest pain.

#### ANALYSIS.

<margin>
This disease is most often contracted through sexual intercourse and other ways. An infant is infected by its mother, a nurse by a child, and vice versa through the lips, leading to the pox.
</margin>

Although this disease is contagious, so much so that it is easily propagated from one person to another—both in generation, insofar as a diseased fetus is produced from infected seminal matter, leading to the <term>pox</term> <note>original: "luem"; referring to Lues Gallica or syphilis</note>...

### ON CONTAGIOUS AND MALIGNANT DISEASES.

<margin>From bodily contact.</margin> This plague <note>original: "luem"; referring to Lues Gallica or Syphilis</note> is more readily produced in one predisposed to it than after its initial generation, when the evil is transplanted into others. However, this does not usually happen in any other way than through bodily contact, since the malignant quality of the pox does not reside in an airborne substance—in the manner of a pestilential poison—but rather in a thicker material. Such bodily contact can be manifold: namely, <margin>Through kisses.</margin> through kisses, when the mouth of another is infected by malignant "French" ulcers; <margin>Through a shared bed.</margin> through a shared bed, with linens and blankets still damp with sweat or "French" discharge; <margin>Through clothing.</margin> through clothing, teeming with virulent discharge, placed against the bare body; <margin>Through sexual intercourse.</margin> through sexual intercourse with an infected person; <margin>Through breastfeeding.</margin> through the sucking of milk from a wet-nurse suffering from the French Pox, etc. <margin>Through scarification.</margin> Among these methods, one also encounters infection through <term>scarification</term> <note>a medical procedure involving making small incisions in the skin to draw blood or fluids</note> performed with shared instruments and <term>cupping glasses</term> <note>original: "cucurbitulis"; heated glass jars used to create suction on the skin</note> in a bathhouse, as is sometimes observed, and of which the present patient complained. 

This man, healthy and unharmed in his later years, underwent scarification a few years ago here in Ulm at a public bathhouse. Shortly thereafter, he discovered the scarified area was being corrupted by foul ulcers. For this reason, he immediately reported it to the <term>Bath-Attendant</term> <note>original: "Balneatori"; bathhouse keepers often performed minor surgeries and bloodletting</note> who, fearing infamy, healed the ulcerated part over and commanded the suffering man to keep silent. The malignancy having been driven back toward the interior in this way, the pox gradually took root, until at last he was afflicted by fixed and most violent nocturnal pains in his joints. When every kind of common remedy was applied in vain, I suspected some underlying malignancy, which a subsequent painful <term>tophus</term> <note>a hard, bony swelling or deposit</note> on the left shin made manifest. The malignancy flowed to that spot because his way of life made his legs weaker; as a weaver, he was forced to carry out his craft for the most part by standing in damp, underground cellars. Wherefore, by special permission of the Magistrate, the patient was admitted to the <term>French Hospital</term> <note>original: "Nosocomium Gallicorum"; a specialized hospital for those suffering from syphilis</note> on August 18th. For three days, he drank a potion consisting of:

> ℞ Recipe: 3 ounces of a decoction of senna leaves.

> Water germander,
> and Buckthorn. Mix.

> and Bitter Apple <note>original: "Colocynth."</note>.

> 12 grains of <term>Sweet Mercury</term> <note>original: "☿ dulcificati"; Calomel, a common mercurial treatment</note>.

After these were taken, matter was drawn out through the bowels many times. Because the "first and second ways" <note>referring to the digestive tract and the circulatory/metabolic systems</note> had been purified in this manner, he underwent bloodletting on August 23rd. Resting for a few days, on the 27th, 28th, 29th, and 30th of August, as well as on the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th of September, a <term>sweating decoction</term> of wood was administered, along with *Theriac* and *Mithrida-* <note>two famous ancient polypharmaceutical "universal" antidotes</note>

Therefore, after a decision was made <margin>prognosis.</margin> by the Medical Council, the patient was indeed accepted for the ordinary cure—though in such a way that the difficulty of restoring health in such an inveterate <note>long-standing and deep-seated</note> disease was made clear at the same time. ### CASE STUDY XI.

#### A six-month-old boy, pustulous over his entire body, and especially in the private areas.

**G**eorge Ganser of Baltzheim, a six-month-old boy born to parents suffering from the **Gallic disease** <note>original: "lue Gallicâ"; a common historical name for syphilis, which was often named after rival nations</note>, displays **Gallic pustules** and foul ulcers around his private parts and over his entire body.

### RESOLUTION.

<margin>This pox is hereditary.</margin>
**A**lthough the malignancy of this pox is such that, due to the firm roots it gradually impresses upon the body of the sufferer, it can very easily be communicated to the fetus through generation—as much because of the impurity of the seed as on account of the harm of the menstrual blood—it could also <column-break/> readily happen here that the infant, due to a naturally weaker constitution from birth, became infected through the embrace of a parent, and especially from the nursing mother. Hence the entire body was made pustulous through bodily contact, the very tender skin being infected by the malignancy; foul ulcers affected the buttocks and neighboring parts, insofar as the reception of a foreign quality is easier there due to the softness and the hot, moist constitution of those areas.

Hence, on December 2, 1625, first <margin>Distillate of wood.</margin> *distilled Guaiac wood* <note>original: "ligni Guajacini"; Guaiacum, or "Holy Wood" from the Americas, was a standard 17th-century treatment for syphilis, believed to cure the "cold" disease through its "hot" properties</note>, which is collected during its decoction through an attached alembic <note>a chemical distilling apparatus</note>, was ordered as a daily drink, lightly sweetened with *Sugar Candy*. This was administered to him at his pleasure and appetite throughout the entire time of treatment, so that, on account of this, sweats of the entire body followed everywhere during sleep and at other times in his delicate constitution. Soon, however, *half a scruple of Dulcified Mercury* <note>original: "Mercurij dulcific. ℈ss."; this refers to Calomel (mercurous chloride), a "milder" form of mercury used as a laxative and to treat the pox</note> was administered mixed with broth, which caused several bowel movements. This dose was repeated on December 3, 4, and 5, with the daily evacuations following with ease of strength. Once the whole body was moderately evacuated, a *cleansing bath* was employed on December 6 and 7, always preceded by a draft of the *distilled Guaiac*. On December 8, for the sake of drawing the malignancy out from the habit of the body, *Caustic Water* [was applied] to the parts...

<margin>Concerning the Coralline of Theophrastus.</margin>

If likewise nothing followed from this administration, he gave it a third time, observing the proper proportion of both time and increase. While the saliva flowed, he rested; but for those complaining of ulceration of the throat and palate, and loosening of the teeth (an evil that no one has yet been able to prevent by art when using mercury), he made a gargle from astringent waters and alum. # OBSERVATION XIV.

## The Treatment of the French Disease by anointing with Mercurial Water.

### To the *Most Famous & Excellent* Mr. ANDREAS Schilling, Doctor of Medicine and Practitioner of the Republic of Strasbourg, GREGORIUS HORSTIUS, Doctor, sends greetings.

I give thanks, most famous man, for the things you have communicated to me. I wonder, however, why your white mercury sublimate, which we commonly call "sweetened" <note>original: "dulcificatum"; likely referring to calomel (mercurous chloride), which was considered a "sweeter" or milder form of mercury than the corrosive sublimate</note>, produced such a salivation <note>Excessive drooling was a common, and often intentional, sign of mercury poisoning used as a "cure" to expel the disease</note>. For if the crude mercury is properly purified, and the sublimate itself is also properly prepared, and from there the operation is carried out through several repeated processes,

<column-break/>

it is rendered altogether mild, so that in a hundred cases it scarcely excites salivation, as we experience here daily. Hence I suspect that our friend Mr. Fuhrmann, of pious memory, must have employed some other mercurial medicine to excite salivation.

<margin>Description of the Coralline.</margin>
His ***Coralline*** <note>original: "Corallinum"; a red precipitate of mercury</note>, as communicated by a certain friend, is described thus: Take 1 pound of the best purified mercury, or even that extracted from cinnabar; 1 pound each of saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate</note> and vitriol <note>sulfates, usually of iron or copper</note>; 3 and a half ounces of plumose alum <note>a form of asbestos or fibrous alum used in alchemy</note>; and a sufficient quantity of distilled vinegar. Mix them: first, let the phlegm <note>the watery part</note> be drawn off, afterward increase the fire for 24 hours; then digest the precipitate with ***Spirit of Wine*** <note>alcohol</note>.

<margin>A Singular Treatment of the Pox.</margin>
But what do you judge of the following treatment of the ***Lues*** <note>original: "Luis"; another term for the "French Disease" or syphilis</note> by a certain celebrated physician in France? He first administers a vomitory <note>an emetic to induce vomiting</note> for two days; on the third day, a purging is instituted through a ***universal extract*** <note>original: "extractum catholicum"; a broad-spectrum purgative</note>; on the fourth day, ***diaphoretic gold*** <note>a preparation of gold intended to induce sweating</note> is administered with ***Theriac*** <note>a famous ancient polypharmaceutical "cure-all" ointment or potion</note> and snake powder. Afterward, the whole body is anointed with a sweat-inducing ***Mercurial Water***, the patient is wrapped in linens, and a sweat is provoked daily.

<margin>A singular diaphoretic gold.</margin>
The description of the ***diaphoretic gold*** is as follows: Take 1 and a half ounces of the best selected and purified quicksilver <note>liquid mercury</note> and 1 drachm of pure gold. Let this be dissolved in ***Aqua Regia*** <note>original: "Aqua Regia"; a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids capable of dissolving gold</note>; but dissolve the mercury in ***Aqua Fortis*** <note>original: "Aqua Forti"; nitric acid</note>. Join the solutions and distill off the watery part through a ***Water Bath*** <note>original: "Balneum"</note>; at the bottom there will remain a precipitate, which should be sweetened <note>washed/neutralized</note> with warm water.

I am writing to you later than I intended, most famous and experienced man, and most honored kinsman. But what was the primary cause of this delay, you might perhaps ask? I will explain. Certainly, it was nothing other than various journeys, some to far distant places and some nearby. Among the distant ones were the trips to Lucerne and Kirchheim. Indeed, four weeks ago, I was called to Lucerne in Switzerland to treat a certain most noble lady, born of the illustrious lineage of the Stewards of Waldburg, who was suffering from dropsy <note>term: hydrops; a condition characterized by the accumulation of fluid in the body's tissues or cavities, often causing severe swelling</note>. 

<column-break/>

Last summer, by the blessing of the Most Holy God and through my own modest efforts, I similarly freed this lady's sister, Elisabeth, the wife of the most noble Count Fugger, from dropsy.

<margin>When thermal baths are appropriate for dropsy.</margin>
This latter woman, after the cure was successfully completed, I sent away to the Swiss baths, specifically for this purpose: that if any remaining traces of the disease were lingering in the internal organs, they might be evacuated and dispersed, and that strength might also be added to the external limbs. By these means, through the grace of God, all the members of her body were strengthened, and she returned to us in good health according to our wishes, and she remains healthy to this day. While I am writing this, a singular and noteworthy case has come to my mind, which I handled this past summer; since I know you are very eager for rare cases, I will not be reluctant to share it with you.

...which like a moth <note>original: tineæ instar; referring to the way moth larvae eat through fabric</note>, little by little, by eating away at the flesh and sometimes the bones, with new small ulcers constantly sprouting up all around, and with foul pus, pierces through with the greatest torment for the sick by day and night: the patient, having suffered for a long time in his left arm, fell into the hands of a certain unskilled impostor, whose useless efforts he used for nearly three-quarters of a year. Finally, after using so many medicines in vain, his parent, meeting me for advice, asked that I visit his son who was in a bad state; and I immediately followed in the footsteps of the one calling me. Having entered the patient's heated room <note>original: hypocausto; a room kept warm by a stove, common in German households of the period</note>, I found not only the left arm swarming with malignant ulcers, but also that an ulcer had ascended even to the socket of the left eye; there, by eating away, it had separated the proud muscle and its neighbor from the bone and devoured it, leaving a large cavity behind, so that he seemed like a second Lazarus <note>A biblical reference to the beggar covered in sores; here used to describe the patient's pitiable, ulcerated state</note>. From this eye socket, this ulcer progressed further to the temples and the crown of the head; there on the crown <note>term: bregma; the anatomical top of the skull</note>, a large and malignant ulcer of horrible appearance, with corruption of the skull bone <note>term: calvariæ; the skullcap</note> and the brain, presented itself to our sight, such as I had never seen a larger one. You may truly believe me, the abscessed brain <note>original: cerebrum apostematum</note>, the size of a goose egg, hung out corrupted beyond the skull and was fermenting like yeast. Having taken up a probe <note>term: specillo; a slender surgical instrument used for exploring wounds</note>, I inserted it into the abscessed brain on the left 

<column-break/>

side and I proceeded little by little with the probe until I reached the back part of the head with it. Having done this, I asked the patient whether he felt any pain from the inserted probe or not? He replied that he felt absolutely nothing. Therefore, having made my prognosis, since the present stench struck the nostrils of those standing by like a rotten egg, I predicted that no hope of a cure shone forth, nor could he remain alive for long, and that he would perish either from convulsions (due to the malignant stench, which is harmful to the nervous system) or from apoplexy <note>term: apoplexia; a sudden loss of consciousness, often associated with a stroke</note>. The outcome of this did not deceive me, since ten days later, with massive convulsions coming on, he exchanged his life for death. Having summoned my surgeon <note>original: Chirurgo; at this time, surgeons were craftsmen who performed manual operations under the direction of a physician</note>, I ordered him to remove a small portion of the abscessed brain, the size of an apple, with a razor, thinking that I would reach a healthy part of the brain; but the operation failed. Therefore, after suitable medicines were applied by the surgeon, I went home; on the following day I was called to the same man in turn, from whom I similarly removed a small portion from the brain, without the slightest sensation of pain. I repeated the cutting even on the third day, and even then no healthy part of the brain was ever seen by me. The aforementioned patient, which almost exceeds all belief, used all his senses intact; there was no diminution, abolition, or de- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "defect" or "depravation"</note>

I would desire a more exquisite investigation <note>original: διάσκεψιν (*diaskepsin*)</note> into what the cause of that ulceration might have been—not according to the common naming, where names are imposed on things at whim, but from the very essence of the matter. I remember a certain woman who, two years ago, was with you for a time and (unless I am mistaken) was also under your care. She was the wife of a certain garrison soldier who previously lived among you. She had an arm teeming everywhere with pipe-like <term>fistulous: ulcers that form deep, tube-like passages into the body</term> and filthy ulcers, such that there also appeared to be decay <note>original: *caries*</note> of the bone underneath. For this reason, she was judged by many to be a hopeless case, until at last she was brought before the entire Medical College by order of the Most Noble Magistrate. Here, having observed the external appearance of the ailment, a suspicion of a "Venereal" infection <note>Syphilis was frequently called the venereal plague or lue venerea.</note> soon arose in me. For this reason, in the presence of my colleagues, I inquired into her medical history, and from the patient's own confession I was made certain that some years before she had been afflicted by cracks in the skin <term>rhagades: painful linear fissures or cracks in the skin, often occurring in the genital or anal regions</term> around her private parts. Because these had been healed over quickly with external remedies, the malignancy turned toward her internal parts; first, tumors appeared, and soon those fistulous ulcers broke out around her arm. Therefore, we considered that we must see to it that a treatment suitable for the French Disease be established for her, especially through the minerals customary to us, which are very effective in aiding a deeply rooted evil. These treatments were carried out by our colleague, Dr. Sebastian Stromayer,

<column-break/>

the Physician-in-Ordinary of the French Hospital <note>A specialized hospital, or *Nosocomium Gallicum*, dedicated to treating syphilis.</note>. Once completed, she was restored to the best of health; those pipe-like ulcers were thoroughly healed after the purification of the body. However, the arm remained entirely contracted <note>Permanent stiffening or shortening of the muscles and tendons due to severe scarring.</note> in the muscular and tendinous parts because of the damage from the preceding ulceration. With this, farewell to you and yours. Written in haste at Ulm, December 15, 1626.

## OBSERVATION XV.

### A continuous fever joined with the malignancy of the Venereal plague.

A certain vigorous military commander, about forty years of age and of a choleric constitution <note>In the theory of the Four Humors, a "choleric" person was thought to be dominated by yellow bile, making them naturally hot, dry, and prone to ambition or anger.</note>, complained in the springtime of the current year *1628* of a continuous, afflicting fever. This was accompanied by a remarkable headache that was most painful at night, as well as "French pustules" <note>Syphilitic skin eruptions.</note> around the forehead, an ulceration of the ear, and an old "creeping rash" <term>serpigo: a general term for spreading skin diseases like ringworm or herpes, here likely a syphilitic lesion</term> on the arms and other parts that had become worse, along with similar symptoms.

# On Contagious and Malignant Diseases.

### RESOLUTION.

This patient, bedridden and finding little relief from the standard remedies for a continuous fever, was already attended by two physicians. However, as the aforementioned symptoms grew more urgent, he summoned me from six miles away. Upon arrival, I inquired into both the past and present state of the patient, and I immediately pronounced that this continuous fever presupposed remnants of the French disease <note>original: "luis"; referring to *Lues Venerea* or syphilis</note>, and it was because of these remnants that the symptoms were rendered more severe. Although the fever certainly required its own specific remedies for the time being, I stated that only a "glassy" <note>meaning fragile or precarious</note> state of health could be expected unless a treatment suitable for the French Disease was applied once the feverish symptoms were tempered. 

Indeed, because this advice seemed foreign to some—given that such sweat-inducing treatments might perhaps reignite the fever or cause a worse relapse—it did not at all displease the laboring patient, who was well aware of his own condition. For this reason, once he had recovered from the fever as much as possible, he traveled here at the end of May. After sharing counsel with my most faithful colleague, **Dr. Sebastian Stromajer**, we observed the following process: namely,

<column-break/>

# ON CONTAGIOUS AND MALIGNANT DISEASES.

## THE RESOLUTION.

<margin>Investigation of the symptoms.</margin>
**W**HEN, during the Dog Days <note>The hot, sweltering weeks of midsummer (July and August), historically believed to be a dangerous time to administer strong medicines or perform surgery</note> of the current year 1625, the parent of the aforementioned patient met with me for a consultation, I immediately declared, after a careful investigation, that a severe case of "malignant psoriasis" <note>original: "Psoram perversam"</note> was present, nearly approaching "Greek leprosy" <note>original: "Lepram Graecorum"; in the 17th century, this term often referred to severe, scaly skin diseases like advanced psoriasis rather than modern Hansen's disease</note>. For this reason, I determined there was still hope for recovery, provided he followed our instructions and diligently applied the appropriate remedies to be prescribed after the summer heat subsided. There had been a dry itch <term>scabies: here used as a general term for a scaly skin eruption</term> since early childhood, caused by "burnt" and salty humors produced by a systemic imbalance <term>dycrasia: a disharmony of the four bodily humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to cause disease</term> of the internal organs. This eventually produced a roughness of the skin due to drying matter accumulating in the pores, and a general itching caused by the corrosive sharpness of that same humor. Branny scales <note>resembling bran or dandruff</note> fell away because of the stickiness of the "burnt" offending matter, combined with a harsh and uneven hardening of the skin. Indeed, the substance of the skin was so weakened that it could not properly expel its waste products, resulting in the skin becoming rough and leathery.

<margin>Goals of the treatment.</margin>
We believed we must focus on three things: first, by opening the natural passages, we would assist the body’s ability to expel waste by flushing out the harmful humors through the bowels; second, to soften and cleanse the deeply rooted skin affliction; and third, to strengthen nature <note>the body's vital force</note> to prevent a relapse.

Regarding the first goal, we began evacuation by means of a laxative mead <note>original: "hydromel laxativum"; a mixture of honey and water infused with herbs</note> made as follows:

> Take: Sharp-pointed dock root, 1 ½ ounces.
> Chicory and sorrel, 6 drachms each.
> Senna leaves, 1 ounce.
> Rhubarb and Larch fungus <note>original: "Agarici"</note>, 1 ½ drachms each.
> Black hellebore bark,
> Prepared Spurge, 2 drachms each.
> Fumitory herb,
> Hart’s-tongue fern,
> Lesser centaury, half a handful each.
> Elder bark, 2 ½ drachms.
> Alder buckthorn, 1 ½ drachms.
> Anise seed, 1 drachm.
> Chopped small raisins, 1 ounce.
> Selected tartar, 2 drachms.
> Galangal,
> Ginger, 1 drachm each.

Let them be infused in 4 pounds of boiling mead. Let it stand for 24 hours; afterwards, let the patient use half a pound every day for a period of eight days. Meanwhile, let the diet be easy to digest, moistening rather than drying. For a drink, let the following decoction be used:

> Take: Sassafras, 2 drachms.
> Sarsaparilla, half an ounce.
> Anise and fennel seeds, 1 drachm each.
> Chopped small raisins, 4 ounces. Boil them

in six measures of water for a daily drink.

In this way, according to the first objective, the body having been purified by

# OBSERVATION XIX.
## *A foul, weeping mange.*

A country youth, 18 years of age, had been afflicted for many years with a foul mange, and a weeping one at that <note>original: "scabies foeda humida"; likely a form of severe eczema or infected scabies with oozing sores</note>. His raw urine testified that this was caused by a corrupted digestion of the internal organs. When he implored medical counsel toward the end of the year 1626, and since he was otherwise of a more robust constitution, we deemed it necessary to work toward purifying the blood mass well, with respect to the antecedent cause, and strengthening the organs of digestion; and as for the immediate cause, the skin should be wiped clean of filth and the superfluous watery matter consumed. First, we completed this partly with common and partly with mineral prescriptions. We therefore first ordered a laxative hydromel <note>a mixture of honey and water used as a carrier for medicines</note>:
Take: Scraped licorice root, 1 and a half drachms.

Oak polypody <note>a type of fern root used as a purgative</note>, 2 drachms.
Tamarisk bark, 6 drachms.
Prepared spurge.
Buckthorn and Dwarf Elder, 3 drachms of each.

A certain peasant from the village of Offelfingen, over 30 years of age, has been suffering for a long time from an influx of fluid and swelling of the foot, along with a moist, creeping skin disease <note>original: "serpígine," a term used for spreading skin conditions like ringworm or herpes</note>. Coming to me for advice toward the end of September in the year 1627, he showed me his urine, which was raw and spiky <note>original: "spiceam"; likely referring to a sediment or appearance suggesting poor digestion</note>. For this reason, I immediately stated that this ailment could not be overcome unless the entire mass of blood was thoroughly purified through appropriate evacuations [purging], while simultaneously employing remedies that would consume the salty, serous humor <note>the watery part of the blood, which in the medical theory of the time was thought to cause irritation if it became too "salty"</note> through the body's pores by the force of sweating, and not neglecting a proper diet. Therefore, for the first eight days, after administering digestive aids, I purged him twice with appropriate medicines. Afterward, I ordered the following decoction:
