## OBSERVATION XXII.

### Elephantiasis conquered by mineral remedies.

**A** certain sixty-year-old man, established in the public office of the prison prefecture, had long suffered from the leprosy of the *Greeks* <note>original: "lepra Græcorum," a term used in this period for severe, scaly skin diseases, often including what we now call leprosy or Hansen's disease</note>. He had hidden the condition for several years by using various internal and external remedies. Finally, he was subjected to the customary examination for lepers, and since most of the signs determined by us in Book 1 of our *Medical Epistles*, section 4, were present, he was pronounced to be separated from the healthy. However, since the Most Distinguished Senate greatly favored this public servant and voluntarily offered sufficient funds to attempt a cure, this task was entrusted to the aforementioned Ordinary Physician of the French Hospital <note>original: "Nosocomij Gallici," referring to a hospital specializing in "the French disease" (syphilis) or similar chronic conditions</note>. After consulting with me, he began by preparing the body's humors <note>a process called "digestion" in early medicine, intended to thin the "thick" fluids of the body before purging</note> twice daily for three days, namely the 24th, 25th, and 26th of March, 1626.

<column-break/>

Having first prepared the patient with a *Magistery of Vitriolated Tartar* <note>potassium sulfate, used as a digestive and mild laxative</note> dissolved in a decoction of raisins, the physician administered a purgative on the 27th day consisting of: Take: *Sweet Mercury* <note>original: "Mercurij dulcificati," also known as calomel</note>, 1 and 1/2 scruples; *corrected Scammony* <note>original: "diagryd. corr.," a potent resinous laxative</note>, 1/2 scruple. Afterward, on the following day, the median vein of the right arm was opened so that nature might be somewhat relieved from the burden of an excess of burnt and corrupt blood. After the bloodletting, the purging was continued on March 31st by administering 7 grains of *simple mineral laxative* and 1/2 scruple of *corrected Scammony*. By this medicine, not only were the bowels loosened several times, but a discharge also occurred twice through vomiting. On the following first of April, a slightly stronger purge was ordered, namely: *Golden Panacea* <note>original: "Panacææ Aureæ," likely a chemical preparation of mercury or antimony</note>, 1 and 1/2 scruples; *corrected Scammony*, 1/2 scruple. The operation of this was also easy, following the pattern of the previous one. The body having been prepared in this way, a sweat-inducing decoction was applied, made from *Guaiacum wood, Sarsaparilla*, with the addition of those things which possess the power of soothing and softening. Six ounces of this were taken twice daily, with 12 grains of *diaphoretic Antimony* <note>a mineral preparation used to induce sweating</note> added; this was repeated several times in a cleansing bath on the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, and 8th of April. On the ninth of April, an evacuation was again instituted, given as: Take: *Golden Panacea*, 1 and 1/2 scruples; *corrected Scammony*, 1/2 scruple. It was given with a broth of small raisin decoction, and it completed its operation through the bowels and vomiting without difficulty. This was done a third time with nearly the same medicines, except that in place of the Anti-

These, along with cleansing baths, were repeated whenever the skin, purified multiple times, took on the color of a boiled crab <note>original: "cancri decocti," referring to the bright red flushing of the skin</note>. This liniment is usually made from a decoction of buckthorn with red wine and pig lard. By its use, the skin was so thoroughly cleansed and restored that he lived healthy and unharmed for three months. However, following a Decree of the Senate for the subsequent quarter of the year—intended to better observe the effects of the cure—he was required to live in isolation. Suddenly, after taking some medicine from a certain empiric <note>original: "Empirici," an unlicensed or self-taught healer often viewed with suspicion by university-trained doctors</note> which had been secretly shared with him, he died from excessive purging <note>original Greek: "ὑπερκαθάρσει" (hypercatharsis), a fatal state of uncontrolled vomiting and diarrhea often caused by harsh laxatives</note>.

## OBSERVATION XXIII.

### Bite of a mad dog.

A boy of two years, four years ago, was bitten by a mad dog <note>a rabid dog</note> in various places around the face and on the head.

<column-break/>

Through the grace of God and the application of a few remedies, he was preserved from hydrophobia <note>rabies; literally "fear of water," the hallmark symptom of the disease in humans</note> and was perfectly restored.

## RESOLUTION.

Since this case occurred on a nearby farm outside the city, the peasant father immediately brought the boy to us, imploring medical aid so that nothing more serious might befall his innocent young son. Because one must work quickly in this affliction to thoroughly uproot the malignancy inflicted by the poisonous bite and prevent it from creeping further inward, it must be blocked with appropriate antidotes. <margin>Indications for the bite of a mad dog.</margin> Therefore, addressing both indications immediately: first, for the exterior, we ordered a cleansing and "extracting" wash. Specifically: two ounces of Old Theriac <note>original: "Theriacæ Veteris," a famous ancient polypharmaceutical paste used as an antitoxin</note>, half a handful of fresh Rue leaves, and one ounce of Syrup of Citron-Vinegar. Let these boil lightly with a sufficient amount of honey-water and be strained by pressing. The wounded parts should be rubbed quite hard and washed with this liquid; then, a poultice of garlic, salt, and turpentine worked together should be applied. However, I decided that an internal remedy was also needed quickly. For this reason, we gave the boy two ounces of the cooked liver of the mad dog, <margin>The liver of a mad dog against the bite.</margin> cut into small pieces. We were confirmed in this experiment by the belief that if this antidote is given before the first twenty-four hours after the bite have passed, the anti-

Afterward, however, by a Decree of the Senate, he was required to live in isolation for the following quarter of the year so that the effect of the cure could be better monitored. ## OBSERVATION XXIII.

### The bite of a mad dog.

A boy of two years <note>The text says "ante quadriennium" (four years ago), which contradicts the boy's age of two; this may be a printer's error or refer to a four-year period of observation</note> was wounded in various places around the face and on the head by the bite of a **mad dog**. By the grace of GOD, and through the application of a few remedies, he was preserved from **hydrophobia** <note>rabies; literally "fear of water," the classic symptom of the disease</note> and perfectly restored to health.

### THE RESOLUTION.

Since this case occurred outside the city on a nearby estate, the rural parent immediately brought the boy, imploring medical aid so that nothing more grievous should be expected for his innocent little son. Indeed, because one must work from the very beginning in this evil to fundamentally uproot the malignancy inflicted by the poisonous bite, and to prevent it from creeping inward, 
<margin>Indications for the bite of a mad dog.</margin>
it must be blocked by appropriate antidotes. Therefore, by looking to both indications immediately: first, we ordered an external cleansing and "drawing" wash, namely: two drams of *Old Theriac* <note>a famous, complex ancient remedy used as an universal antidote</note>, half a handful of fresh *rue* leaves, one ounce of *syrup of citron-vinegar*, let these boil lightly with a sufficient quantity of *hydromel* <note>honey-water</note>, and let it be strained by pressing. The wounded parts should be rubbed quite hard with this strained liquid and washed. Soon after, a *cataplasm* <note>poultice</note> made of garlic, salt, and turpentine worked together should be applied. But I also determined that there was need for a swift internal remedy, for which reason 
<margin>The liver of a mad dog as a remedy against the bite.</margin>
we gave the boy two drams of the **cooked liver of the mad dog**, cut into small pieces. We were confirmed in this by experience, for as long as the first twenty-four hours after the bite have not yet passed, this antidote...

But when these wounds inflicted by canine madness were neglected, I recall that a servant of a certain noble patrician, as well as a tailor of a neighboring Baron, met their deaths in miserable delirium as *hydrophobia* took hold.

More may be read in our *Century of Problems, last Decade, question 2*, and *Book 2 of Medicinal Epistles, section 4*, and in *Master Fabricius, 4th Century of Surgical Observations, Number 88, and Jacopo Caranta, Book 2 of the Metaphysical Decades*.

### THE MEDICAL ANALYSIS.

<margin>Symptoms of malignancy.</margin>
Called three years ago, I shared a German plan of advice, which, translated here into English, reads as follows:
Since the patient [N.] has been affected for a long time by continuous head pains, accompanied by hard and scirrhous <note>original: "scirrhosis," referring to hard, fiber-like tumors or swellings</note> painful tumors, not only around the scalp membrane <note>original: "pericranium"</note> but also in the shins, arms, and breastbone—which are worsened in these places mostly before dinner, in the evening, and at night after the first sleep: it necessarily follows that a chronic illness of this kind arises from a singular malignancy which has its seat in
<margin>The cause and the rooted symptom.</margin>
phlegmatic, viscous, and "tartarous" <note>original: "tartareis," a medical term used by followers of Paracelsus to describe stony or hard deposits in the body, comparing them to the tartar crust in a wine cask</note> humors. In these humors, the disease is rooted, nourished, and produced; its primary characteristic is that it hardens or coagulates within the solid parts of the body. Such a hardening is all the more difficult

<column-break/>

<margin>The origin of the cause.</margin>
to dissolve the more firmly it has taken root over a long period. This is because the origin of this malignant corruption is due to a depraved formation of blood <note>original: "sanguificationi"</note>, caused by a foreign taint impressed upon the liver and spleen (the organs responsible for making blood). Thus, for this reason, the entire mass of blood is invisibly infected by this kind of corrupt "tartar," until, due to the susceptibility of the affected part, it coagulates around the solid parts—namely the bones and the bone-membranes <note>original: "periostia"</note>—causing significant pain.

<margin>Prognosis.</margin>
Truly, since this chronic evil could indeed be eased after so many prescribed sweat-inducing and other medications, yet could not be fully conquered (whereupon the symptoms soon broke out again): it will therefore be necessary—lest bone decay <note>original: "caries ossium"</note>, malignant ulcerations of the stony growths <note>original: "tophorum," hard deposits often found in joints or on bones</note>, and other more serious conditions follow—that a universal Cure be established immediately. This must be done in such a way that appropriate mineral medicines are not neglected, as these, by their specific power, penetrate to the root of the corrupt malignancy and immediately attack it in the liver, spleen, and the entire mass of blood. > **Extract of Diacarthamus**, ½ drachm.
> **Diagrydium**, 7 grains. 
> Mix to make a bolus.

After this, purging followed three times before noon and once after noon; it was quite copious, but occurred without any internal "commotion" or distress. On February 27th, 28th, 29th, and March 1st, 2nd, and 3rd, the sweat-inducing decoction was continued with various additions. Indeed, on the last two days, before dinner, ½ drachm of **Magistery of Vitriolated Tartar** <note>original: "Magisterij Tar. vitriol."; a chemical preparation of potassium sulfate used as a digestive aid.</note> was administered in a draught of plum broth as a preparation, so that on March 4th the previously described purgative could be taken again. This resulted in a moderate evacuation with **a sense of well-being** <note>original: "εὐφορίᾳ" (euphoria).</note>.

<column-break/>

From March 5th to the 9th, the sweats were continued only once daily, while the patient also took **Mineral Bezoar**, gradually decreasing the dose down to 4 grains. Having continued in this manner until now, the patient began to feel better; the hard swellings and indurations were dispersed and resolved, and the pains were entirely conquered.

By Divine Blessing, his former healthy vigor was restored. Therefore, after allowing nature to rest for several days, we finally administered an **Enema** instead of a purge on March 13th. 

<margin>Bloodletting toward the end of the cure.</margin>
On March 14th, we performed a **bloodletting** from the right arm so that the blood, which had been agitated by so many sweats and evacuations, might be "ventilated" <note>An early medical concept of cooling or refreshing the blood after intense internal heat or treatment.</note>.

After this, we prescribed a diet that was simple and **nutritious** <note>original: "εὐχυμον" (euchymous); producing healthy humors.</note>. For the sake of strengthening the body, we recommended several drops of **Paracelsus’s Elixir of Property** <note>original: "Elixiris proprietatis Paracelsi"; a famous tonic made of aloe, myrrh, and saffron.</note> in the morning, and in the evening, **morsels of Species Diambra with Extract of Aloeswood** <note>original: "morsulos ex Specieb. diambræ cum extr. ligni Aloës"; aromatic, warming confections used as a heart and stomach tonic.</note>. By these means, the Patient was liberated from the most severe symptoms noted above, and gave the greatest thanks first to God, and then to **Hygeia** <note>The Greek goddess of health.</note>.

# OBSERVATION XXV.

## Malignity from poisonous metallic fumes, and others, to be cured through Mineral medicines.

<margin>Case 1.</margin>
In former years, a certain citizen of Ansbach <note>original: "Onolsbachii"; a city in Bavaria.</note>, through a poison—perhaps [corrosive] sublimate <note>original: "sublimato"; mercury(II) chloride, a highly toxic mineral salt.</note>—secretly administered to him through the malice of his associates, immediately swelled up in his head, lips, mouth, and his entire body. This was followed by a remarkable burning of the throat, along with an onset of endless convulsions. He was regarded as a hopeless case by everyone. However, the Most Illustrious Mr. Dr. **Tobias Knobloch**, the ordinary physician of that place and my honored friend, administered **Mineral Turpeth** <note>original: "Turpetho Minerali"; basic mercury sulfate, a powerful chemical emetic used in this era to "drive out" poisons through vomiting and purging.</note> three times within twenty-four hours in a sufficiently large dose. A more violent operation [of the medicine] followed, both above and below [vomiting and purging], and after a few strengthening remedies were applied, he was perfectly restored to health by the blessing of God. Thus, we shall hardly conquer the malignity arising from poisonous metallic fumes by any other means than mineral remedies. This is attested by the young son of a certain **Goldsmith** living here,

<margin>Case 2.</margin>

<column-break/>

who, about two years ago, labored under an almost hopeless **Asthma**, with nothing profiting from the remedies usually appropriate for this condition. At last, I was called and immediately suspected that the malignity of mercurial fumes had produced this disease, because the parent confessed that for several days near the onset of this condition, he had been occupied with gilding silver vessels <note>This process, known as fire-gilding, involved dissolving gold in mercury to create an amalgam, which was then heated to evaporate the mercury, releasing highly toxic vapors.</note> in the presence of the boy. Therefore, I quickly administered 12 grains of **Dulcified Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurij dulcificati"; Calomel, or mercurous chloride, used here as a "like-cures-like" treatment.</note> once and then again, by the benefit of which the boy was delivered from imminent, lethal suffocation.

<margin>Case 3.</margin>
In the same way, a certain citizen, while working strenuously in the separation of metallic matter—which remains as dross for goldsmiths—fell into a severe shortness of breath <note>original: "dyspnoeam".</note> on the Calends of September [September 1st], 1627. To him, who was otherwise quite robust, I first administered a purgative:

> ℞. **Compound Mineral Laxative**
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*8 grains.*
> Syrian Powder <note>original: "Pul. syrij"; likely a preparation of scammony.</note>, *6 grains.*
> Dulcified Mercury, *1 scruple.*
> Mix with 2 ounces of
> Rose Conserve for a bolus.

With this evacuation successfully completed, I provoked a sweat in bed twice by using **diaphoretic Antimony** <note>original: "Antimonium diaphoreticum"; a preparation of antimony used to induce sweating.</note> mixed with a little **Theriac** <note>A famous ancient herbal paste used as a universal antidote.</note>. Within a few days, with God's help, the patient was perfectly restored.

<margin>Case 4.</margin>
Finally, a remarkable case of **Ophthalmia** <note>Severe inflammation of the eye.</note> comes to memory, concerning a certain young man of **Nuremberg** <note>original: "Norici".</note>, who was similarly hired here by the Most Distinguished Senate for the separation of metals,

...affected <note>original: "cti"; the suffix of "affecti," continuing from the previous page's description of the goldsmith's son.</note>, who in the month of March 1627 was suffering from the most intense pains in his eyes. When the common medicines were applied, he felt no relief whatsoever, until I was called and a purging medicine was administered, as follows:

At this, like a miracle, once all topical remedies were removed, the immense pain vanished. Therefore, let those who live in metal mines and at such furnaces, as well as goldsmiths, chemical doctors, and similar workers, observe this diligently; and let them always have some appropriate medicines ready at hand, since the saying of the Poet <note>Ovid, *Remedia Amoris*.</note> is also true here: *resist the beginnings* <note>original: "principijs obsta"; the full proverb is "resist the beginnings, for the medicine is prepared too late when the disease has grown strong through long delay."</note>, etc.

## OBSERVATION XXVI.

### Scorbutic Headache.

A fifty-year-old man, of a **Melancholic** <note>In the humoral theory of the time, a "melancholic" constitution was dominated by "black bile," associated with a cold, dry temperament and tendencies toward sadness or anxiety.</note> constitution of body, suffers from a long-lasting headache

<column-break/>

which is worsened in the evening a little before dinner, with groundless fear and a greater than usual sadness occurring at the same time. Simultaneously, spontaneous fatigue, bleeding of the gums, and lead-colored <note>original: "lividæ"</note> spots on the feet and legs also occur.

## RESOLUTION.

<margin>Scorbutic headache is recognized.</margin>
When, in the year 1607, I was practicing medicine at Salzwedel <note>original: "Soltquellæ"; a town in the Altmark region of Brandenburg.</note> in the Old March of Brandenburg, among many other ailments complicated by **scorbutic** <note>Related to scurvy, a disease caused by vitamin C deficiency, though here viewed through the lens of "malignant" humors.</note> malignity, there occurred the so-called *Cephalea* <note>A term for a chronic, deep-seated, and severe headache.</note>. I determined this to be scorbutic, and I pronounced it to be all the more stubborn and long-lasting because of his **Melancholic** constitution. It worsened in the evening before dinner, as that is the time when the melancholic humor usually "boils over," as evidenced by the accompanying *groundless fear and the greater than usual sadness*. Since the *spontaneous fatigue* along with the other added symptoms indicated Scurvy, I followed that particular process of healing (as far as I remember now, twenty years later) which my late Uncle and Teacher, **Mr. Jacob Horst** <note>A prominent 16th-century physician and professor at Helmstedt.</note>, of pious memory, [delivered] in public lectures at the **Julia Academy** <note>The University of Helmstedt.</note>...

...proposed to us in his instructions, which are as follows. **Scorbutic Headache** <note>original: "Cephalæa Scorbutica"; a chronic, severe headache associated with scurvy.</note> arises not only from the obvious faulty qualities and humors, but is joined by a singular corruption of **black bile** <term>atra bilis: according to Galenic medicine, one of the four humors, which when "corrupted" or "burnt" was thought to cause melancholy and chronic diseases</term> specific to this disease. For this reason, the condition is made longer-lasting and more difficult to cure. Therefore, the pharmacy and the diet should be diligently prescribed in the following manner.

<margin>Diet.</margin>
This consists of the regulation of the **six non-naturals** <note>The six factors external to the body that affect health: air, food/drink, sleep/wake, motion/rest, excretion, and passions of the mind.</note>, where first the surrounding air should be temperately warm; its excesses, especially the Northern and Southern winds, should be avoided. Food should be moderate in quantity and easy to digest in quality, possessing a mild "cutting" or thinning quality. The drink should be diuretic, to which a **sachet** <note>original: "nodulus"; a small cloth bag of herbs steeped in a liquid, in this case, beer.</note> for the beer should be added, containing:

> Take: Clove root, 1 ounce.
> Laurel berries, 0.5 ounces.
> Cinnamon,
> Mace, 2 drachms each.
> Ginger,
> Grains of Paradise, 1 drachm each.
> Cut into coarse pieces for the sachet.

Bodily motion should be moderate, though it may be more vigorous at the time the scorbutic potion is taken, before a sweat is promoted in bed afterward through rest. Nighttime sleep is approved, especially two hours after dinner. Finally, the passions of the mind must be resisted as much as possible, as Horace says:

> *Deliver sadness and fears to the bold*
> *winds to carry into the Cretan Sea, etc.* <note>A quote from Horace, Odes 1.26, suggesting that one should cast away anxieties.</note>

<column-break/>

The pharmacy is determined by two things: 1. The cold and dry imbalance of the brain, which must be remedied particularly when the "black bile" matter is abundant, according to the method prescribed for **Melancholic Headache**. 2. The selection of medicines that resist **Scorbutic Melancholy**, namely by mixing those specific to Scurvy with the digestives and evacuants. In this regard, **Scurvy Grass** <note>original: "Cochlearia"</note> easily holds the first place; **Watercress** the second; the **Lesser Celandine** the third; **Water Pimpernel** <note>original: "Anagallis aquat."</note> the fourth; and **Small Stonecrop** <note>original: "sedum minus"</note> the fifth. A confection should also be taken for the cure of the Scorbutic Melancholic Headache, as follows:

> Take: Conserve of Scurvy Grass, 1 ounce.
> Watercress, 6 ounces.
> Borage, Rose, Violets,
> Fumitory, Candied Lemon Peel, 0.5 drachms each.
> Species Diarrhodon Abbatis <note>A cooling, rose-based medicinal powder used to strengthen the heart and stomach.</note>,
> Laetificans Almansoris <note>original: "Lætific. Almans."; a famous "joy-bringing" compound used to treat melancholy and lift the spirits.</note>, 1 scruple each.
> With Syrup of Lemon Acetos <note>A bittersweet syrup made from lemon juice and vinegar.</note>, make a confection.

But if the cure for the Melancholic Headache mixed with the appropriate anti-scorbutics is not sufficient, let us turn ourselves entirely to the **malignancy** <note>The underlying "poisonous" or aggressive nature of the disease.</note> of the Scurvy, and establish a treatment for Scurvy itself, continuing it for three weeks if necessary, with occasional evacuations applied in this or a similar way:

<margin>Cure for Scurvy.</margin>
<margin>Purgation.</margin>

> Take: Purified goat-milk whey, 6 ounces.
> Senna leaves, 0.5 drachms.
> Epithyme <note>original: "Epithymi"; Dodder of Thyme, a parasitic plant highly valued for purging black bile.</note>, 2 drachms.

Let them stay in an infusion overnight; in the morning, let them boil twice or thrice, then be strained, and add: *Syrup of Fumitory* and *Laxative Rose Syrup, 1 ounce of each. Mix.*

Once this or a similar, even stronger, purging medicine has been administered once or twice, a **scorbutic potion** should be prepared. For this, a twofold medical material presents itself: either simple or compound.

<margin>Scorbutic Potion.</margin>
**The simple version is the juice of Scurvy-grass** <note>original: "Cochlearia"; a plant high in Vitamin C historically used to treat scurvy.</note>, **4 ounces at minimum, 5 to 8 ounces at most**, extracted and purified with wine or whey. When this is finished, the clothes should be changed, the skin wiped with moderate friction, and then a temperate lunch and dinner should follow. The second kind is a **distilled water**, which is composed in this way:

Take: **Juice of Borage and Bugloss, 1 pound of each after purification.**

**Scurvy-grass, 2 handfuls.**
**Fumitory, Watercress, Lesser Stonecrop, 1 handful of each (all fresh).**
**Aromatic powder of Roses, 2 drachms.** <note>original: "Spec. Diarrhod. Abb."; Species Diarrhodon Abbatis, a classical Greco-Arabic aromatic powder used to strengthen the heart and stomach.</note>
Let a distillation be made in a **water bath** <term>Balneo Maris: a "Mary's Bath" or double boiler, used for gentle heating in chemistry and pharmacy</term>. However, since the distillate is weaker than the previous potion, its use must be continued for a longer period of time. With these things observed for the aforementioned sufferer, and changing what needs to be changed <note>original: "mutatis mutandis"</note>, we provide relief at that time, not neglecting other matters regarding the correction of symptoms, which are dealt with at greater length in the booklet...

### OBSERVATION XXVII.

->Malignant Pestilential Headache<-

**A** man in the prime of life, 30 years old, *with a ruddy face and a fleshy build, a scholar by profession, suffered a massive headache during a time of epidemic plague. It was so severe that he immediately collapsed from dizziness; this was followed by great anxiety and a weariness in his hands and feet, along with a slight chill that was soon followed by a more intense febrile heat. He suffered from a rapid pulse as well as persistent insomnia and frequent fainting spells.*

### RESOLUTION.

**W**hen I was devoted to my studies at the Academia Julia <note>The University of Helmstedt, founded in 1576.</note> in the year 1607, this case occurred among others at that time. It was shared in public lectures by my Lord Uncle and Teacher, the most distinguished Jacob 

<column-break/>

<margin>The primary indication in the plague.</margin>
Horstius <note>Jacob Horst (1537–1600) was a famous German physician; the author here is his nephew, likely Gregorius Horstius.</note>, First Professor of blessed memory. He determined that this severe headache <term>Cephalæa: a term used for chronic or particularly intense, deep-seated headaches</term> was nothing other than the plague itself. He argued that although the symptom appeared extremely urgent, it should be treated as secondary; instead, one must address the malignant disease which, by its very nature, oppresses the vital principle of life. The patient’s bodily constitution was "hot and moist," and signs of an abundance of blood manifested as a "plethora" <term>plethora: an old medical theory suggesting an overabundance of bodily fluids, particularly blood, which required balancing</term>.

<margin>Prognosis</margin>
The patient’s robust strength offered hope for recovery, provided he diligently obeyed the doctors' advice. Regarding the cure: a malignant and highly dangerous disease indicates that one must immediately use "Alexipharmacs" <term>Alexipharmacs: remedies intended to neutralize poison or ward off contagion</term>. This treatment is achieved through the skillful use of either Theriac, Mithridatium, or an Electuary <note>Theriac and Mithridatium were famous ancient "universal antidotes" containing dozens of ingredients, including herbs, spices, and sometimes honey or opium.</note> such as the following:

<margin>An Alexipharmic Electuary.</margin>
Take: Powder of Scordium <note>Water Germander</note>, Rue seeds,
Gentian root, 3 scruples of each. <note>A scruple is about 1.3 grams.</note>
Mithridatium,
Theriac, 1.5 drams of each. <note>A dram is about 3.9 grams.</note>
Conserve of roses, 1 dram.
With Syrup of Scordium or Citron Vinegar, as much as suffices.
Make an Electuary.

The dose of this Electuary for adults is 1.5 drams, dissolved in rue or rose vinegar and administered to promote sweating. This expulsion of toxins can be aided, when necessary, with external fomentations <note>Warm, medicated compresses</note>, etc. In the meantime, the sweat should be wiped from the face, and rose vinegar should be applied to the nostrils for the sake of strengthening the patient. *The patient's strength*, however, although it had been robust before, was not even

# ON CONTAGIOUS AND MALIGNANT DISEASES

<margin>What the patient's vitality indicates;</margin>
Even if the patient's vitality <note>original: "virtus," referring to the body's natural strength or life force</note> still appears significantly weakened due to the violence of the disease, the situation indicates that strengthening remedies <term>corroborantia: medicines intended to restore strength or "corroborate" the vital spirits</term> must be used immediately after the patient has sweated. Indeed, a malignant disease and a collapsed vitality—or one that is soon to collapse—require medicines that restore strength and resist poison right after the sweating process. For this purpose, we have at hand *Syrup of sweet pomegranates, acids of wood sorrel, citron, and lemon,* and *our own tablets against the plague.* After the sweating was finished in this patient, we gave him *Syrup of sweet pomegranates*; after this was taken twice over the course of half an hour, we provided food—namely, a barley broth <term>ptisana: a medicinal porridge or decoction, usually made from barley, used as a light restorative</term> and a small amount of boiled rockfish <note>original: "piscibus saxatilibus," fish that live among rocks, considered light and easy to digest</note> seasoned with a little rose vinegar. Once he was refreshed by the food, the patient's "plethoric" <term>plethora: an overabundance of blood or bodily fluids, thought to cause disease</term> nature indicated the need for bloodletting. <margin>Permission for bloodletting.</margin> This was supported by his strength, which remained constant for the moment, though we were warned that he could easily slip into weakness, so not much blood was to be drawn. After the blood was drawn from the median vein <note>A common site for venesection in the crook of the elbow</note>, a *Julep* was administered an hour later to temper the feverish heat, composed as follows:

> Take: Water of Lettuce, Wood Sorrel,
> and Holy Thistle—4 ounces of each.
> Syrup of sweet pomegranate juice—1 ounce.
> Highly rectified Spirit of Vitriol <note>original: "Spir. Vitrioli," a potent acid (sulfuric acid) used in tiny, diluted amounts to "cool" the blood</note>—half a scruple.
> Mix to make a Julep, from which he should drink over the following 4 hours.

Six hours after the bloodletting, sleep was ordered. When it failed to come, and fearing a loss of strength, a sleep-inducing *poultice* <term>Epithema: a topical liquid application or compress, often applied to the forehead or heart</term> was prepared in this way:

<column-break/>

> Take: White poppy seeds—1.5 drams.
> Peach kernels—2 drams.
> Citron peel—1.5 drams.
> Waters of Dill, Vervain,
> and Roses—4 ounces of each.
> Mix to make an emulsion for a poultice for the forehead.

At last he began to sleep; in the morning he again used the previously mentioned sweat-inducing remedy, which resulted in a moderate sweat. We continued with the strengthening remedies and a suitable light diet for several days, until the malignancy of the disease was overcome and the patient recovered as desired.

## OBSERVATION XXVII.

### Malignant pestilential headache.

**A** man of mature age, <note>original: "consistentis ætatis"</note> 30 years old, with a ruddy face and a fleshy build, who lived a scholarly life, suffered a massive headache during a time of epidemic plague. It was so severe that he immediately collapsed from vertigo. This was followed by great anxiety and a weariness in his hands and feet, along with a light chill <note>original: "horrore levi"</note> which was succeeded by a more vehement febrile heat. His pulse was rapid, and he was greatly afflicted by insomnia as well as fainting spells.

### RESOLUTION.

**W**hen I was devoted to my studies at the Julia Academy <note>The Academia Julia was the University of Helmstedt, founded in 1576.</note> in the year 1607, my uncle and teacher, the most celebrated Jacob Horstius—formerly the Primary Professor—shared this case among others occurring at that time in his public lectures. He determined that this severe headache <term>Cephalæa: a term used for chronic or particularly intense headaches</term> was nothing other than the plague itself. He argued that although the symptoms seemed extremely urgent, they should be treated as secondary; rather, the disease should be viewed as a malignant force from the "whole substance" <note>An early medical concept suggesting a disease that affects the entire body or its vital essence, rather than just one organ.</note> that oppresses the vital principle. The patient's physical state was hot and moist, and a "plethora" <term>plethora: an overabundance of blood or bodily fluids, thought to be a primary cause of disease</term> was manifest by signs of abundant blood. <margin>Prognosis:</margin> His robust strength provided hope for recovery, provided that the patient diligently obeyed the physicians' warnings. Regarding the cure: a malignant and most dangerous disease indicates that alexipharmics <term>alexipharmacum: a medicine intended to neutralize poison or ward off contagion</term> must be used immediately. This indication is fulfilled by the skillful use of either Theriac, Mithridatum, or the following Electuary:

# On Contagious and Malignant Diseases.

<margin>What the patient's strength indicates.</margin>
Even if the patient's vital strength <note>original: "virtus"</note> still appears to be greatly weakened due to the severity of the disease, this indicates that strengthening remedies must be used immediately after the sweating process. Indeed, a malignant disease and a collapsed (or soon-to-be collapsed) strength require medicines that both restore vigor and resist poison as soon as the sweating is finished. For this purpose, we suggest Syrup of sweet Pomegranates, acid Syrup of Sorrel, Citron, or Lemon, and our Master’s <note>Likely referring to Jacob Horstius’s specific recipe.</note> Tablets against the plague. After this specific patient had finished sweating, we gave him sweet pomegranate syrup; after he had taken this twice within half an hour, we presented him with food, specifically a ptisan <term>Ptisan: a medicinal drink made from barley water or herbal infusions</term> and a small amount of boiled rockfish <note>original: "piscibus saxatilibus"</note> seasoned with a little rose vinegar. Once he was refreshed by the food, the patient's plethoric <term>Plethoric: a medical state characterized by an excess of blood or "fullness" in the body</term> nature indicated that bloodletting was necessary. This was further 
<margin>Permission for bloodletting.</margin>
confirmed by his strength, which remained steady; however, because strength can fail easily in such cases, it was a warning that not too much blood should be drawn. Once the blood was taken from the median vein, a Julep <term>Julep: a sweet liquid medicine, often used as a refreshing vehicle for other drugs</term> was administered an hour later to temper the febrile heat:
> ℞ Lettuce water, Sorrel water,
> Blessed Thistle water, 4 ounces of each.
> Syrup of sweet pomegranate juice, 1 ounce.
> Best rectified Spirit of Vitriol <note>A historically used dilute sulfuric acid, thought to cool the "heat" of a fever.</note>, half a scruple.
> Mix to make a Julep, of which he should drink over the following 4 hours.

Six hours after the bloodletting, sleep was ordered. When it did not come, and fearing a loss of strength, a sleep-inducing Epithema <term>Epithema: a topical compress or poultice applied to the body, in this case to the forehead</term> was prepared in this manner:

<column-break/>

> ℞ White poppy seeds, half an ounce.
> Peach kernels, 2 ounces.
> Citron peel, half an ounce.
> Dill water, Vervain water, 
> Rose water, 3 ounces of each.
> Mix to make an emulsion for a compress
> for the forehead.

Finally, he began to sleep. In the morning, he used the previously mentioned sudorific <term>Sudorific: a medicine intended to induce sweating to "sweat out" a disease</term> again, with moderate success. In addition, we repeated the use of strengthening remedies and a suitable light diet. By persisting in this plan for several days, the malignancy of the disease was defeated, and the patient recovered according to our hopes.

### BOOK THE SECOND OF PART II.

...for the removal of which [plague] one must resort not so much to the ordinary protections of Medicine as to atonements, devout prayers, and true repentance of heart to be offered to God Most High. For God, the Best, Greatest, and Thrice-Holy, who uses secondary and natural causes to bring in, spread, end, and avert the plague, also most mercifully grants that those whom He wishes to be freed from this pestiferous beast should implore the help of Ordinary Physicians with sincere devotion and contrition of heart, and find their help not in vain, but health-giving.

<margin>
What the plague is. 
Compare with *Problems*, decade 10, question 1.
</margin>
*The plague, moreover, is nothing other than a very acute, contagious, and malignant fever, by which the bodies of men are suddenly seized as if by a thunderbolt—not only in the head, heart, and liver, but in all the limbs as well, and especially in the arms and legs—and many of these people perish within a very short interval of time.* From this, it can be gathered that the essence, form, and nature of the pestilence consist of two parts: one, a contagious poison; the other, a malignant fever.

<margin>
The subject of the plague. 
See *Medical Epistles*, book 2, section 3.
</margin>
The subject <note>In this context, "subject" refers to the target or the person susceptible to the disease.</note> is not every human body, but only those which are naturally disposed to receive this pollution.

<margin>
The quality of the pestiferous poison.
</margin>
This poison is imbued with a destructive and harmful quality which, although it arises from the concurrence and mixture of the four Elements and is transfused from one person to

<column-break/>

another by means of the air, is sometimes nevertheless born within us from the boiling mass of the blood itself and, invading people generally, infects the air.

<margin>
F
</margin>
*This fever is malignant and belongs to the order and number of continuous fevers—those afflicting the patient continuously without intermission or apyrexia <note>original: "α​π​υ​ρ​ε​ξ​ί​α", a Greek term referring to a period without fever</note>—and it is an acute fever, raging fiercely with very rapid motion and running its full course.* Those which are most acute, involving extreme putridity and inflammation of the blood, are called "peracute"; this pestilential fever is included in that category, having acquired a notable malignancy in addition to its extreme sharpness.

The bodies of men that are to be immune from the taint of this poison and pestilential fever must be endowed with these three properties: 
1. They must not overflow with superfluous blood and waste-laden juices <term>juices: the "humors," or bodily fluids like phlegm and bile</term>. 
2. They should have moderate and natural excretions through the bowels, urine, sweat, and breath. 
3. They should be strong with vital vigor <note>original: "virtus," referring to the body's innate life-force</note> so that they are capable of resisting the approaching poison. 

However, those bodies which lack these conditions—and either abound in foul juices and blockages <term>blockages: "oppilationes," or obstructions in the vessels and organs</term> collected within the vessels (that is, the veins and arteries), or are not fortified with sufficient strength to drive away this virus <note>original: "virus," used here in the classical sense of "poison" or "venom," rather than the modern germ theory definition</note>, or are accustomed to living softly and delicately—are seized by this plague upon the slightest occasion.

And although everyone about himself...

# ON CONTAGIOUS AND MALIGNANT DISEASES #

<margin>
The nature of those <unclear>p</unclear>rone to fever.
</margin>
Although the person cannot make a judgment for themselves, skilled Physicians can easily discern what should be thought of each one. Among them, those first burdened by the weight of blood <note>original: "sanguinis ablatione"; referring to the theory of plethora, where an excess of blood makes one vulnerable to disease</note> can be relieved by bloodletting and purification. Thus, in cases of urgent necessity, they may move among those infected with the plague more safely than others. The rest, however—those who lack these favorable conditions—ought either to be sent away from contaminated places to distant and more secure locations, or be seriously warned to commit themselves to the treatments and counsel of Physicians before they incur this evil. In this way, by excluding harmful <term>humors</term> <note>The vital fluids of the body—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which were believed to cause disease when out of balance.</note>, they will be less suited to and less exposed to catching this blight; or, if they already suffer an assault of the plague, they will be more quickly restored to health.

<margin>
How bodies may be made safer from the poison.
</margin>
The *intent* <note>original: "Intentio"; the medical strategy or objective</note> against the Plague is twofold: *one is Preservative*, guarding men from the invasion of the plague; the *other is Curative*, healing those already seized by it. Protective medication consists primarily of safeguards preserving against the pestilential <term>miasma</term> <note>A term used for "pollution" or "taint"; it was believed that diseases were spread by foul-smelling air or vapors.</note> and rooting out its causes. This regards not only the prevention of the poison and the malignancy of the fever but also the preparation of impure bodies and their fortification against the <term>bilge-water of excrements</term> <note>original: "excrementorum saburra"; a medical metaphor comparing the buildup of waste in the body to the foul water at the bottom of a ship.</note>, so they are less harmed by this pestilence. This, in turn, is considered in two ways: either as it concerns the guardianship of public health and looks at the whole congregation of men in general—

<column-break/>

—in a certain house, a city, or in a Prince's populous court; or as it weighs the particular benefit of each individual and regards men one by one, each in their own specific case.

<margin>
Preservation against the plague in general.
</margin>
*Preservation against the Plague in general*, concerning a great multitude of people, requires above all else that: 1. The streets, neighborhoods, alleys, and the openings of public sewers—but especially each individual house—be **purged** frequently and diligently of all filth and foul defilements. Experience proves that by this counsel and means alone, the pestilence has been quickly driven out of certain cities. 2. Meetings and assemblies should either be prohibited entirely by the Magistrate, or the population should be distributed into different locations. Alternatively, more rooms should be occupied in every house so that all (or many) do not live together in one room and infect one another. For some, not yet gripped by this corruption <note>original: "tabo"; referring to the infectious rot or discharge</note>, nonetheless infect others with this pestiferous seed <note>original: "rudimento"; the initial "starting material" of the disease</note> lurking in their own clothes and linens. Some carry these contagious miasmas for a long time while appearing healthy; however, as time progresses—with the poison hiding itself for up to a fourth week or even longer—they and others are seized. 3. Commerce and conversations with suspected persons should be conducted in the open air, where the pestilential effluvia <note>Vapors or invisible particles given off by the body.</note>...

...of the paths, so that by not leaping across <note>original: "transiliens"; referring to the movement of "contagious seeds"</note> it cannot disperse itself among others; and certainly not in heated rooms <note>original: "hypocaustis"; rooms heated from below, common in Central Europe, which were thought to trap and cultivate foul air</note>, in which the plague might expand and propagate itself more widely. 4. That two hours each day should be designated for the buyers and carriers of food and necessities of life, during which they may leave the house to purchase what is needed for living, and from whom others not yet contaminated by this pestilence may know to protect themselves.

-> Z 2 <-

Take of:
Sorrel: 2 pounds.

Pomegranate Wine: 6 ounces.
Quince: 5 ounces.
Preserve of Wood-Sorrel: 1.5 ounces.
Species Diamargariton Frigidum <note>original: "Spec. diamarg. frig."; a cooling medicinal powder made primarily of crushed pearls</note>.
Temperate Cordial Species.
Electuary of Gems: 1 drachm of each.
Diamoschu: half a drachm <note>original: "Diamoſch."; a stimulant compound containing musk, ambergris, and spices</note>.
And let a distillation be made according to the art through glass.
Label: **Mithridatium Water of Dr. Horstius.** <note>original: "Mithridatwaſſer"</note> Give 6 spoonfuls for adults and 4 spoonfuls for children in one dose.

Furthermore, two hours after a meal, or seven hours after the onset of the plague, the infected should take a second dose of the Antidote, or my Mithridatium Water, or Theriac, or Mithridatium; let them sweat again, and restore their strength as before. Finally, for the complete dispersion of any remaining plague-seeds, on the second or third day, they should repeat the Lozenges <note>original: "Rotulas"</note> against the plague of our [composition], taking two or three every six hours. Indeed, they should frequently use Syrup of Pomegranate because of the intensity of the burning fever—sometimes by itself, sometimes mixed in the form of a Julep <note>a sweet, medicinal drink used as a vehicle for other drugs</note>, by taking 12 spoonfuls of Sorrel Water and 1 spoonful each of Syrups of Citric Acidity <note>lemon syrup</note> or Pomegranate, especially since these also fight against the malignancy; sometimes taking 6 spoonfuls of sorrel water and mixing in the aforementioned syrups.

It happens, indeed, that those seized by the plague 

<column-break/>

commonly indulge in a deep sleep at the beginning, because the malignancy is drawn back to the Heart, and the infected themselves are in the greatest danger and risk of life; at which time Rue and Vinegar should be applied to the nose, and by every ingenuity, sleep should be driven away. Then, if the bowels are suppressed <note>constipated</note>, the use of the Antidote should be paused for a second time until the following day. And after about the seventh hour from the first onset, or from the first Alexipharmic <note>original: "Alexipharmaco"; a medicine used to ward off poison or infection</note>, a laxative potion should be drunk warm according to the patient's age, fasting for three hours and resting for eight hours from other remedies.

Meanwhile, one spoonful of Pomegranate Syrup can be taken, so that eight hours later the patient may rest a little, and soon after sleep, they should swallow the Antidote in turn to provoke sweat a second time.

Thirdly, bloodletting <note>original: "Sanguinis missio"; the medical practice of withdrawing blood to balance the "humors" or bodily fluids.</note> does not suit everyone equally, both because not everyone is endowed with an equal amount of blood, and because some do not possess enough strength. For those who are overflowing with an abundance of blood and are strong in vigor, only for these is bloodletting beneficial at the seventh or sixth hour, provided that the bowels re-

<column-break/>

-spond <note>This refers to the bowels being "responsive" or open before bloodletting.</note>. For those whose bowels are not loose, after a mild purgative and a light sleep, let them take one spoonful of Syrup of Lemon Acidity or Pomegranate fifteen minutes after bloodletting. And if no bubo <note>original: "bubone"; the painful, swollen lymph nodes that are the hallmark of the bubonic plague.</note> appears anywhere, pierce the median vein of the left elbow; but if something protrudes under the armpits, the Basilic vein; if something breaks out in or under the loins, they should pierce the vein of the knee or the ankle directly on that side. When a bubo breaks out, it is necessary to call a Surgeon to administer local treatments in the proper manner. In his absence, poultices <note>original: "faculi"; small bundles of herbs used as hot compresses.</note> should be prepared from *5 handfuls of marshmallow leaves, 3 ounces each of marshmallow roots and white lilies, half a handful each of agrimony and water germander, and 5 figs.* These two decoctions should be applied alternately to the affected part. Let *Compound Diachylon* <note>A traditional surgical plaster made of lead oxide boiled with olive oil and plant juices, used to soften tumors.</note> also be ready, to be applied three times a day after fomentation <note>The application of warm, medicinal liquids to the body.</note>. After some softening of the bubo, take an onion filled with Theriac <note>A famous ancient "universal" medicinal paste containing dozens of ingredients, including opium and viper flesh.</note> and roasted; let it be crushed and mixed with figs, honey, and flour, and applied. If it has opened, an egg yolk should be added to this mixture. Corrosives and incisions should not be put into action except in cases of the most urgent necessity. Carbuncles <note>original: "Anthraces"; the black, necrotic sores associated with the plague.</note> are remarkably mitigated by wheat chewed by healthy people and smeared on, especially if a *Sapphire* is then held near it and moved in a circle <note>This reflects "sympathetic medicine," where gemstones were believed to possess spiritual or physical powers to draw out poison.</note>.

### OBSERVATION XXIX.

<margin>1611</margin>
->Containing an instruction for the time of the plague in the year 1611, published at the University of Giessen with my colleagues for the benefit of the common people, and translated from the German.<-

<margin>Prevention.</margin>
So that everyone may have an instruction on how to be preserved from the pestilential poison in these dangerous times, and also how to be cured if they should be infected by divine permission, it is necessary to diligently observe the following chapters. First, regarding prevention, care must be taken that the surrounding air is purified. 2. Excess of food and drink should be avoided. 3. Bodies should be cleared of superfluities <note>An excess of "humors" or bodily fluids believed to cause illness.</note>, 4. and defended against the pestilential poison. The surrounding air is purified by frequently lighting bright fires, or by fumigation using juniper wood and its berries, wormwood herb, oak leaves, amber, myrrh, and frankincense; likewise by a powder for smoke, which [is made as follows]:

Take: 4 handfuls <note>original: "Miiij", where M stands for 'manipulus'.</note> of Juniper berries.

### Bezoartic Water of Life by Felix Würk <note>Felix Würk was a 17th-century surgeon and medical writer known for his practical pharmaceutical recipes.</note>.

<margin>Bezoartic Water of Life.</margin>
Take: 1 pound and 4 ounces of Spirit of Wine, separated from its phlegm <note>Pure distilled alcohol.</note>.
*Add into a glass vessel:*
6 ounces of fresh filings of unburnt Hartshorn <note>original: "C. C." or Cornu Cervi; the antlers of a deer, used as a source of ammonia.</note>.
2 drachms of the most select powdered Myrrh.
*Let the sealed glass stand for digestion for eight days; afterwards, separate the Spirit by a Water Bath until dry. Pour the Spirit back onto the dregs, and distill a third time in the same way. Pour that Spirit into a narrow-mouthed glass, and add 2 drachms of fresh filings of Hartshorn.*
1 drachm of the most select powdered Myrrh.
½ drachm of Mithridatium.
2 drachms of Camphor.
*Seal very exactly, and keep for use. The dose for preservation is 1 spoonful.*

## SECOND BOOK OF PART II.

To prepare this water, 6 ounces <note>original: "℥ vi."</note> of the same amount of Bezoartic <note>A term derived from "bezoar," a stone found in the stomachs of animals, believed to be a universal antidote to poison.</note> distilled vinegar may be added; that is, 6 ounces, or 1 ounce for a standard dose.

<margin>
Simpler antidotes.
</margin>

**Simpler remedies should also commonly not** be neglected, especially by those whose circumstances at home are narrow <note>original: "res angusta domi"; a poetic way of referring to the poor.</note>. These include: *Roots of Angelica, Lovage, Elecampane, and Tormentil; fresh Herbs of Rue, Wormwood, Blessed Thistle, and Sage; Zedoary <note>A root similar to ginger.</note>, Root of Butterbur, Sealed Earth <note>A medicinal clay stamped with a seal to guarantee its origin and purity.</note>, Juniper berries*, and their *Rob* <note>A thickened fruit juice or syrup.</note>, etc. Let some of these be used. For those who are accustomed to aiding the stomach with a draught of medicated wine, they may make an infusion from the aforementioned roots and herbs, adding *Betony, Speedwell, Scabious, Scordium, and Pimpernel*, etc. The wealthier may obtain <term>Amulets</term> <note>Objects worn on the body to ward off disease through their occult or magnetic properties.</note> from the apothecaries and wear them over the region of the heart, provided that

<margin>
Caution in wearing Amulets.
</margin>

those which are composed with added substances do not touch the skin, nor should they be kept on at night. No one should leave the house on an empty stomach, but should take bread with butter sprinkled with powdered Rue, followed by a draught of wine or medicated beer; or they should take some of the aforementioned preservative medicines, or chew something simpler in the mouth, such as *Zedoary, Angelica, Lovage, Pimpernel, Citrus peel, Juniper berries, or Laurel berries*, etc. All of these should first be soaked in vinegar and then dried. They may also crush fresh *Rue* in their hands that has been soaked in vinegar,

<column-break/>

or they may carry a <term>Pomander</term> <note>A "scent ball" made of fragrant resins and spices, intended to purify the air the wearer breathes.</note>, which is made in this manner:
Take: 3 drachms each of the purest *Ladanum* <note>A sticky resin from the Cistus shrub.</note> and *Storax Calamita* <note>A fragrant resin used as a fixative.</note>.
1 ½ drachms each of the powders of *Marjoram, Red Roses, Citrus peel, and Cinnamon*.

1 ½ scruples of *Oil of Nutmeg* (expressed).
15 grains each of the *Extracts of Angelica and Zedoary*.

With a sufficient quantity of *Mucilage of Tragacanth* dissolved in *Rose Water*.
**Make a mass for scent-balls.**

<margin>
The Cure.
</margin>

In the treatment itself, the primary focus must be *that the pestilential poison be driven away from the heart*. To this end, an appropriate dose can be sought from the apothecaries,

<margin>
Use of the antidote.
</margin>

respecting the patient's age, whether of the *Curative Electuary*, the *Bezoartic Powder*, or the *Bezoartic Water of Life*, etc. Once these medicines have been administered, sweating should be encouraged for three hours. When the sweat has been wiped away with warm cloths, the linens and shirts should be changed, having first been scented with the smoke of the antidotes mentioned above.

After the sweating, some citrus flesh prepared with sugar, or a certain strengthening broth, should be given. A little later, some strengthening <term>alexipharmacs</term> <note>Antidotes or medicines used to ward off poison or infection.</note> may be granted, such as *strengthening waters, pearled emulsions <note>Medicinal drinks containing crushed pearls, thought to strengthen the heart.</note>, confections*, etc. Foods should frequently be seasoned with rose vinegar, and also with the juice of lemons.

<margin>How to treat bowel obstruction.</margin> ...[of] lemons, citrons, etc. After the first sweating (unless the bowels are completely obstructed), and after five or six hours have passed, the sweating should be repeated a second and even a third time. Those who are forced to interact with the infected should diligently apply the same preventative measures as others: they should not visit the sick on an empty stomach, they should ensure a bright fire with the aforementioned fumigations is lit in the infected houses before they enter, and above all, they should beware of the breath and exhalations of the patients. The rooms of the deceased should be avoided; in these rooms, several portions of <term>quicklime</term> <note>Calcium oxide, a caustic chemical used here to disinfect by "consuming" the plague's "miasma."</note> should be doused with cold water, and its fuming should be continued for two days. Afterward, the windows should be opened, and the aforementioned fumigations should be performed three or four times. Clothing, linens, and so forth should be exposed to the open air in remote locations, etc.

Since the Plague spread widely this summer in the neighboring Duchy of Württemberg, in addition to those things that were formerly in use here, both for the sake of *prevention* and for the *restoration of the infected*, I—having shared counsel with my *most distinguished colleagues*—ordered certain specifically appropriate measures. *Regarding prevention*, we prescribed two types of sublingual lozenges (A), preventive morsels (E E), stomach balsam (E E), pestilential pills (F F), and certain other things contained in previous consultations. After these applications have been repeated, one must ensure that—once the tumor has subsided slightly and its hardness and inflammation have been somewhat eased—an opening is made using a scalpel or a potential cautery <note>original: "cauterium potentiale"; a chemical caustic used to burn through the skin, as opposed to an "actual" cautery which was a hot iron</note> in a circular fashion. Simultaneously, the aforementioned attractants and ripening agents should be added until the malignant matter—aided by internal remedies—is either consumed or brought to suppuration. Always take care, as was mentioned previously, that the wound does not close and heal too quickly <note>If the skin healed before the internal "poison" was fully drained, a relapse was feared</note>.

## APPENDIX TO BOOK II, PART II.
### WHICH CONTAINS A
### TREATISE
# ON SCURVY
### BY
## GREGOR HORST, DOCTOR AT THE UNIVERSITY OF GIESSEN
### IN THE YEAR 1608.
### Proposed for Public Examination in two Exercises.
## SECTION ONE.
### §. I.

<image-desc>Large ornamental woodcut initial 'V' decorated with scrolling vines, leaves, and floral patterns.</image-desc>

VARIOUS and diverse are the diseases by which the human body is afflicted, which nevertheless are all distinguished into *sporadic* <note>original Greek: "$\sigma\pi\omicron\rho\alpha\delta\iota\kappa\omicron\grave{\upsilon}\varsigma$"; referring to diseases that occur occasionally or in scattered instances</note> or *common* <note>original Greek: "$\kappa\omicron\iota\nu\omicron\grave{\upsilon}\varsigma$"; referring to diseases that affect a large portion of the community at once, such as epidemics</note>. For since our body, produced

<column-break/>

from the prolific seed of our parents, exists in a state of perpetual alteration due to the inherent mutability of nature, it is no wonder that it is subject to morbid dispositions, and many kinds at that; this is because the body as a whole is not a simple entity, but is made up of a number of different parts that work together to form a single constitution <note>original: "politiam"; a metaphor comparing the body's internal organization to a "polity" or governed city-state</note>...

<summary>This page serves as the title page and introduction for a specialized treatise on scurvy by Gregor Horst. It begins by classifying diseases into sporadic and epidemic types, citing the inherent instability of the human body as the cause of illness.</summary>
<keywords>scurvy, Gregor Horst, University of Giessen, sporadic diseases, epidemic diseases, pathology, medical constitution</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introductory section of Gregor Horst’s treatise on scurvy. The previous page established that the human body is a complex system of parts organized like a "polity." Here, the text concludes that philosophical definition and begins categorizing diseases into "sporadic" (individual) and "common" (affecting many), setting the stage for where scurvy fits into these medical classifications.</meta>

->ON SCURVY, SECTION I.<-

...and establishes a harmonious whole, so that in this way a single body, though endowed with diverse parts, may provide a proper and adequate subject for the functions of the soul—which acts as the "form," consisting of diverse and manifold faculties. For the soul is the **actualization of a natural body which has life potentially**, as the Philosopher <note>The "Philosopher" refers to Aristotle; this quote is his famous definition of the soul from *De Anima* (On the Soul), Book 2, Text 6.</note> says: namely, the perfection of a natural body that possesses the potential for life, whose parts function as organs. Yet among the manifold morbid dispositions, our bodies are affected in various ways; for this reason, the whole **"Iliad" of diseases** <note>A common Renaissance metaphor comparing a long list of medical troubles to the epic scale of the Trojan War.</note> is reduced to two types: some are **sporadic**, others are **common**.

### II.

**Sporadic diseases** or **scattered ones** <note>original Greek: "Σποραδικοὶ νοῦσοι ἢ σποράδες"</note> are those said to wander here and there in a scattered and dispersed manner, which do not attack many people collectively, but only this or that person individually. See Galen, Book 1 of his commentary on *The Epidemics*, at the beginning. These diseases are elsewhere called **diverse**, since they differ in species and form, and happen to many people from different causes, either at the same or different times—as is evident in **Epilepsy**, **the Stone** <note>Kidney or bladder stones (calculi).</note>, **Pleurisy**, and others. These arise from particular causes in this or that person, especially

<column-break/>

resulting from a poor and inconsistent diet: **for we fall ill from the very things by which we live.** <note>original Greek: "ἐκ τούτων γὰρ νοσῶμεν, οἷς καὶ ζῶμεν"; a quote from the philosopher Plutarch in his *Table Talk* (Symposiacs), Book 8, Question 9.</note>

### III.

**Common and universal** <note>original Greek: "Κοινοὶ καὶ παγκοινοὶ"</note> are those diseases said to attack many people collectively. They either rage only at a certain time in some region—called **epidemic and pandemic** <note>original Greek: "ἐπιδήμιοι, καὶ πάνδημοι"</note>—or they are present with a certain permanence in specific places, regions, or cities, and are called **endemic and local** <note>original Greek: "ἐνδήμιοι καὶ ἐπιχώριοι"</note>.

<margin>Cause of common disease.</margin>
A disease is rendered "common," and thus attacks many at once, when it possesses a common cause that is sustained contrary to nature either in our food or in the air.
<margin>Endemic.</margin>
It is called **Endemic** when it is perpetual and, as it were, peculiar to a certain region, insofar as the air is tainted or the common food supply is corrupted due to the nature of the place.
<margin>Epidemic.</margin>
An **Epidemic**, by contrast, usually rages only at a specific time and mostly draws its cause from a **malignant influence of the stars**, by which a harmful quality is communicated to the air surrounding us. I add "mostly" because an epidemic disease often also arises through **contagion**, where the malignancy is propagated from one person to another in the same city or region. Although Fernelius <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), an influential French physician who sought to harmonize ancient medicine with new observations.</note>, in Book 2, Chapter 11 of *On the Hidden Causes of Things*, maintains...

<meta>This page continues the classification of diseases from page 191, moving from "sporadic" (individual) diseases to "common" diseases that affect whole populations. It addresses the debate over whether "Pandemic" diseases should be a separate category or simply a subtype of Endemic and Epidemic diseases.</meta>

->APPENDIX TO BOOK I, PART II<-

<margin>
Are there such things as Pandemic diseases?
</margin>

...[com]mon diseases not only into Endemic and Epidemic, but also into **Pandemic**, so that they are called **Endemic** or **Epidemic** when the common cause is the air, and **Pandemic** when they arise from a common corruption of food. In this view, they follow *Forestus (Book 6, Observation 1), Ingrassia (Book 1, On Pestilential Contagion, Chapter 18), Marcello Capra (Book on Pandemic Diseases, Chapter 11), Salomon Albert (History of Scurvy, Thesis 14)*, and others. Nevertheless, based on the teachings of Galen and Hippocrates, and along with *Langius (Book 2, Epistle 13), Gerardo Colombo (Book 1, On the Plague, Chapter 2)*, and others, it seems safer to establish that all common diseases are either **Endemic** <note>Diseases native to a specific region or people.</note> or **Epidemic** <note>Diseases that "visit" a population and spread rapidly.</note>. This is because those called **Pandemic** <note>original Greek: πανδήμιοι, meaning "affecting all the people."</note> by Hippocrates and Galen are always contained within the aforementioned categories, as is clear in the first commentary on Book 1 of *The Epidemics*, and likewise in the ninth commentary on Book 1 of *On Acute Diseases*. Indeed, reason itself suggests this, insofar as **Pandemic** diseases—to the extent that they affect many people in one region either permanently or for a certain time—do not differ in their essential nature from **Endemic** or **Epidemic** diseases. For although they sometimes have other preceding causes, such as being produced by the corruption of the air or of food, they do not differ "according to their being" <note>original Latin: "κατὰ τὸ εἶναι" (kata to einai), a philosophical term meaning "according to its essence."</note> or according to their own essential nature, as they possess the same nature, the same subject, and the same mode of injury.

<column-break/>

## IV.

**Epidemic or common diseases** <note>original Greek: Ἐπίδημοι ἢ δηδήμιοι (Epidēmoi ē pandēmioi). The OCR's "δηδήμιοι" is likely a transcription of "πανδήμιοι."</note>—those which attack many people at the same time—are either **pestilential** <note>original Greek: λοιμώδεις (loimōdeis).</note> or **non-pestilential** <note>original Greek: μὴ λοιμώδεις (mē loimōdeis).</note>.

Since the immediate cause for which many people suffer at the same time is not always the same, it follows that Epidemic diseases admit a certain distinction. Some are **pestilential**, that is, plague-like; and of these, some are highly malignant, killing the greater part of the population suddenly, as is evident in the Plague and truly pestilential fevers. Others are less malignant, which indeed kill many, but for not a few, they are survivable, as is seen in the **Hungarian fever** <note>Often identified as typhus.</note> or **petechial fever** <note>A fever characterized by small purple or red spots (petechiae) on the skin.</note>. These occur because of a **morbid secretion** or **exhalation of the air** <note>original Greek: νοσηρὴν ἀπόκρισιν, ἢ ἀναθυμίασιν τοῦ ἀέρος. This refers to the "miasma" theory, where bad air or vapors cause disease.</note> (*Hippocrates, Book on the Nature of Man*), which is more poisonous in the former and less so in the latter, providing the cause and origin for the common evil; hence, contagion is associated with both for the same reason.

Other diseases are **non-pestilential**, being milder than the pestilential ones. These are either common occurrences, such as the **rashes** <note>original Greek: ἐξανθήματα (exanthēmata).</note> of children—namely **measles** <note>original: morbilli.</note> and **smallpox** <note>original: variolæ.</note>—which favorable conditions of the air frequently excite in those bodies in which impurities of the maternal blood still lie hidden; <note>A common early modern medical belief that children were born with "impurities" from the womb that had to be "cooked" out of the body through eruptive diseases like smallpox.</note> likewise **catarrhs**...

### V.

> **Endemic** <note>original Greek: "Ἔνδημοι ἢ ἐνδήμιοι"</note> diseases are those that are common and perpetual to a certain region; they arise from the air or the specific diet of that region, such that by reason of their perpetual cause, they continually afflict many people.

<margin>
From whence comes the goiter of the Alpine people?
</margin>

This is evident in the **goiter** <note>original Greek: "βρογχοκήλη" (bronchocele).</note> of the inhabitants of the Alps and Carnia, where <term>scrofula</term> <note>Swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck.</note> and tumors bloom around the neck. According to *Langius* (*Book 1, Epistle 43*), this comes from the medicated waters they drink, which are especially teeming with <term>mercury</term> <note>original: "hydrargyro." Historically, minerals in the water were blamed for goiters before the role of iodine was understood.</note>. The poisonous quality of the mercury weakens the strength of the brain, exhausts the throat and teeth with <term>rheumatism</term> <note>Used here in the old sense of "flowing" bodily humors.</note>, and congeals these tumors, as *Reusner* states (*On Scurvy, Exercise 4*). Likewise, this is seen in the arthritis and **gout** <note>original: "podagra."</note> of the Marcomanni <note>A Germanic people living in what is now the Czech Republic and surrounding areas.</note> and the

Austrians, due to the dregs of <term>tartar</term> <note>Potassium bitartrate, a sediment that forms in wine casks.</note> which greatly abound in the local wines they consume. It is seen in the **phthisis** <note>original: "phthisi"; pulmonary consumption or tuberculosis.</note> or wasting disease of the Portuguese, which the disposition of the air in that region fosters with a certain constancy, as *Fernel* suggests (*On the Hidden Causes of Things, Book 2, Chapter 11*).

<margin>
From whence comes the consumption of the Portuguese?
</margin>

Indeed, this is manifest in other diseases as well, arising from a perpetual common cause that affects many people of a single region or city at the same time. For the diversity of places and regions contributes greatly to the diversity of diseases, owing to changes in the air and diet. For this reason, as *Hippocrates* attests (*Epidemics, Book 2, Section 1*), the city of Cranon was greatly infested with pestilential and putrid diseases because it was situated in a hollow and southern location.

<margin>
Why was Cranon subject to pestilential diseases?
</margin>

Similarly, in marshy places, ulcers of the head are cured quickly, but those of the legs are cured with difficulty, according to *Aristotle* (*Problem 6, Section 14*). By the same logic, slight wounds to the head are seen to be fatal in Bologna, yet they are very easily cured in Rome.

<margin>
See what the diversity of places does.
</margin>

Conversely, small wounds to the shins are hardly cured in Rome, while in Bologna they admit an easy healing <note>original: "consolidationem."</note>, as *Balduinus Ronseus* attests (*On Scurvy, Chapter 1*). In the same respect, as *Guido* testifies, head wounds are more fatal in Paris <note>original: "Lutetiis."</note> than in Avignon; and conversely, leg wounds are lighter among the latter than the former. This is because, according to *Pareus* (*Surgery, Book 9*), the air in Paris is cold and humid, a constitution which [affects] the brain...

# APPENDIX TO BOOK II, PART II

<margin>A Caution.</margin>
It should be noted here that a certain disease can be **Endemic** with respect to one region, while for others it may be counted among the **Epidemics**, or even the **Sporadic** <note>original Greek: "σποραδων" (sporadōn); diseases that occur occasionally or in scattered instances.</note> diseases. This does not at all undermine the previously stated assertions, because these differences in diseases are not essential but accidental. For it can happen that in a certain region only one person might perish from the plague, even where the plague is truly present, yet it cannot then be called an epidemic.

<margin>English Sweating Sickness.</margin>
Indeed, the sweating fever, or <term>hydropyretos</term> <note>original Greek: "ὑδροπύρετος"; literally "water-fever," referring to the English Sweating Sickness, a mysterious and often fatal disease that struck England in several waves during the 15th and 16th centuries.</note>, was first an endemic disease of **England**, though it later began to be epidemic and contagious to others through travel, as can be seen in *Fracastoro*, Book 2, *On Contagion*, Chapter 5, and *Reusner*, *On Scurvy, Exercise 1*. In the same way, we said above that arthritic pains are endemic to the **Marcomanni** <note>A Germanic tribal confederation; the author suggests they were particularly prone to joint pain due to their climate or lifestyle.</note>, which nevertheless also wander here and there in other regions, after the manner of **sporadic diseases** <note>original Greek: "νούσων σποραδικῶν" (nousōn sporadikōn).</note>.

### VI.

*Scurvy also belongs to the category of Endemic diseases, being an ailment most familiar to northern regions, the treatment of which we now undertake.*

<column-break/>

<margin>Whether Scurvy is an endemic disease?</margin>
For although **Scurvy** <note>original: "Scorbutus"</note> is beginning to exceed its ancestral limits, and thus to become known not only in northern places but also through travel in **Meissen**, **Silesia**, and other tracts; nonetheless, it does not seem that it should be moved from the number of endemic diseases into the camp of the **sporadic** ones, as *Salomon Albertus* suggests in *History of Scurvy, Thesis 32*. By that reasoning, almost no disease would be endemic anymore, because all those diseases called endemic to certain regions are also found for the most part scattered in other places. This is evident in **consumption** <note>original: "phthisi"; a wasting disease, usually tuberculosis.</note>, which is endemic to the **Portuguese**, yet attacks one person here and another there in other locations. We therefore establish that Scurvy is an endemic disease for the northern peoples, in agreement with *Eugalenus* in his *Book on Scurvy*, page 2, and *Langius*, *Book 1, Epistle 42 & Book 2, Epistle 13*, as attested by *Olaus Magnus* in *On the Northern Regions, Book 9, Chapter 38 & Book 16, Chapter 51*. This is because it commonly attacks many in **Denmark**, **Norway**, **Holland**, and other neighboring places, due to a common cause in those regions that fosters and produces this evil, which will be discussed at greater length later.
