<margin>Is Scurvy a new disease?</margin>
Because the opinion of those who claim that **Scurvy** is not a new disease seems likely—for it is found described even in the records of the ancients, as is first evident in **Hippocrates** <note>The famous Greek physician (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) known as the father of medicine.</note>, who accurately describes this disease in his book *On Internal Affections* under the name ***volvulus hematitis*** <note>original Latin: "volvuli hematitis"; a term describing an intestinal or internal obstruction involving blood.</note>, as **Langius** maintains in Book 2, *Letter 14*, in these words: "In this disease it happens that the breath smells foul, the gums recede from the teeth, and blood flows from the nostrils; sometimes ulcers sprout from the legs, some of which heal while others emerge, and the thinned skin turns black." However, although **Ronseus** (in *On Scurvy*, chapter 4) and **Salomon Albertus** (in *History of Scurvy*, thesis 169) reject Langius’s assertion—because Hippocrates adds to those words that such patients are "ready for walking and working," which hardly fits those suffering from Scurvy—one should not necessarily conclude the opposite. For according to **Foës** and **Dodoens**, as attested by **Reusner** (in *On Scurvy*, exercise 1), it is likely that the Greek text was corrupted by the omission of the word *not* <note>original Greek: "ουκ" (ouk).</note>, so that Hippocrates' true meaning was that they were by no means ready for walking and working...

<column-break/>

...which indeed seems consistent when the preceding points are considered: for how can someone be eager to walk whose legs are teeming with various ulcers? Some also maintain that **Hippocrates** described the same disease as <margin>Hippocrates' enlarged spleens.</margin> **enlarged spleens**, according to **Ronseus** in Book 1 of *On Scurvy*, where he considers the words found at the end of the aforementioned Book 2, and according to **Reusner** in the cited place, where Hippocrates' words in *On Internal Affections* regarding diseases of the spleen are recognized. Following Hippocrates are **Celsus** (Book 2, *On Medicine*, chapter 6), **Aretaeus** (Book 1, *On the Causes and Signs of Chronic Diseases*, chapter 14), and other ancients. **Pliny** <margin>Stomakake and Skelotyrbe.</margin> (Book 25 of *Natural History*, chapter 3) describes the disease through the terms ***stomakake*** <note>original Greek: "στομακάκη"; literally "mouth-evil."</note> and ***skelotyrbe*** <note>original Greek: "σκελοτύρβη"; literally "leg-shaking" or "leg-trouble."</note>, where he says that in the army of **Germanicus Caesar** <note>A prominent Roman general and the nephew of Emperor Tiberius, who led campaigns in Germania.</note>, new and unnatural symptoms arose from drinking from a harmful spring on this side of the Rhine, in which the teeth were primarily damaged and the legs would stumble. Some (as **Forestus** in *Book 20, observation 11* attributes to the famous practitioner **Regnerius Snoy** along with **Blienburch**) have given the disease a name based on both symptoms—namely, that the teeth and feet are most affected. As **Salomon Albertus** says, this name was composed with "plain wit" <note>original Latin: "crassâ & pingui Minervâ," an idiom meaning a simple or unrefined approach.</note>, and the illness is called <margin>Gingipedium.</margin> **Gingipedium** <term>Gingipedium</term> from *gingiva* (gums) and *pedes* (feet). Commonly, however, it is called **Scorbutus** or **Schorbutus**, a Latinized term formed either from the Danish language, where this ailment is called *Schorbeck* (meaning "mouth erosion," for which reason some also call it *Schermund*), or from the Dutch *Schōrbuyck*, which signifies a "twisting and gnawing of the belly." But let us not waste more time hunting for names; we believe one should speak with the common folk but think with the learned. For this reason, we proceed to understand the nature of **Scurvy**.

### VIII.

<margin>The limitation of this assertion will appear below in Book 4, Observation 3.</margin> To understand the nature of **Scurvy** more correctly, we must investigate its **primary recipient** <note>original Greek: "τὸ πρῶτον δεκτικὸν" (to proton dektikon), referring to the organ or site first affected by a disease.</note> or first subject. Here the

<column-break/>

**Spleen** <term>Lien</term> <note>The Latin term for the spleen.</note> presents itself, which provides the origin for **Scurvy** because its own function is corrupted in a peculiar way.

To understand this better, we shall briefly determine the true use of the spleen, lest we fall into the common error shared by many. <margin>The spleen is not a receptacle for waste.</margin> These people claim the spleen is dedicated to receiving and purging thick and **melancholic juices** <note>In ancient medicine, "black bile" or thick humors believed to cause physical and mental heaviness.</note> generated by the liver and separated from the blood. However, the office of this organ is something different and more noble: namely, **blood-making** <note>original Greek: "αἱμάτωσις" (haimatosis), the process of forming blood.</note> or a kind of "sanguification." This is clearly suggested by the structure of its substance and vessels, as it is not very different from the composition of the liver. In this sense, perhaps, the spleen was also rightly called a **bastard liver** <note>original Greek: "νόθον ἧπαρ" (nothon hepar).</note> by **Aristotle** in *Book 3 of On the Parts of Animals, chapter 7*. Therefore, what many—following **Galen** (*On Affected Parts, Book 2, Chapter 1*) and **Avicenna** (*Canon, Book 1*)—assert regarding the reception of the waste-like melancholic humor generated in the liver, we reject as improbable. Instead, following **Alexander**, **Aretaeus**, **Plater**, **Caspar Bauhin**, and **Reusner**, we ascribe to the spleen a certain preparation of the blood, so that it is like a <margin>The true use of the spleen.</margin> **secondary liver** <note>original Latin: "jecur secundarium."</note>. For this reason, in its mass and size, it not infrequently resembles a second liver, as seen in the examples of **Fernel**.

<summary>This page discusses the etymology of the word 'scurvy'—including the descriptive term 'Gingipedium'—and argues that the disease originates in the spleen, which the author views as a vital blood-making organ rather than a waste organ.</summary>

# CONCERNING SCURVY, SECTION I.
## Bb 3

*Book 7, chapter 7. Vesalius <note>Andreas Vesalius, the famous 16th-century anatomist.</note>, Book 5 of the Fabric <note>Referring to Vesalius's "De humani corporis fabrica."</note>, chapter 9. Marcellus Donatus, "Miraculous Histories," Book 6, chapter 3. Schenck, Book 9, observation 91.* all testify that the spleen very often takes over the functions of the liver. This is likely what happened in the case of a dropsical <term>dropsical</term><note>Suffering from edema or fluid swelling.</note> and cachectic <term>cachectic</term><note>A state of severe weight loss and muscle wasting.</note> young woman, as **Reusner** determines. As **Coiter** reports in his *Anatomical and Surgical Observations*, for two full years before her death she suffered from extremely heavy nosebleeds, which they could only restrain through bloodletting; yet, upon examination, her liver was found to be whitish, tuberous, uneven, hard, and bloodless.

<margin>In what way the spleen makes blood.</margin> However, the method of that blood-making <note>original Greek: "αἱματώσεως" (haimatoseos)</note> is not defined in the same way by everyone. Some, such as **Franciscus Ulmus** in his *Book on the Spleen*, argue that the thinnest blood—the material for the vital spirit—is prepared in the spleen. Others, as seen in **Reusner's** *On Scurvy*, wish for the more humid and watery parts of the chyle <term>chyle</term><note>A milky fluid consisting of fat droplets and lymph, drained from the intestines during digestion.</note> to be prepared in the spleen and converted into blood. Finally, others—among whose number are **Plater** and **Bauhin**—most truly pronounce that the thicker part of the chyle is drawn in by the spleen for the sake of blood-making. We approved of this opinion in our *Noble Exercises on the Human Body, Exercise 6, Question 6*, and having approved it once, we still defend it: namely, that the spleen assists the work of nutrition insofar as it attracts the thicker part of the chyle to itself through a certain natural affinity. Thus, it not only makes the liver's blood-making more perfect by happenstance, but moreover prepares 

<column-break/>

blood from the attracted chyle for itself and other parts. I say the "thicker" part of the chyle, not absolutely <note>original Greek: "ἁπλῶς" (haplōs)</note> but in some respect <note>original Greek: "πή τι" (pē ti)</note>—specifically in comparison to that material which is communicated to the liver. Thus, it remains true that the spleen "attracts the turbid humors from the belly" <note>original Greek: "ἐκ τῆς κοiliας τὰς ἰκμάδας τὰς θολερὰς" (ek tēs koilias tas ikmadas tas tholeras)</note>, according to **Aristotle** in the place cited and **Hippocrates** in *Book 4 on Diseases*, insofar as the rawer parts of the chyle are diluted by drinkable matter and communicated to the spleen with its help. For although the earthy and thick parts of the chyle cannot be attracted by the spleen without an enormous risk of blockage, this does not apply to earthy and thick parts that are in a natural state, diluted by the benefit of watery or drinkable matter, as will be more evident from what follows. Having now determined the use of the spleen, we must consequently demonstrate how this organ, when its function is impaired, provides the origin for Scurvy.

[The organs] serve the whole body in the digestion <note>The original term "concoctionem" refers to the physiological process of "cooking" or refining nutrients into blood and tissue.</note> of nutrients, namely by introducing a likeness into the foods that can correspond to the substance of the parts, since nourishment is only converted into the nature of the parts when it is of a similar kind, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> in Book 2 of *On the Soul*. 

<margin>Proper digestion of the spleen.</margin>
So also the spleen, through its own proper digestion <note>original Greek: "εὔψησις" (eupsēsis), meaning a perfect "cooking" or refinement of humors.</note>, provides for the whole body by attracting and refining the watery and raw parts of the chyle <term>chyle</term><note>A milky fluid of fats and lymph taken from food in the intestines.</note>. By this means, it not only renders the liver's blood-making <note>original Greek: "αἱματοποίησιν" (haimatopoiēsin)</note> more noble, but additionally prepares and produces blood for itself and for the neighboring parts. However, when this operation is corrupted, so that

<margin>Pollution of the spleen.</margin>
instead of proper digestion there occurs a pollution <note>original Greek: "μόλυνσις" (molynsis), meaning a defilement or staining of the humors.</note>, the rawer and more watery parts of the chyle are not only left undigested, but are further depraved against nature. By disturbing the digestion of the liver and other parts dedicated to nutrition, they produce various symptoms of malnutrition resulting from a specific corruption, and thus they generate Scurvy.

### X.

*Therefore, the internal antecedent cause of Scurvy is raw and watery blood throughout the whole body, but especially collected in the hypochondria <term>hypochondria</term><note>The upper regions of the abdomen, located under the ribs.</note>, failing not by quantity alone, but by a certain specific corruption resulting from the pollution <note>original: "μόλυνσιν" (molynsis)</note> arising from the weakness of the spleen.*

<column-break/>

<margin>
Whether an abundance of melancholic juice is the immediate cause of Scurvy.
</margin>
Many indeed establish that the immediate internal cause of Scurvy is an abundance of a muddy and thick melancholic humor alone, or perhaps mixed with others, which abounds around the spleen and liver and in the veins themselves. This is gathered from the writings of **Wier** (*Observations on Scurvy*), **Echtius** (*Epitome of Scurvy*), **Salomon Albert** (*History of Scurvy*, thesis 16), **Ronsseus** (*On Enlarged Spleens*, chapter 2), **Eugalenus** (*On Scurvy*, page 3), **Forestus** (Book 20, observation 11), and **Langius** (Book 2, Epistle 13). However, they add this caution: that this humor first undergoes a form of corruption peculiar to the Scorbutic disease, by which (as **Eugalenus** says) it depraves the adjacent and neighboring internal organs by its substance, contact, or its quality and vapors. This corrupts their natural temperament until they consent to a community of contagion, and once they have received the stain of infection, they change and spoil the incoming food by impressing upon it a similar form of corruption. We see this similarly when nutrients are corrupted by thin and watery humors in dropsy, or by a specific form of corruption in elephantiasis, the "French Disease" <note>Syphilis.</note>, and similar ailments. But this present assertion is not without doubt, because it presupposes a false hypothesis sought by certain ancients out of ignorance of anatomical matters and defended by more recent writers against reason: namely, that the spleen is a recepta- <note>The word continues on the next page as "receptaculum" (receptacle).</note>

# ON SCURVY, SECTION I.

[the spleen as] a receptacle of the melancholic, waste-like juice that is separated from the blood in the liver, in the same way that we see the gallbladder receive yellow bile <note>original: χολὴν (*cholēn*)</note>; this is an opinion we rejected shortly before as improbable. Furthermore, the very authors we mentioned still seem to doubt this in some way, as they suggest that an abundance of thick and melancholic humors is insufficient to produce Scurvy unless a certain peculiar and specific corruption is added—a property which no one has yet declared or revealed.

<margin>Does Scurvy arise from watery humors?</margin>
Others—whom *Albertus on Scurvy* <note>theses 67 and following</note> mentions and whom *Reusner* follows <note>in his *Book on Scurvy*, exercise 4</note>—establish the immediate internal cause of scurvy to be watery and serous <note>Serum-like or thin</note> humors, characterized by thinness rather than thickness. They base this on the idea that the spleen itself is a receptacle for an abundance of watery matter from what we drink; they argue that when this matter is not properly altered or separated from the blood due to a diseased state of the spleen, it gives rise to Scurvy. However, we cannot in good conscience agree with this opinion, neither regarding its premise (that the true use of the spleen is simply the attraction of watery matter) nor regarding its conclusion (since the symptoms of Scurvy cannot be explained by the nature of overabundant watery matter). Therefore, we propose the immediate cause of Scurvy:

<column-break/>

<margin>The true immediate cause of Scurvy.</margin>
to be raw and ichorous <term>ichorous</term><note>From "ichor," referring here to a thin, watery, and potentially irritating fluid that thins the blood.</note> blood, suffering from a certain specific corruption, which collects in the human body—principally around the nutritional organs—due to the depraved operation of the spleen.

<margin>Crudity</margin>
I say "raw" or "crude" blood because, due to the diseased state of the spleen, the rawer parts of the chyle <note>The milky fluid of digested food.</note> are not diverted from the liver's blood-making process. Consequently, the blood in the veins of the liver and spleen is first depraved by the mixing in of foreign matter; then, the liver’s blood-making <note>original Greek: αἱμάτωσις (*haimatōsis*)</note> is hindered because the material it works on is poorly prepared, specifically because the chyle is not properly purified due to the defect in the spleen.

<margin>Ichor.</margin>
I add "crude and ichorous blood" because the rawer and consequently thicker parts of the chyle are diluted by an overabundance of ichor or serum, and for this reason, they mix more easily with the mass of the blood.

<margin>Corruption.</margin>
Furthermore, I state that it "suffers from a certain specific corruption." For it is inevitable that this raw matter, unfit for perfect alteration or digestion <note>The original term "concoctionem" refers to the physiological "cooking" of nutrients.</note>, acquires foreign qualities. This happens partly from the condition of the matter itself (the preceding foods) and partly because the "efficient cause" <note>A philosophical term for the primary agent that causes a change—in this case, the digestive organs.</note> acts imperfectly; instead of a proper "cooking" <note>original Greek: ἑψήσεως (*hepsēseōs*), meaning boiling or refining</note> or true boiling, a pollution <note>original Greek: μόλυνσις (*molynsis*), a staining or defilement</note> occurs, making the matter more prone to putrefaction. Just as the operations of the spleen and liver are official <note>Meaning they perform a specific "office" or duty for the body.</note>, serving not only themselves, but the whole...

If it happens that the seed is tainted with foreign diseased "tinctures" <note>specific qualities or stains of a disease</note>, then the principles of the diseases are propagated along with the production of the body parts. These diseases were present in the parental model—not all of them, certainly, but only those that have "fixed roots." Examples include **tartaric diseases** <term>tartaric diseases: A category of illnesses, including kidney stones and gout, named after "tartar" (the crust in wine barrels) because they were thought to involve stony deposits in the body</term>, such as the **stone** <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, **arthritis**, **leprosy**, and others. On the other hand, "Sulphurous" and "Mercurial" diseases—namely fevers, inflammations, catarrhs, and the like—are not easily passed on to posterity because they do not have their seeds firmly fixed in the body. This is according to **Quercetanus** <note>Joseph Duchesne, a French physician and chemist</note> in his *Counsel on Arthritis and the Stone*.

<margin>Why a parent with "the stone" does not always produce a child with "the stone."</margin>
However, a person with kidney stones does not always produce a child with stones. This may be because the seeds of the disease have not yet powerfully occupied the anatomy of the human **balsam** <term>balsam: The body’s natural internal preservative or healing power</term>, or because the roots of the disease are overcome by the flowering of the [healthy] seeds. It may also be because the foreign beginnings of the diseases are conquered by the power of the natural balsam in the womb,

<column-break/>

or perhaps because the seeds of the disease have reached the limit of their sterility, as **Petrus Severinus** <note>A Danish physician known for his Hermetic medical theories</note> writes in his book *The Idea [of Medicine]*, chapter 12. We shall apply these principles to those suffering from **Scurvy**, who also pass this evil on to their descendants for the reason that they produce an impure seed. In this regard, the digestive organs—but most especially the **spleen**—are born weaker, so that they are not entirely sufficient to perform their duties. Or, according to the **Hermeticists** <note>Followers of a philosophical and medical tradition emphasizing hidden spiritual and chemical forces</note>, a parent suffering from Scurvy passes such a **congenital** <note>original: "symphyton"</note> disease to the child

<margin>Why Scurvy is propagated to children.</margin>
insofar as the "Scurvy-tartar"—that is, the material proper to Scurvy—has taken root in the blood and the parts themselves. Through long digestion, it has contracted slow "marriages" between bodies <note>chemical or physical bonds</note>, such that it cannot be dissolved by any power of the innate Balsam. Consequently, its harmful **tincture** <note>the essence or imprint of the disease</note> is communicated to the seed and firmly impressed upon it. This is due to the firm union it has with the blood and the Spirit, which mimics the effective nature of the seminal powers. Thus, according to the cycles of maturity and refinement, it brings the diseases of the parents out of invisible treasuries into the body of the offspring. This is especially true when other external causes help, which take root in that specific weakness produced by this disease, about which we must speak next.

### XIII.

*The acquired weakness of the spleen, and consequently of the liver and other parts in Scurvy, arises from what are called "non-natural things," <note>In early modern medicine, the "six non-naturals" were external factors like air, diet, and sleep that influenced health, as opposed to "natural" things like the organs themselves.</note> in which the more distant causes of Scurvy must be sought; among these, thick and foul surrounding air is placed first.*

<margin>Why thick and foul air contributes to Scurvy.</margin>
That this air serves greatly in the generation of Scurvy is most rightly established by **Albert** (in his *Theses on Scurvy*, 44), **Eugalenus** (*On Scurvy*, page 2), **Reusner** (*Exercises on Scurvy*, 4, page 157), and **Wier** (in his *Counsel on Scurvy*), insofar as the humors <note>The body's vital fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> are thrown into disorder by it, the spirits are infected, and the body is rendered sluggish and weak. For this reason, **Hippocrates** (in his book *On Air, Waters, and Places*) and **Aetius** write that the spleen grows large in marshy places; hence **Ronseus** (*On Large Spleens*, chapter 5) established that the inhabitants of such places are most prone to Scurvy-like conditions. **Stegghius** also subscribes to this (*Medical Practice*, book 4, chapter 13) when he says that Scurvy is unknown in arid places but frequent in marshy ones. Furthermore, **Olaus Magnus** (in his *History of the Northern Peoples*, book 16, chapter 51) writes that Scurvy is fostered by the cold exhalation of stone walls, though, as he also attests, it grows milder within wooden-paneled rooms. <margin>How does hot air contribute to Scurvy?</margin> This being established, we do not deny that hot air also occasionally serves the generation of Scurvy, but "by accident," as **Echtius** and **Forestus** argue; it does so insofar as it consumes the thinner humors and thus <term>συμβεβηκὸς: incidentally or by circumstance</term> thickens the blood. It is therefore clear that maritime, lake-side, and marshy locations—which continually breathe out filth and vapors both because of their natural position and because of the flooding and the ebbing of the sea—serve the generation of Scurvy, especially in the Autumn and Spring seasons. It is no wonder, then, that this malady is largely endemic to maritime cities among the Dutch, Danes, Frisians, and others, since they not only continually breathe in such air, but moreover provide an origin for the disease through their customary diet, as will be clear from what follows.

<margin>Fish.</margin>
Furthermore, this category includes fish hardened by smoke—specifically those from lakes and the sea—because a thick and raw blood is generated from them.

<margin>Birds.</margin>
Among the types of poultry, this place is occupied by birds that live in ponds and marshes. Their flesh abounds with excrementitious humidities <note>In humoral theory, these were waste fluids produced by poor digestion that the body could not utilize.</note>, which makes them difficult to digest.

<margin>Cabbage and legumes.</margin>

As **Galen** himself testifies (in *Book 2 of On the Properties of Food, Chapter 44*), such food provides little nourishment but produces copious, raw waste.

## X V.

*Furthermore, bodily exercises—either none at all or ill-timed—as well as the suppression of customary evacuations, contribute to the generation of Scurvy.*

<margin>The harm of idleness.</margin>
Just as "native heat" <note>The internal biological heat believed to drive digestion and life.</note> is overwhelmed and smothered by lazy and inactive idleness—leading to the creation of <term>crudities</term> <note>Undigested or "raw" matter in the body.</note> that easily give rise to Scurvy in a predisposed body—so too does **ill-timed exercise** <margin>The harm of ill-timed exercise.</margin> call this heat (the author of all digestion) away from its work. Because of this, the transformation of food is hindered, and the blood itself is rendered impure due to the leftover waste-like parts; from this, Scurvy is later generated. <margin>Suppression of customary evacuation as a cause of Scurvy.</margin> This happens all the more quickly when customary bodily evacuations are suppressed, causing waste-like blood to remain in the body. This occurs in women when **menstruation** is denied or incomplete, or in certain men—especially older ones—when the **flow of hemorrhoids** (which is otherwise customary, returning at certain times and familiar to their nature) is suppressed beyond the usual, as noted by **Weyer** <note>original: "Wierus"; Johannes Weyer (1515–1588), a Dutch physician.</note> in *Observations on Scurvy*, **Salomon Alberti** in *History of Scurvy, thesis 56*, and **Eugalenus** in *On Scurvy, page 2*.

# SECTION I. ON SCURVY.

It is clear in this way how the immediate cause of Scurvy, which we determined above, is produced and fostered by other more remote causes; it now follows that we turn our attention to those things which are connected to Scurvy as symptoms, and which serve as signs for its recognition.

### XVII.

*The beginning of Scurvy is as long-lasting as it is difficult to recognize, according to **Forestus** <note>Petrus Forestus (1521–1597), a prominent Dutch physician known as the "Hippocrates of Holland"</note>: yet it may be gathered by skillful conjecture from **spontaneous fatigue**, a sensation of heaviness—especially around the **kitchen** <note>original: "culinam"; a medical metaphor for the stomach, where the "first digestion" or cooking of food occurs</note>—tightness of the chest, difficult breathing especially during labor, and urine that is generally thick and white.*

For just as a disease already formed is distinguished from one that is still in the making—which, if the performing cause is removed, does not obtain a permanent disposition—according to **Galen** in *On the Affected Parts, book 1, chapter 2*; 

<column-break/>

so too the beginning of a disease is not made known by the same reasoning as its established state. This is most evident in Scurvy, the beginning of which is recognized with difficulty, because the signs provided seem, for the most part, to be common—fitting not only Scurvy but other affections as well. We add, however, that the beginning of Scurvy must be gathered by **skillful conjecture** from those signs, specifically insofar as those symptoms are diligently compared with their causes and the nature of the subject. Therefore, one must first of all consider whether the person to whom such symptoms happen had parents suffering from Scurvy, whether he is by nature **splenetic** <note>Having a melancholy temperament associated with the spleen</note>, whether he is in a region where this evil is **endemic**, whether he uses a diet of coarse food, and similar factors.

difficult to

</margin>

When these things have been diligently considered, the symptoms themselves must be weighed to see if many concur and can be deduced from the conjunct cause of Scurvy. In the first place, **spontaneous fatigue** presents itself; yet not every kind, but especially that which **Galen** calls **tensive** in *On the Causes of Symptoms, book 2, chapter 5*, where the mass of the body seems as if it were being stretched. This occurs because an **ichorous** <note>watery or thin</note> matter, diluted with impurities and mixed with the blood, is communicated not only to the veins but also to the **habit of the body** <note>the external physical condition or constitution</note>—namely, to the muscular parts themselves—the strength of which must necessarily be greatly weighed down, because...

This occurs mostly around the **organs of digestion** <note>original: "viscera concoctionis"; in early medicine, digestion was viewed as a process of "cooking" or refining food into humors</note>, insofar as the attraction of the spleen is hindered, and crude humors accumulate in the veins and the area around the heart <note>original: "præcordijs"</note>, and eventually throughout the whole state of the body. Because of this, our body is deprived of proper nourishment for each part, and once nutrition is corrupted, how can the strength of our forces be maintained without proper nourishment?

<margin>Whence comes the tightness of the chest?</margin>
Furthermore, we have noted **tightness of the chest** which fatigues such patients. This happens because, due to the abundance of humors collected in the distended **hypochondria** <note>The upper abdomen, just below the ribs; in early medicine, this was thought to be the seat of the spleen and the origin of many "vapors"</note>, and considering their proximity, the **midriff** <note>original: "phrenes," referring here to the diaphragm</note> and the **respiratory organs** <note>original: "organa spiritualia"; the lungs and heart, which were believed to manage the "vital spirit"</note> are simultaneously pressed upon. This occurs in the same way that those suffering from **dropsy** <note>original: "Aqua inter cutem," or "water under the skin"; an old term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid</note>, those who are pregnant, or those who have a protruding belly for some other reason, experience difficult breathing. From this it also happens that in this difficult breathing, nothing is perceived of those symptoms which otherwise necessarily follow diseases of the chest—such as a cough, whistling, rattling, a stabbing pain, and the like.

We said, moreover, that **this malady increases especially during physical labor**, because through

## XVIII.

*As the disease grows more severe, the aforementioned symptoms are further exacerbated. Added to them is the bleeding and flabbiness of the gums, and finally their putrefaction, which is usually accompanied by salivation and foul breath. There is also a weakness of the legs when walking, and sometimes a near-paralysis of them; spots of various colors appear on the shins and sometimes on other parts, which are occasionally followed by loose tumors and, not infrequently, malignant ulcers.*

<margin>Whence the bleeding of the gums?</margin>
For in those, says **Eugalenus** on *page 4 of his Book on Scurvy*, whose nature is robust enough to prevail over the cause of the illness, the body’s innate force and virtue thrusts the evil as far away from itself as possible, depositing the cause of the disease partly in the feet and partly in the gums. First, however, the bleeding of the gums occurs because the sharper and more refined portion of the **faulty matter** <note>original: "materiae peccantis"; the imbalanced humors causing the disease</note>—which is carried upward either by nature’s own "critical" movement or by heat—more easily erodes the tender and moist areas. This is the view held by **Echtius** <note>Johannes Echtius, author of an early epitome on scurvy (1541)</note> and **Forestus** <note>Petrus Forestus (1521–1597), known as the "Dutch Hippocrates"</note> in *book 20, observation 11*. This is because the flesh of the gums is by its nature softer, and because of its **spongy** <note>original: "σομφωδεστέρα" [somphōdestera]; a Greek term meaning porous or spongy</note> and airy texture, it is full of pathways for **ichorous** <note>original: "ichorosum"; referring to a thin, watery, or blood-tinged discharge</note> blood...

### APPENDIX TO BOOK II. PART II.

...easily receives [offending humors], as **Salomon Albert** says in his *History of Scurvy, thesis 99*. Once received, these first cause an **odaxesmos** <note>original Greek: ὀδαξησμὸν; a biting or tingling sensation</note> or a light itching due to their sharp nature, while the gums swell from the excess and saturation of that offending blood. When rubbed, the thin flesh of the gums develops cracks and pours out **ichorous** blood <note>original: "sanguinem ichorosum"; a thin, watery, and irritating discharge common in infected wounds</note>.

<margin>The source of the flabbiness of the gums.</margin>
This bleeding of the gums is followed by flabbiness, through which that thin flesh essentially dissolves due to the volume of offending humor received. This gives rise to a loose swelling of the gums because of **molynsis** <note>original Greek: μόλυνσιν; a defilement, staining, or contamination of the fluids</note> or corrupted digestion. **Reusner**, *Book on Scurvy, exercise 5*.

<margin>The source of the rotting of the gums.</margin>
When the illness is prolonged further, the rotting of the gums follows, so that the small pieces of flesh which cover the teeth like a rampart are corrupted by rot and fall away. Consequently, the teeth are bared and their connections loosened, just as we have known many people in Lower Saxony suffering from confirmed Scurvy, whose teeth were either wobbling so much they could be removed with no effort, or were lost entirely. This happens because of the corruption of the **innate heat** <note>the natural "vital fire" believed by early physicians to power the body's functions</note>, aided by the warm and moist disposition of the gums and surrounding parts. For this reason, such great rot—sometimes even a major **gangrene**—exists, as the interior of the mouth is quite moist and becomes foully soiled by the mass of **anathymiases** <note>original Greek: ἀναθυμιάσεων; vapors or exhalations</note> emerging from the stomach (acting as the "hearth" of digestion), both from the grinding and passing of food, and from the steamy smells 

<column-break/>

emerging from that mass, as **Salomon Albert** says in his *History of Scurvy, thesis 108*. Therefore, it is no wonder that the constant companion of confirmed Scurvy is foul breath along with salivation.

<margin>The source of the foul breath.</margin>
For although some things stink by their own nature—as is seen in **Sagapenum** <note>a bitter medicinal resin</note>, **Asafoetida** <note>a pungent gum-resin often called "devil's dung"</note>, **Castoreum** <note>a secretion from beaver sacs</note>, and similar things, as **Reusner** rightly advises in his *Book on Scurvy, exercise 5, page 305*—wherever a foul smell occurs contrary to nature, it is rightly established as a sign of rot and corruption. This is because, just as from **pepasmos** <note>original Greek: πεπασμὸς; the "ripening" or proper cooking of humors in the body</note>—according to **Albert** in the cited place, thesis 109—comes the **euodia** <note>original Greek: εὐωδία; a sweet fragrance</note> of succulent things that are **euchylous** <note>original Greek: εὐχύλων; having good, healthy juices</note> and beneficial to nature, so conversely, from their corruption and rot, and from the mixture of **kakochylous** <note>original Greek: κακοχύλων; having bad or corrupted juices</note> things, comes **dysodia** <note>original Greek: δυσωδία; a foul stench</note>.

<margin>The source of the saliva.</margin>
We say "with salivation," which, as **Eugalenus** testifies in his *Book on Scurvy, page 16, verso*, not rarely has "empty vomiting" <note>likely dry heaving or unproductive retching</note> as a companion due to the abundance of raw humors. For as **Celsus** testifies in his *Book 2 On Medicine, chapter 2*, and **Xenophon** in *Book 1 of the Education of Cyrus*, it was a great sign of shame among the Persians to spit frequently, as if it indicated excessive greediness or laziness due to neglected exercise. This was based on the principle that salivation, or the frequent spitting of saliva, follows an abundance of raw humors. Likewise, in the present case, this symptom is frequently present in scurvy victims because of corrupted digestions, by which much watery blood is collected; for since in serous humors...

# ON SCURVY, SECTION I.

Since the stomach and adjacent organs are teeming and swollen with **humors** <note>the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health</note>, it can easily happen that these fluids are passed to the throat and the root of the tongue via the esophagus or gullet. This is most clearly seen in those who suffer from vomiting after **excessive indulgence** <note>original: "crapulam"; refers to the sickness following overeating or heavy drinking</note>. This usually begins with salivation, so that the mouth is filled with a certain wateriness until the offending matter is entirely cast out by the **expulsive force** <note>the body's natural ability to rid itself of waste or harmful substances</note>. Furthermore, this salivation is often bloody due to the bloodiness of the gums, whose exuding **ichors** <note>original: "ichores"; thin, watery, or blood-stained discharges from a wound or sore</note> mix with the saliva.

<margin>How is Scurvy contagious?</margin>
From this, it is manifest in what the contagion of the scurvy evil chiefly consists, and how it is spread to others (provided they are predisposed to it): namely, through mutual kisses and the sharing of drinking cups. In the former, the foul breath of another's mouth is drawn in—as potent as fragrant musk—infecting the **Spirits** <note>original: "Spiritus"; the "vital spirits" or subtle vapors believed to animate the body's organs and actions</note> which govern every action. In the latter, the foul saliva is diluted by the shared drink and swallowed. What wonder is it, then, that in **Holland** <note>modern-day Netherlands</note> the scurvy evil creeps so easily and rages even among foreign guests? For in that place, there are as many kisses as there are greetings, especially among women. These are not only young girls (from whom perhaps less harm is expected, both because they are less liable to the disease and also because, as the Poet says:

->—let soft kisses always<-
->delight :<-

<column-break/>

for the more pleasant and delightful a thing is, the less harmful it is, because the appetite follows the imagination, whose power over the humors and spirits is established by many significant arguments); but, alas, even old women—dried up, bloodless, and horrifying to look upon even for infants who still lack the faculty of judgment. If these women were greeted without a kiss, they would complain of a great injury and unusual contempt. What wonder that in the **Hanseatic cities** <note>a powerful league of trading cities in Northern Europe and Germany</note> and Lower Saxony, scurvy is sown with such a rich harvest? It is rare to find a table of guests where several are not scurvy-ridden; yet, despite this, the common custom is observed where cups are shared. These are often of such a size that they hardly need a second filling. Into these cups, scurvy-tainted saliva is deposited not once, but many times during drinking, and it is passed from neighbor to neighbor together with the drink (for in these places, among the common folk, it is considered wicked and dishonest to offer a drink to someone out of the regular order). It is clear from this why, as scurvy worsens, *as **Wierus** says in his observations on Scurvy* <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a Dutch physician renowned for his medical observations and his opposition to witch-hunts</note>, there is a loose and bloody swelling of the gums and a rotting accompanied by a stench of the mouth. Sometimes even the flesh of the gums is consumed down to the roots of the teeth, rendering the teeth entirely wobbling.

Our German people call it **Mouth-Rot** <note>original: "die Mundfaule"</note>, as is clear among others from *Tabernaemontanus’s German book, "The New Treasure of Waters"* <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus (c. 1522–1590) was a famous botanist; his book discusses the healing properties of mineral springs</note> in several places where the virtues of acidic mineral waters for treating this disease are explained.

<margin>How does the contraction of the cheeks occur?</margin>
To these symptoms of the mouth, Salomon Albertus <note>a 16th-century German physician known for his work on anatomy</note> in the cited *Thesaurus, thesis 112*, adds a rare occurrence not observed by others: namely, a contraction of the cheeks. In this condition, the hinge of the mouth—where the lower cheek turns beneath the organ of hearing—stiffens just like the joint of a knee. This happens because a foul humor <note>a "humor" is a bodily fluid; here, "squalid" refers to the thick, corrupt waste products of the disease</note> is deeply absorbed into that joint and its ligaments. Reusner <note>Hieronymus Reusner, an early writer on scurvy</note> in *Exercise 5 on Scurvy, page 279*, writes that nosebleeds very frequently follow. For this reason, following the opinion of the ancients,

<margin>Where do nosebleeds come from?</margin>
he counts these among the signs of scurvy. This is because the scurvy-matter can be diverted to the nostrils through the same veins by which it is carried to the throat. Furthermore, we often see in "splenetic affections" <note>illnesses believed to originate in the spleen, often associated with melancholy or scurvy</note> that nature attempts an evacuation of superfluous waste through a flow from the nose, as is clear from *Hippocrates, book 2 of Epidemics, sections 2 and 3*. But leaving 

<margin>Why is there weakness in the legs when walking?</margin>
these things aside, we proceed to the remaining signs, the first of which is weakness of the legs when walking. For just as in the beginning there is a certain spontaneous exhaustion of the whole body, so as time goes on, weakness of the legs follows. This is because 

<column-break/>

the watery, foul blood <note>original: "sanguis ichorosus"; ichor refers to a thin, watery discharge from a wound or sore</note> communicates its cruder part abundantly to the ligaments, tendons, and the substance of the muscles. This happens partly because such matter naturally tends to sink downward and is cast off by nature toward the less noble and more distant parts of the body. It also happens because the ligaments, tendons, and the nervous parts of the joints attract the glutinous and thicker blood by a "pulling" <note>original: "κατ' ἕλξιν" (kat' helxin)</note> and a certain natural inclination, as Aristotle suggests in *book 3, On the Parts of Animals*. But if 

<margin>How does paralysis of the legs occur?</margin>
this aforementioned matter increasingly forces its way in great quantity into the very bindings of the legs, the legs are, as it were, "loosened." This is why the author of the *Definitions* calls *skelybre* <note>original: "σκέλυβρη"; an ancient term for the leg-weakness associated with scurvy</note> a "form of paralysis" <note>original: "εἶδος παραλύσεως"</note>. It is better called a "loosening of the knee-joints" with Pliny, or the "weakening of the legs" with Langius in *book 1, Letter 42*. This is because not all movement and sensation is destroyed, but each remains somewhat intact, as Salomon Albertus notes in the cited work, *thesis 117*. For this reason, it belongs to that species of paralysis which Quercetanus <note>Joseph Duchesne, a French physician and chemist</note> in *Tetrade, chapter 4*, calls "improper" or "metaphorical" <note>original: "καταχρηστικῶς" (katachrestikos); meaning the term is used loosely</note>. This is because the origin of the evil is not traced back to the beginning of the nerves, but to the weakness of the limb itself, resulting from the abundance of scurvy-matter. Furthermore, 

<margin>Why do spots appear on the shins?</margin>
because of this weakness, spots bloom everywhere on the thighs and shins, which in the beginning are red...

# ON SCURVY, SECTION I.

...[the spots] are to be [observed], resembling those left by fresh flea bites, but they soon turn purple and a leaden-blue color because of **ecchymosis** <term>ecchymosis: the medical term for bruising, where blood leaks from vessels into the skin</term>, by which blood is poured out from the open mouths of the veins, as Hieronymus Reusner notes in his *Book on Scurvy, page 318.* The skin is stained by this because the scurvy-matter is diluted in the blood; since this matter is unfit to be transformed into the actual substance of the body parts, it consequently produces unnatural spots, first on the shins and legs, as these are the parts toward which the scurvy-matter most tends. Indeed, they are sometimes generated in other parts as well, most notably on the back and arms, as is attested by experience and the writings of Pieter van Foreest in *Book 20, Observation 12*, and Balduinus Ronsseus in his *Book on the Great Spleen*. This occurs at that stage when there is a great **corruption of the humors** <term>original: "cacochymia"; an imbalance or "badness" of the bodily fluids</term> and the disease is fully established.

<margin>Why do loose swellings of the thigh and shins occur?</margin>
More often, loose swellings of the thigh and shins follow, due to a certain rush of watery, acrid blood tending downward, combined with the weakness of heat in those parts further removed from the heart—just as we observe the feet swelling in **consumption** <term>original: "phthisis"; a wasting disease, usually tuberculosis</term> and **malnutrition** <term>original: "cachexia"; a state of severe weight loss and muscle wasting</term> while the upper limbs are consumed by wasting.

<margin>Why does atrophy often occur?</margin>
Nor does it matter that experience proves the opposite in some patients, whose legs often become so thin that they scarcely seem to cling to the bones. In these cases, there is a maximum weakness of the "native heat" <note>Early modern doctors believed "innate heat" was the vital energy fueled by the heart that drove digestion and circulation</note>, by reason of which the body is unable to expel the offending matter from the internal organs to the extremities.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, they possess a failing **nutritive power** <term>original: "δύναμιν θρεπτικὴν"; the body's natural ability to absorb nutrients</term>, especially in those parts where the faults of nutrition are otherwise most easily seen. Hence, the feet and legs do not swell because there is simply not enough strength to transfer the offending blood from the veins to those parts; instead, they are consumed by wasting and **atrophy** <term>original: "ἀτροφίᾳ"; the shriveling or wasting away of body tissue</term> because of the debility of the innate heat, which is the principle of all nutrition. But where the depravity of the humor increases, and its sharpness is made greater because the watery and thin parts evaporate away, malignant ulcers frequently follow. This happens because the continuity of the flesh is dissolved by the eroding matter. These are called **Chironian and Telephian ulcers** <note>In medical tradition, these were "incurable" or difficult ulcers named after the centaur Chiron (whose wound would not heal) and King Telephus</note> according to Salomon Albertus and Ronsseus, because they admit a scar only with great difficulty due to their **malignancy** <term>original: "κακοήθειαν"; a medical term for a disease that is stubborn, wicked, or worsening</term> and evil nature, which follows the specific corruption of the scurvy-matter. These and many other symptoms are produced by the nature of the immediate cause of scurvy determined above: namely, that a **tartareous matter** <note>Physicians believed scurvy was caused by "tartar"—salty, stony deposits similar to those found in wine vats—mixing with the blood</note>, mixed with the blood due to the weakness of the spleen, putrefies and generates various unnatural conditions through its own power of thickening and dissolving.

### APPENDIX TO BOOK II, PART II

...constipation, fevers, **fainting spells** <term>original: "lipothymias"; a sudden loss of strength or fainting</term>, headaches, colics, **pleurisy** <term>original: "pleuritides"; inflammation of the lungs and chest cavity</term>, convulsions, arthritis, and many more ailments, but it produces them with deceptive signs, as the most experienced Eugalenus <note>Severinus Eugalenus (1535–1617) was a Dutch physician whose work on scurvy was considered authoritative for over a century.</note> gathers.

Sometimes the **offending matter** <term>original: "materia peccans"; the diseased substance or "bad humor" believed to cause illness</term> in Scurvy excites these very diverse ailments through its own corruption and the accompanying force of coagulation and dissolution, by which, like **Proteus** <note>In Greek mythology, Proteus was a sea-god capable of changing his shape at will; here, it refers to the disease's ability to mimic other illnesses.</note>, it takes on various forms. But I add that diseases of this kind, with their deceptive signs, deceive the inexperienced for the reason that they have a peculiar generation and cure, according to the properties of the Scorbutic matter, compared to others. <margin>From where does the flow of the bowels arise?</margin> And first, regarding the flows of the bowels [diarrhea], they do not consist of raw food just as it was consumed, which happens in **lientery** <term>lientery: a form of diarrhea where food is passed undigested</term>; nor are they even liquid, in unequal quantity, and coming out less densely, as in common diarrhea. Instead, the discharges are more frequently compact, exceeding the amount of food taken in, of various colors, and usually rejected in equal amounts. This happens partly because the matter of Scurvy is somewhat coagulated and separated from the healthy part of the blood, and stimulates the excretory faculty by its **acrimony** <term>acrimony: a sharp, biting, or corrosive quality of bodily fluids</term>, and also because the absorption of the **liver** <term>original: "hepar"</term> is hindered, because of which a large amount of nourishment already altered is rejected together with the offending matter. Indeed, if besides the drossy matter—

<column-break/>

—a greater acrimony is added, sometimes <margin>Where does dysentery arise from?</margin> that flow mimics **dysentery** <note>A severe infection of the intestines resulting in bloody diarrhea.</note>, insofar as some blood is poured out from the **mesenteric veins** <term>original: "venis mesaraicis"; the veins that drain blood from the intestines</term> along with it. This, however, comes out without the shredding of the bowel lining and is separate from the excrement, contrary to what usually happens in true dysentery. <margin>From where does constipation arise?</margin> Just as some scurvy sufferers are seized by a flux, so others are frequently seized by constipation, as Forestus <note>Pieter van Foreest (1521–1597), a prominent Dutch physician known as the "Dutch Hippocrates."</note> notes in *Book 20, Observation 11*, namely when the matter tends toward other parts of the body, and the bile itself—which is the stimulus for the excretory faculty in the intestines—is either not separated from the **liver** <term>original: "jecore"</term> or, once separated, is not sent to the intestines but to some other body part. But if the Scorbutic matter, with its more watery part evaporating or with every exit blocked, grows unnaturally hot so that this heat is communicated to the heart, <margin>Where do fevers in Scurvy come from?</margin> various fevers arise. These are namely slow, continuous, or irregular and intermittent fevers, but which often—as Eugalenus says in *On Scurvy, page 30*—are not similar in any sign to the fevers described by the ancients, except that they sometimes play-act the type of a false **daily, third-day, or fourth-day fever** <term>original: "quotidianæ, tertianæ ac quartanæ"; fevers categorized by how many days pass between spikes in temperature</term>. They express these more by mimicking the timing of the days than by the actual nature of the symptoms. For this reason, experience testifies that these Scorbutic fevers are frequently disordered, so that they occur sometimes twice, sometimes three or four times, and even more often after the third, fourth, fifth, or sixth day, with various **shivering** <term>original: "horripilationi"; the sensation of hair standing on end or "goosebumps" during a fever chill</term>...

### ON SCURVY, SECTION I.

...with chills attacking the patient, usually followed by a burning heat accompanied by an anxiety in the chest <term>original: "praecordiorum"; the area of the body in front of the heart</term>, which is a reliable sign of Scurvy. Indeed, the pulse, even while the fever is active, is found to be large and hard; however, as soon as the heat of the fever subsides, it changes to a small, frequent, and irregular pulse, which is common in ***Scurvy***. What else could produce this variety of febrile symptoms than the ***Scorbutic*** **offending matter** <term>original: "materia peccans"; the diseased substance believed to cause the illness</term>, putrefying in the blood? By the power of its own dissolution and coagulation, it not only mixes with other harmful waste-like humors—which are very easily collected in such an unnatural state—increasing their malice, but it also takes for itself their effects through a certain communication. Because the heart is affected in this way by febrile exhalations, a fever is produced with a singular property peculiar to ***Scurvy***; for this reason, it is not removed by the common treatment for fevers, but by remedies specifically appropriate to this disease.

<margin>Whence fainting arises.</margin> In the same way, ***lipothymia*** <term>fainting or a sudden loss of strength</term> of the spirit and ***swooning*** <term>original: "deliquium"</term> frequently happen to those with Scurvy. This occurs because of foul vapors that are extremely hostile to the primary organ of the **vital faculty** <note>In traditional medicine, the "vital faculty" was the power centered in the heart that distributed life and heat through the blood.</note>, namely the heart, even after slight movement, which excites such evaporation. Therefore, when a seemingly minor disease or fever takes hold of someone, so that while lying down they seem to suffer little or nothing, and yet

<column-break/>

they are suddenly and frequently seized by fainting, you may be certain, says ***Eugalenus***, that they suffer from ***sceletyrbe*** <note>original: "sceletyrbe"; an ancient Greek term used by early modern physicians as a synonym for scurvy.</note>, a fact which the successful cure will prove.

<margin>Whence the pains in Scurvy arise.</margin> Furthermore, various pains follow in ***Scurvy*** when the matter of the disease—namely, the thin, watery blood—acquires a certain sharpness <note>original: "acredine"; a caustic or acidic quality in the bodily fluids.</note> or increases in volume. In the sensitive parts of the body, this produces the immediate cause of pain, which is the **dissolution of unity** <term>original: "solutam unitatem"; a medical theory that pain is caused by the physical separation or stretching of tissues that should be joined</term>. For pain is nothing other than a "sad sensation of tactile qualities," as ***Langius*** <note>Johannes Langius (1485–1565), a famous German physician known for his "Medical Epistles."</note> repeats after others in Book 1, Epistle 41;

<margin>See Medical Problems, decade 3, question 9.</margin> this occurs because of the dissolution of unity in the organ of sense, as we have sufficiently demonstrated elsewhere.

<margin>Headache.</margin> In this way, a continuous and fixed headache arises in ***Scorbutics*** when the offending matter is collected in a dense mass around the sensitive parts of the head by its own sharpness. However, the pain is *interrupted and recurs at intervals* when harmful and biting exhalations rise from the lower parts of the body at certain times. When the ***Scorbutic*** matter is resolved into a vaporous substance and then collected again through coagulation around the membranous parts of the brain, it gives rise to the aforementioned symptom.

<margin>Pain like colic.</margin> But when such a collection of matter occurs in the intestines and neighboring parts, a pain resembling **colic** <term>severe abdominal pain</term> seems to be present. By this, the stomach and intestines are torn apart with various torments and piercing pains, as ***Eugalenus*** affirms on page 63 of his work *On Scurvy*, stating that he has known some...

## APPENDIX TO BOOK II, PART II.

...some who, from such distensions and pains, have suffered a rupture of the peritoneum <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note>. This is why in Northern regions this disease is called ***Schürbauch*** <note>original German: "tearing belly"</note>, because it affects the lower belly with strange griping pains, as *Weyer* <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a Dutch physician famous for his work on both medicine and the occult</note> notes in his *Book on Unknown Diseases*, page 2. This pain is joined with other **pathognomonic** <term>signs that are specifically characteristic of a particular disease</term> signs of Scurvy when it attacks someone. Therefore, it is usually cured only by remedies specific to the disease, through which the **Scorbutic offending matter** <term>original: "materia Scorbutica peccans"; the diseased substance or "humor" believed to cause the illness</term> is dissolved and corrected, which will be more evident in the section on treatment. Sometimes it happens that the offending matter collected around the sensitive parts of the chest mimics pleurisy <margin>Whence false pleurisy?</margin>, which is nevertheless very easily distinguished from true pleurisy when the characteristic signs of the mentioned condition are considered. Here, besides the signs by which Scurvy is recognized, there is a pain in the side recurring at intervals, without a significant cough or sputum <note>mucus coughed up from the lungs</note>, accompanied by a small, soft, and irregular pulse and a lingering fever. These are entirely contrary to true pleurisy, since according to *Galen* <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the foundational authority for medieval and Renaissance medicine</note> (*Book on the Constitution of the Art of Medicine*, chapter 15, and *Book 2 on Affected Places*, chapter 9), in pleurisy there is a stinging pain in the side, an acute fever, and consequently a hard and forceful pulse, a cough, and usually bloody sputum. Furthermore, convulsions <margin>Whence Scorbutic convulsions?</margin> also gradually occur in some Scorbutic patients, such that they eventually become completely contracted until the morbid matter received by the nerves,

<column-break/>

is either resolved on its own through the help of nature or digested and dissolved with the aid of medicines. Truly, it is a wonder what painful tortures of the joints Scurvy sometimes brings in its wake, so that patients seem to suffer from gouty arthritis <margin>Whence Scorbutic arthritis?</margin>, but they do so falsely. This is because these pains do not stay in one place for long, especially at the start of the disease, but wander and move from one place to another. Thus, while we think a joint has been freed from pain, against all hope and expectation you may see new tortures arise in the same spot, either with or without swelling (as *Eugalenus* <note>Severinus Eugalenus, a 16th-century physician whose work was the standard reference for Scurvy for decades</note> observed). This symptom occurs when the offending matter of Scurvy, in a vaporous substance mixed with thin humors, is moved back and forth in various ways within the human body and chiefly affects the sensitive parts of the joints. *Eugalenus* believes this condition is the same as the one *Weyer* says is endemic to Westphalia, Gelderland, and Friesland <note>Regions in the modern-day Netherlands and Germany</note>, called ***die Baren*** <note>likely a regional folk term for "the pains" or "the bears"</note>—as if you were to say a "transfer" or a "migration"—which seems likely because that disease which the Northerners call ***die Baren*** (or, adding a descriptor because of its sudden movement, ***die loopende Baren*** <note>Dutch/German: "the running or wandering pains"</note>) is recognized by the same signs and cured by medicines appropriate for Scurvy. For it appears (says *Henricus a Bra* in a letter to *Forestus* <note>Pieter van Foreest (1521–1597), a prominent Dutch physician known as the "Dutch Hippocrates"</note>) with wandering pains that are extremely agonizing...

# ON SCURVY, SECTION I.

...[pains] in all the members of the body, especially in the back and loins; and first, it usually attacks one particular part, then with swift motion it occupies neighboring parts as well. Indeed, it can be seen that in this plague, often when the pains in the feet are quieted, the shoulder blades are soon affected; once those are calm, the hands are tortured immediately after, and thus the evil itself leaps through all the joints. <margin>See the observations of Forestus <note>Petrus Forestus (1521–1597), a prominent Dutch physician</note>, Book 10, at the end.</margin> However, once those things that are helpful for Scurvy are administered, as Eugalenus <note>Severinus Eugalenus, a 16th-century physician whose work became a standard text on Scurvy</note> testifies, the symptoms mentioned are dispersed and vanish, just as the leaves and fruit of a tree perish once the root is cut out. Hence also *Heurnius* <note>Jan van Heurne (1543–1601), a Dutch philosopher and physician</note> in a letter to the aforementioned *Physician*, rightly refutes those who claim that the disease of the people of Guelders, Westphalia, and neighboring regions

<column-break/>

agrees with the **Little Dragons** <note>original Latin: *Dracunculis*; a term used by ancient physicians to describe Guinea worm or similar parasitic infections</note> of the ancients, when it rather coincides with the disease which the people of Utrecht call **Leaping Gout** <note>original Dutch: *Springende Gicht*</note>, as if it were a leaping joint pain. But that there is a great difference between this joint disease, **the Varen** <note>a local term for a type of wandering pain or gouty affliction</note>, and the **Little Dragons** of the ancients—known today in Meissen, Silesia, and other places as **the Co-eaters** <note>original German: *die Mit-esser*; historically referring to skin parasites or comedones, though here used to distinguish skin/parasitic conditions from internal Scorbutic pain</note>—is sufficiently gathered from *Weyer’s* <note>Johann Weyer</note> *On Unknown Diseases*. From what has been said, it is manifest how Scurvy produces manifold conditions from the specific property of its cause: it follows that we should turn

->ourselves<-

in the following exercise to the prognostics, prevention, and cure.

# ON SCURVY,

## SECTION II.

### §. I.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' inside a square frame with floral motifs.</image-desc>

<margin>
Concerning the prognoses of Scurvy.
</margin>
Before we proceed to the prevention and cure of Scurvy, the prognostic signs must by no means be neglected. Here, it must first be noted that the disease is more severe in those who are born of scurvy-ridden families or even parents <note>The author suggests a hereditary predisposition to Scurvy, a common belief before its nutritional cause—vitamin C deficiency—was understood</note>.

<margin>
Above all, certainty regarding the outcome is required.
</margin>
For just as we seek the means in vain unless we are first certain of the goal, so too is it ridiculous to search for the means of prevention and cure with special diligence at a time when we are still completely ignorant of whether the disease will be dangerous or favorable <note>original Latin: *salutaris*; meaning a disease that follows a "healthy" or predictable path to recovery</note>, curable or entirely lethal. Concerning prognostics

<column-break/>

<margin>
Why must we deal with prognoses?
</margin>
we are therefore rightly concerned in every kind of disease. <margin>Why is the disease more severe in those born of scurvy-ridden parents?</margin>
the fact that Scurvy is more severe in those who are born of scurvy-ridden families or parents. Thus, Salomon Albert <note>Salomon Albert (1540–1600) was a German physician who wrote extensively on scurvy and anatomy.</note> asserts that these people are cured only with great difficulty, and only if the most appropriate treatment is applied; indeed, they are hardly ever cured "root and branch" <note>original: *stirpitus*; meaning a total or foundational cure</note> without the disease leaving some trace, often sprouting back with a resistant malice. Why this happens can be gathered for the most part from what was said above: those who possess this evil by a certain hereditary right have an innate cause for Scurvy—namely, a certain native "weakness of the spleen" <note>In the medical theory of this era, the spleen was responsible for cleansing the blood of "black bile." If it was weak, these impurities built up, causing Scurvy.</note>, which we explained in *Exercise 1, Thesis 12*. This is corrected by medical help only with difficulty, because the cure of hereditary diseases seems exceedingly hard, as is evident from Mercado <note>Ludovico Mercado (1532–1611) was a prominent Spanish physician who wrote a foundational text on hereditary diseases.</note> in Volume 2 at the end of his *Treatise on Hereditary Diseases*. This is because the disease arises from "seed" <note>The reproductive material, believed to carry the health characteristics and "vices" of the parents to the child.</note> corrupted by long-standing and established illnesses, according to Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576) was an influential Italian polymath and physician.</note> in Book 1 of *On Poisons*, Chapter 12. Hence, these things seem to happen through the native constitution. Now, if a habit acquired through custom is difficult to remove, how much more constant is that disposition which arises not from custom, but from nature itself.

<margin>Why a grandfather sometimes produces a scurvy-ridden grandson rather than a son.</margin>
Nor is it an obstacle that sometimes a grandfather suffering from Scurvy propagates this evil not to his son, but to his grandson, with the son acting as the intermediary. For it can happen that the parent possesses an impressed "seal and character" <note>original: *figillationem & characterem*; a medical metaphor suggesting the disease is stamped into the body's essence like a seal on wax.</note> from the grandfather, the activity of which is erased by the strength of the mother's seed and blood; yet it sprouts again in the son if he happens to obtain a mother whose constitution is weaker than the grandmother's (on this, see Mercado in the place cited).

...vigor, so in those patients, over the course of years, that very strength is weakened. It is evident that women are more prone to Scurvy than men, because they are of a colder nature <note>In the "humoral" medical theory of the time, women were considered naturally "colder and wetter" than men, making them more susceptible to diseases caused by sluggish, thick fluids.</note>, as we demonstrated in Book 1 on the Human Body, Exercise 7, last question. They also tend to accumulate a very large amount of dreg-like <note>original: *fæculenti*; referring to "feculent" or sediment-rich humors</note> humor. This is especially true at that time when—as Salomon Alberti <note>Salomon Alberti (1540–1600) was a prominent German physician and anatomist.</note> says in his *Book on Scurvy*, thesis 135—they are found to be sterile due to an inability to receive and conceive the male seed, or otherwise experience their menstrual flow stopping before its time. In such cases, the blood—as if the "sails" of its direction have been changed—is forced to flow back toward the organs of nutrition and undermine their functions. This also occurs most frequently in those women who are not perfectly cleansed of the uterine or postpartum fluids <note>original: *aquis uterinis vel puerperalibus*; referring to lochia or other fluids following childbirth</note> which announce the coming labor while a woman is giving birth.

<margin>Why does the disease worsen around the spring and autumn?</margin>
However, for the most part, the symptoms worsen around the spring and autumn seasons, as Baldwin Ronsseus <note>Baldwin Ronsseus (1525–1597) was one of the first physicians to write a specialized treatise on Scurvy.</note> notes in his *Book on the Great Spleen*, chapter 6. This happens for the same reason that Hippocrates <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460 – c. 370 BC).</note>, in Book 6, Aphorism 55, determined that gouty pains <note>original: *dolores podagricos*; refers to podagra or gout</note> most often attack at these same times. As Heurnius <note>Johannes Heurnius (1543–1601), a Dutch physician known for his commentaries on Hippocrates.</note> notes in his commentary on that aphorism (following Galen), the springtime stirs up the waste products <note>original: *recrementa*; metabolic by-products or "dregs" in the humors</note> that were brought into the body during the winter and drives them toward the weaker parts of the body. Autumn, however, powerfully disturbs the bodily juices <note>original: *succos*; refers to the humors</note> with its atmospheric inequality,

Indeed, nature is undermined because the "native heat" <note>The internal warmth believed to drive digestion and life; a core concept in pre-modern medicine.</note> has been exhausted by the force of the preceding summer. Because of this weakness, and because of the sheer quantity of the "offending matter" <note>original: *materiæ peccantis*; the excess or corrupt humor causing the disease</note>, this heat can no longer master the humors. Consequently, they fall here or there and produce various diseases, as Libanius <note>Likely Georg Liban, a 16th-century scholar and commentator.</note> holds in his notes on the previously cited aphorism of Hippocrates, and as Mercatus <note>Luis Mercado (1532–1611), a leading Spanish physician of the Renaissance.</note> writes in Book 7 *On Fevers*, chapter 2. If anyone wishes to add a quite elegant reason from the Hermetic physicians <note>The "Hermetic" or Paracelsian school of medicine, which used chemistry and alchemy to explain disease.</note> to this reasoning, we shall not object. They say that "tartaric diseases" <note>original: *morbos tartareos*; In Paracelsian medicine, these are diseases caused by the "tartar" or stony precipitates from food and drink, similar to the crust in a wine barrel.</note> worsen around spring and autumn because the impure spirits of tartar are most active at these times; thus, the offending matter produces its "fruits"—namely, the paroxysms or attacks of the symptoms.

Regarding the springtime, the matter is clear: as Quercetanus <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), also known as Quercetanus, a famous Paracelsian physician.</note> notes in his *Consultation on Arthritis* and in Section 2, Chapter 2 of his *Dietetic Polyhistor*, when the Sun enters the "House of the Ram" <note>Aries; this marks the Spring Equinox.</note>, the cold begins to soften. The air and earth are refreshed by the Sun's warm and highly vital rays. The earth, gradually warming and opening its bosom, scatters a "radical humor" <note>A foundational moisture or life-force believed to exist in all living things.</note> into all living beings, by which they revive, sprout again, and finally bring their fruits to maturity, just as this humor is promoted and excited to work by the various degrees of natural "fire" radiating from that great light [the Sun]. ### APPENDIX TO BOOK II, PART II

...scorbutic <note>The text continues from the previous page, completing the word *scorbuticus*.</note>, as *Eugalenus* <note>Severinus Eugalenus (1535–1617) was a Dutch physician whose work on scurvy was considered authoritative for decades.</note> says in his *Book on Scurvy, p. 130*, is caused by a faulty humor <note>original: *humore peccante*; in humoral medicine, this refers to a fluid that has become unbalanced or "corrupt."</note> which affects and weakens the internal organs. This occurs as much by the substance of the humor as by its smoky evaporation and the specific quality of its putrefaction. Once the organs are infected by this, their faculties are damaged, and they are prone to imposing that same corrupt impression on the food they process. In a reciprocal cycle, they return to the incoming nourishment what they received from the faulty humors. These parts then acquire such an unsuitability—due to the contaminating, faulty quality of the humor—that they are rendered unfit for the nutrition of the body. 

Thus, these "silent increments" <note>Hidden, gradual accumulations of the disease.</note> gather until they can no longer be hidden by the body’s innate heat. By a stronger effort of nature, they are diverted to the more remote parts of the body. First, the legs swell; when they can no longer receive the excess, the residue is finally cast back toward the abdomen and the peritoneum <note>The lining of the abdominal cavity.</note>, so that the scurvy presents as a very hard and dense tumor known as <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: *hydrops*; a buildup of fluid in the body's tissues or cavities, today often called edema.</note>. What does the corruption of the gums portend?

But if corruption of the gums occurs—especially gangrenous corruption—we recognize it by certain signs. Once the corruption is complete and the part is dead, our labor to restore it is entirely in vain. <margin>Spots suddenly appearing and vanishing.</margin>

But where the said marks suddenly blossom and in turn vanish, they denote a doubtful duel of nature with the disease, as Salomon Alberti <note>Salomon Alberti (1540–1600) was a German physician known for his anatomical studies.</note> says in section 160. However, according to *Reusner on Scurvy, Exercise 6, page 414*, the **receding** <note>original: *palindromia*; referring to symptoms that "run back" from the surface to the internal organs.</note> of the marks usually signifies an extreme cutting off of strength, insofar as the suddenly blossoming spots in turn disappear because of the weakness of the expulsive faculty. By reason of this, the blood returns to the inner parts, especially to the heart itself, in which the offending matter <note>original: *peccans materia*; the harmful fluid causing the sickness in the humoral system of medicine.</note> leaves a trace of its malignancy and threatens total destruction to the whole.

<margin>What do permanent spots denote?</margin>

In the same way, it is a bad sign for determining the future state of the patient when those spots are permanent; this is because they prove the malignancy and abundance of the matter which was recently held chained by the bonds of the innate heat. For this reason, in those who are dying, and sometimes even in the deceased, 

<margin>Why do spots blossom in some after death?</margin>

we see scorbutic marks of this kind blossom, because the abundant offending matter is moved from the center to the circumference of the body by the heat that remains even after death. For it is not 

<column-break/>

absurd that the effects of heat can survive for some time even in the dead, although death is called the extinction of heat, as we have demonstrated in our *Treatise on the Preservation and Bleeding of Corpses, Problem 1*.

<margin>What do scorbutic ulcers signify?</margin>

Furthermore, it is a bad sign when the marks degenerate into ulcers which admit a scar <note>meaning they are very difficult to heal or close.</note> with difficulty. This is either because they are "atrabilious" <note>caused by black bile, one of the four humors associated with melancholy and decay.</note>, as Ronseus <note>Boudewijn Ronsse (1525–1597), a Dutch physician and pioneer in the study of scurvy.</note> pleased to write in his *Book on Scurvy, Chapter 7*, since the offending scorbutic matter acquires the qualities of black bile when it is exacerbated over a long period, and gains an eroding power due to the exhalation of its thinner parts. **Hippocrates** calls all black-bile ulcers dangerous; for this reason, in *Aphorisms, Book 4, 24*, dysentery from black bile is pronounced lethal. Or [they are difficult to heal] because of the abundance of salty and watery humor <note>original: *serosi*; thin, watery fluid.</note> which is prominent in Scurvy, and which hinders the drying of the ulcer, as Reusner argues in *On Scurvy, Exercise 5, page 355 and following*. 

<margin>Why are scorbutic ulcers difficult to heal?</margin>

Indeed, just as ulcers are called malignant and difficult to heal when corrupted blood flows to them and the part itself suffers from a **dyscrasia** <note>original: *dyscrasia*; an imbalance of the four bodily humors.</note>, according to **Galen** in *Method of Healing, Book 4, Chapter 1*, and *On the Composition of Medicines according to Genus, Book 4, Chapter 1*; **Paré** <note>Ambroise Paré (c. 1510–1590), a famous French royal surgeon.</note> in *Surgery, Book 12, Chapter 10*; and **Aquapendens** <note>Hieronymus Fabricius ab Aquapendente (1533–1619), a celebrated Italian anatomist.</note> in *On Ulcers, Book 3, Chapter 4*. Thus, we believe both causes concur in a **scorbutic ulcer** <note>original: *ulcere sceletyrbico*; 'Sceletyrbe' was the classical term for a disease causing paralysis or lameness of the legs, often identified by early modern doctors as scurvy.</note>, so that they admit a scar with difficulty, because they are among those in which humor flows continuously, which, besides being harmful...
