Nor can it be cured by **flesh-forming medicines** <note>original: *sarcoticis*; from the Greek *sarkotikos*, substances used to promote the growth of healthy new flesh in a wound.</note>, because genuine flesh cannot be generated while this false growth exists, as **Mercado** <note>Luis Mercado (1525–1611) was a leading Spanish physician of the Renaissance.</note> says in *Book 2 on the French Disease, Chapter 7*: "for everything is changed toward the nature of that which is changing it, insofar as that thing is capable of being changed." Having offered these points as an examination of the **prognostic signs** <note>Signs used by a doctor to predict the likely course and outcome of a disease.</note>, it follows that we should proceed to the **prevention** of Scurvy, in which we primarily look to guard against this disease in those who are prone to developing its "kindling" <note>original: *fomitem*; literally "tinder" or "kindling," referring to the internal material that allows a disease to flare up.</note>.

### VI.

<margin>On the prevention of Scurvy.</margin>
->*Those who are prone to Scurvy are protected by a way of life that is contrary to the causes of Scurvy; therefore, they ought to choose air that is warm, dry, and pure in its substance.*<-

<margin>Knowledge of the surrounding air is highly necessary for the Physician.</margin>
Since there is no moment of time in which we do not require the inhalation of air (according to **Hippocrates** in his book *On Airs, Waters, and Places*), and since there is nothing that can equally benefit or harm us more—due to its transformation within our bodies, which we observe daily with the rising and setting of the stars, certain celestial alignments, and the various positions and distances of lands—the quality and disposition of the air must be diligently considered by the Physician. This is noted by **Cardano** <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an influential Italian polymath and physician.</note> in *Book 1 on Preserving Health, Chapter 17*, and **Quercetanus** <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician and chemist who advocated for chemical medicine.</note> in his *Dietary Polyhistor, Section 2, Chapter 2*. This is especially true in the prevention of diseases, since, as **Aetius** and **Paulus Aegineta** <note>Aetius of Amida and Paulus Aegineta were influential Greek medical compilers from the Byzantine period.</note> testify, the surrounding air changes and perverts our bodily **temperaments** <note>The balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which determined a person's health and personality.</note> in various ways according to its own diverse qualities. Indeed, the air is often of greater weight and efficacy than the other **non-naturals** <note>original: *res non naturales*; in Galenic medicine, these were the six factors under a person's control—such as air, food, and sleep—that influenced health.</note>; for it overcomes what medicines and other aids of the medical art could not achieve, simply by a change of location, as Mercado adds in *Book 2 on Preserving Health, Class 2, Article 1, Number 4*.

<margin>What kind of air is suitable for those with Scurvy?</margin>
Therefore, in the prevention of Scurvy for those who are prone and predisposed, the choice of the surrounding air must be considered above all else. We recommend that which is endowed with warmth, dryness, and purity of substance, by which the **vital spirits** <term>spiritus</term> <note>The subtle, vaporous substances believed to circulate through the body to sustain life and function.</note> in our bodies are refreshed. Consequently, all concoctions and digestions become more perfect, whereby the accumulation of the **antecedent cause** <term>causa antecedens</term> <note>The internal predisposition or the build-up of harmful humors that precedes the actual onset of symptoms.</note> is inhibited.

<margin>Artificial correction of the air.</margin>
If such air is not provided by nature, it must be procured by art. This can be done by lighting a bright fire in appropriate places, preferably using woods such as laurel, juniper, rosemary, mastic, and the like, as well as by producing smoke and vapors by throwing...

### VII.

->*Furthermore, food items should be selected from those that possess the power of thinning, cutting, and cleansing: they should provide good nourishment and be easy to digest, which, by a slight astringency, may properly revive the innate heat while preserving the strength of the internal organs.*<- <note>In the medical theory of the time, foods that could "cut" or "thin" were used to break down thick, sluggish fluids (humors) believed to cause disease.</note>

<margin>Broths hold the first place among foods.</margin>
Therefore, among broths and more liquid foods—which rightly hold the first place when taking nourishment—whatever **Mercuriale** <note>Girolamo Mercuriale (1530–1606) was a highly influential Italian physician; the author here disputes his claim that the order of eating foods does not matter.</note> may say, who asserts in *Practical Medicine*, Book 3, Chapter 13, that no specific order should be observed in taking food, we choose those made from young chickens, squabs, and beef. For so great is the efficacy of that acidity that it can "coagulate spirits and dissolve bodies," as **Quercetanus** <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), known as Quercetanus, was a French physician who blended traditional medicine with new chemical theories.</note> says in Book 2 of *On the Signatures of Things*. That is to say, it cuts through thick matter and dissolves it by thinning it, and it "coagulates" or tempers the fervor of spirits or exhaling vapors.

<margin>Suitable meats.</margin>
Among meats, we recommend those from suckling animals: lambs, kids, and then fawns, calves of six or seven weeks, three-month-old bullocks, and **wethers** <note>castrated rams</note>. Among birds, we have at home chickens, capons, and young pigeons. Although it is commonly and falsely said that pigeon meat provides nourishment that is slow to digest, it is actually of good nutrition, so that it offers a most suitable food for the elderly and those subject to **cold conditions** <note>original: *frigidis affectibus*; referring to illnesses caused by an excess of the "cold" humor.</note>, as **Quercetanus** notes in his *Universal Dietetics*, Section 3, Chapter 5.

<margin>
Seasoning of foods.
</margin>
Since a proper preparation of both meat and fish cannot be achieved without suitable seasoning, it should be noted that for seasoning foods, a moderate use of **cinnamon**, **cassia-bark**, **ginger**, **mace**, **nutmeg**, and **saffron** will suffice. Through these, not only is a pleasant taste given to the meals, but the strength of the internal organs is also fortified.

Dips.

<margin>
Sugar is an enemy to those with Scurvy.
</margin>
I say a *little* sugar added, because sweetness is not particularly suitable, insofar as sugar possesses a clogging and "gluey" quality. Therefore, it provides an opportunity for obstructions and the accumulation of **raw humors** <note>original: *crudorum humorum*; in humoral medicine, these were fluids not yet fully "digested" or refined by the body's heat.</note>, as **Quercetanus** <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician and chemist.</note> notes in his *Pharmacology*

> Sweets, says Plautus, are less suitable for a large spleen.

Furthermore, this can be proven from **Galen** (*On the Powers of Simple Medicines*, Book 6) and **Celsus** (*On Medicine*, Book 4, chapter 9); **Talentonius** uses their authority to confirm this opinion in his *Hidden Matters*, Book 3, chapter 19. For this reason, the physicians of **Lower Saxony** <note>A region in Northern Germany where scurvy was common.</note> substituted sugar-syrups with distilled waters and squeezed juices. Daily experience testifies that almost all patients in maritime regions usually reject sweets because they feel themselves harmed by them. What is even more remarkable is that sick children, who otherwise delight in sweets, loathe them—perhaps because from their very first cradles they have some hereditary disposition toward this abominable affliction. This was rightly pointed out by our late friend **Dorncreilius** <note>Tobias Dornkreil (1579–1605), a physician from Lüneburg.</note> in the preface to his *New Dispensary*. ### IX.

*Beyond those things pertaining to the surrounding air and food, it should be noted that this evil is prevented by moderate exercise and by customary evacuations being maintained in the proper manner.*

<margin>Exercises are suitable for those with spleen disorders.</margin>
This is very easily gathered from what we said above in the investigation of causes: for since rest increases spleen-related afflictions, it follows that moderate, suitable exercises are beneficial in Scurvy. This is also evident from the playwright Plautus, where in the play *Curculio*, Act 2, he introduces the pimp Cappadox complaining about his enlarged spleen with these words:

> ->— Now I walk about as if cinched by a belt,<-
> ->*I seem to have twin sons in my belly,*<-
> ->*I fear nothing, except that I, miserable man, might burst in the middle.*<-

To this, after other remarks, the servant Palinurus responds:

> ->— *walk on, that is the best thing for the spleen.*<-

<margin>Customary evacuations should be promoted.</margin>
By the same reasoning, customary evacuations must not be neglected, as they contribute greatly not only to the prevention but also to the cure of this condition, insofar as they hinder the generation of the disease by evacuating superfluities <note>Excess bodily fluids or waste products believed to cause illness.</note>, and they correct and remove what has been generated through the purification of the blood. Hence, experience testifies that women prone to Scurvy feel the paroxysms <note>Sudden attacks or intensification of symptoms.</note> most severely when an obstruction of their menstrual flow occurs. This also appears in certain predisposed elderly men whom Scurvy attacks when their accustomed flow of hemorrhoids <note>Bleeding from hemorrhoids was historically viewed as a natural "safety valve" for the body to release excess or "melancholic" blood.</note> is suppressed. As for the regimen of sleep, waking, and disturbances of the mind, it is easily understood by the principle of opposites, when we consider what we said above in the doctrine of causes. It follows that we should now turn our attention to the treatment itself.

# APPENDIX TO BOOK II, PART II

### X.

<margin>On the cure of Scurvy.</margin>
**The cure of Scurvy is achieved through the help of remedies discovered by rational indications; however, Scurvy, like other afflictions, is not removed while its cause remains. Therefore, in treatment, the cause must first be removed, where one must deliberate on both the performance of bloodletting and purging.**

For even if the Method of Healing, according to *Galen, book 2 of the Method of Healing <note>original: "Methodus Medendi"</note>, chapter 7*, is nothing other than that practice by which the proper use of remedies is prescribed through <term>indications</term> <note>Signs or circumstances that point toward the correct medical treatment.</note> to dispel the disease; nevertheless, this cannot always be done immediately through indications taken from the disease itself. Rather, very frequently, the <term>morbific cause</term> <note>The specific cause that produces the disease.</note> holds the primary place in providing these indications. This is because, more often than not, one must not only remove what has already happened but also prevent what is to come by removing the cause, as *Galen states in book 10 of the Method of Healing, chapter 1.*

<margin>A disease is not cured unless the cause is first removed.</margin>
For we labor in vain in curing a disease at that time when its nourishing cause is neglected. That is to say, not the external cause, which by itself indicates nothing; nor even the <term>containing cause</term> <note>In Galenic medicine, the cause that is present while the disease is active.</note>, which does not establish a specific indication from the disease; but the internal antecedent cause, which consists mostly in the

<column-break/>

contents—whether they are at fault in substance, quantity, quality, location, motion, or rest—as we showed in our *Medical Disputation 17, thesis 40.* We assist this condition, among other things, primarily through the letting of blood and through purging, conducted in the proper manner. Therefore, we must consequently discuss in what way that very thing ought to be done.

### XI.

*Therefore, since the blood in Scurvy is at fault not only in quality but also in abundance, after a mild laxative medicine has been given, one should indicate bloodletting or a substitute evacuation of blood immediately at the beginning, while the disease has not yet grown strong or driven its roots deeper.*

For where, says *Salomon Albertus in his book on Scurvy, §. 240*, the entire body is full of <term>juices</term> <note>The "humors" or fluids of the body which were believed to cause disease if unbalanced.</note> and is suffused with a certain dark redness, and nothing else stands in the way, blood is let promptly and during the early stages. Because once the blood is let, nature is unburdened and the excess is evacuated; the pathways being made wider, there is no doubt that the purging happens more effectively. Indeed, purging itself often follows bloodletting even without further medicine, as *Vallesius says in his book of controversies, chapter 9.* Hence also Horatius Augenius in *book 8 on bloodletting, chapter 3.*

<summary>This page explains the medical logic for treating scurvy by addressing its root causes, specifically through bloodletting and purging. It argues that treatment is most effective in the early stages of the disease to prevent it from becoming more deeply rooted in the body's humors.</summary>

# ON SCURVY, SECTION II.

<columns>

<margin>Why a lenitive is administered before bloodletting?</margin>
When the blood is more abundant than other humors, it is established that one should begin with bloodletting rather than purging. For the less beneficial it is to evacuate pure blood rather than impure, the less appropriate the letting of blood seems to be after purging. However, we have said that bloodletting should be instituted only after a lenitive medicine has been administered. This is because "crudity" <note>An old medical term for undigested or "raw" humors in the body.</note> of the stomach and the primary pathways causes raw juices to be snatched up by the veins to replace the blood, as noted by Gentile da Foligno in his commentary on *Avicenna, book 1, fen 4, chapter 20, question 34.* For this reason, in Scurvy, the bowels and primary pathways should be cleansed of their flood of filth by a lenitive medicine. There is a well-founded hope that, due to the proximity of the adjacent spleen and liver—which by their nature can somewhat free themselves from <term>cacochymia</term> <note>An unhealthy state of the body's humors or fluids.</note>—many of the offending humors will be exhausted from below.

<margin>A soothing enema.</margin>
Therefore, let an enema be administered first, prepared from goat whey or the broth of an aging rooster, in which the following are boiled until a third of the liquid is consumed:
*   Polypody of the Oak root, 1 ounce
*   Mallow leaves, Oregano, and Fumitory, 1 handful each
*   Anise and Fennel seeds, 2 drachms each
*   Hungarian prunes, 8 in number.
In 1 pound of this strained decoction, dissolve:
*   Cassia for <term>clysters</term> <note>Another term for an enema.</note>, 6 drachms
*   Simple Electuary of <term>Hiera</term> <note>A traditional bitter purgative, often containing aloes.</note>, 2.5 drachms
*   Oil of Chamomile and Dill, half an ounce each
*   Strained Honey of Roses, 1 ounce
*   1 egg yolk.

Take:
*   Soothing Electuary of Manna and <term>Diacatholicon</term> <note>A "universal" mild laxative.</note>, half an ounce each
*   Spirit of Vitriol <note>A historical name for diluted sulfuric acid.</note>, 5 drops
*   Sugar, as much as is sufficient.
Let a bolus be made. At Soltquella, in the same case, a pleasant and common Electuary was frequently used by us, the composition of which is:

<margin>Electuary of the extraction of senna.</margin>
Take:
*   Very pungent Cinnamon, 6 drachms
*   Selected Alexandria Senna leaves (stripped from their stalks), 5 ounces.
Having brought these to a single boil with 3 pounds of Malvasia wine, let them sit in infusion for 12 hours; afterward, let them be strained with pressing. In this strained liquid, extract the essence of 9 ounces of raisins washed in wine. To this extraction add:
*   Tamarind pulp
*   Simple Electuary of Prunes
*   Lenitive Electuary, 2 ounces each
*   Distilled Oil of Nutmeg, half a <term>scruple</term> <note>A small unit of weight, about 1.3 grams.</note>.
Let an electuary be made. It is given in doses from 1 ounce to 12 drachms, and is sometimes mixed with other stronger medicines depending on the various intentions of the physician. Furthermore, it will not be inappropriate, after using these solid soothing medicines, to drink a draft of chicken broth or pea broth—not entirely unsalted, but seasoned with a moderate amount of salt. This not only brings the soothing power into action more quickly, but also better and more perfectly washes away the "ballast" <note>original: "faburra"</note> of viscous humors from the primary pathways.

<margin>Should unsalted broths be given after lenitives?</margin>
I said this should be done with broths that are not entirely unsalted, but tempered with moderate salt, so that we do not commit the common error of many who, against reason and experience, follow the common folk and old wives in believing it a sin to provide liquids seasoned with salt, because broth...

# APPENDIX TO BOOK II, PART II

<columns>

...electuary, if it is moderately salted, not only washes out the stomach and intestines, but by the power of the salt it is also rendered suitable for wiping away the very remains of the medicine; for it is a property of salt, as Quercetanus <note>original: "Quercetanus" — Joseph Duchesne (1544–1609), a French physician who championed the use of chemical and "Hermetic" (paracelsian) remedies.</note> says in *The Defense of Hermetic Medicine*, Book 1, Chapter 2, among the other faculties it possesses, to cleanse, to clear obstructions, and to ward off putrefaction and corruption. For this reason, its moderate use is not only harmless but highly necessary and most useful in the preservation of our life—on this, see Marsilio Ficino’s <note>A 15th-century Italian philosopher and physician.</note> *On Obtaining Life from the Heavens*. 

However, by the very fact that we have established that some lenitive <note>A soothing medicine used to ease the bowels.</note> must be administered before bloodletting is undertaken, we do not agree with Reusner <note>Hieronymus Reusner, a 16th-century physician who wrote on scurvy.</note> in his *Exercises on Scurvy*, Exercise 7. <margin>Should bloodletting be attempted before purging?</margin> He maintains that in Scurvy, a vein should never be cut before purging, because, as Galen <note>The Roman-era Greek physician whose humoral theories dominated medicine for centuries.</note> testifies in *The Method of Medicine*, Book 3, Chapter 21, an abundance of "raw" humors <note>Undigested or "crude" fluids in the body believed to cause blockages.</note> prohibits the letting of blood. Yet, corrupt humor around the liver, the spleen, and the neighboring parts threatens a much greater danger than "rawness" does when it is drawn into the veins. We respond to this objection in two ways: first, that bloodletting is not permitted at every stage of the disease, because as the illness worsens, the opportunity for letting blood is considered lost, as the corrupt blood surges back into the more noble organs and brings on more savage

<column-break/>

symptoms; for this reason, by the same logic that bloodletting is postponed until after purging, we determine that it should be omitted entirely. 

Add to this a second point: that the evacuation of blood is permitted in the present instance because Nature, which governs our body, is relieved and unburdened of that which weighs upon it like a heavy pack. Once relieved, she can easily overcome what remains, as is gathered from Galen's *Method of Medicine*, Book 11, Chapter 15. Therefore, if bloodletting is performed first, the subsequent purging of what remains is completed more quickly and perfectly. 

Having settled these matters, it is not without reason <margin>Which vein for phlebotomy?</margin> that one asks: which vein exactly should be cut for the evacuation of blood in Scurvy? Salomon Albert, Wierus <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a Dutch physician.</note> in his *Observations on Scurvy* and his German book *On Unknown Diseases*, page 11, Ronsæus in *On the Great Spleen*, chapter 8, Forestus in Book 20, observation 11, and others incline toward recommending the veins of the left arm above others. This is especially true when—as happens in Scurvy—the spleen is more affected than the liver. The basis of this assertion is drawn from Galen's *To Glaucon*, Book 2, Chapter 2, and *Method of Medicine*, Book 13, Chapter 10, where it is said that in inflammation of the spleen, the inner veins of the left hand should be opened, whereas if the liver is affected, the same should be opened in the right. And in the book *On the Method of Curing by Bloodletting*, Chapter 16, it is said that drawing blood from the left arm greatly assists an afflicted spleen.

# ON SCURVY, SECTION II

<columns>

<margin>
In disorders of the spleen, should a vein be cut in the left arm rather than the right?
</margin>
...the withdrawal [of blood]: because in this way it is done directly from the side that is suffering, and so *in a straight line* <note>original Greek: "kata ixin"—a medical term meaning the bloodletting is aligned with the affected part</note>, according to the symmetry in which right parts correspond to the right and left to the left. Even if in other types of revulsions <note>The practice of drawing blood from a distant part of the body to divert "morbid humors" away from a diseased area</note> we think that alignment of parts, in which left corresponds to left, should not be neglected, nevertheless, in bloodletting we have said that more regard must be given to the directness and the continuation of the vessels and ducts, as noted in *Medical Disputations 16, thesis 34*. For this reason, setting aside the authority of the ancients—so as not to seem to swear by the words of others or approve anything against conscience—we establish, along with certain more recent authors (among whom are Thaddæus Dunus in his *The Art of Evacuation by Bloodletting*, Book 1, Chapter 3 and elsewhere; Reusner in *Exercises on Scurvy*, Exercise 7; and Sennertus in *Controversial Medical Questions*, Disputation 6, Question 5), that in disorders of the spleen, and consequently also in Scurvy, the veins of the left arm have no special privilege. This is because it becomes manifest through the skillful dissection of bodies that there is no branch of the veins in the left arm that has a closer affinity with the spleen than the veins of the right arm. Indeed, all the upper veins are joined with the spleen by means of the liver, insofar as they arise from the ascending *vena cava* <note>The large vein carrying deoxygenated blood into the heart</note>, which nevertheless only reaches the spleen via the *portal vein*. Thus, the blood

<column-break/>

abounding around the spleen is diverted or evacuated through a cut vein in the arm not immediately, but by way of the liver, on account of the anastomosis <note>A connection or opening between two vessels</note> by which the branches of the *vena cava* and the *portal vein* meet and unite in the liver. Furthermore, in choosing the veins of either arm, those people suffer from the same blindness who decide that only the "splenic" or *basilic* vein, or after that the *median* vein, should be cut, but by no means allow the cutting of the *cephalic* or humeral vein in such a case. They are led by the false opinion of their ancestors, arising from an ignorance of anatomical matters, whereby they established one origin for the *Cephalic* vein and another for the *median* and *basilic* veins. Nevertheless, in the human body, these are all the offspring of one propagation and one parent, just as the most celebrated anatomists—Vesalius, Fallopius, Bauhinus, and others—testify after *personal observation* <note>original Greek: "autopsian"—here meaning evidence gained through anatomical dissection</note>.

<margin>
Is there a scrupulous objection to cutting the "liver vein" instead of the cephalic?
</margin>
It is also clear from this what should be thought of those who, following Paul [of Aegina] <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician</note> in *On Medicine*, Book 6, Chapter 40, so greatly recommend for those with spleen issues the so-called *salvatella* vein of the left hand, located between the pinky and the ring finger. Because it is the most remote, we can grant it the power of revulsion (although Dunus, in *The Art of Evacuation by Bloodletting*, Book 2, Chapter 5, against Fuchs, Book 2, Chapter 10, establishes that it should in no way be cut), yet it holds no special privilege...

<margin>
What is to be decided regarding the cutting of the salvatella vein?
</margin>

</columns>

# APPENDIX TO BOOK II, PART II

...that it is on the left side, we attribute it to the same thing, based on the same foundation that we have thus far deduced from anatomical <gloss>direct observation</gloss> <note>original Latin: *autopsia*</note>. Nor does the fact stand in the way that *Valesius* <note>Francisco Vallés (1524–1592), a prominent Spanish physician and personal doctor to King Philip II of Spain</note> in *Book 7 of his Controversies, Chapter 5*, brings forward a new reason: namely, that limbs are accustomed to deposit and expel their waste in a straight line. This is highly doubtful, since waste products tend toward their own receptacles if they are available; if not, they settle in the weaker parts. By this reasoning, we concede that the right part of the body unloads its waste into the glands of the same side behind the ears, around the armpits, and the groin. However, the case is different for the veins, which are distributed throughout the entire body and consequently into the extremities—not to deposit waste (which happens only by accident, as when the blood suffers from an unnatural impurity), but to bring the material for nutrition. Add to this that the same difficulty would remain: for how could the <term>spleen</term> <note>Latin: *lien*</note> deposit its waste into the <term>salvatella vein</term> <note>A vein on the back of the hand, historically believed by physicians to have a direct connection to the spleen</note> of the left hand more than the right, when each is equally distant from the <term>liver</term> <note>Latin: *jecur*</note>, through which the spleen is assisted? Furthermore,

we have said above in the proposed thesis that a "vicarious" evacuation of blood can sometimes be substituted for <term>venesection</term> <note>The surgical opening of a vein</note>—namely at that time when, perhaps, the nature of the patient suggests the provocation of hemorrhoids or the <term>menses</term> <note>Menstrual flow</note> rather than the cutting of a vein.

This is because the peccant matter is most conveniently led through those places toward which its own nature seems to lean, as is gathered from *Hippocrates, Book 1, Aphorism 21*.

### ON SCURVY, SECTION II.

...be made fluid, according to the precept of Hippocrates, and also so that those things which ought to be evacuated are indeed evacuated according to the decree of Galen in his *commentary on Book 2 of the Aphorisms, 9*, where he says: if one thins and cuts through the thick and sticky <term>humors</term> <note>In ancient medicine, these are the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which must stay in balance for health</note> that are in the body and opens the passages through which these are sent and drawn out by purging medicines, then the operation proceeds correctly in all things.

<margin>
Digestion preceding purgation.
</margin>
Therefore, before all else, a <term>digestion</term> <note>In this context, "digestion" (or coction) refers to the process of ripening or "cooking" raw humors so the body can easily separate and expel them</note> or collection of raw humors must be established; specifically, such a kind that can take place in the preparation of the offending humors, where by the thinning of the thick and the thickening of the thin, homogeneous substances are gathered together and heterogeneous ones are separated within the Scorbutic matter, as *Reusner* <note>Hieronymus Reusner (1558–1630), a physician who wrote extensively on scurvy</note> has it in his *7th Exercise on Scurvy*. How such a digestion occurs is beautifully declared by *Mercatus* <note>Luis Mercado (1525–1611), a leading Spanish physician of the Renaissance</note> in *Book 1, On the Right Use of Remedies, Chapter 3*: namely, that in preparing raw and thick matter, we imitate nature. Nature first pours out and thins the humors, and then reduces them to a moderate thickness, just as is evident from <term>chylification</term> <note>The process by which food is turned into chyle in the stomach</note>, by which food is first broken down and melted, but then, in turn, by the force of the acting heat, is coagulated and attains the moderate consistency of chyle. It is also seen in <term>sanguification</term> <note>The process of turning chyle into blood</note>, by which the chyle is first dissolved and then acquires the more solid consistency of blood; likewise,

<margin>
<unclear>Why in</unclear>
<unclear>Scurvy</unclear>
<unclear>the method</unclear>
<unclear>is established.</unclear>
</margin>
from the "cooking" <gloss>coction</gloss> that occurs in every part of the body, by which the blood, first dissolved, is converted into the substance of the parts through a subsequent coagulation. This is done specifically so that the separation of heterogeneous substances can occur in this manner. Although nature does not achieve this same end in offending humors (since they cannot be converted into our body parts due to the "harm" they have acquired), it nevertheless strives to attempt that which is best with the help of medicines—namely, by separating the harmful parts from the harmless. Once this is done, a much easier and less dangerous <term>purgation</term> <note>original Greek: *κάθαρσις* (katharsis)</note> can be established. Therefore, before purgation is performed in Scurvy, nature must be helped to "cook" the raw matter. Consequently, digesting agents must be prescribed which, by their moderate "cutting" <gloss>incisive</gloss>, thinning, and penetrating quality, can serve not only for the preparation of the humor but also for preparing the openness of the passages.

How nature "cooks" noxious humors.

Carrichter refers to this in *On the Body's Medicine*, Book 1, Chapter 41, where <margin>Carrichter’s Powder.</margin>he prescribes a purging powder against Scurvy, which is as follows:

Take: One ounce of Senna leaves. Two drams of <term>Monk’s Rhubarb</term> <note>a species of dock used for its mild laxative properties</note>. One dram each of Anise, Fennel, and Ginger seeds. Let a powder be made, of which he administers half a dram morning and evening. Meanwhile, he prescribes a daily drink made from a decoction of Quince flowers and Sloe <note>wild plums</note>, unless a weakness of the stomach is also present, in which case prepared Coriander and a little Galangal are added in place of the Sloe.

Once these and similar remedies for the preparation and evacuation of the humors have been completed, one must proceed further to correct the <term>contamination</term> <note>original Greek: μόλυνσιν (molunsin); referring to the fouling or corruption of the organ</note> of the spleen and to purify the blood.

### APPENDIX TO BOOK II, PART II

The scorbutic <term>tartar</term> <note>In early modern medicine, "tartar" referred to stony or gritty metabolic waste that precipitated inside the body, similar to the dregs in a wine barrel, causing blockages and pain.</note> must be purified by specific, suitable, and appropriate remedies.

Here, therefore, <term>deobstruent</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐνφρακτικὰ" (enphraktika). While the Greek root literally refers to "obstructing," in this medical context it refers to medicines used to treat "infarctions" or blockages.</note> medicines, which possess the power of clearing out blocked passages and dissolving the obstructing matter itself, are rightly considered. In choosing these, one must look primarily to ensure they are suited both to the organs being affected and to the offending humors. For since an obstructed spleen—infected with corrupt, obstructing matter—leads to a collection of raw blood, we must labor to use medicines that are "cutting," penetrating, and possess a unique property for resisting corrupt scorbutic humors. With these, we may not only open the obstructions but also correct and purify the <term>ichorous</term> <note>thin, watery, or blood-stained discharge</note> scorbutic blood, adding appropriate medicines that evacuate through either the urine or sweat.

This can also be elegantly deduced from the School of the **Hermeticists** <note>Followers of Hermes Trismegistus and Paracelsus who used alchemical processes to create medicine.</note>: for just as elsewhere a coagulation is resolved by dissolution, and a dissolution is resolved by coagulation, so in the present case it is necessary—in order to remove the immediate cause of Scurvy—that we apply those things which dissolve the "tartareous" matter mixed with watery and mucilaginous blood, both in the organs and in the veins. Once dissolved, these things are naturally suited to be driven out 

<column-break/>

partly through the urine and partly through sweat.

<margin>What deobstruent medicines ought to be.</margin> Here, therefore, among the deobstruent medicines, priority is rightly given to those which resist Scurvy by a certain unique property—or, to speak with the **Spagyrics** <note>Alchemical physicians who practiced the art of "separating and recombining" natural substances to extract their medicinal "spirit."</note>, those which possess a copious spirit of "cutting" and penetrating salt. This is apparent in those substances which present to the taste a unique sharpness mixed with bitterness. Among these, the first place is given to the herb **Scurvy-grass** (*Cochlearia*), named for its spoon-like shape (*cochlear*), which **Wierus** describes vividly in his *Observations on Scurvy*, as well as in his *Book on Unknown Diseases*. Following clinical experience with this disease, it is greatly recommended by **Dodoens** (*Medical Observations, ch. 33*), **Eugalenus** (frequently in his *Observations on Scurvy*), **Salomon Albertus** (in the book cited), **Foreest** (*Book 20, observation 11*), and others. This is followed by **Watercress**, **Brooklime** (or Water Pimpernel), **Mustard**, **Horseradish**, and other vegetables of this kind. From among the "fossils" <note>In this period, "fossils" referred to anything dug from the earth, including minerals and salts.</note>, protections are drawn in this disease from **vitriol, alum, tartar of wine**, etc. In these, there is a need for diligent preparation and the "Spagyric" separation of the harmful from the harmless. In all of these resides the quality of "cutting," penetrating, and dissolving the coagulated scorbutic tartar, both in the organs and in the blood itself. For this reason, they serve our current intention best when, after the preceding preparation, they are mixed with those things which strengthen the vigor of the organs.

<margin>To lead the matter where its nature tends.</margin>
...these evacuations should be directed toward mineral springs <note>Original Latin: "acidulos fontes," referring to naturally carbonated or mineral-rich springs believed to have medicinal properties</note>, and patients should be ordered to continue the use of these for some time according to a certain prescribed diet. We must assist nature with suitable remedies, and thus, by mixing in either diuretics or diaphoretics <note>Medicines that promote sweating</note>, we may allow nature to achieve its desired goal. If, therefore, the matter tends toward the urinary passages, those things which facilitate passage through the urinary tracts—both simple and compound—should be frequently mixed with the medicines prescribed to remove the cause of Scurvy. On the other hand, if the disease does not yield to such things and has taken deeper roots, nature must be assisted so that it may achieve the desired result through sweating <note>Original Greek: "Διαφορήσει" (diaphoresis)</note>.

To achieve the purpose of the bath more quickly, some sweat-inducing substance <note>Original Greek: "διαφορητικών" (diaphoretics)</note> should be administered before entering.
<margin>The use of chemical salts.</margin>

He says: "In former times, if any among the crowd of the sick were a bit more delicate, he buried them in an oven from which the baked bread had just been removed, so that by its gentle warmth the remains of the disease might be transferred from the inner recesses of the body to the surface and simultaneously dispersed."

### XIV.

Once these treatments have been performed and continued in the proper manner according to the curative indications <note>In early medicine, "indications" were the signs from the body that pointed toward a specific treatment, such as a fever indicating a need for cooling.</note>, the symptoms usually cease of their own accord when the disease is in its beginning stages. However, when the condition is becoming more severe, the **oral symptoms** <note>Original Greek: *σωματικῇ* (somatikē). In the context of scurvy, this specifically referred to the bodily manifestations in the mouth and gums.</note> and the **leg-trouble** <note>Original Greek: *σκελοτύρβῃ* (skelotyrbē). A classical term used by Pliny and others to describe the "leg-paralysis" or swelling characteristic of scurvy.</note> must be weighed more carefully by the Physician than any other symptoms.

As for the spontaneous fatigue, the feeling of heaviness, the tightness in the chest, difficulty breathing, and similar issues—the explanation of which we proposed in Exercise 1, Thesis 12—the Physician is not overly concerned about these, provided he has vigorously maintained the preceding treatment for the disease. This is because such symptoms cease on their own once the disease is cured, making that philosophical maxim true: *when the cause is removed, the effect is also removed* <note>Original Latin: "causâ sublatâ tolli quoque effectum."</note>. This is also required by the skillful method of healing, in which indications are drawn only from the disease itself, the cause of the illness, and the faculties or strengths of the body, as we have demonstrated from Galen in *Medical Disputations 17, Thesis 9*.
<margin>Should an indication be taken from the symptoms?</margin>
However, when the disease is growing more severe, the symptoms themselves must be carefully observed, as they increase at that time. Sometimes, by their harshness, they so tear apart and consume the patient's strength that there is a fear the strength will fail long before the disease is cured (as Salomon Albertus <note>A 16th-century German physician known for his work on anatomy and scurvy.</note> holds). Sometimes they even degenerate into other diseases, by which means the symptoms often become worse even as the primary disease softens. Regarding <margin>Which symptoms in Scurvy require special care?</margin> this controversy, see Matteo Selvatico <note>Original: "Sylvaticum," a reference to the medieval/Renaissance physician and botanist known for his "Pandects."</note>, *Controversy 17*. For this reason, we rightly address the symptoms of Scurvy during its treatment—namely those by which the strength is significantly weakened, or which provide a cause for the generation of new conditions. Since a Physician never accomplishes anything worthy of praise without the help of nature, the power of the bodily faculties must be carefully considered in every disease, but especially in Scurvy, a disease that truly produces more diverse types of symptoms than others. Therefore, when the disease is worsening, the defects of the mouth and the legs—which appear symptomatically in this condition—must not be neglected; the following rules for correcting them should be noted.

scorbutic blood flowing there, due to the corrupted "spirit of salt" <note>An early term often associated with the balance of minerals in the body; here it implies the blood lacks the necessary "fixing" quality to keep the flesh firm.</note>, is not sufficient to maintain the firm substance of the gums. Therefore, it is right to treat their restoration here, where those remedies are conveniently recommended that possess a contracting and consolidating salt. Among the simple ingredients that offer themselves are Bay leaves, Oak, the bark of the wild plum (Sloe), Plantain, dried unripe Roses, Sage, Bistort root, Alum, Vitriol, Coral, syrup of mulberries, honey of roses, etc. From these and similar items, various medications are composed, the use of which is prescribed in different ways for **softness of the gums** <note>Original Greek: <term>μαλάχη</term> (malachē). This refers to the pathological softening or laxity of the gum tissue.</note>.

<margin>
Against bleeding and flabbiness of the gums in the early stages.
</margin>

Thus, against bleeding and flabbiness in the beginning, a powder such as this is prepared by Albertus: *Take: Flour of Cyperus <note>Galingale</note> and Pennyroyal burnt to ashes, one and a half drachms of each; burnt snail shells, two scruples.*

<column-break/>

*Mix to make a powder, which is to be sprinkled on the gums.* Or, in place of this, let this liniment be prepared: *Take: Juice of Bistort, 2 ounces; juice of unripe Roses, 1 ounce; let them boil in 3 ounces of raw honey until the juices are consumed.* Afterward add two scruples of Alum (split, wrapped in paper, and burnt to ash), one scruple of salt, and one ounce of mulberry syrup. Let a liniment be made, with which the gums are to be anointed. Forestus <note>Pieter van Foreest (1521–1597), a prominent Dutch physician.</note> recommends the juice of Scurvy-grass, as well as its distilled water, with which the mouth is conveniently rinsed after using the previous treatments. For those who dislike ointments, let them use mouthwashes, such as the one recommended by Ronseus <note>Boudewijn Ronsse, author of an early work on scurvy and diseases of the spleen.</note> in *On the Great Spleen*, page 53: *Take: Bistort with Tormentil root, two handfuls of each; Pomegranate rind, 2 ounces; Sumac, 1 ounce; boil in 2 pounds of rainwater down to 1 pound. Strain the liquid, and to the strained portion add 2 drachms of split Alum and 2 ounces of the best honey. Let it be used as a frequent mouthwash.* Wierus <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a Dutch physician.</note>, in his observations on scurvy, proposes in place of this a decoction made from the bark and leaves of Hawthorn and unripe Roses, with Scurvy-grass, watercress, bittercress, and winter cress added, all boiled in chalybeate <note>Iron-fortified</note> water. Dodonaeus <note>Rembert Dodoens (1517–1585), a famous Flemish physician and botanist.</note> in chapter 33 of his *Medical Observations* prescribes a decoction of Hyssop, Rosemary, and Cypress nut, with a few grains of cubebs and nutmeg added, along with rose-honey. Add to these the advice of Crato, number 72, in the *Medical Counsels* published by Scholz.

...not only bleeding and flabbiness, but even the onset of putrefaction <note>The breakdown of tissue, often accompanied by a foul smell; a major symptom of advanced scurvy.</note> shows itself, one must proceed to stronger measures. In such cases, **rectified oil of vitriol** <note>original: "oleum vitrioli correctum"; a highly concentrated form of sulfuric acid, which early modern doctors used in very diluted amounts as an antiseptic and astringent.</note>, or **spirit of Calchans**, is most effective. This is nothing other than the purest dissolved salt, endowed with the greatest power for healing and purifying. By its use, the gums are renewed and the teeth are in turn made firm again. As **Ronsens** writes in *On the Disease of the Spleen, chapter 10*: "For loose teeth, the best remedy is the oil of Calchans <note>Calchans is an old name for vitriol or copperas (metal sulfates).</note>, which is bittersweet and drawn out by the chemical art." You should therefore choose the rectified spirit of vitriol and mix it with strained Honey of Roses, using enough to create a strong acidity. With this liniment, you should rub the gums and other affected parts of the mouth three times every day. If you desire a gargle, take: Water of Plantain and Self-heal, 5 ounces each; Spirit of Calchans, 1 scruple; Honey of Roses, 1 ounce; and Burnt Alum, half a scruple. *Mix and let a gargle be made.* To this also belongs that recipe of **Reusner**: Take selected Guaiac wood <note>A tropical wood from the Americas, often called "Holy Wood," believed to have powerful curative properties.</note>, 1 ounce; make a decoction with Sage, Mouse-ear Hawkweed, and Stonecrop <note>original: "Vermicularis"; often used for its cooling and astringent properties.</note>, 1 handful each; Plantain, Watercress, and Myrtle, 5 handfuls each; and red Rose flowers, 4 portions. Let a decoction be made in 1 pound each of red wine and spring water (or chalybeate water <note>Water infused with iron salts.</note>), boiled down to half the volume. To the strained liquid, add Honey of Roses and rob of walnuts <note>A "rob" is a thick, syrupy concentrate made from fruit juice.</note>, 1 ounce each; and Oil or Spirit of Vitriol, 5 scruples. Let a gargle be made. We use these and similar mouthwashes, which can sometimes be replaced by

<column-break/>

acidic vitriolated springs, where a supply of them can be given to the patients. 

But if certain parts of the mouth become even more foul-smelling and putrid, **Albertus** <note>Salomon Albert (1540–1600), a German physician known for his work on scurvy.</note> advises that they should be rubbed with a new sponge soaked in oil of vitriol (prepared according to the advice of **Matthiolus** <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century herbalist and physician.</note>). In the meantime, the mouth should be washed out frequently with a special distilled liquor, prepared as follows: Take Musk Roses, green Olive leaves (or Privet), 4 handfuls each; Bramble tops, 1 handful; Scurvy-grass or Stonecrop, Watercress, and Rue, half a handful each; Sage, 1 handful; and powdered Myrrh, 2 drachms. If fresh herbs are available, they should be pounded until they release their juice; if dry, let them be macerated together in very fragrant rose water, enough to cover each and every ingredient. Sprinkle with a sufficient amount of sugar and let a distillation of the liquid be made in a *Balneum* <note>A "Balneum Mariae" or water bath, used for gentle, indirect heating in distillation.</note> using glass vessels. 

However, when the disease worsens and the filthy putrefaction of the gums intensifies, **Albertus** says (in section 327) that there is often a need for the work of the hands and for small scissors to cut away the corruption. This must be done with careful judgment, lest we mistake flesh that is only superficially diseased for that which is truly gangrenous <note>original: "syderata"; referring to "sideration," a term for sudden tissue death or gangrene.</note>. For those who shrink from the surgical knife, the useless tissue may be consumed by corrosive and "eating" medicines. Here, Egyptian Ointment <note>A green, corrosive ointment made of verdigris (copper acetate), honey, and vinegar, used to clean wounds.</note> mixed with burnt alum and honey of roses has its place, especially the one described by our friend **Wilhelm Fabricius** in his *Book on Gangrene, chapter 10* <note>Fabricius Hildanus, often called the "Father of German Surgery."</note>.

...astringent and consolidating remedies, which inhibit rot and foul breath, and by their singular properties resist the symptoms of Scurvy, let us correct the condition.

<margin>Which remedies are suitable for the gums.</margin>
Since in many cases Scurvy is deeply rooted in the gums and expresses its ferocity there—insofar as the gums are softened by putrefying "tartaric" blood (according to the **Spagyrics** <note>Followers of Paracelsus who used alchemical processes to prepare medicines; they believed diseases were caused by mineral imbalances like "tartar" or salts.</note>), due to the corruption of their own internal salt—they consequently contract a livid color and decay. This results in a foul odor accompanied by bleeding, because the Scorbutic blood flowing there, due to a corrupted "spirit of salt," is not sufficient to fix and firm the fleshy substance of the gums. Therefore, it is right to treat their correction here. In this regard, those remedies which possess a contracting and consolidating salt are appropriately recommended. Among the **simples** <note>Medicines made from a single herb or ingredient.</note> that present themselves are: leaves of **Laurel** and **Oak**, bark of the **Sloe** (wild plum), **Plantain**, dried immature **Roses**, **Sage**, **Bistort** root, **Alum**, **Vitriol**, **Coral**, **Diamoron** <note>A syrup made from mulberries, often used for throat and mouth ailments.</note>, **Honey of Roses**, etc. From these and similar items, various medications are composed, the use of which is prescribed in different ways for <term>gomalaki</term> <note>original: "γομαλακη"; a Greek term for the softening or loosening of the gums.</note>.

<margin>Against bleeding and flabbiness of the gums in the beginning.</margin>
Thus, against bleeding and flabbiness in the early stages, the following powder is prepared by **Albertus**. <term>Take:</term> <note>original: "R." for "Recipe"</note> Flour of **Cyperus** and **Pennyroyal** burned into ashes, 1.5 drachms of each; pure, burnt **cockle shells**, 2 scruples.

<column-break/>

Mix and let a powder be made, with which the gums of the teeth should be sprinkled. Or, in place of this, let this liniment be prepared. <term>Take:</term> Juice of **Bistort**, 2 ounces; juice of immature **Roses**, 1 ounce; let them boil in 3 ounces of raw **honey** until the juices are consumed. Afterward, add 2 scruples of **feathered alum** (wrapped in paper and burned to ash), 1 scruple of **salt**, and 1 ounce of **Diamoron**. Strain the liquid, and to the strained portion add 2 drachms of **feathered alum** and 2 ounces of the best **honey**. Add to this the advice of **Crato**, number 72, in the *Medical Counsels* published by **Scolzius**.

This is so that the foul breath of the mouth does not occasionally create an intolerable nuisance for both the patients and those standing by while we labor to correct the other defects.

### XVI.

*In **skeletyrbe**, or conditions of the legs and shins, one must look especially to **false paralysis**, loose swellings, variegated spots, and scorbutic ulcers, all of which must be aided by their appropriate remedies.*

<column-break/>

<margin>How false paralysis of the legs is corrected.</margin>
Regarding the first point, which concerns weakness in walking and **false paralysis** <note>Original: *notam paralysin*. A loss of function or "resolution" of the limbs caused by scorbutic buildup rather than a stroke.</note>, the cause of it is known from the previous exercise. Therefore, it is very easily concluded at present that those means should be applied here which resolve and disperse the cause and origin of this evil—namely, the **scorbutic matter** <note>The waste products or "humors" believed to be the source of the disease.</note> clinging abundantly to the tendons and muscles. For this reason, after the general treatment of this condition, we do not advise against frequent fomentations <note>Warm, medicinal compresses or herbal soaks.</note> of the legs and shins. These are made with decoctions of 1 handful each of Melilot, Mallow, and Chamomile; 1 handful each of Mugwort, Motherwort, and Lavender; with the addition of 2 handfuls of juniper berries and 1 handful each of Watercress and **Brooklime** <note>Original: *Becabungæ*. A plant in the speedwell family traditionally used to treat scurvy.</note>. Mix and chop these, and boil them in a sufficient quantity of water for a bath. After the fomentations, an anointing will not be unsuitable; this can be done with oils of Chamomile or Castoreum, marrow from the leg of an ox, or the juices of Radish, Scurvy-grass, and Watercress cooked with common oil to the consistency of a liniment, and other such things. Where loose swellings occupy the legs, **Albertus** <note>Michael Alberti (1682–1757), a prominent German physician and author on scurvy.</note> in his book *On Scurvy*, section 340, prescribes a wash made from things that dry out, consume, and disperse flatulent and **edematous** <note>Swollen with fluid.</note> tumors. Specifically, these are made from lye, brine, sea water or salt water, in which have been boiled juniper berries, Rosemary, Elderflowers, Sage, Chamomile, Wild Radish, **Water-mint** <note>Original: *Sisymbrium*.</note>, a little alum, etc. Furthermore, it is common that applications...

### ON SCURVY, SECTION II.

<margin>
Against spots on the legs.
</margin>
Various colored spots frequently break out in Scurvy, especially around the legs and shins. We correct these using substances that resolve and dissipate blood that has become watery <note>Original: *ichorosum*. Referring to "ichor," a thin, watery discharge from a wound or a morbid thinness of the blood.</note> or infected with "scorbutic tartar," and which has collected under the skin through bruising <note>Original: *ἐκχύμωσιν* (ecchymosis). This refers to the purple or black spots caused by internal bleeding, a classic sign of scurvy.</note>. For this reason, *Wierus* (in his *Observations on Scurvy*) advises that the marks on the legs should be bathed with a decoction of **Juniper berries, Watercress, Lady’s Smock, Winter Cress, Scurvy-grass, Chamomile flowers, Mugwort, Lemon Balm, Marjoram, Thyme**, and similar herbs. From these ingredients, *Salmuth Albertus* describes a specific formula for a fomentation in Section 347, which serves both to draw out hidden marks and to dissipate those that have already appeared. To these are added ointments, where the ingredients of the aforementioned qualities are reduced into the form of a liniment using May butter; or poultices <note>Original: *cataplasmata*.</note>, when these same ingredients are reduced to powders and applied to the marked areas in the form of a poultice with distilled waters of **Scurvy-grass, Winter Cress**, and the like.

<margin>
Against scorbutic ulcers.
</margin>
Finally, although it happens rarely that scorbutic ulcers <note>Original: *ulcera sceletyrbica*. Ulcers specifically associated with the leg-wasting and spotting of scurvy.</note> follow, we subjoin a treatment for them so that nothing is lacking. Nevertheless, we must repeat what we said above: that scorbutic ulcers are difficult to heal <note>Original Greek: *δυσεπούλωτα* (dysepulota).</note>, so much so that they may not improperly be called malignant or "Telephian" <note>A "Telephian" ulcer refers to the legendary wound of Telephus, which could only be cured by the spear that inflicted it; in medicine, it signifies an extremely stubborn or incurable sore.</note>. Furthermore, since an ulcer of this kind—owing to the influx of faulty humors—remains long-lasting even if all treatments are performed correctly,

<column-break/>

according to Galen (Book 4 of *The Method of Medicine*, Chapter 5), the treatment of a scorbutic ulcer is undertaken in vain unless a diligent treatment of the Scurvy as a whole is performed first. Therefore, once the primary requirements are met, we must labor to assist the ulcerated parts as quickly as possible through cleansing and the purging of filth <note>Original: *sordiumque expurgatione*.</note>. For this, a syrup made from dried roses applied over a plantain leaf is first proposed by *Albertus*. To this is added honey of roses and "Thomas" sugar <note>Original: *Saccharumque Thomæum*. A high-quality refined sugar, likely named after the island of São Tomé, a major sugar producer in the early modern period.</note>, which cleanse with a mild astringency and correct the malignancy arising from the influx of humors. Indeed, *Ronsseus* (in *On Great Diseases of the Spleen*, Chapter 9) requires that medicines suited for ulcers of this kind possess both a "digesting" <note>In early medicine, "digesting" meant to promote the maturation and discharge of pus to allow healing.</note> and an astringent faculty, so that they may simultaneously repel what flows in and dissipate what clings to the affected part. Rightly, therefore, they include here the "Cleansing Ointment of Celery," for which the recipe is: **Take half an ounce each of the juices of Celery, Lemon Balm, and Scurvy-grass; 5 drachms of Celandine; and a sufficient quantity of raw honey. Boil to the proper consistency, adding Frankincense, Aloe, and Myrrh, if it seems fit.** When, however, the filth and watery discharges increase further, the ulcerated parts should be purified daily with a decoction of stonecrop <note>Original: *vermicularis herbæ*.</note> or Saracen’s Consound water <note>A plant used for wound healing, often identified as a type of ragwort or goldenrod.</note>, mixed with a few drops of oil of vitriol <note>Original: *ol. vitrioli*. Concentrated sulfuric acid, used in very small, diluted amounts as a caustic or cleansing agent.</note>. Afterward, drying agents ground into a fine powder should be sprinkled on, moving from milder ones to the **Seal of Saturn** <note>Original: *Sigillum Saturni*. An alchemical term for a lead-based preparation. Saturn was the symbol for lead. While toxic by modern standards, lead was used topically for its cooling and drying properties.</note>.

### ADDITION TO BOOK II, PART II, APPENDIX ON SCURVY, SECTION II.

<columns>

...of Saturn, that is, we must proceed to the powder of lead <note>Original: *Saturni*. In the chemical and medical language of the time, Saturn was the name given to lead.</note>, which is made by means of "potential calcination" <note>A process of breaking down a substance using a reactive solvent (a menstruum) rather than direct fire.</note>. In this process, the lead filings are dissolved by pouring an appropriate solvent over them; once the solvent is removed without the use of heat, the lead is crushed into tiny particles <note>Original: *atomos*.</note> in a stone mortar using a lead pestle. 

For those who find powders unpleasant, they should follow the aforementioned washings with the "Lead Liniment of Montagnana" <note>Referring to Bartolomeo Montagnana, a famous 15th-century Italian physician.</note>:

| Recipe: | Amount |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Burnt lead** | 1 ounce |
| **Litharge** <note>Lead oxide.</note> (well-skimmed) | 1/2 ounce |
| **White lead** <note>Original: *Cerussæ*.</note> (washed) and **vinegar** | 2 drams each |
| **Rose oil** | 1 1/2 ounces |
| **Rose honey** | 1/2 ounce |
| **Egg yolks** | 2 |
| **Myrrh** | 2 drams |
| **Wax** | As much as needed |

This makes a liniment with which the cleaned ulcers of the shins are to be anointed while warm. He who desires more information concerning the cure of such ulcers should refer to the works of **Galen**, specifically Book 4 of *The Method of Medicine* and Book 2 of *The Art of Healing, to Glaucon*.

<column-break/>

He should also consult the writings of **Tagault** in Book 3 of the *Institutes of Surgery*; **Fabricius ab Aquapendente** in Book 3 *On Ulcers*, chapter 4; **Ronseus** in the place cited previously; **Ambroise Paré** in Book 12 of his *Surgery*; and others. 

Now, it would remain for us to add the treatment and correction of the other symptoms and subsequent conditions mentioned above. However, since the learned physician will very easily understand through skillful deduction from what has been said—considering how to proceed with appropriate remedies alongside other common treatments according to the diversity of the diseases—we shall therefore bring this to an end here. 

We give immortal thanks to the true <term>Chief Physician</term> <note>Original: *Archiatro*. From the Greek for 'ruling physician' or 'doctor to the king'.</note>, <term>GOD, Thrice Best and Greatest</term> <note>Original: *DEO Ter Opt. Max.* A common scholarly dedication to the Christian God, adapting the Roman title for Jupiter (Optimus Maximus).</note>.

Refers to wines from the Neckar river region in Germany.</note> and similar types, to which sometimes a decoction of **Licorice root**, or an infusion of **Sassafras wood** with smaller raisins, etc., may be added. To this end, then, belongs the seasoning and preparation of food, which is necessary due to a weaker natural heat. CONCERNING THE PAINS OF THE EXTERNAL PARTS.

## OBSERVATION II.

### Regarding chronic gouty
### flows

->To the<-

->Reverend & Most Renowned Man<-

->Lord Balthasar Ment-<-
->zer, Doctor of Holy Theology, Pro-<-
->fessor in the Academy of<-
->Giessen,<-

->PETRUS FUHRMANN<-
->Doctor of Medicine.<-

Greetings. To the most Reverend and Renowned Man, my highly esteemed patron: in order to briefly satisfy your expectation and request, Reverend Dignity, I shall briefly open my judgment—whatever it may be—concerning the diseased disposition by which you have been afflicted for so many years. This judgment is essentially completed in these two points: namely, that I first derive the cause of the disease, the affected location, and the symptoms from their own origins; and in the second place, I shall then demonstrate what ought to be attempted in the cure. As far as the cause of the disease is concerned, it is divided into the remote and the proximate. The remote cause is the "crudity" <note>In 17th-century medicine, "crudity" refers to undigested or poorly processed food and humors that the body failed to transform into healthy tissue.</note> of foods and other things of this kind,

<column-break/>

<margin>Remote causes.</margin>
about which we are not particularly concerned here, since they provide an indication for prevention rather than for the immediate cure of the gout. <margin>Gout.</margin> The proximate cause of the disease is partly material and partly efficient: <margin>Proximate cause.</margin> *that material cause*, according to the dogma of Paracelsus <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), known as Paracelsus; a Swiss physician who revolutionized medicine by using chemicals and minerals rather than just herbs.</note>, *is a volatile and subtle salt* <note>original: "sal est volatilis & subtilis"</note>, which, along with the "fluxions" <note>Flows of harmful bodily fluids or humors.</note> and "Catarrhs" of the Head, insinuates itself into the ligaments and tendons of the joints, and by its vehement sharpness excites intolerable pains. The *Efficient* cause is partly *principal* and partly *assisting*. The *Principal* cause consists primarily in the weakness of the Brain and the Joints, insofar as the moist and cold Brain serves the resolution of vapors and exhalations, by which means the "defluxions" <note>The downward flow of humors from the head to the extremities.</note> are afterwards diverted to the joints, especially when those joints have been greatly weakened either by an innate frailty or from preceding gouty attacks. All these things are promoted by *assisting causes*, which partly foster the imbalance of temperament and partly accumulate the "sinning matter" <note>The "materia peccans" or the specific substance in the body thought to be causing the illness.</note>; such causes include the changing of the seasons, old age, a phlegmatic temperament <note>One of the four classical temperaments, associated with being cold and moist, making one prone to respiratory and joint issues.</note>, a sedentary life, and so forth. From this, therefore, it is manifest which part is the *affected location in this disease*: namely, the *joints along with the ligaments, tendons, and surrounding membranes*. <margin>The location affected in [gout].</margin> Since these parts are endowed with exquisite sensitivity and lack the obvious pathways for the excretion of gouty matter, the "sinning matter" is therefore retained here for a longer time, from which an immense pain...

<sig>Ii 3</sig>
<meta>The catchword "ingens" (immense/great) indicates the sentence continues on the next page: "immense pain is born."</meta>

### BOOK III. OF PART II.

<margin>Derivation of symptoms.</margin>
...is greatly excited, when the subtler parts have been dissipated and the thicker substance gains deep and lasting roots. *The most severe symptoms of the present disease follow, such as heaviness of the head, pains in the joints, swellings, redness, inflammations, injuries, and the hardening and contraction of the limbs,* when the harmful flows <note>In this period, gout was viewed as a "catarrh" or flow of waste fluids from the brain or stomach down into the joints.</note> are communicated to the joints. These unite with the natural "glue" of the joints, gradually drying out the tendons and ligaments, and finally, by separating them from one another, they produce irreparable contortions and dislocations. For as much as nature separates the flowing and moist matter through sweat and hidden transpiration <note>The early modern concept of "insensible perspiration" through the skin.</note>, to that extent the fixed substance remains behind, which frequently generates nodes and tophi <note>original: "tophos" — hard, chalky deposits of uric acid crystals common in chronic gout.</note>. Because of the obstruction and clogging of the nerves, tendons, ligaments, and other vessels, it hinders proper nutrition; thus the weakness of the limbs increases, the organs of motion are weakened, and whatever serous <note>Watery or thin humors.</note> superfluities abound in the rest of the body flow here in crowds, as if to the weaker part. In this way, swelling of the parts usually follows, which, according to its nature, is dissipated now faster, now slower—all of which have frequently attacked your Reverend Dignity for many years.

However, since the aforementioned affliction has not only taken firm roots, but the internal organs have been weakened by the very long duration of the

<column-break/>

disease and the strength of the body has been not a little dissolved, it would be advisable—as is customary in all chronic cases where the corrupt material of the disease cannot be purged all at once, both because of the weaker nature of the body and the unsuitability of the location, which makes it difficult to move the material—that the offending matter be drawn away little by little, the strength of the whole be bolstered, and the weaker external limbs be assisted as much as possible.

<margin>Special indication.</margin>
We shall fulfill these indications through diet, pharmacy, and surgery. First, regarding diet, there is no need for further admonition, since your Reverend Dignity otherwise lives most temperately and even frequently attempts to prevent the generation of crudities <note>Undigested food matter believed to be the source of disease-causing humors.</note> through fasting. Furthermore, your Reverend Dignity knows that all foods of more difficult digestion must be avoided, especially those providing much occasion for dissolution and rot, along with wines that are too potent, affecting the nervous system, and young, thick wines from which the tartar <note>The sediment or crust that forms in wine casks.</note> has not yet been separated. Instead, thin wines, light and weak <note>original Greek: "ὀλιγόφερα" (olygophera) — wines that do not easily cause intoxication or "heaviness" in the head.</note>, are chosen, such as well-purified Neckar wines <note>Wines from the Neckar region of Germany.</note>. From these, a medicated wine should be made in the autumn season according to the following description, the use of which consumes the catarrhs of the brain, strengthens the digestion of the stomach, corrects crudities, and absorbs superfluous moisture in the habit of the body.

<margin>Medicated wine for gouty patients.</margin>
Take: 1 pound of Avens Root <note>original: "Rad. Caryophyllatæ" — Geum urbanum, a root with a clove-like scent used to treat digestive and inflammatory issues.</note>.

Much is attributed to the medicinal waters in the Imperial town of Weissenburg, near Nuremberg, in such cases, as can be seen in the German book which Master Joachim Camerarius, Master Mentzelius, and Master Rosa published on the same, printed at Amberg. I also remember a foot bath made from the more liquid dregs of wine (from which they otherwise extract spirits) being used not without success. But just as this [disease] is truly a Proteus <note>A reference to the Greek sea god who could change his shape; used here to describe the shifting and unpredictable nature of gout.</note>...

### Regarding Gouty patients who are unfit for walking even when the flare-up is absent.

### FROM GREGORIUS HORSTIUS, DOCTOR.

Regarding what you write, Magnificent and Distinguished 

<column-break/>

man, patron, and most esteemed friend, concerning those two gouty patients <note>original: "Podagricis"; Podagra is specifically gout of the foot.</note> who, even when their pains are absent, are unable to walk forward due to excessive weakness of the limbs—even though gouty deposits <note>original: "tophi"; chalky lumps of uric acid common in chronic gout.</note> do not yet appear—I myself have observed this in many cases. I see nothing helps such arthritic sufferers more than the surgical remedy of "little fountains" <note>original: "fonticulos"; also known as "issues," these were small, surgically created wounds kept open to drain "bad humors" from the body.</note> raised in various parts of the body. 

I remember that for many years my colleague, the Professor of Theology, Dr. Balthasar Mentzer <note>A prominent Lutheran theologian (1565–1627) at the University of Marburg and Gießen.</note>, was once so affected. He was helped by the convenient acidic baths of Schwalbach <note>original: "Balneum Acidularum Swabacensium"; Langenschwalbach was a famous spa town.</note> from a particular spring which Tabernaemontanus <note>Jacobus Theodorus Tabernaemontanus (1525–1590), a famous herbalist and physician.</note> calls the "Bubbling Spring" <note>original: "Brodelbrunnen"</note> in his German book *The Water Treasure* <note>original: "Wasserschatz"</note>—and which the locals also call by that name, perhaps because of its more violent boiling. By the benefit of this same spring, I remember the Elder Lord Wolfgang Ernst, Count of Isenburg <note>Wolfgang Ernst I (1560–1633), a high-ranking German nobleman.</note>, was not only freed from the weakness of his joints in his extreme old age but was also preserved from more serious attacks. 

Much is also attributed in such cases to the medicinal waters in the Imperial town of Weißenburg near Nuremberg, as can be seen in the German book which Dr. Joachim Camerarius, Dr. Mentzelius, and Dr. Rosa published from the same public press, printed at Amberg. I also remember a footbath being used with success, made from the more liquid dregs of wine (from which they otherwise draw out spirits). But just as this disease is truly a Proteus <note>A figure from Greek mythology who could change his shape; used here to describe the ever-changing nature of gout symptoms.</note>...

...kept me when I was living outside of Germany, so now a passion seizes me to address you: for I will gladly enjoy the fruit of your sweetest friendship. For that conversation we had here in Frankfurt for several hours a few days ago has not only increased, but increases day by day the fire of love that was lit long ago. Indeed, I intended to discuss many things, but the inconvenience of time prevented my desire from being fulfilled. But does everything come with time? Does the time bring roses? Reason seems to suggest not so much a diversion <note>moving the humors away from the site; original: "aversionem"</note> of the matter, as an evacuation, so that it does not flow to the affected place, etc. Farewell, and be mindful of your Walther, who looks up to you and loves you like a father. Written in haste amid the turmoil of the Frankfurt Fairs, September 17, 1611.

<margin>
Whether sweat-inducing remedies are suitable in Gout
</margin>

And for me, nothing would have been more desirable, Most Illustrious Man and Intimate Friend, than to enjoy further conversation with you, especially regarding certain unique methods used by some French physicians in the treatment of the **Venereal Pox** <note>Syphilis; original: "Luis Venereæ"</note> and other common diseases. Concerning your question about **sweat-inducing remedies in Gout** <note>original: "Sudoriferis in Arthritide"</note>, you judge correctly that the affirmative side can be defended for the sake of both diversion and evacuation. You know that our **Crato** <note>Johann Crato von Krafftheim (1519–1585), an influential imperial physician whose "Consilia" or medical advice were widely studied.</note> in his *Counsels, no. 240*, strongly commends sweats, where he says: *“Guided by both manifold experience and reason, I am certain that the shavings of the best **Stag’s Horn** <note>original: "Cornu Cervi"; a common source of ammonia and a known sudorific in early modern medicine.</note>, tied in a cloth and placed in a drink, both provoke urine and—provided the body is inclined to it—easily dispose the body to sweat, especially if the patients keep themselves in bed in the morning and keep their limbs warm. Those who do this are almost free from gout. For since thick humors cannot flow without watery ones, the best method of preservation is...”*

# ON PAINS OF THE EXTERNAL PARTS #

## BOOK III. OF PART II. ##

The principle is to avoid an abundance of **watery humors** <note>original: "serosorum"; referring to the thin, clear part of the blood then thought to cause swelling and pain in the joints</note> in the diet, and if they accumulate in the body, to expel them in a timely manner through sweats and urines. He [an earlier cited author] repeats the same in Epistle 150, where he says: "certainly, as much as I have learned from long observation and experience, nothing is more suitable than **sweat-inducing medicines** <note>original: "sudoriferis medicamentis"</note> and the continuous use of **Hartshorn filings** <note>original: "limatura Cornu Cervini"; deer horn was often rasped into drinks for its supposed cooling and purifying properties</note> infused in a drink." Solenander also agrees in Section 4, Counsel 24, where he establishes sweating as a useful form of evacuation, and consents to the continued use of a decoction of **sarsaparilla** and **holy wood** <note>original: "ligni sancti"; also known as Guaiacum, a resinous wood from the Americas believed to be a powerful cure for joint pain and syphilis</note>, insofar as in this way the offending humor is evacuated and turned away from the joints, the fleshy parts are strengthened, and the nervous system is moderately dried. However, the specific limitation on how such sweat-inducers are to be used is known from the *Method of Healing*—namely, that after the appropriate general remedies have been administered, one must finally reach that point.

<margin>
Whether mineral sweat-inducing remedies are suitable?
</margin>

But you ask about **Antimonial** <note>remedies derived from the metal antimony, a hallmark of "chemical" or Paracelsian medicine</note> sweat-inducers? I do not deny that they may be conveniently added to the aforementioned, just as we observe in other diseases as well, where **Diaphoretic Antimony**, **Mineral Bezoar** <note>a chemical compound, likely antimony oxide, named after the "bezoar stone" for its supposed ability to drive out toxins</note>, **Diaphoretic Golden Sulphur**, and similar remedies are often used with great benefit. I know a most skilled chemical physician who, according to the nature of the individuals and after the necessary preparations, first established an appropriate purging with the following **Electuary** <note>a medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</note>, which:

<column-break/>

<margin>
Purging Electuary for Arthritis.
</margin>

| Ingredient | Amount |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Hermodactyl** <note>Meadow Saffron, a plant traditionally used (and still used today) to treat gout</note> | 1/2 dram |
| **Corrected Diagrydium** <note>Purified Scammony resin, a powerful and harsh purgative</note> | 1/2 dram |
| **Calcined human bones** <note>Bones burned to a white ash; used in early modern medicine for various ailments, often specifically for bone or joint issues</note> | 1/2 dram each |

Make a very fine powder; add 2 drams of sugar. Dissolve the sugar in **fennel water**. Place over hot coals and when it bubbles, gradually mix in the powder to form an Electuary.

Afterward, he provides pills made from various minerals through a laborious preparation, with an extract of **Theriac** <note>a famous ancient polypharmaceutical "cure-all" containing dozens of ingredients</note> added, by which he provokes sweat for several days, even while the **gouty attack** <note>original: "paroxysmo Podagricorum"</note> itself is distressing the patient, which is successfully dispersed in this way. I add no more, but commend you to the Greatest and Best God, and I heartily pray for your happy return to your ancestral home. Written quickly at **Giessen of the Hessians** <note>original: "Giessæ Chattorum"; the university town of Giessen, Germany</note>, September 25, 1611.

Greetings. I grieve, Most Distinguished and Excellent Man, patron and much-honored friend, that at this age, having scarcely reached your **prime** <note>original: "ακμὴν" (akmēn); the peak or highest point of one's physical health or life</note>, you are so often afflicted by arthritic pains. I read your advice on prevention with pleasure; it is truly worthy of being made public, since with singular diligence you have concisely gathered here, not without good judgment and appropriate limitation, things that are said scattered about by everyone.

The examination of the **preventative pills** <note>original: "Pilularum præservativarum"; these were medicines intended to stop a gout attack before it started by "cleansing" the body</note>
