Antoine le Coq <note>original: "Anton. Gallus"; a 16th-century French physician</note> also holds the same intention as you, whose **Anti-Gout Antidote** is as follows:

<margin>Topical anti-gout remedies.</margin>
Regarding **topicals** <note>medicines applied directly to the surface of the body</note>, I cannot neglect to mention one or two here. The first was shared a few weeks ago by a certain merchant of Augsburg, living with me at the **Ulm mineral springs** at Überkingen. His father was Scheurlin, formerly a celebrated physician of that Republic, who for a very long time prevented gouty pains with a **lye** <note>original: "lixivio"; an alkaline solution made from ashes</note> sufficiently seasoned with salt. When an attack was just about to begin, he immediately submerged his feet into this warmed solution; he never entirely replaced it, but found that the longer it had been kept, the more useful it proved to be.

The second [remedy] is from the Most Noble Vice-Chancellor of the Empire, Lord von Ulm, Free Baron in Erbach, etc. who...

[The Frenchman] recommended, revealed to him by a certain Frenchman like a secret, namely that a powder of **Oriental Bezoar stone** <note>A "stone" found in the stomachs of certain animals, highly valued in the 17th century as a universal antidote and potent medicine</note> should be mixed with rose honey and vinegar under gentle heat and applied to the aching joints like a poultice. ### To the Most Distinguished and Excellent
### Mr. Michael Doring,
### Doctor of Medicine,
### [From] GREGORY HORST, Doctor.

I am glad, Distinguished Mr. Horst, dearest friend, that my advice concerning

<column-break/>

Gout <note>original: "Arthritide"; a general term for joint pain and inflammation, often specifically gout</note> is approved by you. I feel indeed that in the prevention of gout, all the physician's industry is required and aimed for.
<margin>Prevention is of the greatest importance in Gout.</margin>
If he reaches that point of medicine, it will not be necessary for him to be anxious about the cure of a present attack. Therefore, those remedies from whose continued use one may hope for immunity are rightly to be highly valued. Among their number are certainly those pills of mine, not only described in that advice, but also thoroughly examined by me according to all their ingredients. Indeed, I attribute it solely to the use of those pills, alongside God's blessing, that in March of this year I lay ill only lightly with Gout, and that
<margin>Commendation of the pills from the observations</margin>
during the course of September, though seized by it in both feet once or twice at intervals, I was nevertheless able to leave the house—and indeed on foot—and was not forced to hide at home for more than a single day. Namely, I observe that the **digestion** <note>original: "coctionem"; literally "cooking," the process by which the stomach was thought to process food into nutrients</note> of the stomach is aided by them, obstructions of the vessels are cleared, the body is made breathable <note>Through the opening of pores for perspiration</note>, the bowels are reminded of their duty [stimulated], etc. Ever since the month of March, I have taken no medicine besides the said pills. For nearly two months, morning sweats have occurred spontaneously and daily, just as desired. I perceive that I am greatly relieved by them, and that the matter of the **catarrhs** <note>original: "defluxionum"; the "flowing" of harmful fluids from the head down into the joints</note> is removed. Mr. Nicolaus Buschok, an innkeeper over 50 years of age, experiences a clearly similar success from their use; he has suffered from gout for some...

...someone else, likewise, for over twenty years was most severely tortured; so much so that whereas before he was forced to spend the great majority of his time confined to bed, miserably tormented by joint pains <note>original: "doloribus articularibus"</note>, and dared not even taste wine, today—after a similar interval [of using the remedy] as I—he lives free from gout <note>original: "Arthritide"</note> and sometimes invites himself to a little more wine for the sake of cheerfulness. I myself also drink wine moderately for the sake of my stomach without any harm: whether it be Hungarian, Austrian, or Rhenish. Moravian wine, however, being more full of tartar <note>original: "Tartarea"; referring to the sediment or potassium bitartrate found in wine, which early modern doctors believed caused "stone" diseases and gout</note>, I studiously avoid.

<margin>Judgment on the remedy of Antoine le Coq.</margin>
The remedy of Antoine le Coq <note>original: "Antonij Galli"; a 16th-century French physician known for his work on gout</note> contains almost the same ingredients as my pills. I do not doubt it will be profitable for those using it. He established human bones from the joints as a base, so that it might be more specific to the joints. I, however, prefer the human skull, so that the "sending" part <note>The organ from which the disease-causing fluid was thought to originate</note> might be provided for. For that serum <note>A watery bodily fluid or "humor" believed to cause inflammation</note> mostly flows down from the head into the joints was most certainly advised by Charles Le Pois <note>original: "Carolus Piso"; a famous French physician (1563–1633) who argued that many diseases were caused by fluids "flooding" from the head</note> in his most elegant work *On Diseases Arising from a Serous Deluge of Humors*. What Jean Fernel <note>original: "Fernelius"; a highly influential French physician (1497–1558)</note> thinks about the paths through which the matter is carried to the joints, you know even without my mentioning it. I marveled at the proportion of weights in Le Coq's remedy; specifically, that for every ten ingredients, he always increased the weight of each ingredient by one drachma <note>A unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</note>. It is much hotter than my pills; therefore, for bodies [that are]

<column-break/>

phlegmatic <note>original: "pituitosis"; dominated by the humor of phlegm, which was considered cold and moist</note> than for bilious ones, it is far more suitable.

<margin>Use of the said pills.</margin>
Le Coq wishes one drachma <note>The symbol ʒ represents a drachma</note> of his remedy to be taken daily for an entire year. I take half a drachma <note>original: ʒß; the 'ß' or 'ss' stands for *semis*, meaning half</note> of my pills daily in each quarter of the year for thirty days after the Solstices and Equinoxes. Indeed, what do you think of Gessner's <note>Conrad Gessner (1516–1565), a Swiss polymath and physician</note> judgment on remedies of this sort, which he has in Book 3 of his *Letters*, page 97a?
> "I believe," he says, "that medicines must be varied, both because Nature desires different things at different times, and because once accustomed to one thing, she is little moved by it further; and there seems to be a danger lest, by such long use of one so powerful a medicine, the entire habit of the body should be excessively dried out."

<margin>Topical remedies are disapproved of.</margin>
As far as topical remedies <note>Medicines applied directly to the surface of the body, like ointments or poultices</note> are concerned, I do not trouble myself with them. For I persist in that "heresy" with Le Pois (provided that opinion is worthy of the name heresy): that the joints are blamed beyond their desert in ailments born from the transmission of humors, as if they readily admit humors cast down from elsewhere because of their looseness and cavities. Therefore, care is undertaken in vain regarding the "strengthening" of the joints. Let the production of serum be hindered; let the abundance of the same be removed: Gout <note>original: "Arthritis"</note>, believe me, will either never, or most rarely, and at least most mildly, recur. Therefore, I can attribute little to the washing of the feet, by which Scheürlin <note>Likely a reference to the physician Hieronymus Scheürlin</note> is said to have preserved beginning gout-sufferers <note>original: "Podagricos"; those suffering from *podagra* or gout of the foot</note> from further invasion; unless perhaps in that gout which is generated by local congestion; which nonetheless, in my judgment, is most rare—

A <term>Cataplasm</term> <note>a medicated poultice or paste spread on a cloth</note> made from <term>Bezoar stone</term> <note>a mass found in the digestive system of animals, highly prized as a universal antidote and luxury medicine</note>, prepared with rose honey and vinegar, is far too expensive. So much, indeed, can either the confidence or the distrust of the patient do in medicine. etc.

### OBSERVATION VII.

->**False gout with a continuous fever.**<-

A man in the prime of life, Johannes Hafner, a citizen of Ulm, of a fuller body constitution and naturally disposed to an abundance of blood and serous humor <note>the "watery" part of the blood or bodily fluids</note>, fell into a febrile state in the year 1626 near the beginning of October. This was immediately followed by a most vehement pain in the joints of the feet and hands, with subsequent inflammation and swelling.

### THE RESOLUTION.

When I was called, I recognized from the urine as well as other symptoms that a <term>bilious fever</term> <note>a fever traditionally attributed to an excess of yellow bile, often characterized by heat and digestive upset</note> was present. I soon judged that attention must be paid to the following: 1. That the offending matter should be drawn out with suitable medicines; 2. That the imbalance <note>original: "intemperies"</note> of the internal organs should be corrected by alteratives <note>medicines intended to gradually restore healthy metabolic function</note>; 3. That the superfluous serum should be dispersed from the body's habit through sudorifics <note>medicines that induce sweating</note>; 4. and the pain of the external parts—

A **poultice** <note>original: *cataplasma*; a soft, moist mass of material, typically of herbal or mineral ingredients, applied to the body to relieve soreness</note> made from **Bezoar stone** <note>a "stone" found in the stomachs of goats and other ruminants, highly prized as a universal antidote and luxury medicine in the 17th century</note>, prepared with rose honey and kneaded with vinegar, is excessively expensive. Without a doubt, one could achieve the same effect at much lower cost using **prepared hartshorn** <note>original: *C. C. præpar.* (Cornu Cervi); the antlers of a stag, charred or powdered, used as an absorbent</note>, some **Sealed Earth** <note>original: *Terra sigillata*; medicinal clay stamped with a seal of authenticity</note>, or **Bole** <note>a type of medicinal clay</note> or a similar absorbent. But indeed, wealth permits folly. For me, **rye flour** <note>original: *farina siliginea*</note> is sufficient. Some of our local people recommend rye boiled until it bursts in our local **beer**, which is made of wheat (for wheat is an **anodyne** <note>a pain-killing substance</note>); others recommend wine in which common salt has been boiled. Although these two are domestic and of little price, they are hardly inferior in their powers to that most precious remedy. But it is often the case with the Great <note>the wealthy and nobility</note> that they despise cheaper things. So much, of course, in Medicine depends on the patient's confidence or distrust. etc.

## OBSERVATION VII.

### False arthritis with a
### continuous fever.

A man of stable age, **Johannes Hafner**, a citizen of Ulm, of a fuller body constitution and naturally disposed to an abundance of blood and **serous humor** <note>the "watery" part of the blood, then believed to cause swelling and inflammation when in excess</note>, fell into a febrile state at the beginning of October in the year 1626. This was immediately followed by a most vehement pain in the joints of the feet and hands, with subsequent inflammation and swelling.

## RESOLUTION.

<note>The "Resolution" or *Resolutio* is the physician's analysis and plan of treatment.</note>

When I was called and recognized from the urine and other symptoms that a **bilious fever** <note>a fever believed to be caused by an excess of yellow bile, characterized by heat and bitterness</note> was present, I soon judged that I must look to the following: 1. That the offending matter be drawn out with suitable medicines; 2. That the imbalance of the internal organs be corrected through **alteratives** <note>medicines intended to gradually restore healthy function to the body</note>; 3. That the superfluous serum be dissipated from the body's constitution through **sudorifics** <note>substances that induce sweating</note>; 4. and the pain of the external parts...

# OBSERVATION VIII.

# Long-standing pain in the right arm.

A respectable man, nearly sixty years old and of an otherwise robust constitution, but prone to **fluxions** <note>the movement of harmful bodily fluids or "humors"</note> toward his muscular parts, was seized by a pain in his right arm. Although in previous years the pain would subside after repeated evacuation and the subsequent use of the **Baths at Boll** <note>original: *Bollenfium Thermarum*; a famous mineral spa in Germany</note>, the ailment nevertheless broke out again at the start of winter. This occurred even though the patient tried to divert the flowing matter elsewhere by means of a **fontanel** <note>original: *fonticulo*; a small, intentionally created surgical wound kept open to "drain" bad humors from the body</note>. Finally, therefore, he undertook the **sweat-inducing treatment** <note>original: *sudoriferam curationem*</note> that I had long recommended. First, I ordered a **digestion** <note>a preliminary medical step to "ripen" or prepare the humors for expulsion</note> toward the end of May in the past year, 1627, with the following drink:

℞. **Avens root** <note>original: *Rad. Caryophyllatæ*</note>, **Peony root** each ½ ounce.
**Fennel, Licorice** each 6 drachms.

**Rosemary flowers** <note>original: *Fl. Anthos*</note>, **Betony flowers, Arabian Stoechas** each 2 pinches <note>original: *Pij*</note>.
**Galangal** 2 drachms. **Make a decoction in a sufficient quantity of water.**

### OBSERVATION IX.

#### Most intense pain
#### around the left shoulder
#### and shoulder blade,
#### from a boiling over
#### of bile.

A respectable woman exceeding her fortieth year of age, *in the year 1627*, toward the end of *November*, fell into a most vehement pain of the left shoulder and shoulder blade <note>original: *homoplatæ*; the scapula</note>, preceded by a shivering fit. This was followed by excessive heat, sleeplessness, loss of appetite, the secretion of bilious urine, and a dry cough that afflicted her greatly.

<column-break/>

### RESOLUTION.

Since this most vehement pain seized her suddenly, I determined that it arose from the acrimony <note>harshness or sharpness</note> of boiling bilious blood, which the preceding shivering indicated, along with the other signs of fever. For this reason, I immediately aided nature with an Enema. Afterward, I sought to soothe the most vehement pains internally by the administration of *Opiate Laudanum with Magisteries* <note>In early chemistry, "Magisteries" were refined precipitates or extracts believed to contain the full power of a substance.</note>, and externally with a Cataplasm <note>A warm, soft medicinal poultice.</note> made of barley flour, Chamomile, and Melilot <note>Sweet clover</note> with oils of dill and chamomile, egg yolks, etc. 

I did not neglect the concurrent spurious pleurisy <note>original: *pleuritide spuria*; a condition mimicking the sharp chest pain of pleurisy but often attributed to muscle pain or "vapors" rather than lung inflammation.</note> and dry cough, for which tempered pectoral syrups and an appropriate Julep <note>A sweet, liquid medicine.</note> were administered; bloodletting <note>original: *venæsectione*</note> was also performed. Once these remedies were diligently employed, the most vehement pain vanished of its own accord. To expel the remaining bilious matter, a laxative Claret <note>A medicinal spiced wine.</note> was continued with good results for several days. Once or twice, sweat was also provoked using bezoar stone <note>A mass found in the stomachs of certain animals, highly valued as a universal antidote and to induce sweating to "drive out" illness.</note> with Scabiosa water and Blessed Thistle <note>original: *Cardui benedicti*; a herb used to treat digestive issues and fevers.</note>.

Q. B.

### OBSERVATION X.

### Remarkable wandering arthritis following dysentery.

->The Most Illustrious and Excellent<-
->Mr. Augustinus Thonnerus, Doctor, Ordinary Physician<-
->of the Republic of Ulm.<-

->TO GREGOR HORST, Doctor.<-

Greetings. Since some time ago, most Distinguished and Excellent Sir, a patron and colleague to be highly esteemed, you mentioned it would be pleasing to you if I communicated the affliction of "N. N." <note>The abbreviation N.N. stands for *Nomen Nescio*, meaning "I do not know the name," used to protect the patient's privacy.</note> along with its accompanying symptoms, committed to writing—as the case is very rare and not unworthy of investigation. Even though you yourself were employed with me in his care from the onset of the disease, acting as both observer and consultant, so that for you, as a man of great learning, it would not be difficult to describe it and examine its causes; and [I hesitated] lest I "bring wood into the forest" <note>An ancient proverb meaning to do something redundant or unnecessary, similar to "carrying coals to Newcastle."</note>. But since it has pleased you that I should sketch it with my own hand, style, and pen, I would not want to refuse this labor to one requesting it, [as it would] be 

<column-break/>

judged improper, all the more so since I have shown myself benevolent enough to undertake this task in person. Therefore, to fulfill my word and provide what was promised, I transmit this case to you for examination, adorned with a free spirit and supported by reasoning rather than mere authorities. I appoint you as an impartial judge; if these points are to your taste, as I hope, I would not regret the effort spent for <unclear>pious use</unclear>. If not, my intentions should not be blamed (for an indubitable hope shines forth) and my readiness of mind to gratify you.

A learned and honorable man, N. N. ### OBSERVATION IX.

->Intense pain around the left<-
->shoulder and shoulder blade,<-
->arising from a boiling<-
->of bile.<-

A respectable woman, exceeding her fortieth year of age, in the year 1627, toward the end of November, fell into a most vehement pain of the left shoulder and shoulder blade. This was preceded by a shivering-fit <note>original: *horror*; a medical term for the shaking or "creeping" sensation that often precedes a fever.</note>, which was followed by excessive heat, sleeplessness, loss of appetite, the secretion of bilious urine, and a dry cough that afflicted her greatly.

<image-desc>Decorative fleuron ornament in the shape of a cross made of small leaf and flower patterns.</image-desc>

<column-break/>

->THE RESOLUTION.<-

Since this most intense pain seized her suddenly, I determined that it arose from the acrimony <note>harshness or sharpness</note> of boiling bilious blood, as indicated by the preceding shivering-fit and the other signs of fever. For this reason, I immediately aided nature with an Enema. Afterward, I endeavored to soothe the vehement pains internally by the administration of *Opiated Laudanum* with *Magisteries* <note>In early pharmacy, a "magistery" was a concentrated extract or a precipitate prepared with special chemical skill.</note>, and externally with a *Poultice made of barley flour, Chamomile, Melilot, with oils of dill and Chamomile, egg yolks*, etc. I did this while not neglecting the concurrent *false pleurisy* <note>original: *pleuritide spuria*; a condition mimicking the symptoms of pleurisy (lung inflammation) but lacking the same underlying cause.</note> and the dry cough, for which tempered pectoral syrups and an appropriate *Julep* <note>A sweet, liquid medicinal drink.</note> were administered; bloodletting <note>original: *venæsectione*</note> was also applied. 

With these remedies diligently employed, the most vehement pain vanished of its own accord. To expel the remaining bilious waste, a *Laxative Claret* was continued for several days with good results, and once or twice a sweat was provoked using *Bezoar stone* <note>A mass found in the stomachs of animals, highly prized in the 17th century as a powerful antidote and restorative.</note> with *scabious water* and *Blessed Thistle*.

# OBSERVATION X.

## A remarkable wandering arthritis following Dysentery.

### From the most Illustrious and Excellent Lord, Augustinus Thonnerus, Doctor and Ordinary Physician of the Republic of Ulm.

### TO GREGOR HORSTIUS, Doctor.

Much greetings to you. Some time ago, most Illustrious and Excellent man, patron and most esteemed colleague, you mentioned it would be pleasing to you if I were to communicate the condition of N. N., along with the accompanying symptoms, set down in writing. This case is exceedingly rare and hardly unworthy of scientific contemplation. Although you yourself were called to the treatment with me from the start of the illness, and were both a witness and a consultant, it would not be difficult for you, as a learned man, to describe it and examine its causes—lest I "carry wood to the forest" <note>original: *ne ligna in Sylvam*; a Latin idiom similar to "carrying coals to Newcastle," meaning to do something superfluous.</note>. Yet, since you wished for me to sketch it out with my own hand, style, and pen, I judged it improper to decline the labor you requested,

<column-break/>

especially since I have already shown myself quite willing to undertake this duty in person. Therefore, to fulfill my word and stand by my promises, I send this case to you for examination, composed with a free mind and supported by reason rather than merely by authorities, and I submit it to your fair judgment. If these matters are to your taste, as I hope, I shall not regret the effort spent on behalf of our shared practice; if not, my will (in which I have certain hope) and my readiness of mind to please you should not be blamed.

<margin>The disposition of the suffering subject.</margin>
The patient is a learned and honorable man, N. N., exceeding thirty years of age. He was formerly endowed with a fairly fleshy bodily habit and a temperament dominated by melancholy <note>In the humoral theory of the time, a "melancholic" temperament was thought to be caused by an excess of black bile, leading to a serious or somber disposition.</note>, served by thicker blood. This was detectable from the brownish color of his face, a dull and heavy intellect, a calm and modest character, and a <term>paucity of speech</term> <note>original Greek: *ὀλιγομαθιαλαλίᾳ* (oligomathialalia); likely referring to a tendency to speak very little or a slowness in learning.</note>. All his internal organs seem to have fallen to him from nature with a fairly just and convenient <term>balance</term> <note>original Greek: *κράσει* (krasei); the "mixing" or "temperament" of the bodily humors.</note>, corresponding and agreeing with each other; thus, from infancy until last summer, he enjoyed quite comfortable health (except for once, while he was studying at the University, when he was seized by a tertian fever <note>A fever that returns every third day, often associated with malaria.</note>). If the principal members were not as steady as a rock, such health could not have remained uncultivated for so long, since otherwise every kingdom divided against itself [hardly...] <note>original: *omne Regnum, in se divisum, haud...*; a reference to the biblical proverb that a house divided against itself cannot stand.</note>

<margin>Inquiry into the causes of the mentioned symptoms.</margin>
That affliction, by which the patient was so unfortunately and so greatly infested, seems by right and merit to be referred to a wandering and jumping arthritis—and indeed a universal one of the whole body—since no small part was immune from it, nor was there any it did not occupy.

<margin>Universal wandering arthritis.</margin>
Rushing into the neck, it brought on neck-gout <note>original: *trachelagram*</note>; troubling the eyes, eye-gout <note>original: *ophthalmagram*</note>; agitating the tongue, <term>tongue-gout</term> <note>original: *γλωσσάγραν* (glossagran)</note>; penetrating into the shoulders, shoulder-gout <note>original: *omagram*</note>; insinuating itself into the elbow, elbow-gout <note>original: *pechyagram*</note>; flowing into the hands, hand-gout <note>original: *chiragram*</note>; seizing the knee, knee-gout <note>original: *gonagram*</note>; and descending into the feet, it brought on foot-gout <note>original: *podagram*</note>, so that almost no corner of the whole body was left which it did not occupy by creeping through. O shape-shifting and cruel executioner, passing over no joint untouched, to which it has not applied its torments!

<margin>The affected site.</margin>
Direct observation <term>αὐτοψία</term> <note>meaning "seeing for oneself," rather than a modern post-mortem exam</note> shows that the affected site is the joints of almost all the limbs, following the cavities, membranes, ligaments, and tendons, which endure the torture.

Since, however, pain is a symptom of an injured animal action <note>in 17th-century medicine, "animal action" refers to the functions of the brain and nerves, specifically the sense of touch</note>, and indeed of a depraved sense of touch itself, it will therefore have some disease as its leader, which will proceed either from an imbalance of temperaments <note>original: *intemperie*</note> or from a loss of continuity. This did not arise from a sole and naked imbalance alone, because the immense pain exerted itself

<column-break/>

with a conspicuous and not small swelling. Consequently, a loss of continuity <note>original: *continui divisio*; a medical term for a physical disruption or stretching of the tissues</note> was at fault, with the flowing matter either tearing the nervous bodies by its sheer volume, or biting and, as it were, mangling them with its sharper quality. Since the primary qualities—heat and cold—cannot stir up great pain by alteration alone, unless the excess is so great that they pull the continuity apart.

<margin>*Immediate cause.*</margin>
As for the causes, they must be established as either internal or external. The internal are either immediate or mediate. As for the immediate, they can be none other than phlegmatic humors, serous humors, and bilious discharges <note>original: *ichores*</note> (which, like a vehicle for excrementitious superfluities, thin them and make them flow). These do not offend so much by exceeding in the primary qualities of heat and cold, as they do by their secondary qualities, insofar as they are impregnated with salty, nitrous, aluminous, or vitriolic spirits. By their sharp acidity, or their malignant and virulent quality, they provoke pain by gnawing, twitching, and lancing the <term>sensitive</term> <note>original: *εὐαισθήτους* (euaisthētous); parts exquisitely endowed with feeling</note> parts, or by distending them with their volume. To this may be applied that which Hippocrates elegantly and truly recorded in his book *On Ancient Medicine*: *It is not the hot, the cold, the moist, and the dry that has great power of acting, but the bitter and the salty, the sweet and the acid, the tasteless and the harsh; which, even if in their mixture and mutual tempering they are neither perceived nor cause distress, nevertheless when—*

<meta>catchword: nevertheless when—</meta>

# BOOK III. PART II.

...if any of these should be hidden *and exist by itself, it then becomes visible, causes distress to the person, and inflicts harm, etc.* <note>original: "per se extiterit... noxam inferre"</note> In our patient, we must conclude that phlegm-like <note>original: "pituitosos"; relating to phlegm, one of the four bodily humors</note> and bilious thin fluids <note>original: "ichores"</note> are mixed with watery humors; this is because the tumors appearing in the joints are quite hard, stubborn, and difficult to dissolve, accompanied by heat and a yellowish redness. The most atrocious and persistent torture reveals the virulence of the matter.

<margin>Intermediate causes.</margin>
As for the intermediate causes, these can be categorized as those that generate and send the humors, and those that receive them. When watery and phlegmatic humors, along with excessive bilious fluids, constitute the authors of that immense pain, they arise from a "hot imbalance" of the Liver; however, the others emerge from a colder and more humid <term>dyscrasia</term> <note>original: "δυσκρασίᾳ"; an ancient medical term for an unhealthy mixture or "bad temperament" of the bodily fluids</note> of the brain and the stomach. When those superfluous humors are collected in the veins and are unfit for nourishment, they accumulate more and more each day. Eventually, either by their own weight or spontaneously—the barriers having been released—they leap out from the vessels (as if through small holes) like a stream through <term>anastomosis</term> <note>original: "ἀναστόμωσιν"; the opening of the "mouths" of the blood vessels</note> and tend to flow down into the lower parts. Alternatively, because of the quantity or some foreign quality of the fluid, the body's "expulsive faculty" is irritated; seeking to chase out these harmful humors that are contrary to nature, it strives to send them far away and busies itself by depositing them like a heavy pack into the outermost parts of the body.

<margin>External cause.</margin>
Regarding external causes, various coincidences provided no small opportunity for the accumulation of those corrupt humors and the overflow of watery fluids. First, although he possessed a fairly praiseworthy constitution by nature, and his internal organs—intended for the digestion and generation of humors—were so well-tempered that his health remained blameless from childhood until this past summer; yet, due to very serious errors committed in his way of life, he was forced into bad habits. Driven by hunger during times of scarcity, he would greedily consume whatever food was offered without distinction. To quench his thirst, he did not pay tribute to Bacchus <note>The Roman god of wine; the patient could not afford wine</note> but rather to the Waters; especially in this last two-year period, due to the difficulty of the harvest and the high price of wine, he was forced to act as a "water-drinker." Furthermore, in the past, while following a <term>traveling party</term> <note>original: "συνοδίαν" (synodian); a group traveling together, such as a caravan or merchant convoy</note>, he drank beer in great quantities. Consequently, a sickness was impressed upon the internal organs themselves, which often lies hidden for many years until, in the progress of time, the corrupt humors gradually increase and finally burst forth at the slightest provocation.

<margin>Dysentery.</margin>
Last July, he was attacked by a quite severe dysentery which lasted into the third week. Because of the sharpness of the humors, the linings of the intestines were ulcerated, and no small amount of purulent and bloody matter was excreted.

<margin>Arthritis.</margin>
When he seemed to be well-recovered from that illness, he went walking under the hot open sky for the sake of exercising his body and refreshing his mind. Because of the heat of the sun, the humors were melted and driven into a fury; they broke out from all the veins as if they had been unlocked, like a catarrh... <note>The text ends mid-sentence as the humors begin to flow into the joints.</note>

# ON THE PAIN OF EXTERNAL PARTS. 273

...broken out with great force, dripping and working their way into the cavities of the joints, he was seized by universal arthritis <note>original: "arthritide"; a general term for joint inflammation</note>.

But from where did such a great emergence and supply of superfluous humors arise? It is not without reason that we examine the causes more closely. Because of a preceding bout of dysentery, as well as the frequent drinking of water and beer, his natural heat was significantly damaged and weakened. His stomach especially was chilled, as was the brain—partly due to the connection with the sixth pair of nerves implanted in the stomach's opening <note>original: "sexti paris nervorum"; in the anatomical systems of the time, this often referred to the vagus nerve, which links the brain and gut</note>, and partly due to frequent and long stays in cold churches, he was affected by a cold and humid imbalance. This became known from his lack of appetite and excessive salivation <term>ptyalism</term> <note>original: "πυελιζμῷ"; the Greek term for drooling or spitting</note>. He filled several large vessels daily by spitting out humor that was partly watery, partly thick phlegm, and sometimes salty and cold to the touch. He felt that matter descending from his head, and noticed vapors ascending from his stomach, which, having coagulated in the mouth, turned back into water. This happened in the manner of atmospheric phenomena <term>meteors</term> <note>original: "μετεώρων"; early scientists compared the body's internal fluids to weather patterns</note> produced by a circular generation: humid exhalations are carried up to the middle region of the air, condensed by the cold, and fall down drop by drop as rain.

<margin>The cause of a singular convulsion of the tongue.</margin>
On that occasion, exactly one month after the disease began, that marvelous and miserable symptom followed: a certain convulsive movement seizing the tongue. It was agitated in every direction against the patient's will, leaping and stumbling in various ways, much to the shock of those watching. This was accompanied by a constriction of the throat and the danger of suffocation. This fit repeated at intervals, and on a certain day, it invaded almost every hour. It is necessary that either the origin of the nerves or the muscles of the tongue, along with the nerves inserted into them, were damaged. It was not the former, because his mind remained uncorrupted and his senses intact; his speech was not entirely cut off, so that he could implore the help and aid of **GOD**. I would judge that the seventh pair of nerves, destined for moving the tongue and variously dispersed into its muscles, was affected unnaturally. Its branches were either filled with phlegmatic matter or, more likely, imbued with a malignant quality that stimulated the "expulsive faculty" to drive out the hostile substance. However, since that patient was tormented by universal arthritis of the whole body, it does not seem consistent with reason that this evil came solely from a "downpour" from the head, since such a great load of superfluities could not be generated and remain there; rather, it is likely that the matter was collected elsewhere and transmitted, and I would establish such a mode of production.

<margin>The occasion for the generation of abundant thin fluids.</margin>
Since the liquid matter taken in food and drink serves for the distribution <term>anadosis</term> <note>original: "ἀνάδοσιν"; the distribution of nutrients throughout the body</note> of chyle <note>original: "chyli"; the milky fluid produced by the stomach during digestion</note> and the circulation of the blood mass, Hippocrates quite skillfully calls the serum the vehicle of nourishment <note>original: "ὄχημα τῆς τροφῆς"</note>. For it is not

# BOOK III. PART II.

Chyme <note>original: "chymus"; the pulpy acidic fluid which passes from the stomach to the small intestine</note> in the stomach, processed from food, is unable to pass easily into the veins due to its thickness, nor can it easily travel through the very thin and narrow veins of the liver <note>original: "Epatis"</note>, unless a certain thin and watery humidity is mixed with it. The kidneys themselves are destined for the sake of attracting this moisture. From this, the urine later has its origin <term>genesis <note>original: "γένεσιν"</note></term> after being drawn through the emulgent <note>renal</note> vessels and carried down to the bladder through the ureters. Part of it, tempered with the blood, is carried into all the veins and arteries, as it is necessary for the blood's movement. This serum <note>the watery part of the blood</note>, having performed these duties, no longer returns to the vessels when nature is operating normally. Instead, in a well-disposed body, during that third concoction <note>the final stage of digestion occurring in the tissues</note> which takes place in the veins, it is gradually thinned, resolved, and turns into a vapor. This is either evacuated by insensible perspiration <note>breathing or skin evaporation</note> or emitted as sweat. If the kidneys are slower and weaker in attracting this serum, or if the constitution of the body happens to be too dense, so that it can neither exhale through insensible perspiration <term>adelon diapnoen <note>original: "ἄδηλον διαπνοὴν"</note></term> nor be ejected through sweat, then nature labors strenuously upon it. Nature always strives to separate the bad from the good so that it may turn away this burden, which is troublesome to itself, and discharge it elsewhere. Hence, those accumulated watery humors usually flow out from the veins of their own accord, like a river exceeding its bed; or, the expulsive faculty, incited by a sharper and more malignant quality, is accustomed to thrust them toward the furthest limbs.

<column-break/>

Since, therefore, in that sick man—on account of the aforementioned excesses in food and drink, especially on account of excessive drinking <term>polyposian <note>original: "πολυποσίαν"</note></term>, namely a formerly copious intake of beer and water—the watery humors were overflowing in all the vessels. These humors became more congested day by day due to the combined indigestion of the stomach, the "dripping" from the head <note>catarrh</note>, the weakness of the kidneys, and the blockage of sweat. At last, either spontaneously or by the added stimulus of their sheer quantity or foreign quality, they were sent away to the outermost parts. Reaching the cavities of the joints as if a barrier had been placed in their way, they acquired a limit and a fixed seat, being unable to flow further. However, those humors were especially provoked to movement by a triggering cause <term>prokatarktike <note>original: "προκαταρκτικῇ"</note></term>: while the patient was walking under the sun, the scorching rays ignited a fire within him. This stirred up a boiling, like the surging Euripus <note>a strait in Greece famous for its violent, shifting currents</note> or like new wine fermenting in a vat. Foaming over from the larger vessels to the smaller, and then to the smallest, they were diverted to the ends of the limbs. There they became fixed and trapped, which not only produced those tortures of pain but also, by boiling and stirring up inflammation <term>phlogosin <note>original: "φλόγωσιν"</note></term>, brought on a slight fever.

Although various medical protections, both internal and external, were applied to root out all of that <note>original: "πᾶν"</note> affliction, they were all in vain and useless.

### ON PAINS IN THE EXTERNAL PARTS

I had demonstrated to the patient with no small effort of mind that if he truly wished to be liberated from that tyranny of pain, there was a need for sweat-inducing medicines <note>original: "hydroticis"</note> to thin the matter impacted in the nervous system and joints, and to disperse it through perspiration. For some time, the patient ignored this advice with deaf ears—partly because of the interference of a crowd of unskilled people whose mental dullness often slows and overturns the best attempts of physicians, and partly because he pleaded weakness of strength as a <term>Remora <note>original: "Remoram"; a reference to the "suckerfish" believed to stop ships, used here as a metaphor for a lingering obstacle or excuse</note></term> to starting or continuing the cure. Finally, as the pains became urgent and his condition seemed desperate, he gave his consent.

<margin>
Why was China Root approved rather than the "Holy Wood"?
</margin>
However, I remained in suspense and doubt as to which cure would be more profitable. At first glance, because of his <term>excessive salivation <note>original: "πτυελισμὸν" (ptyalismon)</note></term>—arising from a "cold and humid" imbalance of the stomach and brain—a decoction of <term>Holy Wood <note>original: "ligni sancti"; also known as Guaiacum, a resinous wood from the Americas used to treat joint pain and "the French disease"</note></term> seemed not inappropriate. Yet, the prostration of his strength, his nature broken by day and night pains, a total <term>wasting of the body <note>original: "ἀτροφία" (atrophia)</note></term>, and a hotter <term>imbalance of the liver <note>original: "Epatis δυσκρασία" (dyscrasia)</note></term> advised against it. Therefore, I settled on a different opinion—all the more so when I noticed the minds of the patient, his wife, and his mother-in-law were quite averse to its use, with Trigalla <note>likely a nickname for a family member or nurse</note> resisting "with hands and feet" <note>an idiom for resisting with all one's might</note>—so I proposed a decoction of <term>China Root <note>original: "Rad. Chinæ"; the root of Smilax china, a gentler alternative to Guaiacum for delicate patients</note></term> with a portion of Sassafras, relying on these conjectures: 1. Because for several weeks unnatural heat had been observed, and the patient was not free from a lingering slight fever,

<column-break/>

ignited by a mild putrefaction and heat of the serous <note>watery</note> humors due to previous obstructions. 2. Because a hotter constitution of the liver was present. 3. The consumption of all body parts due to a <term>lack of appetite <note>original: "ἀνορεξίαν" (anorexian)</note></term>; for several weeks he took only broths. 4. Weakness of strength. 5. Because he had a fastidious and nauseated stomach, shrinking from and loathing unpleasant things. For the patient was very impatient, soft, and delicate. 6. Because not only watery and phlegmatic humors, but also bilious and salty <term>ichors <note>original: "ichores"; thin, watery, or blood-tinged discharges often considered "malignant" or corrosive in early medicine</note></term>, were the causes of those torments. From this, since China Root is moderate in its active qualities and not excessively harsh in provoking sweats, it resolves superfluous humors while leaving useful ones intact—or at least not depleting them much. Moreover, it is pleasing to the palate and seemed to have the advantage. By adding a portion of Sassafras for the greater comfort of the stomach and to further thin and resolve the thicker humors fixed in the nervous parts, that cure was begun under a happy omen and brought to a conclusion with prosperous success. Taking only a morning sweat-inducing draught once a day, in consideration of his strength, he perspired; his nature could not tolerate the elicitation of two sweats. Bearing it quite well, he sweated abundantly every day. Within 14 days, the pains vanished, and his appetite, which had been prostrate...

...of the neck of those complaining. Others, however, during fevers, cry out that their legs and sometimes their arms are being beaten as if with a pestle. In all these cases, if you were to look at the painful parts, you would say they are unchanged from their healthy state, neither in color, nor in size, nor in general appearance. The Author concludes this assertion not only by recorded observations, but also by rational conjectures that are by no means empty—namely, by establishing that the containing cause of such pains is the settling of a <term>serous humor<gloss>a thin, watery bodily fluid</gloss></term>, rushing all at once into the <term>periostia<gloss>the dense layer of vascular connective tissue enveloping the bones</gloss></term> or the muscles' own membranes. This is confirmed *a priori* <note>from the cause to the effect</note> because manifest evidence of <term>serous pleonexia<gloss>an excess or morbid accumulation of watery fluids in the body</gloss></term> shows itself in the suffering subject. Specifically, it is observed that their urine is copious—far exceeding the amount of liquid they drink—and is thin and clear; and the blood mass (as <term>venesections<gloss>bloodlettings</gloss></term> testify) is seen to be very much diluted with serum. Furthermore, the constitution of the entire body, whether by nature or by an <term>adventitious complexion<gloss>a physical state acquired later in life rather than being innate</gloss></term>, is usually found to be one that is far too ready to collect an abundance of serous superfluity. Since the head is established as a kind of basin and fountain of these "waters," it is judged likely that the serous humor, the cause of the pains, flows down from the head along the membranes, with the liver and spleen assisting in their own way by generating this fullness in the head. It is manifest that this cause of pain is communicated from within the head, rather than from an external source (which would cause a "rain-like" swelling of the skin), insofar as...

From the result <note>original: "A posteriori"; reasoning from effect back to cause</note>, the method of cure and resolution also demonstrates this very thing. This occurs without any sensible swelling of the painful parts, which would not happen if some thicker material humor were mixed with the serum (as we see in the resolution of arthritic pains). I do not doubt that all these things can be adapted to your proposed case. The yellowish color of her face indicates an <term>imbalance<gloss>original Latin: 'dyscrasia'</gloss></term> of the organs of the <term>second concoction<gloss>the stage of digestion believed by early physicians to occur in the liver and blood vessels</gloss></term>, which contributes greatly to this condition; from this, it is easily gathered that emotional agitation through anger causes a copious overflowing of this watery fluid. It is not at all surprising that while fevers afflicted her, periodic pains of this kind were able to subside: as long as Nature was preoccupied fighting the fever, she left the quiet collection of fluids around the membranes alone for a time. Furthermore, the heat of the fever consumed a significant amount of these waste fluids, which is why, after the fever, when the pains returned and Nature reclaimed her old habits, they were observed to be milder.

When they have raged for an hour, more or less, they subside of their own accord, because the influx introducing the pain is very thin and easily dispersed. It leaves behind a sensation of <term>formication<gloss>a tingling feeling like ants crawling on the skin</gloss></term> and weakness, as the effervescence of the thinner serum gradually subsides, and the flow of <term>animal spirits<gloss>the subtle substances believed to flow through nerves to enable movement and sensation</gloss></term>—which were previously quite disturbed—gradually pervades the entire muscular system once again. You correctly add that these pains are eased after a <term>Laconian sweat<gloss>a dry, sauna-like heat treatment</gloss></term> is induced, and also by the use of the <term>Wildbad thermal springs<gloss>original: 'Ferinarum thermarum,' likely referring to the famous healing baths in Wildbad, Germany</gloss></term>. From this, it is clear that the primary goal of treatment consists of two things: namely, to prevent—as much as

<column-break/>

possible—the production of excessive serum in the blood mass and specifically in the head, and to disperse what is in the body's constitution and what already occupies the membranes and boils over at certain times, through sweating, massages, and appropriate moderate exercises. What the use of <term>acidic mineral waters<gloss>naturally carbonated or mineral-rich springs</gloss></term>, thermal baths, sweat-inducing <term>wood decoctions<gloss>medicinal drinks made by boiling woods like Guaiacum, used to "dry out" the body</gloss></term>, and similar remedies can achieve for both goals after appropriate <term>evacuations<gloss>medical procedures like purging or bloodletting to remove excess humors</gloss></term> is obvious to everyone. For this reason, I add no more, for I believe enough has been said to a wise man <note>original: "sapienti sat dictum," a common Latin idiom meaning "a word to the wise is sufficient"</note>. Fare well, Distinguished Sir, and continue to regard me with affection, as you do. Written at Ulm, on the day before the Calends of June [May 31], 1628.

# ON THE PAINS OF THE EXTERNAL PARTS

<margin>Observation of a singular tremor in various body parts.</margin>
...namely, when they move in an **involuntary** <gloss>original Latin: 'præter voluntatem'</gloss> and disordered way, and are convulsed, as it were, with a trembling motion. This frequently happens to elderly women, whose heads continually shake, or to drinkers, whose hands tremble and feet stumble when they have not eaten. However, I consider this particular case to be unique, which occurred to the wife of a certain **schoolmaster** <gloss>original Latin: 'Ludimoderatoris'</gloss> following **childbirth** <gloss>original Latin: 'puerperio'</gloss>. For some unknown reason, for more than twelve years now, her entire left side moves continually while she is awake and against her will, so that her eye perpetually blinks, her lips are constantly opening and closing, her arm jumps, her fingers gesticulate, and her foot never stays still; yet all this occurs without any sensation or pain. When she sleeps, however, everything is at rest.

<margin>Observation of an intermittent tremor of the left side only.</margin>
There is also a certain minister of the Church, about 40 years old, a man of a **melancholic temperament** <gloss>associated in the four humors theory with a somber or anxious disposition</gloss> by nature, but corpulent and full of **vital juices** <gloss>original Latin: 'succi plenus', suggesting a robust or 'moist' constitution</gloss>, who maintains an excellent diet. Two years ago, while standing in the church about to join a new couple in marriage, he felt an involuntary movement in his left foot. Terrified by this, his whole body shuddered, his hair stood on end, and <note>original: 'vox faucibus hæsit' — a classical phrase from Virgil meaning his voice stuck in his throat</note> his voice failed him, so that he could only finish the rest of the ceremony by leaning on the pulpit.

From that time on, as often as he climbed the pulpit, or even when he was worried about a sermon he had to give, a similar tremor invaded the said foot, and from there shook his whole body

<column-break/>

no differently than if he were suffering a **fever fit** <gloss>original Latin: 'paroxysmo febrili'</gloss>, yet he never felt any pain. Inquiring into the cause of this condition, I could find none other than 
<margin>External trigger.</margin>
extreme coldness of the limb and the weakness contracted from it; for he had been accustomed during the summer to place his feet, which were hot from walking, into freezing cold water. Therefore, after a general **purging** <gloss>cleansing of the bowels</gloss> and a **revulsive bloodletting** <gloss>drawing blood from a distant part to divert 'bad humors' away from the affected area</gloss>, I induced sweating several times, bathed the foot in a decoction of suitable herbs, and advised him to visit the **baths of Baden** <gloss>likely the famous spa at Baden-Baden</gloss> in the Margraviate. However, having changed his mind for certain reasons, he visited the **Wildbad baths** <gloss>original Latin: 'Ferinas', referring to the hot springs at Wildbad in the Black Forest</gloss> that year. After using them, he applied ointments made of warm oils, with some relief. But because the **Plague** <gloss>original Latin: 'Pestis'</gloss> broke out soon after his return, renewing his fear and sadness and causing him no small amount of trouble, the ailment flared up again. It even troubled him outside of the sermon when he stood for a long time, and it made his left hand tremulous as well. Thus, on my advice this past summer, he used the Baden baths. At the same time, because of his melancholy, he drank the **Petersthal mineral waters** <gloss>acidic spring waters from the Petersthal region, believed to have medicinal properties</gloss> which are brought there. Although his limbs were remarkably strengthened during the first fourteen days, he felt them grow weak again after continued walking, and he developed an aversion to the mineral waters. Consequently, after a quite troublesome journey, he returned home, not only with his strength exhausted, but also profoundly melancholic...

The case is presented by letter in this manner: A most noble Matron, N.N., 28 years of age and mother of two children, was formerly of a **sanguine constitution** <gloss>historically associated with being energetic and healthy due to a perceived abundance of blood</gloss>, but is now declining toward **melancholy** <gloss>a state associated with an excess of 'black bile', leading to a somber or anxious disposition</gloss>. She eats very little, yet drinks a rather large amount of

<column-break/>

**undiluted wine** <gloss>original Latin: 'meri potus'</gloss>. She began to suffer in her feet; this past May of the current year 1626, she underwent **bloodletting** <gloss>original Latin: 'phlebotomiam'</gloss>, though no prior medicines to aid digestion or purging were allowed. However, the pains she had begun to suffer did not lessen at all; instead, they afflicted her more severely every day at certain intervals. Being unable to endure it, and following the persuasion of a certain **empiric** <note>an 'empiric' was an unlicensed practitioner who relied on trial and error rather than formal medical theory; the term was often used disparagingly by university-trained doctors</note>, she had the **sciatic veins** <gloss>original Latin: 'ischiadicas'</gloss>—commonly called **the gout-veins** <gloss>original German: 'die Gichtadern'</gloss>—cut in both feet about three weeks ago. We do not know if the disease is much different from those which Your Excellence recorded in *Book 1 of Medical Epistles, sections 2 and 3*, except that for one day it mostly ceases, but on the third day it always returns with greater and more terrible pain. Furthermore, the pain never rises above the legs, but fixes its seat most firmly in the soles and the upper parts of the feet above the toes, where the vein was cut. This most cruel **paroxysm** <gloss>a sudden attack or intensification of symptoms</gloss> is prolonged for up to ten hours, with a violent and **spasmodic** <gloss>cramp-like or involuntary</gloss> contraction of the feet, occasionally ceasing for only a very short time. # THE AUTHOR'S 
# Response to the 
# Preceding Case.

<margin>
*Determination of the disease.*
</margin>
This painful condition of the feet, which has now afflicted this most noble Matron every third day for several weeks, has its origin in the nervous and membranous parts of the lower foot. Since it is not without tension, it could be called a **convulsive pain** <note>likely referring to a cramping or spasming sensation</note>. This is generated not through a **primary condition** <gloss>original Greek: 'πρωτοπάθειαν' (protopatheian); a disease starting in the affected organ itself</gloss>, but through a **secondary condition** <gloss>original Greek: 'δευτεροπάθειαν' (deuteropatheian); a "sympathetic" condition where the pain is caused by an issue elsewhere in the body</gloss>. This is because the painful cause is communicated to the affected part from elsewhere, seeing as the pain is not constant but has its own fixed and certain periods of worsening. It undoubtedly takes its origin from **bilious vapors** <note>in the medical theory of the time, "vapors" from excess bile were thought to travel through the body and cause localized pain</note>, which typically worsen every third day. These were originally collected around the splenic and mesenteric veins and acquired a sharp, stinging quality through **adustion** <term>a medical concept where humors "burned" or became scorched by excess internal heat, making them toxic or irritating</term>. 

<column-break/>

In such cases, it is not uncommon for the **vapors** <gloss>original Greek: 'ἀναθυμιάσεις' (anathymiaseis); exhalations or rising fumes within the body</gloss> from such a collection to be communicated to the nervous parts, affecting them severely at intervals rather than constantly. <margin>*Origin of the ill.*</margin> This misfortune may have been occasioned by a certain natural weakness of the receiving part, as well as by a **bloodletting** <gloss>original Latin: 'venæsectio'</gloss> performed on the laboring limb itself against the rules of medical Method. This resulted in a more rapid flow of the offending matter toward the foot, as the innate heat of the laboring subject was further dissipated. <margin>*Prognosis.*</margin> However, just as this condition portends more pain than actual danger, we may console the most noble patient with good hope, provided she does not neglect those things which seem necessary to conquer this enemy. <margin>*The Cure.*</margin> Before all else, to root out the preceding cause, I would recommend the prescribed **chalybeate wine** <term>wine infused with iron or steel, used as a tonic to "strengthen" the blood</term>. She should take a full draught of about 6 ounces <note>original: '℥vj'</note> every day for eight days on an empty stomach, adding at the same time a small portion of **opening powder** <note>a medicine meant to "open" obstructions in the organs</note> weighing 1 scruple <note>original: '℈ j'</note>.

*Peony and Fennel roots, 2 ounces each.*
*Chicory, 6 ounces.*
*Licorice and Polypody fern, as much as needed, 2 drachms.*
*Bark of the root of Dwarf Elder, 4 drachms.*
*Fumitory herb.*
*Hart's Tongue fern, a handful of each.*
*Tamarisk bark, 2 drachms.*
*Choice Senna leaves, 1 ounce.*
*Black Mechoacan, 2 drachms.*
*Select Rhubarb.*
*Hermodactyl, 1.5 drachms of each.*

| Ingredient | Quantity |
| :--- | :--- |

The ingredients are to be sliced and bruised to create a medicinal sachet, to be infused in 6 pounds of thin wine.

Also:
**Take:** **Magistery of Vitriolated Tartar** <note>Potassium sulfate, used as a laxative or diuretic</note> 2 drams.
**Arum starch** 1 dram. Mix and divide into 9 parts. This should be taken along with the iron-infused wine.

After continuing this remedy for eight days, and in consideration of the combined causes of the illness, I would apply a suitable **diaphoretic** <term>a medicine used to induce sweating to expel "corrupt" humors</term> remedy. Specifically, a powder made from **oriental bezoar stone** <note>a mass found in the stomachs of goats, highly prized as a universal antidote and restorative</note>, with **Magistery of Coral** and **Pearls**, tempered in **Speedwell water** with **spirit of lily of the valley**. This should be conveniently repeated four times every week on alternate days. Meanwhile, a proper diet should not be neglected. For the purpose of strengthening the internal organs, I would recommend 3 or 5 drops of **Elixir of Propriety** <note>a famous Paracelsian remedy made of aloes, myrrh, and saffron</note> in a nutritional broth each morning. At the same time, I prescribe a **medicated wine** to be taken at the start of lunch. This is made by an infusion of: Clove root, Scorzonera <note>also known as Viper's Grass</note>, and Peony (each ½ dram); the herbs Sage, Betony, Ground Pine, and true Germander (each 2 handfuls); Flowers of Rosemary, Linden, Sage, and Thyme (each ½ handful); and the tops of Wormwood and Lesser Centaury (each 2 pinches). These should be infused in a vessel of 6 or 7 measures. Finally, if an exacerbation of pain becomes very urgent after the use of the iron-infused wine,

<column-break/>

I would administer **Opiated Laudanum** with Magisteries <note>concentrated extracts</note>, 4 or 5 grains, in a **bolus** <note>a large, soft pill</note> of **Rosemary Conserve**, Betony, or something similar. The use of this is entirely safe for us, as we frequently use up to 8 or 10 grains with happy success in cases of the most vehement and extreme pain. I shall add no more for the time being, lest I overwhelm the most noble patient (who otherwise has an aversion to medicines) with too many prescriptions. May God grant growth through His blessing, He who is praised forever. Written at **Ulm**, June 23, in the year 1626.

## ADDITION.

When I was called in person to this most noble patient shortly thereafter, I was further confirmed in my opinion by the observation of her current symptoms. In those instances where the pains were seasonal and afflicted her most violently, **Camphorated Antihysteric Water** <note>a preparation intended to calm "the vapors" or "hysterical" fits</note>, mixed with **spirit of lily of the valley** and **black cherries**, brought relief that was almost miraculous. In addition to the aforementioned treatments, we prescribed an appropriate internal powder, which consists of:

**Take:** Powdered roots of **Swallowwort**, **Devil's-bit Scabious**, and **Wood Avens**, 1 dram of each.
**Sarsaparilla**, 1 dram.
**Peony root**, ½ dram of each.
Herbs: **Rosemary**, **Sage**, and **Thyme**, 1 scruple of each.
**Species Pleres Archonticon** <note>a restorative powder for the heart and brain</note>.
**Bitter Diamoschu** <note>a musk-based aromatic compound</note>.

### BOOK III, PART II

[Eli]**xir of Property** <note>original: "Elixir Proprietatis"; a famous alchemical medicine made of aloe, myrrh, and saffron, thought to promote longevity and health</note> did some good, she nevertheless passed an almost sleepless night. The affliction is similar to a cruel **colic**. She uses sitz-baths, poultices, ointments, and enemas, from which the pain yields at least for a moment, yet it soon returns. I would give **Opiate Laudanum** corrected with **Magisteries** <term>a "magistery" was a chemical precipitate, often used here to refine or "correct" the harshness of opium</term> if it were provided by you and seemed advisable to you. If you have any other unique remedies, do not be burdened to share them by this messenger, whom we are sending to you for this reason, so that you may help us with your skill. Upset of the stomach and vomiting are not feared as much now as before; only that pain—whether it be in the intestines, or in the parts of the bladder, or in the womb (perhaps in all these lower parts where more matter lies hidden)—causes trouble. To purge through the "upper parts" <note>i.e., using emetics to induce vomiting</note> will be difficult, lest the stomach be disturbed again. In your judgment and skill, provide counsel for the common good. Farewell. In haste, September 28, 1625.

### To the most Distinguished and Excellent Man
## Jacob Eckold, Doctor,
### To GREGORIUS HORSTIUS, Doctor.

<margin>to be given / taken / cause / exacer- / bated.</margin>
**Greetings.** I must in turn inform you of the state of health of our Noblewoman, most Distinguished Sir, etc. From the time I wrote to you, everything has become more relaxed; she felt well and rested peacefully the following night. Because of **strangury** <term>painful, frequent urination where the bladder feels full but only drops are voided</term>, she used **sitz-baths** <note>original: "insessibus"; warm baths where the patient sits in water up to the hips</note> once and again, and she felt well enough from them. She spent the next night sleepless, not however because of a worsening of symptoms, but because she could hardly lie down: for the upper parts of her feet and the buttocks were severely affected by swelling and pain, preventing her from lying down.

<column-break/>

So far she has vomited only once; her appetite is mediocre. Thirst presses remarkably in the morning, but is not troublesome in the afternoon, so that she can even abstain from drinking entirely. I wonder at this one thing: that a sensible coldness rises and enters through the mouth. For she often complains that very cold air rises and reaches as far as her teeth, shaking and affecting them as well as her whole mouth, and is so heavy on the stomach as if she had drunk cold water; this symptom must be suppressed with broths and **Spanish wine** <note>likely a fortified wine like Sherry or Sack, used as a restorative tonic</note>, which has so far seemed to settle the stomach. Yesterday I gave **Spirit of Turpentine**, though not without the risk of her vomiting it back up; she felt better for it and passed a great deal of gas. It is necessary that a copious and impure (almost malignant) matter lies hidden in the lower parts of the belly, which breathes out such a cold vapor. This causes significant difficulty in those same parts, exciting strangury, pain in the **pelvic bone** <note>original: "pectinis"; the pubic region</note>, hardness, burning, and other accidents, which are generally mitigated by sitz-baths. These things, as well as the pains of the external parts—swellings still afflicting her—in my opinion can hardly be corrected otherwise than by the expulsion of that matter through **enemas** <term>liquid injections into the rectum used to clear the bowels</term>. If you think anything else should be tried, do not be burdened to advise me on them, and also with what ointments or **fomentations** <term>warm, moist medicinal applications</term> the swelling and external tumors should be corrected? Farewell.

Oo

### To the most Distinguished and Excellent
### Lord Doctor JACOB ECKOLD,
### GREGORIUS HORSTIUS, Doctor, sends greetings.

At this very moment I receive your letter, most Distinguished and Excellent Sir, etc., which has filled me with singular joy, because it indicates a better state for that Noble and most excellent Matron. I am still entirely of the opinion that, as much as possible, the **harmful matter** <term>peccantem materiam: an imbalance of bodily fluids or "humors" believed to cause disease</term> around the lower parts must be averted, which I agree with you should be done for the most part through enemas, especially if **turpentine** <note>original: "Terebinthina"</note> in substance were added. Nevertheless, I do not doubt that even now nature can be greatly aided by the use of **Spirit of Turpentine** <note>original: "Spiritus Terebinthinæ"</note> mixed with Fernelius’s **Syrup of Marshmallow** <note>original: "Syrupi de Althea Fern."</note>. **With God's help** <note>original Greek: "Συν Θεω"</note>, nature will obtain the victory gradually and day by day, especially since I understand that a moderate appetite for taking food is returning, which I pray for from my heart. Against the swelling of the lower parts, I would continue the steam of a decoction of herbs, where I would especially add **Water Pimpernel** <note>original: "Anagallidem aq."</note> or **Brooklime** <note>original: "Bachbungam"</note> in a greater

<column-break/>

quantity, but use it fresh, on account of the abundance of its **resolving salt** <term>a mineral property believed to dissolve or break down blockages in the body</term>, which evaporates when dried. Internally, before sitting in the **steam bath** <note>original: "vaporarium"</note>, a draft of a decoction of millet with water and wine would not be displeasing; some call it the **Syrup of Saint Ambrose** <note>original: "Syrupum S. Ambrosii"</note>, as you know. Indeed, a half-dram of **Spirit of Dwarf Elder** <note>original: "Spiritus Ebuli"</note> or **Elderberry** <note>original: "Sambuci"</note> added would also assist the internal parts with greater penetration. I would deceive the morning thirst—a sign of a parched liver—with raisins soaked in water and wine, with a **vitriolated conserve of roses** <note>original: "conserva rosar. vitriolata"; rose preserve treated with oil of vitriol (sulfuric acid) for cooling</note>, or even a confection of **Chicory** and **Parsley roots** <note>original: "Rad. Cichorei & Petroselini"</note>. These things in haste in response to yours. Farewell, and also submissively greet the Noble spouses. Written at **Ulm** <note>original: "Ulmae"</note> amid the crowds of the market fairs, October 1, 1625.

### Severe and dangerous pain, affecting the neck, the nape, and the back of the head.
### To the most Distinguished and Excellent

ON PAINS OF THE EXTERNAL PARTS.

Oo 3

A certain Nobleman <note>original: "Magnifico"</note>, who is otherwise perfectly healthy, first began to feel pain in the part of his neck; afterwards the pain occupied the back of the head <term>occiput: the back part of the skull</term> and the nape of the neck <term>nucha: the back of the neck</term>, from which he has now been suffering for almost three months. It returns at certain intervals, although it never entirely vanishes; he does not know how to turn himself except with the greatest distress, and he is forced to lie only on his back, nor can he roll himself onto his sides except with the highest difficulty. He is wretchedly tortured and almost consumed by sleeplessness and pains. This affliction has so far eluded all rational and experimental medicine. I have prescribed a cure of **Guaiac** <note>a medicinal wood from the Caribbean</note> and **Sassafras**, as a primary **head-remedy** <note>original: "Bezoartico capitali" — a "bezoartic" was a sovereign remedy or antidote; here, one specifically for the head</note> [for I am of the opinion that the affliction draws its origin from a certain **downward flow** <term>defluxione: a "dropping" of excess fluids or humors from the brain</term> from the brain into the nerves of the neck and nape, and the vertebrae of the neck, not indeed merely phlegmatic, but which has something of a sharp humor mixed in]; I first applied the necessary preliminary treatments, then local remedies—at first milder ones, and later more powerful ones that almost **redden the skin** <note>original: "rubificantia"</note>, etc. I have chosen to transcribe these things for the sake of sharing the practice; I will inform you of the success of the remedies in due time.

->Farewell, most experienced Man. Given<-

# TO THE AFOREMENTIONED
## Case, the Response
### OF THE AUTHOR.

<margin>An observation similar to the prior one.</margin>
Greetings, etc. I read the case which you added with interest: I had a similar one in previous weeks here in an honorable man, Michael Todel, a **Senator** <note>a member of the city council</note> elected from the commoners seven years ago. He likewise first complained of pain around the nape and the back of the head, so that he was forced to keep his head always held upright. On the outside, nothing of any swelling appeared; but internally, a difficulty in swallowing testified to a swelling of the throat. As time went on, the pain was increased so much that he spent sleepless nights because of it. Finally, the neck and the nape swelled both internally and externally, yet without any significant inflammation; at last, on January 7, a **paralysis** of the hands and arms followed, which was succeeded on January 8 by a **suffocating catarrh** <term>catarrhus suffocativus: a sudden, deadly obstruction of the airway</term>, which took the patient from our midst. In this case, right at the beginning, after providing a **digestive** <note>a medicine to "ripen" or prepare humors for evacuation</note>, I ordered **head pills**; I applied **scarifications** <note>small incisions in the skin</note> for the sake of **drawing away** <term>derivationis: a treatment intended to pull harmful fluids away from the site of disease</term> the fluids; I prescribed **resolving** and **digesting** remedies, both internal (through gargles, **syrups** <note>original: "lambilia" — linctuses to be licked</note>, etc.) and external (through **poultices** <note>original: "cataplasmata"</note>, rubbings, plasters, etc.).

# OBSERVATION XVIII.

## A similar long-lasting pain affecting the neck, nape, and shoulder blades.

**T**o the case proposed with its circumstances, I respond that the origin of this chronic illness was undoubtedly produced by a sticky and sharp downward flow <term>defluxio: the "dropping" of excess fluids or humors from the brain to other parts of the body</term> collected in the aforementioned locations. This has so seized the muscles of the neck and the neighboring membrane-like parts that it has thus far eluded the power of all skillfully prescribed remedies. 

I believe we should see to it that, after repeated evacuations <note>medical treatments intended to clear the body of humors, such as purging or bloodletting</note> directed at the head and the nervous system, a fomentation <term>fomentatio: a warm, medicinal compress</term> be first applied with a large new sponge. This should be soaked repeatedly in the following warm decoction: namely, *Asarum root, Iris, Dwarf Elder root bark, Wild Thyme, Sage, Oregano, Betony, Chamomile flowers, and Elder*. Let these, along with *Castoreum* <note>a medicinal secretion from the scent glands of beavers</note> and *Myrrh*, be steeped and boiled in wine. Use this in the morning and evening for half an hour in the manner described. Afterward, dry the painful parts with a dry cloth warmed by the smoke of mastic <note>a resin from the mastic tree used for its drying and aromatic properties</note>. Once these steps are completed, use *Distilled Galbanum* <note>a gum resin from certain Persian plants</note> *with*

# OBSERVATION XIX.

->Chronic heavy pain in the left thigh.<-

A noble youth, about 20 years of age and prone to **fluxions** <term>fluxiones: the downward flow of excess humors from the head to other parts of the body</term> of the head, complained in **Gießen** in the year 1622 of a heavy, almost superficial pain in his left thigh. I pronounced that this was caused by an **afflux** <note>An "afflux" is a sudden rush of fluid to a part, whereas "congestion" is a gradual buildup</note> rather than congestion. For this reason, after first preparing the body with **digestion** <term>digeſtione: the medical process of softening or "ripening" humors so they can be easily expelled</term> for several days using a decoction of raisins with **Cream of Tartar**, as well as syrup of the five roots and syrup of **Speedwell**, I advised a purging by using **purgative lozenges of Mechoacan** <term>Mechoaca: a root from Mexico used as a powerful laxative</term>, followed afterward by **bloodletting** <term>venæſectione: the surgical opening of a vein to balance the humors</term>.

Once these were completed, I ordered a sweat several times to disperse the **serosities** <note>thin, watery humors</note> from the body's habit, first taking speedwell water distilled with wine, **spirit of dwarf elder**, and a little **Mithridatium** <term>Mithridatium: a complex semi-mythical herbal remedy used as an antidote and general cure-all</term> mixed in. Finally, I ordered the spine around the **sacrum** <note>the bone at the base of the spine</note> to be rubbed externally with **oil of Rue**, **oil of Earthworms**, and **oil of Fennel**, after first using a bath several times made from a decoction of chamomile flowers, speedwell, sage, betony, and juniper berries.

## OBSERVATION XX.

### Superficial pain from frequently recurring Erysipelas.

A noblewoman of a sanguine constitution <note>A "sanguine" temperament was thought to be naturally warm and moist, dominated by blood</note>, who has been sterile for several years following her first childbirth, is frequently afflicted by superficial pain in various parts of her body. Her limbs burn and turn a deep red, showing signs of a "hotter imbalance" <note>original: "intemperiei calidioris," an excess of the heat humor affecting the whole system</note> that distresses her entire body.

## RESOLUTION.

<margin>Identification of Erysipelas.</margin>
When I departed from Hesse in the year 1622, the aforementioned noblewoman sought my advice regarding the symptoms that frequently troubled her. I identified the ailment itself as **Erysipelas** <note>A bacterial skin infection, historically known as "St. Anthony’s Fire," characterized by intense redness and heat</note>—specifically, a "hot tumor" caused by a thin, flammable, and bilious blood. Her sanguine constitution produces this blood due to an irregular menstrual flow and an overly "hot" liver. This condition produces intense superficial pains

<column-break/>

to the extent that the blood is stirred into motion and a "boiling" state by even a minor cause. Because of the blood's thinness and the power of the body's "expulsive faculty" <note>The body's supposed innate ability to push harmful substances away from vital organs toward the skin</note>, it is quickly driven to the surface of fleshy and glandular parts. For this reason, it usually takes hold of the face, breasts, neck, groin, arms, and feet—especially the emunctories <term>emunctoria: parts of the body, like the armpits or groin, through which waste was thought to be expelled</term>. These limbs burn because of the influx of flammable bilious blood and turn a deep red as the skin's natural temperament is altered toward excess. This occurs alongside signs of a hotter imbalance caused by the boiling of the bilious blood, coinciding with a **putrid continuous fever** <term>synocho putri: a 17th-century term for a fever that does not remit</term>.

<margin>The Cure.</margin>
To soothe this ailment, which attacks frequently for the reasons stated, I directed that two things must be considered: namely, prevention between attacks and correction during a flare-up.

<margin>Between attacks.</margin>
Regarding the former, a full course of care should be diligently observed every six months. A "purging" should be performed under the astrological signs of **Cancer, Pisces, or Aquarius** <note>Medical treatments were often timed to zodiac signs associated with water or air to balance the "fire" of the illness</note>. This can be achieved using **Rhubarb** and **Black Mechoacan** <term>Mechoaca nigra: a purgative root imported from the Americas</term>, with a little **Cream of Tartar** added. This should be followed by bloodletting <note>original: "venaesectione"</note>, which she was practicing conveniently at the end of May. One must not neglect those things which assist nature during the monthly cycles; it is often helpful to open the **saphenous vein** <note>A large vein in the leg</note> of the right foot shortly before the menstrual flow begins. Regarding the underlying cause, according to the advice of Solenan—
