"For indeed," says Solenander, "this medicine is based on reason and has clear causes for its effectiveness; it prepares the liver so that it generates as little as possible of that thin, bilious, fatty, and flowing humor <note>The 'humors' were the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to control health</note>, namely by freeing it from obstructions, wiping away the clinging bile, cooling it moderately, and communicating strength to the organ, etc." For this purpose, I also recommended a *conserve made from fresh Chicory roots; and also a Conserve of Roses tempered with a small amount of Spirit of Vitriol* <note>A dilute form of sulfuric acid used in small doses to "cool" the blood</note>, etc. In the meantime, those things which occasionally expel bile and thin humors should not be neglected, where *Rhubarb with cream of Tartar* would be suitable, taken two or three times every month; or the *powder of the same Rhubarb may be sprinkled on Corinthian raisins* <note>Small dried currants</note> *washed in wine*, and taken every week two hours before lunch. Regarding food: one must abstain from fatty, oily, sharp, highly spiced items, noble wines <note>Strong, high-quality aged wines</note>, and similar things.

Among herbs, Sorrel, Spinach, Lettuce, Chervil, etc., are suitable either in the form of a pottage or in salads; here, by the experience of Minderer <note>Raymund Minderer, a prominent 17th-century military physician</note>, the leaves of the **Small Garden Daisy** are highly recommended, as can be seen in his *Military Medicine*. ## OBSERVATION XX.

### *Superficial pain caused by frequently recurring Erysipelas.*

**A** most noble lady, of a sanguine constitution <note>A body type dominated by the "blood" humor, typically characterized as warm, ruddy, and prone to inflammatory conditions</note>, who had been sterile for several years after her first birth, was frequently afflicted by a superficial pain in various parts of her body. Her limbs would become burning hot and deeply red, showing clear signs of an excessively hot imbalance <note>original: "intemperiei calidioris," a disruption of the body's natural temperature balance</note> affecting her entire body.

## THE RESOLUTION.

<margin>
Recognition of Erysipelas.
</margin>

**W**hen I was leaving Hesse in the year 1622, the aforementioned noblewoman sought my advice regarding the symptoms that frequently troubled her. I identified the ailment itself as *Erysipelas* <note>Historically known as "St. Anthony's Fire," this is a skin infection causing painful, red, and swollen patches</note>; specifically, it is a hot swelling caused by a combined humor of blood and bile—thin and easily inflamed. Because her menstrual flow was somewhat irregular, her "hotter" liver produced this humor, which in turn causes the most intense superficial pains

<column-break/>

whenever the blood is stirred into movement or "boiling" by some slight cause. Due to the thinness of this fluid and the power of the body’s "expulsive faculty" <note>The body's natural urge to push harmful substances out toward the skin</note>, it is promptly driven to the surface of the fleshy and glandular parts. For this reason, it usually seizes the face, breasts, neck, groin, arms, and feet—especially the emunctories <note>The parts of the body, such as the armpits or groin, where waste was thought to be gathered and expelled</note>. These limbs burn because of the influx of thin, inflammable, bilious blood, and they turn a deep red because the temperament of the skin is altered beyond its natural state by this excess. The skin is essentially soaked with a greater influx of fluid than its own nutrition requires, accompanied by signs of a "hotter" imbalance due to the boiling of the bilious blood, occurring alongside a putrid continuous fever <note>original: "febri synocho putri," a type of fever that lasted several days without interruption</note>. To soothe this evil, which invaded frequently for the reasons stated, I said that two things must be addressed: namely, preservation between attacks and correction during the attack itself.

<margin>
Between attacks.
</margin>

*Regarding the first*, a regimen for the whole body should be diligently observed every six months. A purging of the system should be performed under the zodiac signs of Cancer, Pisces, or Aquarius <note>Medical astrology dictated that treatments were most effective when the moon was in signs associated with water and moisture</note>. This can be done using **Rhubarb** and **Black Mechoacan** <note>A purgative root from the Americas, related to the Morning Glory</note>, with a little **Cream of Tartar** added. This should be followed by a bloodletting, which she was then conveniently performing at the end of May. Nor should those things be neglected which assist nature when her monthly cycles are approaching; quite often, the saphenous vein <note>A large vein in the leg/foot; bleeding from here was thought to "draw" humors down from the upper body</note> of the right foot was opened shortly before her period began. *Regarding* the antecedent cause, according to the advice...

Solenander, in Section 5, Counsel 13, <note>Reiner Solenander (1524–1601) was a respected German physician</note> advised the same: that for several weeks she should mix two or three parts each of **Wormwood**, **Dandelion**, and **true Germander**, along with **Sorrel**, with a fresh egg. This should be cooked with a little butter and oil into a soft little cake and eaten every morning. For (says Solenander) this medicine is based on sound reasoning and has clear causes for its effectiveness: it prepares the liver so that it generates as little as possible of that thin, bilious, fatty, and flowing humor. ## CHAPTER I.

### On the Nature and Causes of the Convulsive Disease.

<margin>What the malignant convulsive disease is.</margin>
The Convulsive Disease, or Pestilential Spasm, is nothing other than a contagious imbalance <term>intemperies: a medical term from Galenic theory referring to a disturbance in the body's proper mixture of qualities</term> of the nerves and tendons, arising from poisonous mucilages and vapors. Depending on the diversity of [individual] natures, it manifests with preternatural tension and convulsion of the limbs, Epilepsy, Lethargy <note>original: *Veterno*; a state of morbid drowsiness or stupor</note>, Delirium, and indeed sometimes even Madness, with or without fever.

Regarding the causes of this affliction—

<column-break/>

<margin>External causes.</margin>
—one may know from the reports of the sick that the external cause commonly consists of food that is poorly suited and disproportionate for nourishment. This occurs while the poor, destitute of the necessities of life, devour impure and poorly baked bread over a long period during the greatest urgency of hunger. Sometimes they also swallow sour and harsh apples, mushrooms, and the like, engorging themselves on raw, immature, and astringent edibles. From the depraved digestion <note>original: *concoctione*; the process of "cooking" or refining food within the body's organs</note> of these things, raw humors <note>original: *cruditates*; undigested or "raw" substances in the body</note> arise and collect around the mesentery, stomach, liver, and spleen. These are then drawn in by the parts needing nourishment, just like healthy food, because of insatiable desire and intense hunger, eventually inducing a specific and malignant corruption. From the source <note>original: *minera*; literally "mine" or "ore-vein"</note> and fuel <note>original: *fomite*; tinder or touchwood</note> of this corruption, pestilential vapors sometimes break out. Attacking the nervous system, they so irritate and incite the motor power of the nerves that, first shaking the limbs with a convulsive motion, they pinch and stimulate them like the crawling of ants <note>original: *formicatum instar*; this describes "formication," a sensation like insects crawling on the skin, which is a hallmark of ergot poisoning</note>. Not being dispersed or digested by this struggle, but perhaps still prevailing, they insinuate themselves into the innermost nerves. Once this happens, the limbs—with a fierce exacerbation of the disease and pain—are bent and extended in a wondrous manner, and consequently are thoroughly convulsed. Sometimes even the "Herculean disease" <term>Herculeus morbus: an ancient name for epilepsy, so-called because of its perceived strength or because Hercules was said to have suffered from it</term> is produced, and finally the patients are so ruined that either by paralysis...

### CHAPTER II.
#### On the Signs.

<margin>Diagnostic signs.</margin>
The diagnostic signs by which this condition is recognized are not the same or similar among all patients; however, for the most part, they present in the following manner. First of all, the patients perceive a certain crawling sensation <term>formication: from the Latin "formica" (ant), a sensation like ants running over or under the skin</term>, sometimes only in the hands, sometimes only in the feet, sometimes in the hands and feet together, occasionally on only one side, and sometimes on both, as if the part were full of scurrying ants or were otherwise numb. Consequently, the fingers and toes are suddenly and tightly contracted, or very forcefully extended as if they had become stiff; and this tension proceeds from the hands and feet up to the elbow, shoulder, legs, and hips. In a similar fashion, it contracts each of these limbs toward the body, even until the patient either curls up entirely into a ball, or lies rigid, stretched out in length like a long piece of wood, and violently spread out as it were. This extension or contraction

<column-break/>

often persists in the same manner and tenor throughout the entire attack <term>paroxysm: a sudden recurrence or intensification of symptoms</term>, but often it strikes alternately, so that a limb previously distended and rigid might now be bunched up like a ball, or that which was curled into a ball is again pulled apart and extended. Frequently, this convulsion persists in the hands alone, or the arms, or both, and often also in the mouth, lips, eyes, and the entire body. Depending on the nature and abundance of these poisonous vapors, this malignant spasm persists for a long or short time, nor does it cease

<margin>Duration of symptoms.</margin>
until all the vaporous matter has been dispersed and overcome through this shaking and shattering of the limbs. Once it is dissipated, the limbs enjoy rest and peace for as long as it takes for that poisonous source <term>minera: literally "ore" or "mine," used here to describe the internal site where the disease "ore" is produced</term> to be moved anew and again stir up new vapors, which especially infest the nerves; from these, every renewal and worsening of the previous spasms proceeds.

<margin>The site of the affliction is not the same.</margin>
The spasm itself also varies according to the variety of the place which this pestilential matter occupies. For if it has fixed its seat in the head and brain, as most often happens, then—with the spinal cord immediately drawn into sympathy <note>original: *consensum*; a medical theory where one part of the body reacts to an injury or stimulus in another part</note>—the entire nervous system along with the whole body and all limbs are convulsed in a moment. But if the roots [of the disease] are in the hands or feet, on at least one side, or in both, or in any other part of the body...

APPENDIX TO BOOK III, PART II.

<margin>
An unnatural state left after the delirium of the fits.
</margin>
...nevertheless there are some, although few, who begin to rave <note>original: "delirare"</note> even before the onset of the epileptic attack <note>original: "Epilepsiæ insultum"</note>.

This mental disturbance is extended in some to three, four, or even more days, and in certain cases for a very long time. And even though those emerging from the fit <term>paroxysm: a sudden attack or increase of symptoms</term> may return to their original state of mind, they nonetheless behave, live, and walk like drunken men, moving with a high-stepping gait and positioning their legs in a strange and clumsy manner. They do not remember those things that happened to them during the attack, and they complain of no headache, whether present or past. It is rare, however, that these delusions depart without leaving some mark or stigma; sometimes they leave behind a ringing in the ears and heavy hearing, sometimes a blurring of the vision, and occasionally a difficulty with both sight and hearing. Indeed, this evil so pervades many that they are no longer in control of any limb and are contracted on all sides, so that those standing by are compelled to feed and nourish them no differently than infants.

<margin>
Great hunger after the fit.
</margin>
Once the fit has been overcome, almost all the sick are driven by such intense hunger and appetite for various foods that they can hardly be satisfied. If they are given an abundance of food to their heart's content, they ingest and consume an unbelievable amount; yet, they do not perceive any heaviness, pressure, or bulk from the food they have eaten.

<margin>
Diarrhea following.
</margin>
As this malady persists, cases of diarrhea begin to break out

<column-break/>

continually, afflicting them until the total conquest of the condition; and the smaller the quantity of food ingested, the more vehemently the diarrhea presses upon them.

<margin>
Swelling of the extremities and of blisters.
</margin>
Similarly, in the passage of time, the hands and feet in almost most patients swell up, and upon their fingers, large blisters <term>vesicæ: fluid-filled blisters or blebs on the skin</term> full of watery discharge <term>ichor: a thin, watery discharge from a wound or ulcer</term> arise. When these are opened, much serous fluid flows out along the length of the fingers, yet the disease remits none the more, but remains in the same state. Very little sweating is noticed among these same patients.

### ON THE MALIGNANT CONVULSIVE DISEASE.

Qq

The outcomes of the disease were all the more confirmed by examples occurring daily.

<margin>The confirmed outcomes of the disease.</margin>
For all those upon whom the <term>falling sickness: an old name for epilepsy</term> supervened, experienced recurring epileptic attacks for the rest of their lives. In the same way, those who lost their minds, or were turned to madness and rage, for the most part remained in a state of stupor until the end of their lives, without the restoration of their previous discernment and judgment. For it is established by known examples that some survived for fifteen years after the onset of this evil. These people, during the harsh and freezing winter around the months of December and January—at which time the source and root of this plague <note>original: "luis"</note> used to be stirred up, so that the afflicted ought not to be burdened with commands nor provoked by anger—fell back into the same disaster annually. After fifteen years had passed, some were seized by a sudden relapse, ran out into the fields, and leaping into rivers, were drowned in the waters.

It is indeed true, and not without reason, that this condition—just like all other nervous disorders—can be cured and overcome only with the greatest difficulty. This is because it does not follow from other diseases, but arises through <term>protopathia: a primary disease that originates in an organ or system itself rather than being a symptom of something else</term> by its own accord from its own internal causes. Nevertheless, if it has not yet struck deep roots, nor clung to the parts for long, but is in such a state that the <term>pestilential matter: the harmful substance believed by early physicians to cause the illness</term> fixed within can be digested, led

<column-break/>

out, and at the same time it can be prevented from breaking out anew; and furthermore, if strength can be added to the limbs before they are reduced to helplessness <note>original: "ad incitas redactis," a metaphor from a board game meaning to be at a standstill or cornered</note>, then it is not only still entirely curable, but even that which has already lasted for several years can be so mitigated. It can be managed so that it does not waste the patient with such immense cruelty as it usually does, but allows them to enjoy a moderate peace and tranquility, as if a truce had been made.

<margin>The contagious nature of this plague.</margin>
Moreover, this plague is highly contagious, and as experience witnesses, it rarely happens that it does not eventually invade all those who have lived long and closely with the infected, or shared a home with them familiarly. Even so, the manner and movement of the contagion differs greatly from the plague or dysentery, which infect very rapidly. This disease gathers itself and reveals itself gradually over time, in the space of one, two, or six months—sometimes one year—and even more slowly. For it often happens that out of ten or twelve living under the same roof <note>original: "sub eodem lare," referring to the Lares, or Roman household gods</note>, one or two may live free from this plague for a full two years, and only then succumb to the seeds of contagion.

This, however, resulted chiefly from a lack of protection and a scarcity of appropriate remedies, while the evil meanwhile crept here and there at will; whereas after the use of medicines, the greatest part of the sick—even those who already suffered from <term>mania: madness or violent delirium</term> or the falling sickness—

# APPENDIX TO BOOK III, PART II.

...[they] were remarkably relieved and restored to health.

However, because this malignancy tends to rage more violently against those who are forced to endure a meager existence and suffer from a lack of all necessities, it manifests more severely through convulsions as well as other accompanying symptoms—such as <term>mania: madness or wild behavior</term>, rage, diarrhea, dysentery, hunger, and the like—than it does in those of more fortunate circumstances who enjoy the food and care necessary for health. For this reason, experience shows that remedies are offered with more successful results to those who use a refined diet than to those who indifferently consume all manner of food, whether raw or cooked. Therefore, a certain rule of life and an orderly dietary regimen must rightly be established.

## CHAPTER IV.
### On Treatment in General.

<margin>Curative indications.</margin>
Once the affliction is understood from the preceding descriptions, it becomes clear what is required for its treatment and what must be most carefully considered. Since all hope of health is in vain as long as that poisonous material remains in the body, the primary effort in treatment must be directed toward rooting out that <term>corrupt matter: known in Latin as "materia peccans," referring to the harmful substances or "humors" causing the disease</term>.

<column-break/>

Next, since the nervous system has also been so weakened and exhausted by this same matter—to the extent that even if the disease-causing agent is eradicated and the body finds rest, the nerves nevertheless remain weak, languid, and easily prone to convulsions—a second curative goal emerges: to strengthen the weakened nerves. Regarding the first goal, because this pestilential matter rarely originates in the weaker parts themselves, but instead usually settles in other locations from which its transmitted malignancy infects the diseased parts, it is necessary to turn one's eyes toward both the <term>source: literally "fomes" or tinder, the spark of the disease</term> itself and the affected parts during the eradication of this matter.

Furthermore, since it is very well known from the previously established causes and signs that the antecedent or internal cause fostering this affliction is a specific corruption of the contents around the stomach, liver, spleen, and the intervening splenic and mesenteric veins, we must consider here above all else how these viscera may be freed and purged of the <term>offending dross: "saburra," a medical term for an accumulation of foul matter in the stomach</term> right at the beginning. This can be achieved first through a refined lifestyle and a suitable regimen of the <term>six non-naturals: a historical medical concept referring to factors within a person's control: air, food/drink, sleep/wakefulness, motion/rest, excretion/retention, and passions of the mind</term>. These must be diligently observed by the healthy and the sick alike, in order to cut off every opportunity for this evil and to prevent its further growth...

### CHAPTER V.

#### On the rules of Diet.

<margin>Cold must be avoided.</margin>
To this end, therefore, both the healthy and the sick should adopt a correct way of living and look out for themselves diligently, so that the whole body—and especially the extremities, namely the head, hands, and feet—are protected against external cold. They must be especially well-guarded during the months of December and January, since this <term>plague: *lues*, referring here to the epidemic outbreak of ergotism</term> is accustomed to rage more severely and fiercely at this time, not only because of the winter frost, but also by its own nature.

For experience testifies that when this malignancy spreads among the people, the sick complain of nothing more than a cold and southern constitution of the air. By this air—doubtless because poisonous vapors cannot exhale through the closed pores of the skin, and because the biting cold, which is an enemy to the nerves, insinuates itself deeply—the evil is more sharply intensified and aggravated. <margin>A suitable way of living.</margin>
<margin>Hunger is harmful.</margin>

Instead, he should supply as much food and drink as suffices for the preservation of life; for experience clearly proves that this plague not only becomes more common through hunger, but is also more violently intensified and provoked.

<margin>Venus must be avoided.</margin>

Likewise, every other week they should induce a sweat to consume superfluities, and every fourth, sixth, or eighth week—depending on the violence of the evil—they should take a specific purging <term>electuary: a medicinal paste made of powder mixed with honey or syrup</term> to address the underlying cause...

# CHAPTER VIII.

## On the Symptoms that mostly accompany this disease.

Just as all the more serious afflictions attack Nature in its various faculties and body parts, and so assault and torture it that the body is forced to yield to their violence, and repeatedly struggle with many and most cruel accidents, finally succumbing when burdened on all sides: so also the convulsive disease, if any other does, frequently causes the body much business and trouble, and cruelly exercises that same body with many symptoms in various functions. And indeed, such symptoms do not plague every patient, or at least not equally; rather, they affect this one more sharply, and that one more mildly; sometimes they even vanish of their own accord without any effort after the Treatment has begun.

Because, however, the same outcome does not happen for everyone, but most all those who are not helped in time are forced to labor under a defect of health and waste away from the disease through the whole course of their lives, I have therefore decided to observe and note down the symptoms which it was possible <note>original catchword: "licuit"</note> to see in the daily lives of patients...

That irrational hunger usually accompanies a manifest cause, namely a previous lack of necessary foods; then, for the most part, it is caused by some vicious humor—acidic and melancholic <note>In the "four humors" theory of medicine, "melancholic" refers to black bile, which was thought to be cold and dry</note>—which, having been driven into the opening of the stomach, bites and irritates it. For such a humor induces a biting sensation similar to suction; and since the walls of the stomach are constricted and drawn tight, and the food is compressed at the bottom, it brings on a sense of emptiness just like natural hunger,

and an unquenchable desire, regardless of the food already taken. Furthermore, it can happen that while the stomach, due to a lack of food, consumes everything, it so exhausts the opening—and within it the sense of suction and the appetitive faculty—that it desires more intensely and is seized by a hunger that cannot easily be satisfied. If, therefore, <margin>Correction.</margin> this hunger proceeds from a scarcity of food, it must be replenished with suitable foods, as mentioned in the chapter on Diet; however, not all at once, nor with a huge quantity of food, lest the abundance overcome the digestion, and from the undigested mass of food, obstructions of the internal organs, fevers, and similar conditions arise. Instead, from the beginning, food should be given often and in small amounts, and primarily fatty foods should be provided; from there, it should be slowly increased day by day until the hunger is satisfied. <margin>The cause of abnormal hunger.</margin>
I. That irrational hunger most often accompanies a manifest cause, namely a preceding lack of necessary nourishment; thereafter, it is largely caused by some vicious, acid, and melancholic humor, which, being driven into the opening of the stomach, bites and irritates it; for such a humor induces a gnawing sensation similar to suction, and—with the linings of the stomach constricted and tightened, and the food compressed at the bottom—it brings about a sense of emptiness, just like natural hunger,

<column-break/>

and an unquenchable desire, despite food having been taken. Furthermore, it is possible that while the stomach consumes everything due to a lack of food, it so exhausts the opening—and within it the sensation of suction and the appetitive faculty—that it craves more intensely and is seized by a hunger that cannot easily be satisfied. If, therefore, this hunger proceeds from a scarcity of nourishment, it must be restored with suitable foods (as mentioned in the chapter on **Diet**), yet not all at once, nor with a huge quantity of food, lest the abundance overwhelm the digestion, and from an undigested mass of food, blockages of the internal organs, fevers, and similar conditions arise; rather, from the beginning, let food be provided often and in small amounts, and especially fatty foods; from there, let it be slowly increased day by day until the hunger has been satisfied.

<margin>Correction.</margin>
But if indeed it arises from an acid phlegm, let the food first be moderately plentiful, and let one dram <note>original: "ʒj"</note> of bruised nettle seed be cooked with a small amount of the tops of dill in <term>hydromel</term> <note>a mixture of honey and water</note>, with a little olive oil, and let this be given to drink until nausea occurs, and let the throat be irritated with a feather dipped in oil, so that the vomiting of the phlegmatic humor is provoked. Afterwards, the stomach, being relieved of such a burden, may be refreshed with natural food, and this monstrous hunger will be calmed.

If, therefore, it arises from excessive gluttony, food should be taken more sparingly and moderately. If it arises from a poisonous quality, it should not be stopped immediately; rather, once the corrupted humors have been evacuated in this manner, it will be cured of its own accord—provided that more suitable foods are offered thereafter. But if the vomiting is so excessive that it leads to the prostration of the patient's strength, a **Plaster made from wine, rye bread, nutmeg, cloves, cinnamon, and a little quince conserve** <note>original: "diacydony," a thick medicinal jelly or marmalade made from quinces</note> should be prepared and applied to the stomach. Furthermore, a piece of toasted white bread, rubbed with nutmeg powder and soaked in sufficient wine with sugar, should be offered as a broth.

<margin>Diarrhea</margin>
III. **Diarrhea** takes its origin from corrupted and poisonous fluids <note>original: "ichoribus," referring to thin, watery discharges from a wound or diseased part of the body</note> sticking in and around the mesentery <note>the membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</note>, or sometimes even from bile and "melancholy" <note>black bile</note> from the spleen, or from other fluxes descending from the head, according to the physical disposition of each patient. This flow of the bowels should not be checked too hastily; it is wiser to keep it flowing for some time until the vicious matter has been mostly diminished through the use of the convulsive powder and antidote, or until it ceases on its own. If, however, it lasts longer than expected and beyond what the patient’s strength can tolerate, **ignited steel** <note>original: "chalybs ignita"; a common practice where red-hot iron or steel was quenched in a liquid to give it astringent properties</note> should be frequently extinguished in their ordinary drink,

<column-break/>

and rice broth, quinces, wild plums (either preserved or dried), and medlars <note>a fruit resembling a small brown apple, eaten when very ripe</note> should be given. Additionally, one drachm <note>a unit of weight, approximately 3.9 grams</note> of **sealed earth** <note>original: "terra sigillata," a medicinal clay from Lemnos stamped with a seal to guarantee authenticity</note> or true **Armenian bole** <note>a reddish medicinal clay</note>, toasted nutmeg, prepared burnt hartshorn <note>original: "C. <margin>Swelling of the limbs.</margin>
IV. **Swelling of the limbs** arises from poisonous and malignant vapors <note>original: "flatibus"</note>, fluids, and fluxes, which are drawn into the limbs by intense pain or collected there through congestion. These are usually notably consumed and dispersed by means of the **convulsive powder and electuary**. 

<margin>Correction</margin>
However, if the swelling persists longer, it must also be discussed and dissipated with external remedies. To this end, let a lye be prepared from the ashes of vine leaves, birch, beech, or oak—according to one's preference—in which oregano, calamint, or chickweed <note>original: "Alsine"</note> is boiled. Once the herbs are boiled and enclosed in a small bag, the swollen limbs should be fomented with them while warm every day. Once dried, the limbs should be anointed with oil of castor or walnut oil until all the swelling has disappeared.

<margin>Feverish heat</margin>
VI. **Feverish heat** <note>original: "Æstus febrilis"</note> is usually broken by an antidote electuary <note>a medicinal paste made with honey or syrup</note>, or convulsive powder, or **theriac** <note>a traditional "universal" antidote made of many ingredients</note> once sweats have been drawn out. Externally, green water-lily leaves should be applied to the region of the liver and kidneys until they dry out and the heat is extinguished.

<margin>Epilepsy</margin>
<margin>What should be done during an attack</margin>
VII. **Epilepsy** is noticeably erased and inhibited in the same way by the same convulsive remedies focused on purging and sweating. However, if the patient is in the midst of the paroxysm <note>a sudden attack or seizure</note> itself, their limbs should not be entirely restrained, nor allowed to be tossed violently here and there, but should be held so that they can still move a little. Furthermore, the legs and arms should be rubbed well with linens; **rue** <note>a bitter herb used for its stimulant properties</note>, castoreum <note>a substance collected from beaver glands</note>, lavender, oregano, and wild thyme should be held to the nostrils, and with each of these, the hands, feet, temples, crown of the head, and nostrils should be rubbed. Sometimes a soft feather dipped in rue juice may be inserted deep into the nostrils, and a spoonful half-

<column-break/>

-full of rue juice should be offered. All these things should be continued until, the evil having been overcome, the patient returns to their former mind and health. Once these are present, one should proceed with the convulsive medications in the future in the same manner as before.

<margin>Apoplectic Paralysis</margin>
VIII. **Apoplectic Paralysis** <note>original: "Resolutio Apoplectica," a loss of movement or sensation often following a stroke</note>, by which the sick become so stiff that hardly any trace of life can be found in them, rushes in from the moment when poisonous breaths and malignant humors invade the brain with headlong force and block or intercept the carotid veins and arteries, or so acutely injure them with some other pestiferous quality that no function of the body can any longer perform its duty.

This symptom breaks out either from an inflammatory <note>original: "phlegmonosâ," referring to a hot, red swelling</note> disposition of the brain, or from an influx of corrupt and pestilential fluids and vapors into the ventricles of the brain. If indeed the veins and arteries swell with thick blood after immense heat, frenzy, or madness, such an inflammatory disposition should be expected; it immediately requires that the **cephalic vein** <note>the large vein in the upper arm, then thought to be linked to the head's health</note> be opened. The blood should be let out not all at once or in one go, but gradually in several turns, up to sixteen or eighteen ounces. Once the vein is pierced, it can be closed at intervals and then allowed to flow freely until the proper quantity of blood has flowed out. ...the legs and the whole body should be vigorously rubbed with rough, warm linens, and the legs and arms should be frequently and tightly bound to achieve a **revulsion** <term>revulsio: a medical technique intended to draw "excess" blood or harmful humors away from the head toward the extremities</term> of the blood from the head to the lower parts. If such a collapse <term>resolutio: a loss of muscle function or paralysis</term>, lethargy, and a numbness of the individual limbs should follow without any obvious feverish heat, it is born more from the onset of malignant vapors and humors than from any other cause. In such a case, the first and best advice would be that as soon as the patients are seized, a sharp **enema** <note>original: "clyster acris"</note> should be injected to draw the humors away. However, because the poorer classes lack the convenience and opportunity for such equipment, we will not say much about them. Instead, we advise that a feather—dipped in the juice of **rue** <note>a strong-smelling medicinal herb</note>, or in spirits <note>original: "vino sublimato," literally distilled wine or brandy</note> mixed with nutmeg—be inserted [into the throat or nose] to provoke a reaction. The legs, arms, hands, and feet should be rubbed, and the whole body should be smeared everywhere with spirits. The hair of the beard and the pubic region should be plucked by hand, and smoke from burnt hair should be directed to the nostrils to rouse them. All these actions should be repeated alternately until a degree of the patient’s former health shines forth.

<margin>Lethargy</margin>
IX. For **Lethargy** <note>original: "Veterno," a state of deep, coma-like drowsiness</note>, from which the sick can hardly, or not at all, be awakened, it would be best treated by a sharp, revulsive enema. But because the equipment for enemas is often non-existent among the poor, the next best thing is that the lethargic ones be awakened by every possible ingenuity. First, they should be placed in a sunny and bright, yet warm place. Veins that appear swollen with blood should be struck and emptied <note>a reference to bloodletting</note>. **Pennyroyal**, wild thyme, oregano, sage, and similar herbs should be rubbed into the nostrils. The head should be fomented with a decoction of these same herbs made with water and a little vinegar. Glowing hot bricks or stones, covered with a cloth and sprinkled with water and vinegar prepared with juniper berries and sage, should be placed near the bed so that the vapor can reach the head. The skin should even be burned by a piece of oak wood still glowing at the tip, applied to the back of the head, and various pains should be provoked until they are somewhat better.

# CHAPTER IX.

## Concerning certain Universal remedies pertaining to the cure of this disease.

Since this treatise was written and prepared not primarily for the sake of Physicians—each of whom, according to his own wisdom, can investigate the disease and its state and condition from the patients themselves—but rather for the sake of the poor living in the countryside, who are very often deprived of the immediate help of Physicians and the benefit of pharmacies, and whom this disease is most accustomed to attack, we have therefore recorded the greatest part of the remedies with all the diligence we could. We have done so in such a way that anyone from the common people might be able to begin their own cure by their own efforts <note>original: "proprio Marte," literally "by their own Mars," meaning by one's own strength or initiative</note>, without the assistance of a pharmacist. However, since it was impossible to subdue this most atrocious affliction with domestic and therefore weak remedies, and necessity has instead forced out certain stronger and more noble ones to demolish the very root of the evil,

<column-break/>

we have therefore noted down several universal safeguards for each and every person. We have made these public for the common good, so that anyone, according to their means, may seek them from pharmacies. Among these, however, there are three primary ones: namely, the **Convulsive Purgative Electuary** <term>electuary: a medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</term>, the **Convulsive Antidote**, and the **Convulsive Powder**.

### FIRST OBSERVATION.

->*An aneurysm produced on the occasion of bloodletting, and its cure.*<-

<margin>Note Well</margin>
A learned young man, for the sake of preserving his health, underwent bloodletting <term>venesection: the surgical practice of opening a vein to drain blood, a common medical treatment of the era</term> in his right arm. There, as soon as the vein was cut, very bright red blood flowed out abundantly, almost by leaping <note>original: "saliendo quasi," describing arterial spurting rather than steady venous flow</note>; taking little notice of this, the bath-keeper <note>original: "Balneator," a professional who, in addition to managing baths, often performed minor surgeries, cupping, and bloodletting</note> who had performed the procedure bound the wound in the usual manner. Soon, however, a significant pain in the wounded part followed,

FOURTH BOOK, PART II. 320

<columns>
...pain, swelling, and at the very site of the venesection, a tumor the size of a hen's egg, pulsating, yielding slightly to the pressure of the fingers, together with an ensuing inflammation and swelling of the whole arm.

## ANALYSIS.

<margin>
Signs of an opened artery.
See a similar case in Rondelet and Fontanus, book 1, consultation 75.
</margin>
That the bloodletting here was performed less skillfully was evidenced by the very bright red blood flowing out almost in a leaping heap <note>original: "confertim profluens," describing the rapid, pulsating spurt of arterial blood</note>; indeed, an incision of an artery had been made in the place of a vein. Arterial blood differs from venous blood in that it is more "spirituous" <note>Early modern physicians believed arterial blood contained "vital spirits" distributed from the heart, making it brighter and more frothy than venous blood</note> and florid, leaping forth due to the pulse of the artery; whereas when a vein is cut, the color of the blood is observed to be more blackish and is not found to have a leaping force. A Surgeon should note this well so that, if this error occurs contrary to his intention, he may immediately close the artery by applying suitable remedies, which will be discussed later. However, because of ignorance in this case, the wound was only bound in the usual manner; soon, a significant pain in the wounded part followed, along with swelling, because of the blood flowing to the injured part—the "native heat" <term>calore nativo: the innate warmth believed to sustain life and digestion in the body</term> having been not a little weakened by the evacuation of the arterial blood—with a tumor appearing the size of a hen's egg, namely an aneur-

<margin>What an aneurysm is.</margin>

<column-break/>

-ysm, which is produced by a defect in the artery. This is not so much because "spirituous" blood is poured out under the skin from the injured artery—as the ancients believed, for by this reasoning it would quickly be corrupted outside its own place, flow in all directions, and even make the skin livid, as usually happens in <note>original: "ἐκχυμώσει" (ekchymosei), an effusion of blood or bruising</note>—but rather 

<margin>True causes of an Aneurysm.</margin>
it is caused by the dilation of the artery, either in respect to both of its tunics <note>the layers of the arterial wall</note> (which sometimes happens to women in labor, the arteries around the neck becoming so dilated); or by reason of only one tunic, which was what happened here, the artery having been wounded by the phlebotomist <term>phlebotomum: the lancet or the practitioner performing the bloodletting</term>. It was pulsating because it moved along with the dilated artery in respect to the outer tunic. Moreover, it yielded slightly to the pressure of the fingers as the spirituous blood moved back inside into the body of the artery. This occurred along with inflammation of the whole arm, because those things which ought to have prevented such results were not applied. 

<margin>The Cure.</margin>
Having been called in with another Surgeon, and a prognosis first being made—that the condition is not without danger (since an aneurysm, or tumor of an artery, is present, which is determined by many to be altogether incurable, as can be seen in the Classical Authors) and that its cure would be long-lasting—I immediately rejected those things which had been irrationally applied to soften the tumor, and soon ordered those things which the necessity of the case seemed to require. For since by the opening of this tumor 

<margin>An aneurysm must not be opened.</margin>
the patient would be thrown into manifest danger of his life, because along with the spirituous...

<meta>catchword: ...blood [tuoso]</meta>
</columns>

<summary>This page analyzes a botched bloodletting where an artery was punctured instead of a vein, leading to a pulsating aneurysm. Horst explains the physiological differences between arterial and venous blood and argues that an aneurysm is a dilation of the arterial walls rather than a simple internal hemorrhage.</summary>
<keywords>aneurysm, artery, venesection, bloodletting, arterial blood, venous blood, spirituous blood, innate heat, surgery, medical error, dilation</keywords>

### ON CERTAIN SURGICAL MATTERS.

...by the spirituous blood, the principle of life is poured out; an example of this can be seen in *Paré, book 6 of Surgery, chapter 28*. Indeed, the softening and suppuration of a gangrene, and the subsequent "sphacelus" <term>sphacelus: a term for complete necrosis or "death" of a body part</term> and corruption of the part may follow, as is clear in *Forestus, book 1 on tumors, observation 15*. Therefore, a different course of action had to be taken. Although this dangerous aneurysm or tumor could have been prevented with little trouble if I had been present immediately after the artery was cut,

<margin>
A cut artery consolidated with little trouble.
</margin>
as I remember happening in former years in my presence to a certain Noble Senator of the order. In his case, an artery in the arm was similarly cut in place of a vein. In that instance, the opening was immediately closed and a plaster was applied made of fine flour, Armenian bole <note>original: "bolo armeno," a red medicinal clay used as an astringent</note>, sealed earth <note>original: "terra sigillata," a medicinal clay pressed into tablets and stamped with a seal, used as an antidote and astringent</note>, powder of great comfrey, and similar things. Thus the outflow of arterial blood was restrained, and with the help of a stronger bandage, the artery was consolidated again of its own accord. Nevertheless, the cure here became more difficult because I was called later, while in the meantime things had been applied that made the disease worse.

<margin>
Means of cure.
</margin>
Therefore, having ordered a diet and also having applied those things which would prohibit further flow to the affected part—namely, after a general evacuation <note>The practice of "evacuation" usually referred to purging the bowels or further controlled bloodletting to balance the humors</note> had been performed—and avoiding all those things which are naturally inclined to introduce greater inflammation, we applied moderate repellents and astringents to the affected part,

<column-break/>

also succoring the neighboring parts that were swelling and inflamed through suitable means. Gradually, as the swelling of the entire arm subsided, we treated the pulsating tumor with a compound of *Sperniola* <note>original: "Sperniola," likely a cooling preparation made from frog spawn, used in early modern medicine for inflammations</note> dissolved, not neglecting defensive applications in the vicinity. This was done with a quite desired success, so that within the space of three months the arm was totally restored to its former health.

The ancients approached *Aneurysms* through incision, as can be seen in *Paul of Aegina, book 6, chapter 38*, where he exactly describes the method of incision (which *Paré* also repeats from the same source in the cited place). However, he warns that we should abstain from an *Aneurysm* that occupies the armpits, the groin, and the neck, etc.

<margin>
A similar [observa]tion in Jul. Caes. Claudinus.
</margin>
Connect this with *Julius Caesar Claudinus, Consultation 67*, where he proposes a similar case of an *Aneurysm* born from the occasion of a bloodletting. Finally, he also approves of astringent and hardening medicines, where he lists the *Cypress Plaster of Aetius*, the *Iron Dross Cerate of Montagnana* <note>original: "Cerotum de Scoria Ferri," a waxy ointment made from the byproduct of iron smelting</note>, elm bark, sanicle, and a fomentation from a decoction of iron dross with a new sponge, etc. *Paré* in the cited place and *Rondelet à Fonseca, part 2, consultation 53*, recommend a *plaster of fresh cheese with houseleek juice*. To these, the latter also adds salt of prunella <note>original: "salem prunellae," a purified form of potassium nitrate</note> or nitre purified with sulfur, one drachm mixed with two drachms of plantain juice.

<margin>
Lethal outcome of Arteriotomy.
</margin>
A lethal outcome of this kind of arteriotomy <term>arteriotomy: the surgical cutting of an artery</term> in the arm, with a subsequent aneurysm, can be seen in *Libavius in the Medical Chest*...

BOOK FOUR OF PART II.

<margin>
Internal aneurysms in certain cases.
</margin>
...in the *Medical Epistles of Hornungius*, where gangrene set in following a spontaneous hemorrhage, and death followed. Both authors and experience confirm that internal <term>aneurysms: the swelling or dilation of an artery</term> are more often incurable, especially in those who have undergone many treatments of sweating and fluxing to cure the <term>French Disease: a historical term for syphilis</term>. This is due to the blood becoming thinned and overheated, which distends the major arteries into an unnatural width. *Paré* <note>Ambroise Paré (c. 1510–1590), a pioneering French surgeon</note> discovered this in the corpse of a certain tailor, who had died suddenly when an <term>aneurysm</term> of the venous artery <note>In the medical terminology of the time, the "venous artery" referred to the pulmonary vein</note> unexpectedly ruptured. The attending physician here in the French Hospital noted a similar case in recent years involving a young man who, shortly after being admitted for treatment, died suddenly of suffocation. Since the causes of his sudden death were in doubt, the chest was opened after death on my advice. A significant <term>aneurysm</term> tumor was discovered in the Great Artery <note>The aorta</note> near the jugular; the boiling and heat of the blood had provided the occasion for the suffocation. Let the reader add the examples proposed by *Dodoens* in chapter 5 of his *Medical Observations*, as well as those recorded by our own *Marcellus Donatus* near the end of the fifth book of his *Wonderful Histories*.

# OBSERVATION II.

## On the Incision of the Scrotum in a Jaundiced and Dropsical Patient, where many singular things are proposed.

A most noble and energetic man, N. N., had suffered for about three years from <term>Icterus: jaundice, a yellowing of the skin and eyes caused by bile</term>. He was vexed by daily obstructions of the bowels, as the stimulating bile was dispersed through the habit of his body; otherwise, at 26 years of age, he sought medical aid. At the end of May in the year 1623, a plan was shared with my colleague, *Dr. Sebastian Stramayer*. After the primary passages <note>The digestive tract</note> were evacuated, a decoction of an old rooster was prescribed for the sake of digestion, in imitation of *Quercetanus* <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician who advocated for chemical medicines</note>, along with a digestive powder, as follows:
<margin>The first digestion.</margin>
> <insert>Recipe</insert> <note>original: "℞," the traditional symbol for a medical prescription</note> Cream of Tartar, 2 drams.
> Starch of Bryony, 1 dram.
> Magistery <note>A fine powder precipitated from a solution</note> of Red Coral and Pearl, 1 dram of each.
> Mix and divide into 14 parts.

In this manner, the preparation of the humors was carried out for 14 days. Consequently, the regular use of the following pills was ordered, which—
<margin>Evacuation.</margin>

### BOOK FOUR OF PART II.

...I concluded that the material of those tubercles <note>Small, knotty swellings or nodules often found on organs during historical dissections or felt through the skin</note> was a thicker bile, joined with a stickier blood, which the tendinous parts draw in for nourishment. 

<margin>
To what end the decoction of wood was prescribed.
</margin>
Hence we began to consider a decoction of Wood <note>Guaiacum, also known as "Holy Wood," imported from the Americas and used to treat "blockages" and various chronic diseases</note>, seeing as by its benefit, the stubborn obstructions of the mesentery <note>The membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</note> and of the liver itself might—over time—be corrected by cutting into, thinning, cleansing, and evacuating them. This is done not without a strengthening of the internal organs, which a friendly astringent quality, most abundant in the bark, provides. Moreover, so that a more successful operation of the Decoction of Guaiacum Wood with the Barks might be expected, we thought it best to prepare and evacuate that matter which seemed rooted around the mesentery.

<margin>
Preparation before the use of the decoction.
</margin>
The preparation for digestion was as follows:
> Take: Magistery of Vitriolated Tartar <note>original: "Magist. Tart. vitriolati"; potassium sulfate, used as a digestive salt</note> 2 <term>drachms: a unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</term>.
> Starch of Cuckoopint and Bryony, 1 <term>drachm</term> of each.
> Magistery of Red Coral 1 and a half <term>drachms</term>.
> Mix and divide into 8 parts, to be taken each day with a decoction of chicory root.

Following this digestive preparation was the following purgative:
> Take: Croll’s Extract of Panchymagogue <note>original: "Extr. Panchymagogi Crolly"; a famous "all-humor-purging" remedy formulated by Oswald Croll</note>.
> Crystalline or sweetened Mercury <note>original: "Mercurij Crystallini vel dulcific."; likely calomel (mercurous chloride)</note>, 1 <term>scruple: a small weight, about 1.3 grams</term> of each.
> Diagridium <note>A preparation of Scammony, a harsh plant-based laxative</note> prepared with oil of fennel & Spirit of Vitriol, 6 grains.
> Make into 9 pills with syrup of apples.

Label: *The pills to be taken all at once.* <note>original German: "Pilulen auff ein mahl"</note>

However, so great was the obstruction of the Mesenteric veins and the Liver itself, that the evacu-

<column-break/>

-ations did not respond as desired, nor in proportion to the strength of the purging qualities. For this reason, around the end of October, we indeed turned to the decoction of Wood, yet in such a way that by the addition of Golden Diaphoretic Sulfur <note>original: "Sulphuris Aurati diaphoretici"; a compound of antimony used to induce sweating</note>, we might attempt to increase its opening, thinning, and dispersing power in this manner:

<margin>
The prescribed decoction of wood.
</margin>
> Take: Guaiacum Wood 1 <term>pound</term>.
> Bark of the same 4 <term>ounces</term>.
> Make a decoction in 16 <term>pounds</term> [of water].
> Boil the water to a third for a sweat-inducer.
> Take the remains, add:
> Shaved licorice 1 <term>ounce</term>.
> Seeds of fennel and Anise.
> Sharp cinnamon, 5 <term>drachms</term> of each.
> Make a decoction in 20 <term>pounds</term> of water for a daily drink.

In administering the sweat-inducing draught, always in the morning, we added 10 grains of Golden Diaphoretic Sulfur. After continuing these for eight days, a tensing pain in the lowest part of the belly followed, until, as the pain subsided, a tenacious, ash-colored matter, like pitch, was copiously discharged through the bowels. At this point, we decided that nature should be further assisted by the use of an enema, frequently applied, for the preparation of which the following were sent:

<margin>
The effects of the decoction used.
</margin>
> Take: Roots of Marshmallow and white lilies, 2 <term>ounces</term> of each.
> Fennel, Eryngo <note>Sea Holly</note>, Parsley, 1 <term>drachm</term> of each.
> Herbs of Pellitory-of-the-wall, Mercury herb, Veronica, and Fumitory, 4 <term>handfuls</term> of each.
> Flowers of Chamomile and Elder, 2 <term>handfuls</term> of each.

### BOOK FOUR OF PART II.

...of vitriol <note>original: "trioli"</note> as much as suffices to produce a pleasant acidity.

<margin>A persistent hemorrhage follows.</margin>
Despite using these treatments, the heat and thirst nevertheless persisted until March 1624. This was perhaps because the blood was made boiling by bile, which was in turn produced copiously and not secreted through the ordinary channels. Because of this, around the 1st of March, a violent nosebleed seized the patient. The blood flowed at short intervals until the third day; it was copious and for the most part "bilious" <note>yellowish or thin, indicating an imbalance of the humors</note>. On the 4th of March, I was called and arrived, at which time a dripping of blood was again arising toward evening.

<margin>The cause of that hemorrhage.</margin>
Since this symptom occurred partly from the acrimony <note>sharpness or irritating quality</note> of the blood and partly from the weakness of the "retentive faculty" <note>the body's supposed ability to hold onto necessary fluids</note>, I soon proceeded to the following remedies (as the common aids otherwise used to stop blood were of no benefit). However, I first gave a prognosis: either the patient would soon perish from depleted strength, or dropsy <note>edema or swelling caused by fluid buildup</note> would follow. Externally, I immediately applied a Compound of Sperniola <note>A preparation likely derived from frog spawn, used as a cooling agent to stop bleeding</note> dissolved in Frog-spawn Water to the temples, the forehead, and the nasal cavities. Internally, I administered 6 grains of Opiate Laudanum with Magisteries <note>precipitated chemical extracts</note>. By these, an inclination toward sleep and a reduction of the hemorrhage were procured, although it was not yet totally stopped.

<margin>To temper the heat of the blood.</margin>
Therefore, on the 5th of March, I tried to temper the heat of the blood mass, first prescribing an Enema, which consisted of:

<column-break/>

Take: Roots of Chicory and Dandelion, 1 ½ <term>ounces: approximately 28 grams</term> of each.
Herbs of Sorrel, Endive, and Chicory, 2 <term>handfuls: a "manipulus" or the amount a hand can hold</term> of each.
Flowers of Chamomile and Roses, 1 ½ <term>handfuls</term> of each.
The 4 greater cold seeds <note>usually cucumber, gourd, melon, and watermelon</note>, ½ <term>drachm: approximately 3.9 grams</term> of each.
Let them be cut up. <note>original: "f. Kreuter pro decocto aliquot Enematum"</note> Make into herbs for a decoction for several enemas.
Take: Electuary of Hiera <note>A traditional "holy" laxative made of aloes and spices</note>, 3 <term>ounces</term>. <note>original: "f. Latwerg zu 6. Clystieren"</note> Make into an electuary for 6 enemas.
Take: Oil of Violets and Chamomile, 3 <term>ounces</term> of each. Mix.

<margin>To strengthen the powers.</margin>
For the sake of the patient’s strength, "Pearl Water" was of great benefit, prepared as follows:
Take: Water of Chicory and Sorrel, 6 <term>ounces</term> of each.
Black cherries, 1 ½ <term>ounces</term>.
Magistery of Red Coral, 1 ½ <term>drachms</term>.
Pearls, ½ <term>drachm</term>.
Manus Christi with pearls <note>literally "Hand of Christ," a medicinal sugar confection or lozenge used as a restorative</note>, 1 ½ <term>drachms</term>. Mix.

<margin>For the thirst and heat.</margin>
To temper the thirst and heat, we allowed a decoction of chicory root with coral syrup, and the acidity of citron and lemons. However, as the dripping of blood occasionally arose again, toward evening of the same day I administered the aforementioned Opiate Laudanum (7 grains) for a second time. After its use, the blood was stopped, and sleep followed at intervals.

In this way, after correcting that horrible symptom, as I was about to depart for home, I left the following advice dated March 7, 1624, for the most noble patient, namely concerning the hemorrhage...

### CONCERNING CERTAIN SURGICAL MATTERS.

<margin>Plan for the future.</margin>
Now that the hemorrhage <note>original: "hæmorrhagia"</note> has been corrected and the patient's strength has been recovered to some extent, we must primarily focus on the following: 1. that nature be aided through strengthening medicines <note>original: "corroborantia"</note>; 2. that the bowels be kept loose daily; 3. that the imbalance of the liver <note>original: "jecoris"</note>, the spleen <note>original: "Lienis"</note>, and the entire mass of the blood be altered, with the "offending matter" <note>the excess fluids or "humors" believed to cause the illness</note> sent out through the urinary passages as much as possible; and finally 4. that any more serious symptoms be met with suitable remedies.

<margin>Regarding point 1.</margin>
As to the first point, the dietary regimen will be of the greatest benefit. Use foods that are easy to digest, not too hot, and not sharp or irritating. This includes broths of chicken or capon, served alone or with a dissolved egg; a decoction of hulled barley; and decoctions of plums, peas, veal, beef, and so on. For meats, choose chicken, capon, calf, or lamb, prepared either by boiling or by gentle roasting. For side dishes, Italian prunes, dried apples, Damascus plums, hulled barley, and similar items will be suitable. Soft-boiled eggs will also do no harm, as will gudgeon <note>a small freshwater fish</note> if well-cooked with a broth of fresh butter. The daily drink should be a decoction of Sorrel Root <note>original: "Rad. Acetosæ"</note> prepared with burnt hartshorn <note>original: "C.C. usto"; the carbonized antlers of a deer, used as a cooling absorbent</note>; for the sake of variety, a decoction of Tormentil Root <note>a plant used for its astringent properties to prevent further bleeding</note> may be substituted. Occasionally, a decoction of Parsley Root sweetened with sugar may also be drunk.

To suppress the warm vapors rising upward,

<column-break/>

the use of the following decoction will also be helpful: Take 6 ounces of the best sugar and boil it in a measure of water until it is reduced by a quarter. After it is removed from the fire, add half a sliced lemon. Occasionally, with the same intent, a vitriolated conserve of roses <note>rose petals preserved with sugar and a small amount of oil of vitriol/sulfuric acid for acidity</note> may be diluted with the sorrel decoction. However, wine should be avoided entirely.

<margin>Regarding point 2.</margin>
As to the second point: to ensure the bowels are kept open daily, a soothing, softening, and moderately cooling enema <note>original: "Clyster"</note> should be conveniently repeated every other day. This is made from a decoction of the roots of Chicory, sorrel, mallow, melilot, and chamomile flowers, etc., with half an ounce of the "Sacred Bitter" Electuary <note>original: "Elect. Hier. S." or Hiera Picra, a traditional laxative</note>, moisturizing oils, and two egg yolks.

<margin>Regarding point 3.</margin>
As to the third point, for the sake of tempering the liver, the spleen, and the entire mass of the blood, a broth made from a decoction of Chicory roots should be taken twice daily. For greater strengthening, add either 10 grains of Magistery of Coral <note>coral dissolved in acid and precipitated into a fine powder, thought to strengthen the heart and blood</note>, or half an ounce of vitriolated rose conserve, or some syrup of lemon, or sour and sweet pomegranate, or Rob of Currants <note>a "Rob" is a thick fruit syrup</note>, and so on. Care must be taken, however, that the acidity of the flavor does not become excessive and provoke a cough.

<margin>Regarding point 4.</margin>
As to the fourth point, a decoction of Chicory, Fennel, and Parsley roots, prepared in equal parts, will promote the removal of the offending matter through the urinary passages. Finally, should a recurrence of the hemorrhage happen—which God forbid—the internal use of Opiated Laudanum will help, while externally the Compound of Sperniola <note>a cooling preparation often made from frog spawn</note> should be used.

# FOURTH BOOK OF PART II.

...dissolved with Frog’s Spawn Water <note>original: "Aq. Spermatis ranarum"; used in the 17th century for its cooling and soothing properties</note>, applied both to the region of the liver and to the forehead and temples with linen cloths, in the form of a compress <note>original: "epithemata"</note>. Against the failing of strength, let a **Cordial Water** with a Magistery of Corals and pearls <note>a "magistery" refers to a refined chemical precipitate thought to contain the essential virtues of the substance</note> be ready at hand. Against dryness of the tongue, the juice of crabs <note>original: "succus cancrorum"</note> pressed with Plantain water and Houseleek <note>original: "sempervivum"</note>, as well as a mucilage of quince seeds extracted in rose water, then alternately wiped with sloe water <note>original: "aq. prunellæ"; used for throat and mouth ailments</note> prepared with nitre <note>potassium nitrate</note>, will be suitable. Externally, let **Fuchs's Odoriferous Water** <note>a scented medicinal water named after the physician Leonhart Fuchs</note>, mixed with a little rose vinegar, be frequently applied to the pulses and the region of the heart with linen cloths. For the kidneys, let a **camphorated rose ointment** mixed with oil of sweet almonds and chamomile be rubbed on to prevent nephritic pain <note>pain associated with the kidneys, such as stones or colic</note>.

<margin>For obstruction of the bowels, dryness of the mouth, and a dry cough.</margin>
Having left these instructions behind, I was informed shortly afterward that his strength had indeed been moderately recovered; however, he was greatly afflicted by a looming daily obstruction of the bowels, as well as a parched mouth and a persistent, empty cough. Since it cannot happen otherwise than that the bilious wastes—not being rejected through the usual pathways of the intestines but instead committed to the whole mass of the blood—render nature more sluggish in expelling them due to the absence of the excretory faculty's stimulus; therefore, in addition to enemas <note>original: "Enemata"</note> administered on alternate days, we also prescribed a **Laxative Wine** around March 13, 1624.

Fennel, 1 ounce.
Purified Tartar, 2 ounces.

Small raisins, 10 ounces.

Therefore, being called back again on March 18, I prescribed a liniment and a plaster to correct the unnatural disposition of the liver.

℟. Camphorated Rose Ointment, 1 ounce.

℟. Sandalwood Cerate <note>a waxy ointment</note> and Galen’s Cooling Ointment <note>original: "Infrigidatis Galeni"; a traditional formula for "cold cream"</note>, 1.5 ounces each.

Despite all these measures being diligently applied, the desired outcome did not follow. Although many "digestions" <note>treatments to "ripen" or prepare humors for evacuation</note> had been performed, the evil remained rooted in the **mesentery** <note>the membrane attaching the intestines to the abdominal wall</note> and neighboring parts, maintaining its long-standing grip. Thus, neither the enemas nor the stronger prescribed purgatives seemed to draw anything out, except for those daily accumulations of excess waste from the "first concoction" <note>the initial stage of digestion in the stomach</note> found in the primary passages. Therefore, it is no wonder that even the diuretics, though otherwise quite effective, achieved nothing, as the intermediate passages were clearly blocked. For a while, therefore, we allowed nature some rest to restore the patient's strength, frequently using 6 or 8 drops of **Paracelsus’s Elixir of Property** <note>a famous tonic of aloes, myrrh, and saffron</note> with an appropriate liquid; often using vitriolated <note>treated with acid/sulfuric spirits</note> conserve of roses with Magistery of coral and pearls; and often a **tragema** <note>a medicinal powder or confection, often taken after meals</note> was taken, which [was]:

Upon the slightest scratching, first a bilious serum and soon bilious blood would emerge. ### ON CERTAIN SURGICAL MATTERS.

It was considered a favorable omen on June 11, 1626, that an opening was made with a scalpel in the lower part of the right side by Johann Jacob Merck, a most skilled <term>lithotomist</term> <note>a surgeon specializing in cutting for bladder stones, though here acting as a general surgeon</note>. This was followed by a flow of fluid, resembling the water used to wash raw meat, to the measure of 2 <note>units likely being pints or pounds</note>. From this point, the immense gas, the terrible tension and pain, and other symptoms soon abated, so that the patient felt himself snatched from the very jaws of <term>Orcus</term> <note>the Roman god of the underworld; the patient felt he had escaped certain death</note>. Externally, a plaster made of <term>litharge</term> <note>lead monoxide</note>, vinegar, and a suitable mixture of rose oil was effectively applied to treat the skin irritation and the threat of inflammation. The surgical opening was kept open by a <term>pledget</term> <note>a small wad of absorbent material or a wick</note>, through which a great quantity of bilious serum flowed out. In this way, the severe pains of the abdomen subsided; however, the feet nevertheless swelled up to a miraculous degree. Upon these feet, blisters arose and burst of their own accord, also pouring out a copious amount of fluid.

<margin>Scarification of the feet.</margin>
Therefore, we performed <term>scarifications</term> <note>the practice of making small, shallow incisions in the skin to drain fluid</note> on the shins at various times. The evacuation of fluid succeeded so gradually that the patient—who previously could scarcely be moved from one bed to another by six strong men lifting him—was now able to walk back and forth through the heated room without any support. His feet shrank so much they became almost emaciated.

<margin>The Outcome.</margin>
Although the <term>dropsical</term> <note>related to edema or the buildup of fluid in the body</note> swelling of the belly did not subside, his strength nonetheless began to return in some measure. His appetite for food remained constant; he consumed a great variety of foods, both healthy and unhealthy, especially summer fruits in abundance. He also drank goat’s milk whey until he was satisfied. Living in this condition, the sufferer survived through July, August, September, October, November, and most of December, using only those remedies that assisted with his daily bowel movements, until finally, near the end of the year 1626, he suddenly exchanged life for death.

<column-break/>

Although nothing would have been more in accordance with my wishes than to understand the exact state of the internal organs through a skilled dissection, this could not be done due to the distance of the location. However, I was informed by the attending surgeon, Johann Jacob Kielkopf of Geislingen, in a letter dated December 28.

<margin>Post-mortem Anatomy.</margin>
He reported that after first lightly opening the abdomen, ten Wurttemberg measures <note>a "Maß" was approximately 1.8 liters</note> of bilious, serous fluid were extracted. Afterward, the liver came into view, <term>scirrhous</term> <note>hardened and fibrous, often indicating cancer or advanced cirrhosis</note> and hardened, and as dry as wood consumed by rot. <note>original: "die Leber ist gantz hart gewesen / darein zuschneiden / wie in ein faul holtz"</note> The spleen, however, was softer <note>original: "das Milß gar waich"</note>. I believe that because the spleen was in this state, it was still performing some kind of "blood-making" <note>the historical belief that the spleen could take over the liver's role in creating blood</note> in place of the liver during that time. Thus, the condition of the spleen was not found to be unnatural. The <term>mesenteric veins</term> <note>veins that drain blood from the intestines</note> were filled with a substance like glue. <note>original: "die kleine Krößadern beschaffen" — the small mesenteric veins were thus constituted...</note>

<margin>Certain doubts</margin>
From what has been said, certain doubts arise:

<margin>1.</margin> First, is it not strange that the stronger <term>purgatives</term> <note>laxatives intended to "cleanse" the body of bad humors</note> so often achieved so little in their operation? Or was it because they attacked nothing more than the contents of the primary passages, while the intermediate paths were completely blocked by hardened, sticky, <term>tartarous</term> <note>in early modern medicine, "tartar" referred to stony or crusty metabolic waste that built up in the organs, similar to the scale in a wine barrel</note> matter?

<margin>2.</margin> II. Is it not strange that, even after the desired effect was achieved following the <term>cure of the wood</term> <note>likely referring to treatment with *Guaiacum* or "Holy Wood," used for chronic obstructions and "French pox"</note>, a more severe relapse followed in a short space of time from a new outpouring of bile? Was it because the liver was <term>scirrhous</term> <note>hardened or tumorous</note>, and thus the spleen produced blood overflowing with much bile, as will also be made clear from the following observation?

<margin>3.</margin> III. Is it not strange that a long-lasting and copious <term>hemorrhage</term> <note>bleeding</note>, recurring so many times, actually brought some relief? Was it because the entire mass of blood was unburdened in this way of the vast amount of bile mixed into it?

<margin>4.</margin> IV. Is it not strange how the matter of the blood reached the blood-making spleen when the <term>mesentery</term> <note>the membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall and contains blood vessels</note> was completely obstructed and the liver was not drawing it in? Was it because it was taken up through closer paths—namely, the splenic veins inserted into the bottom of the stomach?

<margin>5.</margin> V. Is it not strange how the strengths of the heart were preserved for so long, even though the blood-making process itself was quite unhealthy? Was it because the <term>chylification</term> <note>the process of turning food into chyle during digestion</note> also refreshed the heart with its vaporous exhalation, as it was strong enough in respect to the

<column-break/>

suffering subject?

<margin>6.</margin> VI. Is it not strange that an incision of the <term>scrotum</term> <note>the physician is likely discussing the drainage of fluid from dropsy (edema) which often settled in the lower extremities and scrotum</note> is less dangerous than an incision of the abdomen? Is it because this "solution of continuity" <note>a surgical term for a wound or break in the skin</note> is further removed from the vital principle? Or because the excess fluid is not strained here immediately from the cavity of the abdomen, but rather by a sort of <term>transudation</term> <note>oozing through a membrane</note> through the fleshy and membranous substance of the abdominal muscles?

<margin>7.</margin> VII. Finally, it is not at all strange that the noble medications, though repeated so often, achieved nothing at all. Was it because a confirmed <term>scirrhus</term> of the liver—a total hardening of it—along with completely blocked vessels of the mesentery, was discovered after death?

...possessing a squalid and lean body, with his bowels being more constricted and passing deeply red, bilious urine in the manner of those suffering from fever, frequently exhibiting signs of putrid corruption. For several years, he was afflicted by stomach belching, bloody spitting, and bleeding gums; in the meantime, he was several times afflicted by a bloody flux of the bowels and once even by a continuous fever, preceded by a swelling in the groin. Finally, in the preceding year, a <term>dropsical</term> <note>relating to edema or "hydrops," the accumulation of fluid in the body's tissues or cavities</note> swelling of the belly and feet came upon him. However, although through suitable means—and especially a treatment appropriate for <term>Scurvy</term> <note>original: "Scorbutum"; a disease caused by vitamin C deficiency, though in the 17th century it was often used as a broader diagnosis for various systemic "impurities" of the blood</note> during the spring of the current year, 1627—the said symptoms were eased so much that he seemed to be in excellent health through the preceding summer, nevertheless, as the winter season approached, signs of a relapse began to show themselves. On the following day, for certain reasons and in the presence of Doctor Antonius Rüber, Mr. Andreas Knobloch, and Mr. Johann Daniel Dieterich, I opened the abdomen of the deceased. Soon, the stomach and intestines presented themselves as inflated and blackish, smeared on the inside as if with cobbler’s ink. The kidneys and lungs were in a natural state. The liver was entirely <term>scirrhous</term> <note>original: "scirrhosum"; meaning the tissue had become hardened or scarred, often indicating cirrhosis or a tumor</note> and lumpy, both inside and out, and it showed neither vessels nor blood. The spleen, however, was three times larger than it usually is <term>under natural conditions</term> <note>original: "s. n." or "secundum naturam," meaning according to the normal course of nature</note>, and it was seen to be perfectly healthy, with the <term>parenchyma</term> <note>the functional tissue of an organ as opposed to its connective or supporting framework</note> of the liver being a deep red color and reflecting a fleshy substance. The <term>mesentery</term> <note>the fold of membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall and holds them in place</note> appeared quite glandular, lumpy, and thick, with the <term>mesaraic vessels</term> <note>the mesenteric veins which carry blood from the intestines to the portal vein of the liver</note> being obliterated due to the effusion of blood into the parts of the stomach and intestines.
