### BOOK FOUR OF PART II.

### RESOLUTION.

A MAN of mature age, exceeding his thirtieth year, of a **melancholic** <term>melancholic</term> <note>In the humoral theory of medicine, a melancholic constitution was dominated by "black bile," often resulting in a thin, dry frame and a somber temperament.</note> bodily constitution, whose physical condition was **squalid and lean**; this occurred because the nutritive faculty was deprived of suitable nourishment, inasmuch as the entire blood mass took on an **atrabiliary** <term>atrabiliary</term> <note>From the Latin "atra bilis" (black bile); refers to a state where the blood is thick, dark, and melancholic.</note> quality in such individuals. From this follows a **constricted bowel**, because the stimulus for the excretion of bile is not separated into the intestines in the proper manner due to a **languishing liver**, but is rather left in the blood and scorched. The **bilious urine** is for the said reason: **deeply red in the manner of those suffering from fever**, not because of febrile heat, but rendered so by the weakness of the liver. An example of this matter may be seen in *Dodoens* <note>Rembert Dodoens (1517–1585) was a famous Flemish physician and botanist.</note> *Observation 31*. For this reason, *Akakia* <note>Martin Akakia (1500–1551) was a French physician known for his commentaries on Galen.</note> adds in the additions to *Book 1 of Galen's Art of Curing* that red urine also occurs when, through weakness of the liver or the veins, serum or red discharge is emitted along with the urine. This frequently exhibits signs of putrefaction, yet without thirst, because a **scorbutic** <note>Related to scurvy (vitamin C deficiency), which at the time was often blamed for various "impurities" in the blood.</note> infection of the blood concurred. This is a characteristic of that disease, as may be seen in *Eugalenus* <note>Severinus Eugalenus was a 16th-century author whose work on scurvy was highly influential.</note> *page 33*, that it sometimes exhibits remarkable signs of putrefaction in the urine even if the sufferers complain of no febrile thirst whatsoever and perform

<column-break/>

the usual duties of life. **Belches of the stomach were present**, specifically empty ones, familiar to those with hypochondriac disorders at the time when the stomach's digestion is usually completed. There was **bloody spitting**, occurring both because of the separation of serous blood from the spongy flesh of the gums, and also because the bloody serum of the blood mass was poured out toward the stomach due to the weakness of the liver, and was afterwards gradually communicated to the throat. By this reasoning, *Hippocrates in the Coan Prognostics* declares that much bloody sputum in those with liver disease is immediately fatal in these words: <note>original Greek: "οἷσιν ἡ πατικοῖσι πολὺ πτύαλον, ὀλέθριον εὐθέως"</note> *In those with liver disease, much spitting is immediately fatal.* *Jacotius* <note>Desiderius Jacotius was a 16th-century French physician and commentator on ancient medical texts.</note> in *Book 6, Section 2, Commentary 1, Aphorism 21*, says this happens in those with liver disease for three reasons: namely, weakness of the veins, bad quality of the blood, and finally, a fullness relative to one's strength. Note, however, that *Hippocrates* adds "much" (*polu*), by which a confirmed illness and one placed in the greatest danger is distinguished from a light, long-lasting spitting, in which they do not die "immediately" (*eutheos*), or suddenly. For this reason, in the present patient, such **bloody spitting with bleeding of the gums** was troublesome for several years, as the scorbutic infection gradually occupied the blood mass. By reason of this, the more tender flesh of the gums is affected before the rest by heat, itching, swelling, and also by the putrefaction of the corrupted blood, exhibiting a copious oozing, whence the bloody and copious sputum...

In the meantime, a bloody discharge of the bowel resembling **dysentery** <term>dysentery</term> <note>A severe inflammation of the intestines resulting in diarrhea with blood.</note> occasionally attacked him. This was composed of thick and foul blood, poured out in great quantity through the ends of the veins into the cavities of the intestines. For this reason, the blood was discharged separately from the excrement and without **griping pains** <term>tormina</term> <note>A historical term for severe, twisting intestinal cramps.</note>; it is by this sign that such a bloody discharge in **scorbutic patients** <term>Scorbuticorum</term> <note>Those suffering from scurvy, a disease then associated with "corrupt" blood and internal bleeding.</note> is distinguished from others. Consequently, the blood drawn by bloodletting appeared leaden, leaning toward a greenish hue, and was seen to be thinned by a great deal of leaden-colored serum. This was preceded by a swelling in the groin, as if in the place of an **emunctory** <note>An organ or area of the body—like the groin or armpit—where "superfluous" or "corrupt" humors were thought to be naturally expelled.</note>, where the offending thicker matter had collected, the force of nature having propelled the superfluities toward the exterior. Finally, he was afflicted by a swelling of the belly and an inflation of the feet toward the autumn of the year 1625. This was clearly a species of **dropsy** <term>Hydropis</term> <note>General swelling caused by excess fluid; a common diagnosis for various types of organ failure.</note> which seemed to resemble part **tympanites** <term>Tympanitis</term> <note>A type of dropsy where the abdomen is stretched tight and hollow-sounding, like a drum, due to gas.</note> and part **anasarca** <term>Anasarca</term> <note>Widespread swelling of the skin and underlying tissues.</note>. This was not without suspicion of **scurvy** <term>Scorbutus</term>, for which reason we thought that the malignancy of the scurvy must be addressed at the same time while warding off the evil. Therefore, in the springtime of the current year, I applied a treatment appropriate for scurvy for the duration of a month, by the effect of which he seemed to be very well throughout the entire summer. I hoped for a repetition of that treatment in the autumn,

<margin>
And of the arteries.
</margin>
It is likely that such dangerous vomiting is stirred up not only by the opening of the veins, but even when the mouths of the arteries are filled. This is known both from <term>direct observation</term> <note>original: "autopsia," here meaning visual inspection of the clinical evidence.</note> of arterial blood being cast out along with venous blood, and from the sudden loss of strength by which the vigor of the heart is dissolved. We do indeed concede, as **Galen** <note>A 2nd-century Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> suggests in Book 5 of *On the Affected Parts*, Chapter 5, that blood can be cast up through vomiting from the liver and spleen. Nevertheless, no one will deny that when nature carries out such an expulsion because of a greatly irritated morbid matter, a rejection of arterial blood—the "treasure of life"—also occurs, more or less, from the heart through the arteries. However, we should exclude the observations of those in whom a more robust vital faculty prevents the effusion of arterial blood made <term>all at once</term> <note>original: "athroos," meaning in a single mass or a sudden burst.</note>. We read that such people have sometimes been restored, yet in such a way that most later contracted **cachexia** <term>cachexia</term> <note>A state of physical wasting and malnutrition.</note> and **dropsy** <term>dropsy</term> <note>An old term for edema, or the accumulation of fluid in the body's tissues.</note>, because the organs of the **second digestion** <note>In the humoral system, the liver was thought to perform a "second digestion" to turn food into blood.</note> were greatly weakened; an example of this vomiting can be seen in the works of **Forestus** <note>Petrus Forestus (1521–1597), a prominent Dutch physician.</note>, Book 16, Observation 24. But the condition is rendered more grave, and the danger itself is increased, when black, pitch-like stools are joined with the vomiting of blood; hence

<margin>
Vomiting of blood with black stools is worse.
</margin>

Here, **Jacotius** <note>Jean Jacot, a 16th-century French commentator on Hippocrates.</note> adds in Book 4 of the *Coan Prognostics*, Section 2, Commentary 1, Aphorism 5, that a discharge of this kind occurs when the spleen does not pro-

perly purge the liver and the blood. From this, that muddy matter—long retained in the liver or the **mesentery** <term>mesentery</term> <note>The fold of membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall.</note>—is sometimes corrupted by the delay and becomes perfectly **black bile** <term>black bile</term> <note>One of the four humors; it was believed that an excess or corruption of this fluid caused various diseases.</note>. Sometimes, before such corruption, it is excreted because the bodily faculty is overwhelmed and irritated, being unable to contain the superfluities any longer. Indeed, such black matter mixed with the vomiting of blood indicates an extreme loss of strength, according to Hippocrates: <term>black vomit is troublesome</term> <note>original: "emetos melas, ponēros."</note>. This is because, according to **Duretus** <note>Louis Duret (1527–1586), a French royal physician.</note> in Book 4 of the *Coan Prognostics*, Aphorism 25, black vomit and black stools arise from the same matter and from the same sources. However, this is not contradicted by what **Rodericus Fonseca** <note>A 16th-century Portuguese physician.</note> reports in Part 2, Observation 86, concerning a young man of a somewhat dark complexion, with a weaker stomach and an intensely hot liver, who vomited a black, thick, and tasteless juice every single month for many years, until his declining age. At that time, the juice became acidic, which brought on a <term>dog-like appetite</term> <note>original: "caninam appetentiam," an insatiable or morbid hunger.</note>, and rendered the man so emaciated that he was finally consumed by **wasting** <term>tabes</term> <note>A gradual wasting away of the body, often used to describe tuberculosis or general physical decay.</note>. In this case, something must be attributed to the strength of nature, which immediately separated the collected black matter until the nutritive power became too weak and insufficient; then the offending matter acquired a sharpness and further hindered the work of nutrition in his declining years, as **Cardanus** <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath and physician.</note> notes in Book 4...

# ON CERTAIN SURGICAL MATTERS.

<margin>The reasoning behind the prognosis.</margin>
Aphorism 21 in the commentary on Pietro Maria Locarno <note>original: "Petro Maria Locareno"</note> reports that a vast quantity of dreg-filled blood, over 20 pounds, was once ejected by a patient who nevertheless survived several times, until later, with a weakened liver, he fell into <term>dropsy</term> <note>An old term for edema, or the accumulation of fluid in the body's tissues.</note>. Having carefully considered these and similar cases, we stated that our patient was in mortal danger from the very onset of these symptoms, just as the outcome itself proved. Since I had observed various symptoms of <term>scurvy</term> <note>original: "Scorbuti"; a disease then attributed to "salty" or "tartarous" blood.</note> over so many years, I easily conjectured that the mass of blood was widely overflowing with dissolved <term>scorbutic tartar</term> <note>In early modern medicine, "tartar" referred to stony or gritty deposits in the humors, thought to cause obstructions.</note>. This occurred as "black bile" <note>original: "atrabilariis"</note> wastes collected copiously around the mesentery and spleen, and suddenly fermented with an inherent malignancy, such that the vomiting of blood accompanied by black stools indicated a fatal end.

<margin>First Doubt.</margin>
It is truly a wonder that when the body was opened <note>original: "aperto cadavere," referring to an autopsy.</note>, the kidneys were found to be entirely healthy, even though the patient had complained of back pain for many years. Was it because the burnt, black-bile matter had gradually collected in the veins of the mesentery and spleen, and by its malignancy affected the nervous parts where the <term>mesentery</term> <note>The membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall.</note> is connected to the spine?

<margin>Second Doubt.</margin>
It is a wonder, since the liver was completely <term>scirrhous</term> <note>Hardened or scarred, often referring to what we now call cirrhosis.</note>, how the patient could survive so long. Was it because the spleen <note>original: "Lien"</note> was three times larger than usual and of a healthy substance, taking on the role of an organ of <term>sanguification</term> <note>The process of "making blood," which ancient medicine primarily attributed to the liver.</note>, by which reason the blood was made by the spleen

<column-break/>

instead of the liver? From this, it is no wonder that the blood produced was of a less "praiseworthy" <note>original: "laudabilem," meaning healthy or properly balanced in humoral terms.</note> quality, insofar as the spleen and the gallbladder usually make the liver's blood-making better by separating out foreign materials. But when the spleen makes blood alone, this does not happen; thus, the blood produced is impure, just as is clear from the preceding observation, where blood—though of poor quality—was produced by the strength of the spleen, and by its sharp acidity caused frequent nosebleeds. *Thus **Coiter** <note>Volcher Coiter (1534–1576), a pioneering Dutch anatomist and physician.</note> in his Surgical and Anatomical Observations* noted a spleen larger than usual in the corpse of a man whose liver was putrid and full of pus, while the overall condition of the body remained "melancholic" <note>Dominated by black bile.</note> due to the spleen's blood. *The same author observed a <term>vomica</term> <note>An abscess or cavity filled with pus.</note>, and a quite large one at that, in the lowest part of the liver, with the remaining parts healthy, where undoubtedly the whole body was preserved for a time through the blood-making of the spleen. Thus in **Dodoens** <note>Rembert Dodoens (1517–1585), a Flemish physician and botanist.</note>, chapter 28 of his Observations,* an ulcer is noted on the rounded part of the liver, which for a long time caused severe pain in the right <term>hypochondrium</term> <note>The upper region of the abdomen, just below the ribs.</note>. In *chapter 30*, he also observed a liver corrupted by <term>sphacelus</term> <note>Gangrene or necrosis of the tissue.</note> in a state of <term>cachexia</term> <note>Severe physical wasting.</note>. Likewise, such large purulent abscesses of the liver were noted by **Erastus**, **Jacotius**, **Hollerius**, and **Bauhin**, as **Schenck** reports in *Book 3 of his Observations*, such that the matter of the discharge was communicated to the larger veins. Thus tumors like <term>steatomas</term> <note>Cysts or fatty tumors.</note> were noted by **Trincavelli** in *Book 3, On the Composition of Medicines, chapter 27*. Likewise small boils, with no pain or swelling,

### BOOK FOUR OF PART II.

<margin>From the arteries.</margin>
It is likely that such dangerous vomiting is stirred up not only by opened veins, but also by the unblocked mouths of the arteries, as is seen both from direct observation <note>original: "αὐτοψίᾳ" (autopsia)</note> of arterial blood cast out along with venous blood, as well as from the sudden loss of strength, by which the vigor of the heart is dissolved. We concede indeed, as Galen indicates in *Book 5 of On Affected Parts, Chapter 5*, that blood can be cast up from the liver and spleen through vomiting; nevertheless, no one will deny that—insofar as nature performs such an expulsion when greatly irritated by morbid matter—a rejection of arterial blood, the treasure of life, occurs more or less through the arteries from the heart. But here we must exclude the observations of those in whom a more robust vital faculty prevents the effusion of arterial blood made all at once <note>original: "ἀθρόως" (athroos)</note>. We read that such people were occasionally restored, yet in such a way that most afterwards contracted <term>cachexia</term> <note>A state of physical wasting and malnutrition often associated with chronic disease.</note> and <term>dropsy</term>, because the organs of productive digestion were greatly weakened, as can be seen in *Forestus, Book 16, Observation 24.*

<margin>Vomiting of blood with black stools is worse.</margin>
But the condition is rendered more grave and the danger itself is increased when black, pitch-like stools are joined with the vomiting of blood. Hence Hippocrates in the *Coan Prognostics*: After a hemorrhage, a discharge of black stools is a bad sign <note>original: "μεθ' αἱμορραγίην μελάνων διαχώρησις, κακὸν"</note>. To this, Jacotius adds in *Book 4 of the Coan Prognostics, Section 2, Commentary 1, Aphorism 5*, that a discharge of this kind occurs when the spleen does not pro-

<column-break/>

perly purge the liver and the blood. From this, that dreg-like matter, retained for a long time in the liver or the <term>mesentery</term> <note>The fold of membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall.</note>, is sometimes corrupted by the delay and becomes pure <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "atra bilis"; in humoral medicine, an excess of this was thought to cause melancholy and various physical diseases.</note>. Sometimes, before such corruption occurs, it is excreted by the faculty of the body because it is oppressed and irritated, being unable to contain the superfluities any longer. Indeed, such black matter mixed with the vomiting of blood indicates a total loss of strength, according to Hippocrates: Black vomit is a bad sign <note>original: "ἔμετ. μέλας, πονηρὸς"</note>. This is because, according to Duretus in *Book 4 of the Coan Prognostics, Aphorism 25*, black vomit and black stools arise from the same matter and from the same sources. However, this is not contradicted by what Rodericus Fonseca reports in *Part 2, Observation 86*, regarding a young man of a somewhat dark complexion, with a weaker stomach and an intensely hot liver, who every single month vomited a black, thick, and tasteless juice for many years, until his declining years. At that time, the juice was rendered acidic, such that it brought on a "canine appetite" <note>An old medical term for an insatiable, ravenous hunger (bulimia).</note>, and eventually rendered the man so thin that he was finally consumed by <term>consumption</term> <note>original: "tabe"; a progressive wasting of the body.</note>. For in this case, something must be attributed to the strength of nature, which immediately separated the collected black matter until the nutritional power became too faint and insufficient; then the offending matter acquired an acrimony and further hindered the work of nutrition in his declining age, as Cardanus argues in *Book 4*.

# ON CERTAIN SURGICAL MATTERS.

In his commentary on Aphorism 21, **Pietro Maria Locareno** <note>original: "Petro Maria Locareno"</note> records that a massive quantity of foul, dreg-filled blood—exceeding 20 pounds—was once discharged. The patient survived several such episodes, though he eventually fell into <term>dropsy</term> <note>A condition of swelling caused by excess fluid, often linked to liver or heart failure.</note> because his liver had been so weakened. Having carefully considered these and similar cases, we predicted that our patient was in mortal danger from the very onset of these symptoms, a fact which the eventual outcome confirmed.

<margin>Reason for the prediction.</margin>
Since I had observed various symptoms of **Scurvy** over many years, I easily conjectured that the mass of the blood was currently teeming with dissolved <term>scorbutic tartar</term> <note>Medical writers of this era used "tartar" to describe stony or crusty metabolic waste that settled in the body's organs, much like the sediment in a wine cask.</note>. I believed that waste from <term>black bile</term> <note>One of the four "humors" of ancient medicine; an excess was thought to cause melancholy and various physical obstructions.</note> had collected in great quantities around the mesentery and the spleen, and that these were suddenly effervescing due to their innate malignancy. Thus, the vomiting of blood combined with black stools indicated a lethal end.

<margin>First Doubt.</margin>
Indeed, it was strange that when the body was opened, the **Kidneys** were found to be entirely healthy, even though the patient had complained of back pain for many years. Could it be that the "burnt" matter of the black bile had gradually collected in the mesentery and the splenic veins, and by its malignancy affected the nervous parts that connect the mesentery to the spine?

<margin>Second Doubt.</margin>
It is also a wonder how the patient survived so long when the liver was found to be completely <term>scirrhous</term> <note>Hardened or scarred, similar to what we now call cirrhosis.</note>. Perhaps it was because the **Spleen** was three times its usual size and of excellent substance—acting as the organ of <term>sanguification</term> <note>The physiological process of "making blood" from digested food, which ancient and early modern doctors believed was the primary job of the liver.</note>. Thus, the production of blood was carried out by the Spleen

<column-break/>

in place of the **Liver**. Therefore, it is no surprise that the blood produced was of poor quality, since the Spleen and the Gallbladder usually make the Liver’s blood-making more effective by separating out foreign matter. But where the Spleen alone makes the blood, this purification does not happen. Consequently, the blood produced is impure, just as is evident from the previous observation where blood—though of a poor sort—was produced by the power of the Spleen, and by its sharpness caused frequent nosebleeds. Similarly, **Cotter** in his *Surgical and Anatomical Observations* noted a Spleen larger than usual in the body of a man whose liver was putrid and full of pus; meanwhile, the man’s entire physical state was <term>melancholic</term> <note>A physical constitution dominated by black bile.</note> because of the blood from the spleen. **The same author** observed a <term>vomica</term> <note>An internal abscess or collection of pus.</note> in the lower part of the liver, and quite a large one at that, while the other parts remained healthy; in that case, the whole body was undoubtedly preserved for a time through the blood-making of the Spleen. So too in **Dodonaeus**, chapter 28, an observation is recorded of an ulcer on the outer curve of the liver, which for a long time caused heavy pain in the right side. In chapter 30, he also observed a liver corrupted by <term>sphacelus</term> <note>Gangrene or the death of soft tissue.</note> in a case of <term>cachexia</term> <note>A state of severe physical wasting and malnutrition.</note>. Furthermore, **Erastus, Jacotius, Hollerius,** and **Bauhinus** (as reported by **Schenckius**, book 3) recorded such large, pus-filled abscesses of the liver that the matter from the discharge was communicated into the larger veins. Similarly, **Trincavellus** (book 3, *On the Composition of Medicines*, chapter 27) noted tumors resembling <term>steatomas</term> <note>Fatty cysts or tumors.</note>, as well as boils that appeared with no pain or swelling.

### OBSERVATION IV.

### Hardening of the arm around the joint of the ulna from a fall.

A Noble man, **Patricius Ulmanus**, still in his youth, at the beginning of the year 1626, injured his arm in a fall, with a contusion arising around the joint of the **ulna** <note>One of the two long bones in the forearm.</note>. Having been restored after a fashion, six months later he complained of a hardening of the tendons around the said spot, with a numbness of the fingers in that hand and their contraction frequently occurring.

I advised that for the space of a month, a daily **fomentation** <term>fomentation</term> <note>The application of warm, moist medicinal substances to the body.</note> be applied for a full hour, made from a decoction of sheep’s or calves' feet, along with Marshmallow root, the herbs Mallow, Melilot, Betony, Sage, Ground Pine, Rosemary, etc. When this was finished, the entire arm was to be rubbed with **swallow water** <note>original: "aquâ Hirundinum." A traditional distilled remedy made from young swallows, believed to treat neurological or muscular disorders.</note> with **castoreum** <note>A pungent secretion from beaver sacs, used as a stimulant and antispasmodic.</note>, Sage, and **Spirit of Lily of the Valley**. After these treatments were continued in the prescribed manner, the hardening subsided and was dissipated. However, a certain weakness remained, which was later followed gradually by **atrophy** <term>atrophy</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀτροφία." A wasting away or thinning of the limb.</note>. Consequently, in the spring, we employed the use of the **Boll baths** <note>original: "thermarum Bollensiū." The mineral springs at Bad Boll in Germany, famous for treating muscular and joint ailments.</note>, where not only was whatever residue remained entirely dissipated, but the arm furthermore regained its former strength...

<margin>A similar observation</margin>
I had a similar case twenty years ago in Darmstadt involving a Nobleman of the Court. Falling with his horse, he had violently injured his left arm at the same location of the **elbow joint** <note>original: "articulationis ulnæ"</note>. After medicines were applied, the Surgeon had forgotten to ensure the extension of the arm. Once he had recovered and the wounds were closed, he was unable to extend his arm. Near the insertion of the **biceps muscle** <term>biceps</term>, within the elbow joint itself, there was a hard internal swelling the size of a hen's egg. When he sought my advice, I prescribed a treatment: namely, that a **fomentation** <term>fomentation</term> <note>A warm, moist medicinal compress applied to the body to ease pain or reduce swelling.</note> similar to the one mentioned previously should be applied daily for a month, followed by a suitable anointing. This was intended not only to soften the hardening in turn but also to consume the buildup of fluid, while not neglecting to strengthen the affected part afterward. 

However, since this Nobleman was in charge of taming and exercising high-spirited horses, it was impossible for him to obey my instructions until the year 1610. In that year, he suffered a fracture of his leg from a fall. On my advice, since he was otherwise required to lie in bed for several weeks, he "whitewashed two walls with one jar" <note>original: "unâ fideliâ duos parietes dealbans," a Latin idiom similar to "killing two birds with one stone."</note> by simultaneously making use of the treatments that had been prescribed for his contracted arm. In this way, by the blessing of God, he was perfectly restored—a result for which both the patient himself and other physicians had despaired.

## OBSERVATION V.
### A wound in the cervix.

<margin>The manner of the injury.</margin>
An honest woman, the wife of a weaver here in Ulm, fifty years of age, was injured on September 22, 1626, by a cow. The cow struck her with its horn, catching her in the **genitals** <note>original: "cunnô muliebri," a blunt anatomical term for the vulva.</note> and lifting her upward. At first, her urine was blood-stained, but afterward, pure blood—bright red and transparent, as is characteristic of the arteries—flowed out copiously. 

Since no external injury could be detected on the woman’s members, I immediately concluded that internally her **cervix** <note>original: "collum ipsius uteri," literally the neck of the uterus.</note> had suffered a rupture, along with the significant vessels derived from the **epigastric veins and arteries** <note>Vessels supplying the abdominal wall and pelvic region.</note>. The horn had been braced against the **pubic bone** <note>original: "osse pubis"</note>, by which means the woman had been lifted upward. Had the cow's horn entered above the pubic bone, the entire abdomen would have been wounded and torn open by that violence. 

Therefore, having been called along with a Surgeon, I immediately administered **Manna** <term>manna</term> <note>A sweet, gummy sap from the flowering ash tree, used historically as a gentle laxative.</note> with a decoction of plums to loosen the bowels. I ordered a **defensive** <term>defensive</term> <note>A protective medical plaster or dressing used to prevent inflammation or "deflect" harmful humors from a wound.</note> to be placed around the pubic bone and neighboring parts. Afterward, I also applied moistened linens to the lower abdomen and the **perineum** <note>The area between the genitals and the anus.</note> throughout...

Or is it because that saying of **Hippocrates** <note>The ancient Greek physician considered the father of Western medicine.</note> is true: **Nature is the physician of diseases** <note>original Greek: τῶν νόσων ἰατροὶ αἱ Φύσεις</note>? For nature performs the consolidation of wounds, and all the more quickly the fewer impediments there are. Since this internal injury was in that part which lacks major veins and arteries, it is no wonder that by the power of **innate heat** <term>caloris nativi</term> <note>In early medicine, this was the vital heat believed to be born with a person and essential for life and healing.</note>—which was minimally lost, unlike what happens in external wounds—the healing was prompt. Perhaps the quality of the wound also helped, in so far as the roundness of the horn inflicted a circular wound, which by its own nature might unite more quickly.

# OBSERVATION VI.

## A remarkable wound of the eye, with some additions regarding **Gutta serena**. <term>Gutta serena</term> <note>Literally "clear drop," an old term for a type of blindness (like glaucoma or amaurosis) where the eye looks healthy and clear but the patient cannot see.</note>

### To his most dear brother by the same mother, *Jacob Müller*, Doctor of Medicine and Professor of Mathematics at the University of *Giessen*.

Greetings. The case which you desire to know, my dearest brother, was as follows. In the year 1621, on the 20th of November, Master **Peithmann**, a Westphalian, by some chance or fortune, inflicted a small wound upon himself with a **penknife** <note>original: "cultello scriptorio," a small knife used for sharpening quill pens.</note> in the **cornea** <term>tunicæ corneæ</term> near the transparent part, which however emitted only a little blood-stained fluid. Terrified by this accident, he called for me. Having examined the injury, I predicted a future inflammation of the entire eye. Since such a condition is usually dangerous enough, I decided that he must be aided by every means of preservation. ## THE AUTHOR’S REPLY.

<margin>Blindness <note>original: "Gutta serena."</note> from the collapse of the front chambers of the brain, with the optic nerves wasting away.</margin>
I cannot fail, Most Distinguished Man and honored friend, for the further understanding of **dimness of sight** <term>amblyopia</term> <note>original: "$\dot{\alpha}\mu\beta\lambda\upsilon\omega\pi\acute{\iota}\alpha\varsigma$"</note>, to add the following observation by the celebrated *Spigelius* <note>Adriaan van den Spieghel (1578–1625), an influential Flemish anatomist.</note>, which comes from the communication of Mr. Dr. Fingerlinus, his former student, as follows: A certain woman, still unmarried, having been poorly treated for a hidden cancer, died; a dissection was performed after death for the sake of investigating the preceding cause. Since she had also suffered for twenty years from **blindness** <term>gutta serena</term> <note>Literally "clear drop," this was a term for blindness where the eye appears healthy and clear, as opposed to a cataract.</note> arising from a great weakness of the brain, once the skull was opened, the two front **ventricles** <note>Chambers in the brain which were thought to serve as reservoirs for the "animal spirits."</note> were found to have suffered a collapse and were even fused together, as the optic nerves slowly wasted away. These nerves were twice as small as is usual; by this means, blindness arose even though the eye itself was in no way harmed, especially since

<column-break/>

the eye was nonetheless properly nourished and lived by unharmed veins and arteries. This defect could not be helped, although *Pausanias* <note>Likely the Greek traveler Pausanias, whose writings included accounts of miraculous cures.</note> once claimed that such a blindness was removed following a wound to the forehead. From this it is made clear that an obstruction of the optic nerves is not always—and perhaps very rarely—the cause of **dim sight** or **blindness**, but more often such a collapse [of the brain chambers], and finally a lack of the **inflowing spirit** <note>The "animal spirits" believed to flow from the brain through the nerves to provide the faculty of sight.</note> is assumed. More at another time, when there is more leisure. Fare well. Swiftly from Ulm, on the Ides of August, 1624.

### OBSERVATION X.
## A Remarkable Fracture of the Femur.

<margin>Indications.</margin>
Petrus Kerler of Ulm, a stonemason by trade, fell in the month of November in the year 1624 while in Strasbourg <note>original: "Argentinæ"</note> and broke his left femur <term>femur</term><note>The thigh bone.</note> transversely in two places, as will later become clear. After applying the necessary treatments, he remained under a surgeon's care for nearly six months until the fracture had knitted together. Since the leg was not shortened in comparison to the other, he traveled here to Ulm on foot. However, he complained of an abscess <note>A localized collection of pus.</note> around the affected area, as well as a fistulous ulcer <note>A narrow, abnormal passage or "pipe" leading from an infection to the skin's surface.</note>. Upon his arrival, he implored medical help. We determined that a small fragment of the broken bone was the cause of that long-lasting abscess. Therefore, we decided that the fistulous ulcer should be widened to assist nature in more quickly freeing itself from this foreign matter.

<column-break/>

As these treatments continued, our surgeon, Mr. Baulerus, finally extracted a significant portion of the femur on August 18, 1625, which measured three finger-widths in length. This was a singular miracle of nature, for the body had filled that large gap in the broken thigh bone with such a substantial **callus** <note>The hard new bone tissue that forms around the ends of a broken bone as it heals.</note> that the young man now walks well-restored and without a limp. Furthermore, the length of this femur is not reduced at all. I believe this happened gradually over that long period during which the surgeon skillfully kept the leg extended to match the length of the other. Meanwhile, the separated fragment was moved by natural processes into the spaces between the muscles, which later gave rise to the abscess and the fistulous ulcers.

### OBSERVATION XI.
## Rare Ecchymoses.

Just as an ailment of the eyes—where thin blood seeps out and is poured into the substance of the cornea—is called **enchyamosis** <note>original Greek: "ἐγχύμωσις"</note>, **ecchymoma** <note>original Greek: "ἐκχύμωμα"</note>, or **sugillation** <note>Older medical terms for bruising or the "seeping" of blood under the skin.</note>, as can be seen in our *Medical Problems, Decade 3, Question 2*, so too is this condition sometimes produced in other parts of the body. Concerning this, **Paulus** <note>Paulus Aegineta (c. 625 – c. 690), a prominent Byzantine Greek physician.</note> in Book 4, Chapter 30, says that when flesh is struck by a heavy object...

...if an injury occurs from the outside, with the area being bruised and the small veins there being severed, blood is poured out through the underlying tissue. The Greeks call <unclear>bloody conditions</unclear> <note>original: "καλὰ αἱματώδη"</note> those instances where blood collected under the skin results in what is called a <gloss>bruise</gloss> <note>original: "ἐκχύμωμα" (ekchymoma)</note>. However, it is not only from external causes, but also from internal ones, that such an <term>ecchymosis</term><note>A medical term for a bruise or discoloration of the skin resulting from bleeding underneath.</note> and outpouring of blood beneath the skin occurs.

<margin>Observation 1.</margin>
This will be made clear through the following observations. The first is of a sixty-year-old man who, for two years prior, had been tormented by shifting pains of the kidneys <note>original: "nephriticis"</note> and joints <note>original: "arthriticis"</note>. He had been bedridden for several months and was otherwise of a very full-bodied constitution. He finally complained of congestions <note>The author uses "fluxionibus" to describe an unhealthy flow of bodily fluids.</note> in his head, and on the following night, he noticed a sudden relief from his headache <note>original: "cephalalgiæ"</note>. Unexpectedly, his entire left arm and the upper region of the same side were stained a deep, saturated blood-red color, without any pain or inflammation. Having been called to see him, I determined it to be an ecchymosis arising from an internal cause. A robust nature had propelled a mass of blood—which was threatening <term>apoplexy</term><note>A stroke or sudden loss of consciousness caused by a lack of blood flow to the brain or internal bleeding.</note> due to its "fullness"—toward the nearest external parts of the side where the pain and congestion of the head had been afflicting him. Therefore, I told the patient to have good hope, because such an expulsion of blood was "critical" <note>In Galenic medicine, a "critical" event was a sign that the body was successfully purging a disease.</note> rather than "symptomatic" (harmful), as nature had attempted to separate what was superfluous and move it to a less vital part of the body. I declared that this buildup should be dissipated gradually using "digesting" remedies <note>Medicines intended to break down or "cook" morbid fluids so the body can reabsorb them.</note> and certainly not "repellents" <note>Medicines intended to drive fluids back into the body, which was feared would push the blood back to the brain.</note>.

<column-break/>

By this method, the red color would first acquire a certain lividity (dark blue or purple), and afterward a yellowish hue, in the same way that we frequently see such <term>sugillations</term><note>A historical term for a bruise, particularly one that looks like a black-and-blue mark.</note>—which are sometimes left behind after bloodletting <note>original: "Venæsectiones"</note>—dissipated by nature. For this reason, we ordered the daily application, twice a day, of small bags filled with rye flour, bean meal, and flowers of chamomile and <term>melilot</term><note>Sweet clover, often used in herbal medicine to reduce swelling.</note>. We also administered internal remedies as required by his "fullness" of blood. By this means, this large bruise was gradually broken down, so that finally, after the lividity and yellowness were dissipated, the skin in turn regained its natural color.

A second observation occurred to us in that same year, 1626, 
<margin>Observation 2.</margin>
concerning a six-month-old infant. This child had been seized several times by epileptic convulsions. Finally, as the paroxysms <note>Sudden attacks or fits.</note> were pressing in some way, he suddenly suffered a similar ecchymosis, or effusion of blood into the substance of the skin, around the left eyelid and cheek. By this very occurrence, he was seemingly relieved and appeared to be better in other respects. We stated that in this case, one must abstain from liquids—specifically because of their "actual coldness" which they quickly acquire, giving them the power to "repel" fluids back into the body. Instead, we approached the matter with dry, warming fomentations <note>Warm, dry medicinal applications, like heated cloths or herb bags.</note>, by which the dissipation of the blood was also achieved gradually, just as in the first case.

## OBSERVATION X.

Petrus Kerler, a mason from Ulm, was in Strasbourg in November 1624 when he fell and suffered a double transverse fracture of his left thigh bone <term>femur</term><note>The bone extending from the hip to the knee.</note>, as will later become evident. If a part of the body is struck from the outside and bruised, and the tiny veins there undergo a separation, blood is poured through the underlying area. This is what the Greeks call *by way of blood-filling* <note>original: "κατ’ αἱμάτωσιν" (kat’ aimatōsin)</note>, and when the blood collects under the skin, it creates what is termed an *ecchymosis* <note>original: "ἐκχύμωμα" (ekchymōma); a bruise caused by blood leaking from ruptured vessels into the surrounding tissue.</note>. However, it will be clear from the following observations that such an ecchymosis and the pouring of blood beneath the skin occurs not only from external causes but sometimes also from internal ones.

<margin>Observation 1.</margin>
The first case is that of a sixty-year-old man who, for two years, had been tormented by wandering kidney and joint pains. He had been confined to bed for several months and was otherwise of a very full-bodied constitution. Eventually, he complained of a "flowing" of humors to the head, but the following night he noticed a sudden relief from this headache. Unexpectedly, his entire left arm and the upper region of that same side were stained a deep, saturated blood-red color, without any pain or inflammation. Having been called to the case, I determined it to be an ecchymosis caused by an internal source. Nature, being quite robust, had propelled the excess blood—which was threatening a stroke <term>apoplexy</term><note>In this period, apoplexy was often attributed to a "fullness" of blood pressing upon the brain.</note> due to its abundance—to the nearest external parts of that side where the pain and congestion of the head had been distressing him. Therefore, I told the patient to be of good hope, because such an expulsion was a "critical" sign rather than a "symptomatic" one <note>A "critical" event in early medicine was a sign that the body’s "Nature" was successfully expelling the cause of disease, whereas a "symptomatic" event merely indicated the disease's presence.</note>, as Nature had attempted to separate the superfluous matter and send it to a less vital part. I declared that this influx should be dissipated by gentle "digesting" remedies rather than "repelling" ones.

<column-break/>

By this method, the bright red color would first acquire a livid hue, and afterward a yellow one, in the same way that we frequently see such bruises <term>sugillations</term><note>A medical term for the dark spots of a bruise, often those following bloodletting.</note>—which are sometimes left behind after bloodletting—dissipated by Nature. For this reason, we ordered the application of sachets containing rye flour with the dust of savin <note>A type of juniper often used in topical treatments.</note>, chamomile flowers, melilot, and similar herbs, to be applied twice daily. We also administered internal remedies as required by the patient’s "fullness" of humors. By this means, this large bruise was gradually digested, so that finally, as the livid and yellow colors were dissipated, the skin in turn regained its native color.

*The second observation* occurred to us in that same year of 1626,
<margin>Observation 2.</margin>
in a small boy of six months. He was several times seized by epileptic convulsions; eventually, as the paroxysms were in some way pressing upon him, he suddenly suffered a similar ecchymosis, or effusion of blood into the substance of the skin, around the left eyelid and cheek. By this very occurrence, he was seemingly relieved and appeared to be doing better in other respects. In this case, we stated that liquid remedies should be avoided—since they are endowed with the power of "repelling" due to the actual coldness they quickly acquire—and we approached the matter with dry, digesting fomentations. By these, the dissipation of the blood was gradually achieved, just as in the first case.

# OBSERVATION XII.

## Hemorrhage from a wounded artery.

<margin>Observation 1.</margin>A hemorrhage that follows the wounding of an artery is very often dangerous and not infrequently entirely fatal. An example of this occurred to us in the year 1620, toward the end of April, at the *University of Giessen*. A noble young man, *Johann Ernst von Egloffstein*, a Franconian Knight, suffered a severe hemorrhage in his left hand near the wrist. The external tendons, the circular ligament, and the veins and arteries of that area had been severed. Afterward, an excessive feverish heat followed, as usually happens, along with an extreme weakening of his strength. Although he recovered some strength for several days after the necessary treatments were applied—so much so that we conceived a good hope for his recovery—nonetheless, four days later, the patient erred slightly in his diet and quenched his thirst with too deep a draught <note>Likely referring to drinking too much wine or water, which was thought to disturb the humors during recovery.</note>. A grave hemorrhage of the injured artery broke out again. Since it could be stopped by no skill, his strength (already weakened by the prior loss of blood and the concurrent fever) gradually slipped away, so that 

<column-break/>

shortly thereafter, his vital principle <term>vital principle</term><note>The "spiritus vitalis," or the life force believed to be carried in the blood and distributed by the heart.</note> being exhausted, he paid his debt to nature <note>original: "naturæ debitum solveret"; a common Latin euphemism for death.</note>. 

<margin>Observation 2.</margin>However, a more successful outcome was observed in a certain peasant of the neighborhood. On February 5, 1625, having been wounded in the hand, he suffered a similar rupture of an injured artery. In his case, the hemorrhage of arterial blood broke out repeatedly with a spurting motion <note>original: "cum saltu"; describing the rhythmic spurting characteristic of arterial damage.</note>, and it could not be corrected by any common remedies, although he did not suffer as great a weakness as the previous patient, since the injured artery was not particularly large. This man finally came to my colleague, Master *Sebastian Stromayer*, seeking help for this dangerous bleeding. A tiny amount of *Magistery of Opium* <term>Magistery of Opium</term><note>A concentrated chemical preparation of opium used here as a styptic to stop bleeding.</note> was applied to the wounded artery. By this means, the stubborn hemorrhage—which had completely eluded all other medicines—was soon extinguished, almost miraculously. Afterward, the wound was very easily healed with *Croll's Stictic Plaster* <note>original: "Emplastro Stictico Crolliano"; a famous wound-healing plaster formulated by the alchemist Oswald Croll.</note>.

was added, and on the left side of the tongue there appeared a <term>hypersarcosis</term> <note>original: "ὑπερσάρκωσιν"; a Greek term for an overgrowth of flesh or a polyp.</note> or fleshy excrescence, about the size of an average walnut. It presented without inflammation or significant pain, except that it created a slight impediment to chewing and speech. However, since the root of the growth was not particularly wide, I performed a ligation using a triple-strand silk thread, while simultaneously applying those remedies which might suppress the flow of humors and prevent pain. In this manner, the root having been made thinner, the superfluous flesh was separated by cutting, and the wound was in turn consolidated with little trouble in the usual way. 
<margin>Observation.</margin>
I remember that four years ago, a similar excrescence on the navel of a newborn girl was likewise removed by a ligation that was contracted more every day. Also notable is a history written to me in a letter by the most distinguished and experienced Dr. Barthol. Merclin, which undoubtedly could have been helped similarly at the beginning:
<margin>Observation 3.</margin>
The case is as follows. In the year 1592, a peasant woman from the village of Harthausen was sent to me by the most noble Lady of Reitheim, the mistress of that place, so that I might inspect her and decide what should be done. She had a fleshy growth hanging from her left groin, attached by a long ligament the thickness of a finger—white and sinewy—hanging down below the knee. It was equal in size to the head of a one-year-old child and protuberant with an irregular shape. She reported that in the beginning, it had broken out in the form and size of a wart or a pea, and afterward hung from a stalk like a cherry, and had increased in size day by day.

<column-break/>

<margin>Observation 4.</margin>
Likewise, the same doctor reports that in the year 1614, a midwife from Lauingen named Barbara sought advice on behalf of a newborn girl, because the girl had a tumor hanging from a stalk like a pea from her private parts. When touched, it immediately caused her to let out a most bitter wailing. I advised that a ligation be made at the root with silk thread, and that she should bind it a little tighter every other day. When ten days had passed, it fell off of its own accord. 
<margin>Observation 5.</margin>
To this may also be referred a spongy growth from the female private parts, removed with little trouble by the most distinguished and excellent Dr. Christoph Eisenmenger, whose words written to me are as follows: "To a certain honest woman, after a minor injury sustained during childbirth, a certain spongy substance grew from the right labium, having a thin root and the shape and size of a fig. I ordered its root to be bound with silk thread and tightened more every day. Once this was done, it indeed swelled up considerably, and inflammation followed along with pustules, which, when they broke, yielded <term>ichor</term> <note>A thin, watery, or blood-tinged discharge from a wound or ulcer.</note>. However, after he had frequently sprinkled it with a powder of <term>bole</term> <note>A medicinal earth or clay, often reddish, used to dry wounds.</note>, <term>tutty</term> <note>original: "tutia"; an impure form of zinc oxide used in ointments.</note>, and <term>ceruse</term> <note>original: "cerussa"; white lead, used historically in topical applications despite its toxicity.</note>, the inflammation finally ceased, and on the ninth or tenth day the entire growth fell off, leaving no further trouble behind."

### OBSERVATION XIV.

### The excision of a fatty growth causing blindness.

->From the notes of the same Dr. Merclin.<-

A respected man, Mr. Jacob Ackerman, the Provost of the Neuburg Monastery in Medlingen, had for a long time carried a massive abscess beneath the nape of his neck—which they call a <term>Nata</term> <note>original: "Natam vel Naphtam"; terms used in early modern medicine for large, fatty tumors or sebaceous cysts, often what we would now call a lipoma.</note> or Naphtha—hanging down between his shoulder blades with great discomfort. Wearied by this heavy weight, he entrusted its removal to a surgeon in Ulm, John Jacob Merck, who was highly skilled in the art of <term>excision</term> <note>original: "ἐκτόμῳ"; a Greek term for a specialist in cutting or surgical removal.</note>. After the tumor had been successfully removed by the roots, his vision gradually became duller. As the malady increased daily, around the 75th year of his age, almost all use of his sight began to fail. Therefore, lest he be deprived of all power of seeing, he gave himself over to an oculist to be treated. When the treatment was finished, instead of his vision being restored from its diminished state, it was taken away entirely, so that he now spends his life in darkness and sees the light of heaven no more.

### OBSERVATION XV.

### A wondrous <term>metastasis</term> <note>original: "μετάστασις"; in this historical context, it refers to the shifting or "translation" of disease-causing humors from one part of the body to another, rather than the modern definition relating to cancer.</note> or transfer of ripened offending matter.

It frequently happens that in abscesses, a transfer of offending matter occurs from the "noble" parts <note>The "noble" parts were the vital organs like the heart, brain, and liver.</note> to the "ignoble" parts <note>The "ignoble" parts were the extremities or the skin, which the body used as a dumping ground for excess fluids.</note>, as we have demonstrated here and there in the first and second parts of these observations. However, examples are rare—especially those with a healthy outcome—where nature proceeds in the opposite way and sends away superfluous matter from external parts to internal ones, or from less noble to more noble parts. It pleased us to add two cases of this kind that were communicated to us, the <margin>Case 1</margin> first of which is from the same Dr. Merclin, whose words are as follows: A student from Dillingen, Mr. Christopher Kelner, originally from Ellwangen, had limped for a long time and suffered pain in his hip. Eventually, the head of the femur slipped out of the hip socket and his foot began to waste away. Therefore, for the sake of his health, he was moved to Augsburg to stay with a relative and was recommended to the care of physicians and surgeons. When the treatment did not succeed as desired, the most distinguished...

<margin>Case 2.</margin>
*The second case was noted by my most distinguished colleague, Dr. Johann Widenmann, and is recorded here in his own words as written to me:*

> *I had under my care a woman in her fifties, the wife of Johann Paul, a copper smith; for three whole years she could not leave her house, but was continually forced to keep to her bed or a chair because of a swelling that had arisen around her right knee, yellowish in color, yet without any manifest pain. *the wedged-in matter, contrary to expectation, left its prior location and, by **metastasis** <note>original: "μετάστασιν"; the movement of a disease or its "matter" from one part of the body to another.</note> from a less noble part to a more noble one, was pushed upward to the stomach and rejected through vomiting. By the benefit of this, she was freed from this long-lasting evil and, to the wonder of many, walked about here and there through the city, showing herself to the common people as one wonderfully restored by the blessing of God.*

<margin>Purulent matter transferred from a broken leg below to the urinary tracts.</margin> One should also note here the history of the aforementioned **distinguished Dr. Merclin**, which goes as follows: A student named **Michael Stechlin**, a resident of the College of Dillingen in the year 1598, reported in the presence of the Father Sub-regent, the Surgeon, and myself, that although his leg had been broken and treated for two years, the leg still had to be opened every three months. Unless this was done, he experienced fever, nausea, purulent urine, and coughed-up pus. Whether his account and expectation held true, and whether the foot was opened so many times by the surgeon during each quarter of the year, remains unknown to me, as he never came under my care afterward.

<margin>Dangerous asthma from a cured abscess in the neck.</margin> Furthermore, the same doctor communicates two more cases of a dangerous translation of matter from the periphery toward the interior, the first of which is described in these words: The noble and magnificent Leonhard Plebst, Doctor of Laws and **Counselor to the most Serene Archdukes of Austria**, in the year 1602, suffered—in addition to a <term>cacoethic</term> <note>original: "cacoethicam"; a medical term for a persistent, malignant, or "bad-natured" ulcer that is difficult to cure.</note> ulceration of the whole head and face—from a creeping corrosion of the gums and teeth—

Another case is also relevantly shared here: A noblewoman, the mistress of the Palatine Women’s Quarters <note>original: "Gynæcæi Palatini"</note> in Höchstädt <note>original: "Hochstet"</note>, the widow of N. von Herkheim, had for many years a severely ulcerated foot and an issue <note>original: "fontanellam"; a surgically created or maintained sore meant to drain "bad humors"</note> on the other foot. Tired of the long-term annoyance of these, she had them closed and brought to a scar by a surgeon—despite the advice of myself and many others. Once this was done, a difficulty in breathing immediately took hold of her. Her appetite for eating was not diminished; indeed, by her own account, it became even more vigorous, so that she never dared to

<column-break/>

indulge her desires because of the asthma. Finally, her face and extremities of her hands, along with her abdomen and feet, swelled up because of stagnant humors that no longer had an exit. As the asthma increased and her strength was broken and worn down by the long duration of the illness, she returned her life to nature.

After her death, an abscess was found opened on her left side, near the position of the spleen, which to everyone's surprise she had kept hidden. I was informed that a great quantity of the most foul discharge <note>original: "saniei"; a mixture of blood and pus</note> flowed out of it after she died. From this it is clear that long-standing ulcers or abscesses, into which nature unburdens itself, must be treated cautiously, unless one wishes to throw oneself into a more dismal danger.

### BOOK FOUR OF PART II

...they approached on account [of their condition], complaining of remarkable pain and swelling near the pubic area, begging in a most humble manner that I might help these poor souls for the sake of God. To offer them some aid, I prescribed plasters to lead the tumors to suppuration <note>The process of forming pus to "ripen" an abscess</note>; after these were applied, within the space of a few days, the swellings softened and broke open. From them first flowed pus of a good color; however, not long after, a yellow water like bile emerged, which I saw flowing out with my own eyes.

<margin>The efficacy of Plantain in ulcers.</margin>
Since they were poor women, I advised them to use the juice of Plantain <note>A common medicinal herb, *Plantago major*, used since antiquity to heal wounds and stop bleeding</note>, as well as a decoction of the same with wine, for cleansing and purifying, and later a dried powder to fully close the abscess. And so it happened that one of them, within the space of a few weeks, brought the said abscess to a scar through the benefit of this single simple herb alone.

<margin>Food consumed is ejected through the abscess.</margin>
The other woman, however, keeps her ulcer open even to this day. Through its opening—which is a wonder to hear and see—consumed food and drink, such as cherry pits, pears, cherry broth, beer, and other things, emerge within the space of one hour; a truly marvelous thing. Indeed, at irregular

<margin>Worms ejected through the same.</margin>
intervals, worms—sometimes 4, 5, 7, and even up to 26, the length of a span <note>About 9 inches</note> or more—emerged with great pain and

<column-break/>

troublesome itching. She displayed these to be seen both in my house and in hers. I remember reading in the *Observations* of Schenckius <note>Johann Georg Schenck von Grafenberg (1560–1620), a famous medical chronicler</note> that worms had perforated the intestines of some, accompanied by painful mortification and a grim sensation in the lower belly; Solenander <note>Reiner Solenander (1524–1601), a renowned physician</note> also mentions this in Section 5, Counsel 15. This wretched woman, though she used many medicines on my advice—such as wound-healing decoctions, sweating agents, sulfur baths, and professionally prepared purges in which I sometimes mixed worm-killing ingredients—the abscess could nevertheless not be brought to a scar.

<margin>Raw mercury administered for worms.</margin>
At one point, I administered a bolus of red sugar with <term>quicksilver <note>elemental mercury; historically used as a drastic treatment for parasites or blockages, despite its toxicity</note></term> in a dose of <term>one and a half scruples <note>An apothecary weight; approximately 1.9 grams</note></term>, adding a little conserve of roses and a few drops of oil of spike <note>lavender oil</note>. Through the benefit of this, she expelled a vast quantity of worms, both large and small, both through the lower parts and through the hole of the said abscess; indeed, they still emerge through the same hole daily.

<margin>Perforation of the intestines.</margin>
From these expelled worms, I have come to the suspicion that the intestines of these poor women were perforated; otherwise, the food and drink could not have flowed out. Truly, to this very hour, this woman—who is worthy of pity—is gravely afflicted by the exiting worms, the flowing yellow water, and the sharp, agonizing pains of the lower belly. Written at Kempten <note>original: "Campoduni", the Latin name for Kempten in Bavaria</note>.

### OBSERVATION XIX.

### An ulcer of the navel, through which the excrement of the bowels was cast out.

->*From the letters of the same, dated February 22, 1625.*<-

<margin>A fistulous ulcer of the navel, from which bowel excrement was cast out.</margin>
On January 5th of the current year, I was called to the infant of a certain weaver, a child of a year and a half. Although I was occupied with other business at the time, I was nevertheless moved by the novelty of the matter; springing to my feet at once, I hurried with a quickened pace to the patient's house. Having entered the heated room <note>original: "hypocausto" — a room warmed by an underfloor or stove heating system, common in Central European homes</note>, the parents showed me the infant lying in the cradle, entirely emaciated and wasted away, yet with a belly strangely distended and an injured navel. A linen cloth had been placed over this, as women are accustomed to do for infants; when it was removed, I discovered with the most certain judgment of my eyes that the excrement of the bowels was clinging to it. Afterward, I inspected the navel and noticed a narrow, winding path in the manner of a fistula <note>A permanent abnormal passage between an internal organ and the body surface</note> running toward the interior, from which, in my presence, a foul-smelling discharge <note>original: "sanies putida"</note> emanated. Once this was wiped away, the excrement of the bowels in turn emerged through the said winding path,

### OBSERVATION XX.

### A wound to the head, dividing the frontal bone, dangerous, cured by the application of the trepan.

Regarding dangerous and lethal wounds of the head, we have expressed our mind through various examples in *Book 2 of "Diseases of the Head," the first part of the Observations, and Book 1 of the "Medical Letters," section 17.* To these, we also add here this singular case, which happened as follows. In the year 1626, on the 11th day of October, Georgius Seiß, a peasant in the village of Edelhausen, aged about 40 years, was seriously wounded in the anterior part of the head by a sword during the night. He soon fell into the hands of an empiric <note>An unlicensed or self-taught healer, often viewed with suspicion by university-trained doctors</note>, who performed a perfusion of the skull <note>The pouring of liquids or medicinal washes over the bone</note>

<column-break/>

representing the same appearance and form as that which was secreted through the bowels. I was unwilling to undertake the cure of this ulcer because the infant was exceedingly weak in his strength. I feared lest it might happen to me as it does to others who, not without the loss of their reputation, promise the restoration of desperate conditions; for indeed, not only the navel, but also the intestine in this case was suffering from a malignant ulcer. His strength being consumed, the infant paid his debt to nature <note>A common euphemism for death</note> shortly thereafter.

</margin>
Soon, therefore, we endeavored to counteract the inflammation and to cleanse the discharge daily, not neglecting repeated internal mild evacuations, and also a regulated thin diet. By this method, after two or three weeks had passed, the patient was perfectly restored; he has enjoyed his former health for three years now. It is manifest, therefore, that a trepanation can be granted not only at the beginning, but also during the progress of the disease, provided the strength of the sufferer remains steady.

<margin>The cause of the atrophy in this subject.</margin>
Hence I concluded that not only the most violent and continuous pains of the affected part, but also the <term>fistulous</term> <note>Refers to long, narrow, tube-like ulcers.</note> ulcers themselves, were exhausting all the "praiseworthy juice" <note>original: "succum laudabilem" — referring to the vital nutrients or humors derived from food.</note> from the rest of the body. <margin>The indication for amputation.</margin>

Therefore, with her strength still holding up as best it could, and relying on the hope that once the corrupt limb was removed, the nutritional juice might in turn be shared with the rest of the body—and that this might promote healing all the more quickly in a youthful body where the internal organs were not suffering—we scheduled the amputation of the thigh in the upper part, to be performed by a

skilled surgeon, *Johann Georg Bauler*, (others having despaired of the case) on the 7th of June. With singular industry, using various forceps—larger and smaller—specifically manufactured for this purpose, the major vessels were immediately seized and tied off, so that very little blood at all was lost. Afterward, <term>actual cauteries</term> <note>Metal instruments heated by fire used to sear tissue or bone to stop bleeding.</note> were skillfully applied, especially to the end of the bone; then <term>stegnotic</term> <note>Astringent or blood-stopping.</note> powders were used, particularly in those dangerous places where an eruption of blood seemed most to be feared, such as the "Compound of *Sperniola*" <note>original: "Composito sperniola" — a traditional styptic preparation often containing ingredients like burnt vitriol or frog spawn.</note>, along with applied bandages and the rest of the apparatus which *Mr. Fabricius* diligently describes in the cited place.

Fistulous ulcers had consumed the tendons and nervous parts, providing the cause of the disease. The severed part of the thigh, however, remained healthy, just as we had hoped and expected.

## OBSERVATION XXII.

### A stubborn and long-lasting ulceration of the leg, following the rupture of varicose veins, successfully cured.

How difficult the treatment of <term>varices</term> <note>Varicose veins; swollen, twisted veins usually in the legs.</note> is, is clear from the writings of Rhases, Aëtius, Gradus, Gattinaria, and others, whose assertions Forestus has summarized in Book 29, observations 24 and 25. The methods prescribed by Girolamo Fabricius of Acquapendente <note>A famous Italian anatomist and surgeon (1533–1619).</note> are gentler than the surgery practiced by the ancients.

<column-break/>

(Surgical Operations, part 1, chapter 105). Truly, ulcerated varicose veins usually cause a great deal of trouble for both surgeons and physicians. In this manner, a certain honorable woman, approximately thirty years old and of a <term>sanguine constitution</term> <note>In the theory of the four humors, this suggested a person was courageous, hopeful, and had an abundance of blood.</note>, was afflicted with varicose veins for many years following frequent childbirths. These eventually ruptured in the <term>tibia</term> <note>The shinbone or lower leg.</note> and brought about ulcers of a malignant nature. For a year or two, she sought the help of <term>empirics</term> <note>Often used to describe unlicensed or self-taught healers, sometimes viewed as quacks by university-trained doctors.</note> in vain, and she experienced little relief from the medications applied while her entire leg remained inflamed. Finally, in the year 1623, at the beginning of February, she implored my help.

<margin>Goal of Treatment</margin>
Soon after, while inquiring into the causes of this long-standing evil, I stated that above all, the whole body must be cared for, and then the affected part must by no means be neglected. First, we completed the treatment with appropriate <term>digestives</term> <note>Medicines intended to "ripen" or prepare humors for evacuation.</note> and <term>evacuants</term> <note>Purgatives to remove excess humors.</note>, repeated over several weeks, with bloodletting also applied at the same time. Specifically, I prescribed a decoction of "decrepit rooster" <note>A common historical restorative broth made from an old bird, believed to be easier on the stomach.</note> along with substances that would draw out serous and "burnt" humors in turn. These included <term>Caryocostinum Electuary</term> <note>A purgative paste containing cloves and costus root.</note>, Black Mechoacan powder <note>A root from the Americas used as a laxative.</note> with rhubarb and <term>Magistery of Vitriolated Tartar</term> <note>An early name for potassium sulfate.</note>, Syrup of Buckthorn, and Syrups of Manna, Safflower, and Solutive Roses. <margin>Slow gangrene from an acute illness.</margin>

<margin>In extreme old age.</margin>
This same thing is also prone to happen in extreme old age, as occurred three years ago to a certain eighty-year-old man whose big toe on the right foot gradually turned black with gangrene. Although it was cut off perfectly, even into the completely healthy part, no hope of healing arose; instead, the corruption took hold anew and crept little by little over several weeks toward the upper parts of the foot, until at last, his strength entirely exhausted, he satisfied the debt of nature <note>A euphemism for passing away.</note>.

# BOOK FOUR OF PART II.

<margin>The use of thermal baths should be instituted cautiously.</margin>
A cellar master <note>original: "minister cellæ vinariæ"</note> from the nearby Wiblingen Monastery had been afflicted for many years by a convulsive-like pain in the muscular parts of his left foot. He had frequently managed this with repeated scarification <note>The practice of making small incisions in the skin to draw blood or fluid.</note> on the outer part of the foot. In the month of May, following his own advice without consulting a physician—and without even preparing his body—he went to the Boll baths <note>The mineral springs at Bad Boll, known for their healing properties.</note>. At the very beginning of their use, he noticed a pain near the hip joint caused by a rush of fluids <note>original: "ex affluxu"</note>. After a few days, this pain subsided, but the matter moved downward to the sole and the toes. In that location, it produced swelling and a piercing pain, with the outer skin turning somewhat bluish-black, until a pustular ulceration followed. From this, a watery discharge <note>original: "serosa sanies"</note> flowed copiously and painfully for several weeks. Finally, toward the end of a month’s time, it was healed by the help of the bath.

Therefore, when he had endured the labors of the bath and considered himself restored, before his departure—following his usual custom—he performed scarification not only on his back but also on the outer sole of the suffering foot. With the blood flowing copiously there, he set out on horseback toward Ulm. Before he had even finished half the journey, he noticed a numbness in the entire affected foot, so that he finally reached home with no small amount of trouble.

Since pain and a rush of fluids followed the numbness of the foot,

<column-break/>

<margin>The error of the empiric.</margin>
he immediately called for a neighboring bath-keeper <note>A "balneator" or bath-house operator often acted as an untrained medical practitioner or "empiric."</note>. This man applied what they call "Virgin's Milk" <note>original: "Lac Virginale"; a cooling lotion typically made of benzoin and water, or sometimes lead-based.</note>, even though no heat or inflammation was detected on the exterior. As this treatment continued, the remaining heat—which was otherwise weak—gradually died out in the tips of the toes. For this reason, they called in two of our more skilled surgeons, namely Johann Jacob Merck, a stone-cutter <note>original: "Lithotomum"; a surgeon specializing in the removal of bladder stones.</note>, and Johann Georg Bauler. They immediately saw that the big toe, along with the neighboring one, was totally seized by gangrene <margin>The appropriate goal of the treatment.</margin> <note>original: "sphacelo"; total death of the soft tissue.</note>. Therefore, they rightly rejected that "Virgin's Milk" and applied those things which would inhibit the flow of fluids to the affected part, evacuate the congested matter, and assist the affected part as much as possible. After beginning with general treatments—an ordered diet and daily loosening of the bowels with gentle medications—further fluid buildup was prevented by the "Defensive Plaster of Mr. Wilhelm Fabricius" <note>Wilhelm Fabricius Hildanus, a pioneering German surgeon.</note>. This is described by Chalmeteus in Book 1 of his *Surgery*, Chapter 3, and by Fabricius in his book *On Gangrene*, Chapter 13. It was applied to the healthy part near the ankle joint. Soon, scarification of the affected part was performed, according to Paul of Aegina <note>A famous 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician.</note> (Book 4, Chapter 19). After the corrupt, bloody discharges <note>original: "ichoribus"</note> were carefully cleansed with a decoction of salt, vinegar, and brandy <note>original: "Aquæ vitæ"; literally "water of life."</note>, the "Master’s Egyptian Ointment" <margin>Egyptian ointment with linen cloths.</margin> <note>original: "Aegyptiaco Magistrali"; a traditional sharp ointment made of honey, vinegar, and verdigris (copper acetate).</note> of the aforementioned Fabricius was finally applied on linen cloths. ### A despaired-of Gangrene brought into the extremities by error during a malignant fever.

## OBSERVATION XXV.

### Gangrene of the extremities, born from an internal cause.

### BY THE SAME [AUTHOR].

<margin>The untimely use of mineral waters is harmful.</margin>
In the year 1596, a member of the City Council, Mr. *Christoph Kupfer* of Dillingen, went to the mineral springs <note>original: "acidulas"; naturally carbonated or "acid" mineral waters used for healing</note> on his own advice without first preparing his body <note>16th-century medicine required "preparing" the humors through diet or purging before undergoing a water cure</note>. He drank the waters and was seized by pleurisy <note>an inflammation of the lungs</note>. Neglecting this, he continued drinking as he thought it mattered little; however, the stabbing pain increased even as he sweated, granting him no truce. His dry cough also grew severely worse. Leaving the waters behind, he returned home on June 30. Having

<column-break/>

called for me, his bowels were relieved with an enema <note>original: "clysterio"</note>, a vein was opened <note>the practice of bloodletting</note>, and fomentations <note>warm, medicated compresses</note>, ointments, and treatments to encourage sweating were ordered, but to no effect. On July 7 and 9, delirium set in; on July 12, jaundice <note>original: "Icterus"</note> appeared, with urine tinted like linseed oil. On July 13, a coma took hold of him, from which he could only be roused with difficulty. As July 14 approached (though I could not determine exactly which day of the illness it was, since it began while he was away at the springs), there was an expectoration of thick, foul, blood-mixed matter, accompanied by a collapse of his strength. Toward evening, a bluish-black discoloration <note>original: "livor & nigredo"</note> appeared on the right foot down to the tips of the toes, and likewise on the left hand including the metacarpus <note>the bones of the palm</note> down to the pinky finger; finally, all innate heat and sensation were extinguished. The surgeon *Michael Berchtold*, a man most practiced in his art, left nothing untried that pertained to health, working with untiring zeal and diligence until July 19. However, the atrocity of the disease eluded all the <term>efficacy <gloss>original Greek: ἐνέργειαν (energeian); the active power or "work" of a medicine</gloss></term> of even the most exquisite medicines and snatched away his life. From this, I have learned—as *Rembert Dodoens* experienced in his 27th observation—that this man's internal organs were entirely corrupted, so that the ruin of the exterior parts resulted in the danger and loss of his life.

<margin>An improperly treated burning fever as a cause of gangrene.</margin>
In the same way, the history of the following case is also worthy of note. The cabinetmaker *Michael Kauffmann*, a citizen of Lauingen, suffered from a burning fever. As he himself related to me, a medicine was given—though whether for the sake of purging or to promote sweating...
