### OBSERVATION XXVI.

#### By the Same [Author].

### Gangrene introduced into a <term>cacochymic</term> <note>A body with "bad humors" or an imbalance of the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile)</note> body by the force of a more violent purgative.

<margin>Lazius, Book 8 on the Swabians, page 144.</margin>
**N. N.** <note>A placeholder used for an unnamed person</note>, the Overseer of that house at **Lauingen** dedicated to repairing bridges and roads (commonly called the *Bridge-House*), in the service of the Noble and High-born **Gisela**, wife of Lord **Werner of Schwabeck and Balatshausen**. When this man had gone out for a whole day into a far-distant forest in the harshest winter under bitter cold with his servants, for the sake of hauling large oak logs, he so corrupted his feet with the cold, especially the right one,

<column-break/>

that they were continually cold and numb afterward. With the approach of spring, wishing to purge his body, he took a violently purging medicine from a <term>quack</term> <note>original: "agyrtâ"; a wandering, unlicensed medical practitioner</note>. Immediately, a "translation" <note>A shifting or migration of disease-causing matter from one part of the body to another</note> of the humors occurred into the right foot. These humors, by their malignancy and quantity, suffocated the heat of that part—which was already broken and weak—and completely ruined it. They brought on a sudden gangrene, which, despite the application of many suitable medicines, could not be restored to health without the loss of both the foot and the man's life. From this and other examples, it is clear that it is dangerous to attack bodies filled with impure humors—whether by nature from birth or weakened by external accident—with <term>agonistic</term> <note>Strenuous or aggressive medicines that work by "fighting" the body’s condition</note> medicines. For when humors are violently moved by drugs that act fiercely, they push a portion of the offending matter to the weaker spots, and by strangling the heat of that part, they bring about destruction.

<margin>A caution regarding more violent purgatives.</margin>

...I add. A citizen, he says, of **Lauingen**, named **George Bress**, who traded in various goods, especially iron, once fell backward and struck his right buttock heavily against a mass of iron. Because the pain was tolerable, he made nothing of it. However, after fourteen days had passed and the pain was worsening, he called a Surgeon. Since the Surgeon noticed neither swelling nor redness, he applied a <term>digesting and maturing</term> <note>In early modern medicine, these were poultices intended to soften the skin and draw "corrupt humors" or pus to the surface.</note> <term>anodyne poultice</term> <note>A pain-relieving herbal application.</note>. I forewarned the gathered relatives and kin of the difficulty of a deep incision, lest they be terrified.

<margin>Incision of a deep abscess.</margin>
Therefore, the Surgeon applied his hand, and with a heavy, broad surgical knife that was curved at the tip, he made an incision to the depth of one finger. In one sitting, he drained six <term>barber's basins</term> <note>original: "pelves tonsorias"; these were standard shallow bowls used for bloodletting and catching fluids during surgery.</note> of pus, to the great relief of the patient and the steadying of his strength. After the necessary follow-up care, the man was restored to health without difficulty in a short space of time. From this, I learned the truth of **Aphorism 41, Book 6** <note>A reference to the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, the foundational text of ancient Greek medicine.</note>: that hidden pus, if it gives no outward sign of itself, occurs because of its thickness or the depth of the site.

# OBSERVATION XXIX.
## *By the Same.*
### A fatal abscess of the throat.

<margin>A wooden splinter expelled from the throat.</margin>
**I**N THE YEAR 1624, I was consulted by Banthelius Braun, from Burgau in the Margraviate. He reported that for an entire year, leading up to the autumn of the past year, 1623, he had constantly felt gnawing and stinging sensations in the <term>precordia</term> <note>original: "præcordijs"; the region of the body in front of the heart or the pit of the stomach.</note>. Despite this, his appetite for food and drink had not decreased, nor was he hindered in performing his work. In the autumn of the preceding year, 1623, he coughed up from his mouth a sharp wooden splinter, the length of a finger joint. In January of this current year, 1624, he expelled a longer one, along with much phlegm and blood. From that point, the stinging pain ceased, but he could no longer perfectly swallow any food or drink or pass it down to the stomach; for as

<column-break/>

soon as the ingested items reached the place where the pain had been, they were immediately thrown back up and ejected. It sometimes happened that the entire <term>esophagus</term> <note>original: "œsophagus"; the muscular tube connecting the throat to the stomach.</note>, distended with food, remained swollen all night; in the morning, he would eject the supper he had taken, which remained undigested and raw. Since nothing was being delivered to the stomach, he complained that his strength was being exhausted and he was wasting away.

<margin>The cause of the throat abscess.</margin>
From his reliable account, I observed by certain conjecture that from the time of the last expulsion of the splinter with blood, the area had degenerated into an abscess. By blocking the passage of food to the stomach, this abscess became the cause of the withering and consumption of the entire body. The medications that I had then proposed to be taken by mouth were, I believe, not accepted because of his poverty. In the meantime, he miserably prolonged his life until May, when, finally consumed by the disease, he yielded to nature.

# OBSERVATION XXX.

## A fistulous ulcer around the region of the bladder.

### By the Honorable and Renowned Mr. Johann Faber, Doctor of Medicine, Count Palatine of the Imperial Court, and Chief Physician to the Most Serene Elector of Bavaria.

->TO GREGOR HORSTIUS, DOCTOR<-

<margin>A singular case of toads generated in the belly.</margin>
Greetings and my most ready services, etc. This past spring, at the end of May, I was called to a certain Nobleman who was dangerously ill, and I stayed with him for several days to oversee his care. During that time, the son of a certain farmer, an unrefined man, came to me seeking advice. He was complaining of the most intense gnawing sensations and pains in his lower abdomen, having been miserably afflicted for some time. I conjectured that the cause was <term>intestinal worms</term> <note>original: "lumbricos"; typically roundworms, though the term was used broadly for internal parasites.</note>, and with that intention, I gave him four <term>scruples</term> <note>original: "℈iiij"; a scruple is an apothecary weight equal to about 1.3 grams.</note> of *Diaturbith Powder with Rhubarb* <note>A common 17th-century laxative and purgative composed of turbith root and rhubarb.</note>. And behold! Returning to me after lunch, he brought me a frog, or rather a toad, of a blackish color and covered in small pustules. He said that

<column-break/>

this animal had been rejected and evacuated at the same time as his third bowel movement. However, feeling no relief, he implored me for further help. Therefore, when he was about to go to bed that evening (since I had no other suitable remedy at hand), I administered two <term>scruples</term> each of *shaved deer horn* and *wormwood* in the strongest vinegar. This was intended to stun or "stupefy" any further animals if more were present. Then, on the following morning, I again gave him four scruples of *Diaturbith Powder with Rhubarb*, adding four grains of *Alhandal lozenges* <note>original: "Troch. Alhand."; a potent purgative made from colocynth (bitter apple).</note>. Three more animals, not unlike the first, were expelled along with the most foul-smelling matter, and the patient regained his former health. Of surgical cases, I communicate the following.

<margin>Observation of a fistulous ulcer.</margin>
A man about 33 years old, of a <term>phlegmatic</term> <note>original: "temperamento pituitoso"; one of the four traditional temperaments, associated with being cold, moist, and slow.</note> temperament and a <term>cacochymic</term> <note>original: "cacochymo"; a medical term for an imbalance or corruption of the bodily fluids or humors.</note> habit of body, fell into an ulcerated condition around the region of the bladder due to a certain accidental fall in the year 1620. This was poorly treated and eventually turned into a <term>fistula</term> <note>An abnormal, tube-like passage or tunnel that forms in the body, often draining fluid or pus.</note>, which he endured with difficulty for six years. After various remedies had been applied in vain, he finally called for me. I inspected the affected area and found the place to be extremely moist, ulcerated, and fistulous. It had one quite deep channel near the penis and several other twisting paths, almost like a labyrinth, which I could not fully explore with my instrument. I predicted the danger and that the cure would be uncertain and doubtful, yet not entirely to be despaired of. I therefore established the treatment according to the following indications: 1. since the af-

Since the affliction depended on a defect of the whole body—being soaked in excess moisture due to the weakness of the stomach and liver—I decided that the treatment must focus on preventing that moisture from increasing daily. Secondly, I determined that the moisture already present should be drawn away by suitable aids. 3. The tone and strength of the internal organs must be restored. And finally, the fistula itself must be freed from its <term>callus</term> <note>A hardened, thickened area of skin or tissue around a chronic wound.</note> and putrid flesh, thoroughly cleaned, filled with new flesh, and finally consolidated and healed. *Regarding the first point*, I judged that a proper dietary regimen and the management of the <term>six non-naturals</term> <note>In Galenic medicine, these are environmental and lifestyle factors: air, food and drink, sleep and waking, exercise and rest, excretion and retention, and the "passions of the soul."</note> must be correctly established according to the nature of the disease. > Hartshorn, two <term>drachms</term> <note>original: "ʒ"; about 3.9 grams.</note>.

> is required.

Lastly, by adding two drachms of choice Cinnamon, let it be removed from the fire, well covered, and cooled. After it has settled, let a strained liquid be made through a <term>Hippocratic sleeve</term> <note>original: "manicam Hipp."; a conical fabric filter used by apothecaries.</note> so that the water is as clear as possible. He used the first decoction as a sweat-inducer and the second as his ordinary drink for a month. # BOOK FOUR OF PART II.

Let the younger physicians see that even in those with a <term>cacochymia</term> <note>A Greek-derived term meaning an imbalance or "badness" of the bodily humors or fluids.</note>, tube-like ulcerations <note>original: *fistulosas exulcerationes*</note> can admit a cure, although the singular skill of the Doctor and the prompt obedience of the patient are required. The following case is almost similar regarding the cure, where I left no stone unturned so that I might restore the long-desired health to the sufferer.

<margin>
History of the cure of a malignant ulcer of the nostrils.
</margin>
A girl of about 25 years, the daughter of a citizen and baker here, of a phlegmatic constitution with signs of overabundant watery blood, had labored for several years with ulceration of the nostrils, both inside and out. There were also tube-like swellings <note>original: *fistulosis tuberculis*</note> pouring out watery <term>sanies</term> <note>A thin, often greenish or bloody discharge from a wound.</note> near the corners of the eyes. Although she had frequently used repeated evacuations, bloodletting, and external drying agents, the evil always seemed to get worse. Therefore, at the beginning of May of the current year, she met with me along with her mother for the sake of counsel, imploring medical help and solemnly promising her promptness and obedience.

<margin>
Nature of the suffering subject.
</margin>
Having considered the nature of the suffering subject, I found a phlegmatic imbalance combined with a sharp excess of watery blood. I observed that the head, along with the rest of the body, was "very moist" <note>In the medical theory of the time, an excess of "moisture" or "phlegm" prevented wounds from drying and healing.</note>, as evidenced by the abundance of her menstrual flow at the set time, the watery flows from the eyes,

<margin>

deeper sleep, and other signs. As for the injured part, namely

It showed hard, callous, and swollen edges, pouring out a discharge that was not plentiful but thin; it was accompanied by moderate pain and was not particularly inflamed. This caused the description of the "Ulcer of Chiron" <note>A "Chironian ulcer" was a classical term for an ulcer that was extremely difficult to heal, named after the centaur Chiron who suffered from an incurable wound.</note> written by Celsus to come to mind. <margin>
The malignant ulcer of Chiron.

Therefore, having made a prognosis, I promised a restoration of health, but only after a mutual promise was made that she would obey my instructions for at least two months, both in her diet and in the use of medicines. ...we proceeded to specific remedies. From that point, therefore, for the space of a month, we ordered a sweat-inducing treatment <note>original: *curam sudoriferam*</note>, which was arranged as follows: Take 6 ounces of Guaiac wood, 1 and a half ounces of its bark, 1 ounce of Sarsaparilla, and half an ounce of Sassafras. In this manner, we continued the sweating twice daily, but always ensured that with 5 ounces of the sweat-inducing decoction in the morning, 7 or 8 grains of <term>Diaphoretic Golden Sulfur</term> <note>A preparation of antimony used in the 17th century to promote sweating and "purify" the blood.</note> were allowed. Every fourth day, a purging was also instituted, consisting of: Take half an ounce of Electuary of Tamarind, 2 and a half drams of <term>Caryocostinum</term> <note>A warm, spicy purgative electuary made from cloves and costus root.</note>, and 1 scruple of Prepared Salt of Vitriolated Tartar. <header>TO BOOK IV. PART II.</header>

<margin>The formation of this bladder stone.</margin>
It must be noted that the "material cause" <note>the physical substance from which something is made</note> of this stone is a thick humor <note>in early modern medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids that determined health</note> mixed with a portion of bile. Having sunk down to the kidneys and been thinned by heat and dissolved into tiny parts, it hardens into small grains of sand. However, the thicker part, which cannot be dissolved into vapor or broken down in the manner described, degenerates into small stones. For this reason, there have been constant excretions of sand and pebbles over the past months. Nor was it difficult for the thicker humor, pushed toward the bladder, to get stuck there and finally be compressed, taking on the nature of a stone in the manner explained. Hence come the pains in this Illustrious Man; hence the tortures, as the bladder is provoked by an ill-fitting object. The stone grows larger from the downward flow of sand particles, which, when driven together into one, constitute a greater mass. From this, I easily conclude that the source of this thicker humor depends on the stomach, which is endowed with a cold and moist "intemperament" <note>an imbalance of the primary qualities</note>. This moisture, along with heat in the head, favors the generation of these humors. This is evidenced by the persistent inflammation and bleariness of the eyes <note>original: *lippitudo & ophthalmia*</note>, the force of which causes the eyelids to turn outward. This unnatural heat attracts more fluid, and consequently, a less effective "concoction" <note>original: *concoctio*—the process by which the body "cooks" or digests food into nutrients</note> follows, which should otherwise be perfected by natural heat. Thus, waste products multiply; these are thinned by this heat and poured into various parts of the body, which is why the aforementioned conditions and symptoms follow. Concerning these, the Illustrious Man proposes three questions: 1. Whether the stone

<margin>Three questions.</margin>

<column-break/>

can be crushed and dissolved into tiny parts or sand. 2. If he cannot have his wish in this, he asks whether it can be safely extracted by "section" <note>surgical incision, specifically lithotomy</note>. 3. If the surgery is deferred until the coming spring, what aids may be added to prevent its growth until then. *I respond to the 1st question:* There is no lack of ancient and more recent case histories showing that such a stone can be dissolved. However, *Galen, in his commentary on the 6th book of Epidemics, note 26,* asserts that this condition is cured by surgery alone. I, agreeing with other Excellent men, assert that this stone cannot be crushed. Indeed, the many diuretics that have been tried, far from being able to dissolve the stone into sand, have instead added to its growth. For instance, six months ago, the urine was often blocked, which does not happen at present. A very small stone could easily be pushed to the neck of the bladder, but having become larger, it does not slip down so readily, nor is the urine suppressed. It follows that a tiny stone, inserting itself into the bladder's opening from any side, hinders the exit, but with a larger mass, it cannot occupy the space for urine on all sides. It is also clear from the use of diuretics why he does not currently excrete sand and pebbles; since by such use the veins were made more open, and the substance of the kidneys more relaxed and clear, the path for humors flowing from the kidneys to the bladder became more open. How much value should be placed on this condition

<margin>Can a bladder stone be crushed by medicines?</margin>

### APPENDIX ON LITHOTOMY <note>Lithotomy is the surgical procedure for removing stones from the bladder.</note>

<margin>Is the cutting of the stone safe?</margin>
One may learn from the many writings of **Hippocrates** and **Galen** <note>the two most influential ancient Greek physicians</note> that the "efficient cause" <note>the active agent responsible for a condition</note> must be attributed to the heat of the liver and the kidneys, by which the former seethes and the latter burn. Regarding the second question, one must fly to surgery as if to a **sacred anchor** <note>a Latin idiom for a "last resort" or final hope</note>; however, we can promise nothing certain regarding it, since the remedy is quite precarious and doubtful. Before this surgery, many remedies must be attempted that address both the whole body and the specific part; especially those which, before the operation, halt the onset of the humors, those which assist during the operation, and those which correct complications after the operation. But since, <margin>Whether the growth of the stone can be prevented.</margin> at present, the patient rejects such surgery, we must apply ourselves to "preservation" <note>preventing the condition from worsening</note>. At first glance, this seems not only laborious and difficult, but impossible, since in my judgment the stone will have increased to a greater mass within a few months. However, the law and order of nature are not the same for one following a disordered way of living and the constant use of diuretics <note>substances that increase urine production</note> as they are for one following prescribed aids. Nor do I see the stone increasing in so short a time without an external occasion. I knew a most distinguished Senator here who was held back by such a stone, with a constant excretion of thick humor in the greatest quantity; yet for many months, and perhaps years, it did not grow, which I gather from his specific symptoms. Furthermore, in years past, a certain lawyer was "cut" <note>underwent surgery</note>, and a small fragment

<column-break/>

of the stone was left behind, which in the course of time brought back the previous cruel symptoms. After many months had passed, he was dissected again and the fragment was extracted, to which a tiny growth had adhered, formed after the incision of one year and a half due to a disordered way of living. It will happen differently for this **Illustrious Man** through a correct rule of living and several aids to be taken from **Surgery** and **Pharmacy**. But first, let us weigh those aids taken from Surgery, and whether blood may be let for the sake of preservation. <margin>Does the emission of blood contribute to preservation?</margin> There is no doubt that the "peccant humors" <note>harmful or "sinning" bodily fluids</note> differ from the nature of healthy blood; indeed, it seems the Illustrious patient is <term>cacochymus: a state of having "bad juices" or an imbalance of the four humors</term> rather than otherwise. Truly, although the blood may not "sin" <note>be corrupted</note> as the principal cause, it seems to sin as an "adjunct" cause, since hot humor carries thick and sluggish humors to the deeper parts. Therefore, we approve of some bloodletting from the elbow, which would also benefit the eyes themselves. Regarding <margin>Are issues suitable for preservation?</margin> <term>fonticuli: also known as "issues," these were small surgical incisions or cauterized wounds kept open intentionally to drain "bad humors" from the body</term>, we approve of them by no means. For if we wished to brand them for the sake of preservation and "revulsion" <note>the practice of drawing a disease away from one part of the body to another</note> from the bladder, we would scarcely—not even scarcely—obtain the result in so short a time before the surgery. As for friction <note>medical massage</note>, it is praised in the upper parts for the sake of revulsion, but by no means in the lower parts. Regarding pharmacy, we approve of the customary **Lenients** <note>gentle laxatives</note> and the customary preparatory syrups. Once the preparation is made, a medicine of **Agaric** <note>a type of medicinal fungus used as a purgative</note> with...

# TO BOOK IV. PART II.

<columns>2</columns>

...a little bit of **Rhubarb** <note>original: *Rhabarbari*; used as a laxative</note>, with Syrup of Roses and **Polypody** <note>a type of fern</note>; I would be satisfied with this simple purgation, since the most Illustrious Man has already been sufficiently purged. Nevertheless, we believe that some mild soothing agents are necessary throughout the entire winter season, such as a little **Cassia** <note>a mild laxative pulp</note> and pills made of washed **Aloe**, twice or at least once a week. On the intervening days, however, we highly recommend the use of two ounces of **oxymel** <note>a medicinal mixture of honey and vinegar; original: *oxymellis*</note>, since **Galen** <note>the famous 2nd-century Greek physician</note> in the 4th chapter of his 6th book *On Affected Parts* has these words: *"Oxymel by itself is able to wear down a stone."* We always place great value on this authority for the preservation against and cure of the stone. Next, for the sake of thinning [the humors], we may add lemon juice to his food; because once the thicker matter is thinned, the opportunity for the stone to grow is removed—provided that the oxymel is never omitted. For *pain and burning of the urine*, if it should be particularly pressing, this remedy holds first place: a **Decoction** <note>a concentrated extract produced by boiling medicinal plants</note> made from flowers of the **Water Lily** <note>original: *Nenupharis*</note>, violets, white poppy seeds, **sebesten** <note>a type of plum-like fruit used for its soothing mucilage</note>, and licorice. All of these should be boiled in common water, and this decoction will be able to soothe that burning. As for the Decoction of **Sarsaparilla** <note>original: *Salsa*</note> and **China Root** <note>original: *China*; a root related to sarsaparilla imported from Asia</note>, we completely disapprove of it, because it pours out the humors and drives those that have been thinned toward the kidneys, which increases the material of the stone. Added to this is the fact that the decoction does not correct the poor temperament of the internal organs, which have taken deep root. Furthermore, we disapprove of stronger **diuretics** <note>substances that promote the flow of urine</note>, because they carry down the mate-

<column-break/>

-rial to the bladder, with an increase in the stone and greater pain. The correct standard of living is very well known to the Illustrious Man.

->**Santorio Santorio** and<-
->**Girolamo Teobaldi**,<-
->Physicians of Venice.<-

### CONSULTATION II.

<margin>Three things to be considered in the surgical cutting for the stone.</margin>
<margin>At what time the cutting should be performed.</margin>
<margin>The purging of the offending humors.</margin>

Although in the extraction of a stone <note>the surgical procedure of lithotomy</note> certain rules cannot be prescribed by which a patient might be safely guided—on account of the variety of symptoms that usually arise after the incision, and because what must be done is always determined by the presence of current indicators (for no indication can be drawn from the future)—nevertheless, a certain universal standard can be offered, which is useful and necessary for the patient. Three things must be weighed: first, that which concerns the things occurring *before* the cutting; second, at the *time* of the incision; and third, *after* the incision. Regarding the first: a suitable and favorable time must be chosen, namely, in the Spring; but because this is sometimes inconsistent, there must be a constitution <note>referring here to the weather or climate</note> that does not lean toward the heat. The first defense regarding the whole body will be a suitable purging as documented in our writings: the eyes must always be directed toward the predominating humors, which we shall gather <note>catchword: from ha- (likely *ex haustu* or *ex habitu*)</note>

### APPENDIX ON LITHOTOMY <note>The surgical procedure for removing stones from the bladder; from the Greek 'lithos' (stone) and 'tomia' (cutting)</note>

<margin>
Let it be done without loss of strength.

And this, long before the cutting.
</margin>
...[it is determined] from the state of the whole body, but especially from the evacuation itself, since all diseases arise from a predominance of the **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which pre-modern medicine believed had to be kept in balance to ensure health</note>. Here it must be noted that every purging of the body must be attempted with a minimal loss of strength. Consideration must be given not only to the strength required to endure the purging itself, but much more so to the strength needed to overcome a great illness—such as the incision and the extraction of the stone. Therefore, it should be attempted through **epicrasis** <note>original: *epicrasin*; a medical method of gradually altering and tempering the humors over time rather than all at once</note>, by preparing and purging the dominant humors bit by bit. It should be noted that preparing, thinning, and cleansing agents ought to be administered for several days before the surgery; for if the humors are thinned, they might otherwise rush with greater force to the injured part.

<margin>
But bloodletting should immediately precede.
</margin>
Note thirdly: the letting of blood should not be attempted a long time before the incision, because it would be of little benefit. Blood is drawn out not only to diminish its quantity, but also to act as a **revulsion** <note>A therapeutic technique intended to draw "excess" or "corrupt" humors away from the site of a disease or injury to another part of the body</note> from the affected part; therefore, the closer it is to the incision, the better. The method of drawing blood in repeated instances would be approved, as a better revulsion would occur—a point **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire, whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years</note> often noted—and it would also be done without a loss of strength.

<margin>Diet.</margin>
A proper rule of living must always be established, which looks to quantity, timing, and order. At the beginning of the purging, the quantity and quality should not be excessively thin,

<column-break/>

but should be regulated over the course of time. He should always drink wine that is not "generous" <note>meaning a wine that is not too strong or potent</note>, and it should be diluted with water boiled with **sandalwood** <note>original: *santalis*; often used in early medicine for its cooling and drying properties</note>. Indeed, wine is the vehicle for all the humors, and such a quality is broken by water. Furthermore, Sandalwood—beyond the drying effect which we require—induces strength in the internal organs and settles the humors, from which all [dangerous] accidents are imminent after the surgery.

<margin>
Decoction with Sandalwood and Sorbet.

Friction of the upper parts.
</margin>
For some days before, he should abstain from wine, and in its place drink water with Sandalwood and **Sorbet** <note>original: *Sorbeto*; here referring to the "Syrup of Constantinople," a medicinal preparation used to constrict the bodily vessels</note>; for in this way the narrower passages are made to hinder the transit of humors; thus the water should have a greater quantity of Sandalwood. During all these days, **frictions** <note>therapeutic rubbing of the skin</note> should be applied to the upper parts of the body to evacuate the humors from the lower parts, and he should not exercise the body.

<margin>Enema of rose oil.</margin>
Two or three days before the incision, he should use a **clyster** <note>original: *clystere*; an enema</note> made only of warm rose oil. No other remedy can better assist the suffering bladder than that which is injected through the anus, since the bladder is joined to the rectum. Such oil restrains the blood and strengthens those veins, since the "little forks" of the veins which constitute the internal hemorrhoids proceed from the branches of the **vena cava** <note>the large vein carrying deoxygenated blood into the heart</note>, which are also spread through the bladder.

<margin>Inducing sleep.</margin>
I greatly approve that, two days before the incision, he use those things which can induce sleep; for wakefulness scatters all the humors...

### CONSULTATION III.

It is so evident that this most Illustrious patient suffers from a bladder stone that I judge it futile to search for other causes of impaired urination in him. Since the frequent desire to void, the piercing pain, and a corrosive-like sensation 
<margin>Signs of a bladder stone.</margin>
spread to the tip of the glans <note>The head of the penis.</note>—as if the canal of the penis were ulcerated—bloody urination after riding a horse or traveling in a carriage, the swelling and heat of hemorrhoids, the previous passage of sand-like grains, and the settling of a certain tartareous <note>Stony or sedimentary material, like the "tartar" found in wine casks.</note> material appearing in the urine (which causes the matter to become viscous), all indicate the same. These symptoms, arising from the long duration of the condition which has tortured the Illustrious man for eight years now without any relief from any kind of remedy—or at least very little—can indicate nothing other than a bladder stone, 

<column-break/>

just as learned men and the **Lithotomists** <note>Surgeons specialized in "cutting for the stone."</note> have suspected—and not without reason. They were made certain first by the insertion of a lubricated candle <note>A "bougie" or wax probe; if it hit a stone, the hard surface would leave a visible mark or scratch on the wax.</note> which was slightly scraped at the end, and then by the insertion of a silver catheter, through which they confessed they had felt the stone itself. The stone present is endowed with some roughness and is not smooth like marble, nor coated in some slime; for if it were, it would neither have scraped the candle in its passage, nor produced such notable pain, nor 
<margin>The quantity and quality of this stone is determined.</margin>
so easily caused bleeding during violent movement. However, it is not huge, despite having formed a long time ago, because it does not provoke a significant weight, nor continuous pain, nor a constant dripping of urine, nor **strangury** <note>A condition where urine is passed drop by drop with extreme pain.</note>, nor does it hinder walking down stairs, nor is it felt by a finger inserted through the anus. This has happened because the Illustrious man has used diuretics and evacuants almost continuously, disturbing the source and fuel of the stone; otherwise, it would have increased to a greater mass. 
<margin>The generation of this stone.</margin>
This stone was generated from a predominating **phlegm** <note>One of the four humors; here called "pituita," associated with cold and moisture.</note> partly flowing from the head and partly generated in a cold and moist stomach, with an unsuitable diet and imperfect **attrition** <note>The "cooking" or metabolic breakdown of food in the digestive tract.</note> of food added to the mix. This occurred under the influence of thick and "burnt" bile, generated in an overheating liver, along with excessive heat in the kidneys drawing such matter to themselves, and the immoderate use of diuretics carrying many raw humors to...

...bringing together the affected parts. Due to this same effervescence <note>A medical term of the era describing a "boiling" or agitation of the humors, often associated with excess heat.</note> of the liver and head, along with an uneven temperament of the stomach and other internal organs, he was not only previously subject to **dysentery** <note>Infectious diarrhea with blood.</note>, **lientery** <note>A form of diarrhea where food is passed undigested.</note>, **hepatic diarrhea** <note>Diarrhea attributed to liver dysfunction.</note>, malignant fevers, **phrenitis** <note>Delirium or inflammation of the brain.</note>, and other most serious conditions, but currently he also suffers from an inversion of the eyelids, with redness, tearing, and a flow of viscous and sticky matter leaking at the corners of the eyes. He is also very easily subject to inflammations in any part of the body where he might later suffer some bruising or ulceration from even a slight cause; so much for the condition and its causes.

<margin>The Cure.</margin>
The healing of this condition can be achieved by two means: namely, medicines and surgical operation. Regarding medicines,
<margin>Surgical operation is the only option here.</margin>
in my judgment, he cannot be cured by them, but only by manual operation. This is not because medicines should be entirely forbidden—since **soothing** <term>Epicrastica: medicines used to temper or moderate sharp humors</term> and **pain-relieving** <note>Anodyna</note> remedies will soften the pain (for which purpose *sweet almond oil extracted without heat, mixed with lemon and quince juice* holds the primary role)—but while laxatives and mild emetics <note>Medicines that induce vomiting to clear the system.</note> will check the flow of humors, and milder **diuretics** <note>Medicines that promote urination.</note> may be able to evacuate some of the flowing matter without any harm, and thus can be safely administered; nevertheless, those medicines usually prescribed for

<column-break/>

wearing down, breaking up, and dissolving the **stone** <note>calculus</note> will all be prescribed in vain. Indeed, they clearly harm the liver and the whole body, without being able to break down or expel the stone itself. External medicines will achieve almost nothing except for the relief of pain—which can also be provided by a bath of oil or some plaster applied to the pubic region. As for internal medicines, they are either taken by mouth or injected through a syringe or a **catheter** <note>siphon</note>. Those taken by mouth, if mild, lose their strength in transit; if more potent, they will burn the liver, kidneys, and blood. If injected through a catheter, they will not be retained for long due to the extreme sensitivity of the affected part. Furthermore, in my judgment, the stone has become so hard from its long stay that it could only be crushed with a hammer. Therefore, one must bid farewell to every such medicine. Truly, he can only be cured by an incision made by a skilled **Lithotomist** <note>A specialist surgeon who "cuts for the stone."</note>, which I believe to be the safest operation in this season of the year, in this physical constitution, and at this age. Nor should the concern that he is easily subject to
<margin>How inflammation is to be prevented.</margin>
inflammations be an obstacle; for a total evacuation and **bloodletting** <note>detractio sanguinis</note> must be performed beforehand, and after the incision, some blood should be allowed to flow from the affected part. Finally, the flow of humors must be inhibited with **repellent** <note>Medicines designed to drive humors away from a site of inflammation to prevent swelling.</note> remedies. Thus, the entire cure must be placed in the hands of surgical operation.

### CONSULTATION IV.

Although the signs of a bladder stone are very often ambiguous and so common to certain other conditions that great disputes are stirred up among physicians on the matter, there is nevertheless no occasion for doubt in the case of this Illustrious man.

<column-break/>

<margin>The presence of a bladder stone.</margin>
Whether the defects of his urine, by which he has long been tormented, proceed from a bladder stone is clear, since it was manifestly detected by the insertion of a **catheter** <term>Catheter: A thin tube (at this time usually silver or bronze) inserted into the bladder to search for stones</term> by two most skilled **lithotomists** <note>Surgeons specializing in "cutting for the stone"</note>. Even if all other signs were lacking, this would be enough for a diagnosis of the ailment. Yet, other signs also prove the same: namely, constant **strangury** <term>Strangury: Painful, drop-by-drop urination</term> and **dysuria** <term>Dysuria: General difficulty or pain in urinating</term>, which are greatly worsened by riding on horseback, sitting, walking, or climbing stairs. To these are added a constant **tenesmus** <term>Tenesmus: A continual, painful urge to urinate</term> during urination, a tension in the penis <note>original: "colis tentigo"</note>, and urine that is thick and white with a thick and tenacious **sediment** <note>original: "hypostasi"</note>. Furthermore, there was a frequent excretion of small grains of sand in the past, which has not appeared for many months now. Add to this that smaller stones were formerly passed with intense pain in the loins and occasionally the excretion of blood. During that time, the trouble in urinating persisted—at first more tolerable, because of the smaller and tiny stones left in the bladder—but later it became more severe as the size of the stone increased through the gradual sticking together of falling sand and thick waste. Therefore, the stone of the bladder causes perpetual burning, both by wearing away the tissue with its roughness and by stinging the neck of the bladder with the salty mucus with which it is coated. By its weight, it creates dysuria by blocking the exit of the urine, and by weighing upon the area and with its hardness...

### TO BOOK IV, PART II.

...exasperating [the condition] through all the more forceful movements of the body, it makes all the symptoms worse. Sometimes it also happens that by the flow of thick waste to the bladder, these same evils are sometimes diminished and sometimes aggravated, depending on whether more or less of a milder or sharper material glides downward.

<margin>The nature of the stone.</margin>
Whether indeed there is a single stone in the bladder, or many, or a large or a small one, is entirely difficult to guess; however, this contributes not a little to the ease of the cure. The **Lithotomists** <term>Lithotomists: Surgeons specializing in the manual removal of stones (calculi) from the bladder</term>, who have inserted a **Syringe** <term>Syringa: Here referring to a catheter or probe used to explore the bladder by touch</term> for the sake of testing, assert that a single stone is present. One may also suspect this from the fact that the urine is not totally suppressed, except at very rare and long intervals; and there is less effort and pain in urinating than in those who have several stones, even small ones, as I have learned from the cases of certain people formerly suffering from a stone and dissected after death.

<margin>How large it is.</margin>
The Lithotomists compare the size of the stone to the mass of a chestnut, which is in some way the average size to which bladder stones are observed for the most part to reach. And indeed, it cannot be believed otherwise than that in the space of two years, during which this Illustrious man has been held by this sickness, the stone has grown to this mass, since many small grains of sand were formerly seen to be excreted, which are now retained and can gradually cohere and be glued together; and much tenacious **pituita** <term>Pituita: Phlegm or mucus, considered one of the four humors; here, it acts as the "glue" for the stone</term> 

<column-break/>

rushes by a constant flow to the bladder, which must necessarily catch the stone and cover it as if with a crust. And this is the reason why the Illustrious Lord, for some months now, can no longer endure the aforementioned horse-riding, which nevertheless was sustained a year ago for a quarter of an hour without distress.

<margin>The formation of the stone.</margin>
The formation of the stone, however, was of this kind: thicker matter, especially phlegmatic, communicated to the kidneys and drawing a longer delay there—both because of its own sluggishness and thickness, and perhaps because of some narrowness of the kidneys—was gradually cooked out by their **preternatural heat** <note>In Galenic medicine, "preternatural heat" refers to an abnormal, feverish, or inflammatory heat that alters the body's fluids</note>. As the thinner parts evaporated, it hardened into stones, both very small and sandy, as well as rather large ones. From there, the small stones pushed to the bladder were partly excreted and partly retained; and thus, by the steady influx of small sand and the adhesion of thicker mucus, they acquired a larger mass over the passage of time and joined into one body. The whole body provides phlegm to the urinary passages, especially due to a defect of a more sluggish stomach, which also gathers much waste from an improper diet; as well as from a very humid brain, verging toward some heat, from which a nearly continuous flow, somewhat sharp, also glides down to the eyes. And it happened, by the excessive use of **diuretics** <term>Diuretics: Substances intended to increase the production and passage of urine</term>, that those wastes now flow with greater force than before to the kidneys...

### APPENDIX ON LITHOTOMY.
<note>original: "lithotomia"; the surgical procedure of "cutting for the stone" to remove bladder calculi</note>

...persist, and they turn urine that was once thin into something very thick. <margin>*Prognosis*</margin> From these facts, it is clear that this illness is most dangerous, whether you attempt a cure or neglect it. For in the cure, not a few fail, or are killed by incoming complications; I am speaking of the cure performed by cutting <note>original: "sectione"; surgery</note>. If treatment is neglected, the persistence and magnitude of the pains eventually finish off the patients.

<margin>*A Threefold Inquiry*</margin> Therefore, not without reason, the Most Illustrious Gentleman asks us whether a **calculus** <term>calculus: A stone formed in the bladder or kidneys from mineral deposits</term> can be cured in a milder, less cruel and risky way than by cutting; secondly, whether at least the growth of the stone can be hindered, and those most grave symptoms—from which death looms—can be turned away; finally, whether the cutting can be conveniently and without danger to life deferred until next spring, since his heavy responsibilities hardly allow him to attempt this risky remedy in this season.

<margin>1. *Whether a bladder stone can be cured without cutting.*</margin> To the first, I reply that bladder stones are indeed sometimes cured by the help of medications, which have been tested in many cases, and which the Illustrious Lord could have read about in the works of *Orazio Augenio* and *Ferdinando Epifanio*. Such a remedy was found this year to be most effective in the case of *Girolamo Moneghina of the Order of Friars Minor Conventual* <margin>*Example of a dissolved bladder stone.*</margin> *of Saint Francis*: a plaster made from a white onion boiled in white wine, applied hot to the pubic area. By repeating this twice, the stone he had carried in his bladder for three years was broken into tiny particles,

<column-break/>

passed in the urine, and he regained his former health. Yet, there is hardly anything to be hoped for from the use of these remedies in the case of the Illustrious Gentleman, since he has used many very strong stone-breaking medications for a long time, not only without help, but even with harm—namely, by provoking a greater abundance of **humors** <note>original: "humorum"; the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to control health and temperament</note> toward the bladder than before. From this, I conjecture that the stone formed in him is not crumbly <margin>*The outcome below testifies to this very thing*</margin> and composed merely of little grains of sand clinging to one another, but hard and formed from thick, sticky mucus that has become very firmly hardened—the kind that is only removed by cutting. Therefore, I do not think that **Lithontriba** <term>Lithontriba: Medicines or instruments intended to crush or wear down stones within the body</term> should be attempted again, lest by provoking a greater source of irritation the stone grows more quickly; unless perhaps he wishes to try that external plaster, which can be done without any danger.

<margin>*Surgery is advised.*</margin> But it would be agreeable to attempt the cutting; for although it is not without danger, it is observed to be safe enough if it falls to a skilled craftsman, such as *Giovanni Maria of Norcia, a **Lithotomist** <term>Lithotomist: A specialized surgeon who performs the manual extraction of stones from the bladder</term> living in Venice*. Under his care, I would dare to promise recovery, since the stone is neither so large that it requires a massive wound for extraction, nor so small that it is difficult to grasp, nor so crumbly that it might break and shatter into pieces when caught.

# TO BOOK IV OF PART II.

<margin>
Whether it is possible to hinder the growth?
</margin>
*To the second point, I reply* that the growth of the stone cannot be hindered for a long time, because the flow <note>original: "fluxio"; the movement of "bad humors" or fluids within the body</note> toward the urinary parts cannot be entirely redirected. From the continuous adhesion of waste matter, some growth—even if slow—must inevitably be added to the stone. This is the reason why the symptoms of the stone cannot be lessened, but must necessarily increase in proportion to the stone's growth. 

<margin>
Whether the cutting can be deferred?
</margin>
From this, the solution to the third question is clear: whether the **cutting** <term>cutting: The surgical procedure of lithotomy, where an incision is made to physically remove a stone from the bladder</term> can be deferred for half a year without danger. Since the stone will have turned out larger by that time, the pains will necessarily increase; and perhaps from the constant rubbing against the bladder, an ulcer in its neck or even gangrene will be triggered—conditions under which the cutting should by no means be attempted. Therefore, one must think of the remedy as soon as possible—which, I say, seems to be the only one remaining: the cutting—and the body must be prepared for this. But if at this time the Illustrious Gentleman is either unwilling or unable to do this, every effort must be made so that the evil does not increase and the symptoms of the stone do not grow heavier, as far as that can be managed. 

<margin>
Counsel on hindering the growth of the stone.
</margin>
The growth of the stone will be hindered if the flow is diverted away from the kidneys and bladder; if the regeneration of abundant waste matter is inhibited through the best diet and the strengthening of the affected parts (and especially the head); and finally, if the urinary passages are occasionally cleaned with some mild remedy after a proper purging of the body—namely, so that the waste does not carry bad humors down to the bladder.

<column-break/>

For the diversion of the humors, two **fonticuli** <term>fonticuli: "Little fountains" or issues; small artificial sores kept open by a physician to drain away "excess humors"</term> would be useful: one on the left arm and the other on the right leg, from which much benefit will also be brought to the eyes. Also suitable would be rubbing of the extremities in the morning hours and the frequent use of half an ounce <note>original: "℥ß"</note> of extracted pulp of **Cassia** <term>Cassia: A mild herbal laxative used to cleanse the bowels without irritation</term> shortly before a meal, which will also somewhat soothe the sharpness <note>original: "acrimoniam"; the burning sensation during urination</note> of the urine. With this can be mixed the use of **Aloe** pills with rose juice, if one scruple <note>original: "℈j"</note> is taken once or twice a week shortly before dinner. For the strengthening of the head and eyes, I recommend the use of a conserve of **Anthos** <note>original: "Anthos"; rosemary flowers</note>, **Eyebright**, and Roses in equal portions; let him use two ounces <note>original: "℥ij"</note> after dinner, or in the morning four hours before lunch, for many days. I also recommend the steady use throughout the whole winter of medicated wine with **China** <term>China: China root (Smilax china), a plant used to treat chronic conditions by "purifying" the blood</term>, Mastic, Betony, Eyebright, and Roses. To mitigate the sharpness of the urine, a most excellent powder is made from one part violet-scented white sugar and two parts powder of **Marshmallow** <term>Marshmallow: The root of Althaea officinalis, valued for its mucilaginous properties that soothe internal membranes</term> root, if a spoonful is taken daily in a draught of white wine, about two hours before lunch. Anointing the pubic area with sweet almond oil, expressed without heat, will also be beneficial. Meanwhile, the best possible dietary regimen is also necessary. Let a climate be chosen that is minimally cloudy and subject to winds. The diet, as to its substance, should be of "good juice" <note>original: "boni succi"; meaning highly nutritious and easily digestible</note>; therefore, he should beware of eating many fish, and eat even the good ones sparingly. Let him abstain...

### APPENDIX ON LITHOTOMY.

<column-break/>

...[let him ab]stain from fruits, with the exception of raisins, and cooked apples and pears. Let the meats of domestic chickens, small mountain birds, suckling calf, and kid goat be chosen; likewise, fresh chicken eggs. Regarding the quality of food, sharp and salty things should be avoided, as well as "vaporous" foods like milk, and thick, sticky items such as unfermented dairy sweets and all fried foods. Regarding quantity, dinner should be half as large as lunch. 

Sleep should be moderate, and he should not settle down for it until two hours have passed after taking food. Wine should preferably be white, resembling water in its substance, and not of an intense odor. Walking should be a regular habit, but gentle, and taken before eating. Long periods of sitting are harmful, as is any violent movement, whether from horse-riding or traveling in a carriage. 

But if he contemplates the **cutting** <term>cutting: The surgical procedure of lithotomy, performed to remove stones from the bladder.</term>, he must be purged for about ten days before the operation; however, this should be done with a mild medicine, primarily drawing away the **hot humors** <note>original: "calidos humores"; in humoral theory, these were fluids thought to cause inflammation and irritation</note> which, by their flow, could irritate the bladder and risk inflammation. Therefore, he should take either soluble syrup of roses and manna in a drink, or flowers of cassia in a **bolus** <note>original: "bolo"; a large medicinal pill or soft mass</note>. Then, for five days, he shall take a broth infused with chicory, sow-thistle, dandelion, and purslane, with syrup of vinegar; and on the second day that he takes this broth, he shall see to it that about six ounces of blood are drawn from the **right liver-vein** <note>original: "jecorariâ dextrâ"; the basilic vein of the right arm, traditionally associated with treating liver and abdominal issues</note>. After the sixth day, he shall repeat the aforementioned medicine. The diet during this time must be moderate,

<column-break/>

because a fuller diet would increase **fullness** <note>original: "plenitudinem"; refers to plethora, or an overabundance of blood and fluids</note>, from which the danger of inflammation looms; yet a thinner diet would diminish his strength, which must be robust during the surgery. Three days before the surgery, let him abstain from wine so that the blood may be calmer, and abstain from all salty or spiced food and seasoning. 

The method of operating and cutting is to be left to skilled **Lithotomists** <term>Lithotomists: Specialized surgeons who focused exclusively on the "cutting for the stone."</term>, in whose dexterity the entire safety of the patients resides. After the operation, the same care must be taken for the Most Illustrious Gentleman as would be taken if he had received a wound in the bladder for any other reason. Namely, a thin diet is to be used, without wine, until the **gluing together** <note>original: "agglutinationem"; the healing or closing of the surgical wound</note> of the ulcer. In procuring this healing, I advise this above all: once the danger of inflammation has passed, **Western Balsam** <term>Western Balsam: Also known as Balsam of Peru, a resin used for its antiseptic and healing properties.</term> is most effective for a quick closing when dropped into the wound, with lint fibers soaked in the same balsam also placed over it.

### CONSULTATION V.
#### Translated from the Italian language into Latin.

<margin>
Prevention of the growth of the stone.
</margin>
The regimen which the most noble Lord wishes to observe throughout this winter, so that the growth of the **stone** <term>stone: Also called a calculus; a hard mass formed in the bladder or kidneys.</term> in the bladder may be hindered as much as possible, must be such that, first, fewer **phlegmatic and bilious** <note>original: "pituitoſorum & bilioſorum"; referring to the "humors" of phlegm and yellow bile which were thought to solidify into stones</note> accumulations are generated in the body, and that subsequently the waste products generated and collected are evacuated or diverted from the kidneys and bladder. Following this order will also serve the future **incision** <term>incision: The surgical procedure of lithotomy to remove the stone.</term>, ensuring the easy extraction of the stone and, at the same time, the quick and safe healing of the wound. 1. I recommend that he take the following potion three or four times this winter, five hours before lunch.

Recipe: Leaves of Chicory, Betony, Agrimony.
Maidenhair fern.
Borage, Sow-thistle, half a **pugil** <note>original: "P. β."; a pugil is a "pinch" or a small handful of herbs</note> of each.
Raisins, Damson plums, 
2 **drams** <note>original: "ʒ. ij"; a dram is a measurement of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</note> of each.
Grass roots, 2 drams; boil down to 
3 **ounces** <note>original: "℥. iij"</note>.
Into the strained liquid, infuse overnight:
Senna leaves, half a dram. **Agaric troches** <note>original: "Agar. troch."; medicinal lozenges made from larch fungus, used as a purgative</note>, 
4 **scruples** <note>original: "℈. iiij"; a scruple is about 1.3 grams</note>.

<column-break/>

Violet flowers, Mallow, 1 pugil of each.
Licorice, 1 scruple.
To the pressed liquid add choice **Manna** <term>Manna: A sweet, sap-like substance from the flowering ash tree, used as a gentle laxative.</term>, 
1 ounce.
Mix to make a potion of 4 ounces.

On other days, early in the morning, let him take this small drink, but first let him place himself in a **bath** <note>original: "balneum"; medicinal baths were a standard part of early modern therapy</note> that reaches up to the nipples, made with the following herbs:

Recipe: Pellitory, Violets, Mallow, 
3 **handfuls** <note>original: "M. iij"</note> of each.
Bran, 6 handfuls. **Winter cherry** <note>original: "Alkekengi"; a plant often used to treat urinary issues</note> berries, half a pound. Mix.

The small drink or decoction should be as follows:

Recipe: Mallow leaves, 1 handful. Horsetail, 
half a handful.
Red chickpeas, 2 drams. Winter cherry berries, 
3 in number.
The four large cold seeds, cleaned, half a dram of each.
**Gromwell** <note>original: "Milij ☉" or Milium Solis; a plant named for its stone-like seeds, believed by the "Doctrine of Signatures" to help break up bladder stones</note>, 1 dram. Licorice, 1 scruple.
Boil according to the art to 4 ounces; add to the strained liquid powdered **Sponge stone** <note>original: "Lap. Spong."; a stony concretion found in sponges, used to treat stones in the body</note>, 1 dram.
Mix to make a short potion.

I also recommend the enemas written below for several sessions, at least once every week. The diet shall be such: for drink, let him use sometimes a decoction or **Claret** <note>original: "Clareto"; here referring to a sweetened or spiced wine rather than specifically red wine</note>, sometimes wine tempered and diluted with chicory or mallow water. I recommend beyond measure that **Turkish Sorbet** <note>original: "Sorbetum illud Turcarum"; an early European reference to "sherbet," a sweetened fruit syrup</note>, namely the Constantinople Syrup. Sometimes let him drink barley water with raisins and coriander seeds, according as more or less heat is detected in the body.

### APPENDIX ON LITHOTOMY.
<term>lithotomy: A surgical procedure to remove stones from the urinary bladder, derived from the Greek words for "stone" and "cutting."</term>

For food, I recommend veal. I also recommend mutton—young, roasted, or boiled—mountain birds, thrushes, and partridges. Furthermore, I recommend other small birds, as well as hares and beef, prepared with horseradish, or parsley root, or yellow carrots, or parsnips, or turnips. Also sea fish: flounders, trout, and roasted pike, or those cooked with oil, water, and parsley, and finely chopped. He may also eat cooked peaches, sweet apples, or plums; but he should avoid pork and other waterfowl. I recommend turnips, navews <note>original: "napos"; a type of rapeseed or rutabaga</note>, and yellow carrots, cooked with a little butter in the evening. If a regimen is to be prescribed for the ten or twelve days before the **incision** <note>the surgical cut for the stone</note>, to serve the recovery of the kidneys and bladder and to prevent inflammation from complicating the wound, at that time I recommend, in the evening hours, two fresh eggs laid that very day, and barley cooked with broth, or water with fresh butter, or a **panatella** <term>panatella: A simple bread soup or gruel often given to invalids.</term> made with water and a little butter; also a pancake made of two beaten eggs with a little milk, or an emulsion of fresh melon seeds. In the morning hours, broth with bread, made from roasted or boiled veal. Avoid everything in eating and drinking that could heat the kidneys and bladder.

The **claret** <note>original: "Claretum"; in this context, a spiced, sweetened wine used medicinally</note> should be made watery and not too strong, with as few

<column-break/>

spices as possible. At that time, he should not tire himself by riding, nor should he travel frequently by carriage; he should walk moderately.

For spots on the legs, he should take mustard powder mixed with vinegar into the form of a liniment, and after sweating, he should rub it on his legs. Enemas shall be made with fatty broth, egg yolk, 1 ounce of sugar, and 3 ounces of sweet almond oil in a small quantity, and not very hot; and if perhaps the Most Noble Baron feels **windiness** <note>original: "ventositates"; intestinal gas or flatulence</note>, he should mix in 1 ounce of chamomile oil, etc.

->*Adrian van den Spiegel, Brussels native, Professor of Surgery and Anatomy at Padua.*<-

In order to prepare for that operation, he wished to begin with the use of **mineral waters** <note>original: "acidularum"; naturally carbonated or medicinal spring waters</note>, both for the sake of tempering a rather hot temperament, and also so that, by applying other suitable means at the same time, the primary pathways around the digestive organs, along with the kidneys and bladder, might be further purified. Soon after, having administered one or two enemas here at Ulm, he traveled to the mineral springs at **Überkingen**. There, after repeating several doses of laxative wine, he continued drinking the mineral waters for eight days with **great ease** <note>original: "ευφορια" (euphoria); a state of physical well-being or tolerance of the treatment</note>. This done, he returned in turn to Ulm for the purpose of scheduling the surgery during the waning moon, while the surrounding air was not excessively hot. So that the business might succeed more happily **with God's help** <note>original: "σὺν Θεῷ" (syn Theo)</note>, he used a laxative **claret** <term>claret: A medicinal spiced wine used as a carrier for herbs.</term> for three days, followed by **bloodletting** <note>original: "V.S." (venae sectio)</note> on the day of
<margin>
July 31 / August 10, 1626
</margin>
allowing the body to rest for the following eight days. He observed an exquisite and moderate diet, completely avoided wine, and did not neglect "altering" medicines to temper his bilious blood. These included a conserve of chicory root, rose, candied citron peel, and **magistery of red coral** <note>a refined chemical preparation of coral used as a tonic or antacid</note>, as well as appropriate emulsions, suitable syrups, medicinal broths, and decoctions of herbs and roots. He also received repeated enemas made from emollient

<column-break/>

and cooling decoctions, mixed with oil of roses and violets, etc. Nor did he skip the use of poppy syrup and similar medicines in the evening, which are useful for promoting sleep. After continuing these things, on the 7th/17th of August, having first poured out prayers to God, the Most Illustrious and Noble Hero subjected himself to the surgery of the aforementioned craftsman. The operation was performed immediately according to the wish of His Illustrious Nobility, such that without any delay, at the first attempt, a **stone** <term>calculus: A hard mass or "stone" formed in the bladder.</term> of two ounces—smooth, very solid, and extremely compact—was extracted. Although no physicians were present at this operation (since the Nobleman, out of a notable sense of modesty, did not desire our presence), the wound from the surgery, which was shown to us afterward, testified that it had been performed so perfectly that nothing was left to be desired. But what happened next? Scarcely had the Noble patient been settled back in bed in a proper and suitable manner when, behold! stinging pains arose around the region of the bladder, to such an extent that the first night after the surgery was quite laborious. However, when a **fomentation** <note>a warm, moist medicinal compress</note> was applied to the bladder region, the stinging pain and the retention of urine itself were eased. Finally, along with the urine, clots of blood that had hardened in the bladder were expelled through the wound. Once these were cleared, a quieter night followed. But on the day after the surgery—

### APPENDIX ON THE REMOVAL OF STONES.

On the fourth day, **August 10/20**, stinging pains accompanied by an internal burning throughout the entire lower abdomen below the navel invaded the patient so wretchedly that he spent the entire night crying out in pain. For this reason, we concluded there was a significant inflammation of the bladder and the surrounding parts, especially since the wound and the entire **perineum** <term>perineum: the area of the body between the genitals and the anus.</term>, along with the scrotum, were turning black with bruising. Therefore, with all our skill—using medicines taken by mouth, as well as enemas and injections into the bladder, together with external remedies—we attempted to counter this evil. However, it was entirely in vain; his vital forces succumbed more and more, until this most noble Hero piously breathed his last on **August 13/23** around six o’clock in the morning. His soul lives eternally in heaven; however, his body—which, by the command of the illustrious and most noble deceased, was to be preserved for the journey to his homeland for burial—was found to be in the following condition. 

The head was not opened, but at the request of his attendants was left whole, and was prepared for preservation by the infusion of suitable substances through the nostrils and ears. In the chest, nothing **abnormal** <note>original: "p. n." (praeter naturam)</note> was observed, except that the lungs on the left side were firmly attached to the membrane lining the ribs <note>this likely refers to pleural adhesions, often caused by past respiratory infections</note>. The gallbladder, filled with a large amount of bile, contained **30 stones**; one of these was like a chestnut, yellowish in color and weighing one **drachm** <term>drachm: an ancient unit of weight; one drachm is roughly 3.9 grams.</term>; another was like a hazelnut 

<column-break/>

weighing half a drachm; the rest were smaller, appearing like the seeds of melons, coriander, and millet. The condition of the stomach, spleen, liver, kidneys, intestines, and **mesentery** <term>mesentery: the fold of membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall.</term> was natural, down to the lower position of the rectum. There, the bladder—which was thicker and fleshier than it should be—along with the adjacent part of the aforementioned intestine, was seized by **gangrene** <term>sphacelo: necrosis or the death of body tissue, often due to lack of blood flow or severe infection.</term> due to the excessive inflammation. It was seen to be completely blackening on its interior surface, though otherwise whole and not damaged anywhere else, except in that place where the surgical probe passed through the wound into the neck of the bladder. 

This wound was so situated—though it was already turning livid and black from the spread of the inflammation—that, with respect to its width, it did not reach the **septum** <note>the dividing wall of tissue</note> of the perineum, nor did it affect the anus or scrotum in terms of its length. From this it must be firmly concluded—especially since in the first days the wound was free of any foreign symptoms—that this occurrence did not originate from the wound itself, but from an internal cause of **congestion** <note>original: "plenitudinis"; a medical theory suggesting an overabundance of bodily fluids led to the inflammation</note>. Consequently, once all these parts were removed, the muscular substance of the inner abdomen was also seen to be suffused with black corruption upward as far as the chest cavity. All these things were performed at the request of the ministers of the late Illustrious and Noble Baron; we, the undersigned physicians, who were called and present for the most part...

## CONSULTATION VI.

<margin>Signs of a stone.</margin>
Since many physicians have gathered many consultations for this Illustrious and Noble Lord—which are full and clear regarding the essence of the disease, its cause, the symptoms, and the affected part—I do not wish to waste time on superfluities, but rather, setting aside all digressions, I shall approach the matter itself.

That His Lordship suffers from a **stone of the bladder** <note>original: "calculo vesicae"</note> is clearly evident from the trial with the syringe <note>In the 17th century, a "syringe" or catheter was inserted into the bladder to physically "sound" or feel for the hard strike of a stone.</note>, as well as the quality and location of the pain. For the epigastrium <term>epigastrium: the upper central part of the abdomen.</term>, the pubic region <term>pecten: the pubic bone or the area just above the genitals.</term>, and the **perineum** <term>perineum: the area between the anus and the genitals.</term> are painful, especially during more violent movement. These are indicators that the bladder is affected by a stone, especially since his bodily functions and excrement attest that the bladder of the Noble Lord is not damaged in and of itself. Having detected the stone, we began to consider its safe treatment; however, whether it should be removed by **cutting** <note>This refers to lithotomy, the surgical removal of bladder stones.</note> is doubted, and not without reason, since surgical operation—according to Hippocrates <note>The ancient Greek "Father of Medicine."</note>—is extremely dangerous, especially in an elderly

<column-break/>

<margin>Whether there is any hope for medication</margin>
subject, in a body with a less-than-ideal constitution, and at a time unsuitable for operation. Hence, I have judged that one should not proceed to surgery rashly or precipitously, especially since some hope shines forth in the skillful use of medicines and a more accurate observation of diet. This is possible when the stone is found to be not so hard or large, when the flow of urine is not blocked, the pain is tolerable, movement is comfortable, and much sandy <note>original: "fabulosa," likely a transcription of "sabulosa" (gravel-like).</note> and viscous matter is still freely excreted through the urine. But it is beyond controversy that a long-standing and firmly compacted stone—or one hardened to the density of flint—cannot be crushed, liquefied, or dissolved by any medicines; on the other hand, a soft, rare, and spongy stone can be treated with no difficulty. The safest cure for a stone consisting of viscous material, which

<margin>How the stone may be halted.</margin>
collects and binds together, consists of evacuation, as well as preventing more of it from being generated there. The former is achieved through pharmacy, the latter through diet. Since the Noble Lord possesses a hotter liver and kidneys, a weaker stomach, and a **biliary constitution** <note>A "choleric" temperament in the humoral system, associated with heat and dryness.</note>, the more vehement, hotter, and corrosive remedies must be strictly avoided. Instead, one should remain with detergent <note>Cleaning or purging agents.</note>, opening, and "cutting" <term>incidentibus: medicines intended to "cut" through or break up thick humors.</term> substances, such as gentle and detergent enemas, or a mild vomit, since his nature is inclined toward it. Furthermore, the following remedies are highly beneficial and have very often been proven effective in many cases.

**Recipe:** Seeds of Mallow and Marshmallow, 3 ounces of each.

### APPENDIX ON LITHOTOMY <note>Lithotomy is the surgical procedure for removing stones from the bladder.</note>

<margin>A decoction strongly recommended by Forestus <note>Pieter van Foreest (1521–1597), a prominent Dutch physician known as the "Hippocrates of the Netherlands."</note></margin>
Take: Greater cold seeds <note>original: "fr. major." refers to the seeds of cucumber, melon, gourd, and watermelon</note>, 1 dram each.
Cleaned barley, 2 drams.
Red chickpeas, 2 drams.
Fat figs, 9 in number.
Sebesten <note>A type of plum from the Cordia myxa tree, often used as an emollient.</note>, 7 in number.
Shaved licorice, 6 drams.
Let a decoction be made of all these in 3 pounds of simple water, reduced by half; let him drink of this decoction as he pleases for two days. Or let him take 1 ½ ounces of Syrup of Marshmallow by Fernel <term>Fernel: Jean Fernel (1497–1558), an influential French physician who standardized many medicinal syrups.</term> and 2 ounces of Bean water. Mix for a draft.

For softening the bowels, these should be in use:
Take: Turpentine washed with radish water, ½ ounce.
Barberry grains <note>original: "Gran. Berb."</note>, chopped very small and infused overnight in purslane water, ½ ounce.
Best prepared white amber powder, 1 scruple.
Sweet almond oil, as much as needed. Mix with sugar, let a bolus <term>bolus: a soft, rounded mass of medicine intended to be swallowed, similar to a large pill.</term> be made.

If it is preferred without Turpentine:
Take: Extracted Cassia flowers <note>Cassia was commonly used as a gentle laxative.</note>, 6 drams.
Electuary of Diasebesten <note>A medicinal paste made primarily from Sebesten plums.</note>, 2 drams.
Extract of rhubarb, 1 scruple.
Juice of licorice, ½ dram.
With sugar as much as needed, let a bolus be made.

If a potion is preferred:
Take: Freshly extracted Cassia flowers, ½ ounce.
Electuary of the juice of roses, 2 drams.
Vitriolated tartar <term>Tartarus vitriolatus: Potassium sulfate, used historically as a diuretic and laxative.</term>, 1 scruple.
Mix with as much parsley and pellitory <note>Pellitory-of-the-wall (Parietaria) was traditionally used for urinary tract ailments.</note> water as needed to make a draft.

Or let turpentine pills be taken. This disease does not tolerate stronger remedies, which must also be observed in breaking the 

<column-break/>

stone, where those medicines are most effective which have little substance but much quality <note>Freitag means medicines that are chemically "refined" rather than bulky herbal mixtures.</note>, and do not taste of corrosive substances or lye. Among these I approve of *sweet spirit of salt and vitriol* <note>Diluted hydrochloric and sulfuric acids, used very carefully as "stone-breakers."</note>, likewise *spirit of Turpentine, oil of Crystals, and of amber, Vitriolated Tartar, salt of bean stalks, of Restharrow* <term>Ononidis: Restharrow, a plant with a reputation for "restraining" the plow, used to treat kidney stones.</term> etc.

Finally, I should not pass over in silence the secret of Giovanni Battista Teodosi <note>A 16th-century Italian physician.</note>, by which he claims he was never deceived:

Take: Fresh Marshmallow leaves, 1 ½ handfuls.
Fresh butter, 3 ounces.
Honey, ½ pound.
Let them boil in water as much as needed until reduced to a third. Let a small, hot draft of this be drunk morning and evening.

->These things I have written with a running pen <note>original: "currente calamo," meaning written in haste or informally.</note> due to the constraints of time: may GOD grant that everything succeeds happily.<-

->JOHANN FREITAG,<-
->*Doctor of Medicine*<-
