### APPENDIX ON LITHOTOMY.

...in yours dated September 7, in the year 1625, you grieve over the untimely death of the most Noble and Distinguished Man, Master Adrian Spigelius <note>Adriaan van den Spiegel (1578–1625), a Flemish anatomist famous for his work on the liver; the "Spigelian lobe" is named after him.</note>, a most excellent Anatomist, whom you report contracted a lethal condition from a slight cause—namely, the puncture of a finger. You add a similar observation regarding a respectable Matron who injured the middle finger of her right hand with a fish bone and neglected the injury during the first few days; shortly afterward, there followed intense pain, inflammation of the entire forearm, and even imminent Gangrene, just as you describe at greater length in your 5th century <note>A "century" in early modern medicine refers to a collection of 100 case observations.</note>, observation 2. However, since my friend, the Distinguished Master Christopher Fingerlin, brought back with him from Italy a more fully detailed account of that same distinguished man's case as an eyewitness <note>original: "αὐτόπτης"</note>, I did not want to miss the opportunity to relate the same history to you a little more fully, using the very words recorded by him. The Noble man [he says],

> at 44 years of age, slender, pale, prone to anger, and having spent many days in places where there were unburied corpses, began to complain, after about 40 days, of pain in the left arm. This arose from a puncture of the index finger and was then communicated to the glandular substance <note>Referring to the lymph nodes.</note> under the armpit, where a tumor—not large, but deep—and a pain arose of such nature and magnitude that it gave cause for a fever that lasted a long time; indeed, it recurred many times,

<column-break/>

not yet ceasing, and it took away his sleep. It hindered the movement not only of the entire arm, but of the whole body, weakened his strength, and caused a wasting of the body. This continued until around the 20th day, when the tumor had suppurated <term>suppurated: formed or discharged pus.</term> and the abscess broke open; twenty ounces <note>original: "℥xx"</note> of somewhat bloody, liquid, and foul-smelling discharge flowed out from there over the space of three days, at which point he seemed to be able to lie on the affected side, to sleep, and to feel better. But when that flow ceased, there followed a diarrhea of yellow matter, verging toward blackness—sometimes mixed with slimy and bloody discharge, sometimes without blood, with no pain or at least very slight pain in the belly. Since the fever still persisted along with this excretion, a consultation was held on what should be done. The primary condition was the abscess under the arms, caused by the external occasion of the finger puncture, lasting a long time until it led to a malignant suppuration. In the diarrhea, pus was excreted, which caused great doubt as to whether it was formed from a ruptured abscess in the Mesentery <note>The fold of membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall.</note>, or if it was transmitted from the chest into the bowels through the vena cava and the azygos vein <note>Veins that return blood to the heart; historical doctors believed they could transport "morbid matter" between body cavities.</note>, which is sometimes inserted into the portal vein. The latter was believed to be the case, because pain was felt in the side before the excretion of pus, which diminished once the pus was excreted—following the example of a youth whose arm had been broken, and while pus was being generated but did not flow out from the affected place, it was discharged through the bowels

# TO BOOK IV, PART II, APPENDIX: ON LITHOTOMY <note>The surgical removal of stones from the bladder.</note>

...was flowing, but as the pus began to flow truly from the wound, the discharge of pus through the bowels was halted.

It is added that when the patient felt an abscess <note>original: "apostema"</note> in the glands under the armpits, and feared lest it might recede toward the heart, he saw to it that a seton <note>A "setaceum" or seton was a strip of linen or thread passed through the skin to keep a wound open for drainage.</note> was branded into that place (though somewhat late) by means of a white-hot needle. However, as the pus flowed there in abundance, the condition was so far from being mitigated that instead the glandular bodies themselves were seized by rot, the fever increased, and a massive putrefaction was communicated first to the Spiritual parts <note>In the medical theory of the time, "Spiritual" parts referred to the organs of the chest (heart and lungs) which governed the "vital spirit."</note> and afterwards to the natural parts <note>The "Natural" parts referred to the organs of the abdomen, such as the liver and stomach.</note>. Consequently, he began to cough up bloody phlegm, to lie uncomfortably upon his right side, to feel pains in that same area, to suffer from purulent diarrhea, and to experience great anxieties and a restless bed-rest, until finally, his strength consumed, he expired. Upon opening the body, as he himself had requested, the lungs were found to be rotten,

<column-break/>

half-corrupted, and turning black with various colors. The liver was almost entirely converted into an abscess, which broke through the diaphragm by the sharpness of the foul discharge <note>original: "saniei acrimoniâ"</note>. Thus, all the natural and spiritual internal organs displayed a quite remarkable state of rot, so that it was no wonder he was forced to endure such great anxiety before death. These are the details, Most Distinguished Man, which I wished to communicate regarding the death of the most deserving Spigelius; the history and outcome of this observation, and especially the autopsy, provide an opportunity for lovers of medicine <note>original: "philiatris"</note> to investigate the causes of diseases, which are often linked together. Would that the freedom to investigate the secrets of nature through the anatomy of corpses were granted to us more often. Fare thee well; live according to your desires with your family, and continue to love me as you do. Given at Ulm in Swabia, on the day before the Calends of August <note>July 31st</note>, 1628.

## BOOK III. PART 2.

Obs. 1. Prevention of incipient gouty pains <term>Podagra: A historical term for gout, specifically when it affects the feet.</term>.
2. Regarding long-standing gouty "fluxions" <term>Fluxion: In early medicine, the supposed flow of harmful humors from the head or blood to a specific joint or organ.</term>.
3. Regarding gouty patients who, even in the absence of a paroxysm <note>A sudden attack or flare-up of symptoms.</note>, are unable to walk forward.

### ON THE USE OF THE SCHWALBACH
### MINERAL WATERS. To the Author.

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal woodcut border with repeating floral and scrollwork motifs. Below the heading, the poem begins with a large, ornate square drop cap 'C' decorated with floral and architectural elements.</image-desc>

Star of Physicians, you wish for the sweet-acid liquid
To be celebrated in song, with which GOD adorns the Hessian fields:
Here, where the Schwalbach mountains, touching even the sky,
Surround on all sides, and houses are built among the broken rocks.
A thirsty poet—whose very name is an anagram for "DRUNK" <note>original: *EPOTA*. The poet is playing on the fact that the Latin word for poet, *POETA*, contains the same letters as *EPOTA*, meaning 'drunk' or 'drained'.</note>—
Would hardly do this; he would not celebrate water in verse.
For he consecrates his life as a drinker, just as
The drunken Cratinus <note>Cratinus (c. 510–420 BC) was an Athenian comic poet famous for his talent and his legendary love of wine.</note> said, speaking from more than one wine-skin:
For such a man, wine is the whetstone of genius, and the horse of the prophets,
And the poetic vein is accustomed to return only when unmixed wine <note>original: *mero*</note> is poured in.
But let him first do it who knows that Apollo <note>original: *Phoebum*</note> is the father
Of both the Lyrical and the Medical Chorus:
Who would deny to this Spring verses sprinkled with sesame and poppy <note>A classical metaphor for ornate or "sweetened" poetry.</note>
In your praises, O Spring, if he wished to approach them?
Would he deny a song? Let the Jew Apella <note>A reference to Horace’s *Satires* (1.5.100), a common Roman expression meaning "let someone else believe it, not I"—used here to express deep skepticism.</note> believe it,
Not I: who would forbid the Muses to quench their thirst at the fountain?
You, who surpass the gifts of Bacchus <note>Wine</note>, and all
Riches, and who are better than the treasures of Croesus <note>The king of Lydia famous for his immense wealth.</note>.
Hail, clear Spring! For the health of our kind,
May your pleasing wave bubble up for a long time.
May the dweller of the Rhone visit you, and the dweller of the Rhine,
And may they feel and celebrate your help.
May he whose nerves are weakened by dreadful foot-gout <term>Podagra: A form of inflammatory arthritis, usually in the big toe, historically associated with rich diets.</term>
Leave his crutches <note>original: *sustentacula pedum*, literally "foot-supports".</note> here; may hand-gout <term>Chiragra: Gout specifically affecting the hands.</term> ever tremble before you,
As well as countless other diseases. Return to GIESSEN <note>The University of Giessen, where Horstius was a professor.</note>
One safe and sound: return HORSTIUS
To his studies, so that he himself might compose a song worthy of you;
You could not be read by a better herald.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page's introduction, moving from the divine origin of medicine to the specific history and composition of the legendary antidote, Theriac. # MEDICAL LETTERS BOOK II. SECTION I.

<margin>Where does the name "Theriac" come from?</margin>
—centuries, is Theriac. It is most celebrated, not so much because of the viper flesh used as an ingredient (since the viper is called *echis* and *echidne* <note>original: ἔχις καὶ ἐχιδνη</note> by the Greeks, although in Naples it is called *Tirus*, using an improper and generic name), but rather because it is so named because it resists all poisonous things, among which the bites of beasts—or *thēriōn* <note>original: τῶν θηρίων</note>—are of the greatest concern. This was the view of Bartholomaeus Marantha in the first book of *On Theriac*, chapter 1, though Marco Oddo expressly contradicts him in his first discourse on Theriac and Mithridatium, chapter 7. However that may be, once the facts are understood, let us not be difficult about the words: namely,
<margin>What is Theriac?</margin>
that Theriac is an antidote <term>Alexipharmacum: A traditional Greek term for a remedy used to ward off poison or infection.</term> of such a kind that, with the eventual addition of viper flesh, it was prepared with the greatest diligence and confirmed by the subsequent experience of Andromachus the Elder, physician to the Emperor Nero, so that its composition has been left to posterity even until now. Furthermore, we
<margin>Whether the Theriac of the Greeks can still be made today.</margin>
should not listen to those who claim that in our time the Theriac of the Greeks cannot be prepared at all. Among these people (as cited by Fuchs in book 2 of *On the Composition of Medicines*, chapter 2) are numbered Bernhard Dessenius, and—according to my friend Dr. Michael Doring in his *Examination of Mithridatium*, page 280—Andreas Bürner. For most of the ingredients can still be obtained today, provided we do not spare expense and diligence; and for the few exceptions, effective substitutes fill their place. Hence, we also rightly commend your skill, most expert man and dearly beloved friend, who, having sought out the necessary

<column-break/>

simple ingredients from all sides, wished to subject this most noble antidote to the judgment of physicians in a twelve-fold preparation <note>This likely refers to a large-scale batch or a specific concentrated ratio of the recipe.</note> in the presence of the Honorable Magistrates of the Republic, not without singular praise for your labor and learning. Quercetanus <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician who popularized "chemical" medicine and reorganization of traditional recipes.</note>, in his *Pharmacopoeia Restored*, quite conveniently looks at the reasoning behind the ingredients. He assigns to the first class the lozenges of Squill <term>Trochisci de Scilla: Medicinal lozenges made from sea onion (squill), a common diuretic and expectorant.</term>, the *Hedychroos* <term>Hedychroos: A complex aromatic compound of nearly 20 ingredients (including spices like cinnamon and cloves) used as a base for Theriac.</term>, and the Viper lozenges, as these constitute the base of the composition. In the second class, he places Opium and Saffron <note>original: *Crocum*</note> as painkillers <note>original: *anodyna*</note>, along with their correctives: namely, Sealed Earth <term>Terra sigillata: "Sealed earth," a medicinal clay stamped with an official seal to guarantee its origin and purity.</term>, Acacia, Hypocistis <note>A parasitic plant extract used as an astringent.</note>, and Gum Arabic. To the third class, he ascribes roots, leaves, and fruits that resist poisons and rot. To the fourth class, he assigns aromatics that warm the blood and the spirit and strengthen nature. To the fifth class, he adds the "tears" or resins: Myrrh, Frankincense, Styrax Calamita <note>A fragrant resin often called liquid storax.</note>, and Turpentine, for the defense of our "radical balsam" <note>A Paracelsian term for the innate vital moisture or life-force of the body.</note> against imminent putrefaction. Finally, to the sixth class, he connects the thinning, dissolving, and "de-obstructing" gums. In this way, an account of all ingredients is given (except for three, which will be discussed later). Nevertheless, we do not reject the common distinction into six classes observed long ago and still used today because of the customary method of compounding. According to this method, we also conducted an examination of the Theriac ingredients with you not long ago, with as much diligence as possible, namely—

<meta>The catchword "rum" at the end of the page belongs to the word "nimirum" (surely/namely), which Horstius is using to transition into the specifics of his and Schmidt's collaboration.</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the etymology and definition of Theriac, arguing against contemporary skeptics that the ancient Greek recipe remains viable today. It further outlines a six-fold classification of its ingredients according to the chemist Quercetanus, ranging from the "base" vipers and squill to various resins and aromatics.</summary>
<keywords>Theriac, Andromachus the Elder, vipers, Quercetanus, antidote, pharmacology, Giengen, pharmacy, aromatics, resins</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Gregor Horstius's detailed report to the apothecary Georg Schmidt regarding the inspection and preparation of a batch of Theriac. Having established the history and definition of the antidote on the previous page, Horstius now moves into the practical examination of the specific ingredients used, organized by "Classes."</meta>

-># ON THE COMPOSITION OF THERIAC.<-

...which we conducted in your home on September 29th of the current year.

<margin>Class I.</margin>
## First, you presented the ingredients of the First Class to us, where the following appeared:

### Orris Root from Illyria
<note>original: "Rad. Ireos Illyricæ"</note>
Most fragrant, firm, and excellently cleaned.

### Our local Water Germander,
<note>original: "Scordium nostrum"</note>
Which we chose to keep instead of the Cretan variety, as it is judged to be sufficiently effective—provided that one does not mistake wild garlic or garlic mustard <term>Alliaria: Also known as Jack-by-the-hedge, a common herb with a garlic-like scent.</term> for it. Some might be satisfied by the testimony of the scent alone, for which reason the work of Wilhelm Fabry <note>Guilielmus Fabricius Hildanus (1560–1634), often called the "Father of German Surgery."</note> in his *Century 2 of Surgical Observations*, Observation 94, should be consulted. Since our local water germander grows abundantly in this neighborhood, it would be absurd to mix in the odorless and tasteless Cretan germander that is sold in markets; therefore, we rightly rejected it. Marantha <note>Bartholomaeus Marantha, a 16th-century physician and botanist.</note> approves of the germander that grows in mountainous places, the abundance of which I myself have observed not far from the springs of Bad Ems <note>original: "Thermis Emsensibus"</note> near Koblenz on the Rhine; I would prefer this even to that which grows in marshy areas.
<margin>A Doubt.</margin>
However, a question arises: since the juice of water germander is most resistant to putrefaction—to the extent that the aforementioned highly skilled Fabry suggests the dried plant has less efficacy—should we not prefer the juice, expressed and purified in the springtime, over the herb itself? He teaches that this juice can be preserved in various ways in the passage cited. But let us proceed to

<column-break/>

### Seeds of Wild Turnip,
<note>original: "Semen Buniadis"</note>
Or wild turnip, which according to Galen <note>A foundational Greek physician whose medical system dominated Europe for 1,500 years.</note> should be the Cretan variety, but in its place you have rightly substituted the seeds of Bavarian rampion <term>Rapunculorum: Likely referring to a species of Brassica or Campanula used as a substitute for exotic seeds.</term>, with the agreement of Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs, a famous German botanist.</note> and others; afterwards

### Zedoary
<note>original: "Zedoaria"</note>
Also selected and not at all decayed; this was once used in Theriac in place of Costus. However, we did not need to do that at present because true Costus <term>Costus: An aromatic root from India, highly prized in ancient pharmacy.</term> was ready at hand—resembling white cinnamon, striking the tongue with an aromatic bitterness and the nostrils with a pleasant scent. More on this can be found in the *Aleodarium Marocostino* of Minderer, chapter 3.

### Mountain Germander,
<note>original: "Polium montanum"</note>
Namely the mountain variety, quite pungent, selected and cleaned of its stalks, and full of foliage, flowers, and seeds.

### Aniseed
Most fragrant, with even and mature grains,

### and Marseille Hartwort,
<note>original: "Seseleos Massiliensis"</note>
Which also grows among us; it is not unlike dill seed, somewhat blackish, and striking the tongue with sharpness. Its use in place of the Cretan variety (which is uncertain to us) is rightly commended.

Once these had been coarsely crushed, mixed, and stored in their proper place, we proceeded to the
<margin>Class II.</margin>
## Simple ingredients of the second class,
where the first to appear was

### Cinquefoil Root.
<note>original: "Radix Pentaphylli"</note>

*Recently brought from Italy, with added testimony that they were carefully made during the preceding spring, not rancid or covered with mold, but translucent and yellowish; some call these "pastilles from Tyre" <note>original: "pastillos è Tiro"</note>, because the barbarians call a viper* <margin>Question V.</margin> *Tirus. Although I am not unaware that our serpents have*

<column-break/>

an affinity with vipers, especially the grass snakes <note>original: "Colubris"</note>, which also shed their skins every year in the manner of a viper; nevertheless, I would think that one should not easily depart from viper flesh. This is both because a Theriac antidote made in Germany would soon be called something different from that which is made in Venice and Padua, and also because Andromachus <note>Andromachus the Elder was the court physician to Nero; he is famous for refining the recipe for Theriac by adding viper flesh, believing it essential for neutralizing venom.</note>, and others after him, chose the viper over other species for certain reasons. This can be seen in the Author of *On Theriac to Piso*, chapter 8 <note>A work traditionally attributed to the Roman physician Galen.</note>, as well as in Oddus's *First Sermon on Theriac and Mithridate*, chapter 10, and Marantha, book 1 *On Theriac*, chapter 3: specifically, that the viper is less venomous than the other species which they enumerate in the cited passages. 

Add what we proposed at greater length about fifteen years ago in our *Therapeutic Problems* <note>original: "problematibus nostris therapeuticis"</note>, Decade 10, Question 4. There it is demonstrated that viper flesh enters the Theriac not as if it were a poison leading the way by similarity (as an alexipharmic <term>Alexipharmaca: A medicine intended to neutralize or expel poison from the body.</term> to expel poison), which was the opinion of Marantha and Thomas Jordanus; nor even because a poison can be contrary to a poison, as Joubertus wished; but by that reasoning insofar as a unique alexipharmic power exists in the flesh of vipers, as is confirmed by us at length in the cited place. Let the *Letter of Andrea Bacci to Antonio Porta* be read on this subject, appended to the treatise on medical composition by Marcus Oddus of Padua. If anything

### Squill Lozenges,

carefully fashioned from prepared Squill <note>original: "Scilla"; a sea onion used in ancient medicine as a potent diuretic and expectorant.</note> mixed with the flour of bitter vetch <note>original: "ervi farina"</note>, and dried slowly in the shade, so that neither the flour nor any part of the squill’s skins could be detected in them. If anything here required changing, I would listen to Quercetanus, who, among other things, mentions "transplantation." I remember that Squill was greatly improved by this method when I once transferred one or two bulbs bought in Frankfurt to the medical garden at Giessen. There, I have no doubt that all the praises collected from Serapio, Avicenna, Actuarius, Aëtius, Paul, Galen, Dioscorides, Pliny, and others by Janus Matthaeus Durastantes regarding the excellence of **Scillitic Vinegar** <note>Vinegar infused with squill, used for various ailments.</note> would be far more deserved after such a preparation. He solidly refutes Manardus, Brassavolus, and others who try to deny us the true **Indian Spikenard** <note>original: "Spica Indica"; Nardostachys jatamansi, a highly valued perfume and medicinal herb from the Himalayas.</note>, which, as we noted in passing, can conveniently be pulverized separately.

### Cinnamon,
which, although very well known today, was quite rare in the past, as is especially evident from Galen; see Book 1 *On Antidotes*, chapter 13.

### Long Pepper,
solid, not decayed, and still clearly possessing its stems, which Galen describes in *On Theriac to Piso*, chapter 12, as how it should be selected and distinguished from the counterfeit. Therefore, we rightly wonder at Melichius, who thinks those who mix long pepper into Theriac are in error, since it is even found in the poem of Andromachus <note>Andromachus the Elder, physician to Nero and credited creator of this Theriac formula.</note> itself in Book 1 *On Antidotes*, chapter 6, where he says:
> & let there also be an equal weight of long pepper.

It is worth noting what Pontanus reports in the dispensation of Theriac at the end of Wittichius’s *Medical Observations and Counsels*: that every kind of pepper is the fruit of the same plant, and only differs in respect to ripeness. One who cannot believe this should be sent to where pepper grows <note>A play on the German idiom "wo der Pfeffer wächst," meaning to send someone to a far-off, remote place.</note>, as the German proverb usually says, unless the difference of the plants producing pepper were more fully revealed by Garcia de Orta (Book 1, chapter 22) and other more recent authors. Following in this class are:

<column-break/>

### Hedychroum Lozenges,
<note>original: "Trochisci Hedychroj"; "sweet-colored" lozenges, a complex aromatic compound used as a base ingredient in Theriac.</note>
diligently prepared by you according to Galen. Along with these, you showed us **Oil of Cloves**, which was omitted by prudent counsel so that it might be mixed in near the end of the Theriac’s blending, thereby making the whole composition more perfect. You candidly suggested that you substituted leaves of **Cretan Dittany** <note>original: "Dictamni Cretici"; Origanum dictamnus, a plant famous in antiquity for its healing properties.</note> in place of **Cat-Thyme** <note>original: "Mari"; Teucrium marum.</note>, while meanwhile presenting the dried Cat-Thyme plant obtained at your own expense. I judged this to be genuine, not only from the leaves but also from the scent—it is very well known to me, having been cultivated quite often in the courtly garden at Darmstadt and the academic garden at Giessen, even though Fuchs <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a founding father of German botany.</note>, in Book 2 *On the Composition of Medicines*, did not believe the same could grow in Germany. You can read more about this in Francesco Alessandro, Rad. 3, under the title of Hedychroum Lozenges. There remains:

<margin>Class VI.</margin>
### The sixth class, which contained "The Leaf,"
in whose place you substituted equal parts of **Mace** and **Cloves** according to the Augsburg practice <note>original: "cum Augustanis"; referring to the official pharmacopoeia of the city of Augsburg.</note>. This was not without merit, since the opinion of the ancients regarding "The Leaf" or **Malabathrum** <note>Cinnamomum tamala; the leaf of the Indian cinnamon tree, which was often confused with other aromatics like spikenard in early modern botany.</note> is entirely uncertain, as can be seen from Scaliger (Exercise 146, Section 2), Fallopius (Treatise on Materia Medica, on Book 1 of Dioscorides, chapter 15), and others. However, Garcia de Orta (Book 1, chapter 19) and Fragoso (Treatise 2, chapter 7 *On Exotic Medicines*) describe a different "Leaf" or Malabathrum, which I remember seeing in abundance in the pharmacies of Lower Saxony.

### Cubebs

Substituted in place of **Carpobalsamum** <note>original: "Carpobalsami"; the fruit of the balsam tree (*Commiphora gileadensis*), which was extremely rare and prone to spoilage during transport.</note>, these should be choice, equal-sized large grains, and freed from their stems. Here, Melichius <note>Georg Melich, a 16th-century Venetian pharmacist known for his work on Theriac.</note> takes juniper berries, which nevertheless correspond less to the effects of the ancients' Carpobalsamum than **Cubebs** <note>original: "Cubebae"; *Piper cubeba*, a spicy berry from Java.</note> do. Indeed, Marcus Oddus <note>Marco Oddo, a professor of medicine at Padua.</note> (in the cited place, discourse 2, chapter 3) tries to demonstrate that Cubebs have also been less skillfully substituted by Marantha and others; he instead substitutes **Nutmeg** <note>original: "Nucem moschatam".</note>, and not without reason, while refuting the use of juniper berries, ivy clusters, Cretan carrot, cloves, and cardamom.

### Cardamom,

specifically the smaller kind <note>original: "Cardamomum minus"; *Elettaria cardamomum*, considered more potent than the larger "grains of paradise" variety.</note>, which is sharper and stronger than the larger variety; it tastes somewhat bitter when chewed, and seems to suit Marantha’s <note>Bartolomeo Maranta, a 16th-century physician and botanist who wrote extensively on Theriac.</note> requirements here more than the larger kind.

### Black Pepper,

which is called "Pepper" without any addition by Actuarius <note>Joannes Actuarius, a 13th-century Byzantine physician whose works remained influential in the Renaissance.</note> and almost generally by us today; it should be heavy, thick, with a thin skin, not too wrinkled, and not crumbly (much like how white pepper used to be seen), along with

**Arabian Stoechas Flowers**, still fresh—as much, that is, as such a great distance between places allows—

<column-break/>

<margin>Arabian Stoechas Herb.</margin>
namely with the spikes whole and fragrant, containing mature seeds. When committed to the earth, these have several times produced for us a herb a span in length <note>original: "spithamae"; a span is approximately 9 inches, the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the pinky.</note>, very fragrant, resembling Lavender in appearance. I would not doubt at all that this herb, recently dried in the shade, could be substituted for withered flowers—just as you will perhaps rightly judge along with me from the fresh herb germinating for me this summer, which I have sent to you here.

<margin>Other ingredients besides these six Classes to be ground for certain reasons.</margin>
Once these items had been separately and coarsely crushed according to the aforementioned six classes and set aside, we had to further consider which items must be pulverized by themselves and which must be dissolved according to the rules of the art. Of that former kind was

<margin>To be prepared separately.</margin>
### Agaric,

prepared with wine only, without the addition of any further corrective (a role usually filled by ginger), and formed into lozenges <note>original: "trochiscos".</note>; it should be very white and very fresh. To prevent it from sticking too much to the mortar, it can be ground with some portion of the roots and herbs.

### Myrrh,

transparent, oily, and when broken showing white veins within. Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus, a 16th-century German physician and botanist who pioneered modern pharmacopoeias.</note> adds why it is called "Troglodyte" <note>Historically, the finest grade of myrrh, named for the "Cave-dwellers" (Troglodytes) of the Red Sea coast who traded it.</note>; for its selection, one should consult Marantha and Marcus Oddus.

### Frankincense,

pure and bright, which is hinted at by the "brightness of Frankincense" in the verse description of Andromachus’s Theriac <note>The original recipe by Andromachus the Elder was written as a poem to ensure the dosages and ingredients were not easily altered by copyists.</note>; it should be whole, whitish, and formed of rounded grains.

Fff 2

->**Castoreum**,<- <note>original: "Castoreum"; a bitter, orange-brown oily substance secreted by beavers to mark territory, highly prized in ancient medicine for treating "hysteria" and nervous disorders.</note>

where the scent glands <note>original: "testes"; although these are actually the beaver's castor sacs, they were historically referred to as testicles due to their shape and position.</note> were shown to be still whole, wrapped in their natural membranes, fresh, and possessing a very pungent odor. We are less concerned about the risk of its adulteration because this animal is frequently caught in our Germany; indeed, I recall that several times in my homeland it was brought in by fishermen from the Elbe, that famous river near Torgau and Wittenberg <note>original: "Wirebergam"; likely a variant spelling of Wittenberg, a major center of learning in Saxony.</note>, as Gessner <note>Conrad Gessner (1516–1565), the Swiss "father of modern zoology."</note> also testifies happens elsewhere;

so named because it is believed to be collected from the Dead Sea, otherwise called **Asphalt**. This sample was pure, and when broken, it sparkled like purple—according to Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, the 1st-century author of the most influential herbal in history.</note>, not necessarily in its literal color, but in the vibrancy of its luster, since a "purple brilliance" can be attributed to all colors in that same way;

<margin>Ingredients to be dissolved in a specific manner.</margin>
->**Acacia Juice**,<- <note>original: "Succus Acaciæ"; the sap of the Egyptian *Acacia vera* tree.</note>

which you presented as being carefully pressed from our wild plums <note>original: "prunis sylvestribus"; likely the common sloe (*Prunus spinosa*).</note>, strained, and thickened to an excellent consistency. This is a suitable substitution, since we do not have true acacia juice available to us. Although this substitution does not displease Maranta <note>Bartolomeo Maranta (d. 1571), an influential Italian physician and botanist.</note>, he himself, along with the physicians of Bologna, prefers to take the juice of **Rhus** (or **Sumach**) instead; Marcus Oddus <note>Marco Oddo, a professor at the University of Padua.</note> substitutes fresh **Myrtle** juice, which we also lack in Germany;

<column-break/>

->**Juice of Hypocistis**,<- <note>original: "Succus hypocisthidos"; an astringent juice extracted from a parasitic plant that grows on the roots of the Rock Rose.</note>

which we would rather retain while it is still fresh and endowed with a suitable flavor, rather than using its substitute.

->**Licorice Juice**,<- <note>original: "Succus glycyrrhizæ".</note>

diligently prepared by yourself; it is not scorched, but thickened to such a suitable consistency that, when broken, it shows the same substance of hardened juice inside as is seen on its outer surface.

->**Opium**,<-

whether it be the "tears" <note>The pure latex that naturally seeps from cuts in the poppy pod.</note> or the juice of the poppy, which they call **Meconium** <note>original: "Meconium"; traditionally the juice pressed from the whole poppy plant, which was considered less potent than the pure tears of opium.</note>. Today it is very well known, and you presented it to us while still raw and also dissolved. For although Maranta, following the intentions of the Ancients, would rather desire the tears of the poppy than the expressed juice in this recipe, we nevertheless—along with Oddus—substitute this opium of ours (perhaps expressed by a press), which is heavy, dense, bitter to the taste, and sleep-inducing to the smell. It is a substance that certainly does not fail in its effect, as its extract in **Opiated Laudanum** <note>A potent medicinal tincture containing opium.</note> sufficiently confirms. For this reason, the more recent authors also seem to agree, namely Garcia de Orta <note>A Portuguese pioneer of tropical medicine who lived in India.</note> (Book 1, chapter 4) and Cristobal Acosta <note>A botanist who studied the medicinal plants of the East Indies.</note> (Book of Aromatics, treatise 4, chapter 12).

### Styrax Calamites,
<note>original: "Styrax Calamites"; a fragrant resin from the *Styrax officinalis* tree. The name "Calamites" refers to the reeds (*calami*) in which it was traditionally packed or where the resin was said to collect.</note>
so named because it grows in reeds or canes, which was rare in the time of Galen <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire.</note>, and differed from common Styrax just as Falernian wine <note>A prestigious high-end wine from ancient Rome.</note> differs from that sold in taverns. For this reason, we have not included Styrax full of impurities, but rather that which is selected for its pure, highly fragrant, resinous grains that are white on the inside. For the black, resinous kind with a crumbly consistency and a white, moldy residue is rejected, as Mutonus <note>A reference to a medical commentator on the "Mithridatium," a precursor to Theriac.</note> warns in his *Examination of the Mithridatium*:

### Turpentine,
namely the Cyprian kind, brought from Venice, transparent with a golden color, clear and pure;

### Oil of Nutmeg by expression,
<note>original: "Oleum Nucis Moschatae per expressionem"; oil produced by physically pressing the nutmeg rather than distilling it with heat.</note>
carefully pressed from fresh, fatty, heavy nutmeg that has not been scorched, in the manner taught by Marcus Oddus <note>Marc'Antonio Oddi, a 16th-century Italian physician.</note> (among others) in his third discourse on Theriac, chapter 4. We have substituted this for **Opobalsamum** <note>True Balsam or Balm of Gilead, a rare and expensive resin from the Middle East, often substituted in European pharmacies.</note> along with Maranta <note>Bartolomeo Maranta (c. 1500–1571), a botanist and physician famous for his work on Theriac.</note> and others, setting aside the distilled oil of the same. Although some use that distilled oil, just as they use oil of cloves as a substitute, it is rightly rejected by the arguments proposed by Döringius <note>Michael Döring (died 1644), a physician and author.</note>—my friend and former colleague—in his booklet on **Opobalsamum**. He presents the opinion of those who would rather substitute Peruvian or Toletan <note>Balsam from Toledo, Spain.</note> Balsam, an idea we would not reject if only a supply of that Balsam were available to us over

<column-break/>

time without being adulterated:

### Saffron,
Oriental, with long filaments and a deep red color, most pure, and with a heaviness of scent almost hostile to the nostrils; according to Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a famous Italian doctor and botanist.</note>, a select variety also grows in Austria, which does not yield to the Oriental kind in its characteristics, and which he admits for use in compounding antidotes:

### Silesian Sealed Earth,
<note>original: "Terra Sigillata Silesiaca"; medicinal clay pressed into cakes and stamped with a seal to guarantee authenticity. It was used as an antidote to poison and for treating infections.</note>
which is deservedly substituted for **Lemnian Seal**, since the latter is fraudulent and uncertain, while the former is not only confirmed by public authority, but also approved by its most successful action, which it displays in all malignant conditions:

### Chalcitis,
<note>original: "Chalcitis"; a mineral containing copper and iron sulfates, used for its drying and astringent properties.</note>
not indeed the kind of the ancients, which was numbered among remedies that induce crusting or burning and possess astringent power, and which seemed to hold a middle place between **Misy** and **Sory** <note>Related mineral sulfates used in ancient medicine.</note>. Francesco Alessandro <note>Francesco Alessandro of Vicenza, a medical author.</note> discusses this at length in his *Phoebus or Apollo*, Root 1, against Cardanus, Amatus, Mattioli, Brassavola, and others, in his additions to the **Theriac of Andromachus**. Instead, we use **Roman Vitriol** <note>Iron or copper sulfate.</note> calcined to a yellow color. We believed this should by no means be omitted, contrary to the opinions of Cordus <note>Valerius Cordus (1515–1544), author of the first official pharmacopoeia in Germany.</note>, Dessenius, and others; this is because, besides the black color it provides, it greatly aids fermentation, and because Quercetanus <note>Joseph Du Chesne (c. 1544–1609), a prominent Paracelsian physician known by his Latinized name.</note> determined that the mixture is rendered more excellent by replacing it with a properly prepared Spirit of Vitriol.

Quercetanus <note>original: "cetanus"; refers to Joseph Duchesne (Latinized as Quercetanus, 1544–1609), a prominent French physician and chemist.</note> notes for me on page 608 of his *Restored Pharmacopoeia* that Theriac gains its drying quality from this source, as Leonhart Fuchs <note>original: "Fuch."; a German physician and botanist (1501–1566) famous for his herbal.</note> suggests in the second book of *The Composition of Medicines*. I need not add what Mindererus <note>Raymond Minderer (1570–1621), a German physician.</note> attempts to prove in chapter 6 of his book *On Copperas* <note>original: "Calcantho"; refers to vitriol or copperas, a metallic salt.</note>—namely, that **Chalcitis** <note>A copper-bearing mineral.</note> or its substitute, **Calcined Vitriol**, also possesses a singular power to resist poisons.

### Gum Arabic,
which in the apothecary shops is called "Arabic" by addition, signifies, according to Galen, any type of tear-like resin from a resin-bearing tree. However, Aëtius <note>A 6th-century Byzantine Greek physician.</note> proposes "vermicular" gum, as if he means **Tragacanth**, which Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD) who wrote *De Materia Medica*.</note> says appears like small worms. Nevertheless, we have kept with you well-selected Gum Arabic, which lacks any bitterness or sharp taste.

### Sagapenum,
also called Serapinum, is transparent with the color of myrrh, grainy and fragrant. It has a great affinity with **Galbanum** (or as the Greek word has it, *Chalbano*), much like the similarity shared between Cinnamon and Cassia, or Myrrh and Opocalpasum <note>A resin often used to adulterate myrrh.</note>.

### Opoponax,
<note>A gum resin derived from the *Ferula opoponax* plant.</note>
possessing a reddish-white color on the inside and a saffron-yellow color on the outside; it is fatty in consistency, affecting the nostrils with a heavy odor and the tongue with a very bitter taste.

### Galbanum,
<note>A bitter, aromatic gum resin derived from certain Persian plants.</note>
not full of all the filth of wood and pebbles as is commonly sold in

<column-break/>

the apothecary shops, but selected grains like incense. Galen suggests the method for purifying this in Book 3 of *Medicines According to Kind*, chapter 5.

After all these things have been diligently weighed and observed, **Honey** and **Wine** surpass them in importance. Of the former, a fragrant variety was chosen, pale in color, extremely sharp and sweet to the taste, and in consistency neither too thick, nor curdled, nor very liquid, but continuous and uniform throughout. Marcus Oddus <note>Marc'Antonio Oddi, a 16th-century medical writer.</note> requires these same qualities, among others, when he discusses the nature and selection of honey at length in the third discourse, chapter 12, of his cited book; to this may be added the reading of Marantha <note>Bartolomeo Maranta (d. 1571), a physician and botanist who wrote on Theriac.</note> in Book 1 of *On Theriac*, chapter 30. Regarding the latter—that is, the **Cretan Wine** <note>Also known as Malmsey, a sweet, fortified wine from Crete highly prized in pharmacy.</note>—you promised that you, in your integrity, to whom the entire remaining composition of the Theriac was entrusted, would add it appropriately, being old and perfectly purified. For this reason, since everything has been successfully completed thus far, you poured out for us visitors—and indeed spectators—a generous hand of excellent **Neccatinum** wine <note>Possibly a local vintage or a specific type of sweet "nectar" wine used as a celebratory drink.</note> in place of the Cretan, so that the various tastes of the different ingredients might be thoroughly washed from our tongues. At the same time, a banquet was prepared—not like the one the rancid old man Milo provided for Lucius Apuleius, in which Apuleius himself declares that at that starving feast he was weighed down more by sleep than by food, and dined only on stories—but a most sumptuous one, which a selection of autumn birds and a variety of rare fish, among other things, adorned.

# ON THE COMPOSITION OF THERIAC.

Fff 3

<meta>catchword: que</meta>

Quercetanus <note>original: "cetanus"; refers to Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician and chemist.</note> mentions to me on page 608 of his *Restored Pharmacopoeia* that Theriac acquires its drying quality from this source, as Leonhart Fuchs <note>A German physician (1501–1566), one of the founding fathers of botany.</note> suggests in the second book of his *Composition of Medicines*. I need not add what Raymond Minderer <note>A military physician from Augsburg (1570–1621).</note> attempts to prove in the sixth chapter of his book *On Vitriol* <note>original: "de Calcantho"; Calcanthum or Chalcitis refers to copper-based vitriol.</note>: namely, that Chalcitis—or its substitute, Calcined Vitriol—uniquely resists poisons as well.

->Gum Arabic,<-

which is called "Arabic" in the apothecary shops by the addition of that name, denotes, according to Galen <note>The influential 2nd-century Greek physician.</note>, the "tears" or resin of any resin-bearing tree. However, Aëtius <note>A 6th-century Byzantine physician.</note> refers to it as "vermicular" gum, as if he means Tragacanth, because Dioscorides <note>The 1st-century author of *De Materia Medica*.</note> says it appears in the shape of small worms. Nevertheless, we have kept with you well-selected Gum Arabic that is free from any sharpness or bitterness.

->Sagapenum,<-

also called Serapinum, is transparent like the color of Myrrh, grainy and fragrant. It has a great affinity with Galbanum—or *Chalbano* as the Greek term has it—so much so that just as Cinnamon and Cassia, or Myrrh and Opocalpasum <note>A resin resembling Myrrh, often used as an adulterant or substitute.</note>, share a common nature, so do these resins.

->Opoponax,<-

which is endowed with a reddish-white color on the inside and a saffron-yellow color on the outside; it is fatty in consistency, affects the nostrils with a heavy odor, and touches the tongue with a very bitter taste.

->Galbanum,<-

which must not be full of the impurities of wood and pebbles as it is commonly sold in

<column-break/>

shops, but should be selected in grains like frankincense. Galen suggests the method for purifying it in the fifth chapter of the third book of *On Medicines according to Kind*. 
After all these things have been diligently weighed and observed, Honey and Wine surpass them. Of the former, the variety selected was fragrant, pale in color, and both very sharp and very sweet to the taste; in consistency, it was neither too thick nor solid, nor very liquid, but consistent and unified throughout. Marcus Oddo <note>An Italian medical professor at Padua.</note>, among others, requires these qualities in the third discourse, chapter 12, of his cited book, where he discusses the nature and selection of Honey at length. To this should be added the reading of Bartolomeo Maranta’s <note>A 16th-century physician and botanist.</note> first book *On Theriac*, chapter 30. 
As for the Wine, it should be Cretan wine <note>Often referred to as Malmsey, a sweet, high-alcohol wine favored in pharmacy for its preservative qualities.</note>, aged and excellently purified. Out of your own integrity <note>original: "Candore tuo"; literally 'your brightness/purity,' a formal address to the recipient's character.</note>, to whom the entire remaining composition of the Theriac was entrusted, you promised to add it appropriately. For this reason, having successfully managed all the preparations thus far, you poured out for us—as visitors and indeed as spectators—a generous hand of the finest *Neccatinum* <note>original: "Neccatinum"; likely a sweet, nectar-like wine used as a palate cleanser.</note> in place of the Cretan wine, so that the diverse flavors of the various ingredients would be thoroughly cleansed from our tongues. 
At the same time, a dinner was prepared—not like the one that the rancid old man Milo presented to Lucius Apuleius <note>A reference to Apuleius's Roman novel *The Golden Ass* (2nd century AD).</note>. In that famished banquet, Apuleius declares he was weighed down by sleep rather than food, and dined only on stories. Yours, however, was most refined, adorned with a selection of autumn birds and a variety of rare fish, among other delicacies.

### MEDICAL EPISTLES, BOOK II, SECTION I.

<margin>Humorous matters.</margin>
...with which, the barking stomach being sated, the remainder of the evening was consumed in pleasant conversation, with playful and serious matters mingled together. Among these, a friendly disagreement held almost the first place, in which that most experienced man, Lord Doctor Sebastian Stromajer—my colleague and, in this business also, a most faithful assistant <note>original: "Parastates"; a Greek-derived term for a helper or companion-in-arms.</note>—disputed with you concerning the singular preparation of the Spirit of Roses. You, unless I am mistaken, understood it to be the Spirit of Cherries. I settled this controversy by reciting a humorous story: namely, that in the house of my kinsman, Lord Daniel Leicher, a Senator of Leipzig of pious memory, there once met Lord Doctor Johannes Jessenius, a Professor at Wittenberg, and Lord Doctor Joachim Tancke, a Professor at Leipzig. The former spoke of the singular anatomical matters in which he excelled, while the latter recounted the chemical secrets <note>original: "arcana chymica"; refers to alchemical or early pharmaceutical preparations.</note> most highly commended to him. When finally Jessenius extolled anatomical knowledge to such an extent that he did not hesitate—even making a wager—to slaughter the most robust bull with only a somewhat sturdy needle, provided he were allowed to touch the back part of the head, and this because he had learned through skillful dissection the true origin of the nerves. Tancke then added (whether seriously or in jest, I do not know) that through his knowledge of Chemistry he possessed such a vital balsam that he did not doubt that, by anointing the same, he could revive the mechanical spirits so that he might restore the ox, slaughtered in the aforementioned manner, alive to its former health. Humorous ap-

<column-break/>

-plause was given to both sides, and this story, just as it did for you when you were discussing various matters, settled the friendly contest. In passing, on the occasion of mentioning the aforementioned Jessenius, once my most deserving teacher, I have recounted a noteworthy commemoration of the Hieroglyphic significance of Theriac <note>Theriac was often treated as a "universal medicine" containing the signatures of the entire natural world.</note>, which was performed publicly at Wittenberg in the year 1600, when the most excellent man Andreas Schato, the primary Professor, announced six Doctors with the customary solemnity. Here, according to custom, he preceded the ceremony with a learned and erudite dissertation on contagion. This being done, the most renowned Jessenius, at that time Dean and Pro-chancellor, granted the power of promotion, demonstrating graphically from memory and on the spot that against so many assaults of contagion, Theriac alone was found as a remedy. So that the six present candidates for the Doctorate might always be mindful of this, he assigned to each a single simple ingredient, according to the six classes of ingredients, with a hieroglyphic significance. To the first, who was Melchior Jostelius, a celebrated Professor of Mathematics, he assigned the **SQUILL** <note>original: "SCILLAM"; the Sea Onion, a primary ingredient in Theriac.</note>.
<margin>The Physician becomes skillful.</margin>
He did so because, just as every kind of onion follows the different phases <note>original: "φάσεις"</note> of the moon in its increase and decrease, so too the heavens and the superior bodies must be observed by the Physician, as a singular proof of **SKILL**.
<margin>Prudent.</margin>
To the second in order, Daniel Torschmidt of Freiberg, the **VIPER** was named, as a token <note>original: "Τεκμήριον"</note> of genuine **PRUDENCE**.

### # ON THE COMPOSITION OF THERIAC

...was my former intimate friend, Tobias Tandler of Torgau, of pious memory <note>original: "p. m." (piae memoriae); a standard formula for the deceased.</note>, who for many years served well in both the Philosophical and Medical professions at Wittenberg. To him, from the third class of ingredients, the **ROSE** was dedicated as a symbol of Humanity and Grace. In the fourth place <margin>Pious:</margin> **COSTUS** <note>An aromatic root used in ancient perfumes and medicines.</note> was assigned above others to CASPAR HORN as an incentive for PIETY, since the ancients, as Pliny testifies, sacrificed with Costus. To Stephanus Marcellus, from the fifth class <margin>& Humble,</margin> **Lemnian Earth** <note>A medicinal clay from the island of Lemnos, used as an astringent and antidote.</note> was appropriate, as an honor to humility, which the ancients denoted by the earth. Finally, to the last, <margin>Patient.</margin> Basilius Plinius, the **Beaver** <note>original: "Fiber"</note> was given as a commendation of PATIENCE. The beaver's testicles <note>original: "testes"; also a pun on "witnesses." These were harvested for Castoreum, a substance used in Theriac.</note> also enter into the composition of Theriac; it is said that this animal, unless it wish to be utterly killed, bites them off with its own teeth and throws them to the hunters—though Gesner, in his *History of Animals*, pronounces this story to be more fabulous than true after comparing various authors. By this pleasant enumeration, I would have made your most noble Consuls, the venerable theologians present, and as many guests as were there, quite pensive—in the manner of the human mind, which knows how to lead from one thought to another—had I not immediately turned to you with a joke added: namely, that out of all the ingredients of Theriac, nothing could be more suited to you for the time being than the Symbol of Patience. However, let it not be the Beaver, who avoids the dangers of hunters by biting off his own testicles and inheritance as the fables tell, but rather <margin>Saffron: Symbol of a generous host.</margin> **Saffron** <note>original: "Crocus"</note>, which those skilled in herbal matters say grows more lushly when it is trodden underfoot. Whence Camerarius writes in his *Emblems*:

->The Saffron is trodden so that it may grow more joyfully: O, what great madness!<-
->That you may be able to rise more joyfully, do not refuse to be pressed down.<-

Therefore, may your family estate grow more joyfully, even though it may have suffered some loss for a time through your generosity. The other matters—concerning the fermentation of Theriac, the appropriate time for its preparation and use, as well as its age, which occurred to us in passing during our discourse—I shall not repeat. This is especially so since the most famous Libavius <note>Andreas Libavius (1555–1616), a famous German chemist and physician.</note>, of pious memory, demonstrates these same things quite learnedly in a singular letter communicated to you here, which I possess by good right along with other manuscripts from the surviving library of the most famous physician, the Lord Doctor Sigismund Snizer, of pious memory. In the meantime, fare you well with your whole family, and look kindly upon this brief repetition of your Theriac-related visit. 

Written in haste at Ulm, October 22, 1624.

<meta>This page transitions from a symbolic, social discussion of Theriac’s ingredients to a technical medical inquiry regarding its manufacture. MEDICAL EPISTLES, BOOK II, SECTION I.

## To the most distinguished Mr. Sigismund Schnizer, an exceptional Philosopher and Physician, Greetings.

## Andreas Libavius, Doctor of Medicine and celebrated Philosopher.

<margin>
Question 1:
The time for preparing Theriac.
</margin>
I cannot help but inform you of what was proposed a few days ago at our local pharmacy, and to exercise your mind with a medical problem. I trust this will not be unpleasant for you. One of our local pharmacists had it in mind to compose the **Theriac of Andromachus** <note>original: "Theriacam Andromachi"; a famous "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh and opium, named after Nero's physician.</note>. The first question raised concerned the time of its preparation. For what indeed? Making Theriac in winter, and that among the cold forests of the Germans, near Thuringia at the feet of the most freezing mountains?

<margin>
According to the Ancients: at what time and in what manner.
</margin>
The ancient rule is that the beginning of spring until the start of summer must be chosen for this task, as that is the time when vipers are captured to make **viper lozenges** <note>original: "Trochisci viperini"; small cakes made of processed snake meat used as a primary ingredient in Theriac.</note>. Then, one should set aside the burning heat of midsummer for the **Squill** <note>original: "Scillinis"; referring to sea onions, which required a specific curing process.</note> preparations. Soon after these are perfected, one should move on to the mixing of the Theriac itself. According to **Mattioli** <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli, a famous 16th-century botanist and physician.</note> following Galen's view, this should be done in the sun; but according to Marantha, it should be done at the end of summer or the beginning of autumn while the air is still warm. In this period, a forty-day **fermentation** <term>fermentation: in early modern pharmacy, this referred to a period where the ingredients "ripened" and chemically merged into a single substance</term> must be managed, so that on each 

<column-break/>

individual day it is stirred twice in a large vessel made of metal—silver, pure tin, or gold. (For other metals are rejected during the time of fermentation because they might spoil the composition with their toxicity and their scrapings, or rather their corrosion and efflorescence). Alternatively, one may use a vessel of stone, glass, or glazed ceramic, until the mixing is so perfect that it can be stored, though the **kneading** <note>original: "subactione"; the physical working of the thick, honey-like paste.</note> should not be entirely discontinued. 

Galen, in chapter 14 of *On Theriac, to Piso*, states that once the Theriac is finished, it should be stored in a silver or glass flask, with space left inside for evaporation; it should be uncovered from time to time so that it may better "digest" <note>meaning to chemically stabilize and mature</note> and so that you might use it sooner. The Commentator also allows for a gilded vessel or one made of horn. Galen, in his *Epitome on Antidotes*, rejects tin vessels for all antidotes because they are often adulterated with a mixture of lead; likewise, he rejects those made from impure silver. 

**Nicolaus** <note>Likely referring to Nicolaus Praepositus, author of the influential medieval *Antidotarium*.</note>, however, maintains that in the first month it ought to be worked twice daily, morning and evening, for about half an hour, and afterwards closed and secured with a pressed seal. In the second month, it should be worked once every four days for half an hour; in the third month, every seven days; in the fourth, every ten; in the fifth, every fifteen; and in the sixth month, only once for half an hour. Once this six-month period has elapsed, it is to be kept very well-sealed in a silver or glass flask, according to Galen's advice to Piso—though if it is observed to "boil" <note>original: "ebullire"; referring to off-gassing or bubbling during fermentation</note>, it must be mixed again so it may digest better and come into use more quickly. **Ferrante Imperato** <note>A famous Neapolitan apothecary and natural historian.</note> devoted an entire year to this business. See also **Avicenna** <note>The great Persian physician (Ibn Sina), whose *Canon of Medicine* was a standard textbook.</note>, Book 5, Summa 1, Tract 1.

# ON THE COMPOSITION OF THERIAC.

Theriac has its own stages of life: infancy, puberty, adolescence, old age, and death. It is considered an "infant" after six months. Then its "puberty" and growth begin, lasting until it reaches a stable state for ten years in hot regions, and twenty years in cold ones. It remains in this stable state for ten or twenty years. It begins to decline after twenty or forty years; after forty or sixty years, the Theriac is stripped of its medicinal power. Many others start its four ages from the six-month mark—Infancy, Childhood, Adolescence, and Old Age—such that, if we believe **Johannes de Sancto Amando** <note>A 13th-century philosopher and medical commentator known for his "Expositions" on the works of Galen and others.</note>, the first seven months belong to its "infancy." From then until the end of the tenth month, it enters "youth" in a hot region, which in a cold region must be extended to the twentieth month. Once that time has passed, "old age" begins at thirty years in a hot place and forty in a cold one. However, this calculation does not please others, who assign three or five years to its infancy. During this time, it is narcotic because of the potency of the **opium** <note>Theriac contained significant amounts of opium; aging allowed the raw narcotic effects to mellow as the chemical complexity of the mixture increased.</note> and is hardly useful to any physician except to induce sleep. 

**Johannes de Sancto Amando** says that fresh Theriac is better than old for those purposes for which the **viper** <note>original: "Thirus seu vipera"; the "Thirus" was a legendary or specific type of snake often identified with the viper.</note> is used (which drives poison from the center of the body to the surface). He argues that old Theriac is better in terms of the operation it derives from its "form" or complete composition. Some judge it to be "cold," while others consider it "hot and dry" slightly beyond the second degree. They say that after three years have elapsed, "puberty" follows until the ninth or tenth year, or from the fifth until the fifteenth. After this time, it becomes **alexiteric** <term>alexiteria: substances used to ward off or neutralize the effects of venom, poison, or contagious disease</term> and is effective for curing venomous diseases. They place its "adolescence" from the fifteenth year up to the thirtieth year,

<column-break/>

after which it grows old. It remains effective, however, for a full fifteen years as a **cleansing fire** <note>original: "ignis purgatorius"; used here as a medical metaphor for a remedy that "burns away" impurities or diseases.</note> for all those ailments that **Galen** describes to **Piso** <note>Referring to Galen’s treatise "On Theriac to Piso," a foundational text for this medicine.</note>. There seems to be an error in the book of **Amandus**, where months were written instead of years, for he undoubtedly translated this opinion from **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the influential Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard university text.</note>, though the accounts vary. For he teaches that it is an "infant" until seven months, etc. Let these be compared with the followers of Avicenna. 

**Saludinus** measures "infancy" by the first six months, or as it is written, up to six months. During this time, it is "cold" due to the power of the opium. He assigns "youth" from the second year up to the twentieth, during which time it is "hot." He places its "first old age" when it is thirty years old, at which point it is less hot and less commonly used. However, he extends its period of "coldness" until the second year. For he maintains that it ought to be **fermented** <note>The aging process of Theriac was viewed as a slow fermentation or "digestion" of the dozens of ingredients into a single unified substance.</note> for a whole year, as does **Imperatus**. **Franciscus Alexander** retained the words of Avicenna regarding the ages, although he wishes it to be effective until the thirtieth year, whereas Avicenna reaches forty and even sixty years. These descriptions are truly taken from Chapter 14 of *On Theriac to Piso*, though with some variation. **Galen** says it requires twelve years; some, on the other hand, have used it against venomous bites even after five or seven years. It does not degenerate before thirty years. In less dangerous diseases, even Theriac of sixty years is recommended, but beyond that time it is ineffective. These are roughly the ancient rules for preparing Theriac in Italy—at Rome, Venice, Padua, Naples, Genoa, etc.—which are to be followed as if by a plumb-line.

# MEDICAL EPISTLES, BOOK II, SECTION I.

<column-break/>

And as if **Manlian edicts** <note>original: "Manliana edicta"; a reference to the Roman consul Manlius Torquatus, known for his extreme and harsh severity in enforcing rules.</note> were to be observed, some claim this medicine must not be prepared outside of Italy, or in places similarly arranged and flowing with vipers; as if the workshops of Nuremberg and Augsburg and others should be said to labor at this task in vain. They argue that the air of our region is not similar to that of Naples, nor is the heat, and so forth. Even **Mathiolus** <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a famous Italian physician and botanist.</note> denies that an equivalent can be prepared in Bologna today. But these censors are too rigid—scrupulous, not to say hot-headed and haughty, or possessed of a **dull, unskilled mind** <note>original: "crassa, imperitaque Minerva"; an idiom suggesting someone lacking in wit or intellectual refinement.</note>. For there is no reason Theriac cannot be prepared in other places, even if everything does not respond exactly to Italian breezes. 

**Camerarius** <note>Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), a German physician and botanist.</note> indeed, in his preface to the book of **Marantha** <note>Bartolomeo Maranta (1500–1571), an Italian physician who wrote extensively on Theriac.</note>, does not deny that we—not even the Italians—cannot make the "Neronian" Theriac of Andromachus or Galen <note>Andromachus was Nero's physician; Galen later refined his recipe for Theriac.</note> in the same way as it was made in the best regions of Italy before vipers and other ingredients were brought to light not so long ago by more recent writers. Yet, for that reason, dispensaries and pharmacies were not left without Theriac. If locations are to be judged by the primary qualities of the elements <note>The four qualities: hot, cold, wet, and dry.</note>, some will be judged absolutely hot or cold, while others are so only relatively, such as those in central Italy; and times can occur when our Germany does not yield much to Italy, and regions can be found here no less hot than certain Italian ones. But if nature entirely fails us, let us supply its defect with art and ingenuity, in which we can be greatly helped by

<column-break/>

**chemical operations** <note>original Greek: "ἐγχειρήματα [enkheiremata] Chymica"; referring to hands-on laboratory processes.</note>, although a certain haughty individual, who could bear nothing but his own pure works, mocked chemical fermentations and digestions. Relying on this art, **Johannes Pontanus**, a distinguished physician, composed Theriac in February at Gotha, as **Wittichius**—formerly physician to the **Counts of Schwarzburg** at **Arnstadt** in Thuringia—writes of him. 

I would wish, truly, that it could always be made in spring, summer, and autumn, so that those three seasons might be devoted entirely to the preparation, for that is what nature itself requires, as it brings forth and perfects our local **simples** <note>A "simple" is a single medicinal herb or ingredient used in a compound medicine.</note> during those times. But if all our local ingredients have been collected from our lands, and exotic ones obtained from elsewhere and judged with correct discretion, what stands in the way of even winter—especially a milder one, like the present one—being devoted to the preparation, provided it is lightened by **hypocausts** <note>A Roman-style underfloor heating system, here referring generally to heated rooms.</note> or aided by chemical **furnaces** <note>original: "pyriaterijs"; apparatus used for applying heat in chemical or medical processes.</note>? <margin>Viper lozenges last for a year</margin> **Viper lozenges** <term>Trochisci: small, prepared discs or cakes of medicinal ingredients, in this case made from viper flesh.</term> are to be imported from Italy; if they are well made, they retain their power for up to a year, provided they are kept in a silver vessel or another harmless container and are diligently cleaned of any decay. 

We can also seek **Squill lozenges** from there. **Marantha** indeed wants the work to begin immediately after the viper lozenges are finished, but he who is forced to delay until the end of summer or the beginning of autumn due to the slower preparation of squill lozenges must push back the work, which the nature of our domestic herbs also persuades us to do. For most of them do not ripen any sooner. Thus let the first question regarding the timing be settled:

<margin>Mixing & fermentation.</margin>
approves of mixing in the sun, based on the authority of **Galen**. The same can be read in the works of **Franciscus Alexander** <note>Francesco Alessandro, an Italian medical writer</note>; he likewise writes that it is better mixed in the sun. If it is prepared in winter, the heated room <note>original: "hypocaustum"; a room heated from below, common in laboratories</note> can be made warmer, and the vessel with the pestle or spatula can be slightly warmed; in this way, all the ingredients are more easily worked and later united more exactly. It should be worked after 4 or 5 days, and then again after intervals of 6 or 7, until two months or 40 days have passed. The moody critics seize upon this, concluding that **Theriac** cannot be made unless the sun is blazing, and therefore only in summer, when fermentation must be procured through solar exposure. Truly, the **Peripatetics** <note>The "Peripatetics" were followers of Aristotle's philosophy; here, the author refers to traditional university scholars</note> mock these views from their benches. They claim fire reflects the nature of its fuels, its vapors, and its **Spirit**. Furthermore, they argue that experience testifies that celestial heat, unless it is admitted temperately, is just as much a cause of corruption as elementary fire, from which it does not differ since it exists in similar elementary matter. I leave this dispute to the schools of **Physics**, while in the meantime not denying that "aprication" <note>Exposure to the sun</note> in a skillfully arranged sun-room is useful to some, as even the common people have learned through experience. However, whether **Theriac** must be mixed and fermented in the sun involves a **Refutation** <note>original: "Elenchum"</note> of several questions. It may be granted that it *can* be mixed and worked in the sun; but it does not follow that it *must* be fermented in the sun. In this matter, the nature of the regions must be considered. It is known that in the summer

### MEDICAL LETTERS, BOOK II. SECTION I.

<columns>
In the windows of the sunroom, we mostly use the heat of the workshops, and we heat the material contained in bronze pots over a modest fire of embers (for it must not exceed the limit and stir up a heat that dissipates the **Spirit** <note>In early modern pharmacy, the "Spirit" refers to the volatile active principles or the "life force" of a substance that could be lost if overheated</note>). Soon after removing it from the fire, we work the mixture; by this same art, other observations are made. This is indeed easier in summer and can be done with a smaller loss of embers; but there is no lack of supply in winter and autumn, although at a slightly higher cost, which is of no concern to us as we are not lacking in wood and charcoal. Here we care for the cold of the North Wind only as much as "the wolf cares for the number of sheep, or torrential rivers for their banks," as that famous character of **Virgil's** says <note>original: "Hic tantum Boreæ curamus frigora, quantum Aut numerum lupus, aut torrentia flumina ripas." A quote from Virgil's Eclogue 7, implying that with enough fuel, the external weather is irrelevant to the chemist</note>. Art not only imitates nature but even makes things better; nor does it matter, says **Aristotle**, whether the cooking happens in natural or artificial vessels, provided other things are equal.

<margin>
Several questions on Fermentation.
</margin>
There is a greater dispute regarding **fermentation**. The first question is what it is, so that we do not fight over something unknown; the second, what causes it has, and how these are to be managed so that it turns out well; third, at what time it should be carried out; fourth, in what vessels; fifth, in what place; sixth, how often and when the working <note>the kneading or stirring of the medicinal paste</note> should be repeated; seventh, for how long. At the same time, we must consider whether the method of storage and **preparation** <term>sceuasiæ: from the Greek "skeuasia," referring to the specific technical protocol and equipment used for compounding a medicine</term> should be changed. Other matters will arise in passing.

<margin>
What Fermentation is.
</margin>
I say first that our **alexipharmic** <term>Alexipharmic: a medicine intended to neutralize poison or ward off contagion</term> fermentation is the movement of the Theriacal mass (which consists of a just proportion of mixed simples) driven by its innate heat and **Spirit**, excited by an ex- <column-break/> ternal proportioned heat, until a perfect and homogeneous union of all the altered parts is achieved, possessing **Alexipharmic** virtues. I call it a "movement" because it is an imperfect act between the fermenting agent and the fermented material, of which the former is the moving cause, and the latter is the thing affected by the movement. Even the **pharmacy helpers** <note>original: "Calones officinarum"; literally "workshop drudges," referring to low-level workers who did the heavy manual labor of grinding and mixing</note> know where the name comes from, although the **Mysteries of the Chemical art** teach something deeper. 

Must and other juices are fermented while they are simultaneously separated from their dregs and altered, so that wine emerges from the must, and from other things, their own purified essence. **Bakers** express this matter more closely with their dough; **Pharmacists** have examples of many mixtures through **Electuaries, Juices, Preserves**, etc. **Chemists** do not admit anything that is not essential; nature and the art of the workshops make nothing from the whole. Therefore, with the departure of certain parts, it is always a common fermentation; but the **mystic Chemical** fermentation has none <note>meaning that in "mystic" or high chemistry, the goal is a perfect union without losing any of the substance's "essence" to waste</note>. Care must be taken, however, not to confuse it with **putrefaction**, to which workshop fermentation seems more similar because of the separation [of parts], which has no place in essential fermentation (I do not mean **Aristotelian** putrefaction, but our own artificial kind). **Digestion** and **maturation** are also more about homogeneous things than heterogeneous ones, in which there is not only **combination** <term>σύγκρισις (synkrisis): the joining or mixing together of elements</term> but also **separation** <term>διάκρισις (diakrisis): the discernment or pulling apart of different substances</term>. Our digestion is procured through **pelicanation** <term>pelicanatio: a chemical process of continuous distillation and circulation using a "pelican," a specialized glass vessel with two side-arms that return condensed liquid to the base</term> or circulation, and although it happens that some dreg-like matter separates out, nevertheless:

</columns>
