# ON THE COMPOSITION OF THERIAC.

### [Column 1]

...the name is derived from its ultimate perfection and primary goal.

<margin>I. The Efficient Cause of Fermentation.</margin>
The external cause of fermentation, which is said to produce results by way of activation, is heat. For cold is unable to activate the internal principle, except by accident through <term>antiperistasis</term> <note>original: "antiperistasin"—a philosophical concept where one quality is strengthened by being surrounded by its opposite, such as heat intensifying when surrounded by cold</note>. Heat is either moist or dry. Moist heat is better suited for <term>putrefaction</term> <note>In early pharmacy, "putrefaction" was not just rotting, but a controlled breakdown of organic matter to release its medicinal properties</note>, which is why the art employs water baths, steam, horse manure, or similar inventions. However, if the moisture is gentle, so that it brings the <term>temperament</term> <note>The balance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> to a state of balance—a quality attributed to the season of spring, to blood, and to those of a sanguine nature—I judge it to be better than dry heat, which hinders motion. I would prefer a balanced temperament which, in relation to a weighted temperament, is slightly warmer and therefore more **active** <note>original Greek: "ἐνεργητικώτερον" (energetikoteron)</note>, yet with moderation. But moderate moist heat is also not to be rejected, especially at the beginning. For it can and should be increased by degrees thereafter until perfection is reached, just as it is in the "fermentation of the wise" <note>A reference to alchemical processes</note> and as nature requires in the generation of living things. Those who resist this opinion argue that stagnant humidity causes rot. But if they were to consider the warmth that fosters an embryo in the mother's womb, they would not wander into such childish delusions.

<margin>II. The Cause of Fermentation.</margin>
The other moving or fermenting force is internal, namely that **innate little fire** which exists alongside the Spirit and its corresponding fluid. This is the immediate

<column-break/>

### [Column 2]

mixer and digester, entirely natural, which is evident in common fermentation and in the chemical arts. For those who wish to draw out a "burning liquor" <note>Alcohol or spirits</note> from crushed grain first dilute it with water, then add some wine dregs, or beer yeast, or even a leaven, and set the whole mixture in a moderately warm place. Thus it happens that the Spirit, awakened by the innate heat, permeates everything and calls into action that **fiery Spirit** which previously lay hidden. Let this serve as an example, just as the fermentation used by bakers relies on the spirit of wine, yeast, dregs, pigeon dung, and so on. For otherwise, chemistry corresponds to putrefaction. It is enough, however, if we can perceive from this how the internal principle is awakened by external action, so that afterward that very thing

<margin>The Material Cause of Theriac.</margin>
may be the first and true cause of fermentation. Regarding the matter itself, I say nothing for now. For our own preparation consists of various "miscible species" <note>The numerous herbal and mineral ingredients of Theriac</note> and wine with a suitable amount of honey.

<margin>The Twofold Form of Theriac.</margin>
The "form" is twofold: one relates to the motion itself, and the other to the thing produced by that motion. Inside the vessel, we observe the agitation and the rising of the material into a swollen mass; because of this, it is necessary that the vessels be constructed so that they are not broken by the violence of the reaction, nor the mass allowed to overflow.

<margin>What Kind of Vessels are Required.</margin>
Let the vessels therefore be strong and left one-third empty. Because foreign and "crude" Spirits evaporate during the process, a breathing hole must be left open. This serves as proof that the external heat must not be immoderate. For too much heat would stir the mixture excessively, and beyond...

# MEDICAL LETTERS, BOOK II, SECTION I.

...it would dissipate the raw vapors and even the very essence. Therefore, it must be guided by art, whether in a sun-room <note>original: "solario"</note>, a steam-room <note>original: "vaporarium"</note>, or a heated chamber <note>original: "hypocausto"—an ancient Roman system of underfloor heating</note>.

<margin>The Completion of Theriac.</margin>
They judge the final form by its strength, its blackness, its consistency, and so on. At that point, the fermentation has reached its end. The goal is for the mixture to exist as a **homogeneous** substance according to the nature of its ingredients, in which all parts are so united that they are completely familiar with one another, and every part possesses the same virtues; this cannot happen before the movement ceases and comes to rest. For this reason, Imperatus <note>Ferrante Imperato (1550–1625), a Neapolitan apothecary and naturalist famous for his "Cabinet of Curiosities"</note> did not want any portion of the **Theriac** <term>Theriac: a famous ancient "polypharmacy" or universal antidote consisting of dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh and opium, requiring long fermentation</term> to be removed before the fermentation was complete, because everything would not yet have been reduced to a unity of form. A word to the wise is enough. For not everything can be grasped by words alone.

<margin>When is the Time for Fermentation?</margin>
At what time should the fermentation be established? An astrologer would answer: at that time when the constitution of the heavens is best for the generation and composition of medicines. A physicist <note>In this context, a "Physicus" refers to a natural philosopher or student of nature</note> would choose what is most convenient for the generation of mixtures. A pharmacist and a physician would also look to the scarcity of their supply. Some establish a new batch of **Theriac** when the old is depleted to the point where only enough remains for one year's use. Common people ask about the seasons of the year. I say that one should either look to "natural time," which coincides with the qualities of various locations (and which, because of the damage caused by elemental conditions in our regions, is quite uneven and does not satisfy the intention of the art), or "artificial time," which is prudently adapted with artificial aids and care. It has been said that this is defined by three parts of the year: spring, summer, and autumn—or by such seasonal conditions. This also allows for winters, whatever the grumbling critics may mutter; for them, the shame they bring upon themselves by their revealed ignorance and lack of judgment is punishment enough.

<margin>How much [time]?</margin>
How long should that time be? Surely as long as is sufficient from the beginning to the end. Judgment must be taken from the movement of the matter and the signs of perfection, provided that the helping causes do not fail and leave the **Theriac** imperfect, like a miscarriage or a monster. Some, because they compare its age to that of a human, propose ten months; Imperatus proposes a full year; most propose six months—at least if you are considering only the logic of artificial fermentation. For the judgment is different regarding the ages and the four seasons of consistency. I reject no one, if they can demonstrate they have applied the aids so industriously that they have achieved perfection, whether in a short or long time, provided there is no excessive delay. It is the same in the generation of animals; so too in the philosophical preparation of the "stone" <note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the legendary substance of alchemy said to transform base metals into gold and grant long life</note> and of elixirs. Too much haste is harmful. If you guide the work prudently, it will cook itself, mix itself, and be perfected in a time suitable to its own nature. You might also weigh the critical or "stepped" numbers according to the motion of the moon; in which case seven or nine lunar circuits might suffice. Imperatus looked to the motion of the sun; if he mixed the ingredients at the start of Autumn, then until nearly the same time... <meta>Catchword: men- (likely "menses" or "mensibus," meaning months)</meta>

### ON THE COMPOSITION OF THERIAC.

<margin>The place of fermentation and storage. Note Well.</margin>
...produced the fermentation. Let the place be proportionate to the movement, and at the same time convenient for your storage. A sun-room <note>original: "Solarium"—a room exposed to the sun's heat</note> is suitable in warmer climates; in colder regions, a certain heated chamber <note>original: "hypocaustum"—an ancient system of underfloor heating</note> or a specialized workshop is required. Some keep the mixture in the family dining room, which I do not approve of. For to say nothing of other errors (such as the inequality of qualities when at one time cold dominates and at another the heat is excessive, etc., and the many accidents that can happen from negligent service), I would not want the flatulent and raw spirits which exhale during fermentation to be inhaled into the brain, lungs, and heart. For they are poisonous because of the rawness of the opium, etc. You know, after all, that our opium is not so pure as to meet the standards of the very best. If a dedicated heated chamber is lacking, let a moderate chemical dry-stove <note>original: "stufa sicca Chymica"—likely a small furnace or heated cabinet</note> be prepared in a cellar, a workshop, or a vaulted chamber, in a place well-enclosed and removed from the harmful influence of the [external] parts.

<margin>Agitation or Working the mass.</margin>
How often and for how long must the mass that is fermenting be agitated, and in what place, and in what air? We recognize two types of agitation or "working": one occurs during the initial incorporation itself, the end of which is a uniform form for all parts; the other occurs during the swelling and fermentation. This [second type] is not continuous, but interrupted, and it reaches its end point when the flatulent, watery, and poisonous spirits have been separated, and the essential spirits now begin to emerge. Take as an example the distillation of a "flaming liquor" or "burning water" <note>spirits of wine or alcohol</note> from dregs. You know that the dregs are agitated in the vessel <note>original: "vesica"—the body of a still</note> until they boil up from the bottom and the essential spirits rise—

<column-break/>

—essential spirits, though not without some flatulence, which requires rectification afterward. We do the same in sublimations. But where there are pure essential parts, external agitation is superfluous; instead, the whole is kept in a hermetically sealed vessel in its furnace <term>Athanor: a furnace used by alchemists designed to provide a steady, uniform heat over a long period of time</term>. Thus must one judge the Theriacal mass. It cannot be agitated constantly; yet it should be worked often in the beginning, twice or thrice a day, so that the elementary moisture may depart along with harmful vapors, and the mixing may become more accurate. Meanwhile, let there be no lack of proportional heat. When the essential spirits finally appear, the pharmacist <note>original: "Pharmacopoeus"</note> should beware of manual working; instead, he should place the Theriac, closed on all sides, into his dry-stove, and leave it there until the end of fermentation, meanwhile governing the heat skillfully and prudently. In this way, the essential virtues will be preserved, and although the spirits are raised from the matter, they are nevertheless brought back down again in turn, and united to it once more; at the same time, by this frequent movement, they thin the matter until at last all things come to rest together. Therefore, the vessel—

<margin>The vessel for working the mass.</margin>
—ought to be round at that stage, specifically a large glass flask <note>original: "ampulla"</note> which can be hermetically sealed and at the same time show the movement within. If anything should wish to adhere to the surface, it would easily return to its body by turning the vessel.

<margin>Note Well.</margin>
I do not think any **Theriac** <term>Theriac: a famous ancient "polypharmacy" or universal antidote consisting of dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh and opium, requiring long fermentation</term> has ever been made by this art. Therefore, there is none in which something is not lacking. It is evident, then, how much chemical preparations differ from the common ones of the workshops; however, whichever of those common ones comes closest to this chemical procedure <note>original Greek: "ἐγχείρησιν" (encheirēsin)—a manual operation or method</note>, [the better it is].

...they also attain a not ineffective power. <margin>Chemical Fermentation.</margin> Chemical fermentation belongs to pure essences. But it follows the example of the workshop <note>original: "Officinalium"—referring to standard medicines prepared in an apothecary's shop or 'officina'</note> preparations, and acts as an Ideal of perfection, in which intervals of six, seven, or other days are not strictly observed, but judgment is taken from the state of the substances themselves. When <margin>Note Well. The end of movement.</margin> the movement of fermentation is finished, the external active causes should be removed, and those that stabilize it should rather be admitted. Therefore, I praise those who then remove the Theriac from external heat and <margin>Storage vessel.</margin> place it in a Waldenburg stone vessel <note>original: "vase lapideo Wallenburgico"—high-quality stoneware from Waldenburg, Germany, prized for being non-reactive</note>, or something similar, in a cold cellar. For lead does not contain quicksilver; nor do its scrapings or its decay fail to spoil the Theriac. We also do not want our pharmacist to be too extravagant. Let golden and silver vessels be permitted for kings; let ours use a stone earthenware one for storage. But some say that this agitation does not seem to be necessary. For food in the stomach is better mixed, cooked, and perfected into chyle through rest than if it were stirred with an inserted pestle—and those who cook can prove this very thing. But these people also cannot prevent the exhaling vapors; if art promotes these, it helps nature. As for the fact that the agitation is repeated even after a year,

<column-break/>

I think that is the result of faulty preparation and storage. <margin>The place of working.</margin> The place of "working" <note>original: "subactio"—the physical process of kneading or incorporating the medicinal mass</note> and the air are rightly said to need to be moderately warm, just as it is for fermentation, except in its later progress. For there are degrees of heat, and a delicate composition requires one thing, a medium one another, and a mass that is already strong requires another. It is appropriate to work a firm mixture in the sun, but not a delicate one. For a sharper heat at the beginning dissipates the volatile spirits before they can unite with the fixed parts and take on a bodily form. Nevertheless, the sun can be admitted temperately. Galen seems to have had in mind the vapors of opium, which are more easily dissipated in the open air by the sun's rays than in a closed place where they can harm the person stirring, who should also stand facing away. Is it enough to stir daily for up to 40 days, according to the command of Maranta <note>Bartolomeo Maranta (1500–1571), a physician who wrote a famous treatise on the composition of Theriac</note>? I define nothing, I say: and the followers of Galen themselves disagree on that matter. If everything were done correctly, the time would become known from the movement of the internal principle within the matter. Among so many errors, there must necessarily be disagreement regarding the time. <margin>The ages of Theriac and other common assertions are refuted.</margin> What about the "ages" of Theriac? I laugh, I say, at the talk of its "infancy," "puberty," "adolescence," and "old age." If this thing is to be compared to the ages of men, why is the embryonic state, childhood, and mature and steady age omitted? Why do physicians distinguish puberty and adolescence by such great intervals? When Theriac has reached its finished form, and the movement of fermentation is now at an end, the whole is uniform in nature. It is a fiction that the Opium remains "cold" for the first five years. 1 ounce of **Viper Troches**.

Greetings.
<margin>Doctor Horst,</margin>I have thoroughly read your book of observations and Epistles, most Excellent Lord Doctor Horst, and I read it with great pleasure: for in it I saw the causes of diseases and symptoms reviewed with a clear brevity, and to each was added its own remedies according to a certain reason and method. By following this path, if you weave the rest of what you promise with the same thread, you will, in my judgment, help the medical field in no small way. Moreover, out of your kindness toward me, which both your letters and very friendly greetings attest to, I ask that you not find it burdensome to explain a little more broadly what you said briefly—according to the requirements of your plan—in Book I, Observation XXIV, regarding the **urines of malignant fevers**. You say that in your patient, the urine declined very little from its natural state, which almost everyone asserts happens repeatedly in this type of disease: but they disagree in stating the cause of the matter.

<margin>
The question is raised.
</margin>

<margin>
The opinion of Capivacci.
</margin>

**Girolamo Capivacci** <note>A famous 16th-century Italian physician and professor at Padua</note>, intending to give a reason why in any disease caused by "repletion" <note>An excess of bodily fluids or "humors"</note> a healthy-looking urine is sometimes excreted despite the patient’s poor condition, made a distinction between **sediments**. He argued that one type is born from nourishment and is the cruder portion of the <term>chyle</term> <note>A milky fluid produced during digestion</note> which cannot be turned into nutrition; the other arises from the <term>morbific humor</term> <note>The specific fluid or "humor" causing the disease</note> when it is conquered and subdued by nature. Furthermore, he says both differ, first in the place of their generation—since the nutritional sediment arises in the stomach, while the "humoral" (so to speak) or disease-related sediment arises in the liver or the veins. Next, they differ in the efficient 

<column-break/>

cause, since the nutritional is processed by natural heat, while the disease-related is worked upon by a heat that is, in a way, contrary to nature. From this, he infers that in such diseases, while the body is "cooking" <note>The process of "concoction" where the body matures and prepares to expel disease-causing matter</note> the fluids, both sediments are excreted, sometimes separately and sometimes together; for nature strives no less for the digestion of food than for the <term>pepasmum</term> <note>The ripening or processing of diseased humors</note> of the humor. But because it can happen that the nutritional sediment sinks to the bottom of an excellent-looking urine while the disease-causing humor remains "crude" <note>Unprocessed or raw; not yet ready to be expelled by the body</note>, he provides signs by which one can be distinguished from the other. Having defined these things in a long series, he declares that a physician should not wonder if he sometimes sees a patient die while excreting urine with a natural sediment: for that sediment had its origin in food, not in the disease-causing humor. Although these distinctions seem to be of remarkable use in judging urines, because they are not specific to our current inquiry but pertain to many types of diseases, let us 

<margin>
The opinion of the Conciliator.
</margin>

hear the ***Conciliator*** <note>Referring to Pietro d’Abano (1257–1315), a famous physician known for reconciling conflicting medical views</note>, who, intending to give the reason why in a pestilential or malignant fever (which is our topic) the urines are similar to those of healthy people, says in *Distinction 94* that this happens because nature, terrified by the magnitude and depravity of the rot <note>original: "putredinis," referring to the corruption of humors in the body</note>, does not dare at all to handle the disease-causing matter; remaining untouched, this matter does not change the urine. Thus, this opinion of the *Conciliator* is subordinate to the former one and explains it, while teaching that in these kinds of fevers, the forces of nature do indeed survive...

# ON THE URINES OF PLAGUE VICTIMS.

...toward the digestion of nourishment, but not in the same way toward the disease-causing humor.

<margin>The opinion of Mercurialis.</margin>
**Mercurialis** <note>Girolamo Mercuriali (1530–1606), an influential Italian physician</note> thinks that this man was "entirely wide of the mark," <note>original: "toto, quod ajunt, coelo"</note> as they say, regarding the Goal. First, he says it is absurd to imagine that Nature is "intelligent" <note>In the sense of Nature making conscious, rational choices</note>; however, that thought never occurred to the **Conciliator** <note>Pietro d'Abano (c. 1257–1316), a famous medieval scholar known as "The Conciliator" for reconciling Greek and Arabic medicine</note>, who knew very well that natural action is distinct from the conscious action of an animal. Secondly, as for the claim that Nature is so designed that every part tries to expel what is harmful from itself—and rises up more strongly the worse the offending matter is—this is perhaps granted when Nature is strong; however, one cannot hope for the same when Nature has been overcome. For this reason, Mercurialis neither refutes the opinion proposed by the Conciliator nor offers a better one, just as if he himself, terrified by the difficulty of the matter, had surrendered his hands to the winning cause.

<margin>The opinion of Riolan.</margin>
**Riolan** <note>Jean Riolan the Elder (1539–1605), a French physician</note> and others, whose opinions you also seem to have endorsed, think that the **vital spirits** <note>The "pneuma" or life-force believed to be carried in the blood</note> are primarily attacked by a poisonous quality, and for that reason, clear traces of it are not found in the humors <note>The bodily fluids, such as blood, phlegm, and bile</note>. These men seem to me to have come closest to the mark, yet they cannot yet persuade me to agree completely. For the humors cannot remain healthy for long when the spirits are contaminated, which is clear in "daily fevers" <note>Fevers that recur every day</note>, which are accustomed to change into "humoral fevers" immediately after the first day. Urines similar to those of healthy people ought to be excreted only in the most acute malignant fevers, or only in their

<column-break/>

beginning; yet sense and experience teach us something far different. Let us look at what **Julius Palmarius** <note>Julien Le Paulmier (1520–1588), a French physician</note> says on this matter. ### MEDICAL LETTERS BOOK II. SECTION II.

...the urine has deviated very little from its natural state. But let it be so: suppose the **spirited blood** <note>original: "spirituosum sanguinem"; referring to the blood charged with "vital spirits" in the arteries</note> is most affected against nature; from where does the urine then flow? It is certainly produced in the liver, but it is diffused through all the channels of the veins and arteries in which the spirited blood is stored before it is collected in the bladder and flows out. There are innumerable and very wide **anastomoses** <term>anastomoses: connections or openings between blood vessels that allow them to communicate</term> of the veins into the arteries, and the arteries into the veins. Likewise, the **emulgent vessels** <term>emulgent vessels: the renal arteries and veins, which were thought to "milk" or filter the blood to create urine</term> are almost equal in both types of vessels. Thus it happens that no defect of the blood, even the spirited kind, can be so hidden that some trace of it is not shown in the urine. 

But since those whose humors exceed the proper measure in quality or quantity are more exposed to fevers of this kind, who will doubt that a malignant quality first infects even the **natural faculty** <term>natural faculty: the body's innate power to perform biological functions like nutrition and growth</term>, even if a manifest harm does not always appear in the humors? 

Therefore, **Fernel** <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), a French physician who introduced the term "physiology" and studied how diseases affect the whole body</note> seems to me to have wisely established this as a "disease of the whole substance" <note>original: "totius substantiae morbum"; a disease affecting the very essence of an organ or the body, rather than just a fluid imbalance</note>. If this is denied, it is hardly possible to show why the pulse and urine—the primary and most general signs of other diseases—are not changed in proportion to the severity of the harm in malignant and pestilential fevers. 

But I am surely interrupting your serious occupations. For the rest, farewell, and live most happily through the coming New Year and many thereafter (if there be any). 
From Durlach, December 25, 1624. <note>original: "8. Calend. Jan. Anno 1625"; using the Roman calendar style where the 8th day before the Kalends of January is Christmas Day of the preceding year</note>

*Jordanus* <note>Thomas Jordanus (1539–1585), a physician famous for his work on the "plague-like" epidemics in Moravia</note> determines this more clearly in *On the Plague Phenomenon*, Treatise 1, Chapter 14, demonstrating that urine is a deceptive sign in afflictions of the heart and brain. Whence my predecessor, the illustrious *Verbezius* <note>David Verbezius (1577–1644), a physician in Ulm and former holder of this medical post</note>, rightly says in his *Exercises on the Plague*, page 123, that the urine of the sick is very often similar to the urine of the healthy—specifically, before the poison putrefies the humors, or when it destroys life more quickly than it can corrupt the humors.

On this point, *Mindrerus* <note>Raymond Mindrerus (1570–1621), an Augsburg physician known for military medicine</note> elegantly writes in *On the Plague*, page 98, that sometimes the pulse is praiseworthy [strong and regular] and the urine is very similar to that of the healthy during the plague. The *Conciliator* <note>Pietro d'Abano (c. 1250–1316), a famous medieval scholar who "reconciled" different medical traditions</note> provides the reason: that nature is terrified and does not even attempt to attack the force of the poison. But that reason (he says) is hardly sufficient; rather, it should be attributed to the poison hiding in the "principal part" [the heart]. While the sick might have seemed to suffer only very slightly from this, once a sudden movement of the humor occurred, or a sudden **metastasis** <term>metastasis: the rapid displacement of a disease or its "matter" from one part of the body to another</term>, they have been observed to die instantly.

Hence *Rulandus* <note>Martin Ruland the Elder (1532–1602), known for his work on infectious diseases</note>, in his book *On the Hungarian Sickness* <note>original: "lue Ung."; referring to a typhus-like fever that decimated armies in Hungary</note>, Chapter 3, pronounces that the urine is natural in the beginning because of a pernicious quality occupying the innermost parts of the heart, which has not yet been imprinted upon the remaining humors. *Sarracenus* <note>Jean Antoine Sarrasin (1547–1598), a French physician who wrote on the plague</note>, in *On the Nature of the Plague*, Chapter 5, says that healthy-looking urine arises for this reason: either because nature is weak, or because the **natural faculty** <term>natural faculty: the body's innate power to perform biological functions like nutrition</term> is not yet injured, or—as he judges more likely—because the poison occupies the heart.

But regarding your double objection,

<column-break/>

the first of which is drawn from the generation of urine and its distribution through the whole body, and the second from the disposition of the body suffering from malignant fevers, I respond briefly. But the conclusion is inconsistent, because the serum distributed through the whole body differs greatly from the urine received by the bladder. This is the very point *Jordanus* deduces from the elegantly cited passage of *Galen* <note>Claudius Galen (129–210 AD), the Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years</note>, concluding that something can be gathered from the urine regarding the completed **third digestion** <term>third digestion: the final stage of metabolism occurring in the individual tissues and organs</term> of each part, not **primarily** <note>original: "πρώτως" (prōtōs)</note> but only **secondarily** <note>original: "δευτέρως" (deuterōs)</note>.

## MEDICAL EPISTLES, BOOK II, SECTION II.

...and they contract measles <note>original: "morbillos"</note>. For how is it that the afflictions of smallpox <note>original: "variolarum"</note> and measles are communicated most readily through contagion not to everyone, but only to those who have not yet suffered from them? This is not only because the sick carry a communicable malignancy, but also because a real impurity, left over from the maternal blood, still lurks within those in whom it has not yet been purged by such a "critical" expulsion <note>early modern physicians believed children were born with "impurities" from the womb that were eventually expelled through childhood fevers</note>. Indeed, that hidden impurity is not ignited by contagion unless it reaches its own maturity, in the same way that—according to **Hippocrates'** *On Ancient Medicine*—bitter, salty, sweet, acidic, harsh, and six hundred other things are said to exist within a human. Through their mutual tempering with one another, these are neither seen nor do they cause anyone distress, until they are separated and begin to grow excessive <note>original: "luxuriare"</note>, at which point they constitute the various causes of diseases, as we demonstrated more fully fifteen years ago in the preface to the *Book on the Nature of Man*. Hence it happens that more often in the same household, not everyone is seized by the contagion of smallpox at the same time, but at different times, one after another—not just at intervals of months, but even years. This is also clearly seen in cases of dysentery, malignant fevers, and other afflictions. I very easily concede that the pestilential contagion is far more grave and vehement, for it brings about a similar infection not only by contact or a "fomes" <term>fomes: an object, such as clothing or bedding, capable of carrying infectious organisms</term>, but even from a distance. It does this by a penetrating subtlety and a firm mixture—existing in a certain "slowness" <note>original: "lentore"</note>, according to **Fracastoro** <note>Girolamo Fracastoro (1478–1553), a pioneer of the germ theory of disease</note>—constantly persevering and effectively acting

<column-break/>

to bring about a similar infection. This does not happen to everyone, however, but only to those who are "analogous" <note>meaning "proportionately susceptible"</note> to the body that is breathing out its malignancy through poisonous <term>miasmata</term> <note>original: μιάσματα; infectious vapors or "stains" thought to carry disease</note>. **Fracastoro** rightly declares such an "analogy" to be manifold and most wonderful. Because of it, a certain plague might harm trees and crops but none of the animals; conversely, it might touch certain animals while sparing the crops and trees. And among animals, it picks out humans, or cattle, or horses, or others. But even within the same species, a contagion that affects children and youths might harm none of the elderly, and vice versa. Nor does that which touches males always reach women. Indeed, indiscriminately, some people have felt certain effects while others have not; and while some are among those plague-stricken people, others are not, and so on—thus far Fracastoro. It will not be a wonder, therefore, what is reported from **Dionysius of Halicarnassus** in Book 4 of his *Roman History*, where he writes that there was a certain plague that raged only against virgins and pregnant women. For the same reason, **Giovanni Battista Botero** in Book 3 of the *Universal Relations of the New World* recounts a great pestilence that attacked only younger persons. So too **Gentiles**, as reported by **Minderer** in his *Book on the Plague*, page 53, writes that in his time a certain plague infected only robust men.

# On the Urine of Plague Victims.

...[singular] <note>likely "singularem" based on the preceding page</note> affinity that plague had in the time of the Emperor Charles with the Order of Franciscans, of whom—as **Unzerus** reports in *On the Antidote for Plague* (Book 1, number 124,434), citing the historians **Albert Krantz** and **Funccius**—so many died of the plague over a three-year period? It is not without cause that such an analogy <note>meaning a "correspondence" or "likeness" between the disease and the victim</note> is called marvelous, because just as **the fact of the matter** <note>original: "τὸ ὅτι"</note> is manifest, the **underlying reason** <note>original: "τὸ διότι"</note> remains quite obscure. Indeed, we correctly gather from **Hippocrates** in his book *On Breaths* <note>original: "περὶ πνευμ."</note> that the same things are not beneficial or harmful to every kind of living creature; therefore, body differs from body, nature from nature, and nourishment from nourishment. From this, it follows that a diversity of "staining" <note>the process of infection</note> arises. For this reason, **Mindererus** and others add that no one will be contaminated unless they are susceptible to receiving a similar harm through a likeness of nature, or of humors, or of some other similar disposition. This is because "like things are easily joined and come together," and in those possessing a common quality <note>original: "symbolum"</note>, the transition is easy, as the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle</note> holds. Therefore, that saying of **Galen** has its place here, where he says: **"The greatest factor in the birth of diseases is the readiness of the body about to be affected."** <note>original: "μεγίση μοῖρα γενέσεως νοσημάτων ἔσιν ἡ τοῦ μέλλοντος πάσχειν σώματος ἑτοιμότης"</note>

Nor do we deny that this "preparation" of the body about to suffer contributes greatly here. Authors generally define this

<column-break/>

by stating that those who are **hot and moist** in temperament, prone to putrefaction, overflowing with many humors, and endowed with a looser physical habit, are the first among men to be infected. In this same way, regarding the infection of the air, southern locations are more destructive than northern ones, and thus hot and moist regions are more severely afflicted than cold and dry ones. 

But when we see that very many people during a time of pestilence—even though they are endowed with such constitutions or are even filled with the "bad juices" <term>cacochymia: an imbalance or corruption of the bodily fluids</term> of rotting humors—nevertheless frequently remain immune, even if they are forced to live among the infected; meanwhile, many others are seized by the infection in whom such a disposition is absent. For this reason, **Forestus** <note>Pieter van Foreest, a famous Dutch physician</note> testifies that he himself, while suffering from a simple tertian fever, lived harmlessly among his sisters who were suffering and dying from the plague, without any infection. Indeed, it often happens during various times of plague that some live harmlessly among the infected, yet eventually they are nevertheless forced to experience some of the poison's destruction. 

This happened in recent years to that well-deserving man of medicine, the **Illustrious Mr. Johann Hartmann Beyer**, a physician of Frankfurt. ### MEDICAL EPISTLES BOOK II. SECTION II.

[a certain] <note>completing the word "aegroto" from the previous page</note> sick man, while returning home, was overcome by the force of the disease and forced to pay his debt to nature <note>a common euphemism for dying</note>. According to the testimony of **Girolamo Cardano** <note>an influential 16th-century Italian polymath and physician</note> in the fourth book of *On the Variety of Things*, in his own time at **Basel**, almost only the Swiss inhabitants were infected. A certain trustworthy military commander also reported to me that the same thing happened last year in **Lower Saxony**; he stated that the pestilential infection in the cities of **Halberstadt**, **Aschersleben**, and elsewhere raged far more among the local inhabitants than among the soldiers—the majority of whom were foreigners. Because of this, the soldiers left in the city guards were very little dismayed by the presence of the disease. Furthermore, a person who has suffered from the plague once during an outbreak is almost never infected a second time during that same period of infection. Instead, such a person may afterwards mingle with everyone else without harm, much like the **Psylli** <note>a legendary African tribe renowned for their immunity to snake venom</note> who, after eating a viper's liver, could live among snakes unhurt. It seems we must conclude entirely with **Pieter van Foreest** <note>a famous Dutch physician often called the "Dutch Hippocrates"</note> that the specific and peculiar constitution or "preparation" of the body that makes it vulnerable to the plague is hidden from us; it can be determined neither by our senses nor by our reason, but only by the outcome itself.

**Indeed**, it can also be deduced from this that although we grant the pestilential contagion a great power to do harm, it still necessarily requires a specific "readiness" or disposition within the human body. This is because the plague does not immediately harm every single individual in the manner of other poisons derived from

<column-break/>

minerals, animals, or plants; rather, it affects only those in whom a suitable **passive fitness** <note>original: "ἀξιά ϑεους" (axia theous). The author uses a Greek-derived term to describe a body's specific predisposition to catch a disease.</note> is found. But what is that disposition which vanishes so completely after one has successfully fought off this poisonous plague, so that the survivor can safely breathe in those same poisonous vapors during the same outbreak? How is this state generated in the human body at specific times alongside the pollution of the air? Why does it reach its "maturity" in some people at one point in the plague and in others at a different time? Why, in infected houses, does the contagion strike some people suddenly, while affecting others only after several weeks—with many remaining unharmed after changing their residence, a fact I myself have noted several times during outbreaks? Why are our bodies so disposed not at just any time, but only at specific times when universal causes concur? *This is the task, this is the toil!* <note>original: "hic opus, hic labor erit," a famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid regarding the difficulty of returning from the underworld.</note> We are forced to admit our ignorance here. Along with **Jean Fernel** <note>a prominent French physician who introduced the term "physiology"</note>, we must establish that the cause of the plague is not only an external "active" force, but also a hidden, internal "receiving" cause—a property of the whole substance of the body that is hostile to the vital principle. In this, we flee to the providence of **God**, who is most powerful not only in punishing our sins by corrupting the environment through immediate or intermediate causes, but also in stirring up that internal principle of suffering within us.

<summary>The author explores why the plague selectively infects certain people and nationalities while sparing others, concluding that an internal, hidden "disposition" or susceptibility must exist alongside the external contagion.</summary>

...is [God], by whose will we are what we are. solitary places and withdrawing himself from the company of men. From this fall, since—in my opinion—he collected a great quantity of blood within the cavity of the belly, and since no legitimate remedies were applied which could either dissolve and lead out the clotted blood within, or prevent the influx by bloodletting, or be of use to the affected area through poultices and ointments; it seems likely that this very blood, gradually putrefied, not only occupied the heart, but also, with virulent and malignant vapors <note>In the medical theory of the time, "vapors" were thought to rise from diseased organs to the brain to cause mental disturbance</note> rising upward, sought the very seat of reason, the brain, and along with the imagination, perverted his very thought or reasoning. This last option would perhaps not be entirely foreign to reason, since a virus <note>original: "virus"; in 1625, this term referred to a "poison" or "venom" rather than a microscopic pathogen</note> lying hidden within can be not so much fostered as "excited" by any cause, even sometimes the slightest. But enough of this for now. I recently received as a gift from my brother, Master Johann Baptista, a copy of your *Medical Observations*, and I read it with great pleasure and even greater utility. They are rare and perfect in every respect <note>original: "numeris omnibus absolutæ," a Latin idiom for a work that is complete and flawless</note>. Continue now, and according to the most exquisite sharpness of your intellect, make Medical Studies more and more perfect every day, however and wherever you can. Farewell, most Excellent and Noble Man, and count us both as brothers—as most loving and devoted followers of your most splendid name—among your friends. Nürtingen, September 12, 1625.

**K**now, most Excellent and Renowned man, patron and friend to be greatly honored, that your friendly and long-awaited letter was delivered to me safely by your most Renowned brother. It pleased me for two reasons: first, because it offered an opportunity for us to form a friendship, and second, because it proposed a singular case, memorable in the field of medicine. Regarding the first point: three words, as the common proverb goes, were sufficient for a good cause; therefore, I respond with just as many words, offering my reciprocal goodwill. Regarding the latter point: should I believe the deceased, who reported that he had been bitten by a mad dog about two years prior? Or should I instead conclude that this lethal condition, which resulted in death, was produced by a fall and a contusion of the left hypochondrium <note>The upper part of the abdomen, just below the ribs</note> shortly before the onset of the melancholic deliri-

Although, according to our Scaliger <note>referring to the famous scholar Julius Caesar Scaliger</note>, a retreat to "hidden causes" is rightly called the *Asylum of Human Ignorance* when effects can be conveniently explained by obvious manifest causes, I nevertheless do not see why, in this case, we should not rather agree with the patient. He stated he had been bitten by a mad dog, recalling the similarity of the symptom—that depraved appetite for biting others—which tormented him (who was otherwise rational, a trait peculiar to those with hydrophobia <note>The historical term for rabies, literally "fear of water"</note>), rather than deducing the cause of that melancholic delirium and the subsequent fatal outcome from somewhere else.

...[that the recent injury] contributed little to this disease, not only in fostering and increasing it, but even in accelerating and activating it. To say nothing of those who firmly assert that true rabies can arise from internal causes alone. Although, to confess the truth, I would not wish to defend this opinion as true.

**Diseases perhaps similar to rabies arise from those [internal causes], but never true rabies.**

For I believe it is discovered and placed beyond all doubt—and approved by the unanimous consent of the most highly regarded authors, both ancient and modern—that rabid poison <note>original: "venenum rabidum"</note> can by no means be produced in a man without external contagion and the bite of a rabid animal. But enough on this for now.

<margin>Green wormwood worn inside the shoes for a cold stomach.</margin>
By what reason green wormwood <note>original: "absynthium"; a bitter herb traditionally used for digestive issues and to expel parasites</note>, crushed inside the shoes, should remedy a cold imbalance of the stomach <term>intemperiem: a humoral imbalance where the stomach was thought to lack sufficient heat for digestion</term> through vomiting and nausea, I would wish to be taught by Your Excellence. N. Piso <note>Nicolaus Piso (1527–1590), a French physician known for his practical medical observations</note> observed this remedy, discovered by younger physicians through both reason and experience.

<column-break/>

I do not see a manifest reason for it. However, I have put it to the test, not without success, in the case of a certain noble and illustrious Baron of Limpurg, Hereditary Steward of the Holy Roman Empire <note>The Schenk von Limpurg family held this prestigious ceremonial title in the imperial court</note>, who openly explained and solemnly affirmed that he perceived no small relief from the crushing of this herb.

Whether, indeed, this relief should be properly ascribed to this medicine, or rather to the patient's trust in the Physician—which was very great, and is not infrequently the case—or perhaps because he had previously used many remedies, both internal and external, dedicated and appropriate to the stomach, so that he might have been restored to his former health even without the use of the aforementioned wormwood; you decide. It is incumbent upon Your Excellence to investigate these hidden operations of nature and make them public. For Your Excellence seems born for this task above many others. But I have been longer than I intended, and I abuse Your Excellence's kindness. May Your Excellence fare well for a very long time and most happily, and continue to favor me as you have begun, than which nothing more welcome can happen to me.

EPISTLE ON MEDICINE BOOK II. SECTION V.

...stirred by most kind prayers, he who—through me as interpreter—asks you with great reverence that you do not hesitate to communicate with him, committed to a mindful paper, those things you have thought could be of use to his son, whom he will soon order to depart elsewhere. Although I consider that everything which could be said about our [Mr.] N. is already held in your memory: yet you will not take it ill, I think, when my diligence, or rather my care, begins reverently to approach yours in recalling some of the things which led the course of our deliberation.

That [young man] of ours, when he was first committed to my trust and domestic supervision, showed none of those symptoms which later broke out; a certain member of his entourage, upon his arrival from Austria, had lightly warned me that the youth was sometimes accustomed to be attacked by a small seizure <term>correptiuncula</term> <note>original: "correptiuncula" - a Latin diminutive meaning a "little attack" or minor fit.</note>, creeping out from one side of his flanks, which is nevertheless relieved by subsequent vomiting. It happened at length, that an extraordinary example of this kind of small seizure was exhibited a little later. Then he would press one or the other side with his palm, I believe the right; he would run up and down in the house: soon, exhausted, he would lie down on a cot: twisting his whole body, rolling around: disturbing those standing by with a groan like a turtledove, even breaking out into wailing, no differently than those who are infested with the sharpest torments <term>tormina</term> <note>original: "torminibus" - acute, twisting intestinal pains or "gripes."</note>. Next, he would shrink from all food: or rather, those foods taken earlier—or consumed during the pain at the persuasion of women—he would cast out again, with viscous, yellowish, and even watery bile <note>original Greek: "ὑδατώδει χολῇ" (hydatōdei cholē) - watery bile.</note>.

<column-break/>

And such symptoms <note>original Greek: "συμπτώματα" (symptōmata) - medical symptoms or occurrences.</note> with their associated features occurred first every seventh day <term>VIIana</term> <note>original: "VIIana" - referring to a septenary cycle, a common observation in early modern medicine where illnesses were thought to follow seven-day patterns.</note>; later, once you had already blunted that "executioner" <note>A metaphorical reference to the personified pain or disease.</note> with known medicines, they occurred monthly: coming upon him from the same source after a longer interval. He used, however, at all times a diet that was not inconvenient, and according to the standards of the times and the fare at our house, it was somewhat elegant; but for drink, he took none other than that which, as the common leonine verse <note>A type of rhyming Latin verse.</note> has it, "the Goose drinks" <note>A humorous scholarly idiom meaning he drank only water.</note>. In the jaundiced <term>icteric</term> <note>original: "ictericis" - relating to jaundice, the yellowing of the skin caused by bile issues.</note> attacks of the illness, the difficulty of passing urine also argued that the kidneys and bladder were afflicted. 

But in what way you met that trouble—"to speak of hard things softly" <note>original Greek: "ὡς σκληρὰ μαλθακῶς λέγειν" (hōs sklēra malthakῶs legein) - a Greek proverb about tempering harsh news or dealing gently with a difficult situation.</note>—and with what weapons, both therapeutic <note>original Greek: "θεραπευτικοῖς" (therapeutikois)</note> and dietary <note>original Greek: "διαιτητικοῖς" (diaitētikois)</note>, you fought such a bitter enemy, it is not my place to repeat idly here. We found, however, this most worthy of all observation: as soon as he had sent away the "messenger" of plain and clear water according to your prescription, and had begun to use beer infused with some sort of bile-purging medicines <term>cholalogis</term> <note>original: "Chola-logis" (cholagogues) - substances that promote the discharge of bile from the system.</note> enclosed in a small bag, every terrible thing <note>original Greek: "ἅπαν τὸ δεινὸν" (hapan to deinon) - the whole of the terrifying affliction.</note> was diminished. We were made more secure daily, and hostile irruptions and assaults were long prohibited: so much so that although one or two small invasions wished to be a terror to us [I exclude however that last indication of a small fever, which you, Most Excellent Mr. Stromarius, will be able to explain <note>original Greek: "ἐξηγεῖσθαι" (exēgeisthai) - to interpret or explain professionally.</note>].

...[the symptoms], which you depict so vividly in your letters that it seems there is scarcely any need for a further Apelles <note>A legendary painter of ancient Greece, known for his incredible realism and perfectionism.</note>, except for that part which involves more difficulty than labor. In that regard, I greatly fear that the same thing may happen to us as happened to the aforementioned excellent Painter: having expressed the face of his intended image of Venus with such artistry, no one else could similarly outline and illuminate the rest of the body. In this way, you have quite skillfully noted the various symptoms afflicting him at different times, just as they were observed. Yet, the root and causes of these would scarcely be penetrated at first glance even by a skilled physician with the sharp eyes of a Lynceus <note>A mythological figure from the Argonauts famed for his supernatural eyesight, able to see through solid objects.</note>. Be that as it may, we shall respond to your questions in few words; please take them in good part, since, according to the Philosopher <note>A common reference to Aristotle.</note>, thanks are due even to those who offer probable arguments.

<margin>How diseases are propagated from parents to children.</margin>
You ask first *whether something morbid was derived into the fetus from birth* <note>original: "ἀπὸ γενετῆς" (apo genetes)</note>, even though the perfect health of his noble parents might prove the contrary? Although the unraveling of this doubt serves our purpose but little—insofar as a Physician is compelled to be concerned not with remote and external causes, but mostly with the more immediate ones that foster the condition—nevertheless, it cannot be denied in the least that not a few diseases are propagated from ancestors to posterity. Nothing prevents a parent, who can generate a son similar in external features, from producing one endowed with an internal defect as well,

<column-break/>

insofar as the seed <note>The author uses the term "semen" to describe the reproductive material believed to carry the essential "blueprint" or qualities of the parents.</note> not only represents the whole body in essential likeness, but also includes its qualities. However, this must be understood as referring only to fixed and permanent properties.

<margin>A grandson can also take a likeness from his grandfather.</margin>
Indeed, not only do such diseases of parents sprout again in grandsons, but even those of grandfathers. This occurs when the "seed-force" is obliterated in the father due to hindering causes, so that it does not pass into action, yet it exerts itself in the son. Thus, the following logic is insufficient: "the father is healthy, therefore the son is entirely free from a hereditary condition."

<margin>Why this condition is not hereditary.</margin>
But in truth, since the symptoms invading this noble youth argue for roots that are not at all "fixed" (which all hereditary conditions presuppose), it must be concluded that this disease is not contained within that class at all. 

*It is further asked, whether some trick of the formative power* <term>dynamis</term> <note>original: "δυνάμεως" (dynameōs) — the vital force believed to shape and govern the organs.</note> *regarding the gallbladder is to be blamed—perhaps by fashioning some peculiar passage to the stomach—or some superabundance of yellow bile, or finally, a "consensus" <note>The medical idea that one part of the body can suffer in sympathy with another.</note> of the parts, and by what means the returning evil should be assisted?*

<margin>Determination of this condition.</margin>
The observation of the symptoms and the success of the remedies have sufficiently proven that it is abundant bile, and that it rushes *all at once* <note>original: "ἀθρόως" (athroōs)</note> at certain times toward the stomach. By reason of this, not only is there first a pain of...

# ON THE SINGULAR EFFUSION OF BILE.

...tension around the hypochondria <note>The upper abdominal region just below the ribs, traditionally associated with the liver and spleen.</note>, but also pain in the upper orifice [of the stomach] and bilious belching followed, preceded by a loss of appetite because of foreign matter being communicated to the stomach. Hence, we have remarked more than once that the Distinguished Patient is among those whom Hippocrates calls *those with bitter-bile above* <note>original Greek: "πικροχόλους ἄνω" (pikrocholous ano)</note>, and he declares them most prone to vomiting bile; this is because they have a unique biliary duct leading to the base of the stomach, as more famous Anatomists have noted in some cases.

What wonder is it, then, if the substance of the stomach is provoked by an influx of bile, and other parts are simultaneously drawn into sympathy? This is especially true when the influx of this same bilious humor is communicated to other members, particularly in a body temperament that is otherwise hot and dry, and of a lean constitution. For this reason, we have quite often noted a difficulty and burning of urine <note>A condition known historically as "ardor urinae," often associated with systemic heat or inflammation.</note> occurring toward the end of the paroxysms <note>A sudden attack or increase in the intensity of symptoms.</note>.

<margin>Indications for treatment.</margin>
We believed that right from the beginning, we must look to soothe the onset of the attacks by every means possible, to strengthen nature, and then to prevent the further production of bile. Regarding the first point, we determined that vomiting should by no means be inhibited, because the rejected matter indicates its own need for removal. Meanwhile, we judged that the stomach must be strengthened, the tension-related pains soothed, and the urinary tracts tempered. For this purpose, regarding the stomach:

<column-break/>

On January 12, 1623, we prescribed the following syrup:
*Take:* 
*Syrup of sweet pomegranate, 2 ounces.*
*Citron vinegar, 1 ounce.*
*Cinnamon water, half a drachm.*
*Spirit of vitriol <note>A traditional term for diluted sulfuric acid, used here as a cooling agent.</note>, 4 drops. Mix.*

We attempted to soothe the tension-pains externally with the following remedy:
*Take: Oils of sweet almond, chamomile, and scorpions <note>A traditional preparation where scorpions were infused in oil, believed to be effective against internal pains and stones.</note>, 1 ounce of each. Oil of turpentine, half a drachm. Rose ointment, half a drachm. Mix for a liniment.* 

We also wished to free the urinary tracts from burning through the use of *Syrup of Marshmallow by Fernel <note>Referring to a specific recipe by Jean Fernel, a renowned 16th-century French physician.</note>, mixed with syrup of the two roots and Spirit of Turpentine.* Once the first invasions [of the illness] were overcome in this manner, we similarly brought aid to nature in subsequent attacks, where an external stomach remedy was also prepared for flatulent torments <note>Painful gas or bloating.</note>, consisting of: *Anodyne <note>Pain-killing.</note> ointment and dill oil, half a drachm of each; mastic oil and distilled anise oil, half a drachm of each.* Let it be mixed for anointing the stomach. 

Outside of the attack, we said that nature must be strengthened and the production of bile prevented. For this reason, right from the start, after the labors of the attacks were endured, we advised that evacuation should be instituted at intervals. To this end (since the noble youth abstains from wine), in place of wine, we ordered the following laxative hydromel <note>A medicinal drink made of honey and water boiled with herbs.</note>:
*Take: Chicory root, 6 ounces. Scorzonera <note>Also known as viper's grass.</note>, half a drachm.*
*Eryngo <note>Sea holly.</note>, Licorice, 3 ounces of each.*
*Senna leaves, 1 ounce. Epithyme <note>A parasitic plant, often dodder of thyme.</note>, 1 drachm.*
*Choice Rhubarb, 1.5 drachms. Agaric <note>A type of medicinal fungus used as a purgative.</note>, 5 drachms.*

### LETTERS ON MEDICINE: BOOK II, SECTION IV.

...you describe these symptoms so graphically in your letters that there seems to be little need for a later Apelles <note>Apelles was the most renowned painter of ancient Greece, famous for his realism.</note>, except for that part which involves more difficulty than labor. In that regard, I greatly fear the same thing may happen to us as happened to the aforementioned excellent Painter: having expressed the face of Venus in a painting he had begun, he rendered the work with such artistry that the rest of the body could be similarly outlined and illuminated by no one else. <margin>How diseases are propagated from parents to children.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>A grandson can also take similarity from a grandfather.</margin>
Indeed, not only such diseases of parents, but also those of grandfathers sprout up again in grandsons. In such cases, for various hindering reasons, the trait is erased in the father so that it does not pass into action, yet it exerts itself in the son. <margin>Why this condition is not hereditary.</margin>
In truth, since the symptoms invading the noble youth by no means suggest fixed roots (which all hereditary conditions presuppose), it must be concluded that this disease is not contained in this class. It is further asked whether we should blame some "play" of the formative power <note>original Greek: "δυνάμεως" (dynameos); the vital force believed to shape the fetus.</note> around the gallbladder—perhaps by fashioning some peculiar duct to the stomach—or some superabundance of yellow bile, or finally the consensus of parts <note>The medical concept of "sympathy," where one organ suffers due to the illness of another.</note>? And by what means should this recurring evil be helped?

<margin>Determination of this rare condition.</margin>

### ON THE SINGULAR EFFUSION OF BILE.

...there was not only a feeling of tension around the **hypochondria** <note>The upper part of the abdomen, just below the ribs.</note>, but also pain in the **upper orifice** <note>The cardia, where the esophagus meets the stomach.</note>, followed by the bilious belching of the stomach itself. This was preceded by a loss of appetite, as foreign matter had been communicated to the stomach. For this reason, we have stated more than once that the patient is among those whom Hippocrates calls <term>hypocholos ano</term> <note>original Greek: ὑποχόλος ἄνω; meaning "bilious in the upper parts."</note>. Hippocrates pronounces such people to be very prone to vomiting bile, because they possess a peculiar **bile duct** that leads to the bottom of the stomach, as the more famous Anatomists have noted in certain cases. Truly, what wonder is it if, when the substance of the stomach is provoked by the influx of bile, other parts are drawn into sympathy? This is especially true when the influx of this same bilious humor is shared with other members, particularly in a body temperament that is otherwise **hot and dry**, and of a lean constitution. For this reason, we have frequently noted a difficulty and burning of urine recurring toward the end of these **paroxysms** <note>Sudden attacks or fits of the disease.</note>.

<margin>Indications.</margin>
Right from the beginning, we believed it necessary to focus on soothing the attacks of the paroxysms with every skill, strengthening the "nature" <note>The body's own healing power.</note>, and then preventing the further production of bile. Regarding the first point, we decided that the vomiting should by no means be stopped, because the matter being thrown up indicated that it needed to be removed. Meanwhile, we judged that the stomach must be strengthened, the tensive pains soothed, and the urinary tracts tempered. For this purpose, regarding the stomach,

<column-break/>

on January 12, 1623, we prescribed the following syrup:
> Take: 2 ounces of **Syrup of sweet pomegranates**.
> 1 ounce of **Citric vinegar**.
> half a dram of **Cinnamon**.
> 3 drops of **Spirit of vitriol** <note>A dilute form of sulfuric acid, used as a cooling tonic.</note>. Mix.

We attempted to soothe the tensive pains externally with the following remedy:
> Take: **Oils of sweet almonds, Chamomile, and Scorpions** <note>Scorpion oil was a traditional remedy used to break up stones and soothe internal pain.</note>, 1 ounce each.
> half a dram of **Oil of Turpentine**.
> half a dram of **Rose Ointment**.
> Mix for a liniment.

We also wished to free the urinary tracts from burning through the use of **Fernelius’s Syrup of Marshmallow**, mixed with **Syrup of the two roots** <note>Likely parsley and fennel roots, used for their diuretic properties.</note> and **Spirit of Turpentine**. In this manner, having overcome the first invasions of the illness, we similarly brought aid to "nature" in the subsequent attacks. Where there were also gas-related cramps, an external stomach remedy was prepared from **Anodyne Ointment** <note>A pain-relieving salve.</note> and **Dill oil**, half an ounce each; and **Mastic oil** and **distilled Anise oil**, half a dram each. Let it be mixed for anointing the stomach. Outside of the paroxysm, we stated that "nature" must be strengthened and the production of bile prevented. For this reason, soon after the initial labors of the paroxysms were endured, we advised that an evacuation should be carried out periodically. To this end (since the noble youth is a **teetotaler**), in place of wine, we ordered the following **laxative mead** <note>original: "hydromel laxativum," a mixture of honey and water infused with herbs.</note>:
> Take: 6 ounces of **Chicory root**.
> half a dram of **Scorzonera** <note>Black salsify, used to treat toxins.</note>.
> **Eryngo** and **Liquorice**, 3 drams each.
> 1 ounce of **Senna leaves**.
> 6 drams of **Epithymum** <note>Dodder, a parasitic plant used to purge bile.</note>.
> 2 drams of **Choice Rhubarb**.
> 6 drams of **Agaric** <note>A medicinal fungus used as a purgative.</note>.

However, we immediately countered this with an evacuation using half a dram of the <term>Magistery of Vitriolated Tartar</term> <note>Potassium sulfate, a chemical salt used as a mild laxative.</note> and 2 grains of <term>Diagrydium</term> <note>A potent purgative made from the resin of the Scammony plant.</note> mixed with 2 drams of Red Rose Conserve. To temper the drink, we added a syrup made of the juice of lemons, sour and sweet pomegranates (two ounces of each), and the **Rob** <note>A thick, concentrated fruit juice or syrup.</note> of Barberries and Red Currants (one ounce of each), with enough spirit of vitriol to mix. This was done so that the patient might again enjoy his former health and vigor. 

From this, therefore, it is clear what our opinion is regarding the "neutral constitution" <note>A state where the patient is neither fully healthy nor fully ill, requiring constant management.</note> of this noble patient, and what means we judge necessary for both prevention and cure. May God, the **Chief Physician** <note>original: ἀρχιατρὸς (*archiatros*).</note>, grant that as his years increase, his natural vigor may also grow more and more...

...revised, in the additions of my *Observations, Medical Letters Section 7, Book 1.* The other observation is truly remarkable; for although *Gilbert the Englishman, Brassavola, Fernelius, Mercurialis, Columbus, Johann Matthäus, and others* have observed stones <note>original: "calculos"</note> formed even in the intestines <note>original: "Intestinis"</note>, such a great quantity as both your notes testify has never before been observed by anyone until now.

<margin>Stones of horses expelled through the bowels.</margin>
Regarding stones from horses expelled through the bowels, see the fine discourse by *Libavius in the Cista Medica* <note>The "Medical Chest," a collection of early 17th-century medical writings</note>, *page 182, printed at Nuremberg.* Your Excellency mentions "Cream of Crystal" <note>original: "Cremoris Crystalli"</note> here; I am eager to know whether you mean that *alcohol* of crystal <note>A term for a very fine, purified powder</note>, or the powder of crystal, which is made by heating the crystal in a crucible and throwing it into cold water? It was shaped as if the face of an evil spirit <note>original: "cacodaemonis facies"</note> had been carved into it. I saw this with my own eyes in the presence of the most Noble Baron von Königsegg, and I handled it with my own hands. On the following day, when the patient in turn felt immense pains in his bowels—just like a woman in labor—the lithotomist was called again, and a second stone was removed. The aforementioned stones were indeed large, but very light in weight and brown in color; the lithotomist still keeps them at his home as a memorial of this operation. Now, lest I seem a burden to you, I break off my pen. Farewell, most Excellent Man, whom I must respect most highly; I earnestly ask that you continue to love me in return, as I am most indebted to you for many kindnesses. Given at Kempten <note>original: "Campoduni"</note>, December 7th, in the year 1626.

# ON STONES IN THE HUMAN BODY.

...illustrious man, **Master Doctor Jeremiah Seng**, <note>original: "p. m." for *piae memoriae*, meaning "of pious memory" or deceased</note> my honored colleague. In his gallbladder, more than two hundred stones—almost all four-sided, partly ash-colored, partly yellowish and almost glittering like gold—were found, which the widow of the aforementioned Doctor Seng still has in her possession. The substance of the liver was clearly eaten away; yet, he never once complained of a heavy pain in his right side. Whether such pain ought to be considered a <term>pathognomonic</term> <note>A characteristic symptom that specifically identifies a particular disease</note> sign of these stones, and whether these stones can be crushed and removed by human art, I greatly desire to hear from you, most learned man. Indeed, that a long-lasting and exquisite colic should be ended and put to rest by the excretion of 233 stones through the bowels is very rare, and almost to be counted as a miracle. Many years ago, the father of the most noble man, **Lord Johann Conrad von Wolmershausen**—of Amlishagen, Burleswag, and Neidenfels, etc.—named **Werner**,

<margin>Tartareous globules lurking in the intestines for a long time</margin>
a sixty-year-old man, struggled miserably for a whole year with exquisite tortures of the intestines that evaded all internal and external remedies; finally, he was overcome by the atrocity of the pains. had been prolonged further. # MEDICAL LETTERS, BOOK II, SECTION V.

...one of our magistrates, while still living, fell into <term>dropsy</term> <note>Latin: *hydrops*; an accumulation of fluid in the body tissues or cavities, causing swelling</note>. By God’s grace and my own efforts—though everyone thought she was close to giving birth <note>original: *vicina partui*; her abdominal swelling was so great it was mistaken for late-stage pregnancy</note>—she was cured within four weeks using appropriate medicines. She was able to return to public life and even thanked me for her recovery; only a small, extremely hard area, like a very tough stone, remained in her lower abdomen. 

However, not long after, due to a coarse diet and the suppression of her menstrual flow, she suffered a relapse. Because of her weakened state and a newly contracted <term>cachexia</term> <note>a "wasting" syndrome characterized by weight loss and muscle atrophy</note>—and as you know, relapses are usually far worse than the original illness—the medicines could not save her, and the poor woman exchanged life for death. 

Since her lower belly felt as hard as a rock to the touch, I suspected that something might be hiding in the uterus, perhaps collected water or some other unnatural growth that had made her final treatment difficult or had fueled the disease. Therefore, I performed a dissection in the presence of my surgeon. Once the body was opened, water immediately flowed out in abundance. Truly, what was most astonishing—and something I have never seen in my life—was that all the intestines, everywhere, and both sides around the <term>diaphragm</term> <note>the muscle separating the chest from the abdomen</note> were seen to be covered with many thousands

<column-break/>

of small granules, appearing like grains of hail. Furthermore, the space between the intestines and the <term>mesentery</term> <note>the fold of membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</note> was filled with a sticky mucus, resembling gelatin in its color and consistency. The rest of the internal organs (except for the lungs, which were also spotted with these granules in certain places) were free from any visible defect.

<margin>A stone in the gallbladder.</margin> Moreover, upon opening the gallbladder, I found this stone, about the size of a walnut; I am sending it to you to examine and keep as a gift. Finally, coming to the uterus in the order of the dissection, I found none of the things I had suspected; instead, it was small and flaccid, with some thick menstrual blood remaining in the veins. 

Regarding this case, several points worthy of consideration arise, which might cause doubt for some:

<margin>Doubts.</margin> 1. Is every case of dropsy caused by a "cold" imbalance of the liver, as is commonly held by everyone, whether it occurs in the organ itself or through the influence of other organs?

# ON STONES IN THE HUMAN BODY.

<margin>Does all dropsy come from a cold imbalance?</margin>
...and observed? Concerning the first question, it seems that the notion <note>the prevailing medical theory at the time that dropsy was always caused by a "cold and moist" liver</note> is not universally true, nor consistent with reason and experience, because it has been observed that some patients were greatly harmed by the use of "hot" medicines. My opinion is supported by the *most distinguished Mr. Heinrich Smetius in his Miscellanies, Book 8, Letter 4*, in which mention is made of two dropsy patients whom he cured, contrary to the common method of healing, using only cooling remedies. From this cure, it is clear that not every <term>dropsy</term> <note>Latin: *hydrops*; the accumulation of fluid in body cavities</note> arises from a cooling of the liver. This opinion also seems not to lack supporting reasons, which I would list here were I not afraid of causing your Excellency boredom with my wordiness.

<margin>Why dropsy varies.</margin>
Let us move to the second question. Dropsy is not always of one kind, but differs; this is clearly evident from anatomical dissection. Indeed, when I was staying in Padua <note>Latin: *Patavij*; a major center for medical and anatomical study in Italy</note> for the sake of my studies, I saw a dissected dropsy patient whose liver was seen by everyone to be filled with numerous vesicles full of water. Furthermore, in Marburg <note>Latin: *Marpurgi*</note>, I also saw the liver of a very gluttonous domestic animal entirely full of water vesicles. In this patient of mine, however, not even the slightest trace of injury appeared (even though it was dissected by me into the smallest parts), but it looked exactly like the liver of a healthy person. To the third point: no sensible or notable obstructions were seen by me;

<column-break/>

whether they were observed by others is not known to me. The urine was always very red, and no fever preceded it, nor was any present. Such urine is not usually the result of faulty <term>blood-making</term> <note>Latin: *sanguificatio*; the historical medical theory of how the liver converts food into blood</note>, but rather of a liver that is more burning than it should be. But enough of these matters. Farewell to you and yours, and continue to hold me in your affection. Written in haste at Kempten <note>Latin: *Campoduni*</note>, February 26, 1626.
