...it exhibits a singular bitterness): they testify that its origin is from a thicker bile. The reports concerning stones of the gallbladder found in the *Third Book of Observations* by Schenckius are worthy of note; he cites Kentmann, Fernel, Lange, Coiter, Vesalius, Benivieni, Dodoens, Cardano, Falloppio, Crato, Ferrand, Gemma, Vallès, Forest, and others. However, no mention is made there of a <term>dropsical</term> <note>Latin: *hydropicæ*; a condition of swelling caused by excess fluid</note> affection arising from this, which is why I would say the production of this stone is distinct from the origin of the dropsy. 

<margin>The cause of the hail-like infection.</margin>
As for the addition that the intestines and neighboring parts were infected with an innumerable quantity of granules, resembling hail, I believe this was caused by <term>depraved concoction</term> <note>A term from humoral medicine referring to faulty "cooking" or processing of food and fluids in the body</note>. In this case, the thicker, undigested parts provided the occasion for this evil through <term>adustion</term> <note>Latin: *adustionem*; the "scorching" or overheating of humors, making them thick, dry, or acrid</note>, while in the meantime, a thinner serum collected in the intervening spaces of the abdomen. 

Regarding the additional questions, my mind is known to you from 

<margin>See the Author's *Medical Problems*.</margin>
those things which were formerly proposed by me in my *Medical Problems*, where in *Decade 7, question 9, section 3*, the controversy is decided. There, it is shown through a distinction how dropsy is usually caused not only by heat and cold, but also by a certain substantial corruption, etc.; this will serve for a further declaration of the first question. 

<margin>See book 7 of the *Wonderful History of Medicine* by Marcello Donati, added to chapter 7.</margin>
The second question, whether dropsy can occur while the liver remains healthy <note>Latin: *salvo jecore*</note>, we touched upon in *Book 7, Chapter 7 of the Wonderful History of Medicine*, where this very thing is indeed

<column-break/>

confirmed by many examples: namely, that dropsical tumors have occurred while the liver remained healthy. However, a limitation is added afterward: that "properly so-called" <term>dropsy</term> <note>Latin: *hydrops*</note> must be distinguished from these other swellings. 

Finally, regarding what is asked in the third place—namely, whether such obstructions of the <term>mesentery</term> <note>The membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</note> have been observed as are so very often presupposed by physicians—it seems doubtful, especially since nothing of the sort was observed in the present subject. Here, indeed, I do not deny that it can frequently happen that in similar cases, where one and the same effect usually arises from different causes, we may err in determining the most immediate cause. This is most strongly testified by dissections performed after death. 

Particularly notable is the history of a tumor of the <term>omentum</term> <note>Latin: *omenti*; the fatty "apron" that hangs over the intestines</note>, which appeared to us physicians to be a case of <term>ascites</term> <note>A type of dropsy where fluid collects in the abdominal cavity</note>, until finally, after the opening of the deceased woman, it revealed itself to be a mass weighing 56 pounds, as can be seen in my *Medical Problems, Decade 6, question 10*. Nevertheless, I do not see how obstructions of the mesentery can be entirely denied, even if they do not occur in this or that particular subject. 

Well-known is the story written to me by the most celebrated <term>Bauhin</term> <note>Caspar Bauhin (1560–1624), a famous Swiss anatomist and botanist</note>, who reports that swelling glands of the mesentery, introducing a total obstruction, were the cause of a <term>phthisis</term> <note>A wasting disease, usually referring to tuberculosis</note>; we added this history to *Book 7, Chapter 5 of Marcello Donati's Wonderful History*. Also well-known are those things concerning various collections in the mesentery...

->FROM GREGOR HORSTIUS, DOCTOR.<-

To be sure, there was communicated to me by my colleague, that famous man Doctor Stegmann, while we were by chance speaking of such matters, a rare medical history, not unworthy of obser-

<column-break/>

<margin>A stone rejected from the nostrils through the palate.</margin> vation: namely, concerning a stone the size of a small chestnut which, after a continuous headache, was rejected from the nostrils through the palate. I could not, and should not, fail to transmit this to your Excellence and subject it to your judgment—which is most sharp and skillful in medical matters. It is a case worthy of increasing and adorning our medical observations. It has been confirmed by manifold experience that stones can be generated in various other parts of our body, and even in the head itself. However, in which specific part of the head this one was produced and lay hidden is not entirely certain. Its easy exit confirms that it was generated and held outside the <term>cranium</term> <note>The skull-cap protecting the brain</note>, rather than inside it. Perhaps it acquired its origin near the openings of the <term>cuneiform bone</term> <note>Latin: *os cuneiforme*; now known as the sphenoid bone at the base of the skull</note>, through which the mucous secretions of the brain—having first been received by the <term>pituitary gland</term> <note>In the 17th century, the pituitary was believed to filter waste "phlegm" from the brain down into the nose and throat</note>—flow down or gradually drip into the palate. It likely grew from viscid and corrupt matter collected and sticking there; as it gradually hardened, it formed a space for itself. From this flowing and putrefying material adhering to the fibers—as if from a womb—it sent up foul vapors to the head itself and induced pains. But afterward, when it had hardened sufficiently and could no longer be contained, it prepared its exit. Having emerged through the openings of the palate, it caused this movement in the nostrils, with which the palate is connected through its openings and through the nerves which, arising from the <term>third pair</term> <note>In the anatomical numbering of the time, this referred to branches of what we now call the trigeminal nerve, which supplies sensation to the face and palate</note>, go to the lining of the nostrils and the palate simultaneously.

When an old man was in desperate health with extreme pain in the intestines, though we saw he lacked fever and no tumor was visible, yet he cleared his bowels with daily stools; feeling a weight in the intestines themselves, by a certain fateful guess we thought a stone lay beneath. We ordered enemas of <term>Bdellium</term> <note>A semi-transparent oleo-gum resin used in ancient medicine</note> and our Telinian oil, a saffron <term>malagma</term> <note>A softening poultice or plaster</note>, butter, and a certain decoction to be infused. In the liver of a rower, one very hard, of a diluted flesh color. In the lungs of Albretician the Quaestor, several very hard ones with an even surface and clay color.”*

# ON CALCULI IN THE HUMAN BODY.

Many stones from the bladder are layered with scales like onions, with the layers underneath being of a different color. There are two types besides these. I have both in my possession. A townsman from Bovillae, assisted by our medicines, passed a <term>glassy stone</term> <note>original: *vitreum*; likely a reference to a very hard, translucent urinary stone</note>: surely arising from that famous "glassy phlegm" described by <note>Praxagoras of Cos was an ancient Greek physician who theorized that certain diseases were caused by "glassy" or "acidic" phlegm.</note> Praxagoras. While it was being passed, it had the softness of egg white, but once expelled, it took on the hardness and brilliance of glass. A senator's son ejected many very large ones in the manner of porridge; these later, upon contact with air, hardened into both the appearance and firmness of gypsum. This man is also now in good health. From the joints of those suffering from <term>gout</term> <note>Latin: *podagricorum*; gout often causes the formation of hard "tophi" or chalk-like deposits in the joints</note>—

<column-break/>

resembling brine, aged cheese, and the filings of burnt <term>pyrite</term> <note>a mineral often called "fool's gold," here used to describe the texture of the bodily deposits</note>—we have extracted many stones through the broken skin: they had the whiteness of soapstone and an invincible hardness. From the edge of the eyelid, where clusters of <term>styes</term> <note>Latin: *hordeolorum*; small, painful lumps on the eyelid</note> form, we ordered a small stone to be removed, equal to a grain of wheat in shape, color, and size, but superior in hardness. Pliny writes in his eleventh book that a stone was found in the bellies of heifers, which he names <term>Tofus</term> <note>a porous rock like tufa; Pliny the Elder was a Roman naturalist who cataloged such curiosities</note>, and reports it to be very light. Thus far Scaliger. With these words, fare well with your family. In haste at Ulm, January 31, 1625.

### MEDICAL EPISTLES, BOOK II, SECTION VI.

—regarding that <term>fluxion</term> <note>original: *fluxione*; in Galenic medicine, a "fluxion" was the flow of harmful humors from one part of the body to another, causing swelling or disease</note>, what do you think? Those infected swarmed with pustules and ulcers, almost like **cancers**, not only in the places where the skin had been <term>scarified</term> <note>the process of making small cuts in the skin, often for bloodletting or vaccination</note>, but over almost the entire body. They suffered immense pain in their joints, with such weakness that they could not leave their beds unless supported by others. Of these patients (who were very numerous), some were cured by a <term>decoction of wood</term> <note>original: *ligni decocto*; likely Guaiacum or "Holy Wood," a common 16th-century treatment for skin diseases and syphilis</note> and <term>antidotes</term> <note>original: *alexipharmacis*; remedies used to ward off poison or infection</note>; the rest succumbed to the greatness of the evil. Regarding <term>fly-killing powder</term> <note>original: *μυιοκτόνῳ* (myioctono)</note> and powdered toads, I shall say nothing; but I would like to hear from you what power <margin>A question is proposed concerning crickets.</margin> **crickets** might contribute to these evils, unless more serious matters distract you from an argument of such slight material. *Slight is the subject of the labor, but not slight is the glory*, as the poet said of Bees <note>a quote from Virgil’s *Georgics*, Book 4</note>. And you have indeed approved of this yourself by publishing your books on **Silkworms**. **Pliny** certainly did not wish to overlook crickets; although nothing is found in his work that serves our current purpose. For in *Book 30, Chapter 6*, he records the Greek and Latin names for crickets, as well as their description. In the same book, as well as in *Chapters 4, 8, 9, 12, 13, 14*, and in *Book 29, Chapter 6*, he reviews the manifold uses of <term>locust-crickets</term> <note>original: *tryxalidum*; likely referring to a species of cricket or grasshopper used in ancient pharmacy</note> in medicine.

To these, some authors add other uses, especially against **stones** and difficulties of the bladder; however, **Dioscorides** <note>a famous Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note> ascribes this to locusts, to whose genus they are said to belong, rather than to the genus of cicadas, as **Matthioli** <note>an influential 16th-century Italian physician</note> maintains <margin>Powdered cricket for toothache.</margin> against **Albertus Magnus**. A man of our court, of no small standing, asserts from his own frequent experience that the **powder of crickets** applied to a tooth with cotton wool can soothe its pain.

<column-break/>

But, I say, from all these things there is nothing by which we might ascribe to crickets the power of **stopping blood**; on the contrary, in *Book 30, Chapter 14*, they are said to assist purgations or <term>menses</term>. But another passage in *Book 30, Chapter 6* seems contrary to this, where twenty <term>locust-crickets</term> are ordered to be roasted and drunk in honey-wine against <term>orthopnoea</term> <note>a type of shortness of breath that occurs when lying down</note> for those spitting blood. Should we attribute this to their faculty of drying things out and, as it were, parching them? For perhaps this power exists in locusts and their species—I mean crickets, and even <term>fireflies</term> <note>original: *pyraustis*; a legendary or real insect thought to live in or near fire</note>—as **Bodin** maintains in his *Theater of Nature, Book 3, page 310*. By their touch alone, locusts once parched many things, as histories testify. And the **Locust-Eaters** <note>original: *Acridophagi*; a legendary ancient Ethiopian tribe described by Pliny and Diodorus Siculus as living solely on locusts</note> had bodies that were extremely thin and meager; even though locusts, suffocated by great smoke and preserved with salt, sufficed as a pleasant food for that nation. Perhaps a conjecture about the faculties of crickets can also be drawn from the powers of **ants**, for crickets delight in them and are captured by them. But I await your opinion on this matter. The cited passage of **Pliny** reminds me [*Book 30, Chapter 13*, where he relates that the ash of locust-crickets with honey removes the hard edges of ulcers]. An Englishman, surnamed **Puthman**, who not long ago undertook to cure a nun here who had been struggling for three years with a **cancerous ulcer** in her left breast, was so certain of the perfect success of the cure that he staked his life before our Prince. The edges—

[...growths] that were hard, when anointed with I know not what oil, fell away for the most part without any pain. ### THE CONFESSION OF THE BATHHOUSE ATTENDANT LEONHARD KURMREUTTER.

HE smeared <term>fly-powder</term> <note>original German: *Muckenpulver*; usually a reference to arsenic used as a pesticide</note> upon his leather sharpening-straps for three or four weeks and whetted his <term>bloodletting irons</term> <note>original: *Lasseÿsen*</note> upon them.
He rubbed the <term>scarifying irons</term> <note>original: *Schräpfeisen*; tools with multiple small blades used to nick the skin</note> against a **cricket**, and with these he <term>scarified</term> people who became infected; because of this, their blood stopped flowing, and upon the marks left by the scarification, soot-colored sores and boils erupted.
He dried **toads** and put the powder into a tub with water; he stirred the water and poured it onto the **bath-stove**, from which a steam and vapor were raised.

# MEDICAL LETTERS, BOOK II. SECTION VI.

<margin>How certain things are harmful externally, but less so when consumed.</margin>
...to be dreaded by nature. But this argument is easy to explain. For many things are ruinous upon contact with living blood, which, if you were to eat or drink them, present no trouble and are beyond danger. It is not unknown for serpents, toads, frogs, and so on, to be carried in the stomach—often in great numbers—without the blood itself being infected or malignant ulcers being excited. But if a viper bites someone and mixes its venom <note>original: *saniem*; literally "corrupt blood" or discharge, here referring to venom</note> with the vital juice, even horrible dangers are immediately at hand.

The juice of the Waldensian wolfsbane <note>original: *Toræ Waldensium*; likely a species of *Aconitum*</note>, according to **Gesner**, is not lethal as a drink; but when added as a poison to arrows and committed to the blood, it kills quickly. I would not doubt that the foam and sweat of horses can be drunk without harm. Yet those who quench white-hot <term>lancets</term> <note>original: *phlebotomos*; tools for bloodletting</note> in them, and use them to make small wounds, cause bleeding that does not stop until death. These examples are known to you. Therefore, there is no need for many words. However, it seems strange that such a force, clearly expressed by authors, has not been observed, especially when dealing with a creature so common and unexamined by so many centuries of medicine. But I think the commentaries should be searched more accurately, and experience and analogy consulted more attentively.

<margin>What crickets are.</margin>
Who those crickets of our land are is not agreed upon by everyone. **Matthiolus** notes that **Albertus Magnus** thought they were cicadas, which are nevertheless absent from

<column-break/>

Germany; nor do they endure winters, just as they do not become accustomed to houses. He himself interprets the <term>cockroaches</term> <note>original: *blattas*; a term that historically included various creeping insects</note> of **Dioscorides** and **Pliny** using the German words <term>Grillen</term> and <term>Heimichen</term>, or as we say, <term>Heimen</term> <note>house crickets</note>. He says it is a domestic animal, familiar in Tuscany in wine cellars, latrines, bakeries, baths, etc., chirping on summer nights and fleeing the light, although in the flatness of its body and the thinness of its legs it is said to differ from common crickets. From this we understand (if we wish the explanation of **Matthiolus** to stand) that there are two kinds of crickets: namely, German and Etruscan, both domestic but differing in their legs and backs. We have another kind from the fields, which we call <term>Feldenheimen</term> <note>field crickets</note>, although to some they do not seem to differ in species from the domestic ones, since they are believed to migrate into houses as winter approaches, or to perish, unless one chooses to believe they hide or <term>hibernate</term> <note>original Greek: *φωλεύειν* (phōleuein); to lurk in a den or hibernate</note>. But since **Matthiolus** writes these things, are crickets therefore <term>beetles</term> <note>original Greek: *σίλφαι* (silphai); often used for cockroaches or carrion beetles</note> or the *blattae* of **Dioscorides**? The word *blatta* is indeed a homonym <note>a word with multiple meanings</note>: for sometimes it is a moth that eats skins and clothes; sometimes a small worm eating papers and books; occasionally a small creature born in beehives, which **Aristotle** writes is winged; sometimes it refers to purple dye, or a silkworm; and indeed a black beast similar to beetles or crickets. Nevertheless, because [he] cites **Pliny**...

...the *Commentator* <note>Likely referring to Pietro Andrea Mattioli (Matthiolus), a famous 16th-century commentator on Dioscorides</note> cites, and since it pleased you to record a certain history of this matter, let us seek what is truly consistent with the facts. *It is clear, however, from Book 29, Chapter 6,* <note>Pliny the Elder’s *Natural History*</note> that the cricket is one thing, and the cockroach is another. Indeed, he writes distinctly about each: *The cricket,* he says, *is beneficial for the ears when dug out with its own earth and applied as an ointment; they are hunted by using ants tied to a hair, etc.* <note>original: "Auribus, inquit, prodest gryllus..."</note> *Regarding cockroaches, however, after interposing a medicine made from the tunics of chicken stomachs,* he relates those things which you can easily read there. It will seem, therefore, that *Matthiolus* correctly adapted Pliny’s cockroaches to those of Dioscorides. But in *Book 11, Chapter 28,* another Plinian genus of crickets, which he says is called the *muloikon* <note>original: μυλοῖκον; Greek for "mill-dweller"</note> (or *mulikon, mulabrin, mulakrin*, because it feeds on the flour of mills), is actually Dioscorides' cockroach according to the description. The first kind was the "soft cockroach"; the third was the *silphe bdelyssa* <note>original: σίλφη βδελυσσα; Greek for "stinking beetle" or "stinking cockroach"</note>. You would see no crickets here. *But in Book 11, Chapter 28,* he says, *the cockroach is a child of darkness, fleeing the light and life; it is born in baths especially from the moist vapor.* This is that Tuscan cockroach of Matthiolus, and since it is frequent in our baths and bakeries and loves the darkness, what prevents us from saying that the cricket was also sometimes called a cockroach, so that in some way *Matthiolus* did not wander from the truth? These seem to be the very cockroaches which he writes in *Book 20, Chapter 16* are gathered by the herb fleabane; and in *Book 25, Chapter 9* are called

<column-break/>

*Blattaria* <note>Moth Mullein, an herb traditionally used to repel cockroaches (Blattae)</note>: although I once heard the physician *Abraham Werner* recounting that it happened to him that he placed bread in his hat, in which on the following day he found about 16 crickets gathered. He even carried them into the church <note>original: *templum*</note> with the hat placed on his head, and finally, having noticed his "guests" after he had returned home, he drove them out. He had realized they were in his hat from the noise and from one of them flying out during the sacred rite. There is another passage in the same author <note>Pliny</note> in *Book 11, Chapter 28* concerning <term>beetles</term> <note>original: *scarabæis*</note>, out of which he relates that some excavate hearths and meadows with frequent holes, and are vocal with a nocturnal chirping. There are those who have compared crickets to beetles. 

Therefore, when *Pliny* collected histories from various authors, did he not notice that he was speaking of crickets under the name of beetles? Certainly, both kinds seem to be distributed, namely the field variety as well as the domestic one, unless it must be said that this cockroach is similar to the *Cantharus* beetle, which itself can be a cricket. You think that he designates the same creatures by the name of *Tryxalides*: because in *Book 29, Chapter 6* he reports on the authority of Nigidius <note>Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar and occultist</note> that crickets are of great authority; even greater in the judgment of the <term>magi</term> <note>Ancient Persian priests or sorcerers</note>, since they walk backward, bore into the earth, and chirp at night. And again in *Book 30, Chapter 3*, he says it is an animal similar to a locust, without wings, which is called *Tryxalis* in Greek, and in Latin...

<summary>This page features a scholarly debate on the classification of crickets and cockroaches, citing Pliny the Elder and the physician Abraham Werner to distinguish between these nocturnal insects and their medicinal or superstitious uses.</summary>

# MEDICAL LETTERS BOOK II. SECTION VI.

...though it may not have a name, some judge it to be that which is called a **Cricket** <note>Latin: *Gryllus*</note>. The discovery of the name itself supports this. For "to chirp" <note>Greek: γρυλλίζειν (*gryllizein*)</note> and "to trill" <note>Greek: τριλλίζειν (*trillyzein*)</note> are both terms used by the Greeks for what the Latins call chirping at night, moaning, or grunting. However, since the *Tryxalis* is written to be similar to a locust and to lack wings, it should be considered Dioscorides’ *Asiracon* or *Onon* <note>Greek names for types of wingless insects</note>, which he discusses in his history of the locust; although I would not deny that this beast also chirps at night, and thus has acquired the common name of "cricket." What if the naming of the cricket *generally* <note>Greek: γενικῶς (*genikos*)</note> signifies an insect that chirps at night, flees the light, and lives in the hollows of the earth? Our cricket would thus be a species from the generic class of crickets. You now have the history of the name and the species. Now let us find its **power** <note>Greek: δύναμιν (*dynamin*)</note> in healing or harming. I easily agree with the writer who says that the powder of crickets applied to a **aching tooth** <term>Odontalgia: a common term for toothache in early modern medicine</term> with cotton wool <note>Latin: *lana xylina*</note> settles the pain. This is a quality held in common with many venomous things, such as the lizard, the frog, the *calamitide* <note>A type of green tree-frog</note>, and so on. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note> rubs crickets on the throat and tonsils, and in this way restrains "distillations" <note>The dripping of excess fluids or mucus</note> and roughness. If the *Tryxalis* is one thing and the cricket another, then your argument falls regarding the promotion of cleansing for women after childbirth by applying the ash of *Tryxalids* with honey; although we are not ignorant of the fact that different things can have different uses or modes of action.

<column-break/>

Crickets must possess a great **dispersive power**, or perhaps a **leaping** <note>Greek: σαλτικήν (*saltiken*)</note> or **Gorgonian** <term>Gorgonean: refers to the power of the mythical Gorgon to paralyze or turn to stone; here used to describe the power to instantly halt the flow of bodily fluids</term> power, since they stop the "spirits" <note>The vital forces thought to move through the body</note> so promptly and bind the humors, preventing them from flowing. They are of no less potency than the **mullet fish**, which neutralizes the venom of the **Torpedo** <note>An electric ray known to numb its prey</note>, or **aconite** <note>Wolfsbane, a highly toxic plant</note>, which makes the **scorpion** torpid; or the **Hazel** <note>Latin: *Corylum*</note>, by which serpents and vipers are restrained; or the **Yew** <note>Latin: *taxum*</note> against snakes, and so on. If it were some kind of cockroach, I do not know whether an arsenical and corrosive poison should be attributed to it, such as is found in the **buprestis** <note>A beetle known to be toxic to cattle</note>. For if the **stinking cockroach** <note>Greek: σίλφη βδέλυσσα (*silphe bdelyssa*)</note> is missing, then according to **Aëtius** <note>A 6th-century Greek medical writer</note>, the *buprestis* must be used, whose **erosive or putrefying power** <note>Greek: ἡ σηπτική δύναμις (*he septike dynamis*)</note> is not unknown. This same principle restrains malignant <note>Latin: *cacoëthe*</note> and leprotic ulcers, so that it may now creep into the family of the *tryxalids*. But since experience has shown that the blood does not only stop flowing during **scarification** <term>Scarification: the practice of making small cuts in the skin for medical purposes, often to draw out "bad" blood</term> when the blood-letting knife or scalpel is smeared with the venom or fluid <note>Latin: *sanie*</note> of crickets, but that ulcers have also broken out; consider whether the whole of nature is not opposed to the blood of life, and either chokes or changes the spirit and native heat in the blood with its own poison. Once these are dissipated or changed, the cessation of flow follows naturally, and **putrefaction** follows as its companion. Indeed, when the fluid enters more deeply—as in the bite of a rabid dog or a scorpion—corruption arises in other places as well. In this way, you might say that crickets are **septic** <note>causing rot or infection</note>, because...

### ON MALICIOUS SCARIFICATION.
<sig>Nnn 3</sig>

<margin>The theory of introduced putrefaction.</margin>
They destroy the native heat in the blood and cast it down from its proper form, inducing **putrefaction** <note>In Galenic medicine, putrefaction was the breakdown of the body’s humors when the "native heat" or vital energy could no longer maintain their balance.</note>, which you know occurs with the extinction or calling forth of the native heat and the corruption of the substance. This happens when the bond of the mixture is dissolved because moisture dominates over dryness, and the spirits and remaining heat are utterly suffocated. But enough of this "chirping" <note>original: *gryllizatum*—a pun on the Greek *gryllizein*, "to chirp like a cricket," used here to mean "enough of talking about crickets."</note>. For I do not wish to dispute whether crickets are hot or cold, or if they are narcotic and opiate because they lack blood. It is enough that they are effective as an argument for an adverse disposition and **occult qualities** <term>Occult qualities: properties of a substance that cannot be explained by the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) and are only known through experience.</term>. Anyone who denies these qualities suffers from the same folly as **Erastus** <note>Thomas Erastus (1524–1583), a Swiss physician known for his opposition to Paracelsian alchemy and his belief that all medicine should be explained through manifest physical qualities.</note> once did; he thinks he can understand the "forms" of things while ignoring the most evident experiments, which cannot be explained by primary or secondary manifest qualities.

It seems to you, not without reason, that Puthmann's medicine is metallic. Indeed, such a remedy—which suppresses ulcers of that kind and removes their "lips" <note>The raised, hardened edges of a chronic ulcer.</note>—is prepared from **sublimated mercury** <term>Hydrargyrum sublimatum: also known as corrosive sublimate (mercury II chloride), a highly toxic but powerful caustic used in early surgery.</term> through distillation or by letting it dissolve into a liquid. There is another made from **butter of arsenic** <note>Arsenic trichloride, a heavy, oily liquid.</note>, though it causes the most bitter pain unless it has been corrected by a peculiar art. Others are made from **Litharge** <note>Lead oxide</note>, **Realgar** <note>Arsenic sulfide</note>, **Antimony**, etc. What if he had applied mercury, "killed" <note>original: *mortificatum*—in alchemy, to "kill" a metal meant to change its form or neutralize its metallic nature, often using an acid.</note> by **spirit of vitriol** <note>Sulfuric acid</note>, in the form of an ointment? A **Cancer** <note>In this period, "cancer" referred generally to any persistent, spreading, and "eating" ulcer or tumor.</note> neutralized by arsenic is easily healed, even by a wash of herbs (agrimony and others) alone. A "defensive" against

<column-break/>

pain is a solution of **sulfur**, which is also curative. In diseases of this kind,

<margin>Dissolved sulfur with Mercury for cancer.</margin>
we dissolve sulfur in **spirit of turpentine**, and into the solution we sometimes drop boiling mercury; or we join it with the liquid reduced from the sublimate. It becomes a noble medicine. Those who flee the labor and danger instead boil the sulfur together with arsenic or sublimated mercury, and by the same effort, the medicine is produced, etc. Farewell.
Rothenburg, March 2, Year 1603.

### MEDICAL EPISTLES BOOK II. SECTION VI.

...a certain contagious epidemic, by which more than 70 people have already been infected. The symptoms are plainly the same as those of the **Moravian Disease** <note>original: *Luis Moravicæ*; a historical outbreak of syphilis or a similar treponemal disease described in Moravia in the 16th century</note>, formerly described by **Thomas Jordanus** <note>A famous 16th-century physician who wrote about the epidemics in Moravia</note>. For everyone contracted this evil from **scarification** <term>Scarification: the medical practice of making small incisions in the skin to draw blood</term>, with livid, broad, crusty, and corrosive pustules first arising in the spots where the **cupping glasses** <note>original: *cucurbitularum*; heated glass vessels placed over incisions to create a vacuum and draw out blood</note> were placed. Some of these were painful, while others were painless. These are followed by a general exhaustion of the whole body, pains in the joints, nocturnal headaches, large **phagedenic ulcers** <term>Phagedenic: from the Greek for "to eat"; ulcers that spread rapidly and "eat away" at the surrounding flesh</term>, **gummata** <note>soft, non-cancerous growths typical of late-stage syphilis</note>, **bone-aching pains** <note>original Greek: *ὀϛεοκόποι* (osteokopoi); deep, drilling pains in the bones</note>, small tumors, and inflammations and ulcerations of the mouth; in short, almost everything that usually accompanies the **French Disease** <note>original: *morbum Gallicum*; a common historical name for syphilis</note>. When I was asked by our Senate what the cause of this evil might be, I affirmed it was a contagion spread through contact and **fomites** <term>Fomites: inanimate objects (like clothing or tools) that can carry and transfer infection</term>. This is because, besides those who underwent scarification, no one else was infected—only those who had blood drawn in the same bathhouse, or who had used the services of that specific **bath-keeper** <note>original: *balneatoris*; in this era, bath-house attendants often performed minor surgeries, bloodletting, and tooth pulling</note>. In the other bathhouse, however, no one was infected. For a scalpel, just like other weapons and blades, can be maliciously poisoned so that as soon as it touches the blood, it immediately communicates a venomous quality to it; or rather [since I believe such an inhuman crime would not occur to anyone], when the bath-keeper passed from an infected person to a healthy one and wounded them with the same scalpel, which was still fouled with the virulent stain, that person’s blood

<column-break/>

was corrupted through contagion. Once that blood was corrupted, it could then infect others, with the contagion creeping along in this way infinitely. Furthermore, it is likely that the "seed" of the contagion lurks for a long time in the cupping glasses, the sponges, and the leather straps used to sharpen the scalpels; it causes harm a long time later, only after it is moved and agitated by heat. As for the fact that others attribute the cause to either divine wrath, the stars, or the intemperance of men, these seem to me to be either too general or entirely irrelevant. Truly, I cannot wonder enough that a large part of the infected trust themselves to the faith and care of the very bath-keeper [who infected them]; they expect a remedy from him as if from the very rabid dog or scorpion that bit them, or they commit themselves to **surgeons** or **empirics** <note>Empirics were practitioners without formal university training, often viewed with suspicion by "rational" physicians</note>. Indeed, I have only a few patients so far who use my services and advice, as the rest spurn **rational medicine** <term>Rational medicine: an approach based on logic, theory, and the study of causes, rather than just repeating traditional folk remedies</term> either out of a stupor of the mind or the common error of the masses. However, if I observe anything unique, whether in the cure or the symptoms, I will note it down diligently. Thus far writes Dr. Boxbarter, my singular and old friend. With this, farewell and may you be most happy, most Eminent Sir, and permit me to remain commended to you. Given at **Isny** <note>A town in southeastern Germany</note>, the 10th day before the Calends of April <note>March 23</note>, in the year 1624.

### To the most Distinguished and Excellent Man,

# Mr. MARCUS WIDEMANN, Doctor of Medicine and Official Physician of the Imperial Republic of Isny.

### GREGOR HORSTIUS, Doctor [sends greetings].

<margin>
See Part 2, observation book 2, observation 8.
</margin>
Greetings. While in these wintry days <note>original: *brumalibus hifce diebus*</note> I was attempting to dispel the boredom of the longest nights by selecting the letters of learned men—so that I might finally satisfy the expectations of many with the promised second part of my *Observations and Epistles*—I happened upon your letter, Most Distinguished Man, among others you sent, in which you report a case of malicious scarification <term>Scarification: the practice of making small incisions in the skin to draw blood for therapeutic purposes</term>. What happened once in *Moravia* is known to you from the writings of *Jordanus* <note>Thomas Jordanus (1539–1585), a physician who famously described a syphilis-like epidemic in Moravia spread by shared cupping equipment</note>; what occurred in *Franconia* in our own times is evident from the handwritten letters of *Libavius* and *Snizer*, which I share here for your reading. From those matters concerning the venereal plague <note>original: *lue venerea*; syphilis</note> which will be made public in the second part of my *Observations*, you will find a remarkable case history of a certain weaver, who in the year 1622,

<column-break/>

soon after I had been called to this place, visited me for a consultation. He complained of fixed and very intense nocturnal pains in the joints, for which I prescribed various medicines in vain, until finally in the following year a **tophus** <term>Tophus: a hard, bony outgrowth or swelling, in this case appearing on the shin-bone, typical of advanced syphilis</term> manifested on his shin, preceded and accompanied by the greatest pain. But once the malignancy of the plague was recognized, I investigated the cause and origin of the evil more deeply. The patient reported that he had undergone scarification in a public bathhouse (prior to which he had never complained of any ailment since his early youth); shortly after this was done, the scarified area became corrupted with foul ulcers. The **bath-keeper** <note>original: *Balneator*; bath-keepers in this era functioned as "minor surgeons," performing bloodletting, cupping, and tooth extractions</note>, realizing what had happened and fearing infamy and the ruin of his business, commanded the man to stay silent. He treated the ulcerated part with external ointments and gradually closed the wounds. However, because the infectious matter was driven back toward the interior of the body in this way <note>The author refers to "repercussion," a medical theory where external symptoms are suppressed, forcing the disease deeper into the organs</note>, the plague immediately took root within. It manifested first as fixed nocturnal pains, and later as painful bony swellings along with other signs, so that he could not be restored to health by any means other than the specific treatment for the **French Disease** <note>original: *morbi Gallici*; a common historical name for syphilis</note>, as will be revealed at greater length in my *Observations*. I can easily believe that this infection followed without malice, but rather by chance—perhaps because the scarification instruments had been used unknowingly on someone already infected. However, it does not seem likely,

->To the most Distinguished and Excellent Man,<-

### MARCUS WIDEMANN, Doctor of Medicine and Physician of the Imperial Republic of Isny,

### SENDS MANY GREETINGS TO GREGOR HORSTIUS, DOCTOR.

It was a great pleasure for me, Most Distinguished and Excellent Man, Patron and Friend to be honored with all respect, to read both what you wrote to me and what you shared from the letters of Mr. Libavius and Mr. Schnizer <note>Andreas Libavius and likely Georg Schnizer, contemporary physicians</note>. It is truly remarkable that the same disease sprouted in such widely separated places with almost the same method of invasion, just as the *Brünn-French disease* <note>original: *Brunnogallicus morbus*; a regional name for an outbreak of syphilis in Brno</note> was first seen in Moravia and described long ago by Mr. Thomas Jordanus. For all those mentioned by Jordanus, yourself, Schnizer, and Boxbarter, began to be afflicted by a 

<column-break/>

similar plague after they had undergone scarification <term>Scarification: the practice of making shallow incisions in the skin, often as part of "cupping" to draw out "bad blood"</term>. The primary symptoms of this ailment were these: malignant and foul pustules and ulcers, first erupting in the scarified places and afterwards spreading to the entire condition of the body; violent, fixed pains in the joints, worsening especially at night; a weariness and weakness of those same limbs; and many other symptoms that usually follow the *Venereal Plague* <note>original: *Luem Veneream*; syphilis</note>. Beyond the listed symptoms, it is proven that this evil was related to that Plague because it could not be eradicated by any means other than the specific treatment for the *Venereal Plague*, as can be seen from your letters and Schnizer's. Jordanus himself agrees, placing the cure for this entire evil in the provocation of sweat <note>A common 17th-century treatment for syphilis involving "sweat boxes" and guaiacum wood</note>, as does Crato in Book 2 of his *Medical Epistles*. Regarding Boxbarter's method, I have nothing to say, as he departed this life two years ago, and therefore I have not been able to learn how he treated his patients. Investigating the origin of these infections (excepting the one recounted by Mr. Schnizer), this cause presents itself to me: namely, that the lancets <note>original: *scalpella*</note> which those bath-attendants <note>original: *balneatores*</note> used for scarification were infected with blood, fluid <note>original: *ichore*</note>, or the vapor of someone suffering from the "French disease," from whom they first drew blood through scarification, and then transferred it to others by performing the same service.

This is clearly gathered, I believe, from the fact that all these people were initially healthy, as many...

<meta>catchword: as many (quot-)</meta>

<summary>In this correspondence, Marcus Widemann confirms Gregor Horstius's observations that syphilis was being spread in public bathhouses via contaminated bloodletting tools. He notes that the symptoms and the effectiveness of "sweat cures" prove the disease is identical to the "Venereal Plague" (syphilis).</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the letter from Marcus Widemann to Gregor Horstius. # ON MALICIOUS SCARIFICATION.

...whoever used these scarifications <term>Scarification: the practice of making shallow incisions in the skin, usually as part of a bloodletting or cupping treatment</term>, immediately or soon after, began to suffer first those ulcers in the scarified areas, and then, as time passed, the rest of the symptoms. Meanwhile, those who abstained from scarification remained in their former health. It is worth noting, however, that in the case of the weaver from Ulm, the sickness remained confined to him alone and did not invade others who had entered the same bath and—without a doubt—had also undergone scarification. Yet in Brünn <note>Modern-day Brno, Czech Republic</note> and Windsheim, all those (and there were many) who were scarified in those baths were equally infected. I suspect the same was true for those whom Dr. Schnizer describes, though in his own way.

It is also worth considering that the *Brünn-French disease* <note>original: *Lues Brunnogallica*; a regional name for an outbreak of syphilis</note> lasted from the winter solstice until the spring equinox, while the others had no fixed duration. It will be a pleasure for me, if I live, to see what you yourself record on this matter in the second part of your *Observations and Epistles*; there I shall learn the true causes of all these events, which are well worth our observation. The infection mentioned by Dr. Schnizer was clearly malicious, as was shown by the bathhouse keeper's confession. However, whether the outbreaks in Brünn and Windsheim arose from the malice of the bathkeepers is still doubtful, because in Brünn, after a diligent investigation by the Magistrate, Adam the bathkeeper was found

<column-break/>

innocent, and in Windsheim not even a suspicion of poisoning arose. But were many infected all at once? I believe this could happen because many people were scarified one after another with the same bloodletting knife <term>original: *phlebetomus*; a lancet or tool used to open veins</term> or blade. Thus, they contracted this evil from the same source <term>original: *fomes*; literally "tinder," used here to mean a source or carrier of infection</term>, with the plague spreading itself among many.

Whatever the case may be—whether it arose from intentional poisoning or from the contagion of a scalpel infected with poisonous fluid <term>original: *ichore venenato*; a thin, watery discharge from a wound or ulcer thought to carry disease</term>—the essence and symptoms seem to have been the same. It could be defeated by the same treatment used for the French disease <note>Syphilis</note>, as I hinted at above. And these are the things, Most Distinguished Man, that I have been able to write back to you in haste on this matter. If they meet your approval, I shall feel my labor was worthwhile; if not, let them be a sign of my readiness of mind. Farewell. 

As this year draws to a close, I pray from my heart that the next begins with happy omens for you, proceeds more happily, ends most happily, and returns ever more fortunately. I hope all that you have under your hands [just as you have published previous works for the benefit of the Medical Republic <note>A common term for the international community of physicians and scholars</note> thus far] comes forth successfully. I do not doubt that you will find great favor both with those living now and with all posterity—a prophecy you have read in my other letters which I hope is not in vain.

Given at Isny, December 17, in the year
->1627.<-

### CASE,
->Presented regarding a disposition toward dropsy of the womb:<-
->By the Most Illustrious Man,<-

## MARCUS WOLFFHARD, DOCTOR OF MEDICINE
## and Physician of the People of Biberach.

In the case of a most honorable Virgin, N.N. <note>A placeholder for an anonymous name</note>, I do not yet find what is properly called a dropsy <term>Dropsy: an old medical term for edema or the swelling caused by excess fluid in body tissues</term>. Specifically, I do not see it arising from the three usual types: the liver or the spleen—along with the mesenteric vessels <term>Mesaraic: relating to the mesentery, the membrane attaching the intestines to the abdominal wall</term>—being disposed toward a habitual coldness, or being obstructed, or being hindered by a scirrhus <term>Scirrhus: a hard, cancerous or fibrous tumor</term>, another tumor, or an abscess; for the pathognomonic <term>Pathognomonic: a symptom specifically characteristic of a particular disease</term> signs of all these are absent. However, for nearly the space of a year and beyond, the lower belly gradually began to swell, so that now

<column-break/>

the whole abdomen is raised like a drum <note>original: *instar tympani*; this refers to tympanites, where the abdomen is distended by gas</note>, due to an inflation of the womb and the adjacent parts, and now perhaps also due to a dropsy of the womb. This tumor took its origin shortly after the cessation of menstrual evacuations in a subject fifty years of age, caused by a retained cacochymia <term>Cacochymia: a disordered or unhealthy state of the body's humors or fluids</term>, and a collection and dregs of viscous, thick, and phlegmatic humors. The womb has been chilled and filled with a mucous and varied collection of waste, just as previously from the poorly dispo-

<header>CONCERNING THE INFLATION AND DROPSY OF THE WOMB.</header>
<sig>O oo 2</sig>

...appeared clearly arranged.
<margin>Similar observation</margin>
We saw a similar condition in our Hospital a few years ago in a fifty-year-old Virgin suffering from *cacochymia* <term>Cacochymia: an unhealthy state of the body's humors or fluids, often leading to a breakdown in health</term>, with a subsequent dropsy of the womb, which lasted for three years. In that case, more than once, due to the absence of the characteristic signs <note>original: *pathognomicorum Signorum*</note>, different physicians suspected different things. Finally, after her death, when the body was dissected, not only was the womb found to be filled with blisters full of water, but in the abdomen itself, a foul, bloody, and somewhat purulent discharge <note>original: *saniosa colluvies*</note> amounting to several pints <term>Hemina: a liquid measure approximately equal to half a pint</term> was discovered. From this, it seems the aforementioned Virgin's condition should be attributed to an inflation of the womb, which could easily progress—if proper remedies are neglected—into dropsy of the womb, and eventually, through the involvement of the entire system, into a true dropsy. However, although after a general cleansing of the body (since the subject is cacochymic and filled with phlegmatic waste <note>original: *pituitosâ saburrâ*</note>), carminative <term>Carminative: a medication intended to expel gas from the body</term> and cleansing enemas would be very appropriate; nonetheless, since the patient shrinks back from this remedy due to a vain and false persuasion of ours, in its place, boluses and pills made from properly prepared and washed turpentine could be prescribed. These should be combined with carminatives and medicines specifically for the womb <note>original: *matricalibus*</note>, along with internal strengthening, cleansing, and opening uterine remedies. Indeed, local treatments could also be directed at the gas in the womb, specifically through the use of medicinal hip-baths <term>Insessiones: medicinal baths where the patient sits in a decoction of herbs</term>, fomentations—

<column-break/>

—ointments, and so on. Just as such things have been used with success following the general measures mentioned previously. Finally, a decoction of Sassafras could be prescribed with opening, warming, and carminative womb-medicines in wine, or at the very least, a medicated wine of that sort. While submitting these matters to the judgment of others, I will not be burdened to record specific instructions on what must be done. I have chosen to outline these few things in summary <note>original: *ὡς ἐν τύπῳ* (hōs en typō)</note>, at least to satisfy the request. Written in haste from the Library at Biberach, the last day of September, in the Year 1623.

...to strive toward this goal, so that you might be of service through your many labors, especially in that place where the love of neighbor requires it most. Now that the opportunity has arisen, at the request of Mr. Strauss, I did not want to miss the chance to send these brief remarks to you, both for the sake of fostering our friendship and to satisfy that good man and his wife. I ask most earnestly that you interpret this piece of boldness, such as it is, in the best light.

A case is presented of a certain honorable maiden, regarding whom I hear that last year my advice was also sought—though, as often happens, through a certain old woman and with the patient's name suppressed. (I no longer recall her name, since such things frequently happen, as you know, especially in these populous republics). You have determined that she is suffering not from a true "dropsy" <term>Dropsy: An archaic term for edema, or the abnormal accumulation of fluid in the body's tissues or cavities</term>—of which three species are commonly listed—but rather from an inflation of the womb and adjacent parts, or perhaps even a uterine dropsy. You take your argument from the origin of the affliction: that such swelling began after the cessation of the monthly cycles in a fifty-year-old subject, with the abdomen first increasing in the lower part—which is also noted by *Varandæus* <note>Jean de Varanda (1563–1617), a famous French physician and professor at Montpellier</note> as a sign of incipient uterine dropsy. You identify the preceding cause as a chilled womb, along with *cacochymia* <term>Cacochymia: An imbalance of the body's vital fluids or "humors," believed to cause various diseases</term> and a collection of viscous and phlegmatic humors. You were perhaps led to this conclusion

<column-break/>

not only by considering the nature of the patient, but also, as is added, by the fact that her menstrual cycles were previously poorly regulated. You include for me a most welcome medical history of a fifty-year-old maiden who suffered from uterine dropsy for three years in your hospital <note>original: *Nosocomio*</note>. Her affliction—hardly discernible due to other concurrent signs of unhealthy humors—was sufficiently demonstrated by the autopsy <note>original: *sectio post mortem*</note>.

A similar unique case comes to mind, which the celebrated Physician and Surgeon *Wilhelm Fabricius* <note>Wilhelm Fabricius Hildanus (1560–1634), often called the "Father of German Surgery"</note> wrote to me about in previous years. He described a certain woman whose belly swelled like that of a pregnant woman; her feet subsequently developed a hard swelling that left no pits when pressed. Upon her death, her liver and spleen were found healthy, but the lung was found half-rotted. The removed, swollen womb weighed eighty-seven merchant pounds and was filled partly with a yellow *ichor* <term>Ichor: A thin, watery, or blood-stained discharge from a wound or sore</term> and partly with fatty and oily matter. It is truly remarkable, as *Fabricius* further adds, that in the middle of the womb, along with the aforementioned matter, thick hairs like soft, yellowish wool were found <note>This description suggests what modern medicine calls a "teratoma" or "dermoid cyst," which can contain hair, teeth, or fat</note>. I still have with me a small specimen of this hair that was sent to me. You will see more on this in my response, soon to be published—with God's help <note>original: *σὺν Θεῷ* (syn Theo)</note>—in his *Fifth Century* <note>Referring to "Centuriae," a common way of organizing medical case observations into groups of one hundred</note>. ### ON THE INFLATION AND DROPSY OF THE WOMB.
Ooo 3
<meta>catchword: by the youth</meta>

we are not able to conclude with exactness from external signs those things which nature at play <note>original: "ludens natura"; a common phrase describing nature producing strange or anomalous phenomena</note> (as if abnormally) <note>original: "quasi p. n." (praeter naturam); meaning "contrary to nature"</note> frequently produces in our bodies. This is clear enough from the tumor of the omentum <term>Omentum: A fold of fatty tissue that hangs like an apron over the intestines</term> which, about 16 years ago, deceived many most excellent physicians until, finally, after death, it was found to weigh fifty-six pounds. This is just as we testified publicly several years ago in our "Medical Problems," adding the letters of the celebrated Bauhin and Fabricius <note>Caspar Bauhin (1560–1624) and likely Wilhelm Fabricius Hildanus (1560–1634), two of the most famous medical authorities of the era</note>.

But I return to the present matter, namely your patient. You rightly advise, after a universal cleansing <note>referring to the standard practice of purging the body's humors</note>, enemas to dispel wind, and in their place you substitute pills and boluses made of properly prepared and washed turpentine <note>original: "Terebinthinâ"</note>, combined with carminatives <term>Carminatives: Herbs or medicines used to prevent or expel gas from the gastrointestinal tract</term> and medicines specifically for the womb. You judge that these means should be repeated frequently, while not neglecting internal strengthening remedies in the meantime. Among these, I would judge the *Elixir of Properties* <term>Elixir Proprietatis: A famous alchemical remedy popularized by Paracelsus, made from Saffron, Myrrh, and Aloe, used as a tonic and to regulate the body's systems</term> to be particularly suitable, if properly prepared and administered daily in several drops within syrups or appropriate waters. Meanwhile, a suitable diet should be established along with the other general indications, the determination of all of which is provided by the present condition of the suffering subject. Furthermore, since I see that your Distinguished Self proposes only the common species of dropsy as a foundation, I would gladly expect, through a good

<column-break/>

opportunity in the time to follow, a response to those arguments which I proposed more than a decade ago in the *Additaments of Marcellus Donatus* <note>Marcellus Donatus (1538–1602), a physician who wrote on rare medical cases; the author is referring to his own supplementary notes to that work</note> against the common opinion of the Doctors, and which I also touched upon briefly in my "Therapeutic Problems." In the meantime, I commend your Distinguished Self to God, the Best and Greatest. Written in haste at Ulm, October 15, 1623.

### MEDICAL EPISTLES, BOOK II, SECTION VII.

I also derive greater certainty from the report of the assistant <note>original: "à Juvante"; referring to the medical assistant or practitioner attending the patient</note>.

You know what I advised in the sent note regarding the use of turpentine <note>original: "Terebinthina"; often used in this period as a stimulant and to purge the "humors"</note>. When I made a trial of it, I was not at all disappointed in my hope; it expelled a remarkable amount of wind <note>original: "flatuum"; intestinal or uterine gas</note> together with thick and sticky mucus, resulting in a great relief of the patient’s strength. There even followed a slight reduction in the swelling of the lower abdomen <note>original: "suminis detumescentiâ"</note>, which, however, seems to have returned shortly thereafter. Thus, it is to be suspected that the affected parts, not yet sufficiently cleansed of that mucous, thick, and phlegmatic clutter <note>original: "Colluvie"</note>, are drawing more trouble to themselves. Once this is addressed, I certainly do not doubt that the use of turpentine will thereafter be more convenient, successful, and safer.

Therefore, I would consider a Medicated Wine, prepared with a modest hand for household use, which might sweep out and wash away the waste from both the digestive and genital parts through a gradual treatment <term>Epicrasis: A medical method of gradually evacuating or altering body humors rather than a violent purging</term>. To this, I would perhaps add larch fungus <note>original: "agaricum"</note>, mechoacan <note>original: "mechoacam"; a purgative root from the Americas</note>, and other things that modestly draw away phlegm, and perhaps even some pithy safflower <note>original: "carthamum"</note>, adding penetrating and gas-expelling <note>original: "carminantibus"</note> ingredients as a vehicle. In place of this, I would substitute the use of pills made from washed Cyprian Turpentine, properly prepared with its own corrective ingredients suited to our purpose, and I would order it to be kept as a familiar remedy.

I would even add an anointing of the pubic area and the lower abdomen to assist and promote 

<column-break/>

the use of the internal remedies; and by persisting in these, I would wait a while for a beneficial and desired end.

Committing these things to your Excellency's judgment, I wanted to outline them at least as a sketch <note>original: "ὡς ἐν τύπῳ" (hōs en typō)</note>, leaving them to be specifically polished by you. I would truly prefer all these things to be prepared in your own pharmacy <note>original: "officina"</note>, with you present and standing by, provided the sick woman herself agrees to our wish, which I indeed urge and advise.

As far as the prognosis is concerned, I suspect it is indeed ominous, and I find it to be such from various observations by the Classical authors. Your Excellency knows what **Dodoens**, **Mercado**, **Mercuriale**, **Altomare**, **Saxonia**, **Platter**, and others <note>A list of the most influential medical writers of the 16th and early 17th centuries</note> have proposed in cases of this kind: almost all with a doubtful and ominous outcome. In the meantime, let us do our part, committing what remains to the Highest Power.

I send at the same time a little gift of paper <note>likely a small book or manuscript</note>, which I ask you to look upon with favor; and I pray from my heart that you wish the friendship now begun through letters to be firmly joined in reality. You will certainly always find me most ready to serve you, and I hope for the health of you and yours. Farewell. Written in haste from my study on the Kalends of November <note>November 1st</note>,

->1623.<-

### ON THE INFLATION AND DROPSY OF THE WOMB.

->To the Most Distinguished and Excellent Gentleman,<-

->Lord MARCUS WOLFHARD, Doctor of Medicine and Physician of Biberach.<-

->GREGOR HORST sends greetings.<-

I rejoice, most Distinguished and Excellent man, my much-revered patron and friend, that my letters sent to you on occasion were pleasing to you, as is most clearly evidenced not only by your very kind response but also by the added gift of your writings. Please look with favor upon this slight return-gift <term>Antidoron: From the Greek, a reciprocal gift or a gift given in return</term> (since for the time being I have nothing else at hand from my published books). Furthermore, as far as the diseased state of your young patient <note>original: "Virginis"; typically referring to an unmarried young woman</note> is concerned, I subscribe entirely to your opinion: namely, that there is an inflation of the womb <note>original: "inflationem uteri"; bloating or gas within the uterus</note> tending toward a dropsy of the womb <note>original: "hydropem uteri"; an accumulation of serous fluid</note>. I do not doubt that this condition has been preceded by—and is still accompanied by—a sluggishness and weakness of the feet and the whole body, as well as a numb sensation around the pubic bone <note>original: "pectinem"</note>, the loins, and the legs. For this reason, in married women suffering from this disease, the appetite for Venus <note>referring to sexual desire</note> is rare or 

<column-break/>

non-existent, so that they find no pleasure at all in marital intercourse. There is a heaviness of the womb, like a sort of hanging burden, and the belly is cold to the touch; from this, perhaps, the menstrual cycles have also been watery, discolored, phlegmatic, mucousy, and irregular.

I subscribe to your prognosis without difficulty, especially since over such a long span of time a general imbalance of the whole system has gradually conspired—one that is not simple, but joined with an abundance of phlegm. Since this is long-standing, it must be corrected continuously <term>Dienekes: From the Greek, meaning "uninterruptedly" or "in a continuous manner"</term> as much as possible, both by evacuating and by altering agents. Once these have been sent in advance—as you correctly establish according to the beginning of the Medical Method—more appropriate remedies may be conveniently prescribed afterward.

<margin>The material of remedies.</margin>
Therefore, as far as the material of remedies is concerned, the sick woman must be advised above all else to observe a warming and drying diet. For this reason, she should avoid the Southern wind <note>In traditional medicine, the south wind was considered warm and moist, which was thought to aggravate "phlegmatic" or "dropsical" conditions</note>, underground places, or areas near stagnant water and putrid exhalations.

<margin>Dietetics.</margin>
Let her food be prepared more frequently from roasted meats than from boiled, where the meat of hare, mountain birds, roe deer, and similar animals will be most suitable.

But what is lacking in other nourishments may be compensated for by seasoning, where veal, mutton, beef, and similar meats are seasoned with aromatics: ginger, mace, nutmeg, cloves, and pepper; or with the seeds of anise, cumin, and fennel her- <note>The text breaks off here mid-word, likely "herbis" (herbs)</note>

He recommends a strict warming and drying diet, emphasizing roasted meats and specific spices to counteract the "cold" and "phlegmatic" nature of the illness.</summary>

...[diet], should be prepared with herbs such as Sage, Rosemary, Savory, Marjoram, Thyme, etc. This same rule should be observed with fish, which are to be provided with a sparing hand, and only those that are rock-dwelling <note>original: "saxatilibus"; fish that live among rocks were considered easier to digest and less "slimy" in Galenic medicine</note>. For drink, let there be wine of medium age and potency, since recent wines increase gas and indigestion <note>original: "cruditates"; literally "rawnesses," referring to undigested matter in the stomach</note>, while aged ones, being more noble, may overpower the natural strength. Let the wine be joined with a decoction made by gentle boiling of Sassafras, to which should be added some small raisins <note>original: "passularum minorum"; likely currants</note>, Galangal, Nutmeg, and Cloves. Physical exercise should not be entirely omitted, but should be done gradually so that the strength does not fail; or, in its place, let there be a rubbing of the upper parts of the body with rough cloths. Sleep should only be at night, three hours after dinner, and shorter than perhaps her nature is accustomed to. The bowels and urine should be encouraged daily, and the morning sweats that present themselves should not be hindered. The emotions of the mind should be more spirited, so that a light fit of anger <note>original: "excandescentia"; a warming of the spirits through mild irritation</note> will occasionally do no harm. To this end, I would also recommend the spirit of Elderberry <note>original: "spiritum Sambuci"</note> or Dwarf Elder, which in smaller quantities can be more easily taken several times with Elderberry flower water, Lemon balm water, and the like. We ensure this spirit is prepared every year in our pharmacies through suitable fermentation and digestion; if a supply is lacking, it can be provided. Take 3 drams of Socotrine Aloes, 1 scruple of best Myrrh, half a scruple each of extracts of Aromatic Sweet Flag and Blessed Thistle, 3 grains of Saffron extract, and 5 grains each of Gentian root, Long Birthwort, and Dittany. I have used half a dram of these frequently over several days with success in cases of impurity of the womb and obstruction of the menses arising from thick and phlegmatic humors. But if a "flooding" of the lower belly <note>referring to the accumulation of fluid or "dropsy"</note>—which you propose—should be preceded by a fomentation <note>a warm, moist medicinal compress</note> made from a decoction of Lemon balm, Mugwort, Wall germander, Betony, Sage, Oregano, Laurel leaves, Juniper berries, Laurel berries, Caraway seeds and the like, and followed by the wearing of the following plaster, I hope it will be of the greatest benefit.

<column-break/>

Take 1 dram each of Round Cyperus root, Aromatic Sweet Flag,
and Elecampane; half a dram of Lovage;
half a handful each of Lemon balm root, Water Germander,
and Pennyroyal;
half a dram of Mastic;
2 drams of Frankincense; 1 and a half drams of Myrrh;
1 dram of liquid Styrax;
half a dram of Tacamahaca <note>a fragrant resin from tropical trees</note>;
1 and a half drams of best Ladanum <note>resin from the rockrose bush</note>.
With Wax and Turpentine, make a Plaster.

Truly, I leave all these things to your distinguished judgment. May God, most high and greatest, grant that everything leads toward the restoration of the patient’s former health. Farewell, most distinguished Sir, and continue to hold me in your affection. From Ulm, in haste, on the day before the Calends of November, 1623.

### MEDICAL EPISTLES, BOOK II, SECTION VII: ON SWELLING AND DROPSY OF THE WOMB.

...on the Medical-Surgical Council, and recently he cured the cancerous left breast of a most honorable matron through an incision, with the best success, as I hear. There lives here with us—and lives miserably (I recall Problem 10 of the 6th Decade, published by you for the great benefit of the public and disputed by me in response)—an honorable wife with a tumor of the belly of such a kind that it seems to mimic tympanitis <note>original: "tympanitidem"; a condition where the abdomen is bloated with gas, sounding like a drum (tympanum) when tapped</note> for three years now. Indeed, no part of the tumor yields when pressed with the fingers, though it occupies the entire lower belly or the whole abdomen down to the pubic bone. *Lord Fabricius* <note>Likely the famous anatomist Hieronymus Fabricius ab Aquapendente</note> considered with me whether it was a tumor of the omentum <term>omentum: a fold of fatty tissue that hangs over the intestines</term>, or scirrhous <term>scirrhous: a term for a hard, fibrous, and often malignant growth</term> and hardened glands of the mesentery <term>mesentery: the membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</term>, given the great abundance of gas both within and outside the intestines. But since she is of an excellent physical disposition, with no cachexia <term>cachexia: physical wasting and malnutrition associated with chronic illness</term> but rather a plethora <term>plethora: an excess of bodily fluids, particularly blood</term>, being found with a healthy, ruddy complexion, we believe the cause of the illness must be referred to the womb. For never in her maiden years, nor—

<column-break/>

—in her first or this second marriage, except during her widowhood (and even then not regularly), has she labored with her monthly periods. But in the first year of her second marriage, the midwives judged at that time, based on some movement and swelling of the belly, that she had truly conceived; they were convinced of it then, though perhaps it was a false conception and a mole <term>mola: a mass of fleshy or gas-filled tissue in the uterus, sometimes mistaken for a fetus</term>. Various accounts of complicated gaseous and watery moles, with or without some appearance of dropsy <term>hydrops: an old term for edema or the accumulation of watery fluid in the body</term> of the womb itself—and indeed even of "living moles" mentioned in the authors, and among others in *your Donatus, and Schenck, Book 4 of Observations* <note>Refers to the medical compendiums of Marcello Donati and Johannes Schenck von Grafenberg</note>. But as to what should be concluded in this case of ours, as we greatly desire your expert judgment, I will perhaps provide more details and more accurately very soon. These things certainly in great haste. Farewell, most Distinguished Man, and mindful of our former most friendly favor, do not remain unmindful of helping Streitter’s career happily, wherever God may at some time will it. At Speyer, April 13, in the Year,
->1619.<-

# MEDICAL LETTERS.
## BOOK II. SECTION VIII.
### *On the*
# USE OF THE SETON IN THE PRE-
# VENTION OF APOPLE-
# XY. <note>original: "apoplexiæ"; a historical term for a stroke or sudden loss of consciousness</note>

->*Most Distinguished and Excellent Sir,*<-

# JOHANN JACOB SATTLER, DOCTOR OF MEDICINE AND
# Official Physician of Pfullendorf,

->*TO GREGOR HORST, Doctor and Chief Physician of Ulm.*<-

Most Noble and Distinguished Sir Doctor, the fame of your name, learning, and kindness is such that I do not hesitate to approach your Lordship through these writings, though I am unknown to you. I will, however, explain myself as briefly as I can, so as not to detain your Lordship, who is occupied with various matters of medical practice. The Reverend and Most Religious Lord Prelate N. N., my gracious Lord, being by nature melancholic <term>melancholic: in the humoral system, a temperament associated with black bile, often leading to sadness or anxiety</term> and hypochondriac, has for many years suffered various and severe fluxions <note>original: "fluxiones"; the movement of excess bodily fluids or "humors" to specific parts of the body</note> in his joints, from which

<column-break/>

issues <term>fonticuli: literally "little fountains"; small, artificially created ulcers kept open to drain "bad humors" from the body</term> were created in both arms, and on the outer <note>original: "sylvestri"; literally "wooded" or "wild," likely referring to the lateral or outer side of the foot</note> part of the left foot. Since these did not seem to be enough, a seton <term>seton: a thread or piece of fabric passed through a fold of skin to keep a wound open for continuous drainage</term> was recently employed; it was indeed applied skillfully and now flows copiously and widely. Meanwhile, some charlatan <note>original: "agyrta"; a wandering quack or unlicensed healer</note> or other has instilled a doubt, and threatens the danger of apoplexy from the use of this seton. Your Lordship undoubtedly knows the temperament of melancholics, who are easily frightened by any such idea. Furthermore, a certain empirical physician <note>original: "Empiricus"; a practitioner who relies on experience rather than formal theory, often used disparagingly by academic doctors</note> seems to want to agree with the charlatan, who [considers] the seton... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the catchword "tinus" suggests the next page continues with "protinus" (immediately)</note>

# MEDICAL LETTERS. BOOK II. SECTION VIII.

...[Querceta]tinus <note>Likely referring to Joseph Duchesne (Quercetanus), a famous 16th-century physician.</note> orders it to be discarded, but supports his opinion with no reasons, content with his own experience, which he himself proclaims—namely, that he has often used this kind of remedy but without benefit. Because of this, he condemns this remedy, which was so celebrated among the Ancients, universally and without any exception. These doubts, by which the Reverend Lord patient is distressed, provided the occasion for this writing. 

The question is, therefore: can a Seton <term>seton: a cord or thread passed through a fold of skin to create a "draining" wound, believed to draw out harmful fluids</term> in a body with a more humid brain promote apoplexy <note>original: "apoplexia"; a stroke or sudden loss of consciousness</note> (in a body already prepared for it), or can it rather prevent it? I am not unaware that your Lordship has already, in part, expressed your opinion; but because a charlatan and an untrained practitioner <note>original: "agyrta & Empiricus"; "empirics" were those who practiced based on experience alone without formal theoretical training, often used disparagingly by university physicians</note> have said the opposite, I will add my own opinion. I will do so briefly and submit it to your Lordship's more perceptive judgment, both so that, if the matter is handled well, the Reverend Lord patient may be freed from fear, and so that, if I have wandered from the mark, the error might be corrected from the beginning before it becomes more serious through delay. 

It is well known (since I am writing to a Physician) that apoplexy is the deprivation of sense and motion in the whole body, with injury to the functions of the sovereign soul. It is an affliction of the brain in which the ventricles of the brain are filled on all sides, so that they distend the passages entering the substance of the brain, easily causing a rupture of the tissue <note>original: "continui solutio"; a medical term for a break in the structural continuity of the body, such as a tear or lesion</note>, and the brain is not rarely damaged in its very substance (which was recently seen in a certain deceased Prince

<column-break/>

who, after a disease of no long duration, finally perished from apoplexy). I judge with others that it is not a true disease in itself, but a symptom that follows an obstruction in the pathways. Why I judge so is taught to me not only by the opinion of our Doctors, but also (if I may say so without arrogance) by autopsy <note>original: "αὐτοψία" (autopsia); meaning direct visual observation or dissection</note>. 

But through these means <insert>the seton</insert>, that obstruction is removed; therefore, the evil is not caused, but prevented. Furthermore, that obstruction is mostly caused by phlegmatic <note>original: "pituitosâ"</note> or melancholic matter; this is why the elderly are mostly subject to apoplexy. But once the cause is removed, the affliction is also taken away. Surely it cannot be taken away in a more convenient manner than by drawing out and evacuating that which is harmful from the nearest parts through suitable locations. 

The cold and autumnal constitutions of the air, in which apoplexies most greatly flourish, confirm this same opinion. Likewise, apoplexy is most frequent in cold and humid regions. Therefore, those things which most effectively draw out the phlegm <note>original: "pituita"; one of the four bodily humors, characterized as cold and moist</note>, such as cauteries <term>cauteries: here referring to "issues" or "fontanels," artificial sores kept open to drain humors</term>, especially in the nearest parts, can be beneficial and not harmful. In short, sluggish, thick, and cold phlegm is the chief cause of this evil, which abounds most in this brain. Can any remedy, therefore, be more excellently applied for the prevention of the evil? 

"In one suffering from head pain or pain all around, the discharge of serum <note>original: "sanies"; a thin, greenish or bloody discharge</note> or water flowing through the mouth or nostrils dissolves the sickness," says Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician of antiquity</note>. If the discharge or...
