# ON THE USE OF THE SETON.

[...It is well known (since I am writing to a physician) that] bloodletting cures apoplexy <note>original: "apoplexia"; a stroke or sudden loss of consciousness</note> [in which the head is undoubtedly always in pain]; why then should the Physician, as a servant of nature, not prevent the same disease in the same manner? I consider it more praiseworthy to act like that better Shipmaster <note>original: "Nauclerus"</note> who, foreseeing a storm in time, etc. And our elders, the Arabs <note>referring to medieval Islamic physicians like Avicenna, whose works were foundational to European medicine</note> especially, to whom we owe much, used these remedies successfully in both curing and preventing. I will make an end of this, so as not to detain your Lordship longer than I promised at the start, once I have added this one thing: that a headache which is neither continuous nor universal is not an indicator of some future evil, but is a consequence of a change in nature. Therefore, I judge that this remedy <term>seton: a thread or cord drawn through a flap of skin to create a continuous "discharge" of harmful humors</term> must be insisted upon by all means, as it is most convenient and safest, though painful. If your Lordship also subscribes to this opinion of mine, I shall rejoice to be praised by a man who is himself praised; but if you feel better or perhaps contrary things, I candidly ask, for the sake of our shared studies, that you bring them into the open. You will find me to be a hot-headed <note>original: "cerebrosum"; literally "brained," but used here to mean irascible or stubborn</note> antagonist, but a patient and certainly not ungrateful one. By these things, I wished to earn your Lordship’s goodwill and to place myself in the register of your friends, in whatever place. Farewell, most illustrious man, and regarding Apoplexy, if you deign to give me an answer, you shall hear my doubt: is it an affliction of the heart or rather of the brain? Farewell again. Given the 16th of October, in the year 1623.

<column-break/>

P. S. I ask that you forgive my rushing pen <note>original: "stylo currenti"</note>, which was scratched out around midnight, at which time necessity compelled me to prepare for my journey once again.

### MEDICAL EPISTLES, BOOK II, SECTION VIII.

I did not wish to fail in these matters, all of which I have gladly submitted to the refined judgment of the physicians present. Your Excellence's advice regarding the use of **mineral waters** <note>original: "acidularum," referring to naturally carbonated or medicinal springs</note> did not displease me, provided that the Most Reverend patient had more carefully observed a more suitable time—as I seriously urged—since otherwise there is little hope in such a remedy unless the condition of the surrounding air is favorable. At that time, the air was very much lacking in this regard, being partly northern and partly southern. Regarding the **seton** <term>seton: a surgical procedure where a thread or silk cord is drawn through a fold of skin to create a "running" wound, intended to drain away harmful fluids or humors</term> that was applied, I was informed not long ago by his Overseer. I congratulated the Most Reverend patient on this remedy, although it was painful during the first weeks. I am firmly convinced that there is hardly any more present **pain-reliever** <note>original Greek: "ἀνώδυνον" (anōdynon)</note> for a headache—caused by humors flowing from the **hypochondria** <note>the upper abdomen; in the humoral system, it was believed that "vapors" rose from here to the head</note> and now, through the long passage of time, rooted in the head—than this very thing, provided the Most Reverend patient patiently endures the discomforts of the seton until the suppuration is complete and it begins to flow freely enough. In passing, I quickly listed not just one, but several examples where the seton, applied by me for the most severe headaches arising from these flows, succeeded with great benefit.

However, I understand that a certain **charlatan** <note>original: "Agyrta," a traveling quack</note>, along with a certain **empiric** <note>an unlicensed practitioner who relies on experience alone without formal medical theory</note>, has instilled a doubt in the Most Reverend patient: that the application of a seton brings with it an imminent danger of **apoplexy** <note>a stroke or sudden loss of consciousness</note>. Because of this, Your Excellence is forced to

<column-break/>

propose this question for the sake of the Most Reverend patient: *Whether a stroke can be triggered by a seton in a body with a more moist brain.* To this, I respond not with "three words," as the saying goes, but with a single word: by **denying** it. Convinced by the truth of the matter, I deservedly subscribe to your opinion, especially since your added reasons not only firmly prove the negative but also demonstrate that this very remedy rather preserves one from such an evil.

<margin>What is apoplexy?</margin>
For first, it is correctly established that **apoplexy**—which is a loss of sensation and movement, along with injury to the primary faculties—arises from an organic disease of the brain. This is despite whatever **Giachini** <note>Leonardo Giachini, a 16th-century Italian physician</note> might say to the contrary in this matter; he, against the common assertion of the doctors, establishes that this symptom can also arise from a mere imbalance of temperaments. Hence, in our *Therapeutic Medical Problems* <note>original Greek: "Θεραπευτικοῖς" (Therapeutikois)</note>, we describe the evil as follows: because of this occurrence, men are suddenly struck down, with their primary functions, sensation, and movement abolished, though breathing remains in a way, due to the sudden, unnatural narrowing and blockage of the passages in the brain. While most ancient and modern writers agree on this immediate cause, there is much dispute regarding the *antecedent* cause.

<margin>What is the antecedent cause of apoplexy?</margin>
Commonly, the most severe apoplexy—which **Hippocrates** <note>the ancient Greek physician (c. 460 – 370 BC)</note> states in his *Aphorisms* can in no way be resolved—is defined as...

# ON THE USE OF THE SETON.
<meta>catchword: that.</meta>

...I readily grant that it arises from viscid, thick humors, whether phlegmatic or **melancholic** <note>referring to 'black bile,' one of the four bodily humors thought to cause heaviness or depression</note>, for which reason such **Apoplexy** <note>a sudden loss of consciousness or 'stroke'</note> never ends in paralysis; this is because the offending matter is rightly judged to be unfit for either resolution <note>dissolving</note> or for filling the nerves. However, it is not enough for such matter to abound in this or that part of the brain unless it suddenly obstructs those passages through which the continuous communication of **vital spirits** <term>vital spirits: a refined substance believed to be distilled from the blood and transported from the heart to the brain to enable life and movement</term> from the heart is carried out. For this reason, it is made manifest that in every case of Apoplexy, the **retiform plexus** <margin>The immediate cause.</margin> <note>original: "plexus retiformem," the 'rete mirabile' or network of vessels at the base of the brain</note>—as **Jean Fernel** <note>a famous 16th-century French physician</note> maintained—is obstructed. Yet it is not only this, but also the four **sinuses** <note>the large blood-collecting channels in the brain's membrane</note> meeting together, which in a natural state transfer spirituous blood into the entire substance of the brain, that suddenly suffer such an obstruction. Once the further flow of the vital spirit—as a necessary instrument—is denied, the entire **animal faculty** <note>the power of the soul responsible for sensation and voluntary motion</note> is totally hindered in its operations. Respiration remains in some fashion, by which the different types of the disease are usually distinguished; this operation usually survives to some extent, either because the necessity of the nerves still excites its power for a little while (according to **Galen**), or because of the natural motion of respiration (as **Master Felix Plater** <note>a Swiss physician known for his anatomical observations</note> preferred). We have demonstrated this natural motion of respiration, and how its variation depends only on our intention, at greater length in our first book on *Human Nature*. Or perhaps it is because...

<column-break/>

...on account of the tiny branches of the aforementioned vessels bringing the vital spirit, which are not yet completely obstructed, such a communication still occurs. This may be sufficient for some influx to the pectoral nerves, which perform their duty in assisting respiration—even when we are not thinking of it or even while we are sleeping—out of necessity. It is no wonder, then, that even in those who have died of severe Apoplexy, if we are to trust **Jean Fernel**, **Caspar Bauhin**, **Wilhelm Fabricius**, **Giovanni Valverde**, and others, the cause of the evil was found around the retiform plexus and the remaining sinuses originating from the ascending vessels, rather than elsewhere; the ventricles of the brain were found neither filled nor obstructed. A recent example, worthy of note, confirms this sufficiently. It happened last summer, <margin>See more on this observation in Medical Epistles, book 1, section 17, regarding head wounds.</margin> on the 10th of July, that a certain peasant from the neighboring village of **Göttingen** <note>in the jurisdiction of Ulm</note> was wounded by a puncture from a **two-headed pike** <note>original: "phalange bicipite"</note>. The wound broke the skin through the upper left eyelid, passing all the way into the eye socket without injuring the eye itself. Neglecting the wound in the first few days, he eventually showed it to our **Lithotomist** <note>original: "Lithotomo," a surgeon specializing in "cutting for the stone," but here acting as a general surgeon</note>, a sufficiently skilled surgeon, who took the wounded man into his house and diligently administered suitable external remedies. However, although the small external wound was consolidated <note>healed over</note> quickly enough, around the fifth day the patient nevertheless complained of a headache and a heaviness of the **internal senses**...

->### MEDICAL LETTERS BOOK II. SECTION VIII.<-

<columns>
...when he complained, the aforementioned **Surgeon** <note>original: "Chirurgus"</note> approached me for advice. I promptly visited the suffering man myself and, having soon made a **prognosis** <term>prognosis: a forecast of the likely course and outcome of a disease</term>, I declared the matter to be full of danger—especially during these **dog days** <note>original: "canicularibus," the hottest days of summer, then believed to aggravate diseases and decay</note>—with **convulsions** <note>original: "convulsionibus"</note> and death itself likely to follow very easily due to the matter rotting within. Therefore, having prescribed what seemed useful both for internal use and external application for the **revulsion** <term>revulsion: a traditional medical practice of drawing "bad humors" away from an affected area to another part of the body</term> of the offending matter and the prevention of more serious symptoms, I said that we must wait for the outcome, especially since the location of the injury did not allow for a **trepan** <note>original: "terebrum," a surgical drill used to create a hole in the skull</note> to be used at all. What happened? The wounded man remained in nearly the same state, gradually becoming more affected by stupor, with a beginning of **lethargy** or a **waking coma** <note>original: "Comate vigilante," a state where the patient appears awake but is unresponsive</note>, until on the ninth day he paid his debt to nature <note>a common euphemism for death</note>. Once this occurred, as the Magistrate wished to be certain of the nature of the wound, by his command—and with me and my colleague **Dr. Augustinus Thonner** present—the **skull** <note>original: "Cranium"</note> was opened on July 19th. There, we first discovered that the external wound [which had completely healed and closed in the skin] had not only passed through the upper **eye socket** <note>original: "orbitam"</note>, but also that a sharp piece of the broken socket had remained fixed in the **dura mater** <note>original: "crassa meningem," the "thick membrane" protecting the brain</note>. When the dura mater—otherwise intact—was cut along the length of the crown without damaging the **falciform process** <note>the sickle-shaped fold of the dura mater that separates the brain's hemispheres</note>, a hole through the **pia mater** <note>the delicate innermost membrane</note> into the very

<column-break/>

substance of the brain came into view. From this hole, like a small fountain, **ichor** <note>original: "sanies," a thin, watery discharge from a wound</note> and purulent matter flowed out when the brain was compressed. As the dissection of the brain proceeded further, such a large **abscess** <note>original: "abscessus"</note> was seen—perhaps aided by the heat of the dog days and generated in such a short time—that not only was the upper substance of the brain turned into spontaneously flowing pus [which, as can be seen in the **Conciliator** <note>referring to Pietro d’Abano (1250–1316), a famous physician whose work sought to "reconcile" different medical theories</note>, was incredible to the ancients], but even the two upper **ventricles** <note>fluid-filled cavities</note> of the brain, merging into the third lower one, were completely filled with this purulent matter. Here, one might not undeservedly doubt how the aforementioned patient could have been free from both convulsions and symptoms of **apoplexy** <note>a sudden loss of consciousness or movement, similar to a stroke</note> until the very end of his life. I believe this happened for no other reason than that the injury occupied the upper part, while the **root of the nerves** (which suffers in a convulsion) and the vessels and sinuses (which receive the flow of **vital spirits** and are, as we have said, totally obstructed in apoplexy) remained unharmed. To this also belongs the observation of **Vesalius** <note>Andreas Vesalius (1514–1564), the father of modern anatomy</note> concerning a girl suffering from **hydrocephalus** <note>original: "hydrocephalo," a buildup of fluid in the brain</note> who, never feeling anything of apoplexy, finally died and was found to have the ventricles of the brain entirely distended by a great quantity of fluids. I shall add nothing further, as I have demonstrated this more fully in my first book *On Human Nature*, regarding the Ventricles...
</columns>

<page-num>489</page-num>

<margin>c</margin>The ventricles of the brain <note>the hollow cavities within the brain that circulate fluid</note> were established primarily for the purpose of
<margin>e</margin>receiving and sending away the 
<margin>a</margin>waste products of the brain, as the most
<margin>with</margin>distinguished anatomists indicate to me.
Thus, it is likely that in **catarrh** <note>a buildup of mucus in the nose or throat</note>, **coryza** <note>the common cold</note>,
and similar conditions, a large
quantity of **phlegm** <note>original: "pituitæ," one of the four humors believed to cause sluggishness or blockage</note> frequently
abounds in these ventricles. But to the point: it is sufficiently clear that the most severe **apoplexy** <term>apoplexy: a sudden loss of consciousness or movement, similar to a modern stroke</term> is caused by thick, viscous humors that are difficult to dissolve. Where the condition is less severe, we are compelled to agree with *Carolus Piso* <note>Charles Le Pois (1563–1633), a French physician who argued that many diseases were caused by "serosity" or excess water in the body</note> that it is produced by a mixture of watery fluids. We infer the quality of this material from the manner in which it dissolves, since otherwise a sudden change into **paralysis** would not occur; much less would the offending matter be dispersed from the paralyzed limbs by the usual remedies. Furthermore, we shall not labor too much here in explaining the opinion of *Quercetanus* <note>Joseph Du Chesne (c. 1544–1609), a chemist and physician who followed Paracelsian theories</note>, who attributes this to **vitriolated vapors** <note>acidic or metallic fumes believed to cause chemical reactions in the body</note>, which are very prone to sudden coagulation. He argues that these can suddenly produce such a brain disease—a view also proposed before him by *Theodorus Angelutius*. However, this opinion detracts nothing from our aforementioned assertion, since there can be many preceding causes, all of which necessarily concur in some immediate way to produce the effect. Hence, we also gladly concede to our *Marcello Donato* <note>author of "The History of Remarkable Medicine"</note> that a vapor hostile to the brain—such as the smoke from **lime and coal**—can produce the **stunned disease** <note>original: "morbum attonitum," a term for a sudden seizure or stroke where the patient seems "thunderstruck"</note> in the manner of apoplexy. This happens not because the 

<column-break/>

heart is the primary organ suffering (as *Christoph à Vega* wished), nor even by a tightening through drying (as *Mercurialis* <note>Girolamo Mercuriali (1530–1606), a famous Italian physician</note> preferred), but rather by a certain **narcotic force**, according to *Plater*. This force drives the faulty humors—which are otherwise abundant and flowing—into the vessels and boundaries of the brain. For this reason, we grant that athletic bodies can be seized by **sideration** <note>original: "sideratione," a term for a sudden blast or stroke, often thought to be planetary in origin</note> due to an **inflammatory** <term><gloss>original Greek: Φλεγμονώδην</gloss> inflammatory or full of heat</term> disposition. Though *Galen* used this term improperly, our *Hippocrates* says it happens due to the blockage of the vessels. In those whom this evil invades, the face becomes deeply red, and the vessels of both the eyes and the neck become swollen and tense, as *Curtius Marinellus* describes in his work *On Diseases Besieging the Nobler Faculties of the Soul, Book I.* Hence, we do not deny that a disease similar to apoplexy can also be produced by an immoderate buildup of thin, watery waste, causing the substance of the brain to suddenly subside (according to *Master Plater*), or even by the brain being violently compressed by a blow or a bruise. However, we believe the immediate cause we stated above always plays a part. Although the causes preceding the immediate one can vary, it is most often the case—unless some external, violent, or accidental cause concurs—that it arises from **viscous phlegm**, mixed with or without watery humors. This matter is not only quite capable of producing obstructions, but is also accustomed to being collected in great quantities in the brain, affecting...

# MEDICAL EPISTLES, BOOK II, SECTION VIII.

<page-num>490</page-num>

This horrific affliction <note>referring to apoplexy, or stroke</note> takes its origin in the way we have described: produced daily by an inherited or acquired weakness of the head. It is further provoked by northern and southern atmospheric conditions, by more violent movements of the body and soul, and other irritants, as the examples of stroke victims testify. This can be seen in the works of **Benivieni**, **Foreest**, **Vallériole**, **Augenio**, and others. <note>These were famous medical authorities of the 15th and 16th centuries who specialized in pathology and clinical observations.</note>

But in preventing this condition, what more effective remedy could be devised than a **seton** placed at the nape of the neck? <term>seton: a strip of silk or linen thread passed through a fold of skin to create a "productive" wound, believed to drain harmful fluids from the body.</term> By this method, that which has collected in the substance and cavities of the brain is diverted outward. Furthermore, that which is still in the process of forming is turned away, especially in a patient suffering from vapors rising from the organs of the lower abdomen, which makes them prone to "fluxions" <note>fluid buildup</note> in the head. 

Indeed, if **actual cautery** <note>the application of a hot iron to the skin</note> was able to restore a hopeless stroke victim, as **Marcellus Donatus** records on page 173 of my edition, what might we not hope for from the **seton** regarding prevention, at a time when no signs of the disease have yet shown themselves? Your Excellency knows that in the year 1614, continuous fevers accompanied by an unnatural lethargy were extremely common, as I experienced firsthand in **Hesse** <note>a region in Germany</note> at that time. In those cases, lest the sick sleep the "Sleep of Epimenides" <note>original: "somnum Epimenideum"; a reference to a legendary Greek philosopher said to have slept for 57 years; here meaning a coma or permanent lethargy</note> in their profound stupor, I was finally forced to apply **vesicatories** <term>vesicatories: substances applied to the skin to cause blistering, used to "draw out" internal inflammation</term> to the neck—not just once, but several times—with a most desired success, by God's grace.

<column-break/>

This will be made clear to many in my "Special Observations," which, **with God's help** <note>original: "σὺν Θεῷ"</note> and as requested so many times by my friends, I shall revise for the press this winter. Truly, if a stroke were to be feared from the use of a seton, then at that time, when the feverish humor was swelling everywhere, the use of blistering agents should have been stopped even more. 

I should add nothing further of those who, for many years, due to incurable afflictions of the eyes or nose, have worn setons with the greatest benefit; their brain functions remained fully intact until their very last breath. Among others, a certain nobleman testifies to this in my observations; for him, **Master Wilhelm Fabricius** <note>Wilhelm Fabricius Hildanus (1560–1634), often called the "Father of German Surgery"</note> in the year 1612, 

<margin>See part 3, observation 1.</margin>

while passing through Hesse, placed a seton due to a malignant internal ulcer of the nostrils. I was present and urged this course of action. It was done with such success that afterward, beyond our expectations, he remained in excellent health for many years, until finally he was slowly consumed by a co-occurring **consumption** <note>original: "phthisi"; tuberculosis</note>. During that time, he never complained of any affliction of the head.

I shall gladly look into the doubts regarding the "suffering site"—whether apoplexy is an evil of the heart or rather of the brain. For although it cannot be denied that the heart is also greatly affected here (as the impairment of breathing most strongly testifies), I do not see why the disease should be attributed to the heart rather than the brain. For just as in **syncope** <note>fainting</note> the affliction is said to be primarily in the heart, although...

## BOOK TWO, SECTION IX.

### QUALITIES OF
### CAMPHOR.

<margin>Is Camphor hot or cold?</margin>
Greetings and respect, etc. Not long ago, there was a sharp dispute between two learned men regarding the primary active quality of **Camphor**; one of whom stubbornly held it to be cold, while the other held it to be not just "manifestly" hot (as **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd, the 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and physician.</note> says in his fifth book), but "extremely hot." Why and how it displays such hot effects, I (who was not present at the said contest) have not yet been sufficiently in-

<column-break/>

formed. **Renodeus**, in his work *On Medical Matter* (Book 1, Section 9, Chapter 2), <note>Jean de Renou, a 17th-century French physician.</note> asserts that it affects one like heat through its odor and the "thinness of its spirits," but provokes the body like a cold substance through its other qualities. But I think there is some hallucination here (unless I am hallucinating myself): for what is this odor of Camphor by which heat is inferred? I do not argue about the degrees of the scent, whether it is sharp or sluggish, but whether it is pungent, or harsh, or bitter, etc.

EPISTLE ON MEDICINE, BOOK II, SECTION IX.

these varieties of odors, however, because man has not obtained an exquisite power of smelling, cannot be investigated with extreme accuracy. I consider it a confused matter, and one that can scarcely—if at all—be demonstrated under a simple category of taste, much less appear to affect the mode of heat from this source.

<margin>What odor is.</margin>
Indeed, every odor, according to *Aristotle in his book On the Senses and the Sensible, chapter 5,* is a quality of a mixed body produced by heat, and that heat is twofold: internal and external. The former, acting as the architect of the odor, "cooks" the moisture with the dry and renders it tempered; the latter, from the sun and fire, loosens and thins out the odorous bodies so that they may exhale. But to pronounce everything that is odorous as "hot" because of this, and to deny them coldness entirely, would be too rigorous. No mixture exists that is not made a mixture through heat (of whatever kind)—I speak of that which is considered a mixture truly and naturally, rather than artificially or through mere blending or placement; and such mixable things ought to be **homogeneous** <note>original: h. e. eandem naturam habere—that is, having the same nature</note>, which heat alone gathers together, while on the contrary, it separates **heterogeneous** <note>things of a different nature</note> things. Nevertheless, in no way should all these things be called "hot" as a result. Nor is it permitted to measure the degree of heat by the degree of odor, because a sharper odor is not produced simply because the heat is greater: for glowing iron possesses no odor, but the cause lies properly in the "tasty dry"; for every

<column-break/>

tasty thing is odorous, while odor fails the tasteless, just as a stone is devoid of odor since it has no taste (*Aristotle, in the same place*). So woods return an odor because they are endowed with taste: just as moisture dominates in taste, so dryness dominates in odor, which can be clearly seen in the case of aromatic woods, such as cinnamon and similar things; the drier they are [though it is necessary that they be tasty at the same time], the more odorous they are found to be. I would say it is less correct to argue that the **thinness of parts** <note>A reference to the physical structure or volatility of a substance.</note> proves only the presence of heat: for if this were so, **Oil and Spirit of Vitriol** <term>Spirit of Vitriol: An early name for sulfuric acid; despite its "sharp" and volatile nature, it was classified as chemically cold in the humoral system.</term> and many other things of thin parts—which often vanish into the air of their own accord—would be hot, a claim which experience shatters. And even if they themselves were to act as thinning agents, and were called hot on that account, one should not judge **Attenuants** <term>Attenuants: Medicines believed to thin or break down thick, sluggish "humors" (fluids) in the body to clear blockages.</term> indiscriminately; for some divide thick humors solely by the thinness of their parts, by which they easily insinuate themselves into the innermost parts of the humor and separate them by their motion, such as acids; or they do so by heat combined with thinness of parts and a certain dryness. From this latter group come all sharp things that bite the taste and smell, such as spices, and whatever possesses the power of thinning from the second even unto the third degree of heat and dryness. Hence all diuretics, agents of sweating, digestives, those that disperse swellings, those that clear obstructions, those that move the menses, **lithontriptics** <term>lithontriptics: Medicines used to dissolve or break up bladder or kidney stones.</term>, and those that treat phlegm and melancholy...

<summary>This page explores the Aristotelian theory of odor, arguing that a substance's smell and "thinness" do not always prove it is "hot" in a medicinal sense. It distinguishes between substances that thin the body's fluids through acidity versus those that do so through heat and dryness, like spices.</summary>

# ON THE QUALITIES OF CAMPHOR.
<sig>Qqq 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: not</meta>

...are considered to be preparing or **attenuating** <note>original: attenuantia — substances used to "thin out" thick or sluggish bodily fluids</note> agents, among which not a few are found to be cold. In a similar way, not all **thickening** agents [the opposites of attenuants] are cold—even though, by the law of Logical Canon, "Contraries of contraries" <note>original: Contraria contrariorum — a logical rule suggesting that if one thing has a certain effect, its opposite should have the opposite effect</note> etc., it would follow that all attenuants would indicate heat rather than coldness. I believe, therefore, that these terms are often confused with one another: to be powerful in the strength of attenuating, and to be made of "thin parts"—or distinguished by the thinness of spirits—since the former should be attributed to a **quality** <note>the effect it has</note> and the latter to its **substance** <note>what it is made of</note>. Add to this that Camphor itself is found to be both "thin" and "thick" by reason of its substance. The former is considered good by pharmacists, while the latter—when it is also darkened, black, and tangled with the chips of its own wood (as **Wecker** <note>Johannes Jacob Wecker, a 16th-century physician</note> says in *Antidotes, book 1, f. 17*)—is considered bad. 

Others feel differently; and what is said of vinegar, they also pronounce concerning Camphor: namely, that it both heats and cools. However, a Logical Rule forbids these two opposites from being found in one subject: "Adversaries mutually repel and destroy one another, and if one is truly affirmed, the other must necessarily be denied." Nor would I grant any room for the inference that Camphor heats when applied with hot things (and vice versa); for an effect of this kind must instead be credited to the "super-eminent" heat of the substance that is sucked out by the attractive parts of the Camphor, which then overwhelms the Camphor’s own coldness by its own heat and mass,

<column-break/>

in exactly the same way as **Vinegar** (which according to the testimony of **Galen** <note>The most influential physician of antiquity</note> in *Simple Medicines, book 1, ch. 9; book 4, ch. 12;* and *On Wasting, ch. 8,* is cold). When flowers of cloves are infused in vinegar, it takes on a greater faculty for heating than the simple vinegar possessed by itself. Similarly, **sublimated wine** <note>distilled alcohol or spirits</note>, which is very hot by itself, is made cold in large part by the addition of the seeds of the **field poppy** <note>original: papav. err. — papaver erraticum</note> or **henbane**. 

It is a less forceful argument to say that because Camphor is very easily set on fire, and even burns in water, it must for that reason be extremely hot. For it burns and is ignited by the power of its **airy parts** and because of its **oiliness** <note>original: pinguedinem — fatness or oiliness</note>; for who would assert that everything that burns most easily and immediately is therefore "hottest" in temperature?

Let us consult **Experience**, which is the other leg and pillar of Medicine, and upon which alone we must lean (according to the judgment of **Avicenna** <note>The great Persian physician Ibn Sina</note>) if reason indicates one thing and experience another; for experience cannot be contradicted except **by the deceived** <note>original: τῷ πλάνῳ — to the one who wanders or is in error</note>. Experience reveals that Camphor is so far from being extremely hot that it actually cools in approximately the **third degree** <note>a classification of the strength of a medicine's effect, on a scale of one to four</note>. When applied, it soothes hot headaches, extinguishes glowing inflammations [especially of the **liver**], and frees the kidneys and seminal vessels from excessive heat. Who, even among the bathhouse keepers and traveling herb-sellers, does not know that **Camphorated Ointment**, both white and red, is most effective against **Erysipelas** <note>a painful, red skin infection also known as St. Anthony’s Fire</note>? **Renodæus** <note>Jean de Renou</note> himself writes many things on this in chapter 1, as do others like **Wecker** (*book 1, f. 17, on gums and resins*), **Matthiolus**, **Avicenna**, **Serapio**, the **Physicians of Cologne**, and others. A noteworthy example...

<summary>This page debates the medicinal nature of camphor, arguing that while its chemical volatility suggests heat, clinical experience proves it is a powerful cooling agent used for inflammations and skin infections.</summary>

MEDICAL LETTERS BOOK II. SECTION IX.

not long ago a case presented itself, when a certain woman in a Leper Hospital, suffering intensely from a feverish heat around the upper abdomen <note>original: supremum ventrem — referring to the region of the stomach or chest</note>, on the foolish advice of a foolish old woman, washed her face with rose water [if I remember correctly] to which a good portion of Camphor had been added. You, my teacher, whom I have followed with entirely filial love and honor like a father, and as much as the Avenging Spirit <note>original: ὁ Ἀλάστωρ — a Greek term for a spirit of ill fortune or vengeance, here likely referring to the hardships of life</note> will permit, with God’s help, I shall eagerly follow as long as I draw breath. Live most happily and farewell, most Excellent man, both an ornament and a benefit to our most noble Art, and do not cease to favor me with that singular and sincere love of yours.

### ON THE QUALITIES OF CAMPHOR

And not without reason! Since on both sides, neither arguments nor authorities are lacking. But before we submit the determination of the question, let us begin an inquiry into the nature and origin of Camphor—or *Caphura*, or as it seems to please the most subtle *Scaliger* <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a renowned Italian scholar and physician</note> better, *Capura*. We do this so that we are not accused of that which the aforementioned "Master of Subtleties" criticized in the works of *Cardano* <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath; Scaliger famously wrote a massive critique of Cardano's work</note>, specifically in *Exercise 104, Section 8*: as if the deity of laziness were to be shown to physicians in place of the Elysian Fields, in whose lap the blessed might rest (without ever investigating what Camphor actually is).

<margin>Camphor was unknown to the ancients.</margin>
That Camphor was unknown to the ancient writers is clear enough from *Monardes* <note>Nicolás Monardes (1493–1588), a Spanish physician who described many New World plants</note> in his *Annotations to Mesue*, where he says: "it is a new thing (camphor) which they call the gum of trees." This is also repeated in the *Medical Epistles, Epistle 3* by *Johannes Baptista Theodosius*. *Mattioli* <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), an Italian doctor famous for his commentaries on the Greek botanist Dioscorides</note> in *Book 1 of Dioscorides, chapter 75*, asserts that the ancients—Galen, Dioscorides, and other writers of that era—not only noted nothing about Camphor, but did not even know of it; *Garcia* <note>Garcia de Orta (c. 1501–1568), a Portuguese physician who studied Indian medicine and plants</note> also agrees with this in *Book 1 of Aromatics, chapter 9*.

<margin>Whether Camphor is a bitumen.</margin>
However, there are those who maintain that Camphor is a type of bitumen <note>a naturally occurring flammable mineral substance, like asphalt or naphtha</note>. For this reason, *Falloppio* <note>Gabriele Falloppio (1523–1562), a celebrated Italian anatomist</note> in his *Book on Thermal Waters, chapter 5*, not without reason determined for some that Camphor is a species of Bitumen, because, in the manner of other bitumens, it burns in water. *Fuchs* <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a German physician and botanist</note> in *Book 1 on the Composition of Medicines, chapter 20*, is <term>in agreement<note>original Greek: ὁμόψηφος (homopsēphos) — literally 'sharing the same pebble' or vote</note></term>, thinking that Camphor is a type of Indian bitumen. He writes this because Serapion <note>a name referring to influential medieval Arabic medical writers</note> recorded that a more abundant harvest of camphor is a prognostic sign

<column-break/>

when the sky flashes with frequent lightning, at which time the earth is accustomed to pour forth a bounty of Sulfur and bitumens. This is contrary to the views of *Garcia*, who entirely denies this based on the physical nature of the region where it grows. Likewise, *Agricola* <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the 'father of mineralogy'</note> argued that Camphor was the "flower" of Amber or of a certain Arabian Bitumen extracted through sublimation <note>the process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again</note>; *Libavius* <note>Andreas Libavius (1555–1616), a German doctor and early chemist</note> discusses this in his *Commentary on Alchemical Matters, part 2, book 6, chapter 31*.

<margin>Whether it is the juice of a herb.</margin>
*Platearius* <note>a 12th-century physician from the School of Salerno</note> wrongly declares Camphor to be the juice of a certain herb. But *Capura* is the "tear" (sap) of a tree, says *Scaliger* in the cited location, or the gum of a tree growing in India, as *Mattioli* says, or as *Garcia* has it:

<margin>What Camphor is.</margin>
Camphor is a gum—not the pith or the "heart" of the tree, as *Avicenna* <note>the famous Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> and certain others thought—which, falling into the center of the wood, is then extracted, or it oozes out through cracks. *Scaliger* hints at a description of the tree called *Capur*, but *Garcia* describes it more exactly.

<margin>The qualities of Camphor.</margin>
Regarding the qualities of the medicine, there are diverse opinions. *Falloppio* in his *Book on Ulcers, chapter 10*, uses Camphor as a heating medicine, contrary to *Avicenna* and *Serapion*, who determine that Camphor cools and dries in the 3rd degree. *Mattioli* calls this cooling opinion into doubt, or else declares that we are lacking "true Camphor." He opens his mind more clearly in his *Epistles* on page 137, when he says: "I could by no means persuade myself that Camphor is an extremely cold medicine"; he adds the reason, that it not only ignites...

### MEDICAL EPISTLES, BOOK II, SECTION IX.

...burns most vehemently in water, but also consists of the finest parts and the sharpest odor; when chewed, it heats the mouth and dries it out exceedingly. For this reason, **Fuchs** <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a German physician and one of the three "founding fathers" of botany.</note> in his *Annotations on the lozenges of Purslane, Book 2 on the Composition of Medicines*, rightly decided it should be mixed with somewhat cooling medicines, so that it might carry the strength of the thicker medicines with it to the innermost parts of the body. **Johannes Baptista Theodosius** <note>An Italian physician known for his medical letters (epistles).</note> in *Medical Epistle 49, page 453*, pronounces our Camphor to be abundantly hot. **Dino** <note>Dino del Garbo (c. 1280–1327), an influential medieval Italian physician.</note> in his *Commentary on the 2nd Canon, chapter 3*, pronounces Camphor to be predominantly very cold; and yet, he says, in respect to its powerful odor, one must confess there are hot parts within it. For odor is not produced except by a "smoky operation" <note>original: "fumali operatione"; a reference to the process of evaporation or sublimation.</note>, as **Aristotle** says in *Book 1 on the Senses and the Sensible*; such evaporation does not occur except by heat. **Dr. Minderer** <note>Raymond Minderer (c. 1570–1621), a military physician who popularized various chemical remedies.</note> also seems to lean toward this view, as will later be clear from the way he pronounces camphor to be an <term>alexiterium</term> <note>A medicine used to neutralize poison or protect against infectious disease like the plague.</note>. **Rhases** <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi (865–925), a Persian polymath and physician.</note> in *Medical Matters, Book 3, chapter 22*, pronounces it cold and moist, contrary to **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the most influential philosopher-physician of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> and even **Cardano** <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), who famously debated the nature of substances.</note>. Cardano attributes such great dryness to it that, by drying out the semen, it is said to render young men impotent if carried in their bosoms—an idea for which **Scaliger** <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), who wrote a famous critique of Cardano.</note> not undeservedly refutes him. **Garcia** <note>Garcia de Orta (c. 1501–1568), a Portuguese physician who studied Indian medicine.</note> in *Chapter 1* says that for some time he held Camphor to be hot on account of its odor and the thinness of its parts, but later, being convinced by experiment, he yielded the palm to those who prove it is cold based on its clinical effects.

<column-break/>

<margin>Combined disputes concerning Camphor between Simler and Snizer in the *Medical Clinic*, page 305.</margin>
Nor does he say that the fact it is fragrant contradicts this opinion; since, due to the thinness of its parts, the odor which is on the surface evaporates and exhales very easily. This is the opposite of Sandalwood and Rose, which retain their odor within themselves because of their <term>astriction</term> <note>The quality of binding or contracting tissues; an astringent nature.</note>.

**Crato** <note>Johann Crato von Krafftheim (1519–1585), personal physician to three Holy Roman Emperors.</note> in his *Treatise on the Plague* decides that Camphor is without doubt composed of the finest parts; it heats when combined with hot things, and cools when combined with cold things. See the *Consultations* edited by **Scholz**, near the end of page 1107. You see, Friend, that the present question labors under no small difficulty, with some attributing heat and others cold to Camphor; for which reason I am not surprised that various opinions are still debated among the learned today.

<margin>Foundations of the determination.</margin>
Since, however, a medicine is described in relation to our body insofar as it alters that body (as **Galen** holds in *Book 1 of Simple Medicines, chapter 38*), camphor shall also be considered in that light—not merely how it seems to exceed in cold or hot parts by reason of its own mixture, but insofar as it affects our body in this or that way. A second foundation for our resolution is supplied by **Galen** in *Book 3 on Temperaments, chapter 1*, and *Book 1 of Simples, chapter 2*: namely, that some operations of medicines occur through themselves (*per se*), and others by accident. Nor should we neglect the third foundation, which was proposed by us near the end of *Exercise 2 of the Pharmaceutical Decade*: that the various operations of medicines not infrequently depend on the diversity of their parts.

### ON THE QUALITIES OF CAMPHOR.

Regarding its nature, some not unskillfully declare it to be hot, since it consists of fine and penetrating parts, and since it is flammable in the manner of bitumens, and since it exhales a penetrating and heavy odor, which is the offspring of heat. But even if this is granted, it does not necessarily follow that Camphor also heats with respect to our body, although at first contact it seems to sting the tongue with an impression of heat; for it is established through experience that cooling, rather than heating, follows its use in our body. For this reason, **Garcia** <note>Garcia da Orta (c. 1501–1568), a Portuguese Renaissance physician and pioneer of tropical medicine who worked in India.</note> reports that when applied to <term>ophthalmia</term> <note>A general historical term for inflammation of the eye or conjunctivitis.</note> and eye inflammations, as well as to burns, it restored the coldness of snow. Thus also, for the sake of protection, Camphor is conveniently mixed with other ophthalmic eye-salves during smallpox, preventing and repelling eye inflammations, which I confirm by my own experience. Indeed, the experience of many confirms that even the heat of Venus <note>A poetic reference to sexual desire or "lust."</note> is extinguished by Camphor, hence the common verse:

> Camphor, through the nostrils, castrates males by its scent. <note>original: "Camphora per nares castrat odore mares." This was a common medieval belief that smelling camphor acted as an anaphrodisiac.</note>

Although **Scaliger** <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a celebrated Italian scholar and physician.</note>, in his book against **Cardano**, denies this very thing.

<margin>The reasons brought forward for heat are refuted.</margin>
Nor is the thinness of its parts sufficient proof of heat, because it is not the heat of the compound (which thinness of parts most often demonstrates) that is sought, but the effective heat with respect to our body. Nor is the readiness for inflammation <note>flammability</note> sufficient for Scaliger: for who would say, he asks, that the hottest things

<column-break/>

burn most easily? For fire does not always pass into bodies because of a similarity (I mean a similarity of heat), but some matter is also attracted which can easily admit it because of its rarity <note>In the sense of being porous or having "thin" substance.</note>. Nor finally is the argument drawn from a heavy odor sufficient, as you yourself have demonstrated; to which I add that this odor is not so unique to Camphor that it is not also found in others. For this reason **Bacci** <note>Andrea Bacci (1524–1600), an Italian philosopher and physician.</note>, in Book 5, *On Thermal Springs*, Chapter 4, says that the odor of Camphor was attributed by **Savonarola** <note>Michele Savonarola (1385–1468), a famous Italian physician and grandfather of the friar Girolamo Savonarola.</note> not only to the medicinal waters near the town of Aquarium in Italy, but that **Falloppio** <note>Gabriele Falloppio (1523–1562), the famous anatomist and physician.</note> also established this, because the region of Modena abounds in bitumen, which rivals the odor of Camphor. **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian "Prince of Physicians."</note> also attributes a camphor-like scented power to amber, which **Libavius** <note>Andreas Libavius (c. 1555–1616), a German chemist and physician.</note> proves in his *Commentary, part 2, book 6, chapter 31*, when he says: if anyone, while making oil of Amber, places cotton wool moistened with water on the still, it will emit a smoke with the odor of Camphor.

<margin>Determination of the truth.</margin>
With these things premised, we establish that Camphor is endowed with the power of cooling, not in respect to its composition, but effectively within our body; and this because of the diverse parts which are detected in the same effect. **Libavius** hints at this in *The Apocalypse [of Hermes], part 1, chapter 15*, when he says: Camphor is cold in its medical effect because of the spirits enclosed within it, just as <term>halonitrum</term> <note>Often referring to a type of mineral salt or refined saltpeter.</note> is; but the reason it burns is that it does not exceed the category of sulfurous substances. **Quercetanus** <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1444–1609), a French physician and chemist who championed Paracelsian medicine.</note>, *Defense, Book 1*.

## MEDICAL EPISTLES, BOOK II, SECTION IX.

*Hermes* <note>Likely referring to the Hermetic tradition or works attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, highly regarded by Paracelsian physicians.</note> in chapter 16 determines from the property of the principles of camphor that it is evident, due to its unpleasant odor (even though it burns in water), that it possesses a cooling and narcotic quality. He adds that although its oil may exhibit a certain fiery quality upon the first application, it is nonetheless a most excellent sedative for pains. Because of this operation, Camphor is classified by the Arabs as cold in the third degree. **Quercetanus** <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician and chemist who championed the use of chemical remedies in medicine.</note> repeats the same in chapter 15 of his *Tetrad*, where from the evidence of the scent he attributes to Camphor a "mitigating sulfur," by soothing pain and extinguishing the "raging cause." There is, moreover, a similar operation in Opium, which is also rightly established as cold in effect, although otherwise—on account of its remarkable bitterness joined with acrimony, its heavy odor, and because it very easily catches fire—it is pronounced hot by us in *Decade 9 of Therapeutic Problems, Question 2.* <note>original: "dec. 9. probl. Θεραπ. q. 2." The author refers to his own academic disputes.</note> Thus, from the seeds of poppy, pumpkin, melon, cucumber, and other cold things of that kind, fragrant oils are extracted (according to **Quercetanus** in the cited book), the operations of which nevertheless do not induce heat, but rather rest and cooling. A still greater similarity, which they derive from <term>Halinitrum</term> <note>Saltpeter or Nitre (Potassium Nitrate).</note>, declares this very thing; for who will deny that in prepared nitre—which some call <term>lapis prunellae</term> <note>Literally "plum stone," a medicinal preparation of saltpeter fused into small balls, used to treat sore throats and fevers.</note>—there is a singular power of cooling? As we have demonstrated in *Medical Problems, Decade 3, Question 8*; you may see more praises of this operation in **Quercetanus**...

<column-break/>

...in his *Alexicacus* <note>A title derived from the Greek, meaning "The Warder-off of Evil."</note>, chapter 5, page 351 in my edition; in **Ruland** <note>Martin Ruland (1532–1602), a physician known for his work on the "Hungarian Fever" (likely typhus).</note> on the *Hungarian Disease*, cure 6, page 138 in my edition; in **Unzerus** on *Salt*, chapter 18, and others. Although the volatile and sulfurous nature of this same Nitre is not unknown even to common folk, it is therefore established as likely that this occurs due to a diversity of parts, which the same **Quercetanus** explains at greater length in his book *On Ancient Medical Material*, chapters 3 and 4. Refer also to what **Cunradus** <note>Israel Conradt (1634–1715), a physician and scientist from Danzig.</note> has in his *Marrow of Distillation*, part 1, treatise 21, where he confesses that Camphor is a volatile spirit which is sublimated even by a light heat, and which emulates Saltpeter in its properties. Let us therefore posit that in Camphor also there is a similar Sulfur <note>In early chemistry, "sulfur" referred to the principle of flammability or the oily component of a substance.</note>, dissolving hot exhalations, which—along with a remarkable faculty for drying—is abundant; being endowed with the greatest power of penetrating, it insinuates itself quite deeply, and thus it not only tempers heat, but at the same time even attacks the very subject and hearth of the <term>putrefaction</term> <note>Early modern medicine viewed the plague and fevers as a "putrefaction" or rotting of the body's humors.</note> itself.

<margin>Why Camphor restrains the plague</margin>
It is made manifest from this why classical authors attribute so much to Camphor during times of infection against the pestilential malignancy: for which reason **Crato** <note>Johannes Crato von Krafftheim (1519–1585), a physician to three Holy Roman Emperors.</note> in his work on the plague mixes 3 grains of camphor with a little <term>Theriac</term> <note>A famous ancient "universal" antidote made of dozens of ingredients, including opium and viper flesh.</note> or <term>Mithridatium</term> <note>A complex antidote similar to Theriac, named after King Mithridates VI.</note>, and in *Epistle 103 to Düdith* <note>Andreas Dudith (1533–1589), a prominent humanist and diplomat.</note>, he says that among all <term>alexipharmics</term> <note>Remedies used to ward off poison or contagious disease.</note>, Camphor excels. **Zuvingerus** <note>Theodor Zwinger (1533–1588), a Swiss physician and encyclopedist.</note> also, in an Epistle to Monavius among the Scholzian collection, number 264, commends Camphor dissolved with spirit of wine <note>High-proof alcohol/ethanol.</note> according to the opinion of others, by which method the water of the plague...

<meta>This page concludes the medical correspondence regarding camphor, moving from the theoretical "complexion" (balance of qualities) of the substance to practical applications and expert opinions from contemporary physicians like Hartmann and Minderer. ### ON THE QUALITIES OF CAMPHOR.

The most distinguished **Hartmann** <note>Johann Hartmann (1568–1631), a pioneer of "Chymiatry" or chemical medicine.</note> prepares a remedy for the plague by dissolving Camphor in distilled alcohol, adding a small amount of saffron, used for both prevention and cure during times of pestilence. **Fernel** <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), an influential French physician.</note> also agrees in his *Method*, Book 5, Chapter 21, where he determines that camphor extinguishes warm, malignant vapors. A remarkable praise of Camphor is also given by the late **Dr. Minderer** <note>Raymond Minderer (c. 1570–1621), a famous Augsburg physician known for his "Spirit of Mindererus."</note> in his book *On the Plague*, Chapter 15, where he says: Camphor deserves to be celebrated with our highest praise, not only as a wonder but as a strong and effective <term>alexiterium</term> <note>A medicinal agent used to ward off infection or poison; an antidote.</note>. However, regarding how it exerts its power in defeating poison, perhaps not everyone shares the same opinion. The aforementioned **Minderer** suspects it happens for this reason: when Camphor is taken, it is soon ignited by internal heat as if by fire, and in the manner of a flame consuming putrid exhalations on the outside, it burns in the very center of the body. There, it burns away the polluted spirits—those foul breaths polluted by a filthy <term>miasma</term> <note>The "bad air" or infectious vapor once thought to cause disease.</note> or inhaled breaths contaminated by some stain of poison, already approaching the heart and clinging to the midriff. Thus, pervading the body with a clearly dry and fiery heat, it partly dissipates and expels them, partly consumes them through combustion, and partly corrects and improves them. Therefore, camphor should be placed among the strongest and most powerful antidotes for the plague, whether it be hot or cold, which

<column-break/>

nevertheless everyone is forced to admit is dry. Thus far we have heard the opinions of others, from which our conclusion is finally made clear: Camphor is not to be considered at any given time based on its chemical mixture alone, but according to how it affects our body. Since its cooling effects are more manifest—though we do not contradict those who claim it also heats when used alongside hot substances, aiding their operation as a "vehicle" <note>A substance used to carry or transport a medicine through the body.</note> due to the thinness of its parts—we add our vote to those who grant Camphor the power and effect of cooling. This is true even if it seems to happen not by its "actual heat" (and thus not by a <term>univocal action</term>), but rather by an <term>equivocal</term> <note>In medical philosophy, a "univocal" cause produces an effect like itself (heat produces heat), whereas an "equivocal" cause produces a different effect (like friction producing heat).</note> one, and indeed sometimes even in a way that is **incidentally** <note>original: *κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς* (kata symbebekos). An Aristotelian term meaning a result that occurs as a side effect or by accident, rather than by the primary nature of the thing.</note>. A reading of the cited authors will provide more details. Fare you well, and please look kindly upon these notes written amidst my disturbed and interrupted daily labors. 

Written in haste at Ulm, the day before the Calends of January, in the year 1627 <note>December 31, 1626.</note>. I pray from my soul that this year be peaceful and desirable for you and yours, and indeed for the whole Christian Commonwealth.

->Yours,<-

->*Dr. Gregorius Horstius*<-

Greetings. I ask, Most Distinguished Man, that you set forth your opinion on a marvelous (as it seems to me) example of a foul odor. For a young woman of 17 years was sent from Augsburg <note>The Latin *Augustâ* refers to Augsburg, Germany.</note> (where she was born) here to the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre, so that after her year of probation (as they call it in their custom) was completed, she might be clothed in the habit of a nun <note>original: *monialis*</note> and committed to that order. This woman had barely entered the aforementioned monastery when she was noticed to emit a stench extremely offensive to the other nuns; a stench, I say, like that of a

<column-break/>

rotting corpse, whether she is in the same common quarters <note>original: *contubernio*</note> as the others, or remains hidden in her own vault (which they call a "cell")—for those passing by also smell it. Thus, above all, the body <note>original: σῶμα (*sōma*)</note> of this virgin might not undeservedly be called a tomb <note>original: σῆμα (*sēma*). A play on words common in Greek philosophy suggesting the body is the prison or grave of the soul.</note>. I was called, and having conducted a diligent investigation, I understood that this rot does not flow from a defect of the mouth, stomach, uterus, or any other specific part of the body, but rather that it is the unique constitution <term>idiosyncrasy</term> <note>original: ιδιοσυγϰρασίαν (*idiosyncrasia*); in Galenic medicine, this refers to a person's unique balance of the four humors.</note> of the entire body, to which it has been necessary to resort for explanation whenever similar

<meta>This page continues Dr. Sigismund Snitzer’s description of a young woman suffering from a mysterious and overwhelming body odor. He concludes his inquiry by asking for Libavius's expert medical opinion, after which Andreas Libavius begins his reply, contextualizing the condition within classical and social observations.</meta>

CONCERNING THE SINGULAR FOUL ODOR OF A YOUNG WOMAN. 501

The causes of such effects were hidden; perhaps no differently than when, due to our ignorance of other causes, we attribute things to fortune. The constitution of her body itself moves me to believe this. She is of a blooming complexion, performs all her bodily functions well, has no complaint regarding any part of her body, and, according to the other nuns, possesses no visible blemish. Finally, what uniquely confirms this opinion is that in Augsburg <note>original: *Augustæ*</note> she used many remedies to wash away this stench, but without success. She has two sisters who are also nuns elsewhere, neither of whom is plagued by this evil. Since, therefore—as Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician (980–1037 AD) whose *Canon of Medicine* was a standard text for centuries.</note> well said—Pain and Foul Odor greatly cast down the vital spirit, the nuns will return this virgin to her family home <note>original: *penati*</note> as soon as the harshness of winter has somewhat abated. No reading has provided me with a similar example until now. I remember reading the history of a singular pleasant fragrance <note>original: εὐωδίας (*euōdias*)</note> concerning a certain illustrious man who smelled of musk, but his name does not occur to me now. What do you think about this stench, and whether such a body—stinking, I mean—might have a nature akin to rotting? And how can it be that, within the limits of health and with no functions impaired, the human body comes so close to putrefaction? Is it not more exposed than others to pestilential contagion? Finally, whether there might be hope that the stench will cease as age progresses and the bodily temperament <term>crasi: the specific mixture of humors in an individual</term> changes—please explain this at your leisure.

<column-break/>

I confess I have nothing to offer you in return, except that I may love and honor you as long as I live. Farewell. Given at Bamberg, February 16, 1601.

### Doctor of Medicine.

You tell marvelous things about the girl from Augsburg who smells like a corpse—if indeed it is a marvel that Rufinus smells of breath-mints while Gorgonius smells like a goat <note>Libavius is quoting a famous line from the Roman poet Horace (*Satires* 1.2.27) to show that distinctive body odors have been noted since antiquity.</note>. This occurs without any natural disposition or a distortion of our own sense of smell—which is the reason we do not get along well with polecats, goats, and the like. Or perhaps it is from a neglect of grooming and an acquired vice, just as to us refined and neat people, those dirty farmers, common laborers, shoemakers, skinners, and so on, do not always breathe so pleasantly, nor do they smell at all of the Sabean harvest <note>A poetic reference to the expensive perfumes and incense of Saba (Sheba) in Arabia.</note>. But I understand that this breath has also displeased her parents and relatives since her birth [I believe] in her...

### MEDICAL LETTERS, BOOK II, SECTION X.

...her own fatherland and place of birth. You rightly bring up her **individual constitution** <note>original: ἰδιοσυγκρασίαν (*idiosyncrasian*), a term used in ancient medicine to describe the unique physical and chemical makeup of an individual.</note>, yet I think we must inquire further into what cause has struck her nature away from the disposition of her family and father. Why does it not allow her to breathe human breath like her parents, brothers, and sisters—who, I believe, cause no trouble or offense to others by their breathing? We are not all so delicate that we cannot bear companions and a crowd gathered in the same place, or sit and move where many others are. Therefore, the fault is undoubtedly not in our noses.

It is typical of Musetti <note>Likely referring to a contemporary physician or a specific case known to the author.</note> to haughtily turn away from the scent of a preceding Galenic practitioner; just as it is for the Persian ranks, accustomed to perfumes, to be unable to bear the stench of the Macedonians. I am surprised that the nuns are so delicate and impatient of afflictions that they loathe a "little sister" who smells less than sweet, especially when they are persuaded that they can merit heaven by bravely enduring adversities and performing works of love. Far more holy was that matron who ignored her husband's heavy breath, giving as her reason that she thought marriage should not be abandoned, nor a husband scorned for a stench which she supposed was natural to all men. We are not so overly refined or fastidious. But if it is an **individual constitution**, then the evil began in the first mixing of the seed to form the limbs; and so foul an odor depends on the very form of the bodily temperament <note>original: *craseos*, from the Greek *krasis*, meaning the specific "mixture" or balance of the four humors in a person's body.</note>, as if some

<margin>
Further inquiry into the cause of this stench.
</margin>

<column-break/>

unique and inexplicable logic of the mixtures had brought it about, so that henceforth an **inexpressible quality** <note>original: ἄῤῥητος ποιότης (*arrhētos poiotēs*)</note> of this kind would always follow the constitution and could not be erased unless the mixture itself were dissolved. Whether this is so or not is extremely difficult to investigate or know, being placed beyond human grasp. Thus, the one affirming and the one denying it enjoy equal right, since it is as easy to deny what is said without proof as it is to affirm it—especially when other causes come into view and contemplation. 

For why should we not say that the fault was not in the temperament, but that some external accessory introduced this alteration of the substance, or cast such a stain that she breathes not like a human, but like a corpse? Nor is this contagion always brief; sometimes it dies with the person, an inseparable companion until the final dissolution of the frame. In this category belongs the contamination of the blood and the female nature, being both formed and nourished within the parent: perhaps she suffered something from the mother's nausea, or her consternation and heavy affliction—the sort of stains you know are indelibly branded when mothers are seized by pregnancy cravings <note>original: *malacia*, a term for the "pica" or strange appetites and physical distresses experienced during pregnancy.</note> and strong movements of the soul, or even by the shaking of limbs (such as the hands), the spirit and thoughts being directed toward the conceptus or the tender embryo hiding in the womb. Perhaps she was terrified by a tomb; perhaps the anointing of a corpse occurred; or perhaps a nausea was caused by the foul filth produced from the bellies of those lying ill...

<meta>This page continues Andreas Libavius’s analysis of a young woman’s foul body odor. On the previous page, he suggested the "evil" began at the very first moment her physical substance was mixed. ### ON THE SINGULAR STENCH OF THE GIRL.

...conceived, and was heavily affected by similar things. From there, a mark can be left on the infant. I remember **epileptic boys**, who, when anointed with **oil of amber** <note>original: *oleo succini*; a resinous oil historically used to treat seizures and nervous disorders, known for its very strong, smoky scent.</note>, smelled of something from the grave. When women assist those in labor, the sick, and others, they can easily take in the "seeds" <note>original: *seminaria*; a term used before the germ theory of disease to describe the invisible "seeds" or agents that spread contagion.</note> of disease while they are carrying a child in the womb. I will say nothing of how a fetus might linger too long in the putrid fluids of the menses during conception, or even take its very first beginnings from that time. From such beginnings, foul breaths emerge during the first fermentations of life; but later, even **leprosies** and similar conditions arise. We know that those predisposed from the womb to the **French disease** <note>original: *Gallicum*; a common historical name for syphilis.</note>, **cancers**, **elephantiasis**, and so on, breathe out nothing pleasant, even at times when they seem to be doing well.

But you know these matters better than I. It can be argued that the evil arises from the **crasis** <note>original: *crasi*; the specific "mixture" or balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) that determines a person's health and temperament.</note>, as well as from nourishment, medicines, and other treatments managed through rash care. Furthermore, even at that age when a woman's nature usually changes with the appearance of her menses, no correction was introduced. It is well known that there is great power in these natural turning points, if not to abolish the evil, then at least to inhibit and mitigate it. However, in the generation of a substance from a pre-existing similar act, that fiction of a "new and singular mixing" of the **Elements** <note>The four elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> has no place. If anything happened for that reason, it was an addition or an intermingling, not a fundamental change to her substance. Regarding the coming together of the elements and their qualities...

<column-break/>

...what is the point of producing such fictions? This hardly applies even to rough stones that happen to coalesce from earth and water by chance. Truly, what heats, what dryness, what humidity, or what cold could accomplish so much? A **horse** can bear neither the sight nor the smell of a **camel** because of a total conflict in their natures—this was the basis of **Cyrus’s stratagem** <note>A reference to the Battle of Thymbra (547 BC), where Cyrus the Great used camels to frighten the horses of Croesus’s Lydian cavalry, who could not stand the camels' scent.</note> in the battle against **Croesus**. This girl is not so naturally hateful to humans. And yet, there was a certain father who specifically could tolerate neither the sight nor the breath of his own son, even though he did not recognize him as his own [concerning this, see **Libavius’s *Singularia*** <note>original: *Singularia Libavij*; a reference to Libavius's own published collections of medical and natural wonders.</note>], just as many people are similarly affected by cats. 

Yet this case is not like those. For here the stench comes from manifest causes, alienating everyone who is not accustomed to the rot. You ask whether her body should be considered "related to a putrefying one." You may compare the odors of corpses still wasting away in the process of rot with this breath of a body that is, in its own constitution, healthy. In other respects, I see nothing related, provided her nature remains sound and lively. Those things that rot and ferment by an external heat are dissolved by it and no longer possess the "act of life." As for what the cause of this stench should be thought to be—if I have not fully explained it, I have at least indicated it as clearly as I could. Neither a pleasant nor a foul odor, in itself, prevents the functioning of life. Every living thing is delighted by its own scent, and indeed, animals are born amidst rot <note>A reference to the theory of "spontaneous generation," the belief that certain animals like maggots or flies were born directly from decaying matter.</note>. One must ask whether the woman stinks to herself. If she is not bothersome to you, consider her pleasant—or at least not **repugnant**.

### MEDICAL EPISTLES, BOOK II, SECTION X.

It is possible for someone to breathe out something that seems foreign to them, yet is not adverse to life. Indeed, if you should wish to introduce a contrary habit by force, you might cause more harm. For suffering does not arise from that which is customary. Many people fall into **fainting** <term>original: *lipothymian*; a medical term for a sudden loss of strength or a fainting spell</term> due to the fragrance of sweet odors, even though they have accustomed themselves to foul ones. There was once a man accustomed to lying on hay who, when brought into a fine bed, would lose consciousness until he was returned to his own chamber. The **Hoopoe** <note>The hoopoe bird was notorious in medieval and early modern natural history for building nests out of dung and being associated with filth.</note> rejoices in its own filth and enjoys a pleasant life within it. The violence of a plague is not, by its nature, more familiar to one who smells badly than to one who emits sweet breaths. For the plague is not opposed to filth or perfumes, but rather lies in wait for the vital principle. While it attacks the **constitution** <term>original: *κατάστασιν* (katastasin); the settled state or fundamental disposition of the body</term> and its harmony, it dissipates the spirits and the heat, or makes them foreign to life by changing their natural properties, thus destroying the living being. Not infrequently, nature finds a defense in bad odors—not because they are "bad" in themselves, but because they are effective and occupy the "spiritual powers" <note>In Libavius’s time, "spirits" were subtle fluids believed to circulate through the body to maintain life and motion.</note> so that they might oppose the spiritual poison of the plague, or goad nature into expelling and shaking off the danger before it gains strength and grows, or perhaps to render the body **insensitive** <term>original: *ἀναθή* (anathe); likely from the Greek for "unaffected" or "untouched"</term> so that it rejects the impression of the approaching disease. Thus, some daily saturate their nostrils with the smell of sewers, while others purify and defend themselves and their belongings with **bitumen** <note>A naturally occurring petroleum substance, like tar, often burned as a disinfectant.</note>. But, you will say, the breath of rot can bring on a similar rot. Imagine,

<column-break/>

I say, that this is so; yet with a different disposition, it is possible for one to repel the other by superior force, just as **poison can be killed by poison**. We can only guess rather than say for certain whether this "virus" <note>Here used in the classical sense of a "poison" or "taint," rather than the modern biological sense.</note> would cease if the **humoral mixture** <term>original: *crasi*; the unique balance of fluids in an individual's body</term> were changed. If the condition prevails through the basic elemental properties and other shifting factors outside the "root of nature," you might have some hope. If not, and the substance remains fixed, the affliction will hardly be eradicated. Medicines have some power even over the dead. For you know that corpses are preserved for a long time by embalming and are claimed back from rot. See then if there remains any hope from nourishment, cosmetics, or medicines—if not to uproot the stench, then at least to mitigate and mask it. They say that **Alexander the Great** smelled of **musk** <note>A powerful, heavy scent secreted by the musk deer; ancient sources claimed Alexander’s skin and breath were naturally sweet-smelling.</note> while he was alive; I doubt he did so once he met his fate. And yet the musk-beast, even when killed, breathes out that same odor until the onset of rot destroys the balance of its mixture. My fear is that nourishment dissimilar to the body may eventually bring about a heavy corruption and precipitate the entire body into **Elephantiasis** <note>A term used historically to describe severe skin diseases that made the skin thick and hard, often associated with leprosy.</note> or similar evils. Since such a foul odor is hardly within the normal range for a human under our sky, it may provide an opening for a swifter descent into ruin. However, those who live naked under the **American sky** <note>A reference to the Indigenous peoples of the Americas, who were often described in early travelogues as having distinct bodily odors due to their environment and diet.</note>, though not breathing very pleasantly, may enjoy a different privilege of nature. It is a question more worthy of inquiry: if she were wed to a man, whether...

# CONCERNING THE SINGULAR STENCH OF A GIRL.

...that she would have escaped had she been a conceived offspring? I whisper in your ear that certain women smell most foully during the flowing of the **uterine cleansings** <note>original: *purgamentis*; a common early modern term for menstruation, viewed as a process of purging excess humors from the body</note>. If she was conceived at that time—and it cannot be denied that maternal blood concurs in the act of generation—then the cause, which was hidden so deeply, is brought almost into the open. You will judge it not unworthy of investigation whether she, at such a time (if indeed she suffers her monthly periods), breathes even more horribly, and whether the **taint** <term>original: *virus*; in this period, it referred to a poisonous or foul-smelling secretion rather than a microscopic pathogen</term> is changed, or at least remains in the same kind of stench, increased in degree. It is difficult to search the secret depths of women's mysteries. And yet, so that the cause might be revealed, not just the whole, but every individual part of the whole should have been explored; for instance, whether the sweat separately, and the urine, and the breath emitted from the lungs commonly exhaled the odor like the other parts. In ancient histories, there is an account of a certain woman who had devoted herself to **chastity** <note>original: *lacris*; likely a shorthand or error for *sacris*, referring to a religious or virginal vow</note>; in order to ward off suitors, she composed a fraud by carrying rotting meat between her breasts, the stench of which was so great that no one could help but turn away in disgust from the thought of marriage. This artifice is sometimes so industrious that the trick can scarcely be observed even by the most skilled, as the histories of **Paré** <term>original: *Paræi*; referring to Ambroise Paré (c. 1510–1590), the famous French royal surgeon known for his detailed medical case studies</term> testify. Your account, however, has ensured that there is no room for such suspicion in this person.

For I understand that the remedies at **Augsburg** <note>original: *Augustæ*; the Latin name for the city of Augsburg</note> were seriously applied. She has been condemned to the grave by her own people, and therefore thrust into such a monastery. Nor do I think she suffers from a continuous menstrual flow. I would wish it added, how

<column-break/>

long ago she began to stink, and whether she did so even as an infant; and whether she has ever experienced that flow, whether red or white; what other **goat-like** <note>original: *hircosæ*; a medical term derived from the Latin *hircus* (he-goat), used to describe people with strong, pungent body odor, particularly from the armpits</note> women breathe out; and whether the stench remits at no time, etc. But you have no need of a prompter: so that you might know my mind, I have poured these thoughts into your bosom. Farewell. The day after the Ides of March [March 16], 1601. Rothenburg ob der Tauber.
