...suspended by the temple of Fame, and accepted with open arms by the world of the learned, as your writings prove. But to what end, most grave man, to what end did you write those things? Truly, so that you might benefit those who wish to be relieved by them. So it is; I conceive a hope: and thus you will not be lacking even in the writing of your own hand, while the rest, printed in type, shine in the light. I shall act as those do who, being of lowlier condition and knowledge, attempt to win the favor of men of greater reputation by sending a small gift beforehand: so I do here. I send to your Excellence this *Patience* <note>Likely the title of a manuscript or work Horst is sharing</note> of mine, transcribed among you, and I earnestly pray that you receive it into your house with singular favor. See the cleverness of the sender! Almost like the one who gives a hen and expects an ox in return. I most dutifully beseech you to be willing to help me. We cannot all do everything. <note>original: *Nō poſſumus omnia omnes*</note> **The gods, however, can do all things.** <note>original: *Θεοὶ δέ τε πάντα δύνανται*</note> You, who are the **Alpha of Philosophers**; and who are yourself far superior to others by your spear <note>A metaphor for intellectual prowess</note>, according to the humanity so highly commended to me toward men of the sacred Order, you will by no means be found wanting. Therefore, answer me [I consider it a point of praise to be instructed by a man of such celebrated fame] regarding these **inquiries** <note>original: *ζητήματα* (zetemata)</note> of mine, such as they are, but not written in vain. Not in vain, I say. For while I have now spent twice seven years in the Alps, clinging to them like **Prometheus on Caucasus** <note>In Greek mythology, Prometheus was chained to Mount Caucasus as punishment; Horst feels similarly bound to his post in the mountains</note>, it pleased me to write for piety and spiritual progress (as the pious ancients say), making **Meditations on Snow**.

<column-break/>

Indeed, I wrote them long ago. But while I revise them and apply the finishing touch—for **second thoughts are wiser** <note>original: *δεύτεραι γὰρ φροντίδες σοφώτεραι*</note>—I find things I wish to have explained. Certainly, no one could help me better in that explanation than you. Specifically: I. (from the seventh Meditation) *Why does some snow melt more quickly, while other snow remains longer on the ground?* II. *Is it true that snow hardened by age is converted into crystal?* So indeed says **Master Prosper of Aquitaine** <note>A 5th-century Christian writer</note> in his commentary on Psalm 147, on my page 849. And I have seen **eyeglasses** <note>original: *perſpicilla*; a very early reference to spectacles or lenses</note> manufactured from such hardened snow. *What is the cause of that hardening?* [from Meditation 13.] III. *Why is fresh snow reduced into a mass more quickly than old?* IV. *Does the cold power of straw preserve buried snow?* What is the cause? So indeed **Saint Augustine** affirms in *The City of God*, Book 21, Chapter 4, column 1270. In these matters, because I lack what you can provide, I ask you again and again to satisfy my curiosity. I will not act deceitfully, but with gratitude I will record that I know these things through you as my **Author**, so that your knowledge may turn away my ignorance and that of many others. I also hope your Excellence received the Book of Elegies and the Satire against **Scultetus** <note>Abraham Scultetus, a prominent Calvinist theologian of the era</note>, the follower of Calvin, which I sent previously. I cease: I bid you, most Excellent Man and most certain Patron, to be greeted and to be well. As long as I live, I shall not cease to magnify and honor you. As long as I live, I say. For how many times now, on account of the most bitter pains of **migraine** <note>original: *Hemicraniæ*; literally "half-head" pain</note> on my left side...

Surely so that you might be able to benefit those who wish to be uplifted by them. So it is. I conceive hope: and therefore you will not be lacking in the very writing of your hand, while other things printed in type shine forth in the light. I will act, however, like those who, while they are of a humbler condition and knowledge, attempt to turn the favors of men of greater reputation toward themselves by sending a small gift beforehand: so I do here. I am sending to your Excellence this *Patience* <note>Referring to his work titled "Patientia"</note> of mine, copied out while among you, and I earnestly pray that you look upon it with singular favor in your home. See the cleverness of the sender! Almost like the one who gives a hen and expects an ox in return. I most dutifully beseech you that you be willing to help me. We cannot all do all things <note>original: "Non possumus omnia omnes"</note>. The gods, however, can do all things <note>original: "Θεοὶ δέ τε πάντα δύνανται"</note>. You, who are the Alpha <note>The first or the best</note> of Philosophers; and who are yourself far more excellent than others with the spear, will by no means be lacking in that humanity so highly commended to me toward men of the sacred Order. Therefore respond to me [I consider it a point of praise to be taught by a man of such celebrated fame] regarding these inquiries <note>original: "ζητήματα" (zetēmata); research questions or problems</note> of mine, whatever they may be, but not written in vain. I say not in vain. For while I have now spent twice-seven years in the Alps, clinging to them like Prometheus to the Caucasus <note>Prometheus was a figure in Greek myth chained to a mountain as a punishment; Horst feels similarly bound to his mountain home</note>, it pleased me to write for piety and spiritual progress (as the pious ancients say), 

<column-break/>

making **Snowy Meditations**. Indeed, I wrote them some time ago. But while I review them and apply the finishing touch <note>original: "ultimam manum"</note>—for second thoughts are wiser <note>original: "δευτέραι γὰρ φροντίδες σοφώτεραι"</note>—I find things I wish to have explained. Certainly, no one could help me better in that explanation than you. Namely:

I. (from Meditation seven) Why does some snow melt more quickly, while other snow remains longer on the earth?

II. Whether it be true that snow hardened by age is converted into <term>Crystal<gloss>In the 17th century, it was a common belief that rock crystal (quartz) was actually ice that had frozen so hard it could never melt</gloss></term>? So indeed says Saint Prosper of Aquitaine in his commentary on Psalm 147, on my page 849. And I have seen eyeglasses <note>original: "perspicilla"</note> fashioned from such hardened snow. What is the cause of this hardening? [from Meditation 13.]

III. Why is fresh snow more quickly reduced into a mass than old snow?

IV. Does the cold power of straw preserve buried snow? What is the cause? So indeed Saint Augustine affirms in Book 21 of the *City of God*, chapter 4, column 1270.

In these matters, because I lack that which you may sufficiently provide, I ask again and again that you satisfy my curiosity. I will not act deceitfully, but will note with gratitude that I know these things with you as the Author, so that your knowledge may turn away my ignorance and that of many others. I also hope your Excellence has already received the Book of Elegies and the Satire against Scultetus <note>Abraham Scultetus, a prominent Calvinist theologian</note>, the follower of Calvin, which I sent before. I conclude: most Excellent Man and most certain Patron, I bid you be well and flourish. As long as I live, I shall not cease to value and honor you. I say as long as I live. For how often already, on account of both the most bitter pains of <term>Migraine<gloss>original: "Hemicrania," a pain affecting one side of the head</gloss></term> on the left side,

### To the Reverend and Most Illustrious
### Mr. Master Johann Sebastian Wieland, Imperial Poet Laureate
### Gregor Horstius
### Sends Greetings.

Your most welcome letter, dated May 8th, was delivered to me barely two days ago, Reverend and Most Illustrious Sir, patron and friend to be greatly honored. It was desirable for that very reason: that it might testify to the constancy of your love toward me, to say nothing of the added little gift—namely, your meditation on *Patience*, a thing of which nothing is more easily said, yet nothing is more difficult to practice. I have not yet seen your "Snowy Meditations," but I sufficiently understand your

<column-break/>

intention. Nor do I doubt, although snow is usually a quickly passing atmospheric phenomenon <note>original: "meteoron," which in the 17th century referred to any weather event or "meteoric" substance in the air, including rain or snow</note>, that it provides an occasion for explaining various matters. I remember an immense snowfall that lasted for several weeks in the year of salvation 1606, when, passing through Strasbourg <note>original: "Argentina," the Latin name for Strasbourg</note>, I heard the Reverend Dr. Pappus <note>Johannes Pappus (1549–1610), a prominent Lutheran theologian and professor</note> orating on Snow; that dissertation has no doubt been committed to print. 

He asks, however, why some snow melts more quickly while other snow clings to the earth longer? You know that snow is formed by heat by reason of an antecedent cause, insofar as heat slightly alters the cloud and prepares it for a watery consistency, which is why a lessening of cold precedes the descent of snow. But lest it be produced as rain rather than snow, cold—as the more immediate cause—intervenes, which seizes the cloud while it is still whole but prepared for rain, and constricts it into crumbly particles, not unlike flakes of wool. It is no wonder, then, if some snow melts sooner and some later, either by its own nature—insofar as its freezing is lighter—or in respect to its surroundings—insofar as the melting cause consists of greater activity—not to mention the various qualities of the earth which alter the falling snow according to their own properties. 

Whether, however (as is asked in the second place), snow that has hardened for a longer time is converted into *Crystal*, I strongly doubt, although after—

<meta>This page continues Gregor Horst's scientific response to Johann Sebastian Wieland's "Snowy Meditations." Having discussed the physical origins of snow on the previous page, Horst now moves into a debate regarding the relationship between ice and crystalline stone, citing classical and contemporary natural philosophers.</meta>

<page-num>509</page-num>
### ON THE UNIQUE PROPERTIES OF SNOW.

Pliny holds the very same view as the cited Prosper of Aquitaine. Indeed, Crystal is not produced without water, as Boëtius <note>Anselmus Boëtius de Boodt (1550–1632), a Flemish mineralogist and physician</note> has it in *Book 2 on Gems and Stones, chapter 73*, because a very thin portion of earth must be dissolved by water, or mixed with water sent from elsewhere; then, when the water recedes, it finally hardens into crystal through "snow-shaping" <note>original: νιπλασμῇ (niplasmē)</note>. Hence, Dalechamp <note>Jacques Daléchamps (1513–1588), a French physician and botanist</note> remarks on the passage from Pliny: *Pliny is mistaken. Crystal is formed from a transparent, stony juice, which intense cold freezes and hardens beneath the earth or among the icy veins of rocks.* You may see more on this in Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "father of mineralogy"</note> *Book 6 on the Nature of Fossils*; Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath</note> *Book 7 on Subtlety*; and Diodorus, as quoted by Coelius Rhodiginus <note>Lodovico Ricchieri (1469–1525), an Italian scholar</note> in *Book 1, chapter 10 of Ancient Lessons*. He says the crystal stone is "thickened from pure water," yet not by cold, but by heavenly heat, or as the words go, "by the force of divine heat," and therefore not by the hardening of more intense cold. This is proven by the dissolving of crystal, which by heat does not turn back into water, but into lime or a peculiar salt. It is further proven by the various medicinal uses of crystal, regarding which the aforementioned Boëtius, Quercetanus, Poterius, and others have written.

Nor does the Latin version of the cited Psalm stand in the way (which misled Prosper), since the Greek word *crystallon* <note>original: κρύσταλλον</note> indicates both ice and crystalline stone. However, Dr. Luther—looking to the nature of things rather than the words—understood it as "hail" in his German version, when he says: **He throws his hailstones like morsels.** <note>Referring to Psalm 147:17. Luther’s German Bible uses "Schlossen" (hail) where others used "crystal" or "ice."</note>

The third question follows: namely, why is fresh snow more quickly packed into a mass than old snow? Is it because its brittle, dripping flakes fall in pieces and unite more quickly, since snow, according to the Philosopher <note>Refers to Aristotle, specifically his *Generation of Animals*</note> in *Book 2, chapter 2*, seems to have the consistency of foam? Add to this that the softness following its thinness and rarity, combined with a certain stickiness for the sake of coherence, is greater in fresh snow than in older snow, for which reason it is quite readily coagulated into a mass. Finally, as for the passage from Augustine, the matter will be clear when we distinguish between things that happen by their own nature and those that happen "by accident" <note>original: κατὰ συμβεβηκός (kata symbebēkos) - a philosophical term meaning a secondary or non-essential property</note>. Augustine asks: who gave straw either such a cold power that it preserves buried snow, or such a hot power that it ripens immature fruit? But snow is not preserved under straw by the power of cold; rather, it is preserved because the straw prevents the penetrating heat of the surrounding air from melting the packed snow. This is just as we say in common speech that a fur coat wards off the heat of summer—a fact known to merchants traveling in the heat of the "dog days" <note>The "canicular" days, the hottest part of summer associated with the rising of the dog star, Sirius</note>, who wrap their jugs filled with wine in fur coats when the opportunity arises to defend them from the heat. In the same way, straw ripens—

Sff 3

...promotes this process, not because it possesses any burning power of its own, but by blocking out external heat, so that the innate heat <note>original: *calor insitus*; a vital warmth believed by early modern physicians to be necessary for life and digestion</note> may better ripen <note>original: *concoquat*; literally "cook," referring to the metabolic processing of matter</note> that which is still raw. In other cases, the surrounding heat, by drawing out this innate heat, provides the origin for corruption. To prevent this, housewives also wrap eggs in straw, and thus preserve them longer for the household. I also thank you for the poems you sent; with mutual affection, since I have nothing else at hand for the time being, please accept this Family Poem <note>original: *carmen Gentilicium*; likely a poem celebrating lineage or family honors</note> by our most distinguished friend Hebenstreit <note>Johann Baptist Hebenstreit (1580–1638), a contemporary scholar and educator</note>, and continue to hold me in your favor, as you do. As for what causes chronic migraine pains <note>original: *Hemicraniæ dolores*; pain affecting half the head</note>, I cannot be a prophet, unless perhaps they occur through a "sympathy" with the spleen <note>original: *per consensum splenis*; the medical theory that an affliction in one organ can cause symptoms in another</note>, since they are on the left side, becoming like a scurvy-related headache! If you can teach me the cause, you will find me ready to prescribe remedies; but you must look for the success of the cure from God, the Chief Physician <note>original: *Archiatro*</note>. Fare well, along with your family.

about snow. Indeed, I shall report these findings

my grateful mind. Forgive me, however,
if I still seek clarity on one more thing.
"What is that?" you ask. It is this:
while you deny that snow is transformed into
Crystal, you prove it by the generation of
crystal itself: that it is made from a transparent,
stony juice, which intense cold freezes and
hardens beneath the earth or among the
icy veins of rocks. But the question is not
"from where is Crystal generated?" but
"can snow at last turn into stony Crystal?"
Crystal may have its own origin,
and yet...

# ON THE REMARKABLE PROPERTIES OF SNOW #

...and yet that snow is transmuted into it [crystal]. Those who have seen such crystallized snow bear witness to this, and I myself saw such spectacles in Stuttgart. You know without me telling you (which I add so you may see and laugh at my folly) that crystals can be drawn out from salt of tartar <note>original: *sal tartari*; potassium carbonate, often used in early chemistry and alchemy</note> by the chemical art, or that salt can be changed into crystal, which I myself have attempted more than once. Thus, the generation of crystal does not seem to be just one and the same process. Listen without annoyance to Chyträus <note>Nathan Chyträus (1543–1598), a German poet and humanist scholar</note> singing in his *Venetian Journey* on pages 54 and 55, as follows:

> *A rugged mountain divides the Swiss from the Italian shores,*
> *Part called Adula, the Bernardino of the Mesauco people.*
> *Spring could never reach its inaccessible crags,*
> *Neither Bacchus [wine], Philomela [the nightingale], nor Ceres [grain],*
> *Nor summer has come here: here ice receives the young from the mother’s womb,*
> *And hardens the tender limbs of the shepherds by the force of the cold:*
> *While elsewhere the burning Dog-star [Sirius] parches the dry fields,*
> *There, upon the stiff cliffs, hideous winter holds its kingdom,*
> *And the raging Northwest winds wage war,*
> *And snows built up on the high, lofty mountains*
> *Burden the earth and the jagged rocks:*
> *The mountain itself, roaring with sound, hides its head among the clouds,*
> *And from afar cuts off the fires of Phoebus [the sun] from the cliffs:*
> *All around, crystalline ice, hardened through countless ages,*
> *Stiffens: through the eroded crags the foamy wave*
> *Resounds, and the mountain itself, bordering the stars, shines white, etc.*

What of the fact that in Hebrew, *Korcho* <note>original: *Korcho* (קֶרַח); a Hebrew term for ice or frost</note> has its own word for crystal? From this, Münster <note>Sebastian Münster, a famed 16th-century Hebraist</note> says on the root *Karach* that it means ice, which is almost the same as hoarfrost, except it is more solid and is generated in great cold, as Kimchi <note>David Kimchi, a medieval Jewish scholar and grammarian</note> teaches regarding Psalm 147. Our translator renders it as "Crystal" in Ezekiel 1, where the Chaldean <note>A reference to the Aramaic Targum, a translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> translates "the brilliance of a thing" as *Gelid* [frost or ice]. So says he. Perhaps because, due to excessive frost, it turns to stone and crystal-

<column-break/>

lizes. But enough of these follies and trifles. You, who are an "all-seeing Argus" <note>In Greek mythology, Argus was a giant with a hundred eyes; here, it refers to Horst being an expert observer</note> in this matter, will not take it badly while I grope about blindly. As for what concerns my most bitter migraine pains <note>original: *Hemicraniæ dolores*; severe headaches affecting one side of the head</note>, you have cheered me up by offering me your help in relieving them. Certainly, I myself fear that their cause stems from a "sympathy" with the spleen <note>original: *per consensum splenis*; the early medical theory that an ailment in one organ, like the spleen, could cause symptoms elsewhere, like the head</note>. For I am [suffering] from my illness...

of the disease. They say it is impossible for me to be totally cured. And yet God is able to raise the dead, much more so to drive away these hostile pains through a most experienced physician. I trust, however, that through you this can be entirely accomplished. That is all. Farewell, most excellent man and best patron: may JESUS CHRIST be with us from now and forevermore. Given on the 26th of October, 1626.

# What is the Body?

->The dwelling place of the soul<- <note>original: "Domicilium animæ"</note>
The eyes, the guides of the body and vessels of light
->the signposts of the soul<- <note>original: "indices animæ"</note>
The ears, the judges of sounds
The lips, the folding doors of the mouth
The hands, the laborers of the body
The heart, the vessel of life
The lung, the preserver of air
The stomach, the cook of food <note>In the medical tradition of this period, digestion was often described as a process of "concoction," where the stomach functioned like a kitchen, using heat to "cook" or refine nutrients.</note>
The bones, the strength of the body
The legs, the columns of the body
